sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Ship That Was “Practically Unsinkable”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

In 1911 the British magazine The Shipbuilder brought out a special issue for a giant liner that had just been launched, and it used an adjective that would later become one of history’s great ironies: this ship, it said, was “practically unsinkable”. She was 269 metres long, displaced more than fifty thousand tons and had sixteen watertight compartments; people of the day called her “the pinnacle of human engineering”. Her name was Titanic.

The people of that era believed that if only technology were advanced enough, nature could never threaten humanity again. So when Titanic sailed, she carried just twenty lifeboats, with room for 1,178 people in all — while more than 2,200 people were on board. That figure was perfectly legal at the time, because the lifeboat regulations laid down by the British Board of Trade in 1894 had long since failed to keep pace with the size of ships. In other words, it wasn’t that they got the sums wrong. It never occurred to them that the sums needed doing.

At 11:40 on the night of 14 April 1912, Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. Two hours and forty minutes later she broke in two and sank into the ocean, 3,800 metres deep. More than 1,500 people died.

Brothers and sisters, on the surface the Titanic tragedy was caused by an iceberg. In reality it was caused by a mindset. That mindset was this: I cannot sink.

The Bible gives that mindset a far older name — pride.

In the previous unit we saw together that “selflessness” is the road to revival, the way of life in which Jesus is lifted up and the kingdom of God comes. But the very next question is this: how do we actually live a selfless life? I know selflessness is good, and I long to be selfless — so why does “self” keep pushing its head up again and again?

The answer is one word: humility.

Humility is the starting point of selflessness, and its foundation. Without humility we cannot lay “self” down, because “self” never steps down of its own accord; “self” only lets go when it bows low before God. With humility we can truly let Jesus reign, because there is only one throne: when I come down, the Lord goes up.

And the exact opposite of humility is pride.

Today’s lesson has a very direct title, and one that cuts deep: sin is the fruit of pride.

Notice the cause and effect here. We usually think of sin as a string of “behaviours”: lying, losing our temper, greed, envy, bitterness. So our ways of dealing with sin mostly stay at the level of behaviour: we resolve never to lie again, we work hard at controlling our temper. Yet we find that the branches we cut off grow back, because the root is still in the ground.

Scripture reveals to us that the root of every sin is pride. Pride made angels fall, pride makes people sin, pride breaks relationships, pride divides churches, and pride leaves families wounded on both sides.

In The City of God, Augustine says that pride is “the beginning of all sin”. The twentieth-century apologist C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, calls pride “the great sin”; pride, he says, leads to every other vice — it is the complete anti-God state of mind.

So if we want to enter revival and return to God’s heart, we cannot begin by trimming leaves. We must begin by dealing with pride.

Today we will look at this from three angles: first, the origin of sin — pride separates us from God; second, the fruit of pride — from the Garden of Eden to today’s world; and third, humility as the starting point of selflessness and the key to overcoming sin.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Setting and Context of Two Passages
sections.html:
1. The background of James 4:6

The author of the letter of James is generally held to be James, the half-brother of the Lord Jesus (Galatians 1:19 calls him “James, the Lord’s brother”). At first he did not believe (John 7:5 records, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him”), but after the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7) he became a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9) and presided over the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

This letter was very probably written between AD 45 and 50, which makes it one of the earliest books of the New Testament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — that is, Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution. They lived as strangers in foreign lands, their lives were hard, and yet in the church people had begun to favour the rich and despise the poor, to let their tongues run loose and to compete with one another.

James 4 opens with a piercing question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1) He goes on to say that they ask and don’t receive because they “ask with wrong motives” (James 4:3), and that friendship with the world is “hostility toward God” (James 4:4).

Against that dark backdrop, verse 6 shines in like a ray of light: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” James is quoting an Old Testament text, Proverbs 3:34. In other words, this is not James’s personal opinion. It is a spiritual law that runs through the whole Bible, unchanged from the Old Testament to the New.

Two Greek words here are very important.

“Proud” is ὑπερήφανος (hyperēphanos), formed from “above” (hyper) and “to appear” (phainō); literally, “showing oneself above others”. A proud person isn’t necessarily aggressive, but inside he is always measuring: how much higher am I than whom?

“Resists” is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”. Hear this clearly: God doesn’t merely dislike proud people — God draws up his battle lines against them. When I am proud, I don’t just lose a blessing; I have gone over to stand on the opposite side from God.

“Humble” is ταπεινός (tapeinos), which originally means “low” or “low-lying”, like ground in a hollow. It is a beautiful word: water only flows into low places. Grace is like water — it always runs downhill.

2. The background of Genesis 3

The five books of Moses were written by Moses, in the wilderness years after the Exodus. The first eleven chapters of Genesis are the foundation of the whole Bible, recording four great events: creation, the fall, the flood and the scattering.

The fall recorded in Genesis 3 took place in a perfect environment. That matters enormously. Adam and Eve didn’t sin because they lacked anything, or because they were suffering, or because they had been treated unfairly. They lived in the Garden of Eden, where there was abundant provision, an honourable calling (“to cultivate and keep it”, Genesis 2:15), intimate relationship and God’s presence every day.

In other words, sin is not a problem of environment. Sin is a problem of the heart.

And the serpent’s temptation didn’t start with behaviour either; it started with mindset. First it shook God’s word (“Has God really said…”, Genesis 3:1), then it denied God’s word (“You won’t really die”, Genesis 3:4), and finally it put forward a whole new mindset: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5).

Brothers and sisters, remember the 321 order: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Satan understands that order better than we do. He doesn’t need to force you into sin. He only needs to swap out one of your mindsets.

sections.heading: 3. The Origin of Sin: Pride Separates Us from God
sections.html:
1. That perfect relationship in Eden

In the Garden of Eden, humanity originally lived with God, enjoying his presence and his blessing. It was a perfect relationship, with no sin, no shame and nothing standing between them.

The Bible describes that relationship in a wonderfully tender sentence: “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25)

“Naked, and not ashamed” — this is not only about the body; it is about relationship. It speaks of being completely open, completely accepted, completely safe. They had nothing to prove, because they were already loved.

More beautiful still, God was “walking in the garden in the cool of the day” (Genesis 3:8). The tone of the original suggests a habitual walk. God didn’t drop by now and then; God came every day. The greatest blessing of Eden wasn’t the fruit. It was the God who came every day.

2. The serpent’s words: a mindset swapped

Then the serpent came.

“The serpent said to the woman, ‘You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.’” (Genesis 3:4–5)

“You will be like God” — in Hebrew, כֵּאלֹהִים (ke’elohim), “like God”.

Brothers and sisters, look closely at what this temptation really is. The serpent didn’t tell Eve to kill anyone. He didn’t tell her to steal. He simply planted one thought in her heart: you can be like God.

And so pride was stirred up in the human heart — “I” wanted to be like God.

This is precisely where sin began.

Notice that human beings were created in the image of God from the very start (Genesis 1:27). So the problem was not “being like God”. The problem was wanting to be like God without depending on God — wanting to be God without God. The image God had given, they wanted to seize for themselves; the place God had assigned, they wanted to promote themselves out of. That is the essence of pride.

3. Pride defined: leaving our originally intended position

The 321 vision puts pride very plainly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

The essence of pride is being “self-centred”, wanting to take over God’s place. When we choose to be “our own master”, we no longer let God be Master; when we begin to “make much of ourselves”, we lose the shape of a selfless life.

So sin entered the world. Humanity was driven out of Eden, lost fellowship with God, and lost heavenly glory and authority as well.

The word for “sin”, chatta’t (חַטָּאת) in Hebrew and hamartia (ἁμαρτία) in Greek, at root means “to miss the mark”. People who miss the mark usually don’t miss because their hand is weak, but because they are aiming at the wrong target. Humanity made itself the bullseye, and so every arrow of a lifetime flew off course.

The Reformer Martin Luther, in his Lectures on Romans, defines sin with a wonderfully vivid Latin phrase: incurvatus in se — “curved in on oneself”. Sin doesn’t rush outward; sin curls inward. If someone sees nothing but himself all day long, his world grows smaller and smaller, until at last it is just big enough for him alone.

4. The result of sin: a threefold separation

The result of sin is separation — cut off from God, estranged from others, and broken off from the truth within ourselves. Genesis 3 describes these three separations with perfect precision:

First, broken off from ourselves. “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.” (Genesis 3:7) People began to be unable to accept themselves, and started covering themselves with leaves. From that day on, humanity has invented countless “fig leaves” — degrees, titles, designer labels, social-media filters — all to cover up the self we can’t bear to look at ourselves.

Second, cut off from God. “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8) Notice: God did not hide from people first. People hid from God first. The most terrible thing about sin is not that God no longer wants us; it is that we no longer dare to face God.

Third, estranged from others. “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’” (Genesis 3:12) In one sentence he shifts the blame onto his wife — and onto God. Yesterday it was “bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh”; today it is “the woman whom you gave to be with me”. The moment pride comes in, relationship becomes a battlefield.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that these three separations are exactly what 321 calls the priority of relationships being torn apart? 321 teaches that the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Once sin comes in, all four layers of relationship are severed at the root. So salvation doesn’t only deal with behaviour. Salvation reconnects these four layers of relationship, one by one.

From that moment on, humanity has lived in fear, shame, comparison and struggle. And the root of it all is pride.

5. Confirmation from psychology: we all overrate ourselves

Psychology has a repeatedly confirmed phenomenon called the “above-average effect”. In a study published in 1981 in Acta Psychologica, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that among the American drivers he surveyed, about ninety-three per cent believed their driving skill was better than that of more than half of drivers. That is mathematically impossible.

In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University published an even more searching finding in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: the less competent people are, the more they overrate their competence, because what they lack is precisely the ability to know they are lacking. This later became widely known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect”.

Brothers and sisters, these two studies are really footnotes to the Bible. The most frightening thing about pride is not that it makes me worse, but that it stops me seeing that I am getting worse. It takes away both my eyes and my mirror at the same time.

That is why David prayed: “Who can discern his errors? Forgive me from hidden errors.” (Psalm 19:12)

6. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus is the focal point

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Pride is, at heart, a misplaced focus. When my focus is on myself, I live in comparison; when my focus is on others, I live in envy or judgement; when my focus is on my circumstances, I live in complaint. Only when the focus comes back to Jesus does “self” naturally shrink.

This is also why 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. That day, Eve relied on her brain and not her heart. She “saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise” (Genesis 3:6) — she analysed it three times over, and the more she analysed the more reasonable it seemed, and the more reasonable it seemed the further she drifted from God.

Brothers and sisters, how many times have we, too, analysed things right to the end and talked ourselves into doing the very thing God never asked us to do?

sections.heading: 4. The Fruit of Pride: From Eden to Today’s World
sections.html:
Pride didn’t only cost Adam and Eve their blessing; it has made history replay the same tragedy over and over.

1. Psalm 10:4: the man with his nose in the air

“The wicked, in the pride of his face, has no room in his thoughts for God.” (Psalm 10:4)

The Hebrew of this verse is very vivid. “The pride of his face” is גֹּבַהּ אַפּוֹ (gobah appo), literally “the height of his nose”. We say someone has “his nose in the air”, and the Hebrew is saying exactly the same thing.

Interestingly, a person with his nose in the air faces one inevitable consequence: he can’t see the people on the ground, and he can’t see the God in heaven. All he can see is the tip of his own nose.

So the verse continues: he “has no room in his thoughts for God”. Notice that the psalmist doesn’t say that he “declares with his mouth that there is no God”. Plenty of people confess with their mouths on Sunday that God exists, and then on Monday there is no God in any of their plans. That is what it means to have no room in our thoughts for God.

Pride makes people reject God’s guidance and trust only their own reason, judgement and experience. Such a life ends, in the end, in failure and curse.

Brothers and sisters, here we must ask ourselves a very honest question: of the three most important decisions I have made recently, which one did I first kneel down and bring to God — rather than working it all out myself and then asking God to sign off on it?

2. Four mirrors from history

The Bible gives us four mirrors that show us the fruit of pride.

The first mirror: Satan.

“You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

In just two verses, “I will” appears five times. No passage in the whole Bible is more densely packed with “I”, and it is the most primal specimen of pride there is. And God’s answer takes only one verse: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.” (Isaiah 14:15)

Ezekiel says too: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” (Ezekiel 28:17) Notice that what ruined him was not ugliness but beauty; not lack but splendour. Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous moment is often not when you are at your weakest, but when you are at your most successful.

321 puts it with great precision: selflessness overcomes Satan. Why? Because Satan’s very nature is the self-centred life, and the self-centred life cannot defeat the self-centred life. If you fight pride with pride, both sides are wounded; only selflessness stands on ground where Satan has no foothold at all.

The second mirror: Cain.

Cain, in his pride, rejected God’s warning, envied his brother and killed him. But we often overlook one thing: God came to counsel him first.

“Yahweh said to Cain, ‘Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.’” (Genesis 4:6–7)

God gave him a way to climb down, God gave him a chance, God even warned him of the danger ahead. But pride stopped his ears. And the result? “Cain said to Abel, his brother, ‘Let’s go into the field.’ While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.” (Genesis 4:8)

From “the expression of your face fallen” to “killed him” is a distance of just two verses. Once pride refuses correction, the speed of the fall is staggering.

The third mirror: Pharaoh.

“Pharaoh said, ‘Who is Yahweh, that I should listen to his voice to let Israel go? I don’t know Yahweh, and moreover I will not let Israel go.’” (Exodus 5:2)

“Who is Yahweh?” — these three words are the most arrogant sentence a human being has ever spoken. The result: ten plagues came, the firstborn all died, and at last “the waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen, even all Pharaoh’s army that went in after them into the sea. There remained not so much as one of them” (Exodus 14:28).

It wasn’t that Pharaoh had no chance to repent. But every time a plague passed, the text says that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened. Pride can make a person stiffen his neck at the very same spot ten times over.

The fourth mirror: Nebuchadnezzar.

“The king spoke and said, ‘Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?’” (Daniel 4:30)

And as soon as he said it, the text tells us: “While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky.” (Daniel 4:31) So this king who had swept across the nations “was driven from men, and ate grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky, until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws” (Daniel 4:33).

But the most precious thing about this mirror is that it has a beautiful ending. When the seven periods of time were over, he lifted his eyes to heaven, his understanding returned, and then he spoke the most moving sentence in the whole book of Daniel:

“Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)

Brothers and sisters, hear the hope in this: the proud are not beyond hope — so long as they are willing to lift their eyes to heaven.

3. Why can’t proud people apologise?

Isn’t it the same in our lives today? Pride stops us from taking correction, from apologising, from repenting, even from trusting God.

Why is apologising so hard? Psychology offers a very helpful explanation.

In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”. He showed that when a person’s behaviour contradicts how he sees himself, he feels intense psychological discomfort; and the way people usually resolve that discomfort is not by changing the behaviour, but by changing how they interpret the facts.

In other words, when the self-image “I am a good person” collides with the fact “I did something terrible”, most people don’t revise their self-image. Instead they revise their account of what happened: I had no choice, he started it, it really wasn’t that serious.

Brothers and sisters, this is Adam all over again. “The woman whom you gave to be with me” — I had no choice, she started it, it really wasn’t my fault.

So the more we try to “rely on ourselves”, the deeper we sink into bondage; the more we try to “prove ourselves”, the further we drift from grace. For grace is given to “those who admit they need grace”, and that is the one thing pride refuses most of all to admit.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: pride provokes pride, humility inspires humility

321 has a saying worth engraving on the tablet of our hearts: pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Think about our homes. When a husband and wife quarrel, very often what they’re really fighting about isn’t the thing itself. She raises her voice half a notch, and he raises his a full notch; his face darkens, and she turns and walks out. On the surface they’re arguing about an issue; underneath they’re fighting over a position — who’s right, who’s wrong, who has to back down first.

The logic of pride says: I will never back down first. But when neither of them will lower their head, the result is that neither of them can hold their head up.

The logic of humility says: I will return to my originally intended position first. When one returns to their originally intended position, the other slowly relaxes; when one stops fighting for rights, the other no longer needs to be on guard. That is humility inspiring humility.

321 also teaches us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. How much service is completely right about the “task” and completely broken with the “people”? What God wants is someone who has life first, then relationships, and only then goes out to do the work.

sections.heading: 5. Humility: The Starting Point of Selflessness and the Key to Overcoming Sin
sections.html:
To overcome sin we can’t deal only with behaviour; we have to deal with the root. The root of sin is pride; the secret of overcoming sin is humility.

1. Three sentences of humility

Humility is not a feeling. Humility is three sentences you can honestly say out loud.

Humility is admitting: “I can’t, but Jesus can.”

Humility is admitting: “I was wrong. Lord, have mercy.”

Humility is choosing to lay down “self” and return to living under God’s rule.

The first sentence deals with pride in our ability, the second with pride in our morality, and the third with pride in our position. The hardest one to say is usually the second. Because admitting “I can’t” still lets you save face, but admitting “I was wrong” means handing your face over.

The tax collector’s prayer was a single sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13) And the Lord Jesus’ verdict was: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 18:14)

The Pharisee prayed a long string of words; the tax collector prayed one sentence. But that one sentence was what God heard.

2. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble”

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

This verse reveals a spiritual principle: God does not work alongside the proud, but he delights to walk with the humble.

We said earlier that in Greek the word “resists” is a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against” — shields locked, spears levelled. That is how God faces pride.

Why does God deal so severely with pride? Not because God is petty, but because pride kills people. God resists pride the way a doctor resists cancer cells: what he is fighting is not the person but the thing that is devouring the person.

Peter quotes the very same words: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (1 Peter 5:5) And then he says: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6)

Notice the cause and effect here. It is not “humble yourself and then find your own way up”. It is “humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God”, and then “he may exalt you in due time”. Lifting up is God’s work, not my project.

So humility is not only a virtue; it is a form of spiritual authority. A humble person can carry God’s grace; a proud person cuts off God’s blessing.

Isaiah paints the picture even more beautifully: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” (Isaiah 57:15)

God has two dwelling places: one in the high and holy place, and one in the heart of the humble. Brothers and sisters, will you, this very morning, give up the chair in your heart?

3. The Lord Jesus is our role model of humility

The first of the 321 Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. When it comes to humility, Jesus is not only the teacher; he is the road itself.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

Put this passage side by side with Genesis 3 and you will see an astonishing contrast.

The first Adam: he was a man, yet he wanted to be equal with God.

The last Adam: he existed in the form of God, yet he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.

One reached upward; the other went down. One seized rights; the other laid them down. One left his originally intended position; the other returned to it.

The word “emptied himself” in Greek is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), meaning “poured out”. The Lord Jesus did not lose his divinity; rather, he laid down the rights of his divinity and the display of its glory, and poured himself out into a vessel that people could use.

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. That is exactly Paul’s testimony: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The Lord Jesus himself issues the invitation: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29)

Brothers and sisters, notice: the Lord didn’t say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me”. Nor did he say “and you will succeed”; he said “you will find rest for your souls”. What proud people lack most is not success but rest. Because people who must keep proving themselves can never stop and rest.

4. A photograph and a number

On 14 February 1990, NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, about six billion kilometres from Earth, turned around and looked back at our home. When the photograph came back, Earth took up a single pixel — a faint, pale blue dot hanging in a beam of sunlight.

The astronomer Carl Sagan, gazing at that photograph in his 1994 book Pale Blue Dot, wrote: that’s here. That’s home. That’s us. Every king and every peasant in human history, every war and every triumph, everyone we have ever loved — all of it happened on that mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.

At the other end of the scale, an estimate published in 2013 by Eva Bianconi’s research team in the Annals of Human Biology found that an adult human body is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells — we have only recently managed even a rough count of the cells in our own bodies.

Brothers and sisters, looking outward we don’t know how vast the universe is, and looking inward we don’t know how complex we ourselves are, yet standing in between we often tell God with great confidence: I can handle this one myself.

David sang of it long ago: “When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:3–4)

True humility is not feeling small and so thinking little of ourselves; it is seeing how great God is and so standing in awe. It is not putting ourselves down; it is putting ourselves back in the right place.

5. The humble go the furthest

Some people worry: Pastor, won’t humility mean I get trampled underfoot?

Management studies offer an interesting answer. In 2001 the American researcher Jim Collins published the findings of a five-year study in his book Good to Great. His team screened 1,435 large American companies and found only eleven that had truly made the leap from good to great. The team hadn’t originally intended to look at leadership at all, but the data kept pointing to the same conclusion: these companies were all led by what he called “Level 5 leaders” — people who combined extreme personal humility with intense professional will.

Humility does not equal weakness. Humility moves our strength from “protecting ourselves” over to “fulfilling the mission”. Only someone who no longer needs to prove himself has all his strength free to love others.

The nineteenth-century South African pastor Andrew Murray, in his 1895 book Humility, says that humility is nothing other than the disappearance of “self” in the vision that God is all. That sentence is almost exactly what 321 calls “selflessness”.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: the fivefold change

321 says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

We cannot deal with pride by starting at the last link.

If I change only my “ministry” — serve a bit more, give a bit more — that is covering the root with behaviour, like Adam with his fig leaves. If I change only my “relationships” — try to be a little more polite to people — that is enduring, not being renewed.

Real change has to begin with the mindset: I must settle it afresh that God is God and I am human; I am not the centre of the universe — Jesus is; I don’t need to prove myself, because I am already accepted in Christ.

Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry can finally bear real fruit.

This is also what 321 calls the shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Pride is always human, earthly, temporary and worldly; humility is always of God, heavenly, eternal and godly.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations of 321 are exactly the three pillars for dealing with pride.

Jesus is my role model — he existed in the form of God, yet he emptied himself. When I take him as my role model, my target is no longer “being better than others” but “being as low as Jesus”.

The Bible is my standard — proud people take their own feelings, experience and success as their standard. When the Bible becomes my standard, I have a mirror that never lies. “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, … and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)

The Holy Spirit is my guide — proud people rely on the brain and on themselves; humble people rely on the heart and on the Holy Spirit. 321 says: rely on the heart and you rejoice; rely on the brain and you worry. The wellspring of life flows from the heart.

And the Two Core Values are pride’s ultimate antidote: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. A kingdom can have only one king. If I sit on the throne, Jesus is not on the throne; if Jesus is on the throne, I must come down. This is not a matter of emotion; it is a matter of position. The root of sin is that I am sitting in the wrong seat.

As for the Goal — establish God’s system. A system is a network of relationships. What pride does best is tear relationships down; what humility does best is mend them. So dealing with pride has never been merely a personal devotional exercise. It is kingdom work.

2. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

321 says: the old self lives the self-centred life; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Why not “power overcomes Satan”? Because Satan isn’t afraid of power — Satan himself has power. What Satan fears is selflessness, because a selfless person has nothing on him that Satan can grab hold of. The Lord Jesus said: “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30)

“He has nothing in me” — that is the power of selflessness. Satan could not find a single hook in the Lord Jesus to hang anything on.

Brothers and sisters, so many of our defeats come because we still have too many hooks on us: a flicker of resentment, an unwillingness to forgive, a trace of grudge, a hint of wanting to be seen. Satan doesn’t need great power; he only needs one gentle tug.

3. The 920 practice and 235 relationships

The 920 practice of 321 says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; in them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice that not one of these nine graces is a “power”, and not one can be used for comparison. Fruit grows out of life; it isn’t squeezed out by effort. And for fruit to grow, the tree must first bow low — the branches that bear fruit always hang down.

So the training ground for this lesson is not the pulpit. It is your dinner table, the corridor at the office, the conversation in your group chat. The person who sets you off most easily is the “2” God is giving you today.

And 235 relationships tell us: become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with someone selfless; build “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

No one can deal with pride alone. Because pride’s best camouflage is isolation. A person without a spiritual companion will never hear the one sentence he most needs to hear: “Brother, the way you said that just now wasn’t quite right.”

“The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” (Proverbs 27:6)

Brothers and sisters, is there anyone in your life who can tell you the truth without fear of you turning on them? If not, begin today to ask God to give you a “2”.

4. The Path of Serving

321 describes the Path of Serving in five stages: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First comes the guidance of the Holy Spirit (Spirit), and only then an understanding of Scripture (Understanding); with understanding, life is formed (Life); with life, we can truly serve (Service); and the destination of all service is to let Jesus receive all the glory (God).

The commonest mistake pride makes is to skip the first three steps and charge straight to the fourth. No Spirit, no Understanding, no Life — only Service. Service like that sooner or later turns into a career, a stage, one more extension of “self”.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. That order must never be reversed.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Training Humility into Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. We will use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them out one by one.

Practice 1: A morning prayer of dependence

Every morning, pray: “Lord, help me today not to rely on myself, but to rely on you alone.”

Information: first receive the content of the truth. “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.” (Proverbs 3:5)

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn this sentence from knowledge into illumination. Not “I know I shouldn’t rely on myself”, but “Lord, let me see that in this very matter today I am relying on myself.”

Conviction: truly agree in your heart — without the Lord, even my breath is grace.

Implementation: put this prayer at the very start of the day. Not after you’ve scrolled your phone in bed, but the first thing when you open your eyes; write the sentence by your bed or on your phone’s lock screen.

Evaluation: at night, ask yourself — was there a moment today when this prayer actually made me stop and ask God?

Correction: if it never crossed your mind all day, move the reminder earlier, write it bigger, make it shorter.

Repetition: practise it for twenty-one days in a row. Doing it once isn’t practice; repetition is practice.

Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to do the twenty-one days with you, and report one sentence to each other every day.

Practice 2: Listen first, don’t defend

When someone reminds or corrects you, don’t defend yourself first. First quiet your heart and listen; perhaps God is speaking through them.

Information: “He who hates reproof is stupid.” (Proverbs 12:1b) That’s not a polite sentence, but it is a true one.

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you what your heart is really protecting in the second you start defending yourself — the truth, or your image?

Conviction: I need others to see the self I can’t see. The Dunning–Kruger effect reminds us that my biggest blind spot is precisely that “I don’t know I have blind spots”.

Implementation: set yourself one simple rule — when corrected, count to three, then say: “Thank you for telling me. I need to think about it.” Just that one sentence.

Evaluation: how many times this week did I manage it? How many times did I blurt something out again?

Correction: if you can’t do it in the moment, make up for it afterwards: pick up the phone and say, “What you said the other day — I went away and thought about it.”

Repetition: let “listen first” become a reflex, so you no longer need to remind yourself.

Multiplication: when you need to correct others, use the same gentleness. “Speaking truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15) — love first, then the truth.

Practice 3: An evening examination

Every evening, examine yourself: where am I still self-centred today? Did I let Jesus be Lord?

Information: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Revelation: self-examination is not self-condemnation; it is inviting God to shine his light. Self-condemnation leaves people discouraged; the Holy Spirit’s light sets people free.

Conviction: confessing sin is not a loss; it is a gain. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

Implementation: for three minutes before bed, ask three questions — where today did I grab the Lord’s seat? Whom have I wronged? Toward whom will I humble myself first tomorrow?

Evaluation: look back once a week, on Sunday, and see whether any pattern keeps recurring. That recurring pattern is the place God wants to heal in you this year.

Correction: for that pattern, set one specific small action rather than a vague wish.

Repetition: without missing a day, keep it up for a month.

Multiplication: share what you’ve learned from your self-examination briefly in your small group. Once your weakness is spoken aloud, it becomes someone else’s way out.

A Gentle Reminder

Pride makes people fall; humility lets people be lifted up. To have revival, we must first bow down.

Brothers and sisters, every true revival in history began not on a stage but on the floor; not with applause but with tears.

“If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)

Notice the four conditions God lists — the very first is “humble themselves”. Revival isn’t something we beg into being; it comes when we bow down.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
The root of sin is pride; the starting point of salvation is humility.

When we are willing to admit “I am not Lord” and let Jesus become the centre of our lives, the power of sin loses its grip, and we come back into the blessing of walking with God.

The selfless life begins with humility; the humble life will surely enter revival.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the ship we started with.

The tragedy of Titanic was not that she struck an iceberg, but that when she set sail, no one truly believed they would need the lifeboats.

This morning the Holy Spirit asks each one of us the same question: do you still believe you cannot sink?

If today you are willing to admit “I can sink”, that is not failure; it is the beginning of being saved. Because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6) — when you turn around, the God who had drawn up his battle lines against you becomes the Father opening his arms to you.

So today I want to give you three calls.

First, let Jesus be King. In your heart, truly give up that chair. Not half of it, not just your weekends — the whole chair, your whole life.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. From today on, whenever people praise you for something, turn in your heart and offer it to the Lord; wherever you succeed, remember to say: the Lord did this.

Third, start with one person. Today, go to the person you have always refused to back down to first — one phone call, one message, one sentence: “I’m sorry. I was wrong.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

To have revival, we must first bow down. May we be a people who are willing to bow down before God; may Jesus truly reign as King among us and receive all the glory.

Dear Heavenly Father,
We bow down before you, for you are God and we are human.

Lord, shine your light on us. So often our mouths say you are Lord while in our hearts we sit on the throne ourselves. Forgive our pride — the pride hidden beneath humble-sounding words, the pride dressed up as faithful service, the pride that even we ourselves cannot see.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself, were made in the likeness of men, and became obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Give us that same mind, so that we no longer fight over that chair, but gladly return to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Holy Spirit, be our guide. When we are corrected, give us a heart that is willing to listen; when we are praised, give us a heart that gives the glory to the Lord at once; when we stumble, give us words of confession at once.

Lord, make us low-lying ground that can hold your grace, so that our homes, our small groups and our church may, through humility, receive one another and build one another up, and establish God’s system.
May your kingdom come, may your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Genesis 3:5 says: “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Satan’s temptation starts with “mindset”, not with “behaviour”. Think back to the last time you fell: before the behaviour happened, what mindset had your heart already accepted? Say that sentence out loud, specifically.

James 4:6 says: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” In your current relationships (family, co-workers in ministry, colleagues), which one is stuck in a stalemate where “neither of us will back down first”? This week, are you willing to return to your originally intended position first — and what is the first thing you will say?

blog.title: The Ship That Could Not Sink

blocks.x: Why, when we have dealt with our behaviour, is sin still there?

In 1911 the British magazine The Shipbuilder described a giant liner that had just been launched as “practically unsinkable”. Her name was Titanic. Because everyone believed she could not sink, she carried just twenty lifeboats, with room for 1,178 people in all — while more than 2,200 people were on board.
The following April she struck an iceberg, and two hours and forty minutes later she sank into the deep.
She was not defeated by an iceberg. She was defeated by a mindset. That mindset was this: I cannot sink.
The Bible gives that mindset a far older name — pride.
The root of sin is not behaviour but pride

We usually think of sin as a string of behaviours: lying, losing our temper, greed, envy, bitterness. So our ways of dealing with sin mostly stay at the level of behaviour: we resolve never to lie again, we work hard at controlling our temper. Yet the branches we cut off grow back, because the root is still in the ground.
Go back to the Garden of Eden. The serpent didn’t tell Eve to kill anyone. He didn’t tell her to steal. He simply planted one thought in her heart —
“For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)
Human beings already bore the image of God. So the problem was not “being like God”. The problem was wanting to be like God without depending on God — wanting to be God without God.

So sin came in, and brought a threefold separation: broken off from ourselves, so people covered themselves with leaves; cut off from God, so people hid from his presence; estranged from others, so the first thing Adam said was “The woman whom you gave to be with me”. Yesterday she was bone of his bones; today she is “that woman”.

The vision of Kingdom 321 puts it plainly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.
Why the humble go the furthest

Psychology holds up a mirror. In a 1981 study the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that about ninety-three per cent of the American drivers he surveyed believed their driving skill was better than that of more than half of drivers. That is mathematically impossible. In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger went further: the less competent people are, the more they overrate themselves, because what they lack is precisely the ability to know they are lacking.
The most frightening thing about pride is not that it makes me worse, but that it stops me seeing that I am getting worse. It takes away both my eyes and my mirror at the same time.
That is why the Bible says:
“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)

In Greek, “resists” is a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”. When I am proud, I don’t just lose a blessing; I have gone over to stand on the opposite side from God. And “humble” in the original means “low-lying” — grace is like water: it always runs downhill.

Humility is neither putting ourselves down nor weakness. In Good to Great, the management researcher Jim Collins studied 1,435 American companies and found only eleven that had truly made the leap from good to great; every one was led by what he called a “Level 5 leader” — extreme personal humility combined with intense professional will.
Humility moves our strength from “protecting ourselves” over to “fulfilling the mission”. Only someone who no longer needs to prove himself has all his strength free to love others.
Three practices you can start today
First, every morning pray: “Lord, help me today not to rely on myself, but to rely on you alone.”
Second, when someone reminds or corrects you, don’t defend yourself first — listen first. You can start with this one sentence: “Thank you for telling me. I need to think about it.”
Third, every evening examine yourself: where am I still self-centred today? Did I let Jesus be Lord?
Doing it once isn’t practice; repetition is practice. And practice that never multiplies stops with ourselves — so find a companion and do the twenty-one days together.
In closing
The tragedy of Titanic was not that she struck an iceberg, but that when she set sail, no one truly believed they would need the lifeboats.
The root of sin is pride; the starting point of salvation is humility. When we are willing to admit “I am not Lord” and let Jesus become the centre of our lives, the power of sin loses its grip.
Pride makes people fall; humility lets people be lifted up. To have revival, we must first bow down.
Reflection question: this week, in the relationship where you least want to bow your head, what sentence are you willing to say first?

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today our theme is this — sin is the fruit of pride.
Our key verse is James 4:6: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
In the last lesson we saw that selflessness is the road to revival. But how do we actually live a selfless life? The answer is one word: humility.
Humility is the starting point of selflessness, and its foundation. Without humility we cannot lay self down; with humility, Jesus can reign as King.
Let me begin with a story.

In 1911 a ship was described as “practically unsinkable”. Her name was Titanic. Because everyone believed she could not sink, she carried just twenty lifeboats — enough for only half the people on board.
In April 1912 she struck an iceberg, and two hours and forty minutes later she was gone.
Brothers and sisters, she was not defeated by an iceberg. She was defeated by a mindset. That mindset was this: I cannot sink.
The Bible gives that mindset a far older name — pride.

The letter of James was written by James, the Lord Jesus’ half-brother, around AD 45 to 50, to Jewish believers scattered abroad by persecution. They lived as strangers in foreign lands and their lives were hard, yet in the church they competed with one another and made friends with the world. Into that darkness this verse shines like a ray of light.

The word “resists” is, in the original, a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: when I am proud, I don’t just lose a blessing; I have gone over to stand on the opposite side from God.
The word “humble” in the original means “low-lying”. Grace is like water — it always runs downhill.
First, the origin of sin.
In the Garden of Eden there was originally no shame and nothing standing between. But the serpent said one thing: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)
The serpent didn’t tell Eve to kill anyone. He didn’t tell her to steal. He simply put one thought in her heart: you can be like God.

Brothers and sisters, human beings already bore the image of God. So the problem was not “being like God”. The problem was wanting to be like God without depending on God — wanting to be God without God.
Satan doesn’t need to force you into sin. He only needs to swap out one of your mindsets. Because change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes.
And the result? Sin brought a threefold separation.
Broken off from ourselves — they sewed leaves together and began to cover themselves.
Cut off from God — they hid from the presence of Yahweh God.
Estranged from others — Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me.” Yesterday she was bone of his bones; today she is “that woman”.

Brothers and sisters, pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

In 1981 the psychologist Ola Svenson found that about ninety-three per cent of American drivers believed their driving skill was better than that of more than half of drivers. The most frightening thing about pride is not that it makes me worse, but that it stops me seeing that I am getting worse.
Second, the fruit of pride.
Psalm 10:4 says: “The wicked, in the pride of his face, has no room in his thoughts for God.”
“The pride of his face” in the Hebrew is literally “the height of his nose” — his nose in the air.
A person with his nose in the air can’t see the people on the ground, and he can’t see the God in heaven.
Ask yourself: of the three most important decisions I have made recently, which one did I first kneel down and bring to God?
The Bible gives us four mirrors.
Satan said “I will” five times — and was brought down to Sheol.
Cain refused to listen to God’s counsel — and killed his own brother.
Pharaoh said, “Who is Yahweh?” — and lost his whole army.
Nebuchadnezzar boasted of his own achievements — and was brought low.
But brothers and sisters, Nebuchadnezzar later lifted his eyes to heaven, and he was restored. So the proud are not beyond hope — so long as they are willing to lift their eyes to heaven.

It is the same for us today. Pride stops us from taking correction, from apologising, from repenting. The more we try to rely on ourselves, the deeper we sink into bondage; the more we try to prove ourselves, the further we drift from grace.
321 puts it well: pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
Third, humility is the key to overcoming sin.
Humility is admitting: I can’t, but Jesus can.
Humility is admitting: I was wrong. Lord, have mercy.
Humility is laying down self and returning to live under God’s rule.

The Lord Jesus existed in the form of God, yet he emptied himself (Philippians 2:7). The first Adam reached upward; the last Adam went down. One left his originally intended position; the other returned to it.
“Emptied himself” in the original means “poured out”. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness. It is no longer I, but Christ who lives in me.
“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
Brothers and sisters, a humble person can carry God’s grace; a proud person cuts off God’s blessing.
Grace, like water, always runs downhill. Are you willing, this very morning, to come down low?
Next come three practices.
First, every morning pray: “Lord, help me today not to rely on myself, but to rely on you alone.”
Second, when someone corrects you, don’t defend yourself first. Listen first; perhaps God is speaking through them.
Third, every evening examine yourself: where am I still self-centred today? Did I let Jesus be Lord?

The 321 eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Doing it once isn’t practice; repetition is practice. And once you’ve done it yourself, bring someone else along to do it with you.
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that ship.
The tragedy of Titanic was not that she struck an iceberg, but that when she set sail, no one believed they would need the lifeboats.
Today the Holy Spirit asks us the same question: do you still believe you cannot sink?
If today you are willing to admit “I can sink”, that is not failure; it is the beginning of being saved.
The root of sin is pride; the starting point of salvation is humility. When we admit that we are not Lord and let Jesus become the centre of our lives, the power of sin loses its grip.
Pride makes people fall; humility lets people be lifted up. To have revival, we must first bow down.
Let’s pray together.
Lord, I confess that I am often self-centred; forgive the pride in my heart.
I am willing to lay myself down and humbly seek your face,
that your grace may replace my pride, and your life may overcome my sin.
May Jesus reign as King among us and receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

In 1911 the British magazine The Shipbuilder described a giant liner that had just been launched as “practically unsinkable”. Her name was Titanic.
