That mindset was this: I cannot sink.
The Bible gives that mindset a far older name — pride.

Augustine said that pride is the beginning of all sin. We often think of sin as behaviour, so our ways of dealing with sin stay at the level of behaviour. But the branches we cut off grow back, because the root is still in the ground.
Today we will look at three things: the origin of sin, the fruit of pride, and humility as the key.
First, the background.

The author of the letter of James is generally held to be James, the Lord Jesus’ half-brother, who later became a pillar of the church in Jerusalem. The letter was written around AD 45 to 50, to Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution. They lived as strangers in foreign lands, and yet in the church they competed with one another and made friends with the world.

Two words here are very important. “Resists” is, in the original, a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: when I am proud, I don’t just lose a blessing; I have gone over to stand on the opposite side from God.
“Humble” in the original means “low-lying”. Water only flows into low places. Grace is like water — it always runs downhill.
Now we come to our first point: the origin of sin.

The Bible describes Eden in a wonderfully tender sentence: “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25) No pretence, no defences. They had nothing to prove, because they were already loved.
And the text says that Yahweh God was walking in the garden. The tone of the original suggests a habitual walk — God didn’t drop by now and then; God came every day.
Brothers and sisters, notice: Adam and Eve didn’t sin because they lacked anything, or because they were suffering, or because they had been treated unfairly. They lived in the best place there was.
So sin is not a problem of environment. Sin is a problem of the heart.
Then the serpent came.
The serpent said to the woman: “You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:4–5)
Brothers and sisters, look closely at what this temptation really is. The serpent simply planted one thought in her heart: you can be like God.
Human beings already bore the image of God. So the problem was not “being like God”. The problem was wanting to be like God without depending on God — wanting to be God without God.
Satan doesn’t need to force you into sin. He only needs to swap out one of your mindsets. Because change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes.

321 puts pride very plainly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.
When we choose to be our own master, we no longer let God be Master; when we begin to make much of ourselves, we lose the shape of a selfless life.

The word “sin” at root means “to miss the mark”. People who miss the mark usually don’t miss because their hand is weak, but because they are aiming at the wrong target. Humanity made itself the bullseye, and so every arrow of a lifetime flew off course.
Martin Luther said that sin is being “curved in on oneself”. Sin doesn’t rush outward; sin curls inward.
The result of sin is a threefold separation.
First, broken off from ourselves. They sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves. Today humanity’s leaves are degrees, titles, designer labels and social-media filters.
Second, cut off from God. They hid from the presence of Yahweh God. God did not hide from people first; people hid from God first.
Third, estranged from others. Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me.” Yesterday she was bone of his bones; today she is “that woman”.

Brothers and sisters, psychology has written footnotes to the Bible. In 1981 Ola Svenson found that about ninety-three per cent of American drivers believed their driving skill was better than that of more than half of drivers. In 1999 Dunning and Kruger went further: the less competent people are, the more they overrate themselves.
The most frightening thing about pride is not that it makes me worse, but that it stops me seeing that I am getting worse.
Our second point: the fruit of pride.
Psalm 10:4 says: “The wicked, in the pride of his face, has no room in his thoughts for God.”

“The pride of his face” in the Hebrew is literally “the height of his nose” — his nose in the air. A person with his nose in the air can’t see the people on the ground, and he can’t see the God in heaven.
Plenty of people confess with their mouths on Sunday that God exists, and then on Monday there is no God in any of their plans.
Brothers and sisters, ask yourself an honest question: of the three most important decisions I have made recently, which one did I first kneel down and bring to God?
The Bible gives us four mirrors.

The first mirror: Satan. In Isaiah 14:13–14, in just two verses, “I will” appears five times. And God’s answer takes only one verse: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.”

Ezekiel 28:17 says, “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty.” What ruined him was not ugliness but beauty. The most dangerous moment is often not when you are at your weakest, but when you are at your most successful.

The second mirror: Cain. God came to counsel him first, and even warned him of the danger ahead, but pride stopped his ears. From “the expression of your face fallen” to “killed him” is a distance of just two verses.

The third mirror: Pharaoh. He said, “Who is Yahweh?” The result: ten plagues came, and his whole army was lost. Every time a plague passed, the text says that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened. Pride can make a person stiffen his neck at the very same spot ten times over.

The fourth mirror: Nebuchadnezzar. He boasted that he had built great Babylon as his royal dwelling place by the might of his power. While the word was still in his mouth, a voice came from the sky, and he was brought low.
But this mirror has a beautiful ending. When the seven periods of time were over, he lifted his eyes to heaven, his understanding returned, and he said: “Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.”
Brothers and sisters, hear the hope in this: the proud are not beyond hope — so long as they are willing to lift their eyes to heaven.
Isn’t it the same in our lives today? Pride stops us from taking correction, from apologising, from repenting.

Why is apologising so hard? In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when our behaviour contradicts our self-image, the way we usually resolve the discomfort is not by changing the behaviour, but by changing how we interpret the facts.
I had no choice, he started it — brothers and sisters, this is Adam all over again.
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

When a husband and wife quarrel, very often what they’re really fighting about isn’t the thing itself but a position — who has to back down first. When neither of them will lower their head, the result is that neither of them can hold their head up.
321 also teaches us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks.
Our third point: humility is the key to overcoming sin.
To overcome sin we can’t deal only with behaviour; we have to deal with the root.
Humility is admitting: I can’t, but Jesus can.
Humility is admitting: I was wrong. Lord, have mercy.
Humility is choosing to lay down self and return to living under God’s rule.
The hardest one to say is the second. Because admitting “I can’t” still lets you save face, but admitting “I was wrong” means handing your face over.
The tax collector’s prayer was a single sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” And the Lord Jesus said this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.
“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Why does God deal so severely with pride? Not because God is petty, but because pride kills people. God resists pride the way a doctor resists cancer cells — what he is fighting is not the person but the thing that is devouring the person.
Peter says too: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Lifting up is God’s work, not my project.

Isaiah 57:15 says that God dwells in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit. Brothers and sisters, God has two dwelling places: one in the high and holy place, and one in the heart of the humble. Will you, this very morning, give up that chair?
The first of the 321 Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. When it comes to humility, Jesus is the road itself.
“Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7)
The first Adam was a man, yet he wanted to be equal with God; the last Adam existed in the form of God, yet he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.
One reached upward; the other went down. One seized power; the other laid it down. One left his originally intended position; the other returned to it.
“Emptied himself” in the original means “poured out”. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness. It is no longer I, but Christ who lives in me.
Some people ask: Pastor, won’t humility mean I get trampled underfoot?

First, look up at the sky. In 1990 Voyager 1, about six billion kilometres from Earth, looked back at our home, and in the photograph Earth took up a single pixel. In Pale Blue Dot, Carl Sagan wrote: that’s here. That’s home. That’s us.
Then look down at yourself. In 2013 Eva Bianconi’s team estimated that an adult human body is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells.

Brothers and sisters, looking outward we don’t know how vast the universe is, and looking inward we don’t know how complex we ourselves are, yet we often tell God with great confidence: I can handle this one myself.

And will we lose out? Jim Collins studied 1,435 American companies; only eleven truly made the leap, and every one was led by a Level 5 leader — extreme personal humility combined with intense professional will.
Humility does not equal weakness. Humility moves our strength from protecting ourselves over to fulfilling the mission.
Now for our practices.
First, every morning pray: “Lord, help me today not to rely on myself, but to rely on you alone.”

Proverbs 3:5 says: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.” Put this prayer at the very start of the day — not after you’ve scrolled your phone, but the first thing when you open your eyes.

Second, when someone reminds or corrects you, don’t defend yourself first. First quiet your heart and listen; perhaps God is speaking through them. Here’s a ready-made sentence: “Thank you for telling me. I need to think about it.”
And when you need to correct others, use the same gentleness, speaking truth in love.
Third, every evening examine yourself: where am I still self-centred today? Did I let Jesus be Lord?
David’s prayer was: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.” (Psalm 139:23)
Self-examination is not self-condemnation; it is inviting God to shine his light. Self-condemnation leaves people discouraged; the Holy Spirit’s light sets people free.

The 321 eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Doing it once isn’t practice; repetition is practice. Please find a companion and do the twenty-one days together.
Let’s draw the 321 vision together.
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. A kingdom can have only one king. If I sit on the throne, Jesus is not on the throne. The root of sin is that I am sitting in the wrong seat.
The Goal: establish God’s system.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Because what Satan fears is not power but selflessness. The Lord Jesus said: “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.”
So many of our defeats come because we still have too many hooks on us: a flicker of resentment, an unwillingness to forgive, a hint of wanting to be seen. Satan only needs one gentle tug.
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that ship.
The tragedy of Titanic was not that she struck an iceberg, but that when she set sail, no one truly believed they would need the lifeboats.
This morning the Holy Spirit asks us the same question: do you still believe you cannot sink? If you are willing to admit “I can sink”, that is not failure; it is the beginning of being saved.
2 Chronicles 7:14 says that if God’s people will humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from their wicked ways, he will hear from heaven. The very first condition is “humble themselves”.

So I want to give you three calls. First, let Jesus be King — give up the whole chair. Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. Third, today, go to the person you have always refused to back down to first.
The root of sin is pride; the starting point of salvation is humility. The selfless life begins with humility; the humble life will surely enter revival.
Let’s pray together.

Lord, I confess that I am often self-centred; forgive the pride in my heart — the pride hidden beneath humble-sounding words, the pride dressed up as faithful service, the pride that even we ourselves cannot see.
I am willing to lay myself down and humbly seek your face,
that your grace may replace my pride, and your life may overcome my sin.
Lord, make us low-lying ground that can hold your grace, so that our homes, our small groups and our church may, through humility, receive one another and build one another up.
May your kingdom come, may your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
May Jesus reign as King among us and receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: A Question No One Can Get Around
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to face together a question that is very large, very deep and very real: where, in the end, does sin come from?

This is no obscure seminary topic. Sooner or later it surfaces in every human heart. A mother stands outside a hospital ward in tears and asks, “God, if you are good, why is there so much evil in the world?” A young man stops in his tracks on the road to faith and says, “If God is almighty, why would he create a human being capable of sin? Doesn’t that make sin his responsibility?” An older believer, after a fall, sits in a chair and murmurs to himself, “I knew it was wrong. I really didn’t want to do it. And I still did it — where on earth does this pull come from?”

These three questions are really one question asked three ways. The first asks about the character of God, the second about the source of sin, the third about our own helplessness. And the answer the Bible gives is surprisingly simple — and surprisingly piercing:

God did not create sin. Sin is the result of pride.

Put another way, sin is not a “thing.” It is not an item God added to the inventory of creation. Sin is a “direction”: it is what happens in the moment a creature turns its face away from God and towards itself. Darkness is not a created substance; darkness is what remains when light is blocked. Cold is not a form of energy; cold is what we feel when heat has gone. God made no particles of darkness, and God made no raw material for sin. When the creature chose to leave God — chose “I will be like God” — in that moment sin was born.

So if we press for the source of sin, the Bible does not lead us into a laboratory; it leads us to a heart. Not to a substance, but to an attitude. And the name of that attitude is “pride.”

In the language of 321 we give it a name closer to daily life: the self-centred life. The self-centred life means I am at the centre of my life. It means I want to be my own king. It means I refuse to let God be God and want to sit on the throne in his place. And the cure for sin is not trying twice as hard, nor gritting our teeth in self-restraint. It is selflessness — letting Jesus reign as King, letting God be in his place while I return to mine.

Brothers and sisters, this morning’s message comes down to just two sentences. Please fix them in your mind first: the starting point of sin is pride; the starting point of victory is humility. May God, through his word, plant these two sentences in our hearts.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: James — A Field Manual for the Displaced
sections.html: Our key passage today comes from the letter of James. To hear James’s tone rightly, we first need to know its author, its readers and their situation.

sections.heading: 1. The Author
sections.html:
The author calls himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1). The great majority of witnesses in church history point to James the leader of the Jerusalem church — the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19). John 7:5 says, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” While Jesus walked the earth, this younger brother did not believe in him; but after the Lord rose and appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), he became a pillar of the Jerusalem church.

This matters enormously for today’s theme. A man who once looked at his elder brother with suspicion ends up calling himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” He does not say, “I am the Lord’s brother.” He says only, “I am the Lord’s servant.” Brothers and sisters, here is a living testimony of the self-centred life becoming selflessness. He had a status he could have boasted in, and he laid it down. So when he writes, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble,” it is no slogan. It is the road he himself has walked.

sections.heading: 2. Date and Readers
sections.html:
James is very likely one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written, generally dated to the late AD 40s or early 50s — around the time of the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15, about AD 49). It is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1): Jewish Christians scattered abroad by the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1; 11:19).

They were people who had lost their land and their property and were living as strangers in Gentile cities. Their situation: oppressed by the rich (James 2:6), cheated of their wages (5:4), facing trials every day (1:2). In such conditions two things happen most easily. Outwardly, people complain against God and against their circumstances. Inwardly, they compete with one another, form factions and quarrel. So James 4 opens with the question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1)

sections.heading: 3. The Surrounding Context
sections.html:
James 4:6 does not appear out of nowhere. Look at the order of what surrounds it and we see a clear chain. Verse 1 says wars and fightings come from the pleasures at war in our members; verse 2 says, “You lust, and don’t have”; verse 3 says, “You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures”; verse 4 calls this kind of life “hostility toward God”; verse 5 speaks of the Spirit God has given to live in us: “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”; and then comes verse 6 — “But he gives more grace.”

Brothers and sisters, notice that word “but.” The five verses before it are all human corruption, human grasping, human asking with wrong motives — and straight after comes “But he gives more grace.” The original says μείζονα χάριν (meizona charin), “greater grace.” However deep our sin, God’s grace is greater still; however high our pride, God’s grace is higher still. That is the logic of the gospel.

James then quotes the Septuagint of Proverbs 3:34: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” 1 Peter 5:5 quotes the same line. And from verse 7 James issues ten commands in a row: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7) — all the way to verse 10: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.”

So the structure of the whole passage runs: pride — fighting — hostility toward God — but God gives more grace — submit to God, resist the devil — humble yourselves — be exalted. That is exactly the order of our four key points today. James is not discussing an abstract doctrine. He is writing a prescription for suffering brothers and sisters who are biting and devouring one another, and the name of that prescription is “humility.”

sections.heading: 1. God Did Not Create Sin
sections.html:
Scripture

“God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.” (Genesis 1:31)

“Behold, I have only found this: that God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.” (Ecclesiastes 7:29)

“Let no man say when he is tempted, ‘I am tempted by God,’ for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.” (James 1:13)

Key Words

The “very good” of Genesis 1:31 is, in the Hebrew, טוֹב מְאֹד (tov me’od). Through the earlier days God says “good” (tov) again and again; only on the sixth day, when humankind has been made, does God say “very good.” That “very” is the strongest of intensifiers. It amounts to saying: complete, whole, beyond reproach.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: among all that God made, not one thing was bad. God did not make a “human being with a sinful nature.” God did not make a “broken angel.” Still less did God slip an item called “sin” onto the list of creation. If God had made sin, God would be answerable for sin. But Scripture says flatly: “God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13).

Scripture Interpreting Scripture

The Bible bears consistent witness to God’s nature. Deuteronomy 32:4 says, “The Rock: his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.” 1 John 1:5 says, “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” 1 Timothy 4:4 says, “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving.”

Where, then, does sin come from? Ecclesiastes 7:29 gives the most precise answer: “God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.” “Upright” is יָשָׁר (yashar), meaning straight, not bent; “schemes” is חִשְּׁבֹנוֹת (chishshevonot), the calculations people devise for themselves. God made a straight line; people bent it themselves.

The Greek of the New Testament calls sin ἁμαρτία (hamartia), whose root meaning is “to miss the mark.” Brothers and sisters, when an arrow misses the target, it is not the arrow’s fault, nor the target’s. The archer has aimed off. The essence of sin is not that God made a faulty arrow, but that the creature turned the sights away.

Illustrations and Examples

Augustine, the fourth-century church father, explained evil with a profound idea: evil is not a “being”; evil is “the absence of good.” Just as darkness is not a substance. You cannot buy a bucket of darkness and carry it home, or fill a bottle with darkness and pour it out again. Darkness is simply the state of things when light is absent. Likewise, cold is not a form of energy. Physics tells us that heat is the motion of molecules, and cold is only heat departing. Scientists can lower a temperature further and further until they reach absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, and then they can go no lower — because “cold” has no further amount to add; it is simply heat brought to zero.

Sin is like that. God did not create a substance called “sin.” Sin is the shadow cast when God’s light is blocked, the hollow left when God’s love is refused. That is why you will never “find” the raw material of sin anywhere in creation. You will only find, in the creature’s heart, the act of turning away.

Here is another picture. A piano maker spends two years building by hand a piano with a perfect tone, every string precisely tuned. On the day it leaves the workshop he says, “Very good.” Three months later someone rings to complain that the piano is out of tune. Did the maker build an out-of-tune piano? No. Someone moved it into a damp basement; someone twisted the tuning pins at will. The tension in the strings was the maker’s gift — it is why the piano can make beautiful music. But that same tension, wrongly twisted, becomes a jarring noise.

The free will God gave humanity is that tension. Free will itself is “very good” — obedience without free will is mere machinery, not love. God did not want a set of music boxes; God wanted children who could sing. But if free will is real, then the choice is real, and so are the consequences.

A Saying

The English writer and apologist C. S. Lewis wrote in Mere Christianity: “Pride leads to every other vice: it is the complete anti-God state of mind.” That sentence serves as a footnote in advance to our second key point. God did not create sin; sin grows out of a state of mind that is wholly against God, and the name of that state of mind is pride.

Applying the 321 Vision

The second of the Three Foundations says: the Bible is my standard. When people ask, “Where does sin come from?” human reason offers all sorts of answers. Some say social structures; some say genetic inheritance; some say childhood trauma; some simply say there is no such thing as sin. Each of these may contain a grain of observed truth, but none is the final standard. Our standard is the Bible, and the Bible says: what God made was very good, God tempts no one, and it is people who have searched out many schemes.

This is the first of the fivefold changes — a change of mindset. Brothers and sisters, if your mindset stays at “It’s all God’s doing” or “I was just born this way,” your life will stay forever in the position of a victim. But when your mindset turns to “What God made was very good, and it was I who changed direction,” the door of repentance opens in that very moment. Change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes.

This is also a shift in perspective: from the human point of view to God’s point of view. The human point of view always pushes the blame outward — onto God, onto circumstances, onto other people. God’s point of view brings me back to the door of my own heart, knocks, and says: the door opens from the inside, and the handle is in your hand.

sections.heading: 2. The Root of Sin: The Choice of Pride
sections.html:
Scripture

“The serpent said to the woman, ‘You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.’” (Genesis 3:4–5)

“How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.” (Isaiah 14:12–15)

“Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor. I have cast you to the ground. I have laid you before kings, that they may see you.” (Ezekiel 28:17)

Key Words

The “shining one, son of the dawn” of Isaiah 14:12 is, in the Hebrew, הֵילֵל בֶּן־שָׁחַר (heilel ben-shachar), meaning “the bright one, son of the dawn.” The Latin Vulgate rendered it Lucifer, and that is where the later name “Lucifer” comes from.

The immediate subject of this passage is the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), and the immediate subject of Ezekiel 28 is the king of Tyre. Yet the language of both passages goes far beyond what any earthly king could carry — “I will ascend into heaven,” “I will make myself like the Most High,” “You were in Eden, the garden of God.” So evangelical interpreters through the ages have generally held that, beyond describing the pride of earthly kings, these passages also reveal the figure who stands behind them: the one who first fell through pride.

One thing needs saying here: the Bible never calls Satan an “archangel.” The only one Scripture calls an archangel is Michael (Jude 9). Ezekiel 28:14 calls him “the anointed cherub who covers,” one of the most honoured and glorious of all created beings. Only when we speak as the Bible speaks will we keep our aim true in the details.

The Hebrew word for pride, גָּאוֹן (ga’on), has the root sense of “rising up, being lifted high.” The Greek ὑπερήφανος (huperēphanos) combines “above” (hyper) and “to show” (phainō), meaning “to display oneself above others.” Brothers and sisters, judging by the words themselves, the motion of pride can be put in a single word: “up.”

Scripture Interpreting Scripture

Notice something of the greatest importance: when Adam and Eve were created, they had no sinful nature; when the angels were created, they had no sinful nature either. They did not sin because they were “broken inside.” They sinned because they “chose to rise.” So the starting point of sin is not weakness. The starting point of sin is pride.

The serpent’s technique deserves a close look. First he asks, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1) — first unsettle God’s word. Then he says, “You won’t really die” — next deny God’s word. Finally he says, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil” — at last replace God’s word. Unsettle, deny, replace: those three steps are exactly the same today.

“You will be like God” — in Hebrew כֵּאלֹהִים (ke’lohim). Brothers and sisters, humankind was made in the image of God from the start (Genesis 1:27); humanity was already “like God.” Satan’s lie did not offer something new. It tempted people to seize with their own hands what God had already given freely. That is the common pattern of every temptation: turning “receiving” into “grabbing,” turning a “son” into a “usurper.”

By contrast, Philippians 2:6–8 describes Jesus taking exactly the opposite road: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” One was “not equal with God, yet determined to grasp it”; the other was “equal with God, yet would not grasp it, but emptied himself.” Brothers and sisters, those two roads still lie before us today.

Three Faces of Pride

First, when people want total control of their own destiny, that is pride. James 4:13–14 says, “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.’ Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.”

Second, when people leave God’s word and act as they themselves see fit, that is pride. Judges 21:25 says, “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.”

Third, when people refuse to submit to God and refuse authority, that is pride. 1 Samuel 15:23 says, “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim.”

Supporting Evidence from Psychology

Psychology has made a fascinating discovery. In 1981 the Swedish researcher Ola Svenson published a study in Acta Psychologica. He asked participants to rate their own driving skill, and 93 per cent of the American sample judged themselves to be above the median. Mathematically that is impossible — only half of any group can ever be above the median.

In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University published research in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology that pointed to something even more uncomfortable: the least competent people tend to overestimate their performance the most, precisely because they lack the very ability needed to recognise their own shortcomings. This came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect.”

Another study is often misunderstood. In 1996 Roy Baumeister and his colleagues argued in Psychological Review that violence and aggression often come not from “low self-esteem” but from “threatened egotism” — when someone who rates himself too highly meets with rejection, aggression erupts. In 2003, in a major review in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Baumeister’s team confirmed again that high self-esteem does not necessarily lead to better performance or better relationships.

Brothers and sisters, psychology cannot replace the Bible, but from the side it confirms what the Bible said thousands of years ago: there is a force in the human heart that keeps lifting the self upward, and that force is the very source of broken relationships and behaviour spinning out of control.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 puts it very plainly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Eve’s tragedy was leaving her originally intended position. She was human, yet wanted to be like God. Satan’s tragedy was likewise leaving his originally intended position: he was the anointed cherub who covers, yet wanted to be like the Most High. Brothers and sisters, much of the pain we suffer today at home, at work and in the church also comes down, at root, to leaving our originally intended position: the wife wants to be the head of her husband, parents want to be God to their children, co-workers want to be the Holy Spirit’s spokesman.

And returning to our originally intended position is selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living out that fullness — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Brothers and sisters, when that “I” steps aside, the boundless life of Christ comes in.

sections.heading: 3. The Consequence of Pride: The Cycle of Sin and Death
sections.html:
Scripture

“But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15)

“Now the deeds of the flesh are obvious, which are: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, lustfulness, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these; of which I forewarn you, even as I also forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit God’s Kingdom.” (Galatians 5:19–21)

“For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:23)

Key Words

James 1:15 uses a vivid set of birth words. “Lust” is ἐπιθυμία (epithumia), literally “a strong craving directed at something”; “conceived” is συλλαβοῦσα (syllabousa), to become pregnant; “bears” and “produces” are τίκτει and ἀποκύει (tiktei / apokyei), verbs of giving birth.

Brothers and sisters, James is drawing a family tree in the delivery room: pride kindles lust, lust conceives, the pregnancy gives birth to sin, and sin, full grown, gives birth to death. Four generations under one roof, one unbroken line. This is no figurative exaggeration; this is the physiology of sin.

And notice the two words “drawn away” and “enticed.” “Drawn away,” ἐξέλκω (exelkō), is dragging prey out of its hiding place; “enticed,” δελεάζω (deleazō), is luring a fish onto the hook with bait. This is the language of hunting and fishing. Brothers and sisters, a fish isn’t fooled by the hook; it is fooled by the bait. What it sees is the bait; what it cannot see is the hook. Pride is dangerous precisely because it always comes wrapped in very attractive bait: I’m doing this for justice, I’m doing this on principle, I’m doing this for the good of the church.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture

Pride never stays in the heart; pride always grows into behaviour. Of the “deeds of the flesh” Paul lists in Galatians 5, the first few are bodily indulgence, but a whole string in the middle — hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies, envy — are all breakdowns in relationships. Brothers and sisters, count them: in the list as the Chinese Union Version gives it, eight out of fifteen are matters between people.

Why? Because pride must have someone to compare itself with. Pride isn’t simply liking yourself; pride is “I must be higher than others.” So wherever there is pride, there will be factions; and wherever there are factions, there will be quarrels. James 4:1 asked long ago: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?”

The Witness of History: Jeroboam

The Bible gives us a case study on the scale of a nation. After Solomon died, the people came to Rehoboam and asked him to lighten their labour. 1 Kings 12:8 says, “But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.” As a result ten tribes broke away, with Jeroboam as their king.

Once Jeroboam was king, he reasoned in his heart: “Now the kingdom will return to David’s house. If this people goes up to offer sacrifices in Yahweh’s house at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, even to Rehoboam king of Judah” (1 Kings 12:26–27). So he made two golden calves, setting one in Bethel and one in Dan; he appointed priests who were not Levites and fixed festivals of his own. 1 Kings 12:33 calls it “the month which he had devised of his own heart.”

Brothers and sisters, see this turning point clearly: to keep his own throne, Jeroboam changed the worship of God. That is pride in its most typical form — adjusting God’s affairs to suit my affairs. 1 Kings 14:16 gives the verdict: “because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he has sinned, and with which he has made Israel to sin.”

The consequences were more terrible still. The northern kingdom of Israel had nineteen kings beginning with Jeroboam, and of the eighteen who followed him the Bible passes almost the same verdict: they did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight and walked in the way of Jeroboam. A road opened by pride was walked for more than two hundred years, until in 722 BC the city of Samaria fell to Assyria and the northern kingdom came to an end (2 Kings 17:6–23).

One man’s pride can set the course of a nation for two hundred years. That is why the Bible says, “Before destruction the heart of man is proud” (Proverbs 18:12), and again, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). The higher the position, the greater the damage pride does.

Examples and Data

On 10 April 1912 the Titanic, then the largest liner in the world, sailed from Southampton in England. Press and public alike described her with a phrase that spread far and wide: “practically unsinkable.” Late on the night of 14 April she struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic; in the early hours of 15 April she sank, and more than 1,500 people died. Later inquiries found that her lifeboats could not hold everyone on board, and that although she had received repeated ice warnings before the collision, she had kept up a high speed.

There is also a physical reason icebergs are so deadly. Sea ice is slightly less dense than sea water, so usually only about a tenth of it floats above the surface; the other nine-tenths lie hidden beneath. Brothers and sisters, pride is just the same. The little bit of conceit you and I can see is often just the tenth above the water. The nine-tenths below — the heart that won’t admit it was wrong, the heart that must win, the heart that puts itself in God’s place — is the part that will truly tear the hull apart.

Physics also has its second law of thermodynamics: in an isolated system, entropy (disorder) only ever increases; it never decreases by itself. A room does not tidy itself; a cup of hot water does not get hotter on its own. Life is the same. A heart cut off from God and closed in on itself does not slowly get better by itself; it only moves step by step into deeper chaos. Pride is so frightening precisely because it turns a person into an isolated system.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 has a saying that captures this cycle perfectly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, think about the last argument in your home. Didn’t it start like this? He raised his voice a little, so you raised yours a little more; he ignored you, so you ignored him even more. Pride never exists on its own. Like an echo it provokes pride on the other side, until both are hurt and nothing at all is resolved. Both sides lose.

But the reverse is true as well. When one person softens first and says, “I was in the wrong just now,” the hard heart opposite often softens too. Humility inspires humility; both sides win. Romans 12:21 says, “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

321 also reminds us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. If the pride in our life goes unaddressed, our relationships will certainly suffer; and when relationships go wrong, however busy our ministry, we are only building on sand. Jeroboam turned the order completely upside down: first he grabbed at the work (keeping his throne), then he manipulated relationships (binding the people’s hearts with golden calves), and in the end he paid with his life. Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: 4. Humility Is the Way Out of Sin
sections.html:
Scripture

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.” (James 4:6–8)

“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” (James 4:10)

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29)

Key Words

“Resists” is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, what a sobering statement this is: God himself will draw up his ranks and stand opposite the proud. You may make an enemy of people, you may make an enemy of your circumstances, but whatever you do, do not let God array himself against you.

“Humble” is ταπεινός (tapeinos), originally “low, low-lying.” The New Testament has another word, ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosynē), literally “lowly-mindedness.” It is worth noting that in Greco-Roman culture this word was originally a term of contempt, the trait of slaves and the lowborn. It was the Christian faith that turned it into the highest of virtues — because the Son of God himself walked this road.

“Repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), combining “after, change” (meta) and “mind” (nous): a turning around of the mind. Brothers and sisters, please notice: repentance is not “feeling bad”; repentance is “turning.” 2 Corinthians 7:10 draws the distinction clearly: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.”

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Sin Is Not Fate but Choice

Here is the most liberating sentence in this lesson: sin is not caused by God, nor is it a fate we cannot resist; it is a choice of our free will.

Deuteronomy 30:19 says, “I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants.” Joshua 24:15 says, “But as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” Brothers and sisters, God never made human beings into machines without choice. God gave us free will precisely so that we could love him and obey him “willingly.”

Of course, we must also be honest about the other side of Scripture: in Adam, humanity has fallen under the power of sin (Romans 5:12), and our own willpower cannot save us. So the gospel does not say, “Try a bit harder and you’ll get better.” The gospel says, “He gives more grace.” The choice open to us is not to overcome sin by our own strength, but to choose surrender, letting the Lord who has already overcome reign as King within us. That is why the cure for sin is not self-reproach but repentance; not straining at self-restraint, but humble surrender.

Brothers and sisters, what is the difference between self-reproach and repentance? Self-reproach still has its focus on the self — “How could I be so awful?” In the end it is another form of pride: disappointment with myself for failing to reach the height I set for myself. Repentance has its focus on God — “Lord, I was wrong; I’ve come back.” Judas reproached himself and went and hanged himself; Peter repented, went out and wept bitterly, and later fed the Lord’s sheep. The same fall, a different direction, and a world of difference in the ending.

Illustrations and Examples

In Israel there are two bodies of water, both fed by the same river Jordan. To the north lies the Sea of Galilee: its water is alive, it teems with fish, and the towns on its shore, Capernaum and Bethsaida, bustle with life — most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place there. To the south lies the Dead Sea: its surface lies about 430 metres below sea level, the lowest point on the earth’s land surface, and its salinity is about 30 per cent, so no fish can live in it.

What makes the difference between them? The Sea of Galilee has an inflow and an outflow: the Jordan flows in from the north and out again to the south. The Dead Sea only receives and never gives: its water can leave only by evaporation, so the salt grows ever more concentrated.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: being low is not the same as being humble. The Dead Sea is the lowest of all, yet it is dead, because it only takes and never gives; it is closed in on itself. True humility is not running yourself down and then shutting the door. True humility is opening up — opening to God so that grace flows in, and opening to others so that grace flows out. John 7:38 says, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”

Another picture from everyday life: have you ever noticed that the fuller the ear of rice, the lower it bows its head? The empty ears stand bolt upright. This isn’t poetic fancy; it’s physics — the greater the weight, the greater the turning force, and the deeper the stalk bends. Brothers and sisters, spiritual life is the same. Those who truly have substance within keep their heads low; it is those who are empty inside who need to keep their heads held high.

Psychology and Sayings

June Price Tangney, professor of psychology at George Mason University in the United States, pointed out in a 2000 study in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology that humility is often misunderstood as self-deprecation, but that in psychological terms humility includes an accurate assessment of one’s abilities and limitations, openness about one’s mistakes, not making oneself the centre of attention, and an appreciation of the worth of others.

Brothers and sisters, this echoes the Bible exactly. Romans 12:3 says, “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” Humility doesn’t say, “I’m good for nothing.” Humility is “thinking reasonably” — no more and no less, standing honestly in the place God has arranged for me.

The church father Augustine is generally credited with saying that if you ask the way to the truth, the first thing is humility, the second is humility, and the third is still humility. The saying has been handed down for sixteen hundred years because it names one thing truly: every step deeper into the spiritual life has only one entrance, and that is going low.

Applying the 321 Vision

321’s most central saying is: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order of James 4:7: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” First submit to God, then resist the devil. Many people skip the first sentence and go straight to the second, and the more they resist, the more exhausted they become. Because resistance without surrender is itself another form of pride — it is me doing the fighting, not God.

This is exactly what 321 calls the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. When Jesus truly reigns as King in me, the “I” that wants to lift itself up naturally steps down from the throne. When the glory truly goes to Jesus, I no longer need to fight for my own pride.

And there is that reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. Proud people are always tired, because they must keep calculating, keep guarding themselves, keep maintaining an image. Humble people can rest, because the Lord says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Brothers and sisters, this is the way out.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message within the framework of 321, and you will see that it was one picture all along.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. When Eve wanted to be “like God,” Jesus “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7). The first Adam grasped; the last Adam let go. The pattern we are to learn is not grasping but letting go.

The Bible is my standard. Eve’s failure began with “Has God really said?” The moment people start correcting God’s word by their own feelings, the standard has changed hands. The world today offers a thousand explanations of sin; we have only one standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Galatians 5:16 says, “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” The way to deal with the lusts of the flesh is not to clench our teeth but to walk by the Spirit. This is what it means to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. The problem of sin is, in the end, a problem of the throne. Only one can sit on the throne. When I sit on it, sin has a foothold; when Jesus sits on it, sin loses its foothold.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Satan fell because he wanted glory for himself; humanity fell because it wanted glory for itself. Giving the glory back to Jesus is putting ourselves back in our originally intended position.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. What Jeroboam established was a system of his own — to secure himself, he was prepared to change even the worship of God. God’s system and man’s system differ in one thing only: who is at the centre.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the most important is the first — mindset. From “Sin was made by God; there’s nothing I can do” to “Sin is the result of pride, and I can choose humility.” Brothers and sisters, change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. When daily living changes, relationships change with it; and when relationships are right, ministry has a foundation.

The Priority of Relationships

First with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Proud people turn this exactly upside down — first they handle things, then they sort out people, then they soothe themselves, and only last of all do they grudgingly think of God. This morning, let’s put the order back the right way round.

A Shift in Perspective

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: no longer asking, “Why does God allow sin?” but asking, “What way out has God prepared for me?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: earthly logic is to climb upward; heavenly logic is to go down. The Lord says, “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10).

From the temporary to the eternal: everything pride fights over is very short-lived — winning an argument, saving face in a meeting. Nothing in eternity is won by fighting.

From the worldly to the godly: the worldly view values how much I have; the godly view values how much God gains.

The 920 Practice

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Brothers and sisters, set these nine graces side by side with the list of the deeds of the flesh we read a moment ago in Galatians 5:19–21: on one side the products of pride, on the other the fruit of the Spirit. Which will you bear today?

Pay special attention to “gentleness” and “self-control,” the two that pride fears most. Gentleness is not using your own strength to push people down; self-control is not letting your own desires be king. Once these two start to grow, pride can no longer keep its footing.

235 Relationships

235 reminds us: become a “2” — spiritual companions — with selfless people; establish the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Why do we need a spiritual companion? Because the greatest mark of pride is that it cannot see its own pride. You and I both need someone who can tell us the truth. Proverbs 27:17 says, “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” Brothers and sisters, no one fighting alone can deal with pride, because the very thing that must be dealt with is the “I” that thinks it doesn’t need anyone else.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s work them out one by one through the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: pray every day, “Lord, keep me from making myself the centre; help me to fix my eyes on you.”

Information: first let the truth into your head. You have heard it today — God did not create sin; sin is the result of pride. Please memorise James 4:6.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this sentence from your head into your heart. Ask the Lord to show you one concrete picture: at what moment this week was I making myself the centre?

Conviction: not just admitting, “That makes sense,” but saying, “This is addressed to me.”

Implementation: make this prayer the first thing you say when you open your eyes each morning. It needn’t be long — thirty seconds is enough — but do it every day.

Evaluation: before bed, take two minutes to look back — where was my focus today? On myself, on others, on my circumstances, or on Jesus?

Correction: if you find your focus has drifted, bring it back on the spot. Don’t wait until next week; don’t wait until the next meeting.

Repetition: forty days in a row. For a mindset to become life, it must be repeated; repetition is what turns it into instinct.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister, teach them this prayer, and remind each other.

Practice two: when you want to insist on your own way, stop first and ask, “Is this coming from pride, or from trust?”

Information: James 1:19 says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you hear this question in the three seconds before you’re about to explode.

Conviction: admit one thing — what I am insisting on is not necessarily the truth; very often it is only my pride and my face.

Implementation: decide on a specific action. When you feel the heat rise in your chest and your voice about to go up, take three deep breaths first and silently ask yourself the question.

Evaluation: once a week, take the chance to look back: how many times did I insist on my own way this week? How many of those turned out to be for the truth, and how many just to win?

Correction: if it was just to win, go back and apologise. You needn’t explain at length; “I had a bad attitude the other day — I’m sorry” is enough.

Repetition: don’t give up because you fail two or three times. The old self doesn’t die completely in one go.

Multiplication: share your failures and what you have learned in your small group. Your honesty will set others free to be honest.

Practice three: in relationships, learn to let go of “I have to be right” and choose “I am willing to be humble.”

Information: Philippians 2:3 says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to remind you by name — whose face comes to mind right now? The person you think of and immediately feel, “It’s obviously their fault.”

Conviction: believe one thing — relationships matter more than who is right; people matter more than tasks. Winning the argument and losing the relationship is the worst bargain there is.

Implementation: take the first step this week. A phone call, a message, a cup of coffee — any of these will do. The one who speaks first is not the one who loses; it is the one who is like the Lord.

Evaluation: after you have taken that step, note down what you really feel. Lighter, or more aggrieved? If more aggrieved, it shows I’m still seeking justice for myself.

Correction: bring that sense of grievance to the Lord and hand it over to him. 1 Peter 5:7 says, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.”

Repetition: bowing your head once is not humility; bowing your head as a habit is humility.

Multiplication: when God uses you to restore a relationship, tell that testimony. Humility inspires humility — and that is where both sides begin to win.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please take these two sentences home with you:

Pride takes us away from grace; humility brings us back to God.

Stop asking where sin comes from, and ask yourself: am I still holding on to “self”?

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have come a fair distance today. Let’s gather it up into a few sentences:

The starting point of sin is pride; the starting point of victory is humility. God did not create sin, nor did he create the fall. What God created was free will, so that we could choose him.

What enormous respect that is. God could easily have made a set of machines that never go wrong and kept the universe forever tidy. But he didn’t. He made children who can say “I will,” and in doing so he took the risk of hearing “I won’t.” And when we really did say “I won’t,” he did not destroy us. He sent his only Son, who walked a road exactly opposite to ours — we wanted to go up, he came down; we wanted to be king, he became a servant; we wanted to save our own lives, he gave up his.

Philippians 2:8–11 says, “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The highest place in the universe was won by walking the lowest road. And the Lord has already walked that road for us.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you.

First, admit it. Not admit, “I have a few small faults,” but admit, “There is a self inside me that wants to be king.” Call it by its name — pride.

Second, surrender. Let Jesus be King. Not his being your adviser, not his being your back-up plan, but his being King. Only one can sit on the throne. Please get up and let him sit down.

Third, choose. Today, in the place where it is hardest to bow your head, make one humble choice. A phone call, an apology, a moment of silence instead of self-defence.

May the selfless life grow up within us, and may revival begin in our hearts. For revival has never begun from the pulpit; revival begins from a heart willing to go low. May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)
“Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15)
practices: When you want to insist on your own way, stop first and ask
In relationships, learn to let go of “I have to be right” and choose “I am willing to be humble”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

I confess that sin is not something you made; it is the pride in my heart that has taken me far from you. I confess that I often want to be my own king, to control my own destiny, to act as I please. Lord, please forgive me.
Cleanse me and refine me with your precious blood, and teach me humility. Take me down from my own throne, and let Jesus reign as King in every corner of my life.

Lord, I am willing to let go of “I have to be right” and choose “I am willing to be humble.” I am willing to lay myself down, choose obedience, and live in your grace and light. Holy Spirit, guide me every day, so that my focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on others, not on my circumstances.
Let the selfless life grow up within me, and let revival begin in my heart. To you be all glory, praise and honour, for ever and ever.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Ecclesiastes 7:29 says, “Behold, I have only found this: that God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.” How have you answered the question, “If God is good, why is there sin in the world?” in the past? How has today’s message adjusted your view?

James 4:6–7 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Name one specific situation in which you are currently “insisting on your own way.” If you were to choose humility there, what first step could you take this week?
l073.title: Where Does Sin Come From?
l073.subtitle: Pride Is Where Sin Begins; Humility Is Where Victory Begins
l073.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

blog.title: God Did Not Make Sin

blocks.x: — It Began with an “I will”
Have you ever asked this question late at night: if God is good, why is there so much evil in the world? If God is almighty, why would he create a human being capable of sin?
The answer may not be what you think.
Sin is not a thing but a direction

Genesis 1:31 says: “God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.” Through the earlier days God says “good” again and again; only on the sixth day, when humankind has been made, does God say “very good”. He did not make a human being with a sinful nature, nor did he slip an item called “sin” onto the list of creation.

So where does sin come from? Think about darkness. You cannot buy a bucket of darkness or fill a bottle with it — darkness is simply the state of things when light is blocked. Sin is like that. God made no raw material for sin; sin is the moment a creature turns its face away from God.
Ecclesiastes 7:29 puts it even more plainly: “Behold, I have only found this: that God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.” God made a straight line; people bent it themselves.
Sin begins not with weakness but with pride
What did the serpent say to Eve? “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) What did the shining one say in his heart? “I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14)
Notice one thing: neither of them had a sinful nature to begin with. They did not sin because they were broken inside. They sinned because they chose to rise.

And humankind was made in the image of God from the start; humanity was already “like God”. Satan’s lie never offered something new. It tempted people to seize with their own hands what God had already given freely. Turning “receiving” into “grabbing”, turning a “son” into a “usurper” — that is the common pattern of every temptation.

Jesus took exactly the opposite road. He, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). One grasped; the other let go. Those two roads still lie before us today.
Humility is the only way out

Pride never stays in the heart. James 1:15 says: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; only when humility inspires humility do both sides win.

In Israel there are two bodies of water, both fed by the same river Jordan. The Sea of Galilee has an inflow and an outflow, and its water is alive; the Dead Sea only receives and never gives, its salinity is about 30 per cent, and no fish can live in it. Being low is not the same as being humble. True humility is not running yourself down and then shutting the door. True humility is opening up — opening to God so that grace flows in, and opening to others so that grace flows out.

So the cure for sin is not self-reproach but repentance; not straining at self-restraint, but humble surrender. The order of James 4:7 matters: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” First submit to God, then resist the devil. Resistance without surrender is itself another form of pride.

At home, at work and in the church, so much of our pain comes from one thing: leaving our originally intended position. The wife wants to be the head of her husband; parents want to be God to their children. Returning to our originally intended position means letting man be man and letting God be God.
The starting point of sin is pride; the starting point of victory is humility. God did not create sin. What God created was free will, so that we could choose him.
Today, what will you choose?
Reflection question: this week, what is the one thing where you keep insisting “I have to be right”? If you chose humility there, what is the first step you could take?

notes: Where Does Sin Come From?
Pride is where sin begins
Humility is where victory begins
“God resists the proud,
but gives grace to the humble.” James 4:6
• Greeting: brothers and sisters, good morning — today we face one of the deepest questions
• Key verse: James 4:6, the key sentence of the whole message
• Set the tone in one sentence: the starting point of sin is pride; the starting point of victory is humility
• Preview the four points: God did not make sin; pride is the root; the cycle of sin and death; humility is the way out
Introduction: Three Real Questions
If God is good, why is there sin?
Why make people who can sin?
I didn’t want to — why did I?
God didn’t make sin; it is pride’s fruit
• Three scenes: a mother outside a hospital ward, a young seeker, an older believer after a fall
• The three questions are really one: God’s character, the source of sin, my own helplessness
• Image: darkness is not a created substance, only the state of light being blocked
• In 321 language: the heart of sin is “the self-centred life”; the cure is “selflessness”
Key Verse and Background
James: the Lord’s brother, once unbelieving
Written to scattered, suffering Jewish believers
“But he gives more grace” James 4:6
Pride, fighting — but God gives more grace
• Author: James, the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19); John 7:5 says he did not believe at first
• He calls himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1) — a testimony of the self-centred life becoming selfless
• Readers: Jewish Christians scattered after Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1)
• Context: from James 4:1, fighting born of pleasures, to 4:6, “greater grace”, μείζονα χάριν
God Did Not Create Sin
“It was very good” Genesis 1:31
“God made man upright” Ecclesiastes 7:29
Darkness is not a created substance
Sin is the shadow when light is blocked
• Hebrew “very good”, טוֹב מְאֹד, the strongest form, used only after humankind was made on the sixth day
• James 1:13: God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one
• Greek “sin”, ἁμαρτία, originally means to miss the mark — the archer has aimed off
• The piano illustration: the tension is the maker’s gift; only when wrongly twisted does it go out of tune. Free will itself is very good
The Root of Sin Is Pride
“You will be like God” Genesis 3:5
“Like the Most High” Isaiah 14:14
No sinful nature, yet chose to rise
Sin begins not with weakness but pride
• The serpent’s three steps: unsettle God’s word, deny God’s word, replace God’s word
• Humankind was already made in God’s image; Satan tempted people to seize what God had given freely
• Contrast Philippians 2:6–8: Jesus did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself
• Note: the Bible never calls Satan an archangel; Ezekiel 28:14 calls him the anointed cherub who covers
Three Faces of Pride
Wanting total control of our destiny
Leaving God’s word to do as we please
Refusing to submit to God and authority
Self-centred: leaving; selfless: returning
• James 4:13–14: you are a vapour that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away
• Judges 21:25: there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes
• 1 Samuel 15:23: rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft
• Psychology: Svenson’s 1981 study — 93% rated their driving above the median
• 321: pride is leaving our originally intended position; humility is letting man be man and letting God be God
The Cycle of Sin and Death
“The lust, when it has conceived, bears sin.
The sin…produces death” James 1:15
Pride, lust, sin, death: one unbroken line
Pride provokes pride: both sides lose
• Greek: conceived, συλλαβοῦσα; produces, ἀποκύει — the language of the delivery room
• Drawn away, ἐξέλκω, is dragging out prey; enticed, δελεάζω, is luring a fish with bait — the fish sees the bait, not the hook
• Of the fifteen deeds of the flesh in Galatians 5:19–21, eight are broken relationships
• Everyday example: the echo of an argument — he gets louder, I get louder still, and both sides lose
The Warning of Jeroboam
To keep his throne, he changed worship
“Made Israel to sin” 1 Kings 14:16
Eighteen kings followed the same road
722 BC: the northern kingdom fell
• 1 Kings 12:26–27: he said in his heart, now the kingdom will return to David’s house
• He made two golden calves for Bethel and Dan, appointed non-Levite priests and fixed his own festivals
• The northern kingdom had nineteen kings; the eighteen after him all walked in the way of Jeroboam
• Proverbs 16:18: pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall
• Titanic sank in 1912, and nine-tenths of an iceberg lies hidden below the surface — so does pride
Humility: The Way Out of Sin
“God resists the proud,
but gives grace to the humble” James 4:6
First submit to God, then resist the devil
Not self-reproach, but repentance and surrender
• “Resists”, ἀντιτάσσομαι, is a military term: to draw up in battle array against
• The order of James 4:7: first submit to God, then resist the devil; resistance without surrender is another form of pride
• Self-reproach versus repentance: Judas reproached himself and hanged himself; Peter repented and wept bitterly
• The Sea of Galilee flows in and out, so it is alive; the Dead Sea only receives, its salinity about 30%
• Matthew 11:29: I am gentle and humble in heart… and you will find rest for your souls
Putting It into Practice
Daily: keep me from making myself the centre
Before insisting, stop and ask
Let go of “I must be right”; choose humility
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
• Practice 1: the first prayer of the morning, thirty seconds, forty days in a row
• Practice 2: when your chest grows hot, take three deep breaths and ask: is this pride or trust?
• Practice 3: take the first step this week — a phone call, an apology
• The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
• A gentle reminder: pride takes us away from grace; humility brings us back to God
Closing and Call
Pride is where sin begins
Humility is where victory begins
Admit, surrender, choose humility
Let Jesus be King; all glory to Jesus
• God did not make sin; what God made was free will, so that we could choose him
• Philippians 2:8–11: he humbled himself and became obedient, therefore God highly exalted him
• Three invitations: admit the self within that wants to be king, surrender and let Jesus be King, make one humble choice today
• Revival does not begin from the pulpit but from a heart willing to go low
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, take away my pride
Teach me humility and obedience
May the selfless life grow in me
May revival begin in my heart
• Lead the congregation to pray aloud together, slowly and warmly
• Prayer points: confess pride, ask the Lord to forgive and cleanse, let Jesus reign on the throne
• Blessing: may the grace and peace of the Lord be with all the brothers and sisters
• Close with “May all the glory go to Jesus. Amen.”

Pride, lust, sin, death
Four generations, one unbroken line
• Greek: conceived, συλλαβοῦσα; produces, ἀποκύει — the language of the delivery room

Rivalries, divisions, heresies, envy

• The northern kingdom had nineteen kings; the eighteen after him all walked in the way of Jeroboam (2 Kings 17:6–23)

but gives grace to the humble” James 4:6

• James 4:8: draw near to God, and he will draw near to you
• 321: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan

God gave us free will
so we could choose obedience willingly
“Therefore choose life” Deuteronomy 30:19

• Deuteronomy 30:19: I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life

• Be honest: we cannot save ourselves (Romans 5:12), so the gospel is “he gives more grace”

It is standing honestly where God placed you
