script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 74 of Morning Devotion 321, entitled “Where Does Pride Come From?”

Our key verses are James 1:14–15: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.”
Pride doesn’t appear out of nowhere. It has a root, and that root is sinful desire.
Brothers and sisters, first I’d like you to remember something: when was the last time you said “I want” in your heart?

Perhaps it was last night, scrolling on your phone, when you saw someone’s holiday photos and the words “I want that too” rose up in your heart. Perhaps it was when a colleague was promoted and the thought flashed through your mind, “That should have been me.”
We rarely admit that we are proud, because we think pride looks like swagger. But the pride the Bible speaks of is often quiet.
When a tree grows crooked and you prune the branch, next year it grows back, because the root is still there. Pride is the same, so today we are going to dig down to the root.
The lesson says it clearly: pride is not an inborn personality trait but a wrong choice of the free will.
That is bad news, and it is also good news. The bad news is that we have no excuse. The good news is that if it is a choice, we can choose again.
The author of James is generally held to be James, the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh. He doesn’t call himself the Lord’s brother, only a servant. That in itself is a lesson in humility.
He was writing to Jewish Christians scattered by persecution, who had lost their homes and their property.
Brothers and sisters, in such circumstances, what are people most likely to say? Most likely, “I want.”
But James tells them: the real danger is not the swords of Roman soldiers but that force of “I want” inside you.
First, the root of pride is believing Satan’s lie.
The serpent said to Eve: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)
Notice that Satan didn’t say, “God doesn’t exist.” What he said was, “You will be like God.” He doesn’t ask people to deny God; he asks people to replace God.

This is exactly what 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.
Satan didn’t ask Eve to do a bad thing. He asked Eve to sit in a seat that wasn’t hers.

Brothers and sisters, to this day Satan still works the same way. He will never tell us outright, “Go and sin.” He will say, “You deserve more.” He will say, “You should satisfy yourself.” He will say, “If you don’t look out for yourself, who will?”
These words sound so reasonable. But they all amplify one voice — the voice of “self”.
The bait on the hook is real; the fish really does get to eat. The problem isn’t the bait. The problem is the hook hidden inside it.
So the lesson says: pride does not start with outward behaviour; it starts at the moment the heart begins to believe the lie.
Second, the driving force of pride is the push of sinful desire.
James 1:14 says: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.”
“Drawn away” in the original is a hunting term — luring prey out of its den. “Enticed” in the original is a fishing term — luring a fish onto the hook with sweet-smelling bait.
Brothers and sisters, notice: the subject of both actions is not Satan but “his own lust”.
Satan certainly lays bait, but if there were no appetite in us, the bait could not catch us.
The lie is the match; desire is the firewood.

1 John 2:16 lists three kinds of desire: the lust of the flesh, wanting sensual gratification; the lust of the eyes, wanting to possess more; and the pride of life, wanting other people’s approval and applause.
The senses, possessions, applause. You may escape one of them, but it is hard to escape all three at once.
And Satan can make people fall into it with a single sentence: “I don’t have it; I want it.”

I don’t have money; I want more — and it turns into greed and anxiety. I don’t have status; I want to be noticed — and it turns into comparison and rivalry. I don’t have love; I want others to satisfy me — and it turns into lust and control.
And there is a deeper lie still: “I have it, and I still want more.”
Brothers and sisters, the first lie deceives the poor; the second deceives the rich.
The Bible said it long ago: “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver.” (Ecclesiastes 5:10)

Psychology confirms this too. In 1978 Brickman and his colleagues studied major lottery winners and found that the happiness they felt in everyday life was no greater than that of ordinary people. Researchers call this hedonic adaptation — like a treadmill: we run forward with all our might, but the track is moving backwards at the same time.
We think a little more will make us happy, but instead we end up bound by “more”.
Third, the price of pride is the loss of freedom and blessing.
Pride seems to make people gain, but in reality it makes them lose everything; it turns people from the one in control into the one being controlled.
Those who want money become slaves of money. Those who want power become prisoners of power. Those who want lust become puppets of desire.
Paul says: “For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption.” (Galatians 6:8)
Isaiah 14 records the fallen one saying “I will” five times. And the result? Brought down to Sheol.
But our Lord Jesus, in the garden of Gethsemane, said just one sentence: “Not what I desire, but what you desire.” And the result was salvation for all humanity.
Brothers and sisters, Jesus is my role model.
So today there are three practices.
First, whenever “I want” rises up in your heart, stop and ask: is this from God, or from sinful desire? Give yourself three seconds.
Second, spend a few minutes every day thanking God for the grace he has already given you, replacing “I still want” with “I already have”.
Third, when you want to grab hold of something, choose to let go, and let God satisfy you. The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself.” (Matthew 16:24)
Letting go is not falling; letting go is landing in his hands.
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s conclusion puts it so well: pride begins with “I want”; humility begins with “Lord, your will be done.”
Behind every choice lies a spiritual battle.
The Bible says: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7)
Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can we resist the devil.
Let us no longer believe the lie, no longer obey sinful desire, but let the selfless life replace the pride of “I want”.
Finally, let’s declare together:

Lord, I will no longer believe Satan’s lies; I will no longer let “I want” define my life; for you have given me all I need; you are my greatest satisfaction. Keep me far from pride, living in humility and thanksgiving.
Satan’s lie is: “I don’t have it; I want it.” God’s truth is: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1)
David doesn’t say, “I have everything.” He says, “I shall lack nothing.” A warehouse can be emptied; the shepherd will not walk away.
May Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory go to Jesus. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to Lesson 74 of Morning Devotion 321, entitled “Where Does Pride Come From?”

Our key verses are James 1:14–15: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.”
The lesson states the answer right at the start: pride does not appear out of nowhere. It has a root — sinful desire.
Today we will walk three steps: the root, the driving force, and the price.
Brothers and sisters, first I’d like you to remember something: when was the last time you said to yourself, deep down, “I want”?

Perhaps it was last night, scrolling on your phone, when you saw someone’s holiday photos and the words “I want that too” rose up in your heart. Perhaps it was when a colleague was promoted and the thought flashed through your mind, “That should have been me.” Perhaps someone else was praised, and you smiled on the outside while a small thorn pricked you inside.
We rarely admit that we are proud, because we think pride looks like swagger.
But the pride the Bible speaks of is often quiet, reasonable — even perfectly sensible.
The lesson says something of great importance: pride is not an inborn personality trait but a wrong choice of the free will.
We often say, “I’m just a competitive sort of person — it’s my personality.” We treat pride as a factory setting that cannot be changed.
But the Bible says pride is a choice — pride comes into being at the moment we choose to obey sinful desire and choose to believe a lie.
The bad news is: we have no excuse. The good news is: if it is a choice, we can choose again.
This is exactly the starting point of the 321 fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes.
Let’s first set out the background. Today’s message stands on three books.
Genesis was written by Moses, for the Israelites walking through the wilderness, who said “I want” again and again.

The author of James is generally held to be James, the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh. He could easily have said, “I am the Lord’s brother,” but he called himself only a servant. The letter was written around AD 45 to 50, to Jewish Christians scattered by persecution.
1 John was written by the apostle John late in life, in Ephesus.

Brothers and sisters, more than fifteen hundred years lie between these three books, yet they point to the same source of disease. Humanity changed its tools countless times; the human heart did not change even once.
Our first point: the root of pride is believing Satan’s lie.
The Bible says: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field.” (Genesis 3:1)
In Hebrew the word “subtle” can also be translated “prudent”. Satan’s attacks never come baring teeth and claws; he is reasonable.
Notice his first words. He doesn’t say, “Go and eat.” He says: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
His first words are not a command but a question. First he plants a question mark in the human heart.
Brothers and sisters, Satan never starts with behaviour; he starts with mindset.
Next the serpent said: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)
This is the first lie in human history. At its heart is what the lesson points out: “You don’t need God; you can rely on yourself.”
Notice that Satan didn’t say, “God doesn’t exist.” What he said was, “You will be like God.”
He doesn’t ask people to deny God; he asks people to replace God.
In the original, “knowing good and evil” is not just knowing information; it carries the sense of deciding and controlling.
This is exactly what 321 calls pride — leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place.
Satan didn’t ask Eve to do a bad thing. He asked Eve to sit in a seat that wasn’t hers.
The Bible goes on: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise…” (Genesis 3:6)
Good for food — the lust of the flesh. A delight to the eyes — the lust of the eyes. To be desired to make one wise — the pride of life.
Brothers and sisters, Genesis 3:6 and 1 John 2:16, fifteen hundred years apart, are the same list.
Eve wanted to decide for herself what was right and what was wrong, and that was the beginning of humanity’s fall.
To this day Satan still works the same way. He will never tell us outright, “Go and sin.”
He will say, “You deserve more.” He will say, “You should satisfy yourself.” He will say, “If you don’t look out for yourself, who will?”
The first is in advertisements, the second in feel-good self-help, and the third on the night you feel most wronged.
These words sound very reasonable, but they all amplify the voice of “self”.
The bait on the hook is real; the fish really does get to eat. The problem isn’t the bait. The problem is the hook hidden inside it.
So the lesson says: pride does not start with outward behaviour; it starts at the moment the heart begins to believe the lie.
Our second point: the driving force of pride is the push of sinful desire.
James 1:14 says: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.”
Two vivid Greek verbs are hidden here. “Drawn away” is a hunting term — luring prey out of its den; “enticed” is a fishing term whose root is “bait”.
Brothers and sisters, notice: the subject of both actions is not Satan but “his own lust”.
James blocks both roads of shifting the blame: we can’t blame God, and we can’t blame it all on the devil.
The Lord Jesus said: “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30)
The lie is the match; desire is the firewood.
James goes on: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.”
This is a very clear production line: desire, conception, sin born, death born.
Desire in itself is not yet sin. But if we keep it in our heart and talk with it, it conceives. And what has been conceived will surely be born.

Brothers and sisters, this is a frightening reminder and also one full of hope. Frightening because no sin appears from nowhere; full of hope because, if there is a time of pregnancy, there is time to turn back.
1 John 2:16 says: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.”
The lust of the flesh, wanting sensual gratification. The lust of the eyes, wanting to possess more. The pride of life, wanting other people’s approval and applause.
“The pride of life” in the original means boasting, showing off what one has. It is not only feeling inwardly that I am impressive; it is making sure others know I am impressive.
The senses, possessions, applause — you may escape one of them, but it is hard to escape all three at once.
Satan can make people fall into it with a single sentence: “I don’t have it; I want it.”

I don’t have money; I want more — and it turns into greed and anxiety. I don’t have status; I want to be noticed — and it turns into comparison and rivalry. I don’t have love; I want others to satisfy me — and it turns into lust and control.
The lesson also points out another, deeper lie: “I have it, and I still want more.”
Brothers and sisters, the first lie deceives the poor; the second deceives the rich.
Rockefeller is commonly said to have been asked how much money is enough, and to have answered, “Just a little bit more.”
The Bible said it long ago: “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver.” (Ecclesiastes 5:10)
Paul also says that some, in their greed, have pierced themselves through with many sorrows. No one else pierced them; they pierced themselves.
On this point psychology has produced consistent findings.

In 1978 Brickman and two colleagues published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: some time after their win, major lottery winners felt no significantly greater happiness in everyday life than ordinary people.
Researchers call this “hedonic adaptation”, later often called “the hedonic treadmill” — we run forward with all our might, but the track is moving backwards at the same time.
Psychology can only tell us that the treadmill exists; it cannot tell us how to get off it. The Bible can.
Paul says: “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.” (Philippians 4:11)
Contentment is not a personality trait; contentment is learned.
Our third point: the price of pride is the loss of freedom and blessing.
The lesson says: pride seems to make people gain, but in reality it makes them lose everything; it turns people from the one in control into the one being controlled.
Satan’s promise was “You will be like God” — you will have more power, more freedom. And the result? After eating the fruit, people saw they were naked, began to hide, and began to shift the blame.
Paul says: “You are the servants of whomever you obey.” (Romans 6:16) The Lord Jesus says it even more directly: “Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.” (John 8:34)
Brothers and sisters, people are not choosing between being a slave and not being a slave; they are choosing whose slave to be.
The lesson lists three chains: those who want money become slaves of money, those who want power become prisoners of power, those who want lust become puppets of desire.

Everything addictive shares one feature, called tolerance. The first time, a little is enough; later it takes more and more; in the end it is used only to stop the discomfort. It begins with pleasure and ends with painkilling.
Augustine said: lust indulged becomes habit, and habit not resisted becomes necessity. He also said: our heart is restless until it rests in you.
In Mere Christianity C. S. Lewis says that pride is essentially competitive: it gets no pleasure out of having something, only out of having more of it than the next person.
So pride is bound to make people miserable. Because there will always be someone in the world better than me.

There is one passage in the Bible that shows the end of “I want” more clearly than any other: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)
Count them: how many times does he say “I will”? Five. And the next verse says: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol.”
Solomon said: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)
Paul also warns: “For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption.” (Galatians 6:8)
But our Lord Jesus, in the garden of Gethsemane, said: “Not what I desire, but what you desire.”
Satan said “I will” five times and fell to Sheol; the Lord Jesus said once, “not what I desire,” and saved all humanity.
Brothers and sisters, Jesus is my role model.
Now we come to our practices for daily living.
Practice one: whenever “I want” rises up in your heart, stop and ask yourself, “Is this from God, or from sinful desire?”

This is a pause-button practice. Give yourself three seconds — don’t decide, don’t place the order, don’t answer back. Before bed, evaluate: how many times did I press the pause button today? Then correct: identify the times when you are most likely to give way, and set up your defences in advance.
Practice two: thank God every day for the grace he has already given you, replacing “I still want” with “I already have”.
The best way to drive out darkness is not to fight the darkness but to switch on the light.
David says: “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits.” (Psalm 103:2) He is giving orders to his own soul.
In 2003 research by Emmons and McCullough found that people who wrote down five things each week they were grateful for rated their lives more positively and complained of fewer physical symptoms.
Practice three: when you want to grab hold of something, choose to let go, and let God satisfy you.
The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Denying yourself is selflessness. And denying of self always comes down to something concrete: letting go of a conversation you’ve been determined to win, letting go of a position you’ve always wanted, letting go of a person you’ve been controlling with your emotions, letting go of that app on your phone you know you shouldn’t open again.
Hebrews says: “Be content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.’” (Hebrews 13:5)
Brothers and sisters, I can be content not because what I have is enough, but because the One who has me is good enough.
Letting go is not falling; letting go is landing in his hands.
Let’s take what we have seen today and set it within the framework of 321.
Jesus is my role model: in Gethsemane he showed us “not what I desire”.
The Bible is my standard: without a standard, I will take my feelings as my standard, and feelings always stand on the side of sinful desire.
The Holy Spirit is my guide: what overcomes the flesh is not flesh trying harder, but the Holy Spirit.
The Two Core Values are let Jesus be King and let Jesus receive all the glory. A heart has only one throne: if Jesus is not sitting on it, I am.
The Goal is to establish God’s system. John says: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)

The 920 practice: before every “2”, live the selfless life and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit — the last of which is self-control. And 235 reminds us that the worst thing in dealing with pride is to fight alone. Pride grows fastest in the dark; in the light it won’t survive three days.
Brothers and sisters, today we have walked three steps. The root lies in our mindset, the driving force in our life, and the price shows itself in our daily living.
The lesson’s conclusion says: pride begins with “I want”; humility begins with “Lord, your will be done.”
Behind every choice lies a spiritual battle. Every thought is a vote — a vote for myself as king, or a vote for Jesus as King.
The Bible says: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) First submit to God, and only then can we resist the devil.

I want to issue three calls. First, if there is an “I want” that keeps coming back in your heart, bring it to the Lord today. Second, if you have been bound by something for a long time — so long that you think that’s who you are — that is not who you are; the Lord Jesus said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” Third, if you feel you’re doing fine, with no real problems, please be especially careful, because that is exactly where pride most loves to hide.
Finally, let’s declare together:

Lord, I will no longer believe Satan’s lies; I will no longer let “I want” define my life; for you have given me all I need; you are my greatest satisfaction. Keep me far from pride, living in humility and thanksgiving.
Satan’s lie is: “I don’t have it; I want it.” God’s truth is: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1)
David doesn’t say, “I have everything.” He says, “I shall lack nothing.” A warehouse can be emptied; the shepherd will not walk away.

Let us pray. Dear Heavenly Father, forgive us for setting you aside and sitting on the throne ourselves. Holy Spirit, shine into every corner of our hearts, so that we see the thoughts that are already conceiving, and hand them over to you before they give birth to sin. Heal our discontent, and help us see that what we lack is not things, but you.
Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Hand That Wouldn’t Let Go of the Peanuts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today let’s think together about something very small that nevertheless decides whether our whole life is lived in freedom or in bondage — when, at last, we’re willing to open our hands.

Let me begin with an old, much-told story. A man sets out to catch a monkey. He uses no net and no gun — just a wooden box with a very narrow opening and a handful of peanuts inside. The monkey reaches in and grabs a fistful of peanuts, but a fist full of peanuts is bigger than the opening, and no matter how it pulls, it can’t get its hand out. The hunter walks up; the monkey shrieks in panic and tugs with all its might, yet it simply will not let go. It isn’t the box that has trapped it. It’s trapped by its own hand — the moment it lets go of those peanuts, it’s free to leave.

Brothers and sisters, we are so often just like that. What really traps us is seldom our circumstances; far more often it’s that hand of ours that refuses to open. What holds us captive is not what we lack, but what we can’t bear to give up.

In the last lesson we saw that pride springs from Satan’s lies and from human desire. Satan keeps whispering two sentences into people’s ears: “I don’t have it — I want it.” And once they have it, he switches to another: “I have it — and I want more.” Those two sentences push people into a cycle that never stops — discontent, wanting, getting, discontent again, wanting again. That cycle has no terminus. There’s only ever a next stop.

But our Lord Jesus walked the exact opposite road. He was not mastered by the lie of “I want.” What he chose was “I don’t want.” This is the principle of humility, and it’s the secret of overcoming pride.

Psychology has looked closely at this hand that won’t let go. In 1990, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler published the famous “mug experiment” in the “Journal of Political Economy.” They gave a coffee mug at random to half the participants and then let the two groups trade freely. The result: the people who had been given a mug asked, on average, more than twice what those without a mug were willing to pay. The very same mug meant nothing to me yesterday, yet today, simply because it is “mine,” its value has doubled. This is what’s called the “endowment effect.”

Brothers and sisters, the moment we hang the label “mine” on something, its price changes — and so does our heart. The thing hasn’t grown heavier. We’ve just started gripping it tighter.

So in today’s lesson we’ll follow the text and walk, step by step, along four stretches of road. First, the role model of Jesus — “I have it, but I don’t want it.” Second, Satan’s principle — “I want,” the mindset of possessing. Third, desire is the entry point of pride — a small desire, a big breach. Fourth, the way to overcome pride — the choice of humility.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter of Joy Sent from Prison
1. Author, Date and Recipients
sections.html:
The theme passage of this lesson comes from Philippians chapter 2. Its author is the apostle Paul. It’s generally held that the letter was written between AD 60 and 62, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome. A man in chains wrote a letter in which “joy” and “rejoice” appear more than a dozen times. Brothers and sisters, that in itself is a sermon: freedom isn’t found in our circumstances; freedom is found in a heart that no longer grasps for itself.

The church that received it, in Philippi, was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). Philippi was a Roman colony, home to many retired soldiers; its residents held Roman citizenship, and the city was intensely class-conscious — everyone cared about title, status and honour. To people like these, Paul wrote: have the same mind that was in Christ Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. The Context: A Small Crack in a Church
sections.html:
Why does Paul insert this most exalted passage about Christ just here? Because a small crack had appeared in the church at Philippi. In chapter 4 Paul names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.” (Philippians 4:2) Two co-workers were at odds. He also urges them: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3-4)

Brothers and sisters, notice the word “conceit,” which the Chinese Union Version renders “coveting empty glory.” The Greek is κενοδοξία (kenodoxia), formed from “empty” (kenos) and “glory” (doxa) — literally “empty glory.” People fight and scramble, and what they end up clutching is so often an empty shell. And right after this, Paul uses the same root to describe the Lord: “emptied himself” — in Greek ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), “to pour oneself out until empty.”

People strain with everything they have to fill themselves with “empty glory,” while the Lord willingly “emptied” himself. One single root nails down the message of the whole letter: a church’s problem isn’t its structures; it’s a question of who is willing to empty themselves first.

sections.heading: 3. The Theme Passage, Phrase by Phrase
sections.html:
“Existing in the form of God” — the Greek for “form” is μορφή (morphē). It doesn’t mean outward appearance; it means the true expression of an inner essence. Jesus isn’t merely like God. He is God.

“Didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped” — the Greek for “a thing to be grasped” is ἁρπαγμός (harpagmos), meaning “a prize of war held tight and never released.” Jesus’ equality with God was his by right, not something he had seized; and precisely because it wasn’t seized, he had no need to cling to it. Brothers and sisters, there’s a very deep truth here: the more truly you possess something, the less you need to clutch it; the more insecure a person is, the tighter they grip.

“But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” — the Greek for “servant” is δοῦλος (doulos), a person with no sovereignty of their own at all. He didn’t lose his divinity; he added the identity of a servant. He didn’t become less; he laid himself down.

“He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” — in the Roman world, the cross was a punishment reserved for slaves and rebels. Those people in Philippi who prided themselves on their Roman citizenship must have been shaken to hear these words: the direction we strain so hard to climb is the very direction our Lord went down, all the way down.

This is the key to the lesson. Satan’s route runs upward: I want, I want, I want. Jesus’ route runs downward: emptying himself, humbling himself, obeying, even to death. And God’s response is: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” (Philippians 2:9)

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Role Model of Jesus — “I Have It, but I Don’t Want It”
sections.html:
1. He Already Had Everything

First we need to see one thing clearly: when Jesus said “I don’t want it,” it wasn’t because he didn’t have it. He is the One who possesses all things. “All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.” (John 1:3) All the glory and authority of heaven were already his.

That is exactly why his “I don’t want it” carries such weight. When someone who has nothing says “I don’t want it,” it may be nothing more than resignation. When someone who has everything says “I don’t want it,” that is true denying of self. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.” (2 Corinthians 8:9)

2. The First Showdown in the Wilderness

When the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, Satan played his biggest card: “Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and their glory. He said to him, ‘I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.’ Then Jesus said to him, ‘Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.”’” (Matthew 4:8-10)

Brothers and sisters, look closely at this deal: what Satan offered was “possession,” and the price he demanded was “worship.” He never tells people outright to worship him; he just keeps whispering in their ear, “You could have it.” The Lord’s answer was absolutely decisive. It wasn’t that he lacked the power to gain the kingdoms of the world; it was that he refused to gain them Satan’s way.

This is the first layer of “I have it, but I don’t want it”: I refuse to use methods that don’t fit God’s heart to get even what is rightly meant to be mine.

3. The Final Time, in Gethsemane

But the deepest “I have it, but I don’t want it” came in the Garden of Gethsemane. “He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’” (Matthew 26:39)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord didn’t pretend not to be in anguish. He said, “Let this cup pass away from me” — that was a real struggle. But then he said, “Not what I desire, but what you desire.” Denying of self doesn’t mean feeling nothing. Denying of self means handing over the sovereignty even while you feel it all.

4. Children Are a Blessing, Not a Possession

Let me be clear first: “I don’t want it” is not a denial of blessing, still less a gloomy rejection of life. What it deals with is the heart that rewrites God’s grace into “my property, my pride.” The text gives an example very close to home: our children. “Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.” (Psalm 127:3) Children are entrusted to us by God; they are a blessing. But the moment we treat our children as “my property, my pride, my face,” the trouble begins.

Without realising it, we start treating our child’s grades as our own report card and our child’s career as our own business card. So love turns into control, and care turns into pressure; what the child feels is not being loved, but being graded.

Scripture shows us two parents who did the opposite. Hannah prayed for years before she received Samuel, and as soon as he was weaned she brought him to Shiloh: “I prayed for this child, and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I have also given him to Yahweh. As long as he lives he is given to Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 1:27-28) Abraham took Isaac up Mount Moriah, and God said: “For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” (Genesis 22:12)

Brothers and sisters, neither of them failed to love their child. They simply knew all too well whose child it was. Those who let go are the ones who gain; those who cling are the ones who lose. It’s the same with marriage, with ministry, with wealth and career — the moment we want to “possess,” the struggle begins; the moment we’re willing to “let go” and let Jesus take over, everything finds its order again.

5. Two Convictions That Overcome

The text gives us one very powerful sentence: “Whether I have it or not, I can still not want it.” There are two practices here —

“I don’t have it, and I don’t want it” — this is contentment. “But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.” (1 Timothy 6:6-8)

“I have it, but I don’t want it” — this is denying of self. “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Once we’ve learned both, Satan’s deceptions lose their power. For every bait he uses hangs either on “you don’t have it” or on “you could have more.” A person who neither fears going without nor craves having more gives him nowhere to set his hook.

6. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is that hand clutching the peanuts; selflessness is the moment we willingly let go. And let me stress this: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Satan’s Principle — “I Want”: The Mindset of Possessing
sections.html:
1. Five Times “I Will”

“I want” is the language of pride and the seed of desire. Its earliest and clearest appearance came at the moment the archangel fell: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13-14)

Brothers and sisters, count them: in just two verses, five times “I will.” Satan’s fall didn’t begin with some great sin; it began with “I want.” The 321 vision puts it precisely: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Then in Eden the same script was handed to humanity, word for word: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate.” (Genesis 3:6) “Good for food” is the lust of the flesh; “a delight to the eyes” is the lust of the eyes; “to make one wise” is the pride of life. John sums up these three in exactly the same way: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

2. Want to Possess, and You’ll Be Bound by What You Possess

The text puts it with great insight: “I want” drives people to pursue possessions, and in the end they are bound by the very things they possess.

Want money, and money will control you. Want a reputation, and you’ll be tied up by other people’s opinions. Want relationships, and you’ll be held hostage by your feelings.

Brothers and sisters, someone who cares about money sees their face fall every time the stock market falls; someone who cares about their reputation can lose a whole night’s sleep over a single online comment. How clearly the Lord said it: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

3. Why “Wanting” Never Stops

Neuroscience offers a piercing piece of corroboration here. After years of research, Professors Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson of the University of Michigan proposed that “wanting” and “liking” in the brain are two different systems, and that dopamine mainly drives “wanting,” not “liking.” In other words, the brain can crave something intensely and then, once it gets it, not be all that happy.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that exactly what “I want” looks like? While we’re chasing it, our heart races; once we’ve got it, the thrill lasts three days. After three days, our eyes start searching for the next target.

Psychology also has a famous observation called “hedonic adaptation.” In 1978, Philip Brickman and his colleagues published a study in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” comparing big lottery winners with ordinary people. They found that the happiness of winning fell away quickly, and the winners’ everyday happiness was not much higher than that of the control group. In 2010, Kahneman and Angus Deaton published research in the “Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences” showing that higher income does improve day-to-day emotional well-being, but beyond a certain level the gains clearly level off.

Three thousand years ago Solomon had already said: “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 5:10) What decades of scientific research have concluded, Scripture said in a single sentence.

4. Money as an Example

The text uses money as a particular example: if we want to possess it, money will rule us; but if in our hearts we “don’t want to possess,” money can’t bind us. Such people are free to give generously and use their wealth to advance God’s kingdom, rather than being held captive by it.

Paul’s words deserve to be read slowly, word by word: “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.” (1 Timothy 6:9-10)

Notice that Scripture doesn’t say “money is the root of evil”; it says “the love of money” is. The problem isn’t in our wallet; it’s in our heart. Money in our hand is a tool; money in our heart is a master.

The eighteenth-century evangelist John Wesley left us three sentences in his sermon “The Use of Money”: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can. As his own income grew, his standard of living stayed the same, and he gave away all the rest. In the nineteenth century, George Müller (1805–1898) of Bristol in England cared for more than ten thousand orphans in his lifetime, yet resolved never to ask anyone for money — he asked only God, in prayer. The man who didn’t cling to money became a blessing to countless children.

Psychology confirms this path too. In 2008, Elizabeth Dunn, Michael Norton and their colleagues published a study in the journal “Science”: people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent the same amount on themselves. Once again the Lord Jesus’ words prove true: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35)

5. Applying the 321 Vision

Brothers and sisters, behind “I want” and “I don’t want” lie two different perspectives. The 321 vision says we must shift from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Seen from an earthly, temporary perspective, letting go is a loss. Seen from a heavenly, eternal perspective, letting go is storing things in the safest place there is. “But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:20-21)

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Desire Is the Entry Point of Pride — A Small Desire, a Big Breach
sections.html:
1. The Production Line of Sin

Scripture describes how sin comes into being almost like a production line: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14-15)

Brothers and sisters, notice the four stages: desire, conception, sin, death. Not one step happens suddenly; at every step there’s a chance to call a halt. Sin doesn’t appear overnight. Sin is fed until it grows up.

“Drawn away” and “enticed” are both fishing terms in Greek: “drawn away” (ἐξέλκω) is luring a fish out of its hiding place, and “enticed” (δελεάζω) is tricking it onto the hook with bait. Brothers and sisters, Satan never fishes with a bare hook; there’s always something on it that we genuinely want.

2. Little Foxes and Small Breaches

Pride doesn’t necessarily begin with big things; more often it slips in through “a small desire.” That little bit of “wanting,” that faint trace of “resentment,” can become Satan’s breakthrough point.

“Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom.” (Song of Songs 2:15) Brothers and sisters, Scripture doesn’t say lions ruin the vineyard; it says little foxes do. When a lion comes, everyone runs; when a little fox comes, nobody pays any attention. Yet when the vines are in blossom, the damage a little fox does is deadly.

Paul gives the same warning: “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil.” (Ephesians 4:26-27) The Greek for “place” is τόπος (topos) — “a spot, a space.” The devil doesn’t need us to throw the whole door open. All he needs is a crack.

3. Judas: A Mirror

He had been a disciple, chosen personally by Jesus (Mark 3:19), the one among the Twelve who kept the money. John honestly records his problem: “Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.” (John 12:6)

Brothers and sisters, notice: this wasn’t one massive embezzlement. He “used to steal what was put into it.” A little at a time. And every time, he could convince himself: this is for the Lord’s work too; I give so much; taking a little isn’t going too far. That’s exactly how a small desire grows up.

Then that “thought” came in: “During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him.” (John 13:2) Brothers and sisters, notice the order — first the desire for money had been stored inside him for a long time; only later did the devil put in a specific intention. The breach was one he opened himself; the enemy merely walked in.

How many chances did Jesus give him? The Lord washed the disciples’ feet, Judas’ feet included (John 13:5). The Lord also handed him the dipped piece of bread — in the banquet culture of the time, handing someone that morsel was the highest mark of honour and acceptance: “So when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.” (John 13:26)

The Lord had shown love to the very uttermost. And yet Scripture goes on: “After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him.” (John 13:27) Between “put into his heart” and “entered into him” there stood just one more choice — and still he would not choose humility and repentance.

And how did it end? Thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), and then: “He threw down the pieces of silver in the sanctuary, and departed. He went away and hanged himself.” (Matthew 27:5) Brothers and sisters, he never got to spend a single coin of that money. What desire promises, it never pays out.

Peter fell too; he denied the Lord three times. But Peter “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75) — he turned back. Both men failed. The difference wasn’t the size of the failure; it was where each went after he fell: one toward humility, the other toward despair.

4. The Lesson of Delayed Gratification

In the 1960s and 70s, Professor Walter Mischel of Stanford University in the United States ran the famous “marshmallow experiment.” A child had one marshmallow placed in front of them; if they could wait until the researcher came back before eating it, they would get two. Some children couldn’t hold out for more than a few dozen seconds; others turned their heads away, sang songs, or sat on their hands, and lasted the full fifteen minutes.

I should add that a large-scale replication published in 2018 by Watts, Duncan and Quan in “Psychological Science” found that family socio-economic background accounted for a substantial part of the differences, and that the long-term predictive power claimed early on was not as strong as once thought. Still, the experiment itself reveals something important: in the face of temptation, what works best isn’t gritting your teeth, but taking your eyes off the marshmallow.

Brothers and sisters, that’s exactly what Scripture has always taught. In dealing with desire, the crucial thing isn’t to wrestle it with clenched teeth, but to turn our focus to Jesus. “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” (Hebrews 12:2) The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. Stare at the marshmallow and you’ll lose every time; look to Jesus and you’re free.

5. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. What makes desire so terrifying is that it works as this fivefold change in reverse — one small desire left unaddressed first distorts the mindset, then corrodes the life, then wrecks relationships, and finally destroys the ministry. Judas is the case study of someone who went all the way down that road.

That’s why the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Judas had a ministry. He was one of the twelve apostles; he preached and he cast out demons. But in his life there was a breach that was never dealt with. Brothers and sisters, if the life isn’t dealt with, the bigger the ministry, the harder the fall.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Way to Overcome Pride — The Choice of Humility
sections.html:
1. Root and Fruit

The text puts it very concisely: the root of pride is “I want”; the fruit of humility is “I don’t want.”

2. “I Don’t Want It” Is an Active Declaration of Faith

Choosing “I don’t want” is not passive; it is an active declaration of faith: “Lord, I will not live for myself. Come and reign.”

There is a kind of “not wanting” in this world that is really pretending not to want what we can’t have — disappointment in disguise. A Christian’s “I don’t want” is something else entirely. I don’t want it because I have someone far better; I let go because there is a steadier pair of hands to catch me.

“I don’t want” is not negativity; it is actively trusting in God’s provision. “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1) “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.’” (Hebrews 13:5)

Paul could not have put the secret more plainly: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:11-13)

Notice the words “I have learned.” Contentment is not an inborn temperament; contentment is a lesson learned. Brothers and sisters, if it can be learned, then there is a curriculum, there is practice, there are exams — and it also means that every one of us can learn it.

3. When We Let Go, God Goes to Work

The text says: when we are willing to let go, God goes to work; when we choose humility, God raises us up. This is not a motivational slogan; it is a promise Scripture makes again and again.

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:6-7)

Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first submit to God, and only then can we resist the devil. Many people try to resist the devil directly without first submitting to God, and the harder they try to drive him off, the more exhausted they become. Submission is the foundation of resistance.

“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Our part is simply to go low; lifting us up is God’s part.

4. The Logic of a Grain of Wheat

The Lord used a picture every farmer understands: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat held in your hand is perfectly safe — and it will only ever be one grain. Put it into the soil and it seems to lose everything, yet in exchange it yields a whole field of wheat. Brothers and sisters, hold on, and you keep one grain; let go, and you gain a field. That is the arithmetic of the kingdom of heaven.

5. Words of Wisdom and a Reminder

The English writer C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind, and as long as a person is proud, he cannot know God.

Augustine opens his Confessions by saying to God: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly why “I want” can never stop — our hearts are too big; nothing created can ever fill them. Only God himself can give them rest.

6. Applying the 321 Vision

At this point all of 321’s Three Foundations come together. Jesus is my role model — he had it, but he didn’t want it. The Bible is my standard — not my feelings, but God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — what I can’t give up in my own strength, I can give up by the Holy Spirit. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16)

The Two Core Values are here too. Let Jesus be King — saying “I don’t want” is giving up the throne to him. Let Jesus receive all the glory — no longer coveting that hollow, empty glory. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he existed in the form of God, yet emptied himself. The Bible is my standard — we judge not by what the market says, but by what God’s word says. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the strength to let go isn’t willpower; it’s the power of the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — when a heart is still saying “I want,” it’s we ourselves who are sitting on the throne. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when we stop fighting over that empty glory, the true glory goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A crowd of people all saying “I want” can only build a Tower of Babel; only people who have learned to say “I don’t want” can build God’s house together.

sections.heading: 2. Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place — that is the road of Satan’s five “I will”s. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God — that is the road of the Lord Jesus, who “emptied himself.”

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. This is the most common tragedy in families: both people want to win, so both people lose. The moment one of them is willing to say first, “I don’t need to win this time,” that home begins to come back to life.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Today there’s just one mindset to change: from “possessing is gaining” to “letting go is gaining.”

Our perspective must shift as well: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Through earthly eyes, “I don’t want it” is a loss; through eternal eyes, “I don’t want it” is depositing things into an account that can never decay.

sections.heading: 4. The Priority of Relationships and the 920 Practice
sections.html:
The 321 vision says relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson is exactly what people who have reversed that order most need to hear. Many people grab hold of things first, then people, then themselves, and only at the very end think of God — so they grasp at everything and are worn out by everything.

The 920 practice is very practical here: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” As we practise living out the selfless “0” before them, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23) — which of them doesn’t grow precisely in the moments we say “I don’t want”? Patience is “I don’t want to explode right now”; self-control is “I don’t want to follow my cravings.”

And 235 relationships remind us: don’t try to tough it out alone. Find a brother or sister who is equally willing to be selfless to be your “2,” and remind each other about that clenched hand; then build your “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and pass this lesson on; and finally become a “5,” a team of spiritual comrades. For one person to let go is hard; when a whole group lets go together, it becomes revival.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The text gives us three practices for daily living. We don’t just want to know them; we want to walk them through the eight stages — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they truly become life.

Practice 1: Examine the “I want” in your heart every day

Every day, examine the “I want” in your heart and say to the Lord: “Lord, I give this to you. I refuse to be controlled by it.”

Information: Today we’ve learned that “I want” is Satan’s principle and “I don’t want” is Jesus’ principle.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show me the truest “I want” in my heart. It might be a position, a word of affirmation, a relationship, a sum of money, or an apology from someone else.

Conviction: I believe what the Lord says is true — clinging only binds me; letting go is what sets me free.

Implementation: Every morning, spend three quiet minutes writing down the biggest “I want” in your heart that day, then say to the Lord in specific terms: “Lord, I give this one to you. I refuse to be controlled by it.”

Evaluation: In the evening, look back — did it lead me around by the nose today? Which moment, which remark, pulled me back into “I want”?

Correction: Don’t condemn yourself and don’t make excuses; confess, and hand it over once more (1 John 1:9).

Repetition: Forty days in a row. A change of mindset takes repetition; one moment of being moved won’t change a lifetime of habit.

Multiplication: Tell a brother or sister about this practice, and ask each other once a week: “This week, did you hand it over?”

Practice 2: Ask yourself, “Who am I wanting this for?”

When you’re struggling over possessions, relationships, ministry or position, ask yourself: “Who am I wanting this for?”

Information: Motive determines nature. The very same thing, done for God, is service; done for ourselves, it’s ambition.

Revelation: Ask God to expose my hidden motives. “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9)

Conviction: I admit that even within my most spiritual actions an “I want” may be hiding.

Implementation: At the very moment of each struggle, stop for three seconds and ask: “Who am I wanting this for?” If the answer is “for my own face,” hand it over right there and then.

Evaluation: Once a week, take stock — what was my fiercest struggle this week? What did I really want underneath it?

Correction: Take the part that is “wanting it for myself” and concretely turn it into “wanting it for God’s kingdom.” For example: not asking the Lord to let me be seen, but asking him to use me, even if no one sees.

Repetition: Practise it again and again in the same area until the response becomes instinct.

Multiplication: When someone near you is caught in a struggle, don’t rush to give advice; first sit with them and ask, “Who are you wanting this for?”

Practice 3: Write down one thing you’re willing to let go of

Write down one thing you’re willing to “let go” of, and pray over it, entrusting it to the Lord.

Information: Letting go isn’t giving up; it’s transferring sovereignty.

Revelation: Be still before the Lord and let him point out that one thing — usually the very thing you least want to write down.

Conviction: Believe he can catch it. “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this.” (Psalm 37:5)

Implementation: Write it down today, and write it clearly — the date, the matter, the person; a vague entrusting is no entrusting at all.

Evaluation: Take it out again a month later — have I really let go? Have I quietly taken it back?

Correction: If you’ve taken it back, let go of it once more. Every year Hannah made a little robe and brought it to Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:19) — letting go doesn’t cut off love; it puts love back in its proper place.

Repetition: Rewrite your list every quarter. You’ll find you can lay down more and more, and the space in your heart keeps growing larger.

Multiplication: Tell someone who is struggling right now the story of how God worked after you let go. Your testimony is their Information.

A Gentle Reminder: Two Sentences, Two Roads

Satan says: “I don’t have it — I want it.”

Jesus says: “I have it, but I don’t want it.”

The first brings bondage; the second brings freedom.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, which of the two is your heart repeating?

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Gaining Everything by Not Wanting
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that monkey’s hand at the beginning. It wasn’t the box that trapped it. It was trapped by its own hand.

Pride ensnares us in the net of “I want”; humility brings us into the freedom of “I don’t want.” Jesus lived out, with his own life, the role model of “I have it, but I don’t want it,” and revealed that true glory lies not in possessing, but in laying down.

That’s why Scripture says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9-11)

The end of this road is not “now I have nothing left.” The end of this road is “to the glory of God the Father.” Brothers and sisters, laying down is not the end; laying down is the beginning of letting Jesus reign as King.

This morning I want to invite you to make one very concrete decision: hand over the fistful of peanuts in your hand. It might be a position you’ve clung to for years; it might be someone you’ve never been willing to forgive; it might be a life you’ve designed in advance for your child; it might be a sum of money you’re afraid to give; or it might simply be an “I’m sorry” you’ve been waiting for someone else to say first.

Let us follow his example: choose humility, choose denying of self, gain everything in “not wanting,” and enter true fullness in “letting go.” Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5-8)
declarations: Lord, you are the satisfaction of my whole life.
I no longer chase worldly possessions, nor do I live for myself.
I choose “I don’t want,” and let you reign,
that my heart may find freedom and peace in you.
practices: Write down one thing you’re willing to let go of
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Your Son existed in your form, yet emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and walked the road of the cross. Lord, only this morning have we seen that true glory lies not in possessing, but in laying down.

Lord, forgive us. There’s so much “I want” in our hearts — I want to be seen, I want to be affirmed, I want to be in control, I want everything to be all right. Shine your light on that hand inside us that refuses to open.

Lord, we open our hands now. We give our children back to you, our marriages back to you; our careers, our money, our reputations, our places of ministry — we give them all back to you. We also bring before you that trace of resentment, that little desire; wash it clean with your precious blood, so that we no longer give place to the devil.

Holy Spirit, guide us every day, so that we no longer rely on the brain and ourselves, but rely on the heart and on you. In every moment of struggle, help us to say: “Lord, I don’t want it — what you want is enough.”
May our homes be restored because someone let go first; may our churches be united because someone humbled themselves first; may your kingdom come, and your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

If you were to open your hand after the Lord’s example, what would you be most afraid of losing?

“Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15) Judas’ breach began with that little bit he “used to steal.” Think honestly: is there a little fox in your heart that you’ve been treating as “nothing much”? What concrete action will you take this week to catch it?

blog.title: Satan Says “I Want”; Jesus Says “I Don’t Want”

blocks.x: — A Morning Devotion on Letting Go

People who catch monkeys use no net and no gun. All they need is a wooden box with a narrow opening and a handful of peanuts inside. The monkey reaches in and grabs a fistful of peanuts, and now its fist is bigger than the opening; no matter how it pulls, it can’t get its hand out. The hunter walks up; it shrieks and struggles, yet it simply will not let go.
It isn’t the box that has trapped it. It’s trapped by its own hand.
Satan’s language is “I want”

The earliest voice of pride was heard at the moment the archangel fell: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13-14) In just two verses, five times “I will.”
Satan’s fall didn’t begin with some great sin; it began with “I want.” And he handed the very same script to humanity: you don’t have it — you want it; you have it — and you want more.

And the result? Want money, and money will control you; want a reputation, and you’ll be tied up by other people’s opinions; want relationships, and you’ll be held hostage by your feelings. We think we are possessing things, when in fact the things we possess have come to possess us.

Neuroscience offers a piercing piece of corroboration. Professors Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson of the University of Michigan found that “wanting” and “liking” in the brain are two different systems, and that dopamine drives “wanting,” not “liking.” So while we’re chasing it, our heart races; once we’ve got it, the thrill lasts three days. Three thousand years ago Solomon had already said: “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver.” (Ecclesiastes 5:10)
Jesus’ language is “I don’t want”
“Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6-7)

The original meaning of “a thing to be grasped” is “a prize of war held tight and never released.” Jesus’ equality with God was his by right, not something he had seized; and precisely because it wasn’t seized, he had no need to cling to it.
The more truly you possess something, the less you need to clutch it; the more insecure a person is, the tighter they grip.

His “I don’t want it” carries great weight, because he already had everything. In the wilderness, Satan laid the glory of all the kingdoms before him, and he said, “Get behind me, Satan!” In Gethsemane, he said, “Not what I desire, but what you desire.”
Letting Go Is Not Losing

Children are a heritage from God, a blessing; but the moment we treat them as “my property, my pride,” love turns into control. It’s the same with marriage, career, wealth and ministry — the moment we want to possess, the struggle begins; the moment we’re willing to let go and let Jesus take over, everything finds its order again.

So the conviction that overcomes comes down to one sentence: whether I have it or not, I can still not want it. “I don’t have it, and I don’t want it” is contentment; “I have it, but I don’t want it” is denying of self. Once we’ve learned both, Satan’s bait has nowhere left to hang its hook.
Pride ensnares us in the net of “I want”; humility brings us into the freedom of “I don’t want.” True glory lies not in possessing, but in laying down.
Practices You Can Start Today
1. Every day, examine the “I want” in your heart and say to the Lord: “Lord, I give this to you. I refuse to be controlled by it.”
2. When you face a struggle, ask yourself: “Who am I wanting this for?”
3. Write down one thing you’re willing to let go of, and pray over it, entrusting it to the Lord.
Reflection: What is the fistful of peanuts you are clutching right now? If you opened your hand today, what would you be most afraid of losing?
