Third: why does “rejection” so often not work? Right now, whatever you do, do not think of a white bear. What happened? You thought of one. In 1987, the American psychologist Daniel Wegner conducted the famous white bear experiment: the group told to suppress the thought afterwards thought of the white bear even more often. Why? Because when you try hard not to think of something, your mind keeps checking, “Have I thought of it again?” — and that very act of checking is itself thinking about it. Brothers and sisters, by suppression alone, we will never win.

So what do we do? The Bible’s strategy is “replacement.” When Satan says, “You’re not good enough,” I replace it with God’s word: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” When Satan says, “You don’t have enough,” I declare: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” When Satan says, “Nobody loves you,” I declare: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” The Lord Jesus himself did the same: tempted three times, three times he said, “It is written.” Brothers and sisters, remember that empty house — swept clean, yet empty, and in the end seven spirits more evil came back. We must put off the old self — and even more, put on the new.

Fourth: replace sinful desire with thanksgiving. Sinful desire begins with “I want”; thanksgiving says, “Lord, thank you — I already have.” Scripture says: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” In 2003, a study by Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough found that after ten weeks of writing down five things they were grateful for each week, people’s well-being and optimism rose significantly. Brothers and sisters, God’s grace is there every day; it’s just that our eyes are so often somewhere else.

We must also replace pride with humility. The root of sinful desire is pride — the feeling that “I deserve more”; humility says, “Lord, I am willing to be less, so that you may be more.” The Bible repeats the same sentence twice: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” In the original, “resists” is a military term meaning to draw up in battle array against. Just think — God himself drawn up in battle formation opposite you: what a terrible battle that would be. So between “satisfying ourselves” and “satisfying God,” our choice decides the outcome.

Brothers and sisters, today there are four practices. First, spiritual gatekeeping: every day, check what you have watched and what you have listened to, and whether it glorifies God. Second, renewing your thoughts: replace a wrong thought with a verse of God’s word, and declare it again and again. Third, replacing with thanksgiving: whenever temptation comes, immediately name one thing you are thankful for. Fourth, humble submission: in every choice, ask yourself, “Does this satisfy me, or does it satisfy the Lord?” Please choose one today and begin to practise it.

Brothers and sisters, the power of sinful desire comes from “I want”; the power of holiness comes from “Lord, I don’t want it.” Overcoming sin doesn’t come by suppression but by replacement. When we let the truth in, lies naturally flee. Today the Lord Jesus is standing at the door and knocking. He doesn’t want you to be an empty house, swept clean; he wants to move in. So this morning, don’t just shut one particular door — open the door of your heart to the Lord. Today, in your heart, may sin not reign; may Jesus reign as King; and may all the glory go to Jesus.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we hand you the key to the door of our hearts. Help us to keep watch at the gate; fill us with your word, leaving no empty space for the enemy. Give us sensitive hearts, so that the moment we notice careless thinking, we deal with it at once. Give us thankful hearts, and give us humble hearts, so that we replace pride with humility and sinful desire with thanksgiving, and live a life that is free, holy and yours. Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may you have peace and joy today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the Lord’s peace be with you this morning. Today we come together to Lesson 77 of Morning Devotion 321, entitled “Close the Door to Sin, Open the Door to God.” Our theme verse is Romans 6:12: “Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts.” Brothers and sisters, notice the word “let.” Sin cannot seize the throne by force; it has to wait for you to let it. Satan has no key; Satan only has a hand to knock with. So the first piece of good news today is this: the door handle is not in Satan’s hand; the door handle is in ours.

In our last lesson we came to understand one thing together: sinful desire is the doorway to sin. Satan doesn’t begin by asking us to commit some great evil. He simply sows, very lightly, beside our eyes and our ears, a single seed of “I want.” That seed is so small that we often think, “What harm can this do?” But once the seed falls into the soil of the heart, it sprouts. And so the question arises: when sinful desire has already entered our thoughts — when it has even begun to take shape — what are we to do?

A brother once described his struggle like this: “Every night I go to war with myself. I tell myself a hundred times, ‘Don’t think about it,’ and then I spend the whole night thinking about it. The harder I push it down, the higher it bounces back.” Brothers and sisters, have you heard a struggle like that? It isn’t that you are ungodly; it’s that you are trying too hard. It isn’t that you don’t want to overcome; it’s that you are using the wrong method. Today the Bible wants to tell us: the key to overcoming sin is not suppression but shutting the door; not rejection but replacement. You can never sweep the darkness out of a room with a broom; but just flip the switch, and the moment light comes in, the darkness is gone. Our heart is a room that will always be filled with something. The question has never been “Will it be filled?” but “What will fill it?”

Let’s first stand where these passages were written. Paul wrote Romans around AD 56 in Corinth, to believers living in the imperial capital, surrounded by indulgence on every side. James is quite possibly one of the earliest books of the New Testament; its author, James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh, wrote to Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution. Romans 6:11 speaks first of identity — consider yourselves dead to sin; only verses 12 and 13 speak of action. And the original meaning of the word “instruments” is weapons, armaments. Brothers and sisters, James speaks of what is conceived within; Paul speaks of what is presented outwardly; and between the two stands you — someone with the power to choose.

Our first key point: shut the door on sin. Paul says: “Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness.” Since God says “do not,” it means we are able not to. God never commands us to do something he has not given us the power to accomplish. The next verse goes further: “For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.” Brothers and sisters, the door is locked from the inside, and the lock is on our side. If we choose indulgence, we open the door to sin; if we choose holiness, we shut the door on sin.

Sin works in three stages. First, careless looking and careless listening: outward enticement enters our thoughts. Second, careless thinking: sinful desire is conceived in the heart. Third, careless doing: sinful desire matures and gives birth to sinful acts. Genesis 3 is exactly like this: first Eve “saw that the tree was good for food,” then it was “to be desired,” and finally she “took some of its fruit, and ate.” From eye to heart, from heart to hand. Brothers and sisters, the further along you go, the harder it is to turn back. There is a saying generally attributed to Martin Luther: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair.

So we must guard the gate, and we need a standard. Proverbs says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The original meaning of the Hebrew word for “keep” is to stand sentry like a soldier guarding a city. The heart is not a garden; it is a city. What is the gatekeeper’s standard? Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. And so we have a very simple three-question test: whatever cannot glorify God, cannot build up life and cannot bring peace, we will not watch, will not listen to and will not dwell on. Job said: “I made a covenant with my eyes.” David said: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” Both of them made the covenant before temptation ever arrived.

Our second key point: don’t let sinful desire conceive. James says: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” Here the Bible uses a deeply sobering image — an embryo. A fertilised egg is about a tenth of a millimetre across, almost invisible to the naked eye, and it looks completely harmless; yet it implants, divides, and grows a heartbeat and limbs. Brothers and sisters, sinful desire is just like that: at first it is tiny — so tiny you think, “I’m only thinking about it” — but if it isn’t dealt with, it grows.

There is a very important distinction here, and I want every brother and sister to hear it clearly. Having a sinful desire does not mean you will necessarily sin. Hebrews says: “one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” The Lord Jesus was tempted yet did not sin, which shows that being tempted is not in itself sin. Satan loves two sentences above all: one is “It doesn’t matter,” the other is “I’m finished.” The first makes you indulge; the second makes you despair; and both roads lead to the same place. So when a thought appears, you don’t need to condemn yourself; you only need to deal with it at once.

The earlier you deal with it, the easier it is. Doctors often tell expectant mothers a plain truth: the longer a pregnancy goes on, the harder it is to intervene. Sinful desire is the same. So when you find your heart beginning to “think carelessly,” don’t wait, and don’t bargain with it. What did Joseph do? “He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” He didn’t even keep his garment — no debate, no analysis; he ran. Paul also told Timothy: “Flee from youthful lusts.” Some battles are fought with your feet. In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that neurons that fire together wire together. Every time you think about it, that pathway gets a little thicker; every time you don’t, that path becomes a little more overgrown.

Our third key point, the very heart of today’s lesson: why does “rejection” so often not work? Right now, whatever you do, do not think of a white bear. What happened? You thought of one. In 1987, the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: the group told “not to think of a white bear” afterwards thought of white bears far more often than the control group. He called this the “rebound effect.” Why? Because when you try hard not to think of something, the mind starts two processes at once — one that turns attention away, and another that keeps checking, “Have I thought of it again?” — and that very act of checking is itself thinking about it.

So what do we do? The Bible’s strategy is not rejection but replacement. When Satan says, “You’re not good enough,” I replace it with God’s word: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” When Satan says, “You don’t have enough,” I declare: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” When Satan says, “Nobody loves you,” I declare: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Brothers and sisters, these three sentences are not motivational sayings; they are words God himself has spoken. The Lord Jesus himself did the same: tempted three times, three times he said, “It is written.”

The Lord Jesus also told a deeply sobering parable. When an unclean spirit has gone out and comes back, “he finds it empty, swept, and put in order,” and so he brings seven other spirits more evil than himself to live there. Brothers and sisters, that was a very beautiful house — but it was empty. So simply “giving up” is not enough; we must “exchange.” Paul says: put away the old self, be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new self. Put away, be renewed, put on — it is one complete set of movements. No one takes off their clothes and goes out without putting any on. This is also what 321 says: selflessness is not emptying yourself out; selflessness is letting Christ fill you.

Our fourth key point: replace sinful desire with thanksgiving, and pride with humility. Sinful desire begins with “I want”; thanksgiving says, “Lord, thank you — I already have.” The eyes of “I want” look at what we don’t have; the eyes of “thank you” look at what we already have. Paul says: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” In 2003, a study by Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough found that after ten weeks of writing down five things they were grateful for each week, people scored significantly higher in well-being and optimism than the other two groups. Brothers and sisters, God’s grace is there every day; it’s just that our eyes are so often somewhere else.

We must also replace pride with humility. The root of sinful desire is pride — the feeling that “I deserve more”; humility says, “Lord, I am willing to be less, so that you may be more.” John the Baptist said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The Bible repeats the same sentence twice: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” In the original, “resists” is a military term meaning to draw up in battle array against. Just think — a proud person, and God himself drawn up in battle formation opposite him: there is no harder battle in all the world. James goes on: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil.

So between “satisfying ourselves” and “satisfying God,” our choice decides the outcome. Choose to satisfy yourself, and sinful desire grows; choose to satisfy God, and life is set free. The Lord Jesus is the most perfect role model: existing in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. In the original, “emptied himself” means to pour oneself out; the Lord was not emptied by someone else — he emptied himself. The Lord said: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” Brothers and sisters, self-control is fruit the Spirit bears; it doesn’t come from gritting our teeth. The ultimate answer to sinful desire is not a stronger will but a fuller measure of the Holy Spirit.

Next come the practices. First, spiritual gatekeeping: every day, check what you have watched and what you have listened to, and whether it glorifies God. Set one concrete boundary today: leave your phone in the living room an hour before bed, and in the evening be still for three minutes and ask yourself, “Today, where did my eyes and ears linger longest?” Second, renewing your thoughts: replace a wrong thought with a verse of God’s word. Write the lie on the left side of a sheet of paper and a corresponding Bible verse on the right, and declare it aloud every day, until what comes out of your mouth is God’s word.

Third, replacing with thanksgiving: whenever temptation comes, immediately name one thing you are thankful for — name the person, name the event; no vagueness allowed. That way, temptation becomes an alarm clock reminding you to count your blessings. Fourth, humble submission: in every choice, ask yourself, “Does this satisfy me, or does it satisfy the Lord?” Today, in one concrete decision, choose “you more, me less.” Brothers and sisters, 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Please choose one practice today and keep it up for forty days in a row.

Let’s place today’s content into the blueprint of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — in the wilderness he replaced temptation with the word of God; the Bible is my standard, because the opponent of sinful desire is not our will but God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide, because self-control is the fruit of the Spirit. The Two Core Values: the flip side of not letting sin reign is letting Jesus be King, and letting Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry, and it all begins with the mindset. And don’t fight alone — walk with spiritual companions; that is exactly what our 235 relationships are for.

Brothers and sisters, the power of sinful desire comes from “I want”; the power of holiness comes from “Lord, I don’t want it.” Overcoming sin doesn’t come by suppression but by replacement. When we let the truth in, lies naturally flee. Today the Lord Jesus is standing at the door and knocking. He says: “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him.” He doesn’t want you to be an empty house, swept clean; he wants to move in. So this morning, don’t just shut one particular door — open the door of your heart to the Lord. Today, in your heart, may sin not reign; may Jesus reign as King; and may every victory you win give the glory to Jesus.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you for shining your word into our hearts this morning. Lord, we confess that we so often wrestle with sinful desire in our own strength — the harder we push it down, the more tired we get; the more we fight, the more we lose. Please forgive us. Today we hand you the key to the door of our hearts. Help us to keep watch at the gate; fill us with your word, leaving no empty space for the enemy. Give us thankful hearts, and give us humble hearts, so that we replace pride with humility and sinful desire with thanksgiving, and live a life that is free, holy and yours. Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and give you peace.

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Are Those Three Words So Hard to Say?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we are going to face together a very ancient sickness that has never gone out of date, and receive together a very simple yet supremely effective medicine. The sickness is called pride; the medicine is called humility.

Let me begin with a true story. In the United States, medical malpractice disputes have long been the heaviest burden hospitals carry. The traditional approach was this: when something goes wrong, admit nothing at first and hand everything over to the lawyers. But in 2001 the University of Michigan Health System decided to do the opposite — when a medical error had genuinely occurred, it would take the initiative to explain the truth to the patient and family, apologise sincerely and offer compensation.

Many predicted the hospital would be sued into collapse. And the result? In 2010 Kachalia and colleagues published the data from before and after the programme in the Annals of Internal Medicine: new claims fell from 7.03 to 4.52 per 100,000 patient encounters; cases that actually went to litigation fell from 2.13 to 0.75; and the median time from claim to resolution shortened from 1.36 years to 0.95 years.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? One honest “I was wrong” is more powerful than an entire team of lawyers. Bowing your head is not a loss; bowing your head is the way out.

Yet we all know how hard those three words are to say. A husband and wife quarrel; both badly want to make up, yet neither will speak first. Between parents and children there is love in both hearts, yet all that comes out of their mouths is “What did I do wrong?” Two co-workers in a church fall out over some small matter and stay frozen for years. It isn’t that we don’t know how to apologise; it’s that we can’t bear to bow our heads.

The introduction to the lesson text puts it with great precision: pride drives people away from God; humility brings people back before him. From the fall of the archangel and the sin of Adam to our own weaknesses and failures today, the root of sin has always been the same — pride.

The Bible records how that anointed cherub who covers (Ezekiel 28:14) fell. The prophet Isaiah, speaking through the mouth of the king of Babylon, utters words that shake the heart: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ ” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Brothers and sisters, count them: how many times does he say “I will”? Five. Five “I will”s, and an archangel was hurled down from heaven. Pride has never been “I did something bad”; pride is “I want to sit in the seat that doesn’t belong to me.”

In the Garden of Eden, the serpent’s words to the woman used the same recipe: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Humanity’s fall did not begin with a piece of fruit; it began with a thought — I don’t have to depend on God; I can manage on my own.

The English writer C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind. He was right. For pride is the only sin that the more it grows, the less you can see it in yourself. A greedy person knows he is greedy; an angry person knows he is angry; only the proud person always thinks it is someone else who is proud.

So how is this deepest root of humanity’s sickness to be treated? The Bible gives only one answer, and it has never changed from Genesis to Revelation — humility is the antidote to pride. Only the humble can receive salvation, obtain forgiveness and enter revival.

In the 321 vision we put it even more directly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights that are not ours and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Today, following the three key points of the lesson text, we will walk step by step along this road home: first, humility is the starting point of salvation; second, the humble are forgiven and the proud are rejected; third, humility brings revival and healing.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Younger Brother Who Called Himself a Servant
1. The Author, Date and Readers of James
sections.html:
Our theme verse comes from the letter of James. Its author is generally held to be James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. At first he did not believe in the Lord; John’s Gospel says it plainly: “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” (John 7:5) But after the Lord rose, he appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and this younger brother was utterly changed. He went on to become a leader of the church in Jerusalem, called by Paul one of the pillars of the church (Galatians 2:9), and gave the ruling at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:13–21).

Notice how he introduces himself: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion: Greetings.” (James 1:1) Brothers and sisters, he could perfectly well have written “James, the brother of the Lord” — the most dazzling title in the whole church. He didn’t. He wrote “servant.” The Greek is δοῦλος (doulos): a slave. How deeply a person knows Jesus can be seen from what he calls himself. This book about humility begins teaching humility from its very first verse.

There is another account from church history. Hegesippus, in the second century, left a passage that the church historian Eusebius preserved in his Ecclesiastical History, saying that James was constantly on his knees praying for the people, so that his knees grew calloused, hard as a camel’s. Though this account belongs to tradition, it fits the spirit of the letter of James: the truly humble person is someone on their knees before God.

The letter of James is generally thought to have been written between AD 45 and 50, and is quite possibly the earliest book of the New Testament to be completed. Its readers were “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” — Jewish believers scattered abroad by persecution. They lived in poverty, persecution and trial, and yet in the church there had arisen favouritism, rivalry and mutual criticism.

sections.heading: 2. The Setting of James 4
sections.html:
Chapter 4, where our theme verse is found, opens with a very pointed question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1) Brothers and sisters, the root of conflict in the church is rarely in the matter itself; mostly it lies in the heart. James goes on: “You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” (James 4:2)

Then we come to our theme verse today: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (James 4:6) That phrase “it says” introduces a quotation from Proverbs 3:34. The apostle Peter quotes the same sentence: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (1 Peter 5:5) Two pillars of the Jerusalem church, independently quoting the same Old Testament verse — this in itself is a reminder: this is not James’s personal opinion; it is an unchanging law of the kingdom of God.

sections.heading: 3. Three Key Words in the Original
sections.html:
The first word is “proud,” Greek ὑπερήφανος (hyperēphanos), made up of two roots, “above” (ὑπέρ) and “to appear” (φαίνομαι). Literally it means “to make oneself appear higher than others.” The core of pride is not being highly capable; it is wanting to be seen as higher than others.

The second word is “humble,” Greek ταπεινός (tapeinos), whose verb is ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), meaning “to lower, to bring down, to place beneath.” Interestingly, in Greco-Roman culture this word originally carried a negative sense, describing someone base and lacking ambition. It was the Bible that turned it upside down and made it the highest virtue of the kingdom of heaven — what the world regards as shameful, God has made glorious.

The third word is “resists,” Greek ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, this is a fearful thing to read: God does not merely disapprove of the proud; he draws up his ranks against them as an enemy. There is no battle in all the world with less hope of victory than standing in battle against God.

sections.heading: 4. The Background of Two Other Key Passages
sections.html:
2 Chronicles 7:14, quoted in the lesson text’s third key point, is set at Solomon’s dedication of the temple. After the temple was completed, fire fell from heaven and the glory of Yahweh filled the house, “Yahweh appeared to Solomon by night” (2 Chronicles 7:12) and spoke those words that countless intercessors have quoted. Notice: these words were not spoken to the Gentiles but to “my people, who are called by my name.” Revival has never begun in the world; it begins in the house of God.

Luke 14:11, quoted in the lesson text’s first key point, has an equally important background. Jesus was eating at the house of one of the leaders of the Pharisees, and “he noticed how they chose the best seats” (Luke 14:7). So he told a parable, ending with: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) This saying appears twice in Luke’s Gospel; the other time is after the parable of the tax collector and the Pharisee at prayer (Luke 18:14). Once at the dinner table, once in the temple; once about our seat before people, once about our standing before God. What the Lord is saying is that it’s the same everywhere: in the kingdom of God there is only one way up, and that is to go down first.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Humility Is the Starting Point of Salvation
sections.html: The lesson text’s very first sentence makes the truth plain: salvation does not depend on effort; it begins with humility. If a person will not bow their head and admit they are a sinner, they cannot be saved.

sections.heading: 1. A Law Laid Down by the Lord Himself
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) Brothers and sisters, this is not an exhortation; it is a law. Like gravity, it is always at work whether you believe in it or not. When people grasp upwards, God brings them down; when people bow down, God lifts them up.

The clearest demonstration of this law is the parable in Luke 18. Two men went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood and prayed to himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.” (Luke 18:11–12)

Every word he said was true. He really did fast, he really did give, he really was no extortioner or adulterer. So where was the problem? The problem was that the word appearing most in his prayer was “I” — and while he stood before God, his eyes were fixed on the man beside him. Brothers and sisters, there is a very reliable test for pride: when you are before God, who are you thinking about?

And the other man? “But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ ” (Luke 18:13)

For “be merciful to me” the Greek uses ἱλάσθητί (hilasthēti), from the same root as “atoning sacrifice”; literally it means “be propitiated towards me — grant me the grace of atonement.” And “a sinner” carries the definite article in the original: “me, the sinner” — not one sinner among many, but the sinner. He made no comparison, he offered no explanation; he admitted one thing only: I need God.

The Lord’s conclusion is: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 18:14)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the one who walked out of the temple that day declared righteous by God was not the one with the higher moral score, but the one willing to bow his head. The door of salvation is very wide — wide enough for anyone to come in; but the door is very low — low enough that everyone must bow their head.

sections.heading: 2. Adam’s Tragedy: From Hiding to Shifting the Blame
sections.html:
The lesson text takes us back to the Garden of Eden. After Adam sinned, his first reaction was not to confess but to hide. “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

God came looking for him and asked the first question in the Bible: “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’ ” (Genesis 3:9) Brothers and sisters, of course God knew where he was. When God asked “Where are you?” it wasn’t to locate him but to give him a chance to turn back. God was saying: Come out, child; let’s talk.

How did Adam answer? “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’ ” (Genesis 3:12)

With that one sentence he passed the blame on twice: first to the woman, then to the God who had given him the woman. The lesson text is right — pride cost him the chance to repent. God meant to give him forgiveness; he wanted to give God excuses.

Brothers and sisters, have we made any progress since Adam? When a child breaks a cup, the first words are often “It wasn’t me.” When husband and wife clash, the first words are often “You started …” The mistake itself won’t destroy a person; covering up the mistake will. That is why the Bible says: “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” (Proverbs 28:13)

sections.heading: 3. Confirmation from Psychology: We Are Born Self-Justifiers
sections.html:
Psychology observed this long ago. In 1975 Dale Miller and Michael Ross published a paper in the Psychological Bulletin reviewing a large body of experiments, pointing out that people commonly display a “self-serving bias”: when they succeed, they attribute it to their own ability; when they fail, they attribute it to circumstances or other people.

A little earlier, in 1957, Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when my behaviour contradicts my self-image of “I am a good person,” my mind becomes very uncomfortable; and to get rid of that discomfort, the easiest thing to do is not to change my behaviour but to change my story — to find myself a reason. In their 2007 book, the social psychologists Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson called this mechanism “self-justification”: the longer we justify ourselves, the further we drift from the facts.

Brothers and sisters, psychology tells us the true condition of the human heart; the Bible tells us the way out. Science can describe the symptoms; only the gospel can heal the root of the disease. It isn’t that we are unable to admit our mistakes; it’s that we won’t pay the small price of a little face.

sections.heading: 4. Turning Back Is the Fastest Way
sections.html:
In Mere Christianity C. S. Lewis offers a fine comparison: we all want progress; but if you are on the wrong road, progress means doing an about-turn and walking back to the right road — and in that case the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had this experience? You get on the motorway, drive for twenty minutes, and only then realise you are going the wrong way. The biggest struggle at that moment isn’t the cost of the petrol; it’s the thought, “I don’t want to admit I went the wrong way.” So you console yourself: I’ll drive on a bit and see. And the result? The further you drive, the further away you get.

Confession is the act of taking the exit. It takes a few minutes, but it can save you hours. John puts it very clearly: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

The lesson text says: but Jesus has opened the way home for sinners. As long as we are willing humbly to admit, “Lord, I was wrong,” he forgives at once, heals, and lets us stand up again.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: From Information to Revelation
sections.html:
In the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset, the first stage is Information and the second is Revelation. Information is “I know pride is bad”; Revelation is “Lord, I see that I am that proud person.” How many people stay at the first stage all their lives — hearing sermons for decades without ever once being truly searched by the light.

Brothers and sisters, the work of the Holy Spirit is precisely to turn information into revelation. The Lord said: “When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment.” (John 16:8) The Chinese Union Version renders “convict” as “cause them to reprove themselves” — notice that phrase. The Holy Spirit never deals with us by humiliating us; he shines the light in, so that we see for ourselves, admit for ourselves, turn back for ourselves. This is the third of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not circumstances. The Pharisee’s focus was on himself and on others; the tax collector’s focus was on God. So one went home empty-handed, and one went home justified. Pride makes people perish; humility gives people life.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Humble Are Forgiven; the Proud Are Rejected
sections.html: The lesson text says that the contrast between Saul and David is the most vivid example. Both men were kings of Israel, both were chosen by God, both sinned. Yet their ends were completely opposite. The difference lay not in how heavy the sin was, but in how soft or hard the heart was.

sections.heading: 1. Saul: Pride Wrapped in Pious Reasons
sections.html:
Saul disobeyed God’s command twice. The second time, God commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but he kept King Agag and the best of the cattle and sheep. When the prophet Samuel arrived, what were Saul’s first words?

“Samuel came to Saul; and Saul said to him, ‘You are blessed by Yahweh! I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:13)

Brothers and sisters, how spiritual that sounds! A blessing, and a report of obedience. But Samuel said: “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?” (1 Samuel 15:14) The truth doesn’t change because of how we describe it; the sheep were still bleating.

Saul went on to explain: “They have brought them from the Amalekites; for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the cattle, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God. We have utterly destroyed the rest.” (1 Samuel 15:15) And later: “But the people took of the plunder, sheep and cattle, the chief of the devoted things, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God in Gilgal.” (1 Samuel 15:21)

Look at the three tactics in these words. First, he shifts the blame onto the people. Second, he dresses up the motive as piety — it was meant as an offering to God. Third, notice his wording: “Yahweh your God,” not “my God.” Brothers and sisters, when people are making excuses, even the way they address God gives the truth away.

The lesson text hits the nail on the head: he would not admit his error, but instead used “pious reasons” to cover his pride. This is the hardest pride of all to detect — wrapping my own will up as God’s will.

Samuel’s answer is among the weightiest words in the Old Testament: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:22–23)

There is a startling verbal correspondence here. The Hebrew for “rejected” is מָאַס (ma’as), meaning “to refuse, to cast away.” The same word appears twice in this verse: you have rejected Yahweh’s word, and Yahweh has rejected you from being king. Brothers and sisters, how exact God’s justice is — as we treat God’s word, so God treats our position.

Someone may ask: didn’t Saul later say, “I have sinned”? Yes, he did. “Saul said to Samuel, ‘I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:24) But read on: “Then he said, ‘I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship Yahweh your God.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:30)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What he really cared about was not God’s heart but saving face in front of everyone. His confession was to hold on to his throne. That is not repentance; that is public relations. And so God rejected him and took away his kingship.

sections.heading: 2. David: A Crushed Heart
sections.html:
David’s sin was even more serious. He committed adultery, then arranged the murder of the loyal Uriah, and kept it hidden for nearly a year. The prophet Nathan came and told a parable about a poor man and his little ewe lamb, then pointed at him and said: “You are the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7)

David’s response was a single sentence: “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ Nathan said to David, ‘Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.’ ” (2 Samuel 12:13)

No explanation, no “but,” no “the people.” One sentence of confession, one sentence of forgiveness. Brothers and sisters, God’s forgiveness is never slow; what is slow is our bowing of the head.

David wrote that experience into Psalm 51. He says: “For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.” (Psalm 51:3) And again: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

The Hebrew for “broken” is שָׁבַר (shavar), meaning “shattered, snapped”; “contrite” is דָּכָה (dakah), meaning “crushed, ground down.” Both are heavy words. God doesn’t want us to make our offerings look impressive; God wants a heart that is truly broken. The lesson text puts it well: God does not look at how heavy the outward sin is, but at whether our heart has truly repented.

Brothers and sisters, look at the contrast: Saul offered the best of the cattle and sheep, and God did not accept it; David offered only a broken heart, and God accepted him completely. For an offering can be a bargaining chip I use in exchange, but a broken heart is the surrender of my whole self.

Scripture also says: “For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: ‘I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.’ ” (Isaiah 57:15) God dwells in two places: the high and holy place, and a contrite and humble heart. Brothers and sisters, your heart can become God’s dwelling place.

sections.heading: 3. The Prodigal Son: The Father Interrupted His Bargain
sections.html:
The lesson text says that the story of the prodigal son confirms this truth once again. The prodigal came to his senses in the pigsty and said: “I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.’ ” (Luke 15:18–19)

He prepared three sentences. The first: I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. The second: I am no more worthy to be called your son. The third: make me as one of your hired servants.

But look at what happened when he actually came home. “He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20) And then: “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ ” (Luke 15:21)

Brothers and sisters, the third sentence has vanished. The father didn’t let him finish. Why? Because the first two sentences were repentance, and the third was a bargain — I’ll work, you feed me. The father didn’t want a hired servant; the father wanted a son.

The lesson text says: he made no excuses and hid nothing; he simply came home humbly. The father had long been waiting at the door; he embraced him and restored him. It is never too late to repent, as long as we are willing to turn back in humility.

Brothers and sisters, notice that word “ran.” In the culture of the ancient Near East, an elderly man of standing did not run; to run he had to hitch up his robes, which was unseemly. Yet this father ran. He would rather lose his own dignity than let his son be shamed at the edge of the village. This is our God — he is more eager to forgive than we are to be forgiven.

sections.heading: 4. Confirmation from Psychology and Daily Life
sections.html:
In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning published a famous study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They found that across several tests, the group with the least ability actually rated their own performance the highest. This phenomenon later became known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect.” The reason is simple: if a person doesn’t even know what they lack, they have no way of knowing that they lack it.

Brothers and sisters, this was exactly Saul’s situation, and it is often ours too. The most dangerous thing about pride is not that it makes me go wrong, but that it keeps me from seeing that I have gone wrong. That is why David prayed: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Here is another example from daily life. Two patients walk into the consulting room. The first says, “Doctor, I’m fine — just a bit tired lately.” The second says, “Doctor, it hurts here. It’s hurt for three months and I can’t sleep at night.” Which one can the doctor treat? Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that the doctor plays favourites; the first patient never handed over his illness at all. The Lord Jesus said: “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do.” (Matthew 9:12) It isn’t that the Lord won’t heal the proud; it’s that the proud won’t admit they are sick.

It is generally said that Augustine, in the history of the church, was once asked what the most important lesson of the Christian faith was, and he answered: first, humility; second, humility; third, humility. The saying comes from his letter to Dioscorus. Sixteen hundred years have passed, and the answer hasn’t changed.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Pride Makes Both Sides Lose; Humility Lets Both Sides Win
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a very important saying: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

The conversation between Saul and Samuel is pride provoking pride in action: one excuse draws a rebuke, the rebuke draws a harder excuse, and in the end the throne is gone, and the prophet “came no more to see Saul until the day of his death” (1 Samuel 15:35). By contrast, Nathan says one sentence, “You are the man,” David says one sentence, “I have sinned against Yahweh,” and both men are preserved — and God’s name is preserved too.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. David’s mindset changed — he no longer asked, “How do I get out of this?” but “O God, how do I come back before you?” And so his life was restored, and his psalm has become, for three thousand years, the prayer of countless multitudes of penitents.

This is also what the 321 vision calls the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. Saul kept dealing with “people” and “things” — how the people saw him, how to keep his throne. David dealt with God first — I have sinned against Yahweh. Turn the order upside down and everything falls; put the order right and everything comes right.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Humility Brings Revival and Healing
sections.html: The lesson text says: humility is not only a personal transformation; it is the turning around of a nation. This is a very great promise, and a very solemn order of priority.

sections.heading: 1. The Order of Revival: Humbling Ourselves Comes Before Prayer
sections.html:
God says to his people: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)

Brothers and sisters, notice the four actions here: humble themselves, pray, seek my face, turn from their wicked ways. The lesson text makes a very good point — the first step on God’s road to healing is not “pray” but “humble themselves.”

Why? Because without a humble heart, prayer is merely a form. Someone who still thinks he is right can easily turn prayer into notifying God: Lord, I’ve already decided to do this; please bless it. That isn’t prayer; that is filing a report. The lesson text says it well: humility leads us to admit our limits and let God be Lord again; humility makes us willing to lay down our own will and turn to God’s will.

The Hebrew for “humble themselves” here is כָּנַע (kana‘), meaning “to bring oneself low, to bend the knee, to bow down in submission.” The word was originally military, describing a city or a nation yielding and surrendering in war. Brothers and sisters, how vivid this is — true humbling of ourselves is raising our hands in surrender before God and saying: Lord, I’m done fighting, I’m done striving; you fight this battle.

God’s response is: I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin and heal their land. When we come down an inch, God comes near a mile. This is the law of God’s kingdom.

sections.heading: 2. Nineveh: A City That Bowed Its Head
sections.html:
The lesson text gives Nineveh as an example. Let’s first make the background clear. Nineveh was the great city of the Assyrian Empire, on the east bank of the Tigris, its ruins near today’s Mosul in Iraq. Assyria was the most brutal military power of the ancient Near East, notorious for torture. Jonah refused to go, not because he was timid, but because he did not want God to forgive such an enemy (Jonah 4:2).

Jonah ministered around the eighth century BC, in the time of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). Nineveh finally fell to the combined forces of the Medes and the Babylonians in 612 BC, and with that the Assyrian Empire came to an end. In other words, the message of repentance Jonah preached won that city more than a hundred years of forbearance.

Jonah proclaimed God’s judgement: “Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried out, and said, ‘In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!’ ” (Jonah 3:4)

Brothers and sisters, notice that this was a message with no comfort, no way out and no “unless.” Jonah spoke only of judgement, not of grace. Yet Scripture says: “The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.” (Jonah 3:5)

Even the king did the same: “The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.” (Jonah 3:6)

Brothers and sisters, there are four actions in this verse, and every one of them goes downwards: he rose from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth and sat in ashes. From the highest seat all the way down into the ashes. This is the picture of humbling oneself.

And the result? “God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way. God relented of the disaster which he said he would do to them, and he didn’t do it.” (Jonah 3:10)

The lesson text puts it superbly: humility can turn judgement into blessing and crisis into opportunity. The fate of a whole city turned on whether one king was willing to leave his throne. Brothers and sisters, the fate of a family also often turns on whether one person is willing to bow their head first.

sections.heading: 3. Confirmation from Church History: Every Revival Begins with Confession
sections.html:
Open the history of the church and you will find that every true revival began not with eloquence but with people going down on their knees.

In the autumn of 1904 a revival broke out in Wales that touched the whole world. What the young preacher Evan Roberts proclaimed was not lofty words or great wisdom, but four simple demands: confess and put away every known sin; remove everything doubtful from your life; obey the Holy Spirit’s leading completely; confess Christ publicly. Within a few short months, according to church records of the time, about a hundred thousand people turned to Christ; in many places the taverns closed, and the moral climate of society was transformed.

In January 1907 the same thing happened in Pyongyang on the Korean peninsula. At the Presbyterian winter Bible conference, a local elder, Kil Sun-Joo (later that year one of the first Korean ministers to be ordained), confessed before everyone that he had wronged the estate of a friend who had died, and was willing to make restitution. That confession was like a key that opened the floodgates: the whole congregation fell on their faces, weeping and confessing their sins, and the meeting went on late into the night. This revival came to be called “the Korean Pentecost,” and laid the foundation of the Korean church for the century that followed.

Brothers and sisters, notice what they have in common: the starting point of both revivals was not someone preaching a great sermon, but someone saying in front of everyone: I was wrong.

sections.heading: 4. Two Lessons from the Natural World
sections.html:
God has also written truth into the things he has made.

The first lesson: water flows downhill. All the water in the world flows to the lowest places; high ground cannot hold water, and only a low-lying basin can collect it into a lake. Grace is the same. God’s grace, like water, always flows towards the lowest heart. If you exalt yourself, grace slides right off you; if you bow down low, grace gathers in you into a deep pool.

The second lesson is a warning. Israel has two lakes, both fed by the Jordan River. In the north, the Sea of Galilee has clear water and abundant fish; in the south, the Dead Sea lies about 430 metres below sea level, the lowest point on the earth’s land surface, with a salt content about ten times that of seawater, and almost nothing can live in it.

The same source, both of them low-lying — so why does one have life and the other none? The difference is this: the Sea of Galilee has an inflow and an outflow; the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out.

Brothers and sisters, this reminds us that being low is not the same as being humble. There is a kind of “lowness” that is self-pity and self-enclosure, only taking in and never giving out — a Dead Sea kind of lowness. True humility is open towards God and flowing towards others — having received grace, we let grace flow on. That is why the lesson text’s gentle reminder is so precise: true humility is not putting ourselves down, but admitting, “I need God.”

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a very clear order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

2 Chronicles 7:14 is the very prototype of this order. God didn’t say, “If you plan, publicise and mobilise”; God said, “If you humble yourselves, pray, seek my face and turn from your wicked ways.” First deal with life, then with relationships, and only last of all does it reach the land — that is, ministry and the environment. Revival is not making events bigger; revival is turning human hearts around.

Brothers and sisters, this also brings us to the 321 vision’s “920 practice”: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; as I practise living out a selfless life before them, I bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Notice that the last one is “self-control,” and humility is the very root of self-control: only someone willing to surrender can rein in their tongue and their temper.

Next come the “235 relationships”: become a “2” with someone selfless, spiritual companions to one another; establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, not one of these relationships can a proud person build. For the proud have only an audience around them, not companions; only subordinates, not children.

The lesson text says: today God is still looking for a people willing to be humble. When the church is willing to admit its weakness, when believers lay down their self-righteousness, revival will come to this land. This is precisely the Goal of the 321 vision — to establish God’s system. God’s system is not built on capable people; it is built on people who are willing to kneel.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Humility Is Returning to Our Originally Intended Position
1. The Three Foundations
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model. Paul wrote the most complete model of humility in the New Testament: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8) Brothers and sisters, look at this road: from the form of God to the form of a servant; from the throne of heaven to the cross. He was already in the highest place, yet he walked all the way down to the lowest. It wasn’t that he couldn’t contend; it was that he had no need to. He also said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) This is the only time the Lord directly describes his own heart — gentle and humble.

The Bible is my standard. Not one of the truths we have looked at today is human reasoning: Luke 14:11 is a law spoken by the Lord himself; James 4:6 quotes Proverbs 3:34; 2 Chronicles 7:14 is the procedure for revival laid down by God himself. Brothers and sisters, we don’t humble ourselves according to our feelings; we return to our originally intended position according to God’s word.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. True confession is never forced out of us by people; it is drawn out by the light. The Lord said that when the Holy Spirit comes, he will make the world “reprove themselves,” as the Chinese Union Version puts it (John 16:8). Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you will worry, rely on the heart and you will be glad. We don’t need to fake humility by willpower; we need only open our hearts to the Holy Spirit every day.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King. What is the essence of pride? It is “I want to sit in that seat.” The archangel said “I will” five times; Adam wanted to be “like God, knowing good and evil”; Saul wanted to be honoured “before the elders of my people.” The essence of humility is giving that seat back to Jesus. When Jesus reigns as King, I don’t have to be king; and once I don’t have to be king, I am free.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The moment people compete for glory, relationships break; the moment people give the glory to the Lord, relationships are restored. John the Baptist said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) Brothers and sisters, this is not a declaration of loss; it is a declaration of freedom.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html: The Babylonian system is a system of climbing upwards — “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). God’s system is a system of going downwards — “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20:26). Brothers and sisters, these two systems press completely opposite direction keys. Every day we are adding bricks to one system or the other.

sections.heading: 4. The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness
sections.html:
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Brothers and sisters, remember: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A cup of water poured into the ocean has not disappeared; it has gained the whole ocean.

sections.heading: 5. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. There is only one mindset this lesson sets out to change: bowing your head is not losing; bowing your head is the way to life.

Our perspective must also shift in four directions: from man’s to God’s — Saul cared how people saw him, David cared how God saw him; from earthly to heavenly — the king of Nineveh laid down his earthly throne and saved the whole city; from temporary to eternal — a moment’s face cannot buy eternal forgiveness; from worldly to godly — the world says you only get by fighting, God says you receive by letting go.

sections.heading: 6. The Path of Serving
sections.html: The 321 vision’s Path of Serving is: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides; the Bible gives understanding; our life imitates Jesus; in service we let Jesus reign as King; and in the end we give all the glory to God. Brothers and sisters, every step of this road requires a bowing of the head.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Making Humility Part of Everyday Life
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us four concrete practices. Let’s look at them one by one, and use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Daily Self-Examination

At the end of the day, ask yourself: “In what things was I still proud today? Am I willing to admit it humbly?”

Brothers and sisters, I suggest you check yourself with three very concrete questions. First, did I put someone else down in my heart today? Second, was there something I said today that I knew would hurt, and said anyway? Third, did I take the credit for something today? You can write three lines on your phone or in a notebook — it needn’t be long. David’s prayer is the best model: “Search me, God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23)

Practice 2: A Prayer of Repentance

Take time to come before the Lord alone, admit your wrongs, and ask the Lord to shine his light on you and cleanse you.

Be specific in confession. Don’t just say, “Lord, forgive me all my sins” — that is too general, and general confession doesn’t bring real change. Say: “Lord, what I said to my husband at half past eight this morning was proud. Please forgive me.” Brothers and sisters, the more specific, the more free. For God’s forgiveness is specific: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

Practice 3: Learning to Submit

When someone reminds or corrects you, don’t justify yourself or argue; listen first and examine yourself first.

This is the hardest of the four practices. Let me give you a very practical method called “three seconds and two words.” When someone points out a problem in you, stay quiet for three seconds and don’t answer straight away; then say two words: “Thank you.” When you have calmed down, then work out how much of it is true. Brothers and sisters, the Bible says: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1) And: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19) Being swift to hear is where humility begins.

Practice 4: Interceding for the Nation

Pray humbly for the church, for families and for the nation, asking God to heal the land.

Brothers and sisters, the easiest trap to fall into in intercession is using prayer to accuse: Lord, please deal with those people. But 2 Chronicles 7:14 says, “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves.” When Daniel confessed on behalf of Israel, he said, “we have sinned, and have dealt perversely” (Daniel 9:5) — he counted himself in. Nehemiah did the same: “Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned.” (Nehemiah 1:6) True intercession stands in the gap, not on the high ground.

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages

The 321 vision says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s walk today’s lesson through them.

Stage one, Information. Today we have received clear information: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6); salvation begins with bowing the head; revival begins with humbling ourselves.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation, so that, like David hearing “You are the man,” we see the specific pride in ourselves. Information without revelation only adds knowledge; it doesn’t change life.

Stage three, Conviction. Agree in your heart, truly: God is right and I am wrong; bowing the head really is the way to life. Conviction is not emotional excitement; conviction is a settled resolve.

Stage four, Implementation. Go today and do the hardest thing — make that phone call, say that “I’m sorry,” write that message. Brothers and sisters, if humility doesn’t land in a concrete action, it is only a feeling.

Stage five, Evaluation. Afterwards, look back: when I apologised, did I add, “But you also …”? That “but” is pride slipping back in through the back door.

Stage six, Correction. When you spot it, adjust. Next time, take out the “but,” and let the full stop come straight after “I’m sorry.”

Stage seven, Repetition. Humility is not a one-off decision; it is a lifelong practice. The Lord Jesus spoke of taking up one’s cross daily (Luke 9:23); in the same way, humility is a daily lesson. Bowing the head once is a moment of being moved; bowing the head every day is life.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When your family, your colleagues, your brothers and sisters see that you really are different, you can pass this life on. This is the “3” of the 321 vision — spiritual parents bringing forth spiritual children. Brothers and sisters, we are not trying to train a group of people who understand the teaching on humility; we are trying to multiply a group of people who live out a humble life.

A Gentle Reminder

The lesson text leaves us three reminders, worth copying out and putting up somewhere you will see them.

First, pride drives people away from God; humility draws God near to people.

Second, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Third, true humility is not putting ourselves down, but admitting, “I need God.”

Brothers and sisters, remember this third one especially. Humility is not self-negation; it is not telling everyone you meet, “I can’t, I’m not worthy” — that can sometimes be another form of self-centredness. True humility is accuracy: knowing accurately that God is God and I am human; knowing accurately that I have gifts God has given me, and also the limitation that apart from him I can do nothing (John 15:5). Let God be God and let man be man — this is returning to our originally intended position.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us come back to the lesson text’s closing words. Humility is medicine for the soul, the antidote to pride. Pride makes people fall; humility makes people receive grace. Pride shuts the gate of heaven; humility opens it.

This morning I invite you to be still and ask yourself three questions.

The first question: before God, when was the last time I sincerely said, “Lord, I was wrong”?

The second question: before people, is there someone right now to whom I know in my heart I owe an apology, and I keep putting it off?

The third question: in my affairs, is there something I keep propping up by my own methods, and have never truly entrusted to God?

Let us learn, like David and like the prodigal son, not to run away and not to make excuses, but simply to return to the Father’s embrace. Like the king of Nineveh, let us be willing to come down from the throne. Like our Lord, who was in the form of God, yet willingly took the form of a servant.

When we are willing to be humble, God himself goes to work — dealing with our sin, restoring our life, and making revival begin with us and reach the whole land.

Brothers and sisters, let us begin right here today: laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position; letting God be God and letting man be man; letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (James 4:6)
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” (James 4:10)
“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11)
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, I confess that I often cover my weakness with pride, disguise my mistakes with excuses, and use busyness to escape your searching light. Today I will hide no longer; I choose to be humble before you.
Forgive me and renew me; bring me back into your embrace. Take away those five “I will”s from my heart, and set your throne once again at the centre of my life.
Give me a broken and contrite heart, ears that are swift to hear and a tongue slow to speak, and the courage to be the first to bow my head.
May your grace come upon me, and upon my family, my church, this city and this nation. Heal our hearts, forgive our sins, and bring heavenly revival.
May all the glory be yours, for you are worthy. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Saul said, “I have sinned,” yet God still rejected him; David said, “I have sinned against Yahweh,” and God forgave him at once. Compare 1 Samuel 15:30, “Then he said, ‘I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship Yahweh your God,’ ” with 2 Samuel 12:13, “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ ” What is the difference between these two confessions? In your own experience, have you ever made a “Saul-style confession”?

2 Chronicles 7:14 says: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” Why does God put “humble themselves” before “pray”? This week, towards which specific person or in which specific matter will you bow your head first, so that your prayer is more than a mere form?
l078.title: Humility Is the Antidote to Pride
l078.subtitle: Admitting I Need God; Letting God Be God and Man Be Man
l078.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

blog.title: Bowing Your Head Is the Shortest Way Home

blocks.x: — Humility Is the Antidote to Pride

In the United States, medical malpractice disputes have long been the heaviest burden hospitals carry. The traditional approach was this: when something goes wrong, admit nothing at first and hand everything over to the lawyers. But in 2001 the University of Michigan Health System decided to do the opposite — when a medical error had genuinely occurred, it would take the initiative to explain the truth, apologise sincerely and offer compensation.

Many predicted the hospital would be sued into collapse. And the result? A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in 2010 showed that new claims fell from 7.03 to 4.52 per 100,000 patient encounters, and cases that went to litigation fell from 2.13 to 0.75.
One honest “I was wrong” is more powerful than an entire team of lawyers.

Yet we all know how hard those three words are to say. A husband and wife quarrel; both badly want to make up, yet neither will speak first. Between parents and children there is love in both hearts, yet all that comes out of their mouths is “What did I do wrong?” It isn’t that we don’t know how to apologise; it’s that we can’t bear to bow our heads.
The Root of Sin Has Always Been Pride
From the fall of the archangel and the sin of Adam to our own weaknesses and failures today, the root of sin has always been the same — pride.

The prophet Isaiah, speaking through the mouth of the king of Babylon, wrote words that shake the heart: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ ” (Isaiah 14:13–14)
Count them: five “I will”s, and an archangel was hurled down from heaven. Pride has never been “I did something bad”; pride is “I want to sit in the seat that doesn’t belong to me.”

After Adam sinned, his first reaction was not to confess but to hide. When God asked him “Where are you?” it wasn’t to locate him but to give him a chance to turn back. Yet he passed the blame on twice: first to the woman, then to the God who had given him the woman.

Psychology calls this the “self-serving bias” (Miller & Ross, 1975): success is down to me, failure is down to others. Festinger’s 1957 theory of “cognitive dissonance” puts it even more clearly — when my behaviour clashes with my self-image of “I am a good person,” the easiest thing is not to change my behaviour but to change my story.
Science can describe the symptoms; only the gospel can heal the root of the disease.
The Same “I Have Sinned”, Two Different Endings
Saul and David are the most vivid contrast in the Bible.

Saul disobeyed God’s command, and when the prophet arrived, his first words were: “I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 15:13) Then he shifted the blame onto the people, and claimed the cattle and sheep were meant as an offering to God — wrapping his pride in pious reasons. Later he did say “I have sinned,” but straight away added: “please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel.” (1 Samuel 15:30) What he cared about was not God’s heart but saving face. That is not repentance; that is public relations.

David’s sin was even heavier, yet he answered with a single sentence: “I have sinned against Yahweh.” (2 Samuel 12:13) No explanation, no “but.” He later wrote: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)
God does not look at how heavy the sin is; God looks at whether the heart is truly broken.
The First Step to Revival Is Not Prayer

God promises: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)
Notice the order: the first step is not “pray” but “humble themselves.” Without a humble heart, prayer easily turns into filing a report with God — Lord, I’ve already decided; please bless it.

Nineveh is the best example. Jonah preached only a single message of judgement, yet the whole city repented; even the king “arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes” (Jonah 3:6). Four actions, all the way down — and God relented and did not bring the disaster. The fate of a whole city turned on whether one king was willing to leave his throne.
Church history is the same. The Welsh Revival of 1904 and the great Pyongyang Revival of 1907 both began not with a great sermon, but with someone saying in front of everyone: I was wrong.
Humility Is Not Putting Yourself Down

Israel has two lakes, both fed by the Jordan River. The Sea of Galilee is clear and full of fish; the Dead Sea has almost nothing living in it. The difference isn’t how low they lie, but that the Sea of Galilee has an inflow and an outflow, while the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out.

So being low is not the same as being humble. Self-pity and self-enclosure are a Dead Sea kind of lowness. True humility is not putting ourselves down, but admitting, “I need God”; not denying our own worth, but returning to our originally intended position — letting God be God and letting man be man.

This week, why not try four things: before bed, ask, “Where was I proud today?”; when you confess, name the specific time, the person and the words you said; when someone corrects you, stay quiet for three seconds, then say, “Thank you”; and when you pray for your family, your church and your nation, count yourself in.
Pride shuts the gate of heaven; humility opens it. Bowing your head has never been losing; bowing your head is the shortest way home.
Questions for Reflection
When was the last time you sincerely said to God, “Lord, I was wrong”? Is there someone right now to whom you know in your heart you owe an apology, and you keep putting it off?
