script: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we are going to face together a very ancient sickness, and receive together a very simple medicine. The sickness is called pride; the medicine is called humility. The Bible says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) From the fall of the archangel and the sin of Adam to our own weaknesses and failures today, the root of sin has always been pride. And the Bible gives only one answer — humility is the antidote to pride.

Let me begin with a true story. In the United States, medical malpractice disputes are the heaviest burden hospitals carry, and the traditional approach was to admit nothing and hand it over to the lawyers. But in 2001 the University of Michigan Health System decided to do the opposite: when there had genuinely been an error, it would take the initiative to explain the truth and apologise sincerely. And the result? According to a 2010 study in the Annals of Internal Medicine, new claims fell from 7.03 to 4.52 per 100,000 patient encounters. Brothers and sisters, one honest “I was wrong” is more powerful than an entire team of lawyers. Bowing your head is not a loss; bowing your head is the way out.

Our theme verse today comes from the letter of James. Its author is James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. He could have called himself “the Lord’s brother,” but what he wrote was: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” (James 1:1) The word “resists” is a military term in the original, meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, God does not merely disapprove of the proud; he draws up his ranks against them as an enemy. And the original word for “humble” simply means to bring yourself low.

Our first key point: humility is the starting point of salvation. The Lord Jesus told a parable. Two men went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee said: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.” Everything he said was true, but while he stood before God, his eyes were fixed on the man beside him. And the tax collector? He “wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ ” (Luke 18:13) The Lord said it was the tax collector who went home justified. Brothers and sisters, the door of salvation is very wide, but it is very low; every one of us must bow our head.

Why is bowing the head so hard? Just look at Adam. After he sinned, his first reaction was not to confess but to hide. God came looking for him and asked: “Where are you?” God wasn’t trying to locate him; he was giving him a chance to turn back. But Adam said: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” (Genesis 3:12) He passed the blame on twice. Brothers and sisters, the Bible says: “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” (Proverbs 28:13) The mistake itself won’t destroy a person; covering up the mistake will.

Our second key point: the humble are forgiven; the proud are rejected. Saul disobeyed God’s command, and when the prophet came, his first words were: “I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 15:13) How spiritual! But Samuel said: what then is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle in my ears? Saul made excuses: the people kept them to sacrifice to God. Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest pride of all to detect — wrapping my own will up as God’s will. Samuel said: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) Later he did say, “I have sinned,” but went on: please honour me before the elders. That is not repentance; that is public relations.

David’s sin was even heavier, yet he was forgiven. To Nathan’s one sentence, “You are the man,” David replied with just one sentence: “I have sinned against Yahweh.” (2 Samuel 12:13) No explanation, no “but.” He said: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17) In the original it means shattered and crushed. Brothers and sisters, God does not look at how heavy the sin is; God looks at whether the heart is truly broken. The prodigal son was the same. He had prepared three sentences, and the third was “Make me as one of your hired servants,” but his father didn’t let him finish; he ran and embraced him. The father didn’t want a hired servant; he wanted a son.

Our third key point: humility brings revival and healing. God says: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14) Brothers and sisters, notice the order: the first step is not prayer, but humbling ourselves. The original word for “humble themselves” was a military term meaning to raise your hands in surrender. Prayer without humility is just filing a report with God. Humility leads us to admit our limits and let God be Lord again.

Nineveh is the best example. Jonah preached only one message of judgement: “In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!” (Jonah 3:4) No comfort, no way out. Yet the whole city repented. Scripture says the king “arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes” (Jonah 3:6). Four actions, all the way down. And God relented and did not bring the disaster on them. Brothers and sisters, humility can turn judgement into blessing and crisis into opportunity. Church history is the same: the Welsh Revival of 1904 and the great Pyongyang Revival of 1907 both began not with a great sermon, but with someone saying: I was wrong.

So how do we practise this week? The lesson gives us four practices. First, daily self-examination: before bed, ask yourself, in what things was I still proud today? Second, a prayer of repentance: be specific in confession — don’t just say, “Forgive me all my sins,” but name the time, the person, the words you said. Third, learning to submit: when someone corrects you, stay quiet for three seconds, then say two words: “Thank you.” Fourth, interceding for the nation: like Daniel, count yourself in — “we have sinned, and have dealt perversely.” (Daniel 9:5)

Brothers and sisters, let us come back to the lesson’s closing words. Humility is medicine for the soul, the antidote to pride. Pride makes people fall; humility makes people receive grace. Pride shuts the gate of heaven; humility opens it. This morning I want to ask you three questions: When was the last time I sincerely said, “Lord, I was wrong”? Is there someone right now to whom I owe an apology? Is there something I keep propping up by myself and have never truly entrusted to God? Let us, like David and like the prodigal son, not run away and not make excuses, but simply return to the Father’s embrace. Lay down your rights and return to your originally intended position; let God be God and let man be man; let Jesus be King and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, I confess that I often cover my weakness with pride and disguise my mistakes with excuses. Today I will hide no longer; I choose to be humble before you. Forgive me and renew me; bring me back into your embrace. Give me a broken and contrite heart, and the courage to be the first to bow my head. May your grace come upon me, and upon my family, my church and this nation; heal our hearts and bring heavenly revival. May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” (James 4:10) May the grace of the Lord be with you.

Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we are going to face together a very ancient sickness that has never gone out of date, and receive together a very simple yet supremely effective medicine. The sickness is called pride; the medicine is called humility. The Bible says: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (James 4:6) And again: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” (James 4:10) Today we will follow the lesson’s three key points: humility is the starting point of salvation; the humble are forgiven and the proud are rejected; humility brings revival and healing.

Let me begin with a true story. In the United States, medical malpractice disputes have long been the heaviest burden hospitals carry. The traditional approach was this: when something goes wrong, admit nothing at first and hand everything over to the lawyers. But in 2001 the University of Michigan Health System decided to do the opposite — when a medical error had genuinely occurred, it would take the initiative to explain the truth, apologise sincerely and offer compensation. Many predicted the hospital would be sued into collapse. And the result? A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in 2010 showed that new claims fell from 7.03 to 4.52 per 100,000 patient encounters, and cases that went to litigation fell from 2.13 to 0.75. Brothers and sisters, one honest “I was wrong” is more powerful than an entire team of lawyers. Bowing your head is not a loss; bowing your head is the way out.

Yet we all know how hard those three words are to say. A husband and wife quarrel; both badly want to make up, yet neither will speak first. Between parents and children there is love in both hearts, yet all that comes out of their mouths is “What did I do wrong?” The lesson puts it precisely: pride drives people away from God; humility brings people back before him. The prophet Isaiah, speaking through the mouth of the king of Babylon, describes the fall of that archangel: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’ ” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Brothers and sisters, count them: five “I will”s, and an archangel was hurled down from heaven. In the Garden of Eden, the serpent said, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) — the very same recipe. In the 3-2-1 vision, pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Our theme verse comes from the letter of James. Its author is generally held to be James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. At first he did not believe in the Lord (John 7:5), but after the Lord rose and appeared to him, he was utterly changed and became a pillar of the church in Jerusalem. Notice how he introduces himself: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” (James 1:1) He could perfectly well have written “the Lord’s brother” — the most dazzling title in the whole church — but he wrote “servant.” Chapter 4 opens by asking: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” (James 4:1) The root of conflict in the church is rarely in the matter itself; mostly it lies in the heart. The original word for “resists” is a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”; the original word for “humble” simply means to bring yourself low.

Our first key point: humility is the starting point of salvation. Salvation does not depend on effort; it begins with humility. The Lord Jesus said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) Brothers and sisters, this is not an exhortation; it is a law. Like gravity, it is always at work whether you believe in it or not. When people grasp upwards, God brings them down; when people bow down, God lifts them up. The door of salvation is very wide — wide enough for anyone to come in; but the door is very low — low enough that everyone must bow their head.

The Lord Jesus told a parable. Two men went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood and prayed: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.” (Luke 18:11) Every word he said was true, but the word appearing most in his prayer was “I” — and while he stood before God, his eyes were fixed on the man beside him. And the other man? “But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ ” (Luke 18:13) In the original, “a sinner” carries the definite article — not one sinner among many, but the sinner. The Lord said it was the tax collector who went home justified. Brothers and sisters, there is a very reliable test for pride: when you are before God, who are you thinking about?

Why is bowing the head so hard? Look at Adam. After he sinned, his first reaction was not to confess but to hide. God came looking for him and asked the first question in the Bible: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9) Of course God knew where he was; he asked not to locate him but to give him a chance to turn back. But Adam said: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” (Genesis 3:12) He passed the blame on twice: first to the woman, then to the God who had given him the woman. Brothers and sisters, have we made any progress since Adam? The Bible says: “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” (Proverbs 28:13)

Psychology confirms this. In 1975 Miller and Ross reviewed a large body of research in the Psychological Bulletin and pointed out that people commonly display a “self-serving bias”: success is down to me, failure is down to others. In 1957 Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when my behaviour clashes with my self-image of “I am a good person,” the easiest thing is not to change my behaviour but to change my story. C. S. Lewis offers a comparison: if you are on the wrong road, progress means turning round and going back; the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man. Brothers and sisters, confession is the act of taking the exit. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

Our second key point: the humble are forgiven; the proud are rejected. The contrast between Saul and David is the most vivid. Saul disobeyed God’s command, and when the prophet came, his first words were: “You are blessed by Yahweh! I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 15:13) How spiritual! But Samuel said: “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?” (1 Samuel 15:14) The truth doesn’t change because of how we describe it; the sheep were still bleating. Saul made excuses: the people spared the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to Yahweh your God. Notice his wording — “your God,” not “my God.” When people are making excuses, even the way they address God gives the truth away. Samuel said: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22)

Someone may ask: didn’t Saul later say, “I have sinned”? Yes, he did. But read on: “Then he said, ‘I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:30) Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What he really cared about was not God’s heart but saving face in front of everyone. That is not repentance; that is public relations. In 1999 Kruger and Dunning published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, finding that the group with the least ability actually rated themselves the highest. The most dangerous thing about pride is not that it makes me go wrong, but that it keeps me from seeing that I have gone wrong. The 3-2-1 vision puts it well: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

David’s sin was even more serious: adultery, murder, cover-up. The prophet Nathan pointed at him and said: “You are the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7) David replied with a single sentence: “I have sinned against Yahweh.” And Nathan said: “Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.” (2 Samuel 12:13) No explanation, no “but.” He later wrote: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17) The original word for “broken” means shattered, snapped; “contrite” means crushed. Brothers and sisters, look at the contrast: Saul offered the best of the cattle and sheep, and God did not accept it; David offered only a broken heart, and God accepted him completely. For an offering can be a bargaining chip, but a broken heart is the surrender of my whole self.

The story of the prodigal son confirms this truth once again. He came to his senses in the pigsty and said: “I will get up and go to my father … I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” (Luke 15:18–19) He prepared three sentences. But when he actually came home, “while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck” (Luke 15:20), and he spoke only the first two. The third sentence vanished — the father didn’t let him finish. Why? Because the first two were repentance, and the third was a bargain. The father didn’t want a hired servant; he wanted a son. Brothers and sisters, in the ancient Near East, an elderly man of standing did not run; yet this father ran. He would rather lose his own dignity than let his son be shamed at the edge of the village. This is our God — he is more eager to forgive than we are to be forgiven.

Our third key point: humility brings revival and healing. God says: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14) These are the words God spoke when he appeared to Solomon by night after the dedication of the temple. Brothers and sisters, notice the order: the first step is not prayer but humbling ourselves. The Hebrew for “humble themselves” was originally a military term meaning to yield and surrender. Without a humble heart, prayer is merely a form — it becomes notifying God: Lord, I’ve already decided; please bless it. That isn’t prayer; that is filing a report.

Nineveh is the best example. Nineveh was the great city of the Assyrian Empire; its ruins lie near today’s Mosul in Iraq. Assyria was the most brutal military power of the ancient Near East. Jonah preached only a single message of judgement: “In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!” (Jonah 3:4) No comfort, no way out, no “unless.” Yet Scripture says: “The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.” (Jonah 3:5) Even the king did the same: “he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.” (Jonah 3:6) Four actions, and every one of them goes downwards. And the result? “God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way. God relented of the disaster which he said he would do to them, and he didn’t do it.” (Jonah 3:10) The fate of a whole city turned on whether one king was willing to leave his throne.

Church history is the same. In 1904 a revival broke out in Wales that touched the whole world. What the preacher Evan Roberts proclaimed was not lofty words or great wisdom, but four demands: put away every known sin; remove everything doubtful; obey the Holy Spirit completely; confess Christ publicly. Within a few short months, according to church records of the time, about a hundred thousand people turned to Christ. In January 1907 the same thing happened in Pyongyang. At a Bible conference, a local elder, Kil Sun-Joo, confessed before everyone that he had wronged the estate of a friend who had died, and was willing to make restitution. That confession was like a key that opened the floodgates: the whole congregation fell on their faces, weeping and confessing their sins, and this revival came to be called “the Korean Pentecost.” Brothers and sisters, the starting point of both revivals was not someone preaching a great sermon, but someone saying: I was wrong.

God has also written this truth into the things he has made. Water flows downhill: high ground cannot hold water; only a low-lying basin can collect it into a lake. Grace is the same; it always flows towards the lowest heart. But be careful: Israel has two lakes, both fed by the Jordan River. In the north, the Sea of Galilee is clear and full of fish; in the south, the Dead Sea lies about 430 metres below sea level, with a salt content about ten times that of seawater, and almost nothing can live in it. Where is the difference? The Sea of Galilee has an inflow and an outflow; the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out. Brothers and sisters, being low is not the same as being humble. Self-pity and self-enclosure are a Dead Sea kind of lowness. The lesson’s gentle reminder is spot on: true humility is not putting ourselves down, but admitting, “I need God.”

So how do we practise this week? The lesson gives us four practices. First, daily self-examination: before bed, ask yourself, in what things was I still proud today? I suggest checking yourself with three questions: Did I put someone else down in my heart today? Did I say something I knew would hurt, and say it anyway? Did I take the credit for something? Second, a prayer of repentance: be specific in confession. Don’t just say, “Lord, forgive me all my sins,” but name the time, the person, the words you said. David’s prayer is the best model: “Search me, God, and know my heart.” (Psalm 139:23)

Third, learning to submit: when someone reminds or corrects you, don’t justify yourself or argue; listen first and examine yourself first. Let me give you a very practical method called “three seconds and two words” — stay quiet for three seconds without answering, then say, “Thank you,” and once your heart has calmed down, work out how much of it is true. The Bible says: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19) Fourth, interceding for the nation: pray humbly for the church, for families and for the nation. The easiest trap to fall into in intercession is using prayer to accuse others. Daniel didn’t do that; he said: “we have sinned, and have dealt perversely.” (Daniel 9:5) Nehemiah too said: “Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned.” (Nehemiah 1:6) True intercession stands in the gap, not on the high ground.

Brothers and sisters, let us place today’s lesson within the 3-2-1 vision. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Jesus is our role model: “who, existing in the form of God … emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6–7) The Bible is our standard, and the Holy Spirit is our guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. When Jesus is King, I don’t have to be king; and once I don’t have to be king, I am free. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; life first, then relationships, then ministry. There is only one mindset to change today: bowing your head is not losing; bowing your head is the way to life.

Let us come back to the lesson’s closing words. Humility is medicine for the soul, the antidote to pride. Pride makes people fall; humility makes people receive grace. Pride shuts the gate of heaven; humility opens it. This morning I want to ask you three questions. First, before God: when was the last time I sincerely said, “Lord, I was wrong”? Second, before people: is there someone right now to whom I know in my heart I owe an apology, and I keep putting it off? Third, in my affairs: is there something I keep propping up by myself and have never truly entrusted to God? Let us, like David and like the prodigal son, not run away and not make excuses, but simply return to the Father’s embrace; like the king of Nineveh, be willing to come down from the throne; and like our Lord, willingly take the form of a servant.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. Lord, I confess that I often cover my weakness with pride, disguise my mistakes with excuses, and use busyness to escape your searching light. Today I will hide no longer; I choose to be humble before you. Forgive me and renew me; bring me back into your embrace. Take away those five “I will”s from my heart, and set your throne once again at the centre of my life. Give me a broken and contrite heart, and the courage to be the first to bow my head. May your grace come upon me, and upon my family, my church, this city and this nation; heal our hearts and bring heavenly revival. May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” (James 4:10) May the grace of the Lord be with you until we meet again.

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Doesn’t God Simply Strike Satan Down?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Let’s begin today by facing a question many believers have asked in their hearts but hardly dare say out loud: if God is almighty, why doesn’t he simply wipe Satan out in one stroke? Why let this spiritual war drag on for thousands of years, and let the world suffer so much?

The question is not irreverent. In fact, it is a key. Because when we honestly keep asking, we discover this: it isn’t that God “can’t beat” Satan; it’s that God “doesn’t fight that way”. If the almighty God chose to destroy Satan by sheer power, it wouldn’t take him a single second. But he didn’t do that. He chose the road that looks slowest, weakest and least like victory — he sent his only Son into the world as a man, born in a manger, raised in a carpenter’s home, and in the end nailed up between two robbers.

This is the most staggering truth in the gospel: God did not overpower Satan with might; he defeated him with love and obedience.

Let me begin with a scene from everyday life. A father told me that he and his teenage son had been locked in a cold war for three months. He said, “I’m his father. I raise him, I provide for him, I’ve given everything for him — don’t I have the right to make demands of him?” I asked him, “What is it you want? For him to bow his head, or for him to come home?” He was stunned. Because he realised that every time he had opened his mouth in those three months, he had been fighting over “whether I have the right”, and not once had he been fighting over “how I can win his heart back”.

Brothers and sisters, authority can bring people to their knees, but only humility can bring the heart to true surrender. This continues the truth we saw in the last lesson: humility is the antidote to pride. Today we go a step further and see that humility is not merely a virtue — humility is God’s strategy; it is not merely good character — humility is the strategy that wins.

Last time we saw that pride is the root of all evil, the cause of Satan’s fall and the source of humanity’s sin. Today we ask: how, then, does God deal with pride? The answer astonishes us: God doesn’t crush pride with a greater pride; God dissolves pride with humility.

It is commonly held that when the church father Augustine was asked in a letter what matters most in the Christian faith, he answered: first, humility; second, humility; third, humility. It sounds like exaggeration, but it is profound. For in the kingdom of God, humility is not one virtue among many; humility is the soil in which every other virtue grows. Without humility, even our zeal, our gifts and our service will slowly turn into tools for self-exalting.

In this lesson we will look together at three things: first, God does not destroy Satan by authority but overcomes him by humility; second, humility is God’s strategy for overcoming Satan; third, humility is the strongest weapon in relationships.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: How Philippians 2 Came to Be
sections.html:
Our key passage today comes from Philippians chapter 2. To understand it accurately, we need to know where it came from.

The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece. Acts 16 records that on his second missionary journey Paul, called by a vision in the night, crossed the sea into Macedonia, and Philippi became the first church he planted in Europe. Its first believers included Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, and the jailer whose whole household came to the Lord after the earthquake. The letter is generally thought to have been written around AD 60, while Paul was a prisoner in Rome awaiting Caesar’s judgement.

Notice the contrast: a prisoner bound in chains, with an uncertain future, wrote the most joyful book in the New Testament. The word “joy” recurs more than ten times in just four chapters. Paul isn’t talking about humility from a place of ease; he is talking about it from a prison cell. He isn’t talking about lowliness amid applause; he is talking about it in chains. That is what gives his words their weight.

So why did Paul write this passage in chapter 2? Because although the Philippian church loved the Lord, gave generously and stood firm under persecution, it had a hidden worry: factions and quarrels were beginning to appear among them. In chapter 4 Paul even names two co-workers, Euodia and Syntyche, and urges them to “be of the same mind in the Lord”. So at the very start of chapter 2 Paul says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3–4).

Then Paul does something extremely important: instead of carrying on with argument, he lifts up Jesus Christ and says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). And then comes our key passage today — the section church history calls the “Christ Hymn”. Many scholars believe it was very likely a song the early church sang in worship, which Paul quoted here. In other words, the early church did not treat “emptying himself” as an obscure theological term; it was a confession of faith they sang into their very lives.

The structure of the passage is crystal clear — a deep “V”: down from the glory of heaven, all the way to the manger, to the form of a servant, to death on the cross; then up from the dead, exalted by God to the highest place, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses. Every step down was one he chose himself; every step up was one God did for him. This is one of the most important spiritual laws in the whole Bible: whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Two other passages we will use today also need some background. Isaiah 14 is a lament over the king of Babylon, in which the prophet mocks how this arrogant monarch fell from the heights. Yet as the church through the ages has read it, they have seen behind its five “I will”s a shadow far older than the king of Babylon — the very pride that brought humanity down. Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians facing persecution and tempted to retreat into the rituals of the old covenant; the author wants them to see that the Jesus who humbled himself is the very author and perfecter of their faith.

With this background, we can now turn to today’s three key points.

sections.heading: 1. God Does Not Destroy Satan by Authority but Overcomes Him by Humility
sections.html:
Ever since the creation of the world, Satan has been challenging God’s authority. The prophet Isaiah left us this famous description:

“How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:12–14)

Brothers and sisters, count how many times “I will” appears here. Five, no less. “I will ascend into heaven”, “I will exalt my throne”, “I will sit on the mountain of assembly”, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds”, “I will make myself like the Most High”. The grammar of pride is always the first person; the direction of pride is always upward; the goal of pride is always “like the Most High” — that is, to leave our originally intended position and try to take God’s place.

The Hebrew verb for “ascend” here is alah, which is in itself a neutral word; the Bible also uses it of a burnt offering “going up”. The same movement — what matters is not high or low, but who is lifting me up. When God lifts a person up, it is grace; when a person lifts himself up, it is rebellion.

But look at the next verse: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:15). Five “I will”s pointing upward, answered by a single sentence of God’s judgement pointing down. This is exactly what Proverbs says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

Here is the question: if God has long since pronounced the sentence, why doesn’t he carry it out at once? Why has God tolerated Satan troubling the world for so long? The answer lies not in any limit to God’s power but in the depth of God’s purpose. What God wants is not merely to eliminate an enemy, but to display once and for all, before the whole universe, that “the way of pride is the way of death, and the way of humility is the way of life”.

So God did not erase Satan with a thunderbolt of power. Instead, he sent his Son into the world as a man:

“who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

Two key Greek words here deserve our attention. The first is “emptied himself”, kenoo in the original, meaning to pour out, to make empty. Note carefully: what Jesus emptied was not his divinity — he did not stop being God. What he laid aside was the use of the glory and rights of equality with God. The second is “a thing to be grasped”, harpagmos in the original, meaning something clutched tightly, held on to like plunder that one refuses to let go. Satan’s problem was that he wanted to “seize” a position that never belonged to him; Jesus’ beauty is that he did not cling even to what was rightly his.

Brothers and sisters, do you hear the contrast? One grabs what he does not have; the other lets go of what he already has. One falls because he grasps; the other is exalted because he lets go.

So look at this picture: Satan, who wanted to exalt himself, fell through pride; Jesus, who was willing to lower himself, was exalted through humility. This is a fixed and unshakeable law of the spiritual world — pride drags us down, humility lifts us up. The Lord Jesus himself put this law as plainly as it can be put: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Let me illustrate with a picture from nature. Water by its nature flows downward, and so all the rivers of the earth gather into the sea; and the sea can hold every river precisely because it lies lowest of all. The mountaintop, by contrast, may look highest, yet it cannot keep a single drop of water. People are the same: the lower someone’s position, the more life they carry; the loftier someone’s posture, the less remains with them.

Psychological research confirms this from another angle. In a 1996 study published in Psychological Review, the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues proposed the idea of “threatened egotism”, arguing that aggression and violence often come not from low self-esteem but from a highly favourable view of oneself that has been challenged or offended. In other words, the more someone needs to defend the image that “I’m really something”, the more violently they react once it is questioned. This shows exactly why, if you use authority to crush pride, what you get is not surrender but a fiercer backlash.

Let’s connect this truth with the 321 vision. 321 tells us that the problem of the old self is the self-centred life, and the way out for the new self is selflessness. Satan’s five “I will”s are the self-centred life at its extreme; Jesus’ “emptying himself” is selflessness at its height. And selflessness is not turning ourselves into zero, into nothing; it is placing ourselves in God’s hands, entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

So God’s strategy has never been “force against force” but “humility overcoming pride”. Not by arguing, not by power, not by emotion, but by obedience, trust and the lowliness of love. Brothers and sisters, if this truly turns around in our mindset, the way we relate to people will be completely different.

sections.heading: 2. Humility Is God’s Strategy for Overcoming Satan
sections.html:
In this second key point, we want to see more deeply that humility is not God’s last resort; humility is God’s strategy.

God does not subdue pride with intimidation, because pride is never crushed into submission; it is only provoked into resistance. A law of physics can help us understand this. Newton’s third law of motion says that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. However hard you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard. The human heart is the same. However forcefully you bear down on people, they push back with just as much resistance. This is exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

So God did something no one expected. He had the eternal Son become flesh, become a baby:

“But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone.” (Hebrews 2:9)

The Lord who created the angels now became a man made a little lower than the angels. This was no mistake; this was a plan. For verse 14 goes on to give the reason: “Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14).

Notice the phrase “through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death”. To abolish death, God’s method was — death; to overcome the one who held the power of death, God’s weapon was his own dying. In human logic this makes no sense at all; in God’s wisdom it is brilliant.

The cross looked like defeat; in fact it was the starting point of victory. On that day the sky went dark, the disciples scattered, the religious leaders jeered and the Roman soldiers divided his clothes. Satan probably thought he had won — Jesus was dead! But precisely at that moment of “lowest humiliation”, God’s power was fully displayed; death was overcome, and Satan’s power was stripped away. How forcefully Paul puts it: “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15).

The background of the word “triumphing” is the triumphal procession of a victorious Roman general returning to the city: the chariot in front, the captives behind, the whole city lining the streets. Paul is saying that the cross is Christ’s triumphal chariot. In the world’s eyes it was an instrument of execution; in God’s eyes it was the chariot of victory.

How did Jesus fight this battle? He fought it in a way that looked nothing like fighting. “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). What he spoke on the cross was not a curse but: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Brothers and sisters, this is the mystery of spiritual warfare: Satan tried to win by exalting himself; Jesus won by laying himself down. God’s victory is not suppressing the other side but turning it upside down. He did not pin the enemy to the ground; he made the enemy’s weapons entirely useless.

Jesus answered Satan’s pride with humility, and Satan was defeated so completely that he had nothing left to say. Why nothing left to say? Because Satan could no longer accuse a man who had never sinned yet was willing to die in the place of sinners; every accusation he had fell empty. The proclamation John heard in his vision was: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11). The weapons that overcome the enemy are the blood of the Lamb and a testimony that lays down its life — and both are the fruit of humility.

The same principle still holds today. “He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul learned this from a “thorn”. Three times he begged the Lord to take it away; the Lord did not remove it, but gave him something better: power displayed in weakness.

The prophet Zechariah said the same long before: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6). Brothers and sisters, 321 reminds us to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled. The reason we end up exhausted in the battle is often not that the enemy is too strong but that we are using the wrong weapons — we are fighting with our own might, ability, eloquence and face, so no wonder the fighting wears us out.

Scripture also gives us a living example. How mighty Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, was! He stood on his palace and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). Then God drove him from human society to live with the wild animals, until he lifted his eyes to heaven and his reason returned. His final testimony was: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37). God did not destroy him; God humbled him in order to save him. Brothers and sisters, God’s purpose in dealing with pride has never been to destroy people but to win them back.

sections.heading: 3. Humility Is the Strongest Weapon in Relationships
sections.html:
The third key point brings this truth back into our daily living.

We often want to deal with problems by “authority”. When people don’t submit, don’t listen, don’t cooperate, our most instinctive reaction is to pull rank, raise our voice and put our emotions on display. Parents say, “I’m your father!” Husbands say, “I’m the head of this house!” Co-workers say, “This should have been my call in the first place!” Words like these may bring temporary compliance, but they cannot buy a lasting relationship.

Brothers and sisters, remember these three sentences: power can make people yield; humility can make people turn. Power builds control; humility builds connection. Power changes behaviour; humility changes the heart.

The Lord Jesus spelled this out long ago: “But Jesus summoned them, and said, ‘You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many’” (Matthew 20:25–28).

“It shall not be so among you.” These few words are the watershed between the kingdom of God and the Worldly system. The Worldly system is a pyramid: the higher you are, the more people serve you. God’s system is turned upside down: the higher you are, the more people you serve. Jesus did not abolish authority; he redefined it: authority exists to serve, not to dominate.

So at the Last Supper he did something even his disciples tried to stop — he tied a towel around himself, took a basin of water and washed his disciples’ feet one by one, including Judas, who was about to betray him. Then he said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

On the cross Jesus did not command people to repent; he died for sinners. He loved people through action and won them over through humility. That is why Paul could dare to say: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

Research on marriage and family gives us strong support here. The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington spent many years in his “Love Lab” filming and analysing how couples interact. He and his colleagues found that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is not how often a couple argues but the presence of “contempt” in their interactions — the eye-rolling, the sneering, the looking-down-on-you attitude. What is contempt? Contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship. Conversely, he also found that couples who are willing to accept each other’s influence, and willing to “repair” in the middle of conflict, have the most stable relationships. Being willing to be influenced is what humility looks like in concrete form.

Research on workplaces and teams says the same. A 2013 study by Bradley Owens, Michael Johnson and Terence Mitchell in the journal Organization Science found that humility shown by leaders — acknowledging their own limits, appreciating others’ strengths, being eager to learn — is positively associated with team learning and performance. Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, with her 1999 concept of “psychological safety”, likewise showed that only when those who lead are willing to admit they make mistakes will team members dare to speak the truth. A leader who never admits a mistake earns not respect but silence.

In his 2001 book “Good to Great”, the management scholar Jim Collins studied companies that went from good to great and found that their leaders shared one trait, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: deep personal humility combined with fierce professional will. Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research has brushed against the edge of this truth; how much more has the Lord we believe in lived it out with his whole life two thousand years ago.

A picture often comes to my mind. Two goats meet on a narrow log bridge that only one can cross at a time. If neither will back down, they lock horns and both fall into the water — both sides lose. But if one is willing to lie down and let the other step over it, both cross safely. The one that lay down seems to have lost, but in fact it saved two lives.

In families, churches and teams, when we face conflict, misunderstanding or opposition, if we are willing to lay ourselves down first — to listen first, understand first, give way first — we will discover that humility brings a transformation of the heart rather than grudging compliance in behaviour. James says: “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Solomon says: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

Humility may look like a loss for a while, but its fruit lasts. It wins people’s trust, respect and love. Paul even said to the Corinthian believers who were suing one another: “Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you, that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?” (1 Corinthians 6:7). Brothers and sisters, in God’s ledger, no one who was willing to lose out has ever truly lost.

Scripture holds a beautiful example of this. Jacob had owed Esau a debt for twenty years — he had cheated him out of the birthright and the blessing and fled to Haran. Twenty years later, on his way back, he heard that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men, and he was terrified. What did he do? First he prayed, then he sent gifts ahead of him drove by drove, and finally he himself went on ahead of everyone, and “bowed himself to the ground seven times” (Genesis 33:3). The brother who had come with four hundred men, bent on settling scores, saw this, and the Bible says: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept” (Genesis 33:4). The force of four hundred men was never used; seven bows to the ground melted twenty years of hatred. Brothers and sisters, this is the power of humility.

This is God’s way: not to overawe people with force, but to move them with love.

Let’s connect this back to 321: 321 says “people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things”, and also that the order of service is “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. Many people turn the order upside down — they grab the ministry first, want relationships second, and only care about life last — and the result is that the ministry gets done but the people scatter. We must also remember the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If my relationship with God is right, I don’t need to prove myself in front of people; and only those who don’t need to prove themselves have room to humble themselves.

Then there is the precious 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; in front of each “2”, we practise living a selfless life, and the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that fruit is not grown in a monastery; it is grown in relationships. The person who is hardest to get along with is the very garden God has given you to bear fruit in.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Living Humility Out as a Road
sections.html:
If we sum up today’s message in the language of 321, it becomes very clear.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, humbled himself and was obedient to death; that is the pattern I am to learn. The Bible is my standard — it is not my feelings, my face or my hurt that have the final say, but God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — humility is not a discipline I grit my teeth to keep up; it is fruit the Holy Spirit grows in me.

Second, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: the scene of a conflict is often a battle over the throne — who is King here, me or Jesus? If I insist on winning, it is actually I who am sitting on the throne. Let Jesus receive all the glory: the final test of humility is this — when it’s all over, who has been lifted up, me or the Lord?

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system runs on power; God’s system runs on denying of self. Every time we choose humility, we lay one more brick of God’s system in our own family, small group and workplace.

Next, look at the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. The most important thing in today’s lesson is the first — the change of mindset. I used to think that “winning” meant the other person backing down; now I know that “winning” means their heart being won back. I used to think humility meant losing out; now I know humility is a strategy. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry naturally changes.

321 also often reminds us of four shifts in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective — people see the cross as defeat, God sees it as victory; from the earthly to the heavenly — earth keeps score of who has the upper hand, heaven remembers who was willing to deny themselves; from the temporary to the eternal — how light a moment’s face is compared with eternal reward; from the worldly to the godly — no longer winning by the world’s methods, but by God’s.

And remember: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. In a conflict our focus easily wanders — one moment fixed on our own grievance, the next on the other person’s fault, the next blaming the circumstances. When the focus slips, the heart is thrown into turmoil; when the focus returns to Jesus, the heart is steadied. Solomon says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Finally, the 235 relationships. Become a “2” with a brother or sister who is also pursuing selflessness, supporting and reminding one another; go on to build a “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children and passing life on; then move into a “5”, serving alongside spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team, establishing God’s system together. Brothers and sisters, it is hard for one person to stay humble for long, because pride loves to sprout in isolation; but when two people watch over each other and three generations pass life on to one another, humility can become a culture.

And all of this points to the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God — led by the Holy Spirit, corrected by the Bible, living out the life of Jesus, letting Jesus be King, and in the end letting Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to root them deep in our lives.

Practice 1: In Conflict, Be Still First

Don’t rush to react. Pray first, and let God remind you how to respond.

Information: First let the truth enter your mind — “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). Physiology tells us too that in strong emotion the brain’s amygdala reacts before anything else; the psychologist Daniel Goleman, in his 1995 book, called this “amygdala hijack”, and in that moment our judgement drops sharply. So “being still first” is not passive; it is so that the heart can come back before God.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you — in that conflict, what was I really protecting: the truth, or my face?

Conviction: Acknowledge from the heart that stillness is not losing; stillness is handing the first word to God. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

Implementation: This week, when someone touches a sore spot, first count silently to ten and pray one short sentence in your heart: “Lord, please be King.”

Evaluation: Before bed, think back: how many times today did I rush to answer back? How did those times turn out?

Correction: Identify the one situation, the one person, the one sentence that most easily makes you lose control, and pray over it in advance.

Repetition: Keep at it for forty days in a row, and stillness will turn from a struggle into an instinct.

Multiplication: Teach this practice to your children and your small-group members, and practise it alongside them.

Practice 2: Choose to Lay Down Your Rights

When you are “in the right, in authority and in a position to act”, practise stepping back and letting God speak.

Information: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Revelation: The Lord Jesus existed in the form of God, yet did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped. What he laid down were rights he truly possessed. Brothers and sisters, what we so often cannot lay down are merely rights we imagine we have.

Conviction: Believe that if I give way, God himself will step in; if I take matters into my own hands, God steps back.

Implementation: This week, pick one matter where “I’m clearly in the right” and deliberately don’t fight over it; write it down in your prayer journal and hand it to God.

Evaluation: A month from now, look back: what became of that matter?

Correction: If you find that you are taking revenge through a cold war or silence, that is not laying down your rights; it is fighting by other means, and you need to repent.

Repetition: Practise on small things, so that you can stand firm when big things come.

Multiplication: Tell others the testimony of how God acted after you laid down your rights.

Practice 3: Serve Others in Humility

When a relationship is tense, take the initiative to care for and help the other person, expressing love through action.

Information: “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2).

Revelation: At the Last Supper the Lord washed Judas’s feet. The very man he served was the one about to betray him.

Conviction: Believe that action melts a hard heart better than words.

Implementation: This week, for the person you least want to face, do one small, concrete thing — a glass of water, a word of greeting, a helping hand.

Evaluation: As I did it, was my heart willing, or did it carry a whiff of proving myself?

Correction: If your motives are impure, don’t stop serving; ask the Lord to cleanse your motives, and keep going.

Repetition: Keep doing it, until there is no bitterness left in your heart when you pray for that person.

Multiplication: Share it in your small group and invite a brother or sister to do this practice with you, and you will become each other’s “2”.

Practice 4: Meditate on the Cross of Jesus

Think about how he overcame pride with humility, and ask him to give you the same heart.

Information: Quietly read Philippians 2:5–11, slowly, one verse a day.

Revelation: Ask the Lord one question — Lord, how low did you go? And what am I still holding on to?

Conviction: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). This is not a suggestion; it is a command, and a promise too.

Implementation: Every morning, spend three minutes meditating on the cross, then bless one person who has wronged you.

Evaluation: After doing this for a while, have my feelings towards that person changed?

Correction: If your heart is still hard, tell the Lord honestly about that hard heart and ask him to give you a new one.

Repetition: Build meditation on the cross into your daily morning devotion, as a regular practice.

Multiplication: Gather your family and read a passage of Philippians 2 together at the dinner table.

A Gentle Reminder

Power can subdue people but cannot change them; humility looks weak, yet it can conquer the hardest heart. Jesus’ humility was not retreat; it was the strategy of victory.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s draw today’s message together.

God could destroy Satan by authority, but he chose to win by humility. Because true victory is not destroying the opponent but transforming the heart. The cross of Jesus is the height of humility, and the beginning of victory.

Let’s look once more at that spiritual law. Satan said “I will” five times, and he was brought down to Sheol; but in the Garden of Gethsemane Jesus said: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39) — and he was exalted to the highest place. Brothers and sisters, which kind of words are you speaking today?

How gentle is the invitation the Lord Jesus holds out to us: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). Notice that the Lord did not say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me” — learn my ways. What he promises is not the thrill of victory, but rest for the soul. For only someone who no longer needs to prove himself is truly free.

Peter urges us in the same way: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6). “In due time” — the timetable for being lifted up is in God’s hands, not ours. Our part is simply to go low; the lifting up we leave to God.

So today, let us follow the Lord’s example, and in the face of pride’s challenge and conflict with others, choose humility and choose love.

I want to issue three calls to you. First, in your heart, let Jesus take the throne again — not me as King, but Jesus as King. Second, this week, take the first humble step towards one person — a phone call, an apology, a move to reach out. Third, give all the glory to Jesus — when a relationship is truly healed, remember that it was not your own skill but the Lord’s grace.

Then God’s glory will be revealed through us, pride will be put to shame, humility will triumph, and the showers of revival will surely fall upon this land.

keyVerses: who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. (Philippians 2:6–8)

Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. (Philippians 2:9–11)
declarations: Lord, I want to learn from you — to win not by pride but by humility.
Help me lay down my rights and lay down myself, and live out your gentleness and humility in every relationship.
May your humility become strength in me, so that I overcome pride with love and hardness with gentleness.
practices: Choose to lay down your rights
Meditate on the cross of Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you. You existed in the form of God, yet for our sake you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and were obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Lord, forgive us. So often we try to overpower people with authority, win them with arguments and control them with our emotions, yet refuse to take your way — going low, denying ourselves, moving people with love. Please cleanse us of every “I will” inside us that refuses to let go.

Holy Spirit, work in us today and give us the heart of Jesus. Let us be still first in conflict, give way when we are in the right, reach out in love in tense relationships, and meditate on your cross every morning.
May our families, our small groups and our church be knit together through humility; may pride find no foothold among us.
Be King, Lord, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Isaiah 14:13–14 records Satan’s five “I will”s. Looking back over this week, what has been the strongest “I will” in your heart? If you let Jesus be King in that matter, what would be different?

Philippians 2:6–8 says the Lord Jesus “emptied himself”. In the most tense relationship you have right now, which specific right is God asking you to “lay down”? How do you plan to take the first step this week?
l079.title: Humility Is a Strategy for Victory
l079.subtitle: Humility Is the Antidote to Pride (Part 2)
l079.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

blog.title: Why Doesn’t God Simply Strike Satan Down?

blocks.x: Humility Is a Strategy for Victory

Have you ever quietly asked this question in your heart: if God is almighty, why doesn’t he simply wipe Satan out in one stroke? Why let this war drag on for thousands of years, and let the world suffer so much?

The question is not irreverent. In fact, it is a key. Because when you honestly keep asking, you discover something staggering: it isn’t that God “can’t beat” Satan; it’s that God “doesn’t fight that way”.
Five “I Will”s, One Sentence of Judgement

The prophet Isaiah left us this famous description: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Count them: five “I will”s, no less. The grammar of pride is always the first person; the direction of pride is always upward; the goal of pride is always “like the Most High” — that is, to leave our originally intended position and try to take God’s place.
But the next verse says: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.” Five sentences pointing upward, answered by a single sentence of judgement pointing down.

Faced with such pride, God did not use his power to erase Satan. He did the very opposite — he sent his own Son into the world as a man: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)
Do you see the contrast? Satan grabs at what he does not have; Jesus lets go of what he already has. One falls because he grasps; the other is exalted because he lets go.
The Cross Is God’s Strategy

God does not subdue pride with intimidation, because pride is never crushed into submission; it is only provoked into resistance. It’s like Newton’s third law of motion: however hard you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard. The human heart is the same.

So God chose another way. He let Jesus go to the very lowest place, so that on the cross “through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death”. That day, Satan probably thought he had won. But precisely at that moment of lowest humiliation, God’s power was fully displayed — death was overcome, and Satan’s power was stripped away. Paul says: “triumphing over them in it.” (Colossians 2:15) In the world’s eyes the cross was an instrument of execution; in God’s eyes it was the chariot of victory.
This is the mystery of spiritual warfare: Satan tried to win by exalting himself; Jesus won by laying himself down. God’s victory is not suppressing the other side but turning it upside down.
Humility Is the Strongest Weapon in Relationships
Bring this truth home, and you will feel its weight at once.

When people don’t submit or don’t listen, our most instinctive reaction is to pull rank, raise our voice and put our emotions on display. That may bring temporary compliance, but it cannot buy a lasting relationship.
Power can make people yield; humility can make people turn. Power builds control; humility builds connection. Power changes behaviour; humility changes the heart.

The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington spent many years filming and analysing how couples interact. He found that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is not how often a couple argues but the presence of “contempt” — the eye-rolling, the sneering, the looking-down-on-you attitude. What is contempt? Contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship.

Think of Jacob. He was afraid his brother Esau was coming with four hundred men to take revenge. He didn’t prepare for battle. First he prayed, then he sent gifts, and finally he himself went on ahead of everyone and bowed himself to the ground seven times. And the result? Esau ran to embrace him, and the two of them wept. The force of four hundred men was never used; seven bows to the ground melted twenty years of hatred.
Humility may look like a loss for a while, but its fruit lasts. In God’s ledger, no one who was willing to lose out has ever truly lost.
What You Can Do This Week

First, in conflict, be still first: don’t rush to react; pray first. Second, choose to lay down your rights: when you are in the right, in authority and in a position to act, step back and let God speak. Third, serve others in humility: when a relationship is tense, take the initiative to love. Fourth, meditate on the cross of Jesus: ask him to give you the same heart.

Kingdom 321 reminds us: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. And the order is always life first, then relationships, then ministry — people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things.
God could destroy Satan by authority, but he chose to win by humility. Because true victory is not destroying the opponent but transforming the heart.
Questions for Reflection
In the most strained relationship you have right now, which specific “right” is God asking you to lay down? What first step are you willing to take this week?
