script: Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we come to the second talk on “Humility Is the Antidote to Pride”, and our title is: Humility Is a Strategy for Victory. Last time we saw that pride is the root of all evil. Today we ask: how, then, does God deal with pride? The answer astonishes us — God doesn’t crush pride with a greater pride; God dissolves pride with humility. Listen to today’s theme passage: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, let me first ask a question: if God is almighty, why doesn’t he simply wipe Satan out in one stroke? The answer is not that God can’t beat him, but that God doesn’t fight that way. A father told me that he and his son had been locked in a cold war for three months. He said, “I’m his father — don’t I have the right to make demands of him?” I asked him, “What is it you want? For him to bow his head, or for him to come home?” He was stunned. Brothers and sisters, authority can bring people to their knees, but only humility can bring the heart to true surrender.

Today’s passage comes from Philippians chapter 2. Paul, who wrote this letter, was a prisoner in Rome at the time, around AD 60. A man in chains wrote the most joyful book in the New Testament. Why did he talk about humility? Because there were factions and quarrels in the Philippian church. So Paul didn’t carry on with argument; he lifted up Jesus and said, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5) Brothers and sisters, the answer to problems in relationships is always found in Jesus.

Let’s look first at Satan. Isaiah records him saying: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Brothers and sisters, count them: there are five “I will”s here. The grammar of pride is always the first person; the direction of pride is always upward; the goal of pride is to take God’s place. And the result? “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol.” (Isaiah 14:15) Pride goes before destruction.

Now look at Jesus. He, “existing in the form of God … emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”. In the original, “emptied himself” means to pour out; “a thing to be grasped” means something clutched and never let go. Brothers and sisters, do you see the contrast? Satan clutches what he does not have; Jesus lets go of what he already has. One falls because he grasps; the other is exalted because he lets go. The Lord himself said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) Pride drags us down; humility lifts us up.

To overcome the one who held the power of death, God’s weapon was his own dying. Hebrews says the Lord partook of flesh and blood, “that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). The cross looked like defeat; in fact it was the starting point of victory. Satan thought he had won — Jesus was dead! But at that very moment of lowest humiliation, God’s power was fully displayed. Paul says: “triumphing over them in it.” (Colossians 2:15) The cross is Christ’s chariot of triumph.

Brothers and sisters, this principle still holds today. The Lord said to Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Think of Newton’s third law of motion: however hard you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard. The human heart is the same. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. That is why 321 reminds us to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you are glad; rely on the brain and you are troubled.

Now let’s bring this truth home. When people don’t listen, what is our most instinctive reaction? We raise our voice, pull rank and put our emotions on display. That may bring temporary compliance, but it cannot buy a lasting relationship. Brothers and sisters, remember this: power can make people yield; humility can make people turn. Power builds control; humility builds connection. The psychologist John Gottman spent many years studying how couples interact, and he found that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is “contempt”. What is contempt? Contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship.

The Lord Jesus said: “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) He did not abolish authority; he redefined it: authority exists to serve. Think of Jacob. He was afraid his brother Esau was coming with four hundred men to take revenge. What did he do? He bowed himself to the ground seven times. And the Bible says Esau ran to embrace him, and the two of them wept. Brothers and sisters, the force of four hundred men was never used; seven bows to the ground melted twenty years of hatred. Lay down first, listen first, give way first, and hearts are transformed.

Next, four practices. First, in conflict, be still first: don’t rush to respond; pray first. Second, choose to lay down your rights: when you are in the right, in authority and in a position to act, step back and let God speak. Third, serve others in humility: when a relationship is tense, take the initiative to love. Fourth, meditate on the cross of Jesus: ask him to give you the same heart. Brothers and sisters, walk these practices through the eight stages — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — and then your mindset will truly change.

Brothers and sisters, we are nearly at the end. God could destroy Satan by authority, but he chose to win by humility. Because true victory is not destroying the opponent but transforming the heart. The Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Today I want to issue three calls to you: let Jesus take the throne of your heart again; this week, take the first humble step towards one person; and give all the glory to Jesus.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet for our sake you emptied yourself and were obedient to the point of death. Forgive us for so often trying to overpower people with authority and win them with arguments. Give us the heart of Jesus, so that we are still first in conflict, give way when we are in the right, and reach out in love in tense relationships. Be King, Lord, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless every brother and sister, and give rest to our souls.

Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we come to the second talk on “Humility Is the Antidote to Pride”, and our title is: Humility Is a Strategy for Victory. Last time we saw that pride is the root of all evil, the cause of Satan’s fall and the starting point of humanity’s sin. Today we go a step further and ask a more pressing question: how, then, does God deal with pride? Brothers and sisters, the answer astonishes us — God doesn’t crush pride with a greater pride; God dissolves pride with humility. Listen to today’s theme passage: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

Let me first ask a question: if God is almighty, why doesn’t he simply wipe Satan out in one stroke? Brothers and sisters, the question is not irreverent; it is a key. When we honestly keep asking, we discover this: it isn’t that God can’t beat Satan; it’s that God doesn’t fight that way. If the almighty God chose to destroy Satan by sheer power, it wouldn’t take him a single second. But he didn’t do that. He sent his only Son into the world as a man, born in a manger, raised in a carpenter’s home, and in the end nailed up between two robbers. This is the most staggering truth in the gospel: God did not overpower Satan with might; he defeated him with love and obedience.

Let me describe a real scene. A father told me that he and his teenage son had been locked in a cold war for three months. He said, “I raise him, I provide for him — don’t I have the right to make demands of him?” I asked him one thing: “What is it you want? For him to bow his head, or for him to come home?” He was stunned. Brothers and sisters, he realised that every time he had opened his mouth in those three months, he had been fighting over “whether I have the right”, and not once over “how I can win my son’s heart back”. Authority can bring people to their knees, but only humility can bring the heart to true surrender. Today we will look at three things: God does not destroy Satan by authority but overcomes him by humility; humility is God’s strategy for overcoming Satan; and humility is the strongest weapon in relationships.

First, where the passage came from. The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, and it became the first church Paul planted in Europe; its first believers included Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, and the jailer whose whole household came to the Lord. The letter is generally thought to have been written around AD 60, while Paul was a prisoner in Rome. Brothers and sisters, notice the contrast: a prisoner in chains, with an uncertain future, wrote the most joyful book in the New Testament. Why did he talk about humility? Because factions and quarrels were beginning to appear in the Philippian church; Paul even named Euodia and Syntyche and urged them to be of the same mind in the Lord. So instead of carrying on with argument, he lifted up Jesus and said: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

Let’s look first at Satan. Isaiah 14 records the words of his heart: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Brothers and sisters, count them: there are five “I will”s here. The grammar of pride is always the first person; the direction of pride is always upward; the goal of pride is always “like the Most High” — that is, to leave our originally intended position and try to take God’s place. What matters is not high or low, but who is lifting me up: when God lifts a person up, it is grace; when a person lifts himself up, it is rebellion.

Where do the five “I will”s end? The very next verse tells us: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.” (Isaiah 14:15) Five sentences pointing upward, answered by a single sentence of judgement pointing down. Proverbs puts it even more directly: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18) Brothers and sisters, the Bible gives us a living example. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, stood on his palace boasting of his own might and power; then God made him live with the wild animals, until he lifted his eyes to heaven. His final words were: “those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37) God did not destroy him; God humbled him in order to save him. God’s purpose in dealing with pride has never been to destroy people but to win them back.

Now look at Jesus. He, “existing in the form of God … emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”. There are two key Greek words here. The first is “emptied himself”, which in the original means to pour out; what Jesus emptied was not his divinity — he laid aside the use of the glory and rights of equality with God. The second is “a thing to be grasped”, which in the original means something clutched tightly and never let go. Brothers and sisters, do you see the contrast? Satan’s problem was that he wanted to seize what never belonged to him; Jesus’ beauty is that he did not cling even to what was rightly his.

One grabs what he does not have; the other lets go of what he already has. One falls because he grasps; the other is exalted because he lets go. The Lord himself put this law as plainly as it can be put: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) I often use a picture: the sea can gather every river because it lies lowest of all; the mountaintop looks highest, yet cannot keep a single drop of water. Psychology confirms it from another angle: in a study published in 1996, the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues argued that aggression often comes not from low self-esteem but from a highly favourable view of oneself that has been offended. So, brothers and sisters, if you use authority to crush pride, what you get is not surrender but a fiercer backlash.

Our second key point: humility is not God’s last resort; humility is God’s strategy. Hebrews says: “But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor.” (Hebrews 2:9) Brothers and sisters, the Lord who created the angels now became a man made a little lower than the angels. This was no mistake; this was a plan. Hebrews was written to Jewish believers facing persecution, and the author wants them to see that the one they follow is a Lord who willingly took the lowest road.

Why the incarnation? The passage goes on to explain: “he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil.” (Hebrews 2:14) Hear this clearly: to overcome the one who held the power of death, God’s weapon was his own dying. In human logic this makes no sense at all; in God’s wisdom it is brilliant. John says too: “To this end the Son of God was revealed: that he might destroy the works of the devil.” (1 John 3:8)

The cross looked like defeat; in fact it was the starting point of victory. That day the disciples scattered and the religious leaders jeered, and Satan probably thought he had won — Jesus was dead! But precisely at that moment of lowest humiliation, God’s power was fully displayed. Paul says: “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.” (Colossians 2:15) The background of the word “triumphing” is the triumphal procession of a victorious Roman general returning to the city. What the world saw as an instrument of execution, God saw as a chariot of victory. And how did the Lord fight this battle? “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten.” (1 Peter 2:23) What he spoke on the cross was: “Father, forgive them.” (Luke 23:34)

Brothers and sisters, this principle still holds today. The Lord said to Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Three times Paul begged the Lord to take the thorn away; the Lord did not remove it, but gave him something better. The prophet says too: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6) Think of Newton’s third law of motion: however hard you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard; however forcefully you bear down on people, they push back with just as much resistance. This is exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. So rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled.

Our third key point brings the truth home. When people don’t submit or don’t listen, what is our most instinctive reaction? We raise our voice, pull rank and put our emotions on display. Parents say, “I’m your father!” Co-workers say, “This should have been my call in the first place!” Brothers and sisters, words like these may bring temporary compliance, but they cannot buy a lasting relationship. Remember these three sentences: power can make people yield; humility can make people turn. Power builds control; humility builds connection. Power changes behaviour; humility changes the heart.

The Lord Jesus spelled this out long ago: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) “It shall not be so among you” — these few words are the watershed between the kingdom of God and the worldly system. The worldly system is a pyramid: the higher you are, the more people serve you; God’s system is turned upside down. The Lord did not abolish authority; he redefined it: authority exists to serve, not to dominate. That is why at the Last Supper he tied a towel around himself and washed his disciples’ feet — even the feet of Judas, who was about to betray him.

Research on marriage gives us strong support. The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington spent many years filming and analysing how couples interact, and he found that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is not how often a couple argues but the presence of “contempt” — the eye-rolling, the sneering, the looking-down-on-you attitude. Brothers and sisters, contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship. Conversely, couples who are willing to accept each other’s influence have the most stable relationships. A picture often comes to my mind: two goats meet on a narrow log bridge. If neither will back down, they lock horns and both fall into the water; but if one is willing to lie down, both cross safely. The one that lay down seems to have lost, but in fact it saved two lives.

Scripture holds a beautiful example of this. Jacob cheated his brother out of the birthright and fled to Haran for twenty years. On his way back, he heard that his brother was coming to meet him with four hundred men, and he was terrified. What did he do? First he prayed, then he sent gifts ahead of him drove by drove, and finally he himself went on ahead of everyone and bowed himself to the ground seven times. And the Bible says: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.” (Genesis 33:3–4) Brothers and sisters, the force of four hundred men was never used; seven bows to the ground melted twenty years of hatred. This is the power of humility. 321 reminds us: everyone we relate to is our “2”; as we practise selflessness before each “2”, the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows.

Now for the practices. First, in conflict, be still first: don’t rush to react; pray first, and let God remind you how to respond. Proverbs says: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.” (Proverbs 18:13) In 1995 the psychologist Daniel Goleman described the “amygdala hijack”, showing that in strong emotion our judgement drops sharply. So being still first is not passive; it brings the heart back before God first. Second, choose to lay down your rights: when you are in the right, in authority and in a position to act, practise stepping back. Paul says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath.” (Romans 12:19) Brothers and sisters, if I give way, God himself will step in; if I take matters into my own hands, God steps back.

Third, serve others in humility: when a relationship is tense, take the initiative to care and to help. “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love.” (Ephesians 4:2) This week, do one small, concrete thing for the person you least want to face. Fourth, meditate on the cross of Jesus: each day spend three minutes reading Philippians 2 slowly, and ask the Lord one question — Lord, how low did you go? And what am I still holding on to? Brothers and sisters, walk these practices through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Only when you reach Multiplication is this life truly passed on.

Let’s use 321 to sum up today. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he emptied and humbled himself; the Bible is my standard — it is not my face that has the final say; the Holy Spirit is my guide — humility is fruit the Holy Spirit grows, not something we grit our teeth to keep up. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) The fivefold change begins with the mindset: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The order is life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. Our perspective must shift too: from man’s to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal.

Brothers and sisters, we are coming to the end. God could destroy Satan by authority, but he chose to win by humility. Because true victory is not destroying the opponent but transforming the heart. Satan said “I will” five times, and he was brought down to Sheol; in the Garden of Gethsemane Jesus said: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39) — and he was exalted to the highest place. Which kind of words are you speaking today? How gentle is the Lord’s invitation: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice that the Lord did not say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me”. I want to issue three calls: let Jesus take the throne of your heart again; this week, take the first humble step towards one person; and give all the glory to Jesus.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet for our sake you emptied yourself and were obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Lord, forgive us. So often we try to overpower people with authority, win them with arguments and control them with our emotions, yet refuse to take your way. Please cleanse us of every “I will” inside us that refuses to let go. Holy Spirit, give us the heart of Jesus, so that we are still first in conflict, give way when we are in the right, reach out in love in tense relationships, and meditate on your cross every morning. Be King, Lord, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless every brother and sister; may pride be put to shame, may humility triumph, and may the showers of revival fall upon this land.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Three Seconds After the Blow Are the Real Pulpit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by taking you back to a very concrete scene.

It is a Wednesday evening, and the church’s co-workers’ meeting is under way. Just as it is about to wrap up, one of the co-workers suddenly says: “This was your fault in the first place.” The tone isn’t harsh, but the words are hard; there aren’t many people in the room, but everyone who matters happens to be there. You sit there with a smile still on your face, while inside you have already started gathering evidence — which day you sent the message, which time you reminded everyone, which task was never your responsibility at all. You don’t say a word, but you know full well that if the other person says one more thing, you will spread that whole pile of evidence out on the table.

Brothers and sisters, that moment is the truest moment of our lives. Because a person’s spiritual condition is seen not in how well he speaks from the pulpit but in what rises first in his heart in the three seconds after he has been wronged. The words from the pulpit are ones we have prepared; the reaction in those three seconds is what flows naturally out of our lives.

The most natural human reaction is an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. It is almost instinct. In secondary-school science we learned Newton’s third law of motion: between two bodies, action and reaction are equal in size and opposite in direction. Pride between people seems to obey the same law: you push me once, I’ll push you back once — and usually with a little interest added. You give me one cold word, I give you two; you step back one pace, I step back three. In the end both people are standing where they started, neither willing to move first, and the relationship simply freezes.

This is what the 321 vision keeps reminding us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Pride is never subdued by pride; it is only fed by it. Fire cannot put out fire; only water can.

Yet Jesus’ teaching runs completely against our instincts. He says: “whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39). He wants us to answer pride with humility and overcome evil with good.

Notice that he isn’t asking us to shrink back in weakness, nor to pretend it doesn’t hurt. He wants us to learn his love, a love that goes beyond the world’s logic. Humility is not losing your dignity; it is choosing love. Humility is not retreat; it is victory.

The church father Augustine pointed out in The City of God that pride is the beginning of all sin. C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, likewise wrote that according to Christian teachers the essential vice, the utmost evil, is pride. If pride is the root of the disease, what is the cure? Not a cleverer argument, not a more elegant counter-attack, but humility.

This is the third talk in “Humility Is the Antidote to Pride”. In the first two we saw together that the root of pride is the self-centred life — leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and trying to take God’s place — whereas humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position: let man be man and let God be God. Today we face a more practical question: when someone else’s pride has already struck me in the face, what am I to do?

Brothers and sisters, the answer lies in three pictures: a left cheek turned, a cloak handed over, and an extra mile walked.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Fourth Way on the Mountain
sections.html:
To understand these words of Jesus, we first need to go and stand on that mountain.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew, also called Levi, one of the Lord Jesus’ twelve disciples and formerly a tax collector in Capernaum. A man who had once collected taxes from his own people on behalf of Rome, despised by everyone, later became the one who recorded the charter of the kingdom of heaven — that alone is the finest footnote to grace. The Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christian readers. Matthew quotes the Old Testament again and again to prove that Jesus is the Messiah God promised, the Son of David, the true King of Israel.

Matthew chapters 5 to 7 are the familiar Sermon on the Mount, the first of the five great discourses Matthew records; you could call it the constitution of the kingdom of heaven. In this discourse Jesus says six times over: “You have heard that it was said … but I tell you …” He was not abolishing the law. He said plainly: “Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill” (Matthew 5:17). He was bringing the law back from an external code to the intention in God’s heart.

The passage we read today is the fifth of those six contrasts. The sixth, which follows straight after, is “love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44); and the conclusion of the whole section is: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). In other words, turning the other cheek is not an isolated rule; it is the road to becoming “like the Father”.

“An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth” comes from Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. Many people think God was encouraging revenge, but the very opposite is true. In the ancient Near East, revenge had no upper limit. Genesis records Lamech arrogantly boasting: “If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times” (Genesis 4:24). A life for an eye, a whole clan for a tooth — that is the logic of humanity once it has left God. When God gave “an eye for an eye”, he was putting a ceiling on revenge: compensation could not exceed the damage. And this law was a judicial principle for judges to administer, not a personal licence for revenge.

But by Jesus’ day, this law, originally meant to restrain revenge, had been co-opted into a charm to justify it. People said: “Even the Bible says an eye for an eye — why should I put up with it?” And that is exactly where Jesus takes up the words: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil.”

The Greek word for “resist” is anthistēmi, meaning to stand opposite, to oppose head-on. Jesus is not telling us to take no stand against evil — James 4:7 says plainly, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you”, using the very same word. What Jesus forbids is resisting evil people by evil people’s methods; he forbids us to answer pride with pride. He wants us to change battlefields and change weapons.

There is one more thing we must keep in mind. Judea at that time lay under the iron heel of the Roman Empire. Taxes were heavy, soldiers were arrogant, the people were humiliated. Faced with this, the Jews of the day had roughly three options: the Zealots urged armed revolt, the Pharisees urged separating themselves by the law, and the Essenes simply withdrew into the wilderness — out of sight, out of mind. And on the mountain Jesus opened a fourth way — overcoming evil with humility and love.

Brothers and sisters, two thousand years have passed, and these four ways still lie before us. In the office, at home, in our chat groups, we are still choosing every day: Do I hit back? Do I use a spiritual label to wall myself off from people? Do I retreat into my shell and give them the cold shoulder? Or do I take the Lord’s fourth way?

sections.heading: 1. Jesus Answers Human Pride with Humility
sections.html:
1. The Text: A Saying Often Misunderstood

In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39).

This saying is often misunderstood, as if Christians should let anyone push them around — not make a sound when struck, not seek help when harmed. In fact, what Jesus is teaching is not cowardice but spiritual responsiveness: do not answer pride in pride’s own way, but dissolve hatred with humility.

2. Exegesis: Why Specifically the “Right Cheek”?

Notice one detail: Jesus says the “right cheek”.

The vast majority of people are right-handed. If someone wants to strike the right cheek of the person facing him with his right hand, an open-handed blow from the front won’t reach it; he can only do it with a backhanded flick. In first-century Jewish society, a backhanded slap was not a fight but an insult — a declaration from master to servant, from superior to inferior: you are beneath me. The Mishnah, the compilation of Jewish oral law, records in its tractate on damages, Bava Kamma, that the compensation for an ordinary slap was two hundred zuz, while for a backhanded slap it was four hundred — double. Clearly, in the understanding of the time, it was not a wound to the body but a wound to one’s dignity.

So what Jesus is dealing with is exactly the kind of wound we find hardest to handle: not the wound of a fist, but the wound of losing face.

Then what does “turn the left cheek too” mean? If the other person wants to humiliate you with the back of his hand and you turn the other cheek towards him, he can only strike with an open palm — and an open-handed blow is what passes between equals. This turn looks like conceding defeat, but in fact it is a quiet and powerful declaration: you can strike me, but you cannot decide who I am; my identity in God is not in your hands.

This is not cowardice; this is handing sovereignty back to God.

We need to see this in balance too. Turning the left cheek does not mean forbidding every reasonable defence. When the Lord Jesus himself was on trial and an officer struck him with the palm of his hand, he still spoke up: “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?” (John 18:23). He reasoned, but did not strike back; he pointed out the wrong, but did not curse. 1 Peter 2:23 describes it most vividly: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.”

Brothers and sisters, the key is not “whether I may speak” but “whether my heart is still bent on revenge”.

3. The Cross: We Struck the Right Cheek; He Turned the Left

There is a line in the lesson that shakes me every time I read it: we were the ones who struck the right cheek; the left cheek he turned to us of his own accord.

Let’s pull the camera all the way back to the beginning. God loved the world and placed the Garden of Eden in human hands: “subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth” (Genesis 1:28). What God gave humanity was authority, trust and relationship. And what did humanity do? It listened to the serpent — “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) — and chose to leave its originally intended position and try to take God’s place.

A betrayal like that is far worse than “striking the right cheek”. The created struck the Creator; the beloved betrayed the One who loved.

Yet God did not retaliate. He sent his only, beloved Son Jesus into the very world that had struck his right cheek. The prophet Isaiah foretold the scene long before: “I gave my back to those who beat me, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair. I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). That was not passively taking blows; that was actively bearing them.

Jesus had the power to wipe out all human rebellion. In the Garden of Gethsemane he told Peter plainly: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53). A Roman legion was six thousand men; twelve legions of angels — what a force that would be! But he did not ask. He had the right to take revenge, yet he chose to lay it down. As he hung on the tree, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Paul condensed the whole of this into one of Scripture’s greatest passages: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

The word “emptied himself” is kenoō in Greek, meaning to pour out, to make oneself nothing. This is exactly what the 321 vision calls selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing, not self-annihilation; selflessness is emptying ourselves so that God’s fullness can fill us. Only an empty cup can hold living water.

Brothers and sisters, if Jesus had not “turned the left cheek”, we could never have been restored to relationship with God. Salvation is not God giving up on justice; it is God causing justice and mercy to meet at the cross. He did not strike back; he reached out his hands. He did not condemn us; he died for our sins.

4. Illustration and Science: The Ninety-Second Lesson

The Harvard-trained neuroanatomist Jill Bolte Taylor, in her book My Stroke of Insight, shares a very valuable observation: when an emotion is triggered, the chemicals involved flood into the bloodstream and are then flushed out again, and the whole physiological process takes only about ninety seconds. If we are still angry after ninety seconds, it is usually not because the physical reaction hasn’t finished but because we have chosen to let that thought keep looping in our minds. The psychologist Daniel Goleman, in his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, also used the term “amygdala hijack” for the state in which emotion seizes us in an instant and we have struck back before we’ve had time to think.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a very practical lesson: in the moment you are struck, don’t respond yet. Breathe first, pray first, and move your focus off the other person’s face and onto the face of Jesus.

The 321 vision puts it well: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When my focus is on myself, what I see is my grievance; when my focus is on others, what I see is hatred; when my focus is on my circumstances, what I see is despair. Only when my focus is on Jesus do I see the Lord who turned his left cheek for me, and only then can my heart soften.

Remember too: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. When we rely on the brain, the more we think, the angrier we get, and the more we tally things up, the more unfair it all seems; when we rely on the heart, the Holy Spirit can work in those ninety seconds. Rely on the heart and you are glad; rely on the brain and you are troubled. For out of the heart flows the wellspring of life.

5. Applying 321: Let Jesus Be King, Starting in Those Three Seconds

The first of the Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. However Jesus faced humiliation, that is how I face humiliation. He did not strike back, so I will not strike back.

The first of the Two Core Values is: let Jesus be King. The most concrete moment to let Jesus be King is those three seconds — when my “self” leaps up to administer justice, I say to the Lord: Lord, this seat is yours, not mine. I step down; you step up.

This is where the fivefold change begins: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; and when relationships change, ministry will bear real fruit. Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — the fivefold change begins with the mindset.

The mindset to change today is this: being struck does not mean I have failed; not striking back when I am struck is how I win.

sections.heading: 2. Defusing Conflict with Humility, Overcoming Pride
sections.html:
1. “Why Should I Have to Put Up with This?”

When we are misunderstood, hurt or wronged, the natural reaction is: “Why should I have to put up with this?”

Brothers and sisters, listen to the subject of that sentence — “I”. Why should I; I did nothing wrong; I was only doing it for everyone’s good; I’ve served for so many years. However many times “I” appears in a sentence shows how big the “self” is. This is the response of pride.

But Jesus teaches us: overcome pride with humility.

Letting go of the attitude “I’m right, I deserve respect” and choosing to respond with forgiveness and gentleness not only sets us free, but also gives the other person’s heart a chance to be moved.

Notice the words “sets us free”. Many people think forgiveness lets the other person off the hook, but in fact the first person forgiveness releases is yourself. The psychologist Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet of Hope College in the United States and her colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science in 2001 which found that when participants recalled a grudge and nursed unforgiveness, their blood pressure, heart rate, facial muscle tension and skin conductance all rose markedly; and when, in their imagination, they chose empathy and forgiveness, these stress responses dropped significantly.

In other words, unforgiveness is a punishment you pay for yourself. You think you’ve locked the other person in prison, but in fact you’re the one bringing him his meals every day.

Proverbs said it long ago: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). A gentle answer is not powerless; it is the only power that can put the fire out.

2. Coat and Cloak: Don’t Let Things Get in the Way of People

Scripture says: “If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also” (Matthew 5:40).

This was a startling thing to say at the time. The “coat” is chitōn in Greek, the tunic worn next to the skin; the “cloak” is himation, the outer robe, which the poor wore to cover themselves by day and used as a blanket at night. The law of Moses specially protected this cloak: “If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What would he sleep in?” (Exodus 22:26–27).

In other words, the cloak was expressly safeguarded by law; no one could hold on to it. And Jesus says: let him have even this.

What does that mean? It means — don’t let possessions and entitlements become stumbling blocks in relationships. I clearly have the right, I could clearly sue, I clearly have a case; but for love’s sake I can choose not to use that right.

Paul said the same thing to the church: “Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you, that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?” (1 Corinthians 6:7).

Brothers and sisters, if we quarrel over face or profit, the relationship will break; if we lay down the “self” for love’s sake, we gain back real connection.

The 321 vision says: people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. The order is life first, then relationships, then ministry. How many families have seen brothers stop speaking to each other for good over a plot of land, a sum of money, or a word of apology never spoken. The things stayed; the people left.

John Gottman, the marriage researcher at the University of Washington, spent many years observing how couples interact and identified the “Four Horsemen” of relationships — criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling — of which he considers “contempt” the strongest predictor of divorce. What is contempt? Contempt is pride putting on a facial expression and walking out the door: that cold laugh, that roll of the eyes, that “What would you know?”

So to save a relationship, the first thing is not to prove who’s right but to wipe the contempt off our own faces.

3. The Extra Mile: The Distance at Which Love Gains Influence

“Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.” (Matthew 5:41)

The Greek word for “compel” is angareuō. It comes from the courier conscription system of the Persian Empire and later became a legal privilege of the Roman army: a soldier could press any civilian of an occupied territory into carrying his pack for one Roman mile. A Roman mile was a thousand paces, about 1,478 metres today.

Picture the scene: a Jewish youth walking along the road, and a Roman soldier dumps dozens of kilos of equipment onto his back. How he must have hated it! But he had no choice but to carry it, and when exactly one mile was up, he would throw it down hard on the ground and walk off without a backward glance.

Jesus says instead: when you’ve finished that mile, say — I’ll walk another mile with you.

No one compels you to walk that mile. On the first mile you are a slave; on the second, a free man. The first mile is law; the second is grace. The first mile is duty; the second is love. Between the first mile and the second, sovereignty comes back into your hands: he is no longer compelling you; you are choosing to love him.

There is a man in Scripture who was “compelled” with the very same word. “As they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name, and they compelled him to go with them, that he might carry his cross” (Matthew 27:32). That “compelled” is angareuō in the original. Simon was only a traveller passing by, forced to carry the cross of a condemned man. But Mark’s Gospel records a detail: he was “the father of Alexander and Rufus” (Mark 15:21). Later, in Romans 16:13, Paul sends greetings: “Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.” Many commentators believe this is the same Rufus and his family.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The mile he was compelled to walk became the mile that brought his whole family to salvation.

Going the extra mile means laying down our own will and thinking of others. This “extra mile” is often the distance at which love gains influence and a relationship is won back.

The social psychologist Robert Cialdini, in his book Influence, points out that “reciprocity” is one of the most universal rules of behaviour in human society: when people receive kindness, they naturally feel a pressure to return it. What does that mean in relationships? It means the extra mile you walk leaves a place in the other person’s heart. Of course, we don’t go the extra mile to manipulate anyone; we go the extra mile because the Lord went countless extra miles for us. But God is often pleased to use such a mile to soften a hardened heart.

Dr Martin Luther King Jr. wrote these famous words in Strength to Love: “Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.”

4. Applying 321: The 920 Practice and Relationships Where Both Win

The 920 practice in the 321 vision fits right here. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; in front of them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice: almost every one of these nine graces can only be grown amid the friction of relationships. Without people who try your patience, you can’t grow patience; without people who make you want to explode, you can’t grow gentleness; without people who make you want to hit back, you can’t grow self-control.

So the person who strikes your right cheek is not only your difficulty; he is also a field God has given you.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When I stop answering him in his own way, the cycle is broken right here with me. Breaking that cycle takes one person who is willing to stoop down first. Brothers and sisters, may we be the ones who stoop down first.

sections.heading: 3. David’s Humility: The Overcomer Who Would Not Grab Power
sections.html:
1. The One Hunted Was Not a Sinner but a Righteous Man

David’s life is a living testimony of “turning the left cheek”.

He was hunted by Saul not because he had done anything wrong, but because he was successful and praised. The women came out singing: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). From that day on, “Saul watched David” with a jealous eye (1 Samuel 18:9).

Brothers and sisters, how true to human nature this is. Sometimes we come under attack not because we did something wrong, but because we did something right. It’s like being “struck on the right cheek” — wronged, envied.

Suffering that comes from our own mistakes is somewhat easier to accept; suffering that comes from our faithfulness is especially hard to bear. David hid in the wilderness for about ten years — living in caves, feigning madness, taking refuge in enemy territory — and through those ten years he faced just one question every day: God, what on earth have I done wrong?

2. The Knife in the Cave

At last the opportunity came. Saul, pursuing David with three thousand chosen men, went into a cave to relieve himself — and David and his men were hiding in the depths of that very cave (1 Samuel 24:1–3).

His men immediately said: “Behold, the day of which Yahweh said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you’” (1 Samuel 24:4). Now the time had come!

How reasonable it sounded. The timing, the place, the mood of the men — even “God’s promise” — everything lined up. Many of life’s great falls happen not when the temptation is obvious, but when the temptation looks very spiritual.

David quietly cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. But Scripture records: “Afterward, David’s heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt” (1 Samuel 24:5).

Notice that what he cut was only a piece of cloth, not a life. Yet even cutting a piece of cloth troubled his conscience — that is a sensitive heart. Brothers and sisters, spiritual sensitivity doesn’t wait for a great wrong before it takes alarm; it feels the sting even over the corner of a robe.

Then he said to his men: “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:6).

“Anointed” in Hebrew is mashiach — the very word “Messiah”. What David meant was: Saul’s position was given by God; removing him is God’s prerogative, not mine. He chose humility and chose to leave the judgement to God.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride, on the other hand, is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and trying to take God’s place. In that cave David held to his originally intended position.

3. God Himself Vindicated Him

David came out of the cave, called out to Saul from a distance and held up the piece of robe in his hand. And what happened? Saul wept aloud and said to David: “You are more righteous than I; for you have done good to me, whereas I have done evil to you” (1 Samuel 24:17).

A piece of robe not used to kill was more powerful than a sword.

More precious still, David didn’t hold back just once. In 1 Samuel 26 the same opportunity came again; his officer Abishai said, “Now therefore please let me strike him with the spear to the earth at one stroke, and I will not strike him the second time.” And David still said: “Don’t destroy him; for who can stretch out his hand against Yahweh’s anointed, and be guiltless?” (1 Samuel 26:8–9).

Restraint once may be good manners; restraint twice is real life.

In the end God himself vindicated David, raised him up as king and made him the most glorious king in Israel’s history. Paul says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

“Give place to God’s wrath” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “rather give way”, but literally it is “leave room for the wrath”. It means: you step back first, so that God has room to come in and work. The reason we so often don’t see God’s vindication is that we keep occupying that place ourselves.

4. The Way Up Is the Way Down

This reminds us: true authority is not won by fighting for it, but received through humility.

Jesus says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). Peter also says: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6).

Notice those three words: “in due time”. God’s lifting up runs on God’s timetable. Waiting is the truest test of humility.

Psychology has a famous study: the “marshmallow experiment” carried out by the Stanford psychologist Walter Mischel in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Researchers placed a marshmallow in front of a child and said: if you can wait until I come back before eating it, you can have two. Follow-up studies found that the children who had been better able to wait generally showed better self-control and better ability to cope with frustration as adolescents. In recent years some scholars have also pointed out that a family’s socio-economic background and how trustworthy the child’s environment is are equally important factors — if a child learns early on that adults’ promises are often broken, of course he won’t want to wait.

Brothers and sisters, that second half is actually the more precious reminder. Whether we can wait depends on whether we trust the One who made the promise. David could wait in that cave because he knew the God who had anointed him, who never breaks his word.

So David sings in the Psalms: “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this: he will make your righteousness shine out like light, and your justice as the noon day sun. Rest in Yahweh, and wait patiently for him” (Psalm 37:5–7).

God’s way of lifting us up is not self-promotion but self-humbling. Humility is not a sign of weakness; it is the starting point from which God means to exalt you.

5. Applying 321: Spiritual Companions in 235

Through David’s ten years in the wilderness, God did not let him walk alone. God provided Jonathan for him. “Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:3). When David was at his lowest, “Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose, and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16).

This is the 235 relationship of 321: first find someone selfless and become each other’s “2” — spiritual companions; then build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, when we are misunderstood, what we need most is not a crowd who will help us curse people, but a Jonathan who strengthens our hand in God. Ask God for a Jonathan of your own, and ask him to make you a Jonathan for someone else.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
When we set today’s message back into the 321 framework, it becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he turned his left cheek, so I turn mine too. The Bible is my standard — not my emotions, not how others see me, but the Lord’s word decides how I respond. The Holy Spirit is my guide — in those ninety seconds it is the Holy Spirit who is in charge of my heart, not my hot temper.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — I no longer act as judge in my own case; let Jesus receive all the glory — whether I am praised or misunderstood, in the end all the glory goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A community full of revenge builds a human system; only a community that forgives one another and bears with one another is God’s system.

The core lesson is this: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And every picture we’ve looked at today — turning the left cheek, handing over the cloak, walking the extra mile — is one and the same thing: laying down the “self”. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). “It is no longer I who live” — that is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” — that is fullness without limit.

Our perspective must shift too: from the human perspective to God’s perspective — people see that I’ve lost out, God sees that I’ve become like him; from the earthly perspective to the heavenly — earth argues over who was right and who was wrong, heaven remembers who loved whom; from the temporary perspective to the eternal — the cloak is temporary, the soul is eternal; from the worldly perspective to the godly — the world says you’ve only won if you’ve won, God says you only gain by giving up.

The Path of Serving is the same road: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. Turning the left cheek looks like a single movement, but in fact it is the whole road from Spirit to Understanding to Life to Service to God.

And the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry. If our lives lack humility, our relationships will keep breaking; and if our relationships keep breaking, however big our ministry grows, it is a house built on sand.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared four practices for us. Let’s follow the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — and put them into effect one by one.

Practice 1: The Right-Cheek Practice

When someone misunderstands or criticises you, don’t rush to defend yourself; bless them first.

Information: Copy Matthew 5:39 onto a card and put it where you will see it every day.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you — who struck your “right cheek” most recently? In that moment, what was really stung in your heart: the facts, or your face?

Conviction: Say to the Lord, “You are right”, not merely “It would be better to do it this way.” Conviction means handing over sovereignty.

Implementation: This week, whenever someone points out your fault, first count silently for ninety seconds, then open your mouth and speak one word of blessing over them.

Evaluation: Before bed, ask yourself: did I replay that conversation in my head today?

Correction: If you did, turn your focus back to Jesus and look at the face that was struck for you.

Repetition: Keep at it until “bless first” becomes your natural response.

Multiplication: Teach this practice to your family and your small-group members.

Practice 2: The Left-Cheek Practice

When you are treated unfairly, choose to lay down your rights and ask God for the strength to love.

Information: Read Matthew 5:40 and 1 Corinthians 6:7.

Revelation: Ask God — what is the “cloak” I’m clutching and won’t let go of right now? A sum of money? An apology? A word of vindication?

Conviction: Acknowledge that before God, relationships matter more than things, and people matter more than tasks.

Implementation: Choose one matter you have every right to fight over but decide not to, and concretely let it go.

Evaluation: After letting it go, does my heart feel lighter, or am I still counting my losses?

Correction: If you’re still counting, count them out one by one to God, and then entrust them to him.

Repetition: Every time something similar comes up, make the same choice.

Multiplication: When someone one day asks you why you didn’t fight, tell them the Lord’s words.

Practice 3: The Extra-Mile Practice

In your relationships, give a little more, understand a little more, forgive a little more.

Information: Read Matthew 5:41, and remember those extra 1,478 metres.

Revelation: Ask God to show you one person — the one with whom you only want to finish the “first mile” and then turn away.

Conviction: Believe that the second mile is not wasted; it is the distance at which love gains influence.

Implementation: This week, do something for that person that they haven’t asked for and that you have no obligation to do.

Evaluation: As I did it, was my heart willing, or was I forcing myself?

Correction: If you were forcing yourself, first ask the Lord to renew your heart, then do it a second time.

Repetition: Let “one more mile” become a habit of your daily living, not an occasional good deed.

Multiplication: Take a brother or sister with you and walk that second mile together.

Practice 4: Turn Your Eyes to Jesus

Meditate on his humility and forgiveness on the cross, and ask that his heart would become your heart.

Information: Read Philippians 2:5–8, Luke 23:34 and 1 Peter 2:23.

Revelation: In stillness, look at that scene — as he was being nailed to the cross, whom did he pray for?

Conviction: Acknowledge that none of my grievances comes to even a ten-thousandth of what he suffered.

Implementation: Every morning, spend three minutes bringing before the Lord the person most likely to sting you that day.

Evaluation: This week, has my focus been more on Jesus, or on myself, on others, on my circumstances?

Correction: Turn your focus back — however many times a day you need to, it’s never too many.

Repetition: Let “turning my eyes to Jesus” become the first thing I do every time I’m hurt.

Multiplication: Share your experience, so that others may be comforted too.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Humility is not weakness but strength under restraint; it is not indulgence but choosing to respond in the way of love.

These two sentences matter a great deal, and we need to distinguish them clearly.

Strength under restraint means I have power in my hands, but I choose not to use it. Not striking back when you have no power is called helplessness; not striking back when you do have the power — that is humility. Jesus had twelve legions of angels at his command; that is why his not striking back carries weight.

Choosing the way of love means that humility does not equal doing nothing. In the face of real harm, the boundaries that should be set must still be set, the police who should be called must still be called, and those who need protecting must still be protected. The Lord Jesus has never told anyone who is being abused to stay in danger. Humility deals with the revenge in my own heart; it does not cancel out practical wisdom in the real world.

When you are willing to turn the left cheek, you overcome not only your enemy but also yourself.

And to be honest, the hardest one to overcome has never been the person who struck you; it is the “I” inside you that refuses to let go.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, what we have seen today is a different kind of King.

Jesus chose to overcome pride with humility. He did not passively take the blows; he actively loved. One who passively takes blows is a victim; one who actively loves is an overcomer. The same lowly posture — but with a different heart inside it, the outcome is completely different.

His “turning the left cheek” is the starting point of salvation; his “going the extra mile” is the road of revival.

From heaven to the manger was one mile; from the manger to the cross, another mile; from the cross to the door of your heart and mine, yet another mile. All the way he came, and not a single step of it was compelled.

When we follow his heart, we will discover that humility is not losing but gaining; not falling back but being lifted up by God.

So this morning I want to extend an invitation to you. Picture a face in your heart: the person who misunderstood you, the person who hurt you, the person who still hasn’t apologised to you to this day. Then say to the Lord: Lord, I hand the right to judge back to you. You are King; you are in charge of this. I am willing to turn the left cheek; I am willing to walk the extra mile.

Let us dissolve hatred and rebuild relationships through humility, overcome in love, and be lifted up in humility.

May Jesus be King in our families, King in our church, King in every moment when we are offended. May all the glory go to him.

keyVerses: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also. If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also. Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two. Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you.” (Matthew 5:38–42)
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. (Matthew 23:12)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord, I will no longer answer pride with pride; I will overcome the evil of the world with your humility.
When someone strikes my right cheek, give me a heart of love and patience, so that I put forgiveness in place of revenge and gentleness in place of hardness.
May your humility become my glory, so that I find freedom in letting go and victory in obedience.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. We were the ones who struck your right cheek; your left cheek you turned to us of your own accord. Had you not refused to strike back, we could not stand before you today.

Lord, forgive us — forgive us for talking about humility with our lips while keeping accounts in our hearts; forgive us for the sneers we never voiced, the counter-attacks wrapped up in spiritual language, the grievances we replay again and again.
Holy Spirit, work within us. When we are misunderstood, hold back our tongues; when we are wronged, hold up our hearts; when we have the power to take revenge, remind us that the seat belongs to you.
Give us the heart of David, so that we would rather wait for your timing than snatch our own justice; give us the heart of Christ, so that we can bless those who strike us.
May our families be healed through humility, may our church be united through humility, and may Satan find no breach among us.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 5:39 says: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.” Share: what was the most recent experience that made you feel “struck on the right cheek”? What was the first reaction that rose in your heart at the time? If you could do it again, what would you do?

1 Samuel 24:6 says: “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed.” Share: is there something right now that you are holding in your hand, ready to “stretch out your hand” at any moment? Are you willing to hand it over to God? What is the “second mile” you will walk this week?

blocks.x: Subtitle: Humility, the Only Antidote to Pride
The Three Seconds After You’re Wronged Are the Real Pulpit

It’s a Wednesday evening co-workers’ meeting, and just as it is about to wrap up, someone suddenly says: “This was your fault in the first place.” The tone isn’t harsh, but the words are hard. There’s still a smile on your face, while inside you have already started gathering evidence — which day you sent the message, which time you reminded everyone, which task was never your responsibility at all.
That moment is the truest moment of our lives.

Because a person’s spiritual condition is seen not in how well he speaks from the pulpit but in what rises first in his heart in the three seconds after he has been wronged. The words from the pulpit are ones we have prepared; the reaction in those three seconds is what flows naturally out of our lives.

The most natural human reaction is a tooth for a tooth. In science class we learned Newton’s third law of motion: action and reaction are equal in size and opposite in direction. Human pride obeys the same law — you give me one cold word, I give you two; you step back one pace, I step back three. In the end both people are standing where they started, neither willing to move first.
Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Fire cannot put out fire; only water can.
We Struck the Right Cheek; He Turned the Left
Jesus says: “whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.” (Matthew 5:39)

This saying is often misunderstood, as if Christians should let anyone push them around. Not so. Notice that he says the “right cheek”. The vast majority of people are right-handed; to strike the right cheek of the person facing you, an open-handed blow from the front won’t reach — you can only do it with a backhanded flick. In first-century Jewish society, a backhanded slap was not a fight but an insult — a declaration from superior to inferior: you are beneath me.
So what Jesus is dealing with is exactly the kind of wound we find hardest to handle: not the wound of a fist, but the wound of losing face.

And if you turn the other cheek, the other person can only strike with an open palm — and an open-handed blow is what passes between equals. This turn looks like conceding defeat, but in fact it is a quiet and powerful declaration: you can strike me, but you cannot decide who I am.
At a deeper level: we were the ones who struck the right cheek.

God placed the Garden of Eden in human hands, yet humanity chose to leave its originally intended position and try to take God’s place. A betrayal like that is far worse than striking the right cheek. Yet God did not retaliate; he sent his only, beloved Son into the very world that had struck his right cheek. He had the power to ask the Father for more than twelve legions of angels, but he did not ask; hanging on the tree, he said only: “Father, forgive them.”

Paul says: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6–7) In the original, “emptied himself” means “poured out”. Only an empty cup can hold living water.
If Jesus had not turned the left cheek, we could never have been restored to relationship with God.
The Extra Mile Is the Distance at Which Relationships Are Won Back
Jesus said two more things that run just as much against our instincts: let him have your cloak also; and whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.

The cloak was a poor man’s blanket at night, and the law of Moses expressly forbade keeping it; yet Jesus says, let him have even this. The point is: don’t let possessions and entitlements become stumbling blocks in relationships. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. How many families have stopped speaking for good over a plot of land or a sum of money — the things stayed, but the people left.

As for the “mile”, that was the legal distance a Roman soldier could press a civilian into carrying his pack — about 1,478 metres. The first mile is duty; the second is love. Between the first mile and the second, sovereignty comes back into your hands: he is no longer compelling you; you are choosing to love him.
That extra mile is often the distance at which love gains influence and a relationship is won back.

The person in Scripture who best knew how to “turn the left cheek” was David. He was hunted by Saul not because he had done wrong but because he had done right. When the opportunity came, he said: “Yahweh forbid that I should … stretch out my hand against him.” (1 Samuel 24:6) He left the judgement to God, and God himself vindicated him and raised him up as king.
True authority is never won by fighting for it; it is received through humility.

Humility is not weakness but strength under restraint; it is not indulgence but choosing to respond in the way of love. When you are willing to turn the left cheek, you overcome not only your enemy but also yourself.
And to be honest, the hardest one to overcome has never been the person who struck you; it is the “I” inside you that refuses to let go.
Questions for Reflection
This week, for whom is God asking you to go the extra mile? Who is the person with whom you only want to finish the “first mile” and then turn away?

Right-cheek practice: copy Matthew 5:39 where you’ll see it; count silently for ninety seconds, then speak a blessing.
Left-cheek practice: name the “cloak” you’re clutching — a sum of money? An apology? A word of vindication?
920 practice: everyone we relate to is our “2”.
Almost every one of the nine graces of Galatians 5:22–23 can only be grown amid the friction of relationships.
The person who strikes your right cheek is not only your difficulty; he is also a field God has given you.
Putting it into practice (2)
Extra mile: give more, understand more.
Eyes on Jesus: let his heart be your heart.
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction,
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Extra-mile practice: this week, do something for someone that they haven’t asked for and you have no obligation to do.
Eyes on Jesus: every morning, spend three minutes bringing the person most likely to sting you before the Lord.
Walk through the eight stages one by one, stressing Evaluation, Correction and Repetition — repeat until “bless first” becomes your natural response.
The last stage is Multiplication: teach this practice to your family and small-group members.
235 relationships: ask God for a Jonathan of your own, and to make you a Jonathan for someone else.
Summary: the 3-2-1 vision
Jesus is my role model, the Bible my standard,
the Holy Spirit my guide; let Jesus be King,
let Jesus receive all the glory.
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal: establish God’s system.
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Turning the cheek, giving the cloak, walking the second mile are all one thing — laying down the self.
Galatians 2:20: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Four shifts: from man’s to God’s, earthly to heavenly, temporary to eternal, worldly to godly.
The order is always life first, then relationships, then ministry; the fivefold change begins with the mindset.
Closing and call
His turned cheek: the starting point of salvation;
his extra mile: the road of revival.
Humility is not losing but gaining;
not falling back but being lifted up by God.
One who passively takes blows is a victim; one who actively loves is an overcomer — the same posture, a different heart, a different outcome.
From heaven to the manger was one mile, from the manger to the cross another, and from the cross to the door of your heart yet another.
Gentle reminder: humility is strength under restraint; boundaries must still be set, and those who need protecting must still be protected.
Call: picture a face and say to the Lord, “I hand the right to judge back to you.”
May Jesus be King in our families, in our church, and in every moment when we are offended.
Prayer of response and blessing
Lord, I hand the right to judge back to you.
I am willing to turn the left cheek;
I am willing to walk the extra mile.
May all the glory be yours.
Lead the congregation in praying aloud together, in a quiet, warm tone.
Confession: talking about humility with our lips while keeping accounts in our hearts; counter-attacks wrapped up in spiritual language.
Ask the Holy Spirit to hold back our tongues, hold up our hearts, and remind us that the seat belongs to God.
Bless families with healing, the church with unity, and pray that Satan finds no breach.
Close with “In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen,” and read the declarations of faith.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is the third talk on “Humility Is the Antidote to Pride”, and our title is “Turn the Other Cheek, Go the Extra Mile”. In the first two talks we saw that the root of pride is the self-centred life — leaving our originally intended position and trying to take God’s place. Today we face a more practical question: when someone else’s pride has already struck me in the face, what am I to do? The answer lies in three pictures: a left cheek turned, a cloak handed over, and an extra mile walked.

Brothers and sisters, picture this. At a co-workers’ meeting, someone suddenly says: “This was your fault in the first place.” There’s still a smile on your face, while inside you have already started gathering evidence. That moment is the truest moment of our lives. A person’s spiritual condition is seen not in how well he speaks from the pulpit but in what rises first in his heart in the three seconds after he has been wronged. Newton’s third law of motion says: action and reaction are equal in size and opposite in direction. Human pride is the same: you give me one cold word, I give you two. That is why the 3-2-1 vision reminds us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Fire cannot put out fire; only water can.

Let’s first go and stand on that mountain. The Sermon on the Mount is the constitution of the kingdom of heaven. “An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth” comes from Exodus 21:24. Many people think God was encouraging revenge, but the very opposite is true. When God gave this law, he was putting a ceiling on revenge, and it was administered by judges. But by Jesus’ day it had been co-opted into a charm to justify revenge. The Jews of the day had three options: the Zealots revolted, the Pharisees separated themselves by the law, and the Essenes withdrew into the wilderness. But on the mountain Jesus opened a fourth way — overcoming evil with humility and love. Brothers and sisters, two thousand years have passed, and these four ways still lie before us every day.

Jesus says: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.” (Matthew 5:39) This saying is often misunderstood, as if Christians should let anyone push them around. Not so. What Jesus teaches is not cowardice but spiritual responsiveness — don’t answer pride in pride’s own way, but dissolve hatred with humility.

Notice one detail: he says the “right cheek”. To strike the right cheek of the person facing you with your right hand, you can only do it with a backhanded flick. At that time, a backhanded slap was not a fight but an insult — a declaration from superior to inferior: you are beneath me. The Mishnah records that the compensation for a backhanded slap was double. Brothers and sisters, what Jesus is dealing with is exactly the kind of wound we find hardest to handle — not the wound of a fist, but the wound of losing face. If you turn the other cheek, the other person can only strike with an open palm, and an open-handed blow is what passes between equals. This turn looks like conceding defeat, but in fact it is a quiet declaration: you can strike me, but you cannot decide who I am.

There is a line in the lesson that shakes me every time I read it: we were the ones who struck the right cheek; the left cheek he turned to us of his own accord. God placed the Garden of Eden in human hands, yet humanity wanted to take God’s place. A betrayal like that is far worse than striking the right cheek. Yet God did not retaliate; he sent his only Son into the very world that had struck his right cheek. He could have asked the Father for more than twelve legions of angels, but he did not ask; hanging on the tree, he said only: “Father, forgive them.” Paul says he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). In the original, “emptied himself” means poured out — exactly what 321 calls selflessness. Only an empty cup can hold living water.

When we are wronged, the most natural reaction is: “Why should I have to put up with this?” Listen to the subject of that sentence — “I”.
