“But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,
being made in the likeness of men”
Philippians 2:7
Key points:
1. Open with the lesson title and key verse; read Philippians 2:7.
2. State the theme of the lesson: humility is not weakness; it is strength under control.
3. Preview the three points: not low self-esteem, laying down our rights, returning to our originally intended position.
He plainly could — yet he chose not to
Peter drew his sword; the Lord stopped him
“Do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father,
and he would send me twelve legions of angels?”
Matthew 26:53
Key points:
1. Describe the scene in Gethsemane where Peter draws his sword; read Matthew 26:53.
2. Explain that a legion was about 5,000–6,000 men; twelve legions is about 70,000 of heaven’s host.
3. Stress: it was not that he couldn’t; he had the power and did not use it.
4. Illustration: a strong man holding a seven-day-old baby — his strength isn’t less, just gathered in.
Key Passage and Background
Philippians: written by Paul in prison in Rome
Philippi: a Roman colony obsessed with status
Discord in the church — Paul lifts up Christ
“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus”
Key points:
1. Philippians was written around AD 61–62, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome.
2. Philippi was a Roman colony, a city of discharged veterans, intensely concerned with status and standing.
3. There was discord in the church (Euodia and Syntyche); Paul doesn’t debate who is right but first lifts up Christ.
4. Philippians 2:6–11 is the early church’s Christ Hymn: the first half descends, the second ascends.
Humility is not low self-esteem
Pride says “I’m the best”; low self-esteem, “I’m the worst”
Yet the subject is always “I”
Not seeing yourself as low — not looking at yourself
Romans 12:3: think reasonably
Key points:
1. Lesson point: low self-esteem is really another form of being self-centred.
2. Read Romans 12:3; in the original, “think reasonably” means to be clear-headed.
3. Illustration: the funfair mirror and the distorting mirror both reflect only yourself; humility swaps the mirror for a window.
4. Numbers 12:3: Moses was very humble — yet he was the man who parted the Red Sea.
Humility is laying down our rights
Form: he was God from the beginning
Grasped: he had no need to cling to it
Emptied: what he poured out were his rights
Philippians 2:6–7
Key points:
1. Read Philippians 2:6–7 phrase by phrase.
2. Three key words in the original: form (morphē), grasped (harpagmos), emptied (kenoō).
3. Principle: those who truly possess something don’t need to clutch it; the insecure hold on tightest.
4. What he emptied out was not his divinity but his rights.
Four rights Jesus laid down
The right to be God (John 17:5)
The right to receive glory (Isaiah 53:3)
The right over life and death (John 10:18)
The right to be respected (1 Peter 2:23)
Key points:
1. Take the four rights in the lesson’s order, each with one verse.
2. The right to be God: John 17:5 and 2 Corinthians 8:9.
3. The right to receive glory: Isaiah 53:3 — he deserved a crown and received thorns.
4. The right over life and death: John 10:18; note the “nevertheless” in Matthew 26:39.
5. The right to be respected: 1 Peter 2:23 — he didn’t answer back because he entrusted himself.
Return to our originally intended position
The angels fell because they left their place
Sin’s most primitive shape: leaving one’s place
“Didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling”
Jude 6
Key points:
1. Read Jude 6 and point out that the angels fell because they didn’t keep their originally intended position.
2. The most primitive shape of sin is not an action but leaving one’s place.
3. God is God and man is man; the Father is the Father and the Son is the Son; a leader is a leader and a servant is a servant.
4. Genesis 1, “after their kind”: order is not a restriction; order is grace.
Pride steps out; humility steps back in
Pride says: I will make myself like the Most High
Satan says: you will be like God, knowing good and evil
Humility says: I am not Lord; he is
Isaiah 14:14
Key points:
1. Isaiah 14:13–14: five “I will”s, ending with “I will make myself like the Most High”.
2. Contrast with Philippians 2: one plainly had it and laid it down; the other plainly did not have it and tried to snatch it.
3. Genesis 3:5: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” is where every tragedy begins.
4. Proverbs 16:18: pride goes before destruction.
Let man be man and let God be God
Knowing all was in his hands, he knelt to wash feet
Sure of who you are, you can let go of your posture
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
John 13:15
Key points:
1. John 13:3–5: “knowing that all things were in his hands”, he then knelt to wash feet.
2. Washing feet was the work of the household’s lowest slave; that night the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest.
3. Principle: only when you are sure of who you are can you let go of your posture; security comes from knowing God’s love.
4. Illustration: the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, so it is salty and bitter; the Sea of Galilee has an inlet and an outlet, so it is full of life.

5. The secret: not “I can’t”, but “I entrust”.
Humility is strength under control
A fire hose: the point is to grip it
A nuclear plant: safety lies in the control rods
Collins: Level 5 leadership
Personal humility plus intense professional will
Key points:
1. Humility is not loss but a choice to lay down; not weakness but a willing lowering of oneself in order to obey God.

“Originally intended position” is a biblical idea
“Didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling”
Sin’s most primitive shape: leaving one’s place
God is God, and man is man
The Father is the Father, the Son is the Son (Jude 6)

The king of Babylon’s five “I will”s
“I will make myself like the Most High” Isaiah 14:14

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today’s lesson is titled: Lay Down Our Rights, Return to Our Originally Intended Position.
Our key verse is Philippians 2:7: “but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.”
Brothers and sisters, humility is not weakness; humility is strength under control.
Let’s go back first to one particular night. The Garden of Gethsemane, torchlight flickering, Judas arriving with the soldiers. Peter draws his sword and cuts off a man’s ear.
But the Lord stops him and says: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53)
A Roman legion numbered roughly five to six thousand men. Twelve legions is more than seventy thousand of heaven’s host.
Brothers and sisters, it was not that he couldn’t; he had the power and did not use it. He plainly could — yet he chose not to.
Have you ever watched a big, tall father holding a newborn baby? His hands tremble, every movement slows right down. His strength hasn’t diminished one bit; he has simply gathered it in.
That isn’t weakness; it is restraint within love.
Paul wrote this letter to the Philippians in a prison in Rome. A man in chains wrote a letter brimming with joy.
Philippi was a Roman colony, home to discharged veterans — a city that cared intensely about status and standing. And discord had arisen in the church.

How did Paul deal with it? He didn’t convene an arbitration hearing, didn’t analyse who was right and who was wrong, didn’t draw up new regulations. He did something far more fundamental — he lifted up Jesus Christ. He said, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

Brothers and sisters, the verses that follow are a hymn of the early church. The first half goes down step by step, all the way to the bottom; the second half says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” (Philippians 2:9)
The one who descended to the lowest place was raised by God to the highest.
The first point: humility is not low self-esteem.
Some people think humility means saying, “Oh, I’m hopeless.” Brothers and sisters, that isn’t humility; it is just another way of being self-centred.
The proud person says, “I’m the best”; the person with low self-esteem says, “I’m the worst.” What they say is opposite, but the subject is the same: “I”.
So true humility is not seeing yourself as low; it is not looking at yourself at all.

Paul says: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3) In the original, “to think reasonably” means: to be clear-headed.
I often say that low self-esteem and pride are both mirrors; humility is a window. In a mirror you see only yourself; a window lets you see the sky and lets the light come in.

Scripture says: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3) And Moses was the man who stretched out his staff and parted the Red Sea. Clearly, humility is in no way a lack of strength.
The second point: humility is laying down our rights.
“Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6–7)

“Form” means he was God from the beginning. “Grasped” means to clutch tightly — he already had it, so he had no need to cling to it for dear life. “Emptied” means poured out; what he poured out was not his divinity but his rights.
Brothers and sisters, the more truly someone possesses something, the less they need to clutch it; the more insecure someone is, the tighter they hold on.
He laid down four rights.
First, the right to be God. He shared the glory of the Father, yet he became a baby who had to learn to walk.
Second, the right to receive glory. He deserved a crown, and received thorns.
Third, the right over life and death. He said: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” (John 10:18)
Fourth, the right to be respected. “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back.” (1 Peter 2:23)
Brothers and sisters, he didn’t answer back — not because he had nothing to say, but because he entrusted himself. Not “I can’t”, but “I entrust”.
The third point: return to our originally intended position.
How does the Bible describe the fall of the angels? “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place.” (Jude 6)
Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: not adultery, not theft, but “didn’t keep their first domain” — they left their originally intended position.
So the most primitive shape of sin is leaving one’s place.

God has appointed every person a place. God is God, and man is man; the Father is the Father, and the Son is the Son; a leader is a leader, and a servant is a servant. Order is not a restriction; order is grace.
Pride is stepping out of position; humility is stepping back into position.
The king of Babylon said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14)
The serpent said to Eve: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)
“Like God” — these words are where every human tragedy begins.
Humility is admitting: I am not Lord; he is.
The Lord himself returned to the servant’s place.
Notice the order in John 13: it was “knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” that he then knelt down to wash the disciples’ feet.
Brothers and sisters, only when a person is sure of who he is can he let go of his posture.
He said: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15)
In the 321 vision we say: let man be man and let God be God. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.
So how do we practise this week? Four things.
First, lay down the right to control: this week, ask about your child’s homework only once, and don’t follow up a second time.
Second, respect other people’s roles: pray for seven days for the person you least submit to in your heart, and affirm one thing to his face.
Third, serve without seeking a return: do three unseen acts of service, and when you’ve done them, tell no one.

Fourth, give thanks continually: every night before you sleep, write down three things you’re thankful for. “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:18)

Brothers and sisters, these four things are all small — small enough that you can start today. But change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes; change your living and your relationships change.
Brothers and sisters, humility is not loss but return; not powerlessness but surrender; not being trampled on but being lifted up by God.
The Lord said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)
Peter said: “that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6)
Our part is to go low; God’s part is to lift up. Try to rush the timing, and you’ve stepped out of position again.
This morning, open that clenched hand and say to the Lord: Lord, this is yours, not mine.
Let us pray together.

Lord, I want to learn your ways — to lay down my own rights and return to the originally intended position you have set for me. No longer insisting on my own will, no longer fighting for control, but wanting only to obey your will. Be Lord in my life and receive the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you. May you live a life of humility all your days, just as he did — with the heart of a servant, glorifying the Father in heaven.
Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today’s lesson is titled: Lay Down Our Rights, Return to Our Originally Intended Position.
Our key verse is Philippians 2:7: “but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.”
Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to begin with one sentence, and I ask you to keep it in your heart: humility is not weakness; humility is strength under control.
Let me start with a question: in your heart, what is humility?

The world often equates humility with weakness. Fight whenever you can, because if you don’t fight you lose; giving way means you’re useless. The nineteenth-century philosopher Nietzsche called the humility and submission that Christianity teaches a “slave morality”.

In my pastoral work I often meet a certain kind of brother. At work he is highly capable, and his staff respect him. But at home he treats his wife and children in exactly the same way: he demands, he corrects, he directs.
One day, with red eyes, he asked me, “Pastor, out there I get everything right. Why is it that at home I get everything wrong?”
Brothers and sisters, his problem wasn’t ability; it was position.
Let’s go back to one particular night.

It is late, after the Passover meal, in the Garden of Gethsemane, and torchlight is flickering between the olive trees. Judas arrives leading the officers and soldiers. The blood rushes to Simon Peter’s head; he draws his sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest’s servant.
But Jesus stops him. He says: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the weight of that sentence. In the Roman army a legion numbered roughly five to six thousand men. Twelve legions is more than seventy thousand of heaven’s host. On the very night he was bound and led away, he held in his hand the authority to summon seventy thousand angels.
It was not that he lacked the power; he had the power and did not use it. It was not that it was taken from him; he laid it down himself.

Have you ever watched a big, tall father holding a baby only seven days old? His hands tremble, every movement slows right down. His strength hasn’t diminished one bit; he has simply gathered it in. That isn’t weakness; it is restraint within love.
Paul wrote this letter to the Philippians in a prison in Rome, around AD 61 to 62. A man in chains wrote a letter brimming with joy.

Philippi was a Roman colony, home to many discharged veterans, and it cared intensely about status and standing. And this church had its troubles: in chapter 4 Paul names two sisters, urging them to be of one mind in the Lord.
Brothers and sisters, in a spiritual church the commonest breach is not heresy but “contending” — contending over who is right, contending over face, contending over who matters more.
Paul didn’t convene an arbitration hearing or analyse who was right and who was wrong. He lifted up Jesus Christ and said, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

Many scholars regard the verses that follow as a hymn of the early church. The first half goes down step by step, all the way to the cross; the second half says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” (Philippians 2:9) The one who descended to the lowest place was raised by God to the highest.
Now we come to the first point: humility is not low self-esteem.
Many people think humility means thinking little of yourself, putting yourself down, or waving your hand in front of others and saying, “Oh no, not me, I’m hopeless.”
Brothers and sisters, that isn’t humility; it is just another way of being self-centred. Have you noticed that someone who keeps saying “I can’t” is actually talking round and round the word “I”?
The proud person says, “I’m the best”; the person with low self-esteem says, “I’m the worst.” What they say is opposite, but the subject of the sentence is exactly the same.
So true humility is not seeing yourself as low; it is not looking at yourself at all.

The standard of Scripture puts it with great precision: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3)
In the original, the word for “think reasonably” means: to be clear-headed, sound-minded.
Brothers and sisters, the Bible’s definition of humility is not “underestimating” but “being sober”.
Because the measuring rod isn’t in my hand; it’s in God’s.
So where does humility come from? The root of humility is a heart that fears God.
Scripture says: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3)

Moses was the man who dared to stand before Pharaoh and stretched out his staff so that the Red Sea parted — and the Bible says that the humblest man on all the earth was him. Clearly, humility is in no way a lack of strength.

The prophet Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne, and cried out: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips.” (Isaiah 6:5) He was not humbled because people had humiliated him; he was humbled because he saw God.
Seeing God, we see ourselves clearly.
I often use this picture: low self-esteem and pride are both mirrors; humility is a window.

The funfair mirror makes you look tall and huge — that is pride; the distorting mirror makes you look squat and small — that is low self-esteem. Whichever mirror it is, the only person you ever see is yourself. Humility replaces the mirror with a window: a window lets you see the sky and lets the light come in.

The American psychology professor June Price Tangney, in a study published in 2000, pointed out that the core of humility is not self-deprecation but an accurate assessment of one’s own abilities and limitations — a kind of “forgetting of the self”.
Brothers and sisters, on this point the best psychology in the world has walked right up to the Bible’s front door.
The second point: humility is laying down our rights.
“Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7)
There are three key words here.
“Form” refers not to outward appearance but to essence — he was God from the beginning.

“Grasped” means to clutch tightly and never let go. His equality with God was his already, not something he had snatched, so he had no need to cling to it. Brothers and sisters, the more truly someone possesses something, the less they need to clutch it; the more insecure someone is, the tighter they hold on.
“Emptied” means poured out. He did not pour away his divinity; what he emptied out were his rights.
He laid down four rights.

First, the right to be God. He prayed to the Father: “Now, Father, glorify me with your own self with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” (John 17:5) This Lord who upholds all things became a baby who had to learn to walk. Paul says: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor.” (2 Corinthians 8:9)

Second, the right to receive glory. Isaiah prophesied long before: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease.” (Isaiah 53:3) He deserved a crown, and received thorns.
Brothers and sisters, what we find hardest to let go of is often not money but “being affirmed”.

Third, the right over life and death. He said: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” (John 10:18) The cross was not an accident; he walked up to it himself.

In the Garden of Gethsemane he prayed: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) Notice that “nevertheless”: before it, a real struggle; after it, complete obedience. Humility isn’t the absence of feeling; humility is feeling it and still obeying.
Fourth, the right to be respected. Peter wrote: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23)
He didn’t answer back — not because he had nothing to say. Had he chosen to argue, no one could have out-argued him. This is the secret of humility: not “I can’t”, but “I entrust”.
Brothers and sisters, what do we mean by “strength under control”?

A fire hose under high pressure can knock a grown man off his feet. Yet the focus of a firefighter’s training is never how to make the water blast harder, but how to grip it. A system’s maturity lies not in its maximum output but in its brakes. People are the same.

Paul learned this lesson too. He had the right, yet he said: “Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 9:12)

In “Good to Great”, the management scholar Jim Collins sifted through 1,435 large American companies and identified eleven that were truly great. The leaders of these companies shared one feature: extreme personal humility combined with intense professional will.
Even the world’s management research has discovered it: the highest positions are kept for the lowliest posture.
The third point: return to our originally intended position.

“Originally intended position” is not a phrase we invented; the idea comes from the Bible itself. Describing the fall of the angels, Scripture says: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place.” (Jude 6)
Brothers and sisters, look closely: not adultery, not theft, but “didn’t keep their first domain”. So the most primitive shape of sin is leaving one’s place.
God is God, and man is man; the Father is the Father, and the Son is the Son; a leader is a leader, and a servant is a servant. Order is not a restriction; order is grace.
Pride is stepping out of position.

In Isaiah 14 the prophet uses the arrogance of the king of Babylon to point to a deeper fall behind it. There are five “I will”s in a row, each one higher than the last, and the final one shows his hand: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14)
Brothers and sisters, this is Philippians 2 played in reverse. Jesus was equal with God, yet did not grasp at it; this one was not equal with God, yet tried to seize it.
Satan paved this same road into the Garden of Eden. He said: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) “Like God” — these words are where every human tragedy begins.
Scripture says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18) The next step after stepping out of position is always a fall.
Humility is stepping back into position.

John 13 records that evening. The text first says, “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (John 13:3), and only then that he rose from supper, wrapped a towel around his waist, poured water into the basin and washed the disciples’ feet.
Brothers and sisters, it was knowing that all things were in his hands that he then knelt down to wash feet.

In those days washing feet was work done by the lowest slave in the household. That night the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest, and not one of them would pick up the basin. In the end, the one who picked up the basin was the Lord. He said: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15)

Only when a person is sure of who he is can he let go of his posture. Why do we find it impossible to let go? Because we aren’t sure we are loved, and so we have no choice but to use our rights to prove we still matter.
This principle must land in every real relationship.

In the family, a husband must not use his authority to press others down. The command Scripture gives husbands is: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.” (Ephesians 5:25) The place of the head is not a place for pressing down; it is a place for giving yourself up.
A wife need not fight for control, because the whole passage rests on this: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21)
A leader seeks not status but service: “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26)

Brothers and sisters, think of a stone arch bridge. It has no nails and no steel; it stands because every stone keeps its place. Let a single stone shift outward by an inch, and the whole arch comes down.
So how do we practise this week? The lesson gives us four practices.

First, lay down the right to control. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on the one thing you most often reach out to control, then say to the Lord: the sovereignty over this belongs to you. Concrete action: this week, ask about your child’s homework only once, and don’t follow up a second time.

Second, respect other people’s roles. Ask God to show you the person in a position over you that you least submit to — not the person you dislike most, but the one you secretly think “has no business being there”. Concrete action: pray for him for seven days, and affirm to his face one thing he has done well.

Third, serve without seeking a return. The Lord said: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does.” (Matthew 6:3) Concrete action: this week, do three unseen acts of service, and when you’ve done them, tell no one.
Brothers and sisters, when you keep quiet about it, is there a little itch inside you? That little itch is the “self” still there.

Fourth, give thanks continually. “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:18) Concrete action: every night before you sleep, write down three things you’re thankful for. In 2003 the psychologists Emmons and McCullough found that people who recorded things they were grateful for each week were more optimistic about the future and reported fewer physical complaints.
Brothers and sisters, let’s draw the 3-2-1 vision together.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system.

The mark of the old self is the self-centred life; the mark of the new self is selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the boundless — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)
So we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Today we are changing the very first link — exchanging the old mindset that “humility means being taken advantage of” for the new mindset that “humility is returning to our originally intended position”.
Brothers and sisters, humility is not loss but return; not powerlessness but surrender; not being trampled on but being lifted up by God.
Jesus laid down his rights in heaven and gained the glory of all the earth.
The Lord said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

Peter said: “that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Notice the words “in due time” — the timetable is in his hands. Our part is to go low; his part is to lift up. Try to rush the timing, and you’ve stepped out of position again.
This morning I want to issue three calls to you.

First, turn from the mirror to the window. Second, loosen that clenched hand and say to the Lord: this is yours, not mine. Third, return to your originally intended position — if you are a husband, return to the place of giving yourself up; if you are a leader, return to the place of serving.
And above every one of these places, we all share just one originally intended position: we are servants, and he is Lord.
Let us pray together.
Lord, we confess that we have misunderstood humility all along; we thought letting go meant losing. Please forgive us.
Lord, we have seen you. You plainly could, yet you chose not to; you knew that all things were in your hands, yet you knelt down to wash your disciples’ feet.

Lord, I want to learn your ways — to lay down my own rights and return to the originally intended position you have set for me. No longer insisting on my own will, no longer fighting for control, but wanting only to obey your will. Bear in us the fruit of self-control; be Lord and receive the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you and keep you. May you live a life of humility all your days, just as he did — with the heart of a servant, glorifying the Father in heaven.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Lord of the Universe, Asleep in a Manger
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Before we open the Bible, let’s first grow quiet together and picture a scene in our hearts.

It is an utterly ordinary night. Outside the town of Bethlehem, in a borrowed shelter for animals, a baby is wrapped in cloths and laid in a feeding trough. The inn has kept no room for him; this world’s first response to him is “no room”. And yet this baby lying in the manger is the one through whom all things were made, the King whom angels worship day and night without ceasing. The Lord of the universe has shrunk himself to the size of a baby.

Brothers and sisters, this is not just a heart-warming Christmas story. It is the greatest descent in the universe, and the deepest humility in all of history.

The lesson we enter today is titled “Laying Down the Right to Be God”, the first lesson in the series “Jesus’ Role Model”. The first of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is “Jesus is my role model”. We often say we want to imitate Jesus, but to imitate him we must first see one thing clearly: what exactly did he lay down?

Astronomers tell us that the observable universe is roughly ninety-three billion light years across, while the earth we stand on is only a little over twelve thousand seven hundred kilometres in diameter. Set the earth in such a universe and it doesn’t even count as a speck of dust. And yet, brothers and sisters, the distance between man and God is immeasurably greater than the distance between man and the universe. For that is not a difference of size; it is the difference between creature and Creator, between the finite and the infinite.

Yet Jesus crossed it. He did not send an angel in his place, nor call to us from far off in heaven. He crossed that eternal chasm himself, became man and lived among us. The apostle John sums up the whole mystery in a single sentence: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14)

Brothers and sisters, right at the start I want to ask you three questions, and these three questions are the three stretches of road this lesson will walk.

The first question: when you “have”, can you lay it down? When you have authority, resources, reputation, talent — can you still serve like a servant?

The second question: when you “can”, do you still rely on God? When you’ve done something so often that you could do it with your eyes shut, do you still pray first?

The third question: when you “know better than others”, do you still submit? When you can plainly see more clearly than your boss, understand more than your parents, are more mature than your leader — are you still willing to stay in your place and submit?

Some people draw near to God only when they “can’t”, call on God only when they “have nothing”, and learn humility only when they “have no standing”. But Jesus was not like that. He laid down when he “had”, relied when he “could”, and submitted while he held his “position”. That is the role model we are learning from today.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A City Obsessed with Status Receives a Letter About Going Down
sections.html:
To understand Philippians 2, we must first get to know the man who wrote the letter, the people who received it, and the city itself.

The writer was the apostle Paul, and when he wrote he was in prison. From the mention of “the whole palace guard” in Philippians 1:13 and “Caesar’s household” in 4:22, the great majority of evangelical scholars conclude that he was imprisoned in Rome, around AD 61. Notice this detail: a prisoner bound in chains wrote the most joyful letter in the New Testament; a man who had lost his freedom teaches us what it means to lay down our freedom gladly and willingly.

The recipients were the church at Philippi, founded by Paul on his second missionary journey around AD 49–50 and recorded in Acts 16 — the first time the gospel set foot on European soil. Its first members were a remarkable mix: Lydia, a merchant in purple cloth, of high social standing; a slave girl possessed by a spirit and exploited by others for profit, of the lowest standing of all; and a jailer of the Roman Empire, representing public authority. Three people of utterly different status became brothers and sisters in the same church. What would enable them to live together in harmony was certainly not human self-cultivation, but the humility of Christ.

Now look at the city. Philippi began as a small gold-mining town; in 356 BC it was enlarged by Philip II, king of Macedon, who named it after himself — that is where the name “Philippi” comes from. In 42 BC, Antony and Octavian defeated Caesar’s assassins Brutus and Cassius on the plain of Philippi. After the war Rome settled large numbers of veterans there, and Philippi became a Roman colony enjoying the “Italian right” — its residents held Roman citizenship and its legal privileges.

Brothers and sisters, this point is crucial. Philippi was a city that took pride in “status”. Acts 16:21 records that the men who accused Paul made a point of calling themselves “Romans” — their sense of superiority leaps off the page. The very air of the city was thick with one message: climb higher; make sure people see you’re above everyone else. And it was in such a city that Paul wrote a passage about “going down”. He did not tell them to give up their citizenship; he reminded them: “For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).

Now look at the context. Philippians 2:5–11 is not a theological treatise appearing out of nowhere; it is the ground of an exhortation. Just before it Paul says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3–4) Why say this? Because there was friction in the church. By chapter 4 he even names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.” (Philippians 4:2) Two co-workers at odds, and the whole church affected.

How does Paul deal with the problem? He doesn’t call a mediation meeting or draw up a set of rules. He does something far more fundamental — he sets Jesus Christ before their eyes. He says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). The way to resolve tension between people is not first to change others but first to change our mindset; not first to deal with the issue but first to return to Christ. This is exactly what the 321 vision says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, then ministry changes.

Many scholars call Philippians 2:6–11 the “Christ Hymn”; it was very likely sung in the worship of the early church. Its structure is very clear. Verses 6–8 are a staircase going all the way down — from the form of God, to emptying himself, to the form of a servant, to the likeness of men, to humbling himself, to obedience unto death, to death on a cross. Verses 9–11 go all the way up: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

Brothers and sisters, remember this shape: first down, then up. The world teaches us to climb up; the Bible teaches us to go down. The world says that when you reach the top you gain glory; the Bible says that when you go all the way down, God will lift you up. How clearly 1 Peter 5:6 puts it: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.”

Now let’s follow the lesson and walk down these three steps one at a time: laying down the right that comes with “having”, laying down the right that comes with “being able”, and laying down the right that comes with “position”.

sections.heading: 1. Laying Down the Right of “Having”: From Glory Down to Humanity
sections.html:
1. The Text: He Had It, Yet Did Not Grasp It

“who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6)

2. Light from the Original: “Form” and “Grasped”

The Greek word for “form” is morphē. It refers not to an outward shape but to “the form that displays the essence”; Greek has another word, schēma, for an external, changeable appearance. Paul uses morphē here, and the meaning is very clear — Jesus did not merely “look like God”; in his essence he was God. John 1:1 says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He was not later raised up to be God; he always was.

Interestingly, in verse 7 Paul says he took “the form of a servant”, and he uses the same word, morphē. This tells us he is truly God and he truly became a servant; his divinity was not pretended, and his servanthood was not an act.

The second key word is “grasped”, in the Greek harpagmos. Its root means “to plunder, to seize by force”; it can refer to a prize of war to be clutched at all costs. So the sentence means: Jesus did not regard “equality with God” as something he must grip tightly in his fist and let no one touch.

Brothers and sisters, here we meet the sharpest contrast in the whole Bible.

In Genesis 3:5 the serpent says to Eve: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Man was not God, yet wanted to be “like God”.

In Isaiah 14:13–14 the fallen one says: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” He was not the Most High, yet wanted to be “like the Most High”.

Do you see it? The way of Satan and Adam was: “not God, yet trying to seize God’s position.” The way of Jesus was: “God from the beginning, yet not clutching God’s rights.” One snatches upward; the other gives downward. This is exactly what the 321 vision puts its finger on: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

3. Emptying Himself Is Not Losing His Divinity but Laying Down the Right to Use It

Verse 7 says he “emptied himself”. The Greek is ekenōsen, literally “poured out, emptied”.

We must interpret this very carefully here, so as not to go astray. What Jesus emptied himself of was not his divinity. On earth he still forgave sins, calmed storms and received worship; Colossians 2:9 says, “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily.” What he emptied himself of was “the right to use his rights as God” — he willingly set aside the privilege of summoning heaven’s armies at any moment, of being spared all suffering, and gladly entered a body that knew hunger, weariness, tears and death.

He had the right to be God, yet chose the limitations of being human. He could have commanded angels to serve him, yet chose to serve people; he need not have suffered, yet chose to bear the agony of the cross for us. In the Garden of Gethsemane he said with his own lips: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53) It was not that he couldn’t; it was that he wouldn’t.

2 Corinthians 8:9 puts it in the most moving of sentences: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.”

4. An Illustration: What If You Had to Become a Snail?

The lesson offers a powerful comparison: if we had to turn from human beings into animals, we would all find it hard to accept; how unimaginable, then, is the humility of the God who created the universe being willing to become one of the creatures he made.

The British writer C. S. Lewis uses a similar picture in “Mere Christianity”: if you want to get some sense of what the Incarnation means, think how you would like to become a slug or a crab. Merely imagining it makes us squirm — because that is going down several levels.

But brothers and sisters, the gap between a human and a snail is still the gap between one creature and another. The gap between God and man is the gap between the infinite and the finite. Scientists estimate that the human body is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells (Bianconi et al., 2013, “Annals of Human Biology”), and the precise design of every one of those cells points to the Creator. And this Creator actually entered a body made of cells — a body that could hunger, thirst, tire and bleed.

Why would he do this? There is only one answer — for love. This is humility: not being forced down, but willingly coming down for love. Bowing your head because you are forced is called humiliation; only bowing it willingly is called humility. Many people in this world are pushed down by circumstances — that isn’t humility, it’s helplessness. Jesus had every right not to come down, yet chose to come down. That is humility.

5. A Generation Climbing Up, a Saviour Coming Down

Psychological research holds up a mirror to the face of our age. Jean M. Twenge and colleagues, in a study published in 2008 in the “Journal of Personality”, found that from 1979 to 2006 the scores of American college students on the Narcissistic Personality Inventory showed a marked upward trend. She later co-wrote, with W. Keith Campbell, the book “The Narcissism Epidemic”, arguing that contemporary culture constantly reinforces a sense of self that says “I’m the most important, I’m the most special.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the very air we breathe every day. Advertising tells us “you deserve it”, and social media keeps inviting us to show off our most glamorous side. The whole world’s gravity pulls upward, toward the self. Yet in that air the Bible points to a Saviour who went down and says: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.

What is the “having” in our own lives? It may be a little authority — you’re a manager, a parent, a small-group leader. It may be a few resources, some talent, a little time. Laying down the right of “having” doesn’t mean throwing these things away; it means no longer treating them as grounds for “I can be above others”, but as vessels through which “I can serve others”.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem.

The phrase “emptied himself” is the most perfect demonstration of selflessness. But brothers and sisters, be sure to remember: selflessness is not having nothing, not self-denial in the sense of self-rejection, not regarding yourself as worthless. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When Jesus emptied himself, he did not become any less God; rather, he let God’s love pour out to all humanity through a finite body. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) “It is no longer I who live” — that is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” — that is the fullness without limit.

And the outcome? Philippians 2:9 says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” Notice that “therefore”. He was not exalted first and then humbled; it was because he humbled himself that God exalted him. Laying down is not losing; laying down is where gaining begins.

sections.heading: 2. Laying Down the Right of “Being Able”: Relying on the Father in Everything
sections.html:
1. The Text: The Son Can Do Nothing of Himself

“Jesus therefore answered them, ‘Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.’” (John 5:19)

2. Background: Words Spoken Under the Threat of Death

These words were not spoken on a quiet hillside; they were spoken under enormous pressure. John 5 records that beside the Pool of Bethesda Jesus healed a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years — and that day was the Sabbath. So the Jews persecuted him. Jesus answered, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.” (John 5:17) The moment those words were out, the situation escalated: verse 18 says the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. It was at that very moment that Jesus spoke verse 19. People were plainly out to kill him, and yet he said, “the Son can do nothing of himself.”

3. Exposition: Not a Lack of Ability, but the Nature of a Relationship

We must be very careful not to misread this as “the Son is inferior to the Father”. Orthodox evangelical faith holds to the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit are of one substance, equal in power and equal in glory. The “can’t” Jesus speaks of is, in the Greek, ou dynatai ... aph’ heautou — “cannot of himself”. This “cannot” is not a deficiency of ability but an unwillingness rooted in relationship — he is so completely one with the Father that he never would, and never will, take any independent action apart from the Father.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we can trace this theme through:

“I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

“I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things.” (John 8:28)

Brothers and sisters, did you notice? In all Jesus’ life, not one action, word or judgement was done “of himself”. He did not lean on his divinity to take shortcuts; he depended entirely on the Father’s guidance. The four Gospels record again and again that he withdrew into the wilderness to pray, rose before dawn to pray, prayed all night. He could work miracles, and still he prayed; he could teach, and still he first listened for the Father’s voice.

The lesson puts its finger on our sore spot in a single sentence: for us, we pray only when we “can’t”; once we “can”, it’s easy to rely on ourselves. But the role model Jesus gives us is this — even when he could, he chose to depend.

4. An Illustration: The Greatest Danger Isn’t Not Knowing How, but Thinking You Know

There is a very famous psychological finding here. In a study published in 1999 in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology”, Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University reported that in tests of grammar, logical reasoning and sense of humour, the people who performed worst were the most likely to overestimate their own ability and ranking — what came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect”. Their explanation: if a person lacks a certain skill, he also lacks the skill to recognise that he lacks it.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the lesson says: in spiritual service, in work, in decision-making, the greatest danger is not “not knowing how” but “thinking you know how”.

Picture a scene from everyday life. Someone who has just passed their driving test grips the wheel with both hands, keeps checking the mirror and slows down at every junction. And the old hand with twenty years behind the wheel? One hand on the wheel, chatting on the phone, wondering what’s for dinner. Which one is more likely to have an accident? Not the one who doesn’t know how — the one who knows it all too well.

The spiritual life is the same. A new believer reads the Bible like digging for treasure and prays like breathing; but someone who has served for years may preach from old notes, pray in the same old words and run Sunday by the same old routine. Inside they think, “I know this one,” and so God gets shown to a seat on the side.

The Lord Jesus could not have been more emphatic: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) And Proverbs says: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

5. True Humility Is Not Admitting Weakness but Admitting Need

This sentence from the lesson is worth memorising: true humility is not admitting weakness but admitting need. The humble, however experienced, still depend on God; the proud, however helpless, still want to rely on themselves.

Psychological research on humility points the same way. June Price Tangney of George Mason University, in a paper published in 2000 in the “Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology”, argued that humility is not self-deprecation but involves several components: an accurate assessment of one’s abilities and achievements, the ability to acknowledge one’s mistakes and limitations, openness to new ideas, and turning one’s attention away from the self toward the larger whole.

Brothers and sisters, notice that last one — turning one’s attention away from the self toward the larger whole. Isn’t that just what the 321 vision says? Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

The 321 vision has a saying that is the very key to this point: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Everything we do flows from the heart.

“Once I can, I rely on myself” — that is relying on the brain; “even when I can, I still depend” — that is relying on the heart. The third of the Three Foundations is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. The pattern of Jesus’ ministry on earth is precisely the pattern of a man wholly led by the Holy Spirit — Luke 4:1 says he “was led by the Spirit into the wilderness”, and Luke 4:14 says he “returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee”. He did not go it alone on the strength of his own divinity; what he modelled was a life obedient to the Holy Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, if you exchange the mindset “I can, so I do” for “even though I can, I will first ask God”, your life will be different.

sections.heading: 3. Laying Down the Right of “Position”: Submitting to Sinful People
sections.html:
1. The Text: He Went Down with Them

“And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.” (Luke 2:51)

2. Background: A Twelve-Year-Old Boy and Three Days of Searching

Luke 2:41–52 records the only event from Jesus’ childhood that is written down in any detail. Every year at Passover, Joseph and Mary went up to Jerusalem. The year Jesus was twelve, when the feast was over, they had travelled a day’s journey home before they discovered the boy was not among their relatives. They went back to Jerusalem and searched for three days, and finally found him in the temple.

At thirteen a Jewish boy became a “son of the commandment”, formally taking on responsibility for keeping the law; twelve was the age of preparation. How does Scripture describe the scene? “After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them, and asking them questions. All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.” (Luke 2:46–47)

He was brilliant beyond others; even the most learned rabbis of the day were amazed. And when Mary, after three days of anguish, asked him why he had treated them like this, he answered: “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49) These are the first words Jesus speaks in the Bible, and his very first sentence declares his relationship with the Father. By human logic, he could well have stayed on in the temple to keep debating and teaching; after all, he was right — he of all people should be occupied with his Father’s affairs.

But the next verse says: “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them.”

3. Exposition: Submission That Lasted Eighteen Years

The Greek word for “subject to” is hypotassō, originally a military term meaning “to rank oneself under someone”; it is not a forced capitulation but a voluntary ordering. Even more noteworthy is the tense of the verb: Luke uses the imperfect with a participle, indicating a continuous, long-running state.

In other words, this was not a single concession but a long stretch of years. Luke 3:23 says that when Jesus began his ministry he was about thirty years old. From twelve to thirty — nearly eighteen years — the Bible is almost entirely blank: no miracles, no sermons, no crowds; only a carpenter’s workshop in Nazareth. Mark 6:3 records that later the people of his home town said, “Isn’t this the carpenter?”

Brothers and sisters, think about it: the Creator of the universe spent eighteen years measuring timber, planing timber, nailing timber, submitting to a foster father and a mother. And Luke 2:52 says: “And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.” The years of submission were not wasted years; they were years of growth.

There is a very deep truth here: the sinless Jesus submitted to sinful parents; the perfect Lord obeyed imperfect people. Joseph was only his legal father; and Mary, though highly favoured, was also someone who needed a Saviour — she herself sang: “My soul magnifies the Lord. My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47). In calling God “my Savior” she shows that she too was among those being saved.

Hebrews 5:8 says: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” He did not first learn to obey and then become the Son of God; he was the Son of God and still learned obedience.

4. An Illustration: When You Know More, Do You Still Submit?

The lesson asks a very sharp question: when we know more than our boss, more than our parents, more than our leaders, can we still humbly submit?

This is a real tension. A young co-worker fresh out of seminary, head full of new methods, watches the old pastor run meetings the same way he has for thirty years and thinks: this is wrong; it should be done like that. He may well be right. But as soon as he opens his mouth with an “I know better than you” tone, it is no longer a question of right and wrong; it is a question of pride and humility. The 321 vision puts it exactly: pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

Management research confirms this truth too. In a study published in 2013 in “Organization Science”, Bradley P. Owens, Michael D. Johnson and Terence R. Mitchell found that leaders’ “expressed humility” — a willingness to acknowledge their own limitations, appreciate others’ strengths and stay open to new views — was positively related to their followers’ work engagement, job satisfaction and intention to stay. Of course, we are not humble because it works; we are humble because that is what Jesus is like.

Scripture’s teaching is consistent: “Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1). “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (1 Peter 5:5)

Of course, we must also keep the Bible’s proportions: submitting to authority does not mean going along with sin. When human commands conflict with God’s commands, the apostles’ answer is clear: “We must obey God rather than men.” (Acts 5:29) Jesus submitted to Joseph and Mary, but he never once went along with sin. Laying down the right of “position” means laying down my pride and my own opinions — not laying down God’s standard.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Return to Our Originally Intended Position — Let Man Be Man and Let God Be God

The 321 vision says that the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. In the temple Jesus first established his relationship with the Father — “I must be in my Father’s house”; then, carrying that settled identity, he went back to Nazareth to submit to people.

Brothers and sisters, this order matters enormously. Someone whose standing before God is insecure will always fight for standing before people; only someone who knows for certain who he is has the strength to take a place beneath others. Jesus didn’t need to “stay in the temple and debate” to prove he was the Son of God, because he already was.

The lesson says: don’t insist on “I know better than you”, but choose “I am still willing to submit”. This is exactly what 321 says — humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position; let man be man and let God be God. In the home at Nazareth, Jesus let Joseph be the father, let Mary be the mother, and let the heavenly Father be God. He took nobody’s place.

This is also the foundation of “235 relationships”. To become a spiritual companion — someone’s “2”; to establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; to form a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of comrades — the first condition is this: am I willing to stand beneath others? Am I willing to give the credit away? Am I willing, when I am right, still to choose to submit? Without this step, relationships can never be established.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Three Layings-Down on the Road of Selflessness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set these three layings-down back into the framework of the 321 vision.

1. The Three Foundations Match the Three Layings-Down

Laying down the right of “having” matches “Jesus is my role model”: we no longer ask what others do; we ask what Jesus does. The world’s role models climb up; Jesus’ role model goes down.

Laying down the right of “being able” matches “the Holy Spirit is my guide”: being able doesn’t mean I’m right; being experienced doesn’t mean God wants me to do it this way.

Laying down the right of “position” matches “the Bible is my standard”: I submit not because that person deserves it but because God’s word says so; I lay down my opinion not because I’m wrong but because the Bible stands above my feelings.

2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King; Let Jesus Receive All the Glory

Brothers and sisters, what does “laying down the right to be God” mean? In the language of 321, it is “let Jesus be King”.

Inside each of us there is a little throne. If “self” sits on that throne, we will clutch our “having”, boast of our “being able” and fight for our “position”; if Jesus sits on that throne, we will naturally be able to lay them down. The question has never been “how much should I lay down?” but “who is on the throne?”

And the end of this road is already written in Philippians 2:11: “to the glory of God the Father.” All of Jesus’ descent comes in the end to glory. He himself said: “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” (John 17:4) Brothers and sisters, someone who is willing to lay down does not lose glory; he puts glory back where it always belonged.

3. The Goal: Establish God’s System

The Worldly system is a pyramid: those on top press down on those below. God’s system is turned upside down: those on top hold up those below. Jesus said: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) If someone won’t lay down “having, being able, position”, what he establishes will inevitably be a human system — resting on ability, seniority and rank. Only if someone is willing to lay them down can what he establishes be God’s system — resting on grace, on the Holy Spirit, on submitting to one another.

4. The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless: Humility Overcomes Pride, Selflessness Overcomes Satan

Isaiah 14 records five “I will”s — I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High. This is the manifesto of pride, the self-centred life at its extreme.

Philippians 2, by contrast, records a whole chain of “laying down” — not considering equality with God a thing to be grasped, emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, humbling himself, becoming obedient, even to death. This is the road of humility, selflessness at its fullest.

These two roads met head-on in history. In the temptation in the wilderness Satan said to Jesus, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” (Matthew 4:9) It was a shortcut to glory without going to the cross, and Jesus refused it. He defeated the one who would not submit by submitting, and overcame the one so full of “self” by selflessness. This is what the 321 vision keeps stressing: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most is not a powerful Christian but a Christian with no “self”; because you cannot get a grip on someone who isn’t gripping anything.

5. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective

321 says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with mindset. Most people’s mindset is: to lay down is to lose. This lesson tells us otherwise: laying down is not losing; laying down is the beginning of finding freedom. Once this mindset changes, life begins to change; when life changes, the choices of daily living change; when daily living changes, relationships at home, at work and in the small group change; and when relationships change, ministry will bear real fruit. That’s why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Some people have served for years and built large ministries, yet their relationships are in chaos — and the reason is often that three things have not been laid down: having, being able, position.

Our perspective must shift too: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From man’s perspective, Jesus being born in a manger was a failure; from God’s perspective, it was the beginning of salvation. Seen from earth, eighteen years as a carpenter were years buried in obscurity; seen from heaven, they were perfect obedience. Seen in the short term, laying down means losing out; seen from eternity, “God also highly exalted him.”

6. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice says: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; with that person we practise living the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, look at these fruits: patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, self-control — which of them doesn’t require us first to lay ourselves down? If you don’t lay down “I’m in the right”, you can’t be patient; if you don’t lay down “I’m too busy”, you can’t be kind; if you don’t lay down “I want it”, you can’t exercise self-control. All nine graces grow on the tree of selflessness. And 235 relationships — becoming someone’s “2” as a spiritual companion, establishing a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, forming a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of comrades — every level needs someone to bow their head first.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Turning Mindset into Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them out layer by layer.

Practice 1: Practise Laying Down in What You “Have”

When you have authority, position or resources, choose to serve humbly.

This week, write down three things you “have”, and for each one think of a way to serve someone with it. If you have a car, give an elderly member a lift to the meeting; if you have professional expertise, look over a document for a brother who needs help; if you have time, make a phone call to ask after someone.

Practice 2: Practise Depending in What You “Can Do”

Even when you know it well, pray first and seek God’s heart.

Pick the one thing you’re most practised and most confident at — leading a Bible study, giving a presentation, cooking a meal — and before you start, be still for three minutes and entrust it to God. The more familiar something is, the more you need to pray; because that is exactly where you’re most likely to forget God.

Practice 3: Practise Submitting in Your “Position”

Respect the authority God has established, and learn to experience blessing through submission.

Think of someone you “know more than” yet must submit to — perhaps a boss, a parent, a spouse, a co-worker. This week, over one thing you would normally have fought for, choose to say: “All right, I’ll do it your way.” Then notice what God does in your heart.

Taking These Three Practices Deeper Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Stage one, Information: write down what you heard today. Philippians 2:6–8, John 5:19, Luke 2:51 — three passages, three layings-down. Copy them into your notebook and put them up where you’ll see them.

Stage two, Revelation: ask God to turn the information into light. Information only reaches the head; revelation reaches the heart. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, which is the ‘having’, the ‘being able’ or the ‘position’ that I cling to most?” Let the Holy Spirit point out that specific name, that specific thing.

Stage three, Conviction: acknowledge from the heart that God is right. Not “I know I ought to lay it down”, but “I believe laying it down is better than holding on.” Conviction is the surrender of the will, not merely the agreement of the mind.

Stage four, Implementation: do at least one this week. Don’t try all three at once — just one, but really do it. Implementation is the bridge by which a mindset enters daily living.

Stage five, Evaluation: each evening spend three minutes looking back — where did I grab hold again today? Seeing it honestly is the beginning of progress.

Stage six, Correction: once you see it, adjust. If today you grabbed the top spot in front of your family, go and apologise tomorrow; if today you charged through in your own strength, tomorrow pray first and then move. Correction is not remorse; it is turning around.

Stage seven, Repetition: doing it once won’t change a person; doing it again and again will. Jesus submitted again and again for eighteen years — how can we hope for a three-day crash course?

Stage eight, Multiplication: bring someone along with you. This week, share what you’ve learned through the practice with a brother or sister, or invite a companion to do these three practices with you. The 321 vision says that life is multiplied — when you lay down, others get to see what laying down looks like.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder: Laying Down Is Not Losing
sections.html:
Laying down is not losing; laying down is the beginning of finding freedom. When you are willing to lay down the right to “be God”, you become more like “the Son of God” — Jesus Christ.

Why does laying down bring freedom? Because the one who grips is not free. Hold on to face, and face ties you up; hold on to position, and position ties you up; hold on to “I’m right”, and that “right” ties you up. A clenched fist can catch nothing; only an open hand can receive.

The Lord Jesus said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Brothers and sisters, rest is not having nothing to do; rest is selflessness — having no “self” left to fight for.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that manger where we began.

When Jesus laid down the right to be God, he did not lose his honour; rather, he revealed the glory of his love. He entered the world in the form of humility, so that through him we might gain life and gain salvation.

He teaches us that humility is not weakness, but being able and still willing to obey; not being forced to lay down, but choosing to lay down for love.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: what if Jesus had insisted on his right to be God? He would still be God, still seated on the throne; the angels would still worship him; he would not have lost a thing. The ones who would have lost are us — we would have stayed in our sin for ever, separated from God for ever, with no way home for ever. He laid down, so that we could gain. That is the gospel.

So today, through this lesson, God asks us a question: what are you still clutching in your hand?

Perhaps it’s a title, and you can’t bear to hand over the baton. Perhaps it’s an “I know this better than anyone”, and you won’t listen to others. Perhaps it’s control in a relationship, and it has to be done your way. Perhaps it’s an old wound you’re gripping tightly, refusing to forgive. Brothers and sisters, not one of those things can be carried into eternity. But every time you let go for love, heaven writes it down.

The 321 vision says: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. This morning I want to invite you to do something very simple and very deep — open your hand, and in your heart say to the Lord: “Lord, this seat is yours, not mine. I come down; you go up.”

When we learn humility like this from Jesus, we too are walking the road of selflessness, living a life that truly glorifies God.

Today, may you serve people where you “have”, depend on God where you “can”, and willingly submit where you hold a “position”. May Jesus reign as King in your home, reign as King in your work, reign as King in your heart. All the glory to him.

keyVerses: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)
declarations: Lord, you existed in the form of God, yet you did not insist on your equality with the Father, but emptied yourself and took the form of a servant.
Help me to learn your ways: not proud when I have, not self-reliant when I can, not self-exalting when I hold a position.
Help me to depend on you in everything and obey your will.
May your humility become my glory; may your likeness become my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
practices: Practise laying down in what you “have”
Practise depending in what you “can do”
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you.

Lord Jesus, this morning we have seen your humility. You existed in the form of God, yet willingly emptied yourself; you could have commanded angels, yet chose to serve sinners; you could have stayed in the temple to teach, yet chose to go back to Nazareth and submit. Lord, before you we have nothing to say; we can only bow our heads and worship.

Lord, we confess that we are often proud when we have, self-reliant when we can, and self-exalting when we hold a position. We cling to things that will surely pass away, and let go of you. Please forgive us.

Holy Spirit, shine your light on us now and point out the one thing we are gripping tightly in our hands. Give us the strength to let go today. Give us the mind of Christ, so that we gladly go low for love — not forced, but willing.
Lord, we give our families to you, our work to you, our service to you. Reign as King among us, and receive all the glory.
We ask this in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
discussion: Philippians 2:6–7: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” Share: in your life right now, which “having”, “being able” or “position” is hardest for you to lay down? Why is it hard?

Luke 2:51: “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them.” Share: has there been a time when you plainly felt you were right, yet chose to submit? How did God later bless you through it? If something like that is happening now, how do you plan to respond?
