blog.title: The One Who Had the Right — and Didn’t Use It

blocks.x: Three Layings-Down That Begin at a Manger

That night, outside the town of Bethlehem, in a borrowed shelter for animals, a baby was wrapped in cloths and laid in a feeding trough. The inn had kept no room for him; this world’s first response to him was two words: no room.

And yet this baby was the King whom angels worship day and night. The Lord of the universe had shrunk himself to the size of a baby. This is not just a heart-warming festive story; it is the deepest humility in all of history.

From a prison in Rome, Paul wrote to Philippi — a city full of Roman veterans, where everyone took pride in their citizenship. The very air of the city said: climb higher. And it was precisely there that he wrote a passage about “going down”:
“who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7)
1. Laying Down When We “Have”

The Greek word for “form” refers to the form that displays the essence — Jesus did not merely look like God; in his essence he was God. And the original word for “grasped” means a prize of war to be clutched at all costs.
He had it, yet did not grasp it.

He could have commanded angels to serve him, yet chose to serve people; he need not have suffered, yet chose to go to the cross. This is humility: not being forced down, but willingly coming down for love. Bowing your head because you are forced is called humiliation; only bowing it willingly is called humility.
2. Depending When We “Can”

Jesus said, “the Son can do nothing of himself.” (John 5:19) This “cannot” is not a deficiency of ability but an unwillingness rooted in relationship — he is so completely one with the Father that he would never take a single independent action apart from the Father.

We are often the opposite. When we can’t, we pray desperately; once we can, we rely on ourselves. In 1999 Kruger and Dunning of Cornell University published a famous study: in a range of tests, the people who performed worst were the most likely to overestimate their own ability — what came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect”.
The greatest danger has never been “not knowing how” but “thinking you know how”. True humility is not admitting weakness but admitting need.
3. Still Submitting When We Hold a “Position”

The twelve-year-old Jesus sat among the teachers in the temple, and even the most learned rabbis of the day were amazed at his answers. By human logic, he could well have stayed on to keep teaching. But Luke 2:51 records that he went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.

From twelve to thirty — nearly eighteen years — the Bible is almost entirely blank: no miracles, no crowds, only a carpenter’s workshop in Nazareth. The sinless submitted to the sinful; the perfect obeyed the imperfect. And Luke goes on to say that he increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and people. The years of submission were not wasted years; they were years of growth.

Inside each of us there is a little throne. If “self” sits on that throne, we will clutch our “having”, boast of our “being able” and fight for our “position”; if Jesus sits on it, we will naturally be able to lay them down. The question has never been “how much should I lay down?” but “who is on the throne?”

A clenched fist can catch nothing; only an open hand can receive. Had Jesus insisted on his right to be God, he would not have lost a thing; the ones who would have lost are us. He laid down, so that we could gain — that is the gospel.
Laying down is not losing; laying down is the beginning of finding freedom. When you are willing to lay down the right to “be God”, you become more like the Son of God — Jesus Christ.
Reflection: Today, what is the “having”, the “being able” or the “position” in your hand that you are most reluctant to let go of? Are you willing to hand it over for love?
