Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 83
“But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”
Philippians 2:7
• Greet the brothers and sisters; explain that this is the second lesson in the series “Jesus Our Role Model”.
• Read the whole key passage, Philippians 2:5–11.
• Set the tone in one line: the world pursues glory; Jesus laid it down.
• Invite the congregation to be still and prepare their hearts for the Holy Spirit to shine on their motives.
An age that longs to be seen
Every post waiting for a heart
Every video counting its views
Afraid of being overlooked, afraid to be quiet
A hunger to be seen and lifted up
• Open with a question: if the whole world wanted to see you and praise you, would you reach out and take it?
• The spirit of the age: Jean Twenge and W. Keith Campbell’s The Narcissism Epidemic (2009) shows American college students’ NPI scores rising steadily since the 1980s.
• Explain: longing to be loved and accepted is not in itself a sin; the question is to whom we bring it.
• Ask: am I waiting for the Father’s acceptance, or for the applause of the crowd?
Glory: something to pursue, or to lay down?
In the world’s eyes, glory is pursued
In Jesus’ eyes, glory is laid down
True glory is not being honoured by people
But being willing to serve in humility
• Key line: in the world’s eyes, glory is something you pursue; in Jesus’ eyes, glory is something you lay down.
• Jesus is the King of kings, yet he came into the world in the form of a servant.
• Illustration: an old preacher who served a rural church for over thirty years; at his memorial someone said, “Pastor never made us remember his title — but he made us remember Jesus.”
• 321: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to it and letting God be God.
Key Passage and Background
Philippians 2:5–11
A book of joy, written by Paul in prison in Rome
Philippi: a Roman colony obsessed with status
A church competing for glory — Paul lifts up Christ
• Author: Paul; generally dated AD 60–62, during his first imprisonment in Rome; known as “the Epistle of Joy”.
• Philippi became a Roman colony in 42 BC; many residents were veterans who prized citizenship and rank. Acts 16:12 calls it the foremost city of the district.
• Philippians 4:2: Euodia and Syntyche are urged to think the same way in the Lord; 2:3: do nothing through rivalry or conceit.
• This “Christ Hymn” is shaped like a “V”: from the highest down to the cross, then exalted to the highest — the exact opposite of Satan’s “I will ascend into heaven” in Isaiah 14:13.
• 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry.
Emptied himself
“But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,
being made in the likeness of men” Philippians 2:7
Emptied (kenoō): to empty oneself
Servant (doulos): a slave at the very bottom
• Greek ekenōsen, from the verb kenoō, “to empty, to make empty”; in theology, the doctrine of kenosis.
• Clarify: he did not empty himself of his deity (Colossians 2:9); what he laid down was the right to use the honours of his divinity and to be seen.
• morphē (form) means a form matching the essence; homoiōma (likeness) means outward resemblance — he really became a servant; it was no act.
• doulos was a slave in Roman society, with no status and no name; a Roman citizen in Philippi would have been shocked to read this.
Laying down a right ≠ having no right
“Didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped”
Philippians 2:6
Grasped: a prize clutched and never let go
He was worthy — and chose to lay it down
• Philippians 2:6, “grasped” (harpagmos): “a prize of war to be clutched and never let go”.
• Key distinction: laying down a right and having no right are two different things. A man with no money isn’t generous; a man with no standing isn’t humble.
• His humbling of himself is glorious precisely because he was worthy of it all along.
• Application question: what right that is “rightfully mine” am I holding in my hand?
He deliberately turned away from glory
Born in a manger, raised in a carpenter’s home
He could ask for twelve legions — and didn’t
When the crowd would crown him, he withdrew
He entered Jerusalem on a young colt
• Luke 2:7, the manger; Mark 6:3, the carpenter; Isaiah 53:2, no good looks or majesty.
• Matthew 26:53: couldn’t I ask my Father to send me more than twelve legions of angels? He had it, yet didn’t ask.
• John 6:15: after the five loaves and two fish the crowd wanted to make him king by force, and he withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
• Matthew 21:5: a donkey’s colt, not a warhorse; in the ancient Near East kings returned in triumph on warhorses, while those on donkeys came seeking peace.
• John 4:34: my food is to do the will of him who sent me.
The lesson of the moon
The moon gives off no light of its own
It reflects only about 12 per cent
It simply stands in place, facing the sun
Step out in front, and it becomes an eclipse
• Scientific fact: the moon gives off no light of its own; its albedo is about 12 per cent, reflecting only a small fraction of the sunlight that falls on it.
• Picture: we don’t need to shine by ourselves; we only need to stand in the right place and face the true Light.
• The eclipse warning: when we step out in front and block God’s light, we not only fail to shine; we create darkness.
• John 5:41, 8:50, 7:18: he did not receive glory from men.
• 321: from the self-centred life to selflessness; Galatians 2:20, it is no longer I who live.
Whoever would be first must be a servant
“Whoever wants to become first … shall be bondservant of all”
Mark 10:44
“The Son of Man also came not to be served,
but to serve” Mark 10:45
• Mark 9:35: the disciples argued about who was greatest; the Lord said to be last of all and servant of all.
• Servant (diakonos) originally meant a waiter serving at table — the root of “deacon”; bondservant (doulos) is a slave.
• Read the full verse, Mark 10:45, including “and to give his life as a ransom for many”.
• Contrasting picture: the disciples climbing up, the Lord walking towards the cross.
Today’s trap
Turning service into status
Turning an office into an identity
Ordination: an affirmation and commission
As a status symbol, it strays from God’s heart
• Ordination was the church’s affirmation and commission, beautiful in itself; as a status symbol it strays from God’s heart.
• The symptom: no longer longing to serve the Lord but longing for titles and applause; ministry becomes a race for status.
• Matthew 23:8–12: don’t be called “Rabbi”; all of you are brothers; whoever exalts himself will be humbled.
• “Rabbi” (Hebrew rabbi) literally means “my great one”; the Lord is dismantling a structure that assigns seats by forms of address.
Not a title, but a mission
“Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus”
Ephesians 1:1
“What do you have that you didn’t receive?”
1 Corinthians 4:7
• Ephesians 1:1: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God” — a description of a trust, not a title.
• Romans 11:13: “I glorify my ministry” (the original is doxazō, “to give glory”) — in order to provoke his own people and save some of them.
• 1 Corinthians 4:7: who makes you different? What do you have that you didn’t receive?
• Picture: showing off a present someone else gave you is a comical sight.
An office is a function, not an identity
The fivefold ministry: for perfecting the saints
Ephesians 4:11–12
Bach ended his scores: “To God alone be the glory”
Collins: Level 5 leaders are humble
• Ephesians 4:11–12: the fivefold ministry is “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ”.
• Picture: in an operating theatre, surgeons and cleaners each have their place — they work together rather than compete over who is higher (see 1 Corinthians 12).
• Illustration: Bach (1685–1750) wrote J.J., “Jesus, help me”, at the top of his scores and S.D.G., “to God alone be the glory”, at the end.

• Research: Collins, Good to Great (2001), Level 5 leadership — personal humility plus professional will; Owens et al. (2013, Organization Science) found leader humility positively related to team performance.
• 321: 235 relationships rest on selflessness; pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.
If I glorify myself
“If I glorify myself,
my glory is nothing” John 8:54
Kabod: originally weight, heaviness
Glory is weight, not volume
• John 8:54 in full: if I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me.
• Hebrew kabod originally means “weight, heaviness”; Greek doxa means radiance made visible.
• A line to remember: true glory is weight, not volume. People of weight don’t need to be loud.
• Isaiah 42:8: I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.
Impressive is not the same as glory
Don’t do your giving before men
to be seen by them (Matthew 6:1)
The only difference: to whom does the glory go?
Loving men’s praise more than God’s praise
• Compare Matthew 6:1 with Matthew 5:16: both are done before people; the difference is to whom the glory goes.
• Good done with the glory going to God is light; good done with the glory going to ourselves is a performance.
• John 12:43: for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise — their faith was not the problem; their order of priorities was.
• The spotlight effect: Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky (2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) found people overestimate how much others notice them by about double.
• Hebrews 4:13: all things are naked and laid open before his eyes.
He laid aside his garments and washed their feet
“He took a towel and wrapped it around his waist …
and began to wash the disciples’ feet” John 13:4–5
Knowing who he was, he could bend down
Those who can’t bend down are often unsure
• John 13:4–5: garments laid aside, towel around the waist, water poured, feet washed — the work of the lowest slave in the household.
• Note: that night he washed twelve pairs of feet, including Judas’s.
• John 13:3 is the key cause and effect: he knew who he was, where he came from and where he was going, so he could bend down.
• Application: those who can’t bend down are often not too proud but too unsure of who they are in God.
• Mark 12:43: the poor widow’s two small coins count most in God’s accounts.

“Not to us, Yahweh, not to us” Psalm 115:1
Treasure in clay vessels: the power is of God
2 Corinthians 4:7
“He must increase, but I must decrease” John 3:30
• The double negative of Psalm 115:1: not to us, not to us — say it only once, and our hands would still reach out.
• 2 Corinthians 4:7: treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.
• John 3:30: he must increase, but I must decrease.
• 321: the Two Core Values — let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. Notice the word “all”.

Am I doing this for God, or to be seen?

Don’t let your left hand know what your right is doing
• Practice 1: Psalm 139:23–24, ask God to search you; before serving, be still for ten seconds and say, “Lord, this is for you.”
• Practice 2: Matthew 6:3–4, not even your left hand should know what your right hand does — the hardest audience to guard against is yourself.
• Hebrews 11:6: believe that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.
• Research: Dunn, Aknin and Norton (2008, Science) — people who spend money on others are happier.

Learn to call brothers and sisters by name
Learn to appreciate others
See their worth; don’t compare who’s higher

• Research: Festinger’s 1954 social comparison theory — comparison is instinctive, and Satan’s handiest weapon.
• Concrete step: praise three people’s service specifically, naming details rather than giving general praise.
