Form, morphē: true nature, not disguise
Grasped, harpagmos: clutched and never let go
Emptied himself, ekenōsen: poured himself out
Not deity poured out, but the right to glory
• Morphē, form: the true outward form that flows from one’s essential nature, not a disguise.
• Harpagmos: a prize of war clutched and never let go; Jesus did not treat equality with God as something he had to grip tightly.
• Ekenōsen: literally “poured himself out”; orthodox faith: the incarnation is deity plus humanity, not deity minus something.
• Remember: emptying himself was not losing himself; emptying himself was laying down a right.
• Foot washing, John 13:13–15: “I really am the Lord, so I wash feet.”
Can an Office Sin?
An office cannot sin; people do
When people treat an office as a status,
the office is humanised and secularised
Exalt the title, and you lose reverence for the office
• Ask the question and pause: can an office sin?
• The office of pastor was established by God to shepherd people; it cannot sin in itself — it is people who sin.
• When people treat an office as a status, one person falls and the world despises the whole office and God’s calling.
• Isaiah 42:8: I will not give my glory to another.
• God does not compete with man for glory, nor will he ever hand it over to man, because that would destroy man.
The Lesson of the Moon
The moon’s albedo is about 12 per cent;
it has no light of its own, yet lights the night
Its glory lies in facing the sun
Its greatest danger: thinking the light is its own
• The moon’s albedo is about 0.12; it reflects just over a tenth of the sunlight, yet that is enough to light the night.
• Everyone who serves is a moon; the moment of praise is the most dangerous.
• When the moon turns its back on the sun, it becomes the biggest patch of darkness in the dark.
• Collins, Good to Great: in eleven companies that made the leap to greatness, the leaders’ common trait was profound humility.
• Compare Matthew 23:12, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
First Identity: Brothers and Sisters
All of you are brothers. (Matthew 23:8)
Scribes and Pharisees loved top seats and being called Rabbi
Redwoods: over 100 metres tall, roots only a few metres deep
Roots intertwined, the whole forest stands together
• Background to Matthew 23:6–7: they loved the place of honour at feasts, the best seats in the synagogues, and being called Rabbi in the marketplaces.
• “Rabbi” originally meant “my honoured one, my master”; Jesus wants to tear down the ladder of rank stacked up out of forms of address.
• California redwoods: the tallest exceed 115 metres, yet roots go only 2–4 metres deep; they stand because their roots intertwine as a forest.
• Baumeister and Leary’s 1995 “need to belong” theory: stable, caring bonds are a basic psychological need.
• 321’s 235 relationships: 2 spiritual companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
Second Identity: Servants
Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.
(Matthew 20:26)
The Son of Man came not to be served,
but to serve, and to give his life
• Background to Matthew 20:20–24: the mother of Zebedee’s sons asks for the seats at his right and left; the ten are indignant.
• Two Greek words: diakonos, servant (one who waits at table; later “deacon”); doulos, bondservant (belonging wholly to his master).
• In the kingdom of God, the way up is the way down.
• Greenleaf, “The Servant as Leader” (1970): test a good leader by whether those he leads grow healthier and freer.
• 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships more than things.
Third Identity: Slaves
Made free from sin, having become servants of God.
(Romans 6:22)
You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20)
The servant with a pierced ear: I stay because of love
• Romans 6:22 has two movements: made free from sin, become servants of God; there is no third way.
• 1 Corinthians 6:19–20: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you are not your own, you were bought with a price.
• Exodus 21:5–6: the willing servant’s ear is bored through with an awl; the hole is a lifelong mark: I stay because of love.
• Deci and Ryan’s “self-determination theory”: obedience that comes from embracing and internalising a value is the strongest and most lasting motivation.
• Galatians 2:20: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Fourth Identity: Prisoners
I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus
on behalf of you Gentiles. (Ephesians 3:1)
My bonds have advanced the Good News (Philippians 1:12)
Bunyan: twelve years in prison, The Pilgrim’s Progress
• Ephesians 3:1 and 4:1: Paul does not say Rome’s prisoner but “the prisoner of Christ Jesus.”
• The very same chain: to the Romans an instrument of punishment, to Paul an office.
• Philippians 1:12–13: his bonds advanced the Good News; it became evident to the whole palace guard that they were in Christ.
• 2 Timothy 2:9: I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal, but God’s word isn’t chained.
• Bunyan: from 1660, twelve years in Bedford jail; The Pilgrim’s Progress, published in 1678.
Fifth Identity: Condemned Prisoners
Like men sentenced to death,
made a spectacle. (1 Corinthians 4:9)
No longer of the world, no longer living for ourselves
When Stephen was martyred, the Lord stood up for him
• Background to 1 Corinthians 4:8: the Corinthians thought they were already filled, already rich, already reigning, and were splitting into factions.
• Theatron, spectacle, means the theatre; epithanatios describes those already condemned and awaiting execution.
• In the Roman arena such people came out last; the whole crowd knew they would not walk out alive.
• 1 Corinthians 15:31: I die daily.
• Acts 7:55–56: Stephen saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God; Colossians 3:1 says seated, here he stands.
The Ladder of Five Identities
Brothers and sisters, servants, slaves, prisoners, condemned prisoners
The further you go, the more you lay down self
On the world’s ladder you climb up — and are left with only yourself
On heaven’s ladder you step down — and are left with only Christ
• Link the five identities together and draw them as a downward ladder.
• The further you go, the more you lay down self; the more you lay down self, the more you live out the glory of Christ.
• This is the very road the Lord himself walked: the form of God, the form of a servant, the likeness of men, death on a cross.
• Philippians 2:9, “Therefore God also highly exalted him” — notice the word “Therefore.”
Point Three: Lay Down Freedom, Gain Greater Freedom
If the Son makes you free,
you will be free indeed. (John 8:36)
Don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh,
but through love be servants to one another. (Galatians 5:13)
• John 8:36: true freedom is a release of identity, being redeemed from the power of sin.
• Galatians 5:1, stand firm and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage; Galatians 5:13, through love be servants to one another.
• 1 Peter 2:16: not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
• Freedom and serving are not opposites; it is the person bound by face who is least free.
The String, the Pressure, and Nothing to Boast Of
The jam experiment: four times the choice, a tenth the buyers
The string looks like a limit, yet it makes the kite fly
Pressure outside cannot crush us — Christ is within
Of him and to him are all things. Romans 11:36
• Iyengar and Lepper’s 2000 jam experiment: with 24 jams about 3 per cent bought; with 6 jams about 30 per cent bought.
• Four times the options, yet the purchase rate fell to a tenth — “choice overload.”
• A kite’s string looks like a restriction but is the reason it flies; a snapped string means not freedom but a fall.
• At sea level each square centimetre bears about a kilogram of air pressure — over ten tonnes on the whole body — yet there is equal pressure within.
• 1 Corinthians 4:7, what do you have that you didn’t receive; Romans 11:36, of him, through him, to him.
Putting It into Practice (1)
Change the way you address people:
call one another brother and sister
Cultivate a servant’s attitude:
do everything as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23)
• Practice one: within a week, start calling at least three people “brother” or “sister”; the eight stages begin with Information, Revelation and Conviction.
• Practice two: every day do one act of service no one will know about or thank you for, forty days in a row.
• Point to Colossians 3:23–24: work as for the Lord, and not for men.
• Stress evaluation after implementation: is the heart sweet or resentful?
Putting It into Practice (2)
Willingly lay down your rights:
drop the argument and the control at home, church and work
Reflect on your identity:
meditate on “I am a slave of Christ”
• Practice three: choose a conversation you would normally fight to the end; listen to the end first, then respond, and swallow that “I told you so.”
• Practice four: every morning, let your first words to the Lord be, “Today I am your servant; please send me.”
• The second half of the eight stages: Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — a practice needs a time frame, a companion and the potential to multiply.
• The 920 practice: everyone around me is my “2”; before them I live out the “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.
The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
Three Foundations, Two Core Values, One Goal
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
• The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
• The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
• The worldly system is a pyramid; God’s system is turned upside down: the higher up you are, the more people you serve.
• Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
• The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — the order cannot be reversed.
Closing and Call
True honour is not what you are called,
but that people see Jesus when they see you
Therefore God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9)
Exaltation is the result of humbling
• Return to the opening business card: true honour is that people see Jesus when they see you.
• The Roman general needed reminding who he was; Jesus knew from the beginning who he was, and so dared to bend down.
• Only those who know who they are before God are unafraid to humble themselves.
• Call: lay down one specific right to glory today.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, you laid down the right to glory;
help me to be your servant willingly.
Let Jesus be King;
let Jesus receive all the glory.
• Lead the congregation in reading the declaration of faith together.
• Read Philippians 2:9–11; all say together, “Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.”
• Blessing: may the Lord give us a gentle and humble heart, so that when people see us they see Jesus.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are looking together at the next talk in “Jesus Our Role Model” — laying down the right to glory. Our key passage is Philippians 2:5–8: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

Brothers and sisters, let me start with a question. If someone gave you a blank business card and you could print only one line on it — the identity you most want people to know you by — what would you print?

In Roman times a victorious general was given a “triumph.” A laurel wreath, a chariot, the cheers of the multitude. The church father Tertullian records that a man stood behind the general, leaning close to his ear and reminding him over and over: remember that you are only a man.

In that very same era, another King entered a city. No chariot, only a donkey’s colt; no laurel wreath — a few days later, only a crown of thorns. He was worthy of all glory, yet of his own accord he laid down the right to glory.

Paul wrote this letter while he was in prison in Rome, around AD 60. Philippi was a Roman colony; many in the city held Roman citizenship, and what they valued most was status and face. The city that loved face the most received the letter that cared for face the least. Just before our key passage Paul says: do nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility.

Point one: an office is not a title. Ephesians 4:11–12 says God gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? An office is a function, not a rank; a verb, not a noun.

Let me ask you a question: can an office sin? No. It is people who sin. But when people treat an office as a status, then when one person falls, the world despises the whole office and no longer even respects God’s calling. Brothers and sisters, when people exalt titles, they lose their reverence for the office. God said long ago: I will not give my glory to another. God does not compete with man for glory, and he will never hand his glory over to man.

In the original, “emptied himself” means poured himself out. But hear this clearly: what Jesus poured out was not his deity, but the right to glory. He really was the Lord, yet he took off his outer garment and washed his disciples’ feet. He said: if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet…

Think of the moon. The moon gives off no light of its own; it reflects just over a tenth of the sunlight, and yet it lights up the whole night. The moon’s glory lies in facing the sun; the moon’s greatest danger would be to think the light was its own. Brothers and sisters, every one of us who serves is a moon.
Point two: our true identity in the Lord is fivefold.

First, brothers and sisters. The Lord says: all of you are brothers. California’s redwoods stand more than a hundred metres tall, yet their roots are only a few metres deep. Why don’t they fall? Because they grow in forests, and their roots intertwine. When the wind comes, every tree is held up by the whole forest.

Second, servants. The Lord says: whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. And he says the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve. Brothers and sisters, in the kingdom of God, the way up is the way down. The higher the position, the heavier the responsibility; the more honoured the standing, the more we need to learn to bend down. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Third, slaves. Romans 6:22 says we have been made free from sin and have become servants of God. We were bought with a price; we no longer belong to ourselves. In the Old Testament, a willing servant could have gone free, but if he said, “I love my master; I will not go out free,” his master bored his ear through with an awl. That pierced ear was a lifelong mark: because of love, I chose to stay.
Brothers and sisters, true freedom is not having no master; it is choosing the right master.

Fourth, prisoners. Paul does not say, “I am Rome’s prisoner”; he says, “I am the prisoner of Christ Jesus.” The very same chain was an instrument of punishment in others’ eyes, and an office in his. More than three hundred years ago, John Bunyan was locked up for twelve years for preaching the gospel, and in his cell he wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress. They could lock up Bunyan’s body, but they could not lock up the word of God.

Fifth, condemned prisoners. Paul says we are like men sentenced to death, made a spectacle. When Stephen was martyred, he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Elsewhere the Bible says the Lord is seated; only here does it say he stood up. For a condemned prisoner who was lowly in the world’s eyes, the King of heaven rose to his feet.
Point three: lay down your freedom and gain a greater freedom. True freedom is not “I do whatever I want”; it is “I let the Lord do whatever he wants.”

There is a famous jam experiment: when twenty-four kinds of jam were set out, only 3 per cent of people bought any; when only six were set out, 30 per cent bought. Four times the options, yet a tenth of the purchases. Brothers and sisters, unlimited options don’t make people freer; they only make people more anxious. The real lightness of life comes from having only one Master.
Paul says: of him, and through him, and to him are all things. He is the beginning, he is the way, he is the end — where in the middle is there any room for our names?

So today there are four practices. First, change the way you address people — learn to call one another brother and sister. Second, cultivate a servant’s attitude — whether the task is great or small, do it as for the Lord. Third, willingly lay down your rights — at home, at church and at work, take the initiative to drop the argument and let go of control. Fourth, reflect on your identity — meditate on “I am a slave of Christ.”
Brothers and sisters, a practice needs a time frame, it needs a companion, and it needs to multiply.

True honour is not being called Pastor So-and-so or Leader So-and-so; it is that when people see you, they see the likeness of Jesus. The more we lay down human glory, the more God receives his glory in us.
The Roman general needed someone to remind him who he was; our Lord did not — he knew from the beginning who he was. And precisely because he knew who he was, he dared to bend down and wash feet.

Let us pray together. Lord, you laid down the right to glory and took the form of a servant, becoming our example of serving. Help me to lay down the praise and position people give, and in my serving to seek your pleasure alone. Let me be your servant willingly, a blessing to my brothers and sisters, glorifying your name all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may we lay down one right to glory this very day. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are looking together at the next talk in “Jesus Our Role Model” — laying down the right to glory.

Our key passage is Philippians 2:5–8: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

The world’s glory is found up high; Jesus’ glory is found down low. Today we will look at three things: an office is not a title; our fivefold identity in the Lord; and how laying down our freedom actually gains us a greater freedom.

Brothers and sisters, let me start with a question. Suppose someone handed you a blank business card and you could print only one line on it — the identity you most want people to know you by. What would you print?
Some would print a job title, some a place of service, and some a relationship. That little card is really a mirror; it shows what our hearts value most.

In Jesus’ day Rome had a grand ceremony called the “triumph.” A general came home from victory, wore a laurel wreath and stood in a chariot, riding through streets packed with people while the crowds shouted his name. It was the highest glory a man could receive in his lifetime.

The church father Tertullian records that at such a moment a man stood behind the general, leaning close to his ear and reminding him over and over: remember that you are only a man. Brothers and sisters, that is the most honest reminder there is — and also the one most easily drowned out by cheering.

In that very same era, another King entered a city. No chariot, only a donkey’s colt; no laurel wreath — a few days later he wore a crown of thorns. He was worthy of all glory, yet of his own accord he laid down the right to glory.

Paul wrote this letter in prison. In it he mentions the whole palace guard and those of Caesar’s household, so most scholars believe it was written during his imprisonment in Rome, around AD 60 to 62.

The church in Philippi was the first church Paul planted in Europe. It began with a woman who dealt in purple cloth, a demon-possessed slave girl and a jailer — three people from completely different social classes who became one family in Christ.

Philippi was a Roman colony. Many residents held Roman citizenship and held being Roman as their highest pride. It was an honour-and-shame society, where titles and forms of address were declarations of status; a slave had the least honour of all, and the cross was the greatest shame.

Brothers and sisters, it was to just such a city, the city that loved face the most, that Paul wrote the letter that cared for face the least. He says first: do nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.
Point one: an office is not a title.

Ephesians 4 says: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.”

Brothers and sisters, listen to the purpose: the perfecting of the saints, the building up of the body of Christ. An office is a job, not a rank; a verb, not a noun. From “I have been sent to serve” to “I am a person of standing” is only a single step — yet it is the distance between heaven and earth.
There are three key words in our key passage.

“Form” in the original is morphē — the true outward form that flows from one’s essential nature, not a disguise. “Existing in the form of God” means he was fully God all along; and “taking the form of a servant” was not playacting either.
“A thing to be grasped” is harpagmos, a prize of war clutched and never let go. Equality with God was his from the beginning, but he did not treat it as something he had to grip tightly.

“Emptied himself” is ekenōsen, literally “poured himself out.” Hear this clearly: what he poured out was not his deity; what he poured out was the right to glory. Emptying himself was not losing himself; emptying himself was laying down a right.
He really was the Lord, yet he took off his outer garment and washed his disciples’ feet. He said: if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: can an office sin?

The office of pastor was established by God to shepherd the flock; the office itself cannot sin — it is people who sin. But when people treat “pastor” as a rank, then when a particular pastor falls, people conclude that the office has lost its dignity, and in the end they no longer respect God’s calling.
Remember this: when people exalt titles, they lose their reverence for the office.

God said long ago: I am Yahweh, that is my name; I will not give my glory to another. God does not compete with man for glory, nor will he ever hand his glory over to man, because that would destroy man.

Let’s look up at the moon. The moon gives off no light of its own. Its albedo is only about 12 per cent — it reflects back just over a tenth of the sunlight — and yet that is enough to light up the whole night.

The moon’s glory lies entirely in facing the sun; its greatest danger would be to think the light was its own. Brothers and sisters, every one of us who serves is a moon. When someone says, “You preached so well,” that is the most dangerous moment of all.

In his research for Good to Great, Jim Collins found that the leaders who took companies to lasting greatness shared one trait: they were profoundly modest, gave the credit to others and shouldered the responsibility themselves. The Bible said it long ago: whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
Point two: our true identity in the Lord is fivefold.

First, brothers and sisters. The Lord says: “But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers.” The background is pointed — the scribes and Pharisees loved the place of honour at feasts and loved being called Rabbi.

California’s redwoods are the tallest trees on earth; the tallest of them stands over 115 metres high, yet their roots are only two to four metres deep. Why don’t they fall over? Because their roots intertwine, and when the wind comes, every tree is held up by the whole forest.

In 1995 the psychologists Baumeister and Leary put forward the theory of “the need to belong”: stable, caring bonds are a basic human psychological need. That is exactly what 321’s 235 relationships say: join with a selfless person to form a “2,” build the “3” of spiritual parents and children, and become the “5,” a team of spiritual comrades.

Second, servants. Jesus says: “Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

The mother of Zebedee’s sons came asking for seats, and when the other ten disciples heard, they were indignant — not because the two shouldn’t have asked, but because they themselves hadn’t asked first. Brothers and sisters, the old self is still arranging the seating even in the presence of Jesus.
In the kingdom of God, the way up is the way down. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.
Third, slaves. Paul says: “But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.”

Notice the two movements: made free from sin, and then become servants of God. There is no third way — a person is either a slave of sin or a slave of God. We were bought with a price; we no longer belong to ourselves.

The Old Testament has a beautiful picture of this. A servant served for six years and in the seventh could go free; but if he said, “I love my master; I will not go out free,” his master bored his ear through with an awl. That hole was a lifelong mark: I could have gone, but because of love I chose to stay.

True freedom is not having no master; it is choosing the right master. Deci and Ryan’s self-determination theory found the same: obedience that comes from embracing and internalising a value far outstrips motivation driven by outside pressure. The strongest force is not compulsion but willingness.
Fourth, prisoners. Paul calls himself “the prisoner of Christ Jesus.”

He does not say, “I am Rome’s prisoner.” The very same chain was an instrument of punishment in Roman eyes, and an office in Paul’s. He says: my bonds have turned out to the progress of the Good News; God’s word isn’t chained.

In 1660, the English preacher John Bunyan was thrown into Bedford jail for refusing to stop preaching the gospel, and was held there, all told, for twelve years. No pulpit, no congregation, no title — only a pen. Released in 1672, he was imprisoned again for preaching in 1675, and it is generally held that The Pilgrim’s Progress was written during that shorter spell in prison.
Brothers and sisters, they could lock up Bunyan’s body, but they could not lock up the word of God. The focus is Jesus, not our circumstances.

Fifth, condemned prisoners. Paul says: “For, I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last of all, like men sentenced to death. For we are made a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men.”

Some in the Corinthian church thought they were already reigning as kings. Paul answers: do you think you’re sitting in the stands, reigning as kings? We apostles are the condemned prisoners marched into the middle of the arena, saved for the final act. We no longer belong to the world, and we no longer live for ourselves. He puts it without the slightest ambiguity: I die daily.

As Stephen was being stoned to death, full of the Holy Spirit, he looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Elsewhere the Bible says the Lord is seated; only here does it say he is standing. For a condemned prisoner who was lowly in the world’s eyes, the King of heaven rose to his feet.

Brothers and sisters, put these five identities together: brothers and sisters, servants, slaves, prisoners, condemned prisoners. It is a gradual road of humility. The further along you go, the more you lay down self; the more you lay down self, the more you live out the glory of Christ.
On the world’s ladder, people climb up, and at the top there is nothing left but themselves; on heaven’s ladder, people step down, and at the bottom there is nothing left but Christ.

This is the very road the Lord himself walked. And then Scripture says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” Notice that word — “Therefore.” Exaltation is the result of humbling.
Point three: lay down your freedom and gain a greater freedom.

In the world’s eyes these five identities grow ever less free; but in the Lord it is exactly the opposite. Only when we lay down our own control can we be led by the Holy Spirit; only when we lay down our own face can we serve sincerely; only when we lay down our own glory can the glory of Christ be seen.
True freedom is not “I do whatever I want”; it is “I let the Lord do whatever he wants.”

Paul says: don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another. Brothers and sisters, freedom and serving have never been opposites. A person who cannot be at peace without others’ approval may look impressive, but is in fact the least free of all.

People today assume that freedom means the more options the better. In 2000, Iyengar and Lepper carried out a famous experiment in a supermarket: when twenty-four kinds of jam were set out, only about 3 per cent of people bought any; when only six were set out, about 30 per cent bought. Four times the options, yet a tenth of the purchases. Unlimited options don’t make people freer; they only make people more anxious. The real lightness of life comes from having only one Master.
Think of a kite, too. The string looks like a restriction, but it is the very reason the kite can fly. If the string snaps, the kite does not gain its freedom; it begins to fall.

Standing at sea level, our bodies bear well over ten tonnes of atmospheric pressure, yet we are not crushed, because there is an equal pressure inside us. Brothers and sisters, the pressure outside cannot crush us, because Christ is within. That is why Paul says: of him, and through him, and to him are all things.

There are four practices today, and we will put them into practice with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

First, change the way you address people. This week, change how you address at least three people, calling them “brother” or “sister.” Each night ask yourself: did someone’s title change the way I spoke to them today?

Second, cultivate a servant’s attitude. Colossians says: whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men. Every day, deliberately do one act of service that no one will know about and no one will thank you for. Afterwards ask yourself: is my heart sweet, or resentful?

Third, willingly lay down your rights. Ask the Lord to show you which right you are least willing to lay down — the right to have the last word? The right to receive an apology? This week, choose a conversation you would normally have fought to the bitter end, and listen to the end first before you respond.
Fourth, reflect on your identity. Every morning, let the first words you say when you open your eyes be to the Lord: today I am your servant; please send me.

Brothers and sisters, a practice needs a time frame, it needs a companion, and it needs to multiply. The 920 practice says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” The hardest person to get along with beside you today is God’s lesson for you to live out selflessness.
Let’s set this lesson within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he laid down the right to glory; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide — only the Holy Spirit can make a person willing to go low, because the flesh only ever climbs upwards.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The worldly system is a pyramid; God’s system is turned upside down — the higher up you are, the more people you serve.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; only humility inspiring humility brings a win for both. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today we ask first for a change of mindset — from “a title is glory” to “an office is a trust.”
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that business card we began with.

True honour is not being called Pastor So-and-so or Leader So-and-so; it is that when people see you, they see the likeness of Jesus. The more we lay down human glory, the more God receives his glory in us.

The Roman general needed someone to remind him, “Remember that you are only a man,” because he could so easily forget who he was. Our Lord needed no one — precisely because he knew who he was, he dared to bend down and wash feet. Only those who truly know who they are before God are unafraid to humble themselves.

Let us pray together. Lord, you laid down the right to glory and took the form of a servant, becoming our example of serving. We confess that we often spend our whole lives striving for the things you spent your whole life laying down. Forgive us.

Help me to lay down the praise and position people give, and in my serving to seek your pleasure alone. Let me be your servant willingly, a blessing to my brothers and sisters, glorifying your name all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord give us a gentle and humble heart, so that whatever position we are in, when people see us, they see Jesus. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Introduction: An Age in Which Everyone Wants to Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we are going to reflect together on a lesson that looks very small, yet takes a whole lifetime to learn: learning to hide ourselves, so that Jesus is seen.

We live in an age unlike any before it. One mobile phone is a television station; one account is a stage. That in itself is not a bad thing, and God uses these tools to spread the gospel too. But, brothers and sisters, this age has quietly planted a mindset in our hearts: being seen means you have value, and not being seen is as good as not existing.

There was a sister who had served on the worship team for three years. One Sunday she wasn’t on the platform at all; she was down on the floor setting out chairs and looking after the children. After the service she sat in her car and suddenly felt like crying. She said, “I was doing exactly the same thing — for the Lord. But nobody saw it, and I feel as if today was wasted.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had a moment like that? You did something good that nobody knew about, and your heart felt a little empty; you were overlooked once, and your heart felt a little sour. That little emptiness, that little sourness, is a very honest signal. It is telling us that inside our service there still lives an “I” that badly wants to be seen.

And our Lord Jesus, with his whole life, walked a path that ran in exactly the opposite direction.

He was the King of kings, yet he chose to be born in a manger, to grow up in Nazareth, and to spend thirty years as an unknown carpenter. With a single word he could still the wind and the waves, yet again and again he charged those he had healed, “Tell no one.” When the crowds wanted to make him king, he withdrew alone to the mountain. He had every “right to glory”, and time after time he laid it down.

That is the theme of this lesson: laying down the right to glory.

In the vision of Kingdom 321 we often say that the old self is self-centred and the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. And the side of pride that is hardest to detect hides inside our service — I am still serving God; I would just like to be seen by people a little while I’m at it.

The lesson puts it beautifully: true glory does not lie in being seen, but in letting Jesus be seen.

Today we will follow the lesson’s four key points and learn step by step: first, Jesus chose a way of serving that was “hidden” rather than “famous”; second, what people see should not be me, but Jesus; third, submarine service — being seen by God is better than being seen by people; fourth, facing ourselves honestly — on whom, in the end, is my focus?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Light of the Sermon on the Mount, and the Hiddenness in Mark
sections.html: Before we come to the key points, let’s set out the background clearly. Once you understand the background, the weight of these words is completely different.

sections.heading: 1. The Author, Audience and Times of Matthew’s Gospel
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, who had been a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9). In those days a tax collector held a job his own people despised. Yet the Lord Jesus said to him, “Follow me,” and he got up and followed him. The man least likely to be used by God went on to write the first book of the New Testament; and throughout that whole book, when he mentions himself, he honestly labels himself “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3). Brothers and sisters, that in itself is a silent sermon: a person changed by the Lord is no longer in a hurry to put a crown on his own name.

Matthew is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish believers. That is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament so heavily, explaining again and again that “this was to fulfil what the prophet said”, in order to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah the Jews had awaited for so many years.

sections.heading: 2. The Sermon on the Mount: The Charter of a Brand-New Kingdom
sections.html:
Our theme passage comes from Matthew 5 and belongs to the “Sermon on the Mount” (Matthew 5–7), the charter of the Kingdom of Heaven proclaimed by the Lord Jesus. He begins with the Beatitudes, turning our whole set of values upside down — blessed are the poor in spirit, blessed are those who mourn, blessed are the gentle. Straight after that he says, “You are the salt of the earth … You are the light of the world.”

Notice the order: first comes the “life” of the Beatitudes, and only then the “influence” of salt and light. This is exactly what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. We don’t start by working out how to shine; we first let our life be renewed by the Lord, and the light shines out naturally.

There is one more very important thing. In the very same discourse, right at the start of chapter 6, the Lord Jesus says, “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1).

Matthew 5:16 tells us to let our light “shine before men”, yet 6:1 says, don’t do it “before men”. Do these two sayings contradict each other? Not at all. The difference is not whether we are seen, but who receives the glory once we have been seen. The conclusion of 5:16 is “glorify your Father who is in heaven”; the motive in 6:1 is “to be seen by them”. The very same good deed can be a lampstand, or it can be a stage.

“To be seen by them” in the original Greek is πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι (pros to theathēnai). The verb’s root, θεάομαι (theaomai), means “to look at, to watch as a spectator”, and the English word theatre comes from this very root. The Lord Jesus’ point is a sharp one: don’t turn good works into a performance. No wonder he goes on to use the word “hypocrites” — in Greek ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs), which originally meant “an actor wearing a mask on the stage”.

sections.heading: 3. The “Messianic Secret” in Mark’s Gospel
sections.html:
Several of this lesson’s other passages come from Mark. Scholars point to a distinctive feature of this book which they call the “Messianic secret” — Jesus repeatedly forbids people to make him known.

After cleansing the man with leprosy he says, “See you say nothing to anybody, but go show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them” (Mark 1:44). After healing the deaf man with the speech impediment, “He commanded them that they should tell no one, but the more he commanded them, so much the more widely they proclaimed it” (Mark 7:36).

Why? Because the Messiah the Jews of that day had in mind was a political liberator who would overthrow Rome. Had Jesus allowed the crowds to exalt him on their own understanding, the way of the cross would have been drowned in human enthusiasm. He had to walk the whole way of the cross first; only then would people truly understand who he was.

Mark 1:45 records the result: once his fame spread, “Jesus could no more openly enter into a city, but was outside in desert places.” Brothers and sisters, fame never comes free.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus Chose a Way of Serving That Was “Hidden”, Not “Famous”
sections.html:
Right at the outset the lesson points to a surprising fact: in the Gospels, Jesus often avoided the crowds and refused to be exalted by people.

Scripture: Three Deliberate Withdrawals

The first was after a healing. “Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, ‘I want to. Be made clean.’ When he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was made clean. He strictly warned him, and immediately sent him out, and said to him, ‘See you say nothing to anybody’” (Mark 1:41–44).

The second was after a busy day. “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The evening before, “all the city was gathered together at the door” — the most “successful” night of his ministry. The next morning, before it was light, he did not go out to receive applause; he withdrew to the wilderness to meet with the Father.

The third was when the applause was loudest. After feeding the five thousand with five loaves and two fish, “Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). Notice the words “by force”. This is the hardest kind of pressure to refuse — not pressure to sin, but pressure to be king.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: He Is the Servant Who “Will Not Strive, Nor Shout”

Why did Jesus act this way? Matthew gives us the best explanation. Matthew 12:15–19 records: “Jesus, perceiving that, withdrew from there. Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all, and commanded them that they should not make him known: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, ‘Behold, my servant whom I have chosen; my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations. He will not strive, nor shout; neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets.’”

“They should not make him known” is not polite modesty; it is the portrait of the Servant that the prophet foretold some seven hundred years earlier. True authority has no need to strive; he is so great that he does not need to prove himself.

The lesson is spot on: Jesus would not let people make miracles the foundation of their faith, nor let fame replace the way of the cross. What he sought was not for people to praise him, “How great you are,” but for people to turn and say, “How great God is!”

The God Who Hides Himself

This disposition is not Jesus’ alone; it is the disposition of the triune God. Isaiah 45:15 says, “Most certainly you are a God who has hidden yourself, God of Israel, the Savior.”

The word for “who has hidden yourself” in Hebrew is מִסְתַּתֵּר (mistatter), from the root סָתַר (satar, to hide). It is in the reflexive form, meaning “to make oneself hidden”. God is not hidden by anyone else; he chooses to hide himself.

And notice the context of this verse. Isaiah 45 is about Cyrus, king of Persia. More than a hundred years before Cyrus was born, God called him by name: “I have called you by your name” (Isaiah 45:4). All his life Cyrus never came to know this God — the text says, “though you have not known me” — and yet God used him to set the exiled Judeans free to return home. Brothers and sisters, this is the God who hides himself: he works behind the scenes of history, leaving no signature and no photograph, yet moving the course of the whole world.

He does not need to be publicised; he only needs to be revealed.

An Example from Life: The Invisible Light

There is a beautiful scientific fact here. Light itself is actually invisible. Look side-on at a beam of sunlight in a vacuum and you will see no beam at all; the reason we can see the shaft of light from a cinema projector is that dust in the air scatters it. In other words, the presence of light is made known through the things it illuminates. Light never shines for its own sake.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the Lord Jesus meant by “You are the light of the world”. When a Christian truly shines, what people remember is not the light, but the path it lit up.

Applying 321: Pride Is Leaving Our Originally Intended Position; Humility Is Returning to It

The 321 vision says that pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Jesus’ withdrawal in John 6:15 is the perfect demonstration. The crowd wanted to give him a throne — a premature, cheap throne that bypassed the cross. Had he accepted it, he would have left the position the Father had appointed for him. Withdrawing to the mountain was returning to that position — letting the Father be the Father and the Son be the Son.

Our temptations today are often variations on that same temptation: someone wants to set a crown on your head, and it is not the crown the Father means to give you. Brothers and sisters, learn to withdraw to the mountain.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: What People See Should Not Be Me, but Jesus
sections.html:
The lesson’s second key point brings us back to the theme passage.

Scripture: A Lampstand Is Not a Stage

“You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:14–16)

This passage is often misread as “Christians should be bold about putting themselves forward”. Look carefully at three details.

First, the Lord says, “You are the light of the world,” not “You must find a way to become light.” This is identity. John 8:12 says, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” Our light is moonlight, borrowed from him.

Second, the picture the Lord uses is a “stand”, a lampstand. A lampstand’s job is to hold the lamp up high so that its light reaches further. The lampstand itself never gives off light, and nobody walks into a room and compliments the lampstand. Brothers and sisters, we are the lampstand, not the lamp.

Third, the passage concludes, “and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” If good works don’t carry people’s eyes to the Father in heaven, they are only a handsome performance.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: The Witness of the Early Disciples

When Peter healed the man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate, everyone was amazed. Peter immediately moved the focus away from himself: “By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all” (Acts 3:16).

In this one short verse, “his name” appears twice. Peter did not say, “Our faith is so great.” He said, “By faith in his name.”

Now look at Acts 4:13: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” What amazed the council was not their education, not their eloquence, but this — “these two men had been with Jesus.”

That is the highest praise there is. When people look at you, what they recognise is the fragrance of Jesus. Second Corinthians 2:14 says, “Now thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place.” What is the nature of a fragrance? You can smell it, but you can’t grasp it; it lingers on a person, but it isn’t that person’s own.

An Example from Scripture: He Must Increase, but I Must Decrease

John the Baptist understood this better than anyone in the whole Bible. When his disciples came to him, jealous, and said, “Everyone is coming to him,” John’s reply became the motto of servants of God in every generation since:

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

In the original, “increase” is αὐξάνω (auxanō, to grow) and “decrease” is ἐλαττόω (elattoō, to lessen, to become smaller). This is a continuing action in progress — not a one-off decision, but a lifetime of letting yourself become smaller.

And the Lord Jesus’ verdict on him was this: “Among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer” (Matthew 11:11). Brothers and sisters, do you see the wonderful contrast? All his life he worked at becoming smaller, and the Lord said no one was greater than he.

Psychology: We Want to Be Seen More Than We Think

Psychology has a thoroughly documented phenomenon called the “self-serving bias”. In a classic 1975 review, Dale Miller and Michael Ross showed that people tend to credit their successes to themselves and blame their failures on circumstances. A 1981 study by the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson in Acta Psychologica was even more direct: among the American drivers surveyed, about 93 per cent believed their driving skill was above the median. Mathematically, that is impossible.

Brothers and sisters, this is not meant to condemn us; it is meant to make us honest. If we overrate ourselves even behind the steering wheel, how much more in the pulpit, or when we are being praised? The Bible’s diagnosis came earlier and goes deeper: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9)

sections.heading: Applying 321: Jesus Is the Focal Point
sections.html:
What the 321 Vision Says: Jesus Is the Focal Point — Not Ourselves, Not Others, Not Our Circumstances.

The lesson’s words are worth memorising: if Jesus is the focal point of our service, we can be used by God; if the focal point is ourselves, then even if we are lifted up, we will soon fall. True “fame” is not people remembering my name, but people coming to know the name of Jesus through me.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Submarine Service — Being Seen by God Is Better Than Being Seen by People
sections.html:
The lesson uses a vivid picture: Jesus calls us to be “submarines”, not “aircraft carriers”.

A Picture: The Aircraft Carrier and the Submarine

In human eyes an aircraft carrier is dazzling. It is like a floating city; wherever it goes, every satellite in the world can see it. A submarine is the exact opposite: it moves silently through the deep sea, giving off no light and making no sound, straining even to keep its own position hidden. It puts its greatest effort not into being seen, but into not being seen.

But, brothers and sisters, though the submarine is unseen, at the decisive moment it can exert enormous influence. What an aircraft carrier fears most is often the very submarine it cannot find.

The lesson draws a crucial conclusion: spiritual life is not measured by exposure, but by depth.

Science Bears It Out: What Can Be Seen Is Only Ever a Small Part

The natural world preaches this truth everywhere. Sea ice has a density of about 920 kilograms per cubic metre, and seawater about 1,025, so the part of a floating iceberg that shows above the surface is only about a tenth of its volume. What really decides how stable it is and how big it is lies in the nine-tenths below the water.

Plants are the same. In a study published in 1937, the American botanist H. J. Dittmer measured the root system of a single rye plant and found that the roots alone ran to some six hundred and twenty kilometres, and with the root hairs added the total length came to more than ten thousand kilometres. Above ground you see a grass a few dozen centimetres tall; below ground, out of sight, are more than ten thousand kilometres of lifelines.

Brothers and sisters, where will you put your effort? Into the tenth that shows above the waves, or the nine-tenths in the deep?

Scripture: The Father Who Sees in Secret

The Lord Jesus’ teaching could not be clearer: “But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6).

The Greek for “in secret” is κρυπτός (kryptos), meaning “hidden, concealed”; the English word cryptography comes from it. The Father is right there in that hidden place: he is not waiting for you in the applause; he is waiting for you behind the closed door.

In the same chapter the Lord speaks of three things — giving, prayer and fasting — and all three times he closes with the same pattern of words (Matthew 6:4, 6:6, 6:18). Three repetitions mark the Lord’s emphasis.

And his verdict on the other kind of person is this: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2). In the original, this phrase is commercial language, meaning “the receipt has been issued; the account is settled in full.” Brothers and sisters, this is a very solemn word: the moment human applause breaks out, the account in heaven is closed. Do you want to collect now, or collect then?

The lesson says it well: this is the spiritual order of glory — it isn’t that people see you first; it is that God sees you first.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: Every Servant of God Has Taken the Lesson of “Hiddenness”

The lesson mentions Moses, John the Baptist, Elijah and Paul, and it is a very accurate observation. Almost everyone God has used mightily was first prepared in hiddenness.

Moses spent forty years in Pharaoh’s palace; at forty he struck out in his own strength, and ended up fleeing into the wilderness. Acts 7:30 says, “When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.” Forty years of shepherding: God was wearing away a prince’s “self”.

Before Elijah’s great victory on Mount Carmel, God first said to him, “Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan” (1 Kings 17:3). He had to be hidden by the brook before he could stand on the mountain.

And John the Baptist? “The child was growing and becoming strong in spirit, and was in the desert until the day of his public appearance to Israel” (Luke 1:80). The wilderness was his seminary.

Nor did Paul, after he came to faith, rush off to hold evangelistic rallies; rather, “I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus” (Galatians 1:17).

And our Lord himself spent thirty of his thirty-three and a half years in Nazareth. “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them … And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:51–52). Thirty years hidden, three and a half years of ministry — that ratio deserves our quiet meditation.

The Witness of History: A Prayer Meeting No One Saw

On 13 August 1727, in a little village in eastern Germany called Herrnhut, “the Lord’s watch”, a group of Moravian Brethren believers who had fled from Bohemia experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit during a communion service. After that revival they held no great evangelistic rallies. They did just one very unremarkable thing: they divided into shifts and prayed in turn, twenty-four hours a day, without a break. That prayer went on for more than a hundred years, and the missionaries later sent out from this little village reached the West Indies, Greenland and Africa. A group of people whose names nobody remembers prayed in secret for a hundred years and changed the history of modern missions.

The New Testament has a man like this too. Colossians 4:12 says, “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.” The Greek for “striving” is ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnizomai), a word from the arena, for wrestling and combat. Where no one could see, he wrestled for his brothers and sisters.

Applying 321: Hidden in Christ

The lesson is exactly right: “hiding ourselves” is not running away from the community; it is choosing to hide ourselves in Christ. Colossians 3:3 says, “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” This is precisely what 321 calls selflessness.

Note this: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Brothers and sisters, put a drop of water on a table and it soon dries up; put a drop of water into the ocean and it will never dry up. Being hidden is not disappearing; it is entering into the infinite.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Facing Ourselves Honestly — On Whom, in the End, Is My Focus?
sections.html:
The lesson’s fourth key point turns the blade towards ourselves. In a generation where anyone can become a “celebrity”, we need all the more to examine ourselves: who, in the end, is the focus of my service?

Three Honest Questions

The lesson gives us three questions. Answer them quietly in your heart; there’s no need to say them aloud, because God already knows.

First, when people mention my service, is it my name they remember, or the name of Jesus?

Second, when someone else is praised, do I feel jealous or resentful inside?

Third, when others speak of what Jesus has done through me, am I quick to add, “Actually, I also …”?

The third question cuts deepest. That little “Actually, I also …” is often said lightly, naturally, wrapped in spiritual packaging, yet it gives away the real longing at the bottom of the heart: I want to be seen too.

Scripture: The Most Dangerous Kind of Piety

The Lord Jesus’ severest criticism of the Pharisees was not that they lacked piety, but that their piety was put on for people to see. “But they do all their works to be seen by men. They make their phylacteries broad, enlarge the fringes of their garments” (Matthew 23:5).

Notice that what they wore were “phylacteries”, boxes holding Scripture, and that in itself was not wrong (Deuteronomy 6:8). What was wrong was the motive — turning God’s word into an ornament for themselves.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most dangerous kind of sin, because it wears the robe of piety. The lesson asks very honestly whether we are truly “hidden in Christ”, or are still wrapping the “self” in a spiritual robe.

Psychology: The Spotlight Effect

In 2000, Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky of Cornell University in the United States published a famous series of experiments and named the “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on a very embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room full of people, then asked them to guess how many people had noticed. On average the participants guessed about half; in reality only about a quarter had.

The conclusion: we grossly overestimate how much attention other people pay to us. We always feel that a spotlight is following us around overhead, when in fact most people are busy looking at the one over their own heads. Brothers and sisters, this is very liberating news: the image you are working so hard to protect is not being watched by nearly as many people as you think. You can let it go.

Another study points us in an even more beautiful direction. Elizabeth Dunn of the University of British Columbia in Canada, Michael Norton of Harvard University and their colleagues published research in the journal Science in 2008 which found that people who spent money on others were happier than people who spent the same money on themselves. The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

Famous Words

The evangelist D. L. Moody is generally credited with saying that a man’s character is what he is in the dark. And Paul puts it even more plainly: “For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends” (2 Corinthians 10:18).

Applying 321: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

If this kind of self-examination rests only on our own effort, it soon turns into another form of law, and can even become a new pride — “I understand humility better than other people do.”

The 321 vision reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Self-examination is not dissecting ourselves; it is opening our heart and letting the Holy Spirit shine his light in.

That is why David prayed like this: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). He did not say, “I will search myself.” He said, “Search me.”

Only true humility can let people see nothing but Jesus. And true humility is not something I manufacture; it is something the Holy Spirit works out within me.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Letting Jesus Be Seen Is Letting Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson is the very heart of the 321 vision in a single sentence: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. Philippians 2:6–8 says, “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” “Emptied himself” in Greek is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to pour out, to make oneself empty”. His glory was not snatched from him; he emptied himself. This is what “laying down the right to glory” means.

The Bible is my standard. We don’t judge by feelings whether “this counts as pride”; we let God’s word take the measure. Matthew 6:1 is a measuring rule, and John 3:30 is a measuring rule too.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Hiding ourselves is not suppressing ourselves. Suppression is forcing the self down by effort, and sooner or later it springs back; the work of the Holy Spirit is to make us genuinely no longer crave that position inside.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. There can be only one lead actor on a stage. When I step back one pace, he comes forward one more; if I don’t step back, I block him from view.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Isaiah 42:8 says, “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” Glory is not something we can grab, nor something we should try to.

Establish God’s system. The Worldly system is a pyramid: the higher you go, the fewer people there are and the more visible they become. God’s system is a body, and its most vital organs are often hidden deepest inside. First Corinthians 12:22 says, “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” The heart never goes up on stage, yet it never stops for a moment.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The heart the lesson describes, the one in a hurry to add “Actually, I also …”, is the self-centred life of the old self. And “letting Jesus be seen” is the selflessness of the new self.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan fell precisely because he wanted to raise his own seat higher. Isaiah 14:13–14 records his thoughts: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” Those five “I will”s are the template for all pride.

Our Lord walked in exactly the opposite direction: from heaven to the manger, and from the manger to the cross. Pride climbs upwards; humility goes downwards. But God’s law is this: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12).

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a team, as soon as one person starts grabbing the credit, everyone else immediately turns defensive and starts keeping score, and the ministry grinds to a halt; on the other hand, as soon as one person gives the credit away, the whole atmosphere of the team relaxes.

The Fivefold Change and the Shift of Perspective

What this lesson brings is exactly the fivefold change that 321 speaks of: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Where is the change of mindset here? From “I only have value when I’m seen” to “Being seen by God gives me value.”

It is also a shift of perspective: from man’s view to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the Worldly to the godly. Human applause is temporary; God’s reward is eternal.

And remember the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people turn it upside down and rush into ministry first; the ministry grows big, but the life inside grows empty. The Lord Jesus lived in Nazareth for thirty years before he came out to minister for three and a half.

The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. We practise living out a selfless (0) life, so that in that person the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit are borne — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that not one of these nine graces is called “fame”. And what is the nature of fruit? Fruit isn’t for the tree to eat. An apple tree never eats its own apples.

235 relationships: become a “2” with someone who lives selflessly, build “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — and become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. What is the greatest joy of spiritual parents? That their children surpass them. A true spiritual father is overjoyed when, one day, people talk about his son without needing to mention his own name at all.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking It Through with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives four practices for daily living. We will use 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work each one out in practice.

Practice 1: Serving in Secret

Deliberately do some acts of service that nobody knows about — visiting, giving, interceding — without seeking anything in return.

Information: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3).

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to show you that serving in secret isn’t losing out; it is banking the account in heaven.

Conviction: Settle it truly in your heart — the Father sees in secret, and that is enough.

Implementation: This week, do one good deed that nobody at all will know about; when it’s done, don’t post about it and don’t share it in your small group.

Evaluation: Afterwards, ask yourself: did I feel a little let down because nobody knew? That little disappointment is exactly the place the Lord wants to heal.

Correction: If you do feel let down, hand it over in prayer and say to the Lord, “This one was for you.”

Repetition: Once a week, for a whole year.

Multiplication: Don’t go teaching others how to do it; live it out, so that people are drawn to it.

Practice 2: Redirecting the Glory

When people praise you, turn at once to the Lord and say, “All of this is his grace.”

Information: “But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Revelation: Praise is like a ball: as soon as you catch it, pass it straight on; hold it too long and it sticks.

Conviction: I am a channel, not a reservoir.

Implementation: Prepare a sentence of your own, such as “Thank you — this really is the Lord’s grace.” Neither pretending nor taking the credit.

Evaluation: Watch for two extremes — accepting every word of it, or protesting too much. Sometimes protesting too much is a way of fishing for more praise.

Correction: Name the people who really deserve the credit, including the ones behind the scenes.

Repetition: Treat every compliment as another round of practice.

Multiplication: When you praise others, point the glory to God as well — “I can see God at work in you.”

Practice 3: The Focus Check

Ask yourself one question every day: today, did I make people see more of me, or more of Jesus?

Information: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Revelation: At the end of the day, let the Holy Spirit replay the day’s footage.

Conviction: Believe that this self-examination is not self-reproach; it is being loved.

Implementation: Every night, for one minute before you sleep, quietly ask this question.

Evaluation: Once a week, look back: in which situations am I most likely to turn the camera on myself?

Correction: For the situation where you stumble most easily, make a decision in advance.

Repetition: Let it become a bedtime habit, as natural as brushing your teeth.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion, become each other’s “2”, and ask each other this question every week.

Practice 4: Submarine Prayer

Pray for hidden service, asking God to let his glory be revealed in the hidden places.

Information: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6).

Revelation: See the members of the church whom no one sees — the ones setting out chairs, the ones washing cups, the mother at home praying for her children with tears.

Conviction: Believe that God sees them, every single one, without missing anyone.

Implementation: This week, pray for three “hidden” co-workers, and send each of them a short message to tell them, “I prayed for you.”

Evaluation: Do I only pray for the people on the platform?

Correction: Widen your intercession list to include people who will never be named.

Repetition: Once a week.

Multiplication: Lead your small group to pray together for the unseen, so that everyone’s eyes are turned towards them.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: True Glory Is the Radiance Hidden in Christ
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the lesson’s gentle reminder: “being seen by God” is worth more than “being seen by people”. When you are willing to be hidden in Jesus, in his own time he will let his glory shine through you. Don’t be in a hurry to be seen.

Jesus laid down the right to glory and chose to be a hidden servant. He did not pursue fame, yet he has influenced all of humanity; he did not pursue applause, yet he has brought the nations to bow before his name. Philippians 2:9–11 says, “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

Look at the order: first he emptied himself, then the Father exalted him. He did not fight for a single inch for himself, yet the Father gave him the name above every name.

First Peter 5:6 says, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” The timetable is in God’s hands, not ours; all we have to do is humble ourselves, and wait.

So today I want to issue a call to you, brothers and sisters.

First, hand over the microphone. The microphone you have been gripping all this time — today, pass it to Jesus.

Second, turn the camera around. Stop pointing it at yourself and focus it on the Lord who is worthy of the glory.

Third, be willing to go down into the deep. If God has not yet let you be seen, don’t be anxious: he is thickening your steel hull, so that you can dive deeper and travel further.

True glory is not the brilliance of being seen, but the radiance hidden in Christ. When we choose to be “hidden”, God’s glory can shine brightly on the earth through us.

This morning, let us declare together: Lord, I want to be a submarine in your hand — not asking to be seen, only asking to be used by you.

keyVerses: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:14–16)
“Most certainly you are a God who has hidden yourself, God of Israel, the Savior.” (Isaiah 45:15)
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you.

You existed in the form of God, yet you willingly emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. You had every right to glory, and time after time you laid it down. Lord, when we see you, we see what true greatness is.

Lord, forgive us. So often, while we serve you, we quietly keep a seat for ourselves; with our lips we say, “Glory to the Lord,” yet in our hearts we hope someone will remember our name. Cleanse our motives with your precious blood.

Holy Spirit, be our guide, so that deep within we truly no longer crave that position — not by suppressing it, but by being filled and satisfied with you. Teach us to serve in secret and to pray in the hidden place.
Lord, we are willing to be the lampstand and not the lamp; to be a submarine and not an aircraft carrier; to be the moon, reflecting your light.
Make our whole lives vessels through which Jesus is seen and God the Father is glorified.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: The Lord Jesus repeatedly charged people “that they should not make him known” (Matthew 12:16), and when the crowds wanted to make him king, he even “withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). In your present service or work, is there an “opportunity to be lifted up” from which you need to learn to step back? What is hardest for you about stepping back?

Question 2: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6). Share a time when you “served in secret”: nobody saw it at the time — what did you honestly feel inside? If you believe the Father truly sees in secret, what is one thing nobody will know about that you are willing to do this week?
