“Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father” (John 14:12). Name one specific person God has placed beside you whom you need to build up. What one concrete thing do you plan to do for them this month?

blog.title: Hiddenness in Three Movements

blocks.x: The People God Truly Uses Are Those Who Know How to Hide Themselves

We live in a generation full of stages and spotlights. One mobile phone is a film studio; one account is a stage. Day and night the algorithm whispers the same sentence in our ear: you only exist if you’re seen.

Interestingly, psychology warned us about this long ago. In 2000, Thomas Gilovich and colleagues at Cornell University named the famous “spotlight effect”: participants who walked into a room wearing an embarrassing shirt thought about half the people there had noticed; when the others were actually asked, only about a quarter had. The light we thought was shining on us had never even been switched on.
We overestimate how much people are watching us, and underestimate how much God is watching us.
Jesus Walked the Opposite Way

He was the King of kings, yet he was born in a manger and spent thirty quiet years in a carpenter’s workshop in Nazareth. With a single word he could still the wind and the waves, yet again and again he charged those he had healed, “Tell no one.” He did miracles without seeking applause, and served people without seeking a name; what he let people see was not himself, but the glory of God the Father.
John the Baptist put it most beautifully. When his disciples complained that “everyone is coming to him,” John replied: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

In the original it means: let him grow larger and larger, and let me grow smaller and smaller. The direction of a whole life is to let my own shadow grow shorter and shorter, and his light grow longer and longer.
Hiddenness in Three Movements

Step one: be hidden in the body of Christ. Jesus is the head of the church, and we are members of his body. Every member has its function, but none can be glorified on its own. The joints are the least noticeable part of the body, yet they carry the weight of the whole; the most important service in the church is often the service no one sees. So in serving, say “we” more and “I” less.

Step two: help others to be more successful than yourself. The Lord Jesus says: “He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these.” (John 14:12) Moses gave some of his own honour to Joshua; Elijah brought Elisha to maturity. They were not jealous; instead they rejoiced that their spiritual sons were being used by God. This is a spiritual parent’s heart — I can go unseen, as long as you are brought to maturity.

Step three: lay down status and authority. After his resurrection the Lord said: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Therefore, you go.” The authority is in his hands, yet the action is handed to his disciples. Some people think laying down means retiring, but in God’s kingdom laying down means transforming: we lay down the identity of leader and support others in the role of servant; we lay down the power of control and bless others with a parent’s heart. Laying down is not losing; it is an upgrade.
Seen by People, or Seen by God?
Service seen by people brings brief applause; service seen by God brings eternal reward. People forget, and the list may leave your name off — but God does not forget.
God does not look at how many people see you; he looks at how many people you are willing to let see Jesus. Hiding yourself is not losing your worth; it is letting your worth be fully used by God.
May every one of us become that kind of person — not asking to be seen, only asking that Jesus be seen; not seeking glory, only seeking that the glory go to the Lord.
Question for Reflection

In your present service or work, what is the one thing you most want to be “seen”? If you handed it over to God completely — letting him increase and you decrease — what would your heart find hardest to let go of?

• Illustration: Bernstein is generally credited with saying the hardest player to find in an orchestra is one willing to play second violin.
• The lesson: true team service lets people see no individual, only Jesus.
• 321: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.
Helping Others Succeed More Than Yourself
“The works that I do, he will do also”
“And he will do greater works than these”
John 14:12
Building others up is greater than succeeding yourself
• Read John 14:12 in full; “greater” refers to the scope and fruitfulness of the work.
• Compare Acts 1:8: from Jerusalem to the uttermost parts of the earth.
• John 16:7: it is to your advantage that I go away.
• Ask: “My leaving is to your advantage” — could you say that?
The Example of Moses and Elijah
“You shall give authority to him”
Numbers 27:20
“Let a double portion of your spirit be on me”
2 Kings 2:9
• Numbers 27:18: God tells Moses to lay his hand on Joshua.
• “Authority”, Hebrew הוֹד (hod), majesty, splendour — given out of his own.
• 2 Kings 2:10: Elijah replies, “You have asked a hard thing.”
• The lesson: their successors accomplished greater works than they did, yet they were not jealous.
A Spiritual Parent’s Heart
Saul raged; Moses would have rejoiced
The difference is not the song but the heart
Level 5 leaders: humility plus will
The window and the mirror: credit to others
• 1 Samuel 18:7–8: Saul is enraged on hearing “David his ten thousands”.
• Collins, Good to Great (2001): from over 1,400 companies, eleven great companies were identified.
• Level 5 leaders: extreme personal humility plus intense professional will.
• In success, look out of the window and credit others; in failure, look in the mirror and take responsibility.
• 1 Corinthians 3:6: but God gave the increase.
The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
Everyone I relate to is my “2”
Live out the selfless “0”; bear the ninefold fruit
235: companions, parents and children, team
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
• The 920 practice: with every “2”, live out selflessness (0) and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.
• A fruit tree does not eat its own fruit; not one of the nine graces is for ourselves.
• 235 relationships: 2 spiritual companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
• 2 Timothy 2:2, four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others.
Laying Down Status and Authority
“All authority has been given to me”
“Therefore, you go”
Matthew 28:18–19
He steps back; the kingdom leaps forward
• Key: the authority is in the Lord’s hands, yet the action is handed to his disciples.
• Matthew 28:20: I am with you always, even to the end of the age.
• The lesson: he did not carry on taking first place himself, but raised up many more to complete the mission.
• No longer limited to one body and one place, he is present through the Holy Spirit with thousands upon thousands of disciples.
Laying Down Is Not Retiring but Transforming
Lay down leadership; support others as a servant
Lay down control; bless with a parent’s heart
Laying down is not losing but an upgrade
The great tree feeds the seedlings
• The lesson’s key line: in God’s kingdom, laying down means transforming.
• Illustration: Simard, 1997, Nature — trees pass carbon, nitrogen and water through underground mycorrhizal networks.
• The oldest, largest trees send nutrients to the seedlings in their shade — a picture of spiritual parents.
• Warning: hold a position long enough and it grows into your flesh — from “I am serving” to “it can’t be done without me”.
Humility Overcomes Pride
“Whoever wants to become first … shall be bondservant of all”
Mark 10:44
Pride provokes pride; both sides lose
Humility draws out humility; both sides win
• Read the whole of Mark 10:42–45; διάκονος is one who waits at table, δοῦλος a slave.
• In the world, authority grabs upwards; in God’s kingdom, authority flows downwards.
• Isaiah 14:13: Satan left his originally intended position and wanted to take God’s place.
• 321: humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan; Galatians 2:20, no longer I.
God Raises Up Others Where We Lay Down
Gideon: from 32,000 down to 300
“Lest Israel brag against me”
Judges 7:2
Treasure in clay vessels; glory to God
• The lesson: he can raise up others in the places where we lay things down.
• Judges 7:2: God was not weakening Gideon, but removing everything that might take a share of the glory.
• 2 Corinthians 4:7: because the clay jar is plain, people see the treasure inside.
• John 12:24: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone.
The Reward of Being Seen by God
Seen by people: brief applause
Seen by God: eternal reward
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly”
Matthew 6:4
• Matthew 6:1, “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them.”
• The Lord Jesus says “in secret” again and again: our Father does not need us to switch on the light to see.
• Hebrews 6:10: God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work.
• The 321 shift of perspective: from the temporary and earthly to the eternal and heavenly.
Putting It into Practice (1, 2)
Say “we” more, “I” less
Actively support others’ gifts
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction,
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
• Practice one, Information: Ephesians 4:16, every joint, each part working.
• Implementation: name at least one co-worker in every report, for forty days.
• Practice two, Information: John 14:12, he will do greater works than these.
• Implementation: write down three names, pray for them daily, and do one concrete thing.
• Evaluation: when they are praised, is my heart joyful or sour?
Putting It into Practice (3, 4)
Step back; let the younger generation serve
Be faithful where no one sees
Hand over one ministry this quarter
Do three unknown good deeds this week
• Practice three, Information: Matthew 28:18–19, the authority is in the Lord’s hands, the action handed to the disciples.
• Implementation: hand it over completely — the responsibility, the resources, the platform — and don’t take it back when it’s less than perfect.
• Practice four, Information: Matthew 6:3–4, let your merciful deeds be in secret.
• Evaluation: that little itch to have it known is the evidence that the self-centred life has not yet stepped down.
• Multiplication: teach those you build up to go and build up the next person.
The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard
The Holy Spirit is my guide
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Establish God’s system
• The Three Foundations: the three movements of hiddenness are the road the Lord Jesus himself walked first.
• The Bible is my standard: Ephesians 4:15–16, John 14:12, Matthew 28:18–20, Colossians 3:3.
• The Two Core Values and the Goal: a system can be passed on; a star cannot.
• The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — the order cannot be reversed.
Closing and Call
Not asking to be seen, only that Jesus be seen
Not seeking glory, only that the glory go to the Lord
Willing to be hidden, God’s glory shines
“He must increase, but I must decrease”
• The lesson’s closing words: the people God truly uses are those who know how to hide themselves.
• The gentle reminder: God does not look at how many people see you, but at how many people you are willing to let see Jesus.
• Luke 24:31, Emmaus: they recognised him, and then he vanished.
• The call to four decisions: be a joint, be a spiritual parent, loosen your grip first, be faithful in secret.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, I am willing to learn your way
Even while used by you, to keep hiding myself
May my whole life give glory to you alone
May the Lord bless and keep you. Amen
• Lead the congregation in reading the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
• Confession: we crave applause, we fear being overlooked, our hearts turn sour when others are praised.
• Pray for the church: no more fighting over positions, only building one another up.
• Close with Psalm 115:1, then bless the congregation.

script: Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we are looking together at a beautiful lesson called “Hiddenness in Three Movements”. It belongs to the series Jesus Our Role Model — laying down the right to glory. Our key verse is John 3:30: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Brothers and sisters, this was not a fine phrase spoken when things were going well; John the Baptist said it as his following kept draining away.

We live in a generation full of stages. One mobile phone is a film studio; one account is a stage. But psychology tells us something very interesting. In 2000, Thomas Gilovich and colleagues at Cornell University named the “spotlight effect”: they had participants walk into a room wearing an embarrassing shirt; the participants thought half the people had noticed, when in fact only about a quarter had. That light had never even been switched on. Brothers and sisters, we overestimate how much people are watching us, and underestimate how much God is watching us. And our Lord Jesus walked a path that ran in exactly the opposite direction.

Our key passage has another verse, Colossians 3:3: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Brothers and sisters, notice that in the original the word “hidden” is in the perfect tense, meaning it has already been hidden. The Bible does not tell us to go and hide ourselves; the Bible says we have already been hidden. Hiddenness is not a goal I must strive to achieve; it is a position I have already received. Hidden in God now, revealed in glory one day.

Step one: be hidden in the body of Christ. Ephesians 4:16 speaks of the body “being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part.” Jesus is the head of the church, and we are members of his body. Brothers and sisters, the joints are the least noticeable part of the body; no one ever praises their own knee joint. But let one joint go wrong and the whole person can’t move. The most important service in the church is often the service no one sees, which carries the weight of the whole body.

Scientists estimate that an adult human body has about thirty-seven trillion cells, and not one of them has a name of its own. Or think of a symphony orchestra: without the second violins there is no harmony. Brothers and sisters, true team service lets people see no individual, only Jesus. So the first practice is very down to earth: in serving, say “we” more and “I” less.

Step two: help others to be more successful than yourself. The Lord Jesus says: “He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these.” That is John 14:12. Brothers and sisters, which teacher would ever say, “You will do greater things than I”? Yet our Lord said it. Building others up is greater than succeeding yourself.

Moses gave some of his own honour to Joshua; Elijah brought Elisha to maturity, and when Elisha asked for a double portion of his spirit, he did not refuse. They were neither jealous nor competitive; instead they rejoiced that their spiritual sons were being used by God. Brothers and sisters, this is a spiritual parent’s heart. 321’s 920 practice says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; with them we live out a selfless life and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. And 235 relationships say: first spiritual companions, then spiritual parents and children, and only last a fivefold-ministry team.

Step three: lay down status and authority. After his resurrection the Lord said: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Therefore, you go.” Brothers and sisters, listen to that — the authority is in his hands, yet the action is handed to his disciples. He takes one step back, and the kingdom takes a great step forward. Some people think laying down means retiring. It doesn’t. In God’s kingdom, laying down means transforming; laying down is not losing, but an upgrade.

Finally, the hidden life brings out a deeper glory. Service seen by people brings brief applause; service seen by God brings eternal reward. The Lord Jesus says: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” That is Matthew 6:4. Brothers and sisters, people forget, and the list may leave your name off — but God does not forget.

There are four practices today. First, in serving, say “we” more and “I” less. Second, take the initiative to encourage and support the development of other people’s gifts. Third, learn to step back and let the younger generation take up the work of service. Fourth, choose to be faithful in completing what the Lord has entrusted, in places where no one sees. Brothers and sisters, all four can begin this week.

The lesson’s gentle reminder puts it so well: God does not look at how many people see you; he looks at how many people you are willing to let see Jesus. Hiding yourself is not losing your worth; it is letting your worth be fully used by God. May every one of us become that kind of person — not asking to be seen, only asking that Jesus be seen; not seeking glory, only seeking that the glory go to the Lord. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let us pray together. Lord, I am willing to learn your way: even while you are using me, to keep hiding myself. Let me serve humbly in the team, find joy and contentment in building others up, and experience true freedom in laying down position. May my whole life give glory to you alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may we all become people who are hidden, yet shine, this very day.

Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we are looking together at a beautiful lesson called “Hiddenness in Three Movements”. It belongs to the series Jesus Our Role Model — laying down the right to glory. Our key verse is John 3:30: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Brothers and sisters, this was not a fine phrase spoken when things were going well. When he said it, John the Baptist’s disciples were drifting away; everyone was going over to Jesus. Yet he said: let him grow larger and larger, and let me grow smaller and smaller. This morning we are going to learn this lesson together.

We live in a generation full of stages and spotlights. One mobile phone is a film studio; one account is a stage. Day and night the algorithm whispers in our ear: you only exist if you’re seen; you only have value if you’re liked. But, brothers and sisters, psychology gives us a reminder. In 2000, a team led by Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University, with Savitsky and Medvec, published experiments in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology that named the famous “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked: how many people noticed your shirt? The participants guessed about half; in reality only about a quarter had.

The conclusion is blunt: we always assume we are standing under a spotlight, when in fact the light was never even switched on. Brothers and sisters, we overestimate how much people are watching us, and underestimate how much God is watching us. How, then, can we keep hiding ourselves even while God is using us greatly? The Bible gives us the three movements of hiddenness: first, be hidden in the body of Christ; second, help others to be more successful than yourself; third, lay down status and authority. Philippians 2 says the Lord Jesus “emptied himself”; in the original that means he poured himself out. Emptying is not becoming zero; it is making room, so that God’s glory can come and dwell.

Our key passage has another verse, Colossians 3:3: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Colossians is one of the Prison Epistles Paul wrote while a prisoner in Rome. At that time a heresy was going around the church that exalted my knowledge, my experience, my spiritual discipline; Paul’s answer was to turn people’s eyes back to Christ. Brothers and sisters, notice that in the original the word “hidden” is in the perfect tense, meaning it has already been hidden. The Bible does not tell us to go and hide ourselves; the Bible says we have already been hidden. Hidden in God now, revealed in glory one day.

Now to step one: be hidden in the body of Christ, and learn to serve as a team. Ephesians 4:15–16 says: “we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase.” Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the head of the church, and we are members of his body. There are two key words here: “knit together” in the original means bound closely together; “joint” in the original means a joint, a point of connection. The strength of the body does not lie in one especially large muscle, but in every joint being connected in the right place.

In 1 Corinthians 12 Paul explains it even more thoroughly: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” Brothers and sisters, the joints are the least noticeable part of the body; no one ever praises their own knee joint. But let one joint go wrong and the whole person can’t move. The lesson puts it very realistically: if one member sticks out too far, the whole body loses its balance. The most important service in the church is often the service no one sees, which carries the weight of the whole body.

Science gives us an astonishing picture. In 2013, researchers at the University of Bologna in Italy estimated that an adult human body is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells — and not one of those cells has a name of its own. Or think of a symphony orchestra: Bernstein is generally credited with saying that the hardest player to find in an orchestra is the one willing to play second violin. Yet without the second violins there is no harmony. The lesson says that true team service lets people see no individual, only Jesus. So the first practice is very down to earth: in serving, say “we” more and “I” less.

Step two: help others to be more successful than yourself. The Lord Jesus says: “He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.” That is John 14:12. Brothers and sisters, just think how astonishing this is. What a teacher fears most is a student who surpasses him; a master craftsman will often keep one trick back. Yet our Lord not only keeps nothing back — he declares with his own lips: you will do greater works than I. “Greater” here refers to the scope and fruitfulness of the work: when the Holy Spirit came, the gospel spread from Jerusalem to the uttermost parts of the earth.

The Bible gives us two pairs of role models. God said to Moses: “You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey.” That is Numbers 27:20. Brothers and sisters, God did not tell Moses to produce a separate portion of honour for Joshua; God said: give him some of yours. True succession means cutting off a piece of yourself. Elisha said to Elijah: “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” Elijah did not get angry; he only said, “You have asked a hard thing.” Their successors accomplished greater works than they did, yet they were neither jealous nor competitive.

The opposite example is Saul. The women sang: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” And Saul was very angry. Brothers and sisters, it is the same song: Moses would have rejoiced to hear it; Saul heard it and flew into a rage. The difference is not in the song; it is in the heart. Management studies confirm it too. In Good to Great, Jim Collins studied more than 1,400 companies and identified eleven truly great ones, and found that their chief executives were all “Level 5 leaders” — extreme personal humility combined with intense professional will. When things went well, they looked out of the window and gave the credit to others; when things went badly, they looked in the mirror and took the responsibility themselves.

This is a spiritual parent’s heart. What parent anywhere is jealous because their children have done better than they have? 321 has a precious practice called the 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; with them we live out a selfless life and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Brothers and sisters, a fruit tree does not eat its own fruit. And there are 235 relationships: first spiritual companions, then spiritual parents and children, and only last a fivefold-ministry team. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

Step three: lay down status and authority. After his resurrection the Lord said to his disciples: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Therefore, you go and make disciples of all nations.” Brothers and sisters, notice these words: “therefore, you”. By human logic it ought to run: since the authority is in my hands, therefore I will go. But the Lord says: therefore, you go. He holds the authority in his hand, yet hands the action over to his disciples. He did not carry on taking first place himself; he raised up many more people to complete the mission. He takes one step back, and the kingdom takes a great step forward.

The lesson has a superb sentence here: some people think laying down means retiring, but in God’s kingdom laying down means transforming. We lay down the identity of leader and support others in the role of servant; we lay down the power of control and bless others with a parent’s heart. Laying down is not losing; it is an upgrade. Brothers and sisters, the Canadian forest ecologist Suzanne Simard published research in the journal Nature showing that the trees in a forest are linked to one another through underground mycorrhizal networks; the oldest, largest trees quietly send nutrients to the seedlings in their shade. Isn’t that a picture of spiritual parents?

The Lord Jesus made this principle plain long ago. He said: “Whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all.” In the world, authority grabs upwards; in God’s kingdom, authority flows downwards. Brothers and sisters, Satan fell precisely because he would not stay in his originally intended position. 321 puts it clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

The lesson says that when we choose to hide ourselves, God is freer to use us, and he raises up others in the places where we lay things down. Brothers and sisters, think of Gideon. God said: the people with you are too many, lest Israel brag against me, saying, “My own hand has saved me.” From thirty-two thousand down to three hundred: God was not weakening Gideon; he was removing everything that might take a share of the glory. Paul says: we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God. Because the clay jar is so plain, people notice the treasure inside.

Service seen by people brings brief applause; service seen by God brings eternal reward. The Lord Jesus says: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” Brothers and sisters, people forget, and your name gets missed off the year-end thank-you list — but God does not forget. 321 says: turn from the human, earthly, temporary perspective to God’s heavenly, eternal perspective. Which one do we want?

The lesson gives us four practices. First, practise team spirit: in serving, say “we” more and “I” less. This week, every time you share or report, name at least one co-worker, and keep it up for forty days. Second, the blessing of building others up: take the initiative to encourage and support the development of other people’s gifts. Brothers and sisters, write down three names, pray for them every day this month, and do one concrete thing for them. And when they are praised, ask yourself honestly: is my heart joyful, or a little sour?

Third, the practice of laying down position: learn to step back and let the younger generation take up the work of service. This quarter, pick out the ministry you do most comfortably and hand it over completely — the responsibility, the resources, the platform — and when they do it less than perfectly, don’t take it back. Fourth, a heart for quiet service: choose to be faithful where no one sees. This week, deliberately do three good deeds nobody knows about, and when you’ve done them, tell no one — tell only your Father in heaven. Brothers and sisters, if there’s still a little itch inside to have it known, that little itch is the evidence that the self-centred life has not yet fully stepped down.

Let’s set today’s message inside the 321 framework. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the three movements of hiddenness are the road the Lord himself walked first; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide — when to let go, whom to hand over to, how to let go, all of it needs the Holy Spirit’s leading. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, a system can be passed on; a star cannot. The fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry, and this order cannot be reversed.

Let’s return to the lesson’s closing words. Jesus did not seek a stage of glory; he chose to hide himself and give the glory to the Father. Luke’s Gospel records that on the day of his resurrection the Lord walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and when their eyes were opened and they recognised him, “he vanished out of their sight.” Brothers and sisters, look at the order: they recognised him, and then he vanished. This morning the Lord comes among us in just the same way. May every one of us become that kind of person — not asking to be seen, only asking that Jesus be seen; not seeking glory, only seeking that the glory go to the Lord.

Let us pray together. Lord, I am willing to learn your way: even while you are using me, to keep hiding myself. Let me serve humbly in the team, find joy and contentment in building others up, and experience true freedom in laying down position. Lord, we confess that inside us there is an “I” that badly wants to be seen; have mercy on us and forgive us. May our families, small groups and churches no longer fight over positions, but only build one another up. May my whole life give glory to you alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may we all become people who are hidden, yet shine, this very day.

sections.heading: Introduction: The One Thing We Most Want to Hold On To — and Can Least Hold On To
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning let’s think together about a subject everyone would rather avoid, yet everyone must one day face: my life and my death — in whose hands, in the end, do they really lie?

So much of what people do today circles around one single longing — control. We buy insurance because we want to control accidents; we get health check-ups because we want to control illness; we save for retirement, fill our schedules and draw up life plans because we want to control time. The calendar on our phone is packed solid, the figures in our bank account rise and fall, and behind them all hides the same sentence in the heart: “I want to be in charge of my own destiny.”

And yet a single, sudden pandemic brought the whole world’s calendar to a standstill at once; a single phone call in the middle of the night can rewrite a family’s plans of many years. We have seen it with our own eyes: what we can control is far less than we imagine. We may have our hands on the steering wheel, but we cannot command the weather on the road.

In 1966 the psychologist Julian B. Rotter put forward the theory of “locus of control,” dividing people into those with an “internal” locus and those with an “external” one: the internal type believes outcomes lie in their own hands, the external type believes outcomes are decided by forces outside them. Half a century of later research has broadly shown that an internal locus is associated with higher achievement motivation and a lower sense of helplessness. But Rotter’s theory also left a problem unsolved: if a person attributes everything to his own control, then when he meets the things he truly cannot control — illness, death, other people’s choices — his whole world collapses.

What the Bible gives us is neither the “internal” nor the “external” locus, but a third way: God’s control. Not I in control, nor fate in control, but the Lord who loves me and gave himself for me in control. Jesus walked this road first.

I once heard the testimony of an older brother. He had planned his whole life meticulously, and in the year he retired he scheduled the next twenty years: the first year, a trip around the island; the second, study abroad; the third, time with his grandchildren. Then, three months into retirement, a single diagnosis cancelled every one of those plans. In his hospital room he said something very deep to his pastor: “All my life I’ve been arranging my days, and only today have I discovered that my days were never mine.” Brothers and sisters, that may sound like despair, but in fact it is the beginning of freedom. Because only when I finally admit that my days are not mine will I ask: then whose are they?

The book of James made this plain for us long ago: “Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away. For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that’” (James 4:14–15). Notice that James does not tell us not to plan. He tells us to put four words in front of our plans — “If the Lord wills.”

We have already looked together at the first two lessons in the example of Jesus: he laid down the glory of heaven and humbled himself to become a man; he laid down his standing as one to be served, tied a towel around his waist and washed feet. Today we shall see the third thing he laid down, and the deepest of all — he laid down sovereignty over life and death.

He had every right as God, yet he chose to lay it down. He did not live for himself, nor did he die for himself. He lived for the Father, and he died for the world. This is the highest height of humility, and the highest height of freedom too. Brothers and sisters, please remember this sentence today: true freedom is not found in control, but in obedience.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter of Joy Sent from Prison
sections.html:
To understand the message of “laying down the right over life and death,” we must first go and stand beside the man who wrote this letter.

The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. It is generally held that the letter was written between AD 60 and 62, while Paul was under house arrest in Rome awaiting Caesar’s judgement. In other words, the man who wrote “Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” was at that moment standing quite literally on the threshold between life and death. He was not discussing life and death in a study; he was discussing life and death beside his chains.

The church in Philippi, which received the letter, was the first church Paul planted in Europe. Acts chapter 16 records how Paul, following the vision of the man of Macedonia, crossed the sea; beside the river outside Philippi he met Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, and in the middle of the night in a prison cell he led the jailer and his whole household to the Lord. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were proud to hold Roman citizenship; on its streets the talk was “We are Romans.” But Paul said to them, “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). It was a great reversal of perspective: your true registration is not in Rome — it is in heaven.

Philippians 2:6–11 is regarded by many scholars as a “Christ hymn” the early church was already singing. Paul quotes this hymn not to set out some lofty Christology, but to deal with something very practical — in the church at Philippi some were forming factions, some were chasing empty glory, and two sisters, Euodia and Syntyche, were at odds with each other. Paul’s remedy was not a technique of mediation but a role model: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5).

The hymn has a clear direction: down, down, and further down still — and then God lifts him up on high. From the form of God to the form of a servant; from the form of a servant to death; from death to death on a cross. In the Roman Empire the cross was a punishment reserved for slaves and rebels; by law a Roman citizen could not be crucified. For the Philippians, so proud of their Roman citizenship, the words “death on a cross” marked the lowest point they could possibly imagine.

The other half of today’s theme passage, Romans 14:7–8, has an entirely different background. Romans was written around AD 57, while Paul was in Corinth preparing to go up to Jerusalem. In the Roman church, Jewish and Gentile believers lived under one roof and argued endlessly over whether to eat only vegetables and whether to keep special days. How did Paul handle it? He did not begin by ruling who was right and who was wrong; he lifted everyone straight to a higher place: you are arguing over “whether I have the right to do this,” but you have forgotten something far more basic — you are not your own at all.

Two passages: one tells how Jesus laid it down, the other tells why we should lay it down. Together they make today’s message: Jesus laid down the right over life and death, so we too are able to lay it down; Jesus, having laid it down, received the highest name, so we, having laid it down, receive true freedom.

sections.heading: 1. Jesus Laid Down Sovereignty over Life and Death and Lived in the Father’s Will
sections.html:
The life of Jesus was not of his own arranging.

“For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). This is Jesus’ most concise explanation of his whole life. He came, not by his own wish; his schedule was not in his own hands.

Beside the well at Sychar he said to his disciples, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). Brothers and sisters, notice the word “food.” In Greek it is βρῶμα (brōma), the real food that goes into the mouth and sustains life. Jesus did not say, “Doing the Father’s will is my hobby,” nor “It is my duty.” He said it is my food. Without it you go hungry; without it you die. For Jesus, obedience was not an obligation added from outside, but his very way of staying alive from within.

From his birth, his baptism and his temptation in the wilderness, to his ministry in Galilee and his passion in Jerusalem, every step Jesus took was in the Father’s hands. Never once did he pray to save his own life. When he was told that Herod wanted to kill him, he did not run for cover but said, “Nevertheless I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the next day” (Luke 13:33); when the time had fully come, “he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). His comings and goings were decided not by circumstances, but by the Father’s timetable.

The most profound scene of all is in the garden of Gethsemane. “He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire’” (Matthew 26:39). Brothers and sisters, the Chinese Union Version renders this verse with the word “will” twice, and behind both stands the Greek verb θέλω (thelō), “to will, to desire”; then in verse 42, when Jesus prays again, “your desire be done,” the noun θέλημα (thelēma), “will,” appears. Jesus did not pretend he was not in anguish. He asked; he said, “if it is possible.” True obedience is never numbness; it is handing over your own will while fully awake and in full anguish.

We must take special note: this was not the Father forcing the Son. Jesus himself put it very plainly: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father” (John 10:18). Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the subject of this lesson. Jesus had authority over life and death — he had authority to lay down his life, and authority to take it up again. It was not that he had no rights; he had the right and chose to lay it down. That is what humility is. A man with no money is not called generous, and a man with no authority who lets go is not called humble. Humility is this: I clearly have it, and yet for love I lay it down.

The writer of Hebrews says, “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). “Obedience” in Greek is ὑπακοή (hypakoē), which literally means “to listen from underneath.” The first act of obedience is not doing but listening; not first exerting ourselves, but first bowing our heads. Why do people not obey? Because they stand too high to hear.

Let me use a picture from everyday life. Have you ever flown? When a plane comes in to land through thick fog, the pilot actually cannot see the runway. At that moment he must hand the plane over to the guidance of the control tower and the readings of his instruments, descending step by step as instructed. The most dangerous thing he could do is go by his own feeling and say, “I think the runway is over there.” Aviation has a technical term for this: “spatial disorientation.” When a pilot lacks any external reference, the vestibular system of the inner ear gives false signals about the aircraft’s attitude, so that he “feels” he is flying level when in fact he is banking and falling. The pilot training handbooks of the US Federal Aviation Administration teach explicitly that under instrument conditions a pilot must trust his instruments, not his feelings. Brothers and sisters, this is a precise picture of the spiritual life. In the fog of life, the most dangerous thing is not that we cannot see, but that we trust our own feelings. The role model Jesus gives us is this: look up, listen to the voice from the tower, and land as the Father directs.

“Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation” (Hebrews 5:9). It was precisely because he obeyed to the point of death that “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Notice that “therefore.” Jesus’ glory was not won by striving; it was received through laying down. This is an unchanging law of God’s kingdom: the way down is the way up.

This is exactly the first of the Three Foundations in the 321 vision — Jesus is my role model. The 321 message says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person must keep hold of the steering wheel, must know the next step, must always keep a way out. The selfless person can say: Lord, I don’t know, but you know, and that is enough. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. What Jesus did in Gethsemane was to let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, is there a “cup” in your life that you have long been trying to push away? You can ask as honestly as Jesus did. But once you have asked, are you willing to add that one sentence: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire”?

sections.heading: 2. Living for the Lord: The Resolve of Paul’s Whole Life
sections.html:
Paul understood deeply the role model of Jesus laying down his life, and so he distilled his own life into a single declaration.

“according to my earnest expectation and hope, that I will in no way be disappointed, but with all boldness, as always, now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” (Philippians 1:20).

The word “magnified” is the Greek μεγαλύνω (megalynō), meaning “to make great, to be honoured as great.” Mary’s song of praise opens with the very same word: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:46). Paul’s meaning is clear: my body is a mirror, a stage; whether the play performed on that stage is a play of living or a play of dying, as long as the audience sees Christ exalted, my play has succeeded.

Brothers and sisters, this is the highest height of the spiritual life — life no longer has two possible endings, only one purpose. If I live, the purpose is that Christ be honoured as great; if I die, the purpose is still that Christ be honoured as great.

So he goes on: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Paul does not say, “I live for Christ.” He puts it even more radically: to me to live is Christ. Christ is not one part of my life; Christ is my life itself.

If this sentence had only its first half, it would be an ideal; if it had only its second half, it would be escapism. Only the two halves together make freedom. For if he lives, he can preach the gospel; if he dies, he can return to the Lord’s embrace. He says himself: “But I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better. Yet to remain in the flesh is more needful for your sake” (Philippians 1:23–24). Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Paul’s dilemma is not a dilemma of “is it better to live or better to die,” but a dilemma of “both are good.” If even death counts as gain to a man, what in this world can still threaten him?

At Miletus Paul said to the elders of Ephesus: “But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God” (Acts 20:24). He placed his own life behind his “race” and his “ministry.” Life is not a contest of length; it is a choice of direction.

Through church history, many have taken up this same resolve. The twentieth-century missionary Jim Elliot (1927–1956) wrote in his journal in October 1949 words that are still quoted today: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Seven years later, in January 1956, he and four fellow workers were killed on the banks of the Curaray River in Ecuador by the very people they had gone to reach with the gospel. He was only twenty-eight. He gave the life he could not keep and gained the reward he could not lose; and in time many from that people turned to Christ.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945) wrote in The Cost of Discipleship: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” On 9 April 1945 he was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp, less than a month before the Nazis surrendered. He did not lose; he handed over what he could not keep.

Psychology confirms this from another angle. The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor E. Frankl (1905–1997) observed in the concentration camps that those who survived were often not the physically strongest, but those who still held in their hearts a “why” to live for. In Man’s Search for Meaning he quotes Nietzsche: “He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.” From this Frankl developed “logotherapy,” arguing that our deepest drive is not the pursuit of pleasure but the pursuit of meaning. Brothers and sisters, if we have no reason larger than ourselves, we will not come through suffering larger than ourselves. The Christian’s answer is the most solid answer of all: to me to live is Christ.

Let me use an everyday example to explain “magnified.” When we look at the moon at night, it seems very bright. But the moon gives no light of its own; all its light is reflected from the sun. The moon does its job best not when it strains to shine by itself, but when it faces the sun squarely and blocks nothing. Brothers and sisters, this is what Paul means by “as always, now also Christ will be magnified”: I don’t need to shine by myself; I only need not to block him. And what is it that blocks him? Very often it is that big, thick “self.”

So we too should have this same resolve. Don’t treat “living for the Lord” as a burden; see it as immense grace. For if Jesus had not first died for us, we would never have had the chance to live for him. Paul says it very directly: “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15).

This is exactly the Two Core Values of the 321 vision — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Letting Jesus be King answers the question “Who has the final say?”; letting Jesus receive the glory answers the question “Whom am I living for?” Paul’s Philippians 1:20 is the most beautiful duet of these two core values. And it is precisely the shift of perspective that 321 speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man calculates, “How many years have I got left?”; God calculates, “How much fruit have you borne for me?”

sections.heading: 3. “Living for Myself” Is Satan’s Most Dangerous Lie
sections.html:
One of the things people say most often is: “I live for myself.” It sounds free, independent and modern, but in fact it is one of Satan’s cleverest traps.

The Bible says it very clearly: “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself” (Romans 14:7). Brothers and sisters, notice that Paul does not say, “You ought not to live for yourselves.” He says, “None of us lives to himself.” This is not an exhortation; it is a statement of fact. Human beings have never had the option of “living for themselves.” If we are not living for the Lord, we are living for some other master; if we do not die to the Lord, we die to sin.

Why? Because we are created beings. A created thing can never define itself. A fish out of water is not free — it is suffocating; a kite whose string has snapped is not liberated — it is falling. So-called “living for myself” is in reality handing my thoughts and choices over to another, unseen master. Satan’s first lie, spoken to man in Eden, was this: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). From that day on, the self-centred life became the root of humanity’s fall, and pride the root of every problem. Satan never needs you to worship him; he only needs you to worship yourself.

Jesus put this in the most decisive terms: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24). At this point the Chinese Union Version adds a small-print note explaining that Mammon means wealth. Jesus did not say you “may not” serve two masters; he said you “cannot” — this is not a moral prohibition but a fact of existence. The human heart has only one throne.

Money in itself is not sin. Money is a very good servant but a very bad master. The issue is not how much money you have, but who sits on the throne of your heart. Jesus told the parable of a rich fool (Luke 12:16–21): his land yielded abundantly, so he pulled down his barns and built bigger ones, and told his soul to take its ease, eat, drink and be merry. In just a few verses he says “I” and “my” five times over — my crops, this is what I will do, my barns, all my grain, my soul — yet not once does he mention God, nor anyone else at all. And the result? “But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’ So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God” (Luke 12:20–21). Brothers and sisters, his failure lay not in being rich, but in this: there was only one person in his life — himself.

Psychology has some profound observations here too. The American cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker (1924–1974) argued in The Denial of Death (1973) that many of the driving forces of human civilisation actually spring from the fear and denial of death; people strain to build “immortality projects” — careers, reputations, fortunes, descendants — so that they can believe “I will not disappear.” The book won the Pulitzer Prize in 1974. Later the social psychologists Greenberg, Pyszczynski and Solomon (1986) developed from it “Terror Management Theory,” and a large body of experiments has shown that when people are reminded that they will die, they cling more tightly to their own worldview, value money and status more highly, and more readily look down on groups unlike their own. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What psychology describes is exactly what the Bible says: those who fear death spend their whole lives as slaves. The letter to the Hebrews said it long ago: “and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:15).

A picture often comes to my mind. A man stands in a boat and pushes hard against the pier. He thinks he has pushed the pier away, but in fact he has pushed himself further and further from the shore. “Living for myself” is just like that: you think you are pushing away other people’s interference, but in fact you are pushing yourself out towards a lonely island. Satan doesn’t need to build you a prison; he only needs to persuade you to row away from the shore with your own hands.

Bronnie Ware, an Australian palliative-care nurse, spent many years with dying patients and later gathered what she heard into The Top Five Regrets of the Dying (2011). The book records that many people regretted at the end that they had worked too hard, had not kept up their friendships, had not let themselves be happier, and had not had the courage to express their true feelings. Brothers and sisters, notice this: no one on their deathbed regrets that “my title wasn’t high enough” or “my savings weren’t large enough.” What people care about at the very end is all relationships. This is exactly the order 321 speaks of: people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things; first life, then relationships, then ministry.

So “living for myself” looks clever, yet it is the most tragic choice; “living for the Lord” looks like loss, yet it is the most glorious life. Jesus said, “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25). This is the greatest paradox in the gospel: what you clutch, you lose; what you let go, you gain.

Seen from the 321 perspective, this is precisely the battlefield where “selflessness overcomes Satan.” Satan does not win by intimidation; he wins by persuading you that “you can be your own master.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When everyone in a family says, “I live for myself,” the result is that they wear one another down; when someone in a family is first to say, “I live for the Lord,” love begins to flow. Brothers and sisters, in what matter today are you still secretly sitting on the throne of your own heart?

sections.heading: 4. Laying Down the Right over Life and Death and Living Out the Freedom of Selflessness
sections.html:
Jesus laid down his authority over life and death and entrusted it wholly to the Father, and he invites us to learn the same resolve.

“For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Romans 14:8). This is the Christian’s freest declaration — I do not belong to myself; I belong to the Lord. Elsewhere Paul says it even more bluntly: “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

“You are not your own” — brothers and sisters, if these words come from the mouth of the enemy, they are bondage; if they come from the mouth of the Saviour, they are release. For if I do not belong to myself, then I don’t have to carry my success or failure alone, I don’t have to calculate my future alone, and I don’t have to fear my death alone.

When we lay down our craving to control “the length of our life” and “the arrangement of our life,” we become truly free. No more anxiety over security, no more fear over success or failure, because we know that our life and death are in the Lord’s hands. In the days when he was being hunted, David prayed, “My times are in your hand. Deliver me from the hand of my enemies, and from those who persecute me” (Psalm 31:15). Job, having lost everything in a single day, said, “Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name” (Job 1:21). Esther, at the moment when life and death hung in the balance, said, “if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16). Daniel’s three friends, standing before the furnace, said, “But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:18). Brothers and sisters, these people stood firm not because they knew the outcome, but because they knew whom they belonged to.

This is what 321 calls “selflessness.” Please be sure to remember: selflessness is not having nothing, not self-erasure, not passive resignation. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and living out the fullness. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). “It is no longer I” is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” is the fullness. A cup is emptied not so that it can stay empty, but so that it can be filled.

Jesus used a grain of wheat to picture this: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Brothers and sisters, notice the two outcomes: if it does not die, it “remains by itself alone”; if it dies, it “bears much fruit.” If the grain protects itself, its end is not destruction but this — to be only one grain for ever. That is the truly frightening thing. Many lives do not fail; they simply remain one grain from beginning to end.

Let’s look at the limits of life from another angle. An adult’s resting heart beats about seventy times a minute — around a hundred thousand times a day, around thirty-six point seven million times a year; live to eighty, and it comes to about two point nine billion beats. Every beat is grace, and not one of them beats because we commanded it. Have you ever ordered your own heart to beat? No. From the moment you were formed in your mother’s womb, your life has never been in your own hands. The psalmist says, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). We number our days not to make ourselves anxious, but to gain wisdom.

The English writer C. S. Lewis (1898–1963) has a much-quoted line in Mere Christianity: aim at heaven and you will get earth thrown in; aim at earth and you will get neither. This is exactly the shift of perspective 321 speaks of. When you turn from the temporary to the eternal, you do not lose the present; for the first time you truly possess it.

Describing the overcoming saints of the last days, Revelation says: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11). Brothers and sisters, notice the order here: first the blood of the Lamb, then not loving their lives. It is not that we are brave first and then God loves us; it is because he loved us first that we find the courage to let go. Our selflessness is not squeezed out by gritted teeth; it is melted out of us by the love of the cross.

And so I live no longer haggling for myself, and no longer afraid of death, because for those who believe in the Lord, death is no longer the end but a homecoming. “Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). Brothers and sisters, the one who can lay down life and death is a person the world has no more bargaining chips to threaten. That is freedom.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Road from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the four key points of today’s lesson are in fact the most central road of the 321 vision. Let’s string them together.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he had authority over life and death and chose to lay it down. This is our pattern: not a theory but a life actually lived. The Bible is my standard — I do not judge the meaning of life and death by my feelings; I declare, according to Romans 14:8, “If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” The Holy Spirit is my guide — that sentence in Gethsemane, “not what I desire,” was not squeezed out by willpower; it was upheld from within by the Holy Spirit. Brothers and sisters, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be glad, rely on the brain and you will be troubled. For out of the heart flow the issues of life.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — if he truly is King, then the schedule of my life and death belongs on his desk, not locked away in my drawer. Let Jesus receive all the glory — Paul says, “Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death”; that is giving all the glory back to him in full.

The Goal. Establish God’s system. Only a person who can lay down life and death is able truly to commit himself to a work that will outlive him. The Worldly system is built with “me” at the centre, so when the person leaves, the system falls apart; God’s system is built with Christ at the centre, so when the person leaves, the system remains and goes on multiplying.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The mark of the self-centred life is that it must be in control: control of outcomes, control of other people, control of its own lifespan. Selflessness is not having no self at all, but entering into the fullness — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. When Satan tempted Jesus in the wilderness, the heart of all three temptations was the same sentence: “Be your own master.” And all three of Jesus’ answers took the same stand: it is written.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today’s lesson begins with “mindset.” When your mindset shifts from “my life is mine” to “my life is the Lord’s,” your life changes with it; when your life changes, the priorities of your daily living change; when your daily living changes, your relationships with family and co-workers change; and when relationships change, ministry bears real fruit. The order cannot be reversed: first life, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The shift of perspective. If we look at life and death from man’s perspective, death is deprivation; from God’s perspective, death is being brought home. From the earthly perspective, long life is the greatest blessing; from the heavenly perspective, faithfulness is. From the temporary perspective, being taken advantage of is loss; from the eternal perspective, nothing offered up for the Lord is ever wasted. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938 and still running today, has followed several hundred participants over the long term, and its current director, Robert Waldinger, has pointed out many times that the strongest predictor of happiness and health in later life is neither wealth nor fame but good relationships. Brothers and sisters, even secular long-term research points to the same thing — people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” The most practical arena for laying down the right over life and death is not the martyr’s scaffold but the home, the office, the group chat. When you no longer fight to have the last word for yourself, you are living out the “0” in front of that “2” — the selfless life. And the selfless life naturally bears the fruit of the Spirit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Nine graces, one fruit of the Spirit, one life — that is 920.

The 235 relationships. When you lay yourself down, you can become a “2” with another selfless person, supporting each other and praying for each other; you can establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; you can join all the saints to become the “5,” spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team. Brothers and sisters, someone still living for himself cannot build 235, because his hands are full — clutching himself.

The Path of Serving is walked the same way: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First let the Holy Spirit guide, then let the Bible open our eyes, then life is shaped, and only then comes true service, and at last all the glory is given to God. The focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances.

sections.heading: 6. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared four practices for us. Let’s take them one by one, and use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deep.

Practice 1: The daily prayer practice. Each morning when you open your eyes, let your first words to the Lord be: “Lord, today I live for you.” Don’t just think it silently; please say it out loud. The power of a declaration is this: your ears will hear your mouth, and your heart will follow your ears.

Practice 2: The practice of entrusting life and death. In danger, before a test result, at a major decision, or in any moment of uncertainty, declare: “My life and death are in your hands.” (See Psalm 31:15.) Exchange anxiety for declaration, and imagination for trust.

Practice 3: The practice of letting go of control. This week, deliberately say “I want” one time less, and “Lord, what do you want me to do?” one time more — especially when you disagree with your family. Letting go of control is not abandoning responsibility; it is giving the throne back to the Lord.

Practice 4: The practice of living for the Lord. Whether at work, at home or in ministry, put one question in front of every choice: “Will this let Jesus be honoured as great?” If the answer is no, then however advantageous the thing may be, it is not worth it.

Now let’s walk these four practices once round the full circle of the eight stages.

Stage 1, Information. Today you have heard a new message: Jesus had authority over life and death, and he chose to lay it down; and I am not my own — I was bought with a price. Please copy the theme passage onto a piece of paper and put it where you will see it. If information never enters our eyes and ears, it can never change our life.

Stage 2, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to let this word drop from your head into your heart. Be still for three minutes and ask the Lord: “Lord, in what matter am I still gripping the steering wheel?” The answer the Holy Spirit gives is usually more specific than you expect.

Stage 3, Conviction. Revelation without conviction is only being moved. Conviction is making a decision: from today on, I acknowledge that my life and death are not mine. You can say to the Lord, “Lord, I agree that you are right and I am wrong.”

Stage 4, Implementation. Don’t wait for something big before you practise. This week, choose one specific small thing to begin with: a plan you can’t bear to give up, a remark you badly want to win back, a person you are used to controlling. Each time you let go is one time of putting it into practice.

Stage 5, Evaluation. Each night before sleep, take three minutes to look back: was there a moment today when I grabbed the steering wheel back again? What was the situation? Who was involved? What emotion was it? Please write it down specifically; don’t just say vaguely, “I didn’t do well.”

Stage 6, Correction. For the one thing your evaluation has uncovered, make one small adjustment. For example: tomorrow, when I meet the same situation, I will first take a deep breath and pray, “Lord, you are King,” before I open my mouth. Keep the correction small enough that you can really do it tomorrow.

Stage 7, Repetition. Brothers and sisters, a change of mindset is never a one-time decision but a repetition of hundreds and thousands of times. Brain science tells us that repeated behaviour strengthens the connections of neural pathways; spiritual practice is the same. Let go once today, let go once more tomorrow, and three months from now letting go will have become your reflex.

Stage 8, Multiplication. When this message bears fruit in you, pass it on to one person. This week, find a brother or sister, share Romans 14:8 with them, and pray for them. If the change in a life does not multiply, it stops with you; once it multiplies, God’s system begins to be built.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the very end the lesson leaves us a gentle reminder, and a very precious one: “living for myself” is an earthly end point; “living for the Lord” is a heavenly starting point. When we lay down our control over life and death, the life of Jesus is made manifest in us.

Jesus’ humility was not merely his attitude; it was his very way of life. He laid down the glory of heaven, he laid down his standing as one to be served, and at last he laid down authority over life and death, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross, so that we might receive eternal life.

Today he calls us to take up his resolve: no longer living for ourselves but for the Lord; no longer afraid of death, but giving even our death to the Lord. When we learn to lay down the right over life and death, we will be able, in every day of our lives, to live out that true freedom and glory.

Let us respond to the Lord together with the lesson’s declaration of faith:

Lord, I am willing to lay down the right over life and death, no longer living by my own strength and no longer afraid of death. May both my life and my death glorify you. If I live, I live for you; if I die, I return to you. In life or in death, I belong to you.

Brothers and sisters, may we do just one thing all our lives — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:5–9)
“For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Romans 14:7–8)
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you.

Thank you for sending your only beloved Son to be born for us and to lay down his life for us. Lord Jesus, you had authority over life and death, yet for love you laid it down; in the garden of Gethsemane you said to the Father, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” You were obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. This morning we bow down in worship before you.

Lord, forgive us. So often our mouths say you are King while our hands grip our own steering wheel. We are anxious about tomorrow, afraid for our health, calculating gains and losses, losing sleep over other people’s opinions. Lord, please loosen our fingers from the steering wheel, one finger at a time.

Holy Spirit, please work within us, so that what we have received today will be not only information but revelation; not only being moved but conviction; not only a decision but implementation, every single day.

Help us, from today on, to say sincerely every morning, “Lord, today I live for you”; to say with quiet confidence in moments of uncertainty, “My life and death are in your hands”; and to say humbly in moments when we are offended, “Lord, what do you want me to do?”
Whether we live or die, may we always be the Lord’s; may Christ, as always, be magnified in our bodies.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Discussion 1: Jesus said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father” (John 10:18). Jesus “had the power” and chose to lay it down. Please share: in your life right now, what is one thing you “have the right” to insist on, but could choose to lay down for love? Once you have laid it down, what change do you expect to see?

Discussion 2: Paul said, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Please share honestly: what are you most afraid of losing? If you placed that one thing in the Lord’s hands, what concrete differences would there be in your daily living? Please pray for one another, and agree together on one practice to put into action this week.

blog.title: Are You Really in Control of Your Own Destiny?

blocks.x: — Jesus Our Role Model (Part 3): Laying Down the Right Over Life and Death

We buy insurance because we want to control accidents; we get health check-ups because we want to control illness; we save for retirement, fill our schedules and draw up life plans because we want to control time. Behind the packed calendar on our phone hides the same sentence in the heart: “I want to be in charge of my own destiny.”

And yet a single pandemic brought the whole world’s calendar to a standstill at once; a single phone call in the middle of the night can rewrite a family’s plans of many years. We may have our hands on the steering wheel, but we cannot command the weather on the road.
1. He Had the Authority, Yet Chose to Lay It Down
With his whole life Jesus tells us this: true freedom is not found in control, but in obedience.

He laid down the glory of heaven, he laid down his standing as one to be served, and at last he laid down the deepest thing of all — sovereignty over life and death. “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8).
But he was not forced. Jesus put it very plainly: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again” (John 10:18).

Notice this: it was not that he had no rights; he had the right and chose to lay it down. A man with no money is not called generous, and a man with no authority who lets go is not called humble. Humility is this: I clearly have it, and yet for love I lay it down.

And the result? “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Notice that word: “therefore.” Jesus’ glory was not won by striving; it was received through laying down. The way down is the way up.
2. “I Live for Myself” Is the Most Costly Sentence
One of the things people say most often is: “I live for myself.” It sounds free, but in fact it is the cleverest of traps.

For the Bible says that none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself (see Romans 14:7). This is not an exhortation; it is a statement of fact. If we are not living for the Lord, we are living for some other master. A fish out of water is not free — it is suffocating; a kite whose string has snapped is not liberated — it is falling.

Jesus told the parable of a rich fool. His land yielded abundantly, so he pulled down his barns and built bigger ones. In just a few verses he says “I” and “my” five times over, yet not once does he mention God, nor anyone else at all. The end: “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20). His failure lay not in being rich, but in this: there was only one person in his life — himself.
3. Letting Go Is Where Freedom Begins

In his Roman imprisonment Paul wrote: “Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” (Philippians 1:20). He was not discussing life and death in a study; he was discussing life and death beside his chains.

So it is with us: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). If these words come from the mouth of the enemy, they are bondage; if they come from the mouth of the Saviour, they are release. For I don’t have to carry my success or failure alone, and I don’t have to fear my death alone.

This is what 321 calls “selflessness.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness — it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. If a grain of wheat protects itself, its end is not destruction but this: to be only one grain for ever.

Starting this Monday, try four small things: each morning say out loud, “Lord, today I live for you”; in moments of uncertainty declare, “My life and death are in your hands”; say “I want” one time less and ask “Lord, what do you want me to do?” one time more; and before every choice ask, “Will this let Jesus be honoured as great?”
Living for myself is an earthly end point; living for the Lord is a heavenly starting point.
Reflection Question
Today, what is one thing you have “every right” to insist on, yet could choose to lay down for love?
