brief12.title: Laying Down the Right Over Life and Death
notes: Jesus Our Role Model (Part 3)
Becoming obedient to the point of death,
yes, the death of the cross.
Philippians 2:8
Key points:
1. First read the full theme verse, Philippians 2:8: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

2. Explain that this is the third lesson in the series on Jesus our role model: the first two covered laying down the glory of heaven and laying down his standing as one to be served; this lesson covers laying down sovereignty over life and death.
3. Set the tone in one sentence: true freedom is not found in control, but in obedience.
4. Keep the tone warm; invite the brothers and sisters to receive quietly together.

brief12.title: In Whose Hands Are My Life and Death?
notes: Insurance, check-ups, plans
One longing behind them all: control
Yet one phone call can rewrite everything
True freedom: not control, but obedience
Key points:
1. Everyday scene: buying insurance, getting check-ups, saving for retirement, filling the calendar — behind them all is “I want to be in charge of my destiny.”
2. Contrast: one pandemic brought the whole world’s calendar to a standstill; one phone call in the night rewrote a family’s plans.
3. Psychology note: Julian B. Rotter’s (1966) “locus of control” theory — internal and external.
4. Name the problem: someone who relies only on internal control collapses when meeting what truly cannot be controlled.
5. Closing line: true freedom is not found in control, but in obedience.

brief12.title: Theme Passage and Background
notes: “We live or die, we are the Lord’s”
Romans 14:8
Paul wrote Philippians in a Roman prison
on the threshold between life and death
Key points:
1. Background: Philippians was written around AD 60–62, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome awaiting judgement.
2. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship; yet Paul said, “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).
3. Romans was written around AD 57; chapter 14 deals with believers’ disputes over eating only vegetables and keeping special days.
4. Theme passage in full: Romans 14:7–8.
5. Stress: the man who wrote these words was at that moment standing on the threshold between life and death.

brief12.title: Living in the Father’s Will
notes: “I have come down from heaven,
not to do my own will” John 6:38
“My food is to do the will
of him who sent me” John 4:34
Key points:
1. Quote John 6:38 and John 4:34.
2. Original-language note: “food” is the Greek brōma, the food that sustains life; for Jesus obedience was not a duty but his way of staying alive.
3. Illustration: without food you go hungry, without it you die — Jesus treated doing the Father’s will like eating.
4. Point out that Jesus’ comings and goings were decided not by circumstances but by the Father’s timetable.

brief12.title: Not What I Desire
notes: “Not what I desire,
but what you desire” Matthew 26:39
Power to lay it down and take it again
Having the right and laying it down: humility
Key points:
1. Read the full verse, Matthew 26:39; explain that “will” is the Greek thelēma.
2. Stress that obedience is not numbness: Jesus asked; he said, “if it is possible.”
3. Key verse: John 10:18 — he had power to lay it down and power to take it again.
4. Illustration: a man with no money is not called generous, and a man with no authority who lets go is not called humble; humility is having it and laying it down.
5. 321 application: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is returning to our originally intended position and letting God be God.

brief12.title: Whether by Life or by Death
notes: “Christ will be magnified in my body,
whether by life or by death” Phil 1:20
“For to me to live is Christ,
and to die is gain” Phil 1:21
Key points:
1. Read the full text of Philippians 1:20–21.
2. Original-language note: “magnified” is the Greek megalynō, the same word as in Mary’s “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:46).
3. Illustration: the moon gives no light of its own but reflects the sun; I don’t need to shine, I only need not to block him.
4. Testimony: Jim Elliot (1927–1956), journal entry of 1949 — giving what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.
5. Psychology note: Viktor E. Frankl’s logotherapy — we need a reason larger than ourselves.

brief12.title: Living for Myself Is a Lie
notes: “None of us lives to himself,
and none dies to himself”
Romans 14:7
Not living for the Lord is living for Satan
Key points:
1. Read Romans 14:7; stress that this is a statement of fact, not an exhortation.
2. Explain: if we are not living for the Lord, we are living for some other master.
3. Illustration: a fish out of water is not free — it is suffocating; a kite with a snapped string is not liberated — it is falling.
4. 321 application: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride the root of every problem; Satan doesn’t need you to worship him, only to worship yourself.

brief12.title: You Cannot Serve Two Masters
notes: “You can’t serve both God
and Mammon” Matthew 6:24
The rich fool spoke only of “I” and “my”

Key points:
1. Read the full verse, Matthew 6:24; explain that Mammon means wealth.
2. Stress that Jesus said “cannot,” not “may not” — the human heart has only one throne.
3. Illustration: money is a very good servant but a very bad master.
4. Tell the parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21): he said “I” and “my” five times over, yet never mentioned God.
5. Psychology note: Becker’s The Denial of Death (1973) and Terror Management Theory (Greenberg et al., 1986); compare Hebrews 2:15.

Only a grain that dies bears much fruit

2. Key line: from the mouth of the enemy these words are bondage; from the mouth of the Saviour they are release.
3. Illustration: the grain of wheat in John 12:24; the end of a grain that will not die is not destruction but to be only one grain for ever.
4. Quote Galatians 2:20: “no longer I” is selflessness; “Christ lives in me” is the fullness.

3. Stress: true obedience is not numbness; Jesus asked; he said, “if it is possible.”
4. Application question: is there a cup in your life that you have long been trying to push away?

brief21.title: Having Authority, Choosing to Lay It Down
notes: “I lay it down by myself. I have power
to lay it down, and to take it again” Jn 10:18

The way down is the way up

4. Read Philippians 2:9 and notice the “therefore”: glory was not won by striving but received through laying down.

brief21.title: Paul’s Resolve
notes: “Christ will be magnified in my body,

Key points:

brief21.title: To Live Is Christ
notes: “For to me to live is Christ,
and to die is gain” Phil 1:21

Not a struggle — both are good
Key points:

brief21.title: Living for the Lord Is Grace
notes: “He died for all, that those who live

Jim Elliot’s journal and testimony
Key points:

2. Reminder: if Jesus had not first died for us, we would never have had the chance to live for him.
3. Testimony: Jim Elliot (1927–1956), journal entry of October 1949; martyred in Ecuador in January 1956, aged only twenty-eight.
4. Testimony: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), The Cost of Discipleship — “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die”; executed on 9 April 1945.
5. Psychology note: Viktor E. Frankl (1905–1997) and logotherapy; we need a reason larger than ourselves.

brief21.title: The Most Dangerous Lie
notes: “None of us lives to himself,
and none dies to himself”
Romans 14:7

Key points:

2. Explain: if we are not living for the Lord, we are living for some other master; if we do not die to the Lord, we die to sin.

4. Quote Genesis 3:5: Satan’s first lie was “you will be like God.”

brief21.title: You Cannot Serve Two Masters

Key points:

brief21.title: The Rich Fool

Treasure for himself, not rich toward God
Key points:

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to the third lesson on Jesus our role model, and its title is “Laying Down the Right Over Life and Death.” Our theme verse is Philippians 2:8: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” In the first two lessons we saw that Jesus laid down the glory of heaven, and that he laid down his standing as one to be served. Today we look at the third thing he laid down, and the deepest of all — he laid down sovereignty over life and death.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you a question: in whose hands are your life and your death? We buy insurance because we want to control accidents; we get health check-ups because we want to control illness; we save for retirement and fill our schedules because we want to control time. Behind it all is the same sentence in the heart: I want to be in charge of my own destiny. And yet a single pandemic can bring the whole world’s calendar to a standstill at once; a single phone call in the middle of the night can rewrite a family’s plans of many years. We may have our hands on the steering wheel, but we cannot command the weather on the road. So Jesus tells us with his life: true freedom is not found in control, but in obedience.

Today’s theme passage has a second part, in Romans 14:8: “For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” Brothers and sisters, did you know? When Paul wrote Philippians, he was imprisoned in Rome, awaiting Caesar’s judgement. He was not discussing life and death in a study; he was discussing life and death beside his chains. That is why these words carry such weight.

The first key point: Jesus laid down sovereignty over life and death and lived in the Father’s will. He said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). And he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). Brothers and sisters, notice the word “food.” In the original it means the real food that goes into the mouth and sustains life. For Jesus, obedience was not an obligation added from outside; it was his daily breath and his daily bread.

The most profound scene of all is in the garden of Gethsemane. He prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). He did not pretend he was not in anguish; he asked. True obedience is never numbness; it is handing over your will while fully awake. And he said it very plainly: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself” (John 10:18). Brothers and sisters, it was not that he had no rights; he had the right and chose to lay it down. A man with no money is not called generous; having it and laying it down — that is what is called humility.

The second key point: living for the Lord was the resolve of Paul’s whole life. He said, “Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” (Philippians 1:20). And he said, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Brothers and sisters, the moon gives no light of its own; all its light is reflected from the sun. So it is with us: I don’t need to shine by myself; I only need not to block him.

The third key point: “living for myself” is Satan’s most dangerous lie. People so often say, “I live for myself.” It sounds free, but in fact it is a trap. The Bible says, “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself” (Romans 14:7). Brothers and sisters, notice that this is not an exhortation; it is a statement of fact. If we are not living for the Lord, we are living for some other master. A fish out of water is not free — it is suffocating; a kite whose string has snapped is not liberated — it is falling.

Jesus said, “You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24). Mammon means wealth. He said “cannot,” not “may not” — because the human heart has only one throne. Money is a very good servant but a very bad master. Jesus told of that rich fool (Luke 12:16–21): in just a few verses he says “I” and “my” five times over, yet not once does he mention God. God said to him, “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you.” His failure lay not in being rich, but in this: there was only one person in his life — himself.

The fourth key point: laying down the right over life and death and living out the freedom of selflessness. Paul says, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Brothers and sisters, if these words come from the mouth of the enemy, they are bondage; if they come from the mouth of the Saviour, they are release. For I don’t have to carry my success or failure alone, and I don’t have to fear my death alone. Jesus said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). The end of a grain that will not die is not destruction, but to be only one grain for ever. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, let’s practise four things. First, each morning say out loud to the Lord, “Lord, today I live for you.” Second, whenever you meet uncertainty, declare, “My life and death are in your hands.” Third, say “I want” one time less, and ask one time more, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” Fourth, before every choice ask, “Will this let Jesus be honoured as great?” And take them deep through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, please remember this: living for myself is an earthly end point; living for the Lord is a heavenly starting point. Jesus’ humility was not merely his attitude; it was his very way of life. Today he calls us: no longer living for ourselves but for the Lord; no longer afraid of death, but giving even our death to the Lord. When we lay down the right over life and death, the life of Jesus is made manifest in us. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let us declare together: Lord, I am willing to lay down the right over life and death, no longer living by my own strength and no longer afraid of death. May both my life and my death glorify you. If I live, I live for you; if I die, I return to you. In life or in death, I belong to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and give you peace.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we come together to the third lesson on Jesus our role model, and its title is “Laying Down the Right Over Life and Death.” Our theme verse is Philippians 2:8: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” In the previous two lessons we saw that Jesus laid down the glory of heaven, and that he laid down his standing as one to be served. Today we look at the third thing he laid down, and the deepest of all — he laid down sovereignty over life and death. He did not live for himself, nor did he die for himself; he lived for the Father, and he died for the world. This is the highest height of humility.

Brothers and sisters, let me begin with a question: have you noticed that so much of what we do in life actually circles around one single longing — control? We buy insurance because we want to control accidents; we get health check-ups because we want to control illness; we save for retirement and fill our schedules because we want to control time. Behind the packed calendar on our phone hides the same sentence in the heart: I want to be in charge of my own destiny. And yet a single, sudden pandemic brought the whole world’s calendar to a standstill at once; a single phone call in the middle of the night can rewrite a family’s plans of many years. Brothers and sisters, we may have our hands on the steering wheel, but we cannot command the weather on the road.

I once heard the testimony of an older brother. He had planned his whole life meticulously, and in the year he retired he scheduled the next twenty years. Then, three months into retirement, a single diagnosis cancelled every one of those plans. In his hospital room he said, “All my life I’ve been arranging my days, and only today have I discovered that my days were never mine.” In 1966 the psychologist Julian Rotter put forward the idea of “locus of control,” dividing people into an internal type and an external type. But the theory leaves a problem: if a person attributes everything to his own control, then when he meets the things he truly cannot control, his whole world collapses. The Bible gives us a third way. James 4:15 says, “For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.’” Brothers and sisters, the Bible does not tell us not to plan; it tells us to put four words in front of our plans — “If the Lord wills.”

Let’s first look at the background. The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul; it is generally held that the letter was written between AD 60 and 62, while he was under house arrest in Rome awaiting Caesar’s judgement. In other words, the man who wrote “Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” was at that moment standing quite literally on the threshold between life and death. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship, yet Paul said to them, “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). The other theme passage is in Romans 14. At the time the Roman church was arguing endlessly over eating only vegetables and keeping special days. Paul did not begin by ruling who was right and who was wrong; he lifted everyone to a higher place: “If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.”

The first key point: Jesus laid down sovereignty over life and death and lived in the Father’s will. Brothers and sisters, the life of Jesus was not of his own arranging. He said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). This is Jesus’ most concise explanation of his whole life. His schedule was not in his own hands: when Herod wanted to kill him, he went on his way; when the time had fully come, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. His comings and goings were decided not by circumstances, but by the Father’s timetable.

Beside the well at Sychar, Jesus said to his disciples, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). Brothers and sisters, notice the word “food.” In Greek it is brōma, the real food that goes into the mouth and sustains life. Jesus did not say doing the Father’s will was his hobby, nor that it was his duty. He said: it is my food. Without it you go hungry; without it you die. For Jesus, obedience was not an obligation added from outside, but his very way of staying alive from within. Brothers and sisters, is our obedience three meals a day, or an occasional snack?

The most profound scene of all is in the garden of Gethsemane. “He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire’” (Matthew 26:39). Brothers and sisters, the word for “will” here in Greek is thelēma — desire, will. Notice this: Jesus did not pretend he was not in anguish. He asked; he said, “if it is possible.” True obedience is never numbness; it is handing over your own will while fully awake and in full anguish. This morning, is there a cup in your life that you have long been trying to push away?

But we must take special note: this was not the Father forcing the Son. Jesus himself said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again” (John 10:18). Brothers and sisters, this is precisely today’s subject. It was not that he had no rights; he had the right and chose to lay it down. A man with no money is not called generous, and a man with no authority who lets go is not called humble. Humility is this: I clearly have it, and yet for love I lay it down. That is why Philippians 2:9 says, “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” Notice that word — “therefore.” Jesus’ glory was not won by striving; it was received through laying down. The way down is the way up.

The second key point: living for the Lord was the resolve of Paul’s whole life. He said, “according to my earnest expectation and hope, that I will in no way be disappointed, but with all boldness, as always, now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” (Philippians 1:20). “Magnified” in Greek is megalynō, meaning to be honoured as great; Mary’s song of praise uses the very same word. Brothers and sisters, at night the moon is very bright, but the moon gives no light of its own; all its light is reflected from the sun. The moon does its job best not when it strains to shine, but when it blocks nothing. I don’t need to shine by myself; I only need not to block him. And what is it that blocks him? Very often it is that big, thick self.

So Paul goes on: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Brothers and sisters, Paul does not say, “I live for Christ.” He puts it even more radically: to me to live is Christ. Christ is not one part of my life; Christ is my life itself. And he says, “But I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better” (Philippians 1:23). Do you see it? Paul’s dilemma is not about which side is better, but that both are good. If even death counts as gain to a man, what in this world can still threaten him?

Living for the Lord is not a sacrifice; it is grace. For if Jesus had not first died for us, we would never have had the chance to live for him. Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15). Brothers and sisters, the missionary Jim Elliot wrote in his journal in 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Seven years later, in Ecuador, he was killed by the very people he had gone to reach with the gospel; he was only twenty-eight. And in time many from that people turned to Christ. He did not lose; he handed over what he could not keep.

The third key point: “living for myself” is Satan’s most dangerous lie. One of the things people say most often is, “I live for myself.” It sounds free, but in fact it is Satan’s cleverest trap. The Bible says it very clearly: “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself” (Romans 14:7). Brothers and sisters, notice that Paul does not say, “You ought not to live for yourselves.” He says, “None of us lives to himself.” This is not an exhortation; it is a statement of fact. A fish out of water is not free — it is suffocating; a kite whose string has snapped is not liberated — it is falling. Satan’s first lie in Eden was this: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). From that day on, the self-centred life became the root of humanity’s fall. Satan never needs you to worship him; he only needs you to worship yourself.

Jesus put this in the most decisive terms: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24). Mammon means wealth. Brothers and sisters, Jesus said “cannot,” not “may not.” This is not a moral prohibition; it is a fact — the human heart has only one throne. Money in itself is not sin; money is a very good servant but a very bad master. The issue is not how much money you have, but who sits on the throne of your heart. It is like a man standing in a boat pushing hard against the pier: he thinks he has pushed the pier away, but in fact he has pushed himself away from the shore.

Jesus told the parable of a rich fool (Luke 12:16–21). His land yielded abundantly, so he pulled down his barns and built bigger ones, and told his soul to take its ease, eat, drink and be merry. Brothers and sisters, in just a few verses he says “I” and “my” five times over, yet not once does he mention God, nor anyone else at all. And then God said to him, “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?” His failure lay not in being rich, but in this: there was only one person in his life — himself. In The Denial of Death the thinker Ernest Becker says that people strain to build “immortality projects” so that they can believe “I will not disappear.” This bears out exactly what Hebrews 2:15 says: the Lord came to deliver those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

The fourth key point: laying down the right over life and death and living out the freedom of selflessness. Paul says, “For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Romans 14:8). And he says, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Brothers and sisters, if these words come from the mouth of the enemy, they are bondage; if they come from the mouth of the Saviour, they are release. For if I do not belong to myself, then I don’t have to carry my success or failure alone, I don’t have to calculate my future alone, and I don’t have to fear my death alone. When he was being hunted, David said, “My times are in your hand.” When he had lost everything, Job said, “Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away.” They stood firm not because they knew the outcome, but because they knew whom they belonged to.

Brothers and sisters, please be sure to remember: selflessness is not having nothing; it is not self-erasure. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and living out the fullness. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). “It is no longer I” is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” is the fullness. A cup is emptied not so that it can stay empty, but so that it can be filled. Jesus said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Notice this: the end of a grain that will not die is not destruction, but to be only one grain for ever. Many lives do not fail; they simply remain one grain from beginning to end.

Brothers and sisters, let’s practise. First, the daily prayer practice: each morning when you open your eyes, let your first words to the Lord, said out loud, be: “Lord, today I live for you.” Don’t just think it silently; please say it out loud, because your ears will hear your mouth, and your heart will follow your ears. Second, the practice of entrusting life and death: in danger, before a test result, at a major decision, declare: “My life and death are in your hands.” Psalm 31:15 says, “My times are in your hand.” Exchange anxiety for declaration, and imagination for trust.

Third, the practice of letting go of control: this week, deliberately say “I want” one time less, and “Lord, what do you want me to do?” one time more — especially when you disagree with your family. Letting go of control is not abandoning responsibility; it is giving the throne back to the Lord. Fourth, the practice of living for the Lord: whether at work, at home or in ministry, before every choice ask one question: “Will this let Jesus be honoured as great?” Brothers and sisters, please take these deep through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let go once today, let go once more tomorrow, and three months from now letting go will have become your reflex.

Let’s string the 3-2-1 vision together. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he had authority over life and death and chose to lay it down; the Bible is my standard — according to Romans 14:8 I declare that whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s; the Holy Spirit is my guide — that word of obedience in Gethsemane was not squeezed out by willpower. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; and the order is life first, then relationships, then ministry. And the 920 practice is right beside you — everyone you relate to is your “2”; live out the selfless “0” before them, and you will bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson leaves us a gentle reminder, and a very precious one: living for myself is an earthly end point; living for the Lord is a heavenly starting point. Jesus’ humility was not merely his attitude; it was his very way of life. He laid down the glory of heaven, he laid down his standing as one to be served, and at last he laid down authority over life and death, becoming obedient to the point of death, so that we might receive eternal life. Today he calls us to take up his resolve: no longer living for ourselves but for the Lord; no longer afraid of death, but giving even our death to the Lord. When we learn to lay down the right over life and death, we will be able, in every day of our lives, to live out that true freedom and glory. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let us declare together: Lord, I am willing to lay down the right over life and death, no longer living by my own strength and no longer afraid of death. May both my life and my death glorify you. If I live, I live for you; if I die, I return to you. In life or in death, I belong to you. Heavenly Father, forgive us: so often our mouths say you are King while our hands grip tightly to our own steering wheel. Please loosen our fingers, one finger at a time. Holy Spirit, may what we have received today be not only information, but become revelation, conviction and daily implementation. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and give you peace.

sections.heading: Introduction: To Be Respected Is the Deepest Longing of Our Hearts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to ask you first to be quiet for thirty seconds and recall one thing: the last time something left you feeling really uncomfortable inside — did it have to do with “not being respected”?

Perhaps it was in a meeting, where you were cut off before you had finished putting forward your idea; perhaps it was at home, where you had worked all day for your family and all you got back was, “What’s the big deal?”; perhaps it was at church, where you had quietly served for years, yet when the new leadership came in, no one remembered your name; perhaps it was in a group chat, where you posted something you had written with real care, and it was met with silence — no one replied.

That feeling is not necessarily anger. More often it is a dull, unspoken ache. We replay the scene over and over in our minds, imagine how we should have answered back at the time, and wish someone would say a fair word on our behalf.

Why does “being respected” tug at us so strongly? Because being understood, accepted and appreciated makes us feel that we have worth and that we are secure. In their classic 1995 paper “The Need to Belong,” published in Psychological Bulletin, the psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary showed that “belonging” is one of the most basic of human motivations: our longing to be accepted is as deeply rooted as our need for food and safety. Leary went further and proposed “sociometer theory,” suggesting that our self-esteem is really like a thermometer we carry around with us; what it measures is not how good we are, but how far we are accepted by others.

This is the truth about us: every day we walk around holding that thermometer. One approving glance from someone else, and the temperature rises; one cold response, and it falls. Our emotions are held hostage by other people’s attitudes, and our worth is priced by other people’s opinions.

And yet, brothers and sisters, Jesus showed us another way with his whole life — laying down the right to be respected, and still choosing love.

He was misunderstood, rejected, humiliated, even nailed to a cross, yet with a gentle, humble and obedient heart he still fulfilled the will of God. Not once did he fight for the respect he was due, because in his heart there was a greater aim: that the Father should receive the glory, and that sinners should receive life.

So today we are going to see one truth together: true humility is not being looked down on by others; it is no longer fighting for respect for ourselves.

Notice the difference between the two. Being looked down on is something others do to you; no longer fighting for respect for yourself is a choice you make before God. The first you cannot control; the second you can practise every day. A life like this is the very height of what the 321 vision calls “selflessness” — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Written to Suffering Believers
sections.html:
Our theme passage today comes from 1 Peter chapter 2. To grasp the weight of these words, we need first to go back to the scene in which the letter was written.

Author, Date and Recipients

The author of this letter is the apostle Peter. At the very beginning he introduces himself: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1). These five place names all lie in the region of present-day Turkey; they were five provinces of Asia Minor in the Roman Empire.

The letter is generally dated between AD 62 and 64, on the very eve of the emperor Nero’s persecution of the church. At the end of the letter Peter writes, “She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you” (1 Peter 5:13). Church tradition generally holds that “Babylon” here is a code word for Rome.

The recipients are called people “living as foreigners.” The Greek word is parepidēmos, meaning a foreigner residing somewhere temporarily, a traveller without citizenship. In the cities where they lived they were second-class people; and now that they believed in Jesus, they were regarded by their neighbours, their colleagues and even their own families as a strange crowd. Later Peter puts it very bluntly: “They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, blaspheming” (1 Peter 4:4).

Historical and Cultural Setting: A World That Lived and Died by Honour and Shame

To feel the force of this letter, we must understand one feature of the first-century Mediterranean world: it was an “honour and shame culture.” In that society a person’s most important asset was not property but “face.” To be insulted and not hit back was to be seen as weak, as less than a man.

It was in exactly that atmosphere that Peter wrote words that go almost against the grain of heaven and earth: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten” (1 Peter 2:23).

“Cursed” in the original is loidoreō, meaning to revile and humiliate someone to their face; “threaten” is apeileō, a counter-attacking intimidation. Peter says the Lord Jesus did neither. He did not answer back, and he did not threaten.

Then what did he do? He “committed himself to him who judges righteously.” “Committed” in the original is paradidōmi, meaning to hand something over into another person’s hands. In the original this verb is in the imperfect tense, indicating a continuous, ongoing action — not gritting his teeth and bearing it once, but placing himself back into the Father’s hands again and again.

The Surrounding Context: From Household Servants to the Whole Church

Interestingly, Peter’s words here were first addressed to “servants” (1 Peter 2:18). In the Roman Empire a household servant had no channel of appeal at all; if his master was harsh, he simply had to take it. To these people, who had fewer rights than anyone, Peter says: though you have no rights on earth, you have in heaven a Lord who judges righteously.

Then Peter widens this principle to the whole church: “For you were called to this” (1 Peter 2:21). So following in the footsteps of Christ’s suffering is not a special calling for a few, but the shared calling of everyone who has received grace.

“Example” in the original is hypogrammos. In Greek this word referred to the line of writing that a teacher wrote across the top of a wax tablet when ancient schoolchildren learned to write; the pupils traced it over, stroke by stroke. Peter’s meaning is this: Jesus has written his life on that top line, and the lesson of our whole life is to trace over it.

The background of Philippians chapter 2 is also worth mentioning. Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), and its citizens were proud of their status as Roman citizens; what they cared about most was rank and honour. Paul wrote to them around AD 60 to 62 from prison in Rome, and to these people who prized status above all he said that Christ “emptied himself.” “Emptied” in the original is kenoō, meaning to pour out, to make empty. He did not lose his divinity; rather, he laid down the glory and respect he had every right to enjoy.

Brothers and sisters, please remember these two words: hypogrammos, the copybook line; kenoō, emptying. Today’s lesson is about tracing over Jesus’ line of writing and learning to empty ourselves.

sections.heading: 1. Rejected by the Crowds, Jesus Chose Silent Obedience
sections.html:
The People He Had Helped Became the People Crying for His Crucifixion

What did Jesus do in his three and a half years of public ministry on earth? He healed the sick, set the captives free and preached the gospel of the kingdom of heaven. The blind saw, the lame walked, lepers were cleansed, the deaf heard, the dead were raised, and the poor had good news preached to them.

Yet on the night he was arrested, not one person stood up to speak for him.

Pilate stood before the crowd and gave them a choice: “But the governor answered them, ‘Which of the two do you want me to release to you?’ They said, ‘Barabbas!’” (Matthew 27:21).

Who was Barabbas? Mark’s Gospel tells us he was “bound with his fellow insurgents, men who in the insurrection had committed murder” (Mark 15:7). In other words, the crowd would rather have a murderous thug than the Lord who had healed them.

Pilate asked again: “‘What then shall I do to Jesus, who is called Christ?’ They all said to him, ‘Let him be crucified!’” (Matthew 27:22).

At that moment Jesus, who had helped countless people, was treated by the crowd as worse than a bandit.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Prophet Saw It Long Before

This was no accident. More than seven hundred years earlier Isaiah had seen it: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him” (Isaiah 53:3).

“Despised” in Hebrew is nivzeh, from the root bazah, meaning to regard as worthless, not worth a second glance. The most piercing part of the whole verse is the last line: “we didn’t respect him.” Not “they,” but “we.” Isaiah counts himself in.

The apostle John sums it up in one sentence too: “He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him” (John 1:11).

And how did Jesus respond? Isaiah had written that down long before as well: “He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

Jesus did not defend himself. He bore the humiliation in silence and let God vindicate him.

Scientific Confirmation: Rejection Really Does Hurt

Someone may say: it’s only rejection — grit your teeth and it’ll pass; is it really that serious?

In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger and Matthew Lieberman of the University of California, Los Angeles, together with Kipling Williams of Macquarie University in Australia, published a well-known brain-imaging study in the journal Science. They had participants play an online ball-tossing game called “Cyberball.” Partway through, the two other “players” suddenly stopped throwing the ball to them and shut them out. The result: the “dorsal anterior cingulate cortex” in the participants’ brains became markedly active — and this is one of the very regions that becomes active when our bodies are in pain.

In other words, the pain of being excluded runs, in the brain, on the same circuitry as physical pain.

So, brothers and sisters, when you feel heavy inside because you have been left out in the cold, it is not that you are too fragile; it is the reality of how God made us. And more importantly, it also means that when Jesus was rejected by the crowds, what he bore was real, genuine pain. He was not numb; he held it in.

True Humility Is Trusting in God’s Justice

So we must distinguish between two things: the silence of cowardice and the quietness of trust.

Cowardly silence comes from not daring to speak; the quietness of trust comes from knowing there is a higher Judge. Peter says it plainly: the Lord Jesus “committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). And Paul says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Peter reminds us: “But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God” (1 Peter 2:20).

Notice the words “with God.” They are the key to the whole verse. In man’s eyes, patient endurance is being taken advantage of; with God, patient endurance is commendable. The same thing, two perspectives, two values.

So when we are misunderstood or rejected, we don’t need to rush to prove we were right. We need only ask ourselves one question: “Is my conscience clear before God, before others and before myself?”

“Conscience” in the original is syneidēsis, which literally means “knowing together” — the truth that I know together with God. 1 Peter 3:16 says: “having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.”

So if our conscience is clear, we can, like Jesus, quietly entrust ourselves to the God who searches the heart.

Applying the 321 Vision: From Man’s Perspective to God’s

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision is very clear: we must learn the shift of perspective — from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

The moment of rejection is precisely the watershed of perspective. Seen from man’s perspective, I have lost; seen from God’s perspective, I am being shaped. Seen from the earthly perspective, I have lost face; seen from the heavenly perspective, my reward is accumulating. The Lord Jesus said: “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven” (Matthew 5:11–12).

And this is exactly the first of what 321 calls “the Three Foundations”: Jesus is my role model. In the place of rejection we do not look at how others treat us; we look at how Jesus walked through it.

sections.heading: 2. Rejected by His Disciples, Jesus Still Chose to Receive and Restore Them
sections.html:
The Deepest Wounds Often Come from Those Closest to Us

Rejection by the crowds was painful enough, but there is a deeper pain still — the pain that comes from people you chose with your own hand and led personally for three and a half years.

Judas betrayed him. “Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests, and said, ‘What are you willing to give me, that I should deliver him to you?’ They weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver” (Matthew 26:14–15).

How much were thirty pieces of silver? The Old Testament law has a very particular provision: “If the bull gores a male servant or a female servant, thirty shekels of silver shall be given to their master” (Exodus 21:32). Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation paid for a slave gored to death by an ox. In other words, the price Judas put on the Lord Jesus was the price of a slave’s life. The prophet Zechariah had foretold this very sum long before, and described it like this: “Yahweh said to me, ‘Throw it to the potter, the handsome price that I was valued at by them!’ I took the thirty pieces of silver, and threw them to the potter, in Yahweh’s house” (Zechariah 11:13) — what a bitter irony that is.

And Peter? This disciple, who had sworn so confidently, said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew 26:35). Yet a few hours later, “Peter remembered the word which Jesus had said to him, ‘Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.’ Then he went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75).

How Jesus Treated His Faithless Disciples

If you were Jesus, what would you have done?

Most of us would probably do one of three things: scold them, accuse them, or keep our distance from then on. But Jesus did not scold, did not accuse and did not hold a grudge.

On the contrary, after his resurrection he went looking for them himself. “When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle, and said to them, ‘Peace be to you’” (John 20:19).

Look at this picture: the doors were locked, and so were their hearts. They were hiding there, full of shame and fear. And the risen Lord’s first words were not, “Why did you run away?” but “Peace be to you.”

Then by the Sea of Tiberias, “when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it” (John 21:9), and Jesus said, “Come and eat breakfast!” (John 21:12).

Brothers and sisters, pay attention to that “fire of coals.” The word John’s Gospel uses is anthrakia, and it appears only twice in the whole New Testament: once in the high priest’s courtyard, where Peter stood beside a fire of coals and denied the Lord three times (John 18:18); and once here. The Lord Jesus deliberately lit the same kind of charcoal fire — he wanted to bring Peter back to the scene of his fall, and then heal him in that very same setting.

Then the Lord asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Three questions, answering to three denials. Jesus was not trying to shame Peter; he wanted to heal his broken heart and restore his calling: “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16).

In fact, Jesus had prepared Peter’s restoration even before he fell: “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32). The Lord did not start looking for a solution after the fall; before the fall he had already said, “when once you have turned again.”

A True Testimony: Corrie ten Boom and the Guard

The family of the Dutch woman Corrie ten Boom was arrested during the Second World War for hiding Jews, and her sister Betsie died in Ravensbrück concentration camp. After the war Corrie travelled widely, preaching God’s forgiveness. In 1947, after a meeting in Munich, a man came up and held out his hand to her — and she recognised him as one of the guards from the camp. He told her he had become a Christian and asked for her forgiveness.

Corrie later wrote honestly in her book Tramp for the Lord that in that moment her hand hung frozen at her side; she could not hold it out. She prayed silently, asking the Lord to give her the power to forgive. Then, she said, in the instant she obediently stretched out her hand, a warm current flowed from her shoulder down her arm, and tears sprang to her eyes. That forgiveness, she said, did not come from her, but from the love of God.

Forgiveness is often not something we do once we feel it; we first obey and do it, and the feeling follows afterwards.

Psychological Confirmation: The Cost of Unforgiveness

Forgiveness is not only a spiritual lesson; unforgiveness also carries a measurable physical cost. In 2001 Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet of Hope College and her colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science. They asked participants to imagine, in turn, “not forgiving” and “forgiving” someone who had wronged them. They found that while imagining unforgiveness, participants’ blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension all rose significantly, and they reported more anger and a greater sense of losing control; while imagining empathy and forgiveness, these physiological measures were markedly lower.

Holding a grudge is punishing your own body for someone else’s wrong. Another psychologist of forgiveness, Everett Worthington of Virginia Commonwealth University, has organised the process of forgiveness into a set of practices, reminding us that forgiveness is an ability that can be learned and practised, not a gift reserved for a few saints.

Applying the 321 Vision: First Life, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

Brothers and sisters, did you notice the order in which the Lord Jesus restored Peter? He first asked, “Do you love me?” and only then said, “Tend my sheep.”

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: first life, then relationships, then ministry. Not first making up for the lost work, but first repairing the love. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Peter first needed to realign his love before the Lord; only then could he face his own failure, and only then could he go and feed others.

This is also the beautiful picture of the “235 relationships”: the Lord Jesus and Peter first became a “2” — a pair of spiritual companions honest with each other; then Peter became spiritual parent to others, building the “3”; and finally, with the other apostles, he became part of the “5,” spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team.

So when we are misunderstood or hurt by those closest to us, can we, like Jesus, choose not to retaliate, not to accuse, but to go on loving?

Jesus’ love gave his disciples fresh strength; his humility built up those who had failed once again. This is true humility: laying down the right to be respected, and choosing to forgive and to entrust others with responsibility again.

sections.heading: 3. Forsaken for a Time by the Father, Jesus Still Obeyed to the End
sections.html:
The Deepest Cry from the Cross

On the cross Jesus bore immense suffering. The Roman cross was universally acknowledged as the cruellest punishment in the ancient world. The Roman philosopher Cicero, arguing a case in court, called crucifixion “the most cruel and disgusting penalty,” and said that a Roman citizen should not even hear the word. The Jewish historian Josephus called it “the most wretched of deaths.”

And yet, as the Gospels record it, Jesus did not cry out in pain at the scourging, nor weep at the humiliation.

He spoke seven sayings in all from the cross, and the first time he cried out with a loud voice was this one: “About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, ‘Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?’ That is, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” (Matthew 27:46).

The ninth hour is three o’clock in the afternoon. Before that, “from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour” (Matthew 27:45). For three whole hours the sun gave no light and the whole land lay in pitch darkness.

This Was the Deepest Loneliness of His Life

Brothers and sisters, notice this: Jesus did not cry out because of the nails; he cried out because of his separation from the Father.

From all eternity the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Three in One, had been perfectly united, never separated for a single moment. And in that moment, because the sin of humanity was laid upon him, that intimate fellowship was veiled.

Paul explains why: “For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). And Isaiah says: “Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

Jesus bore the sin of the world, and the Father turned his face away from him. That is a pain beyond imagining.

Yet Jesus still chose to obey to the end, until he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Light from the Original Language: Two Key Words

The first word is “forsaken.” The Greek is egkataleipō, meaning to leave behind, to abandon and leave uncared for.

Remarkably, this same word appears again in Hebrews 13:5: “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.’”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? This is the light of Scripture interpreting Scripture — on the cross Jesus experienced egkataleipō so that we would never experience egkataleipō again. He was forsaken by the Father so that we would never again be forsaken.

The second word is “It is finished,” in the original tetelestai. It is a perfect-tense verb, meaning “it has been completed, and its effect continues for ever.” The scholar Adolf Deissmann, studying ancient papyrus documents, found that this word was often written on receipts, meaning: the debt is paid in full.

So the Lord Jesus’ final declaration on the cross was not “I am finished,” but “The debt is paid.”

The Words He Cried Came from a Psalm

There is another detail that is often overlooked: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” was not something Jesus made up on the spot; it is the first verse of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?” (Psalm 22:1).

In that era, quoting the first line of a psalm was a way of pointing to the whole psalm. And how does Psalm 22 end? “For he has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, Neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard” (Psalm 22:24).

That is to say, what Jesus quoted in his darkest hour was a psalm that begins with a cry and ends in victory. His faith did not waver — he still called him “my God.”

An Illustration from Life: Only Those Who Have Walked the Valley Understand It

There is a very simple comparison: if you want to show someone that you understand the road they have walked, the best way is not to explain how hard that road is, but to let them see the mud on your shoes.

We often see this around us: a mother who has lost a child does not most need a perfect theological answer; what she needs is another mother who has also lost a child, sitting beside her and saying nothing at all.

That is just how Hebrews describes our Lord: “For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

So, brothers and sisters, when we feel lonely and abandoned, Jesus understands better than anyone. He is not a God far off in heaven, but a Saviour who has walked the road of rejection and knows what pain is. He is willing to walk with us through the season of rejection, and to say within us: don’t give up — I am with you.

The Lord himself promised with his own lips: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision: The Focus Is on Jesus
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances.

When we are rejected, our focus easily slides towards three places. Slide towards ourselves, and we fall into self-pity: “Why me?” Slide towards others, and we fall into bitterness: “How could he do this?” Slide towards circumstances, and we fall into despair: “What will become of me if this goes on?”

Only when we fix our focus on Jesus do we discover that he walked this road before us — and he walked it to the end.

The writer of Hebrews says: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2).

“Despising its shame” — not that it didn’t hurt, but that because he saw a greater joy, the shame was outweighed. This is what 321 means by turning from the temporary to the eternal.

sections.heading: 4. Holding to Humility amid Rejection: Laying Down the Right to Be Respected
sections.html:
He Had the Power, but Chose Not to Use It

We must see one thing clearly: it was not that Jesus lacked the power to strike back; he had the power and did not use it.

In the garden of Gethsemane, when Peter drew his sword and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant, Jesus said to him: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53). A Roman legion numbered about six thousand men, so twelve legions would be more than seventy thousand angels. He had the power to take revenge, the power to escape the shame of the cross, but he did not do it.

He chose to lay down his power and chose to forgive: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Notice the tense of this prayer. In the original it is the imperfect, indicating that he kept on saying it — as the nails were driven in, blow after blow, he asked again and again for forgiveness for those who were nailing him.

Humility Is Not Losing to Others but Winning over Ourselves

When we are rejected or misunderstood, our most natural reactions are three: we want to prove ourselves, we want to retaliate, we want to be understood.

But the role model of Jesus reminds us: humility is not losing to others; it is winning over ourselves.

The 321 vision puts this very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

You see, this is exactly the picture of the cross. Satan’s way is, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God!” (Isaiah 14:13); Christ’s way is that he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7).

One leaves his originally intended position and grasps upward; the other returns to his originally intended position and goes downward.

And the outcome? “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5).

So 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Sayings and Testimonies

The English writer C. S. Lewis devotes an entire chapter of Mere Christianity to pride. He points out that pride is the very centre of all evil, “the complete anti-God state of mind”; and he observes something very profound: pride is essentially comparative — a person is proud not of having something, but of having more of it than others.

This explains exactly why the need to be “respected” is so hard to lay down — because we are constantly comparing ourselves with others. Who is noticed more, who is affirmed more, who is remembered more.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in The Cost of Discipleship (published in 1937), reminded the church that the call of Christ is a call to come and die for him. He himself was later martyred in a Nazi prison, sealing these words with his life.

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl recorded his observations of the concentration camps in Man’s Search for Meaning. Everything can be taken from a man, he said, but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, others can take away your face, your position and your reputation, but they cannot take away your freedom to “choose humility.” No one can ever take that from you.

We Lay Down Our Rights So That God May Be Glorified

For the idea of “rights,” the New Testament has a very important word: exousia — authority, entitlement. The apostle Paul had the right to make his living by the gospel, yet he said: “Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:12).

What Paul laid down was not his responsibility but his right. The question he asked was not, “Am I entitled to this?” but, “If I do this, will the gospel be hindered?”

We lay down “the right to be respected” so that God may receive the glory. For when we choose to forgive, God’s love is made manifest in us.

The Lord Jesus said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). And Paul says: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Brothers and sisters, let’s place today’s message within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back; that is our copybook line. The Bible is my standard — when I am rejected, I go not by my feelings but by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — because by our own willpower we can’t hold out for three days; only the Holy Spirit can bear the fruit of patience and gentleness in us.

The Two Core Values: Let Jesus be King — in the moment I am misunderstood, who sits on the throne of my heart? My sense of grievance, or Jesus? Let Jesus receive all the glory — I don’t defend myself, not because I am big-hearted, but because I want him to receive the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A community whose members don’t fight for respect, yet respect one another, is the truest form of God’s system on earth.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And “the right to be respected” is the self-centred life’s most attractive and least detectable disguise. It looks so reasonable: I have given so much — of course I deserve to be noticed.

But selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and living out the fullness. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

“It is no longer I” — that is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” — that is the fullness.

Notice: selflessness does not mean having no sense of self-worth; it means no longer needing to draw our self-worth from other people’s opinions. For my worth has already been priced by the cross.

The Fivefold Change and the 920 Practice

321 says that the change of a life is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living.

Today’s lesson has just one mindset to change: being respected is not a right I must hold on to, but a gift I can lay down.

And the arena for practice is 920. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” Before the colleague who misunderstands you, before the family member who ignores you, before the brother who forgets you, practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and then let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine of its expressions: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

You will find that seven of these nine graces can only be borne within relationships. A person with no difficult people in his life cannot bear patience; a person with no enemies cannot learn kindness.

So, brothers and sisters, the person who rejects you is not your obstacle — he is your orchard.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Truth into Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. Let’s use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to deepen them one by one.

Practice 1: Quietly Entrust

When you are misunderstood or rejected, don’t defend yourself first; pray to the Lord first.

Information: copy out 1 Peter 2:20–23 once, so the truth enters your mind. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show you before whom you most often rush to defend yourself. Conviction: acknowledge before God that my innocence does not need my own mouth to protect it. Implementation: from today, set a “twenty-four-hour rule” — after being misunderstood, pray for twenty-four hours first, then decide whether to respond. Evaluation: each week, review how many times this week I spoke first and prayed afterwards. Correction: turn the time spent defending myself into time spent praying. Repetition: keep it up for forty days and let it become a habit. Multiplication: share this practice with a brother or sister and invite them to do it with you.

Practice 2: Choose to Forgive

Think of someone who has hurt you, bless them, and ask the Lord to heal your heart.

Information: read Ephesians 4:32: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). Revelation: ask the Lord to let you see the far greater debt of which you yourself have been forgiven. Conviction: acknowledge that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision. Implementation: write down that person’s name and pray specifically for three good things for them. Evaluation: notice whether your chest still tightens when you think of them. Correction: if there is still bitterness, change your prayer from “Lord, change him” to “Lord, heal me.” Repetition: pray for them for thirty days. Multiplication: when someone around you is caught in bitterness, walk through this process with them once.

Practice 3: Respond with Love

Reach out in care to someone who has ignored you, following Jesus in dissolving the distance with love.

Information: reflect on John 20:19 — it was Jesus who took the first step towards that group behind locked doors. Revelation: ask the Lord to show you the person you have been “waiting to speak first.” Conviction: accept one fact — the one who reaches out first is not the loser but the one who is like the Lord. Implementation: this week, take the initiative to send a greeting, arrange a meal, or offer a small gesture of care. Evaluation: record the other person’s response, and record your own feelings too. Correction: if they are cold, don’t withdraw your love; just adjust your expectations. Repetition: let reaching out become your normal way, not a one-off experiment. Multiplication: take a younger brother or sister with you to visit someone.

Practice 4: Examine Your Conscience

Ask yourself every day: “Is my conscience clear today before God and before others?”

Information: read Acts 24:16: “In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men” (Acts 24:16). Revelation: set aside five minutes before sleep and be still, letting the Holy Spirit search you. Conviction: believe that a clear conscience matters more than a spotless reputation. Implementation: each night write one sentence — “Today, in this matter, I was right before God” or “Today, in this matter, I fell short towards someone.” Evaluation: at the weekend, look back over the seven days’ entries. Correction: to anyone you have wronged, apologise promptly and make it right promptly. Repetition: keep it up for a whole season. Multiplication: lead your small group in keeping a week-long conscience journal together.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, I want to give you these tender words from the lesson: being rejected does not mean you have failed; on the contrary, it is an opportunity to become more like Jesus.

Rejection is a testing of faith, and a perfecting of love.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed the same group of people since 1938, for more than eighty years, and its current director, Robert Waldinger, points out that the clearest conclusion of the study is this: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout life is neither wealth nor fame, but good relationships.

And good relationships are never sustained by respect we fight for; they are watered by the humility that lays down its rights.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Jesus’ humility was not merely outward gentleness but inner strength — laying down the right to be respected, and still choosing love and forgiveness.

He was rejected by people, yet he did not reject people; he was humiliated, yet he still honoured others.

A life like this is the glory of the cross.

And the Bible tells us where this road ends: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9–11).

Brothers and sisters, the way down turns out in the end to be the way up. The hand that lets go turns out in the end to be the hand that is lifted high.

So this morning, let us answer this call together: let us follow Jesus, learning to love amid rejection and learning humility amid the loss of respect.

Let Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and let the glory go to the Lord who was crucified.

keyVerses: “For what glory is it if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating? But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God. For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps, who didn’t sin, ‘neither was deceit found in his mouth.’ When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:20–23)

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8)
prayer: Lord, when I am rejected and misunderstood, help me to remember your example on the cross.
I am willing to lay down the right to be respected, not arguing for myself, asking only that your love be made manifest in me.
Lord, I confess that there is a self in me that longs to be noticed and longs to be affirmed. Deal with my self-centred life through your cross, and live out selflessness in me by your Holy Spirit.
Heal my heart, wounded by rejection, and remove the bitterness that has grown in me from not being respected.
Lord, I want to be like you — choosing to forgive, choosing to accept, choosing humble obedience.
Reign as King in my family, my workplace and my church, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). Please share a time when you were misunderstood but chose not to defend yourself. During that time, how did you entrust yourself to God? How did God later vindicate or comfort you?

“And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). In your relationships right now, is there someone you are still waiting to apologise first? If today you were to take the first step towards them as Jesus did, what could that first step be?

blog.title: When He Was Cursed, He Didn’t Curse Back

blocks.x: Another Road You Can Choose When You Are Not Respected

Have you ever had an experience like this? In a meeting you are cut off before you have finished speaking; at home you work all day and all you get back is, “What’s the big deal?”; at church you quietly serve for years, yet when the new leadership comes in, no one remembers your name.
That feeling is not necessarily anger. More often it is a dull, unspoken ache.

In their classic 1995 paper “The Need to Belong,” the psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary showed that belonging is one of the most basic of human motivations. Leary even compared self-esteem to a thermometer we carry around with us: what it measures is not how good we are, but how far we are accepted by others.
This is the truth about us: our emotions are held hostage by other people’s attitudes, and our worth is priced by other people’s opinions.
Rejection Really Does Hurt

In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger of the University of California, Los Angeles, and two fellow researchers published a brain-imaging study in the journal Science. When participants were shut out in an online ball-tossing game, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex in their brains became markedly active — and this is one of the very regions that becomes active when our bodies are in pain.
In other words, the pain of being excluded runs, in the brain, on the same circuitry as physical pain.
So if you feel heavy inside because you have been left out in the cold, it is not that you are too fragile. It really does hurt.
And this also means that when Jesus was rejected by the crowds, what he bore was real, genuine pain. He was not numb; he held it in.
He Had the Power, but Chose Not to Use It

For three and a half years on earth Jesus healed the sick, set the captives free and preached the gospel of the kingdom of heaven. Yet on the night he was arrested, not one person stood up to speak for him. When Pilate asked the crowd whom he should release, they shouted for Barabbas, a man who had committed murder in the insurrection.

Those closest to us wound us more deeply still. Judas sold him for thirty pieces of silver — under Old Testament law, the compensation paid for a slave gored to death by an ox. Peter boasted that he would die with him, yet a few hours later he denied him three times.
How did Jesus respond?

He did not scold, did not accuse and did not hold a grudge. After his resurrection he went himself to that group behind tightly locked doors, and his first words were, “Peace be to you.” By the sea he lit a fire of coals — the same kind of charcoal fire beside which Peter had denied the Lord three times — and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Then he gave him back his calling: “Tend my sheep.”

And on the cross, though he could have asked the Father to send more than twelve legions of angels, he did not ask. What he said was: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).
Peter later remembered his Teacher like this: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23).
Humility Is Not Losing to Others but Winning over Ourselves

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
So true humility is not being looked down on by others; it is no longer fighting for respect for ourselves.

Notice the difference between the two. Being looked down on is something others do to you; no longer fighting for respect for yourself is a choice you make before God. The first you cannot control; the second you can practise every day.
This week you can try practising four things:
1. Quietly entrust. When you are misunderstood, don’t defend yourself first. Set yourself a twenty-four-hour rule: pray for a day first, then decide whether to respond.

2. Choose to forgive. Think of someone who has hurt you and pray specifically for three good things for them. If your chest still tightens, change your prayer from “Lord, change him” to “Lord, heal me.”
3. Respond with love. Reach out in care to someone who has ignored you. The one who reaches out first is not the loser but the one who is like the Lord.
4. Examine your conscience. Each night set aside five minutes to ask yourself: Is my conscience clear today before God and before others?
Being rejected does not mean you have failed; on the contrary, it is an opportunity to become more like Jesus. Rejection is a testing of faith, and a perfecting of love.
For the Bible says that the way down turns out in the end to be the way up: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).
A Question to Leave with You
At this moment, the first name that comes to mind — the person who has made you feel disrespected — what is the first small thing you are willing to do for them?

2. Theme passage: 1 Peter 2:20–23; its heart is “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back.”
3. Also read Philippians 2:5–8; “emptied himself” is the Greek kenoō, meaning to pour out, to make empty.
4. Set the tone at the start: true humility is not being looked down on by others; it is no longer fighting for respect for ourselves.
Respect: our deepest longing
Cut off mid-sentence in a meeting
Your effort met with “What’s the big deal?”
Years of serving, and no one remembers
That dull ache — do you know it?
Key points:

2. Give three everyday scenes: cut off in a meeting, effort made light of, years of serving that no one remembers.

Jesus points to another way
Belonging: our most basic need
(Baumeister and Leary, 1995)
True humility is not being looked down on
but no longer fighting for respect

1. Baumeister and Leary’s 1995 paper “The Need to Belong,” published in Psychological Bulletin.
2. Leary’s sociometer theory: self-esteem is like a thermometer measuring “how far we are accepted.”

A letter to suffering believers
Peter writes to foreigners in Asia Minor
Around AD 62–64
“This is commendable with God.”
(1 Peter 2:20)
Key points:
1. 1 Peter 1:1: written to those living as foreigners in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia.
2. “Living as foreigners” is the Greek parepidēmos, temporary residents without citizenship — second-class people in society.
3. Church tradition generally holds that “Babylon” in 1 Peter 5:13 is a code word for Rome.
