5. “Example” is the Greek hypogrammos, the copybook line schoolchildren traced over.
Jesus rejected by the crowds
Three and a half years of healing and preaching
The night of his arrest, no one spoke for him
The crowd cried: Release Barabbas!
(Matthew 27:21)
Key points:
1. For three and a half years Jesus healed the sick, set the captives free and preached the gospel of the kingdom.
2. On the night of his arrest not one person stood up to speak for him.
3. Barabbas had committed murder in the insurrection (Mark 15:7), yet the crowd preferred him.
4. Pilate asked again, and they all said: Let him be crucified! (Matthew 27:22).
The prophet saw it long before
“He was despised and rejected by men,
a man of suffering and acquainted with disease.”
(Isaiah 53:3)
Most piercing: “we didn’t respect him”
Key points:
1. Isaiah 53:3 was written more than seven hundred years before the event.
2. “Despised” is the Hebrew nivzeh, from the root bazah, meaning to regard as worthless.
3. Most piercing is “we didn’t respect him” — not “they,” but “we.”
4. John 1:11: he came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.
5. Isaiah 53:7: as a lamb led to the slaughter, so he didn’t open his mouth.
Entrust yourself to the righteous Judge
Exclusion and physical pain share a circuit
(Eisenberger et al., 2003, Science)
Ask only: Is my conscience clear?
From man’s perspective to God’s
Key points:
1. The “Cyberball” experiment by Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams, Science, 2003.
2. When excluded, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex becomes active, sharing circuitry with physical pain: rejection really does hurt.
3. Distinguish the silence of cowardice from the quietness of trust; Romans 12:19, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.”
4. “Conscience” is the Greek syneidēsis, “knowing together”; see 1 Peter 3:16.
5. 321 application: turn from man’s, the earthly and the temporary perspective to God’s, the heavenly and the eternal.
Jesus rejected by his disciples
Judas sold the Lord for thirty pieces of silver
The price of a slave gored by an ox
(Exodus 21:32)
Peter denied him three times
Key points:
1. The deepest wounds often come from those closest to us.
2. Matthew 26:14–15: Judas himself went and asked, “What are you willing to give me?”
3. Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation for a slave gored to death by an ox (Exodus 21:32).
4. Zechariah 11:13 had long foretold this very sum, calling it with irony “the handsome price.”
5. Peter boasted, “Even if I must die with you” (Matthew 26:35), and fell a few hours later.
The Lord came to those behind locked doors
Doors locked, hearts locked too
“Peace be to you.”
Three questions by the fire: Do you love me?
Key points:
1. John 20:19: the doors were locked for fear of the Jews — doors locked, hearts locked too.
2. The Lord’s first words were not a rebuke but “Peace be to you.”
3. The fire of coals in John 21:9 is the Greek anthrakia, found only twice in the New Testament.
4. The other is John 18:18, where Peter stood beside a fire of coals and denied the Lord.
5. The Lord brought Peter back to the scene of his fall and healed him in that very same setting.
Forgiven and entrusted again
“Tend my sheep.”
Unforgiveness raises blood pressure and heart rate
(Witvliet et al., 2001, Psychological Science)
Key points:
1. Three questions answer to three denials; the aim was not to shame him but to restore his calling.
2. Luke 22:32: before the fall, the Lord had already said, “when once you have turned again.”
3. The 2001 Psychological Science study by Witvliet, Worthington and colleagues: unforgiveness raises blood pressure and heart rate.
4. Optionally add Corrie ten Boom’s testimony of forgiving a concentration camp guard in Munich in 1947.

Forsaken for a time by the Father
Darkness over the land, sixth to ninth hour
“My God, my God,
why have you forsaken me?”
(Matthew 27:46)
Key points:
1. Cicero called the Roman cross the most cruel and disgusting penalty; Josephus called it the most wretched of deaths.
2. Matthew 27:45: from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour; the ninth hour is three in the afternoon.
3. The only loud cry among the seven sayings from the cross: the loneliness of separation from the Father, not physical pain.
4. 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Isaiah 53:6: he was made sin on our behalf.

“Forsaken”: egkataleipō
“I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”
(Hebrews 13:5)
“It is finished”: the debt is paid
Key points:
1. “Forsaken” is the Greek egkataleipō, meaning to leave behind, to abandon and leave uncared for.
2. The same word appears in Hebrews 13:5: I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.
3. Scripture interpreting Scripture: he experienced egkataleipō so that we would never experience egkataleipō.
4. “It is finished” is the Greek tetelestai, a perfect tense; Deissmann, studying papyri, found it on receipts meaning “the debt is paid in full.”
5. “My God, my God” comes from Psalm 22:1, a psalm that ends in victory (verse 24).
He understands your loneliness
He was forsaken so we never will be
“Touched with the feeling of our infirmities”
(Hebrews 4:15)
