Key points:
1. Hebrews 4:15: we have a high priest who can be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.
2. Illustration: the best way to show you understand someone’s road is to let them see the mud on your shoes.
3. Frankl, Man’s Search for Meaning: the last of the human freedoms is the freedom to choose one’s attitude.
4. Matthew 28:20: I am with you always, even to the end of the age.
5. 321 application: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not circumstances.
Having power, choosing not to use it
“Do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father,
and he would send more than twelve legions of angels?”
(Matthew 26:53)
He chose to lay down power and to forgive
Key points:
1. Matthew 26:53: a legion was about six thousand men, so twelve legions would be more than seventy thousand angels.
2. It was not that he lacked the power to strike back; he had the power and did not use it.
3. Hebrews 12:2: for the joy set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame.
4. 1 Corinthians 9:12: what Paul laid down was not his responsibility but his right (Greek exousia).
Father, forgive them
“Father, forgive them,
for they don’t know
what they are doing.”
Key points:
1. The prayer in Luke 23:34 is in the imperfect tense: as he was nailed, he kept on asking for forgiveness.
2. Those he asked forgiveness for were the very people nailing him.
3. Compare our three natural reactions when rejected: wanting to prove ourselves, to retaliate, to be understood.
4. Ephesians 4:32: just as God also in Christ forgave you.
Humility is winning over ourselves
Pride: leaving our position, grasping power
Humility: laying down power, returning to our position
Pride provokes pride: both sides lose
Humility draws out humility: both sides win
Key points:
1. 321 core: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place.
2. Contrast Isaiah 14:13, “I will ascend into heaven,” with Philippians 2:7, “emptied himself.”
3. Proverbs 16:18 and 1 Peter 5:5: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.
4. C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity: the essence of pride is comparison.
5. Humility is not losing to others but winning over ourselves: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
Practices 1 and 2
Quietly entrust: pray first, respond later
Choose to forgive: bless the one who hurt you
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction,
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
1. Read out Practices 1 and 2 from the lesson one by one; don’t skip any.
2. Model the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
3. Practice 1 can use a “twenty-four-hour rule”: pray for a day first, then decide whether to respond.
4. Practice 2: change your prayer from “Lord, change him” to “Lord, heal me.”
Practices 3 and 4
Respond with love: reach out to one who ignored you
Examine your conscience: clear before God?
“A conscience void of offense toward God and men”
Key points:
1. Practice 3: take the first step towards the person you have been waiting to speak first.
2. The one who reaches out first is not the loser but the one who is like the Lord (John 20:19).
3. Practice 4: be still for five minutes each night, let the Holy Spirit search you, and write one line in a conscience journal.
4. Harvard Study of Adult Development: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout life is good relationships, not wealth or fame.
321 summary: from self-centred to selfless
Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, glory
“It is no longer I who live”
(Galatians 2:20)
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
3. Galatians 2:20: “no longer I” is selflessness; “Christ lives in me” is the fullness.
4. The 920 practice: everyone we relate to is our “2”; bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.
5. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.
The glory of the cross
Rejected, yet he did not reject people
Humiliated, yet he still honoured others
The way down is the way up
Glory to the Lord who was crucified
Key points:
1. He was rejected by people, yet he did not reject people; he was humiliated, yet he still honoured others.
2. Philippians 2:9–11: therefore God also highly exalted him.
3. Call: learn to love amid rejection, and learn humility amid the loss of respect.
4. Point to the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, I lay down the right to be respected
Not arguing for myself
Asking only that your love be made manifest in me
May all the glory be yours. Amen
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in praying line by line after you; slow your pace.
2. Intercede for three kinds of people: those being misunderstood, those caught in bitterness, those feeling lonely.
3. Close with a blessing: may the Lord’s love be made manifest in us, and may the glory go to him.
4. Optionally preview the next talk: Jesus Our Role Model (Part 5).

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we come together to the fourth talk in the series “Jesus Our Role Model”: laying down the right to be respected. 1 Peter 2:23 says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Can you do that? I can’t. But the Lord Jesus did. This morning, let’s see how he walked this road.

Brothers and sisters, I’d like you first to recall something. The last time you felt that dull heaviness inside, did it have to do with “not being respected”? Perhaps you were cut off before you had finished speaking; perhaps you worked all day and all you got back was, “What’s the big deal?”; perhaps you served for years, yet no one remembered your name. Why does it hurt so much? Because being understood, accepted and appreciated makes us feel that we have worth. Back in 1995 the psychologists Baumeister and Leary showed that belonging is one of our most basic human needs. But brothers and sisters, Jesus pointed to another way.

Brothers and sisters, this letter was written by the apostle Peter, around AD 62 to 64, to believers “living as foreigners” in five provinces of Asia Minor. They were already second-class people, and once they believed, their neighbours slandered them too. Peter says to them, “But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God.” Notice the words “with God.” In man’s eyes, patient endurance is being taken advantage of; with God, patient endurance is commendable. The same thing, two perspectives. And the word for “example” in the original refers to the copybook line a teacher wrote for schoolchildren to trace over. The Lord has written his life on that top line, and the lesson of our whole life is to trace over it.

Brothers and sisters, what did Jesus do in those three and a half years? He healed the sick, set the captives free and preached the gospel of the kingdom of heaven. Yet on the night he was arrested, not one person spoke for him. Pilate asked, “Which one do you want me to release?” They said, “Barabbas!” Who was Barabbas? A thug who had committed murder in the insurrection. At that moment Jesus, who had helped countless people, was treated as worse than a bandit. In fact, more than seven hundred years earlier Isaiah had written: “we didn’t respect him.” And Jesus did not defend himself. Like a lamb led to the slaughter, he didn’t open his mouth.

Brothers and sisters, someone may say: it’s only rejection — grit your teeth and it’ll pass; is it really that serious? In 2003 Eisenberger and her colleagues published a brain-imaging study in the journal Science: when people are excluded, the region of the brain that becomes active runs on the same circuitry as physical pain. So rejection really does hurt. If you feel heavy inside, it is not that you are too fragile. But Jesus’ quietness was not cowardice; it was trust. Scripture says, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.” So when we are misunderstood, we don’t need to rush to prove anything. We need only ask one question: Is my conscience clear before God, before others and before myself?

Brothers and sisters, rejection by the crowds was painful enough, but there is a deeper pain still — the pain that comes from those closest to us. Judas sold the Lord for thirty pieces of silver, the very sum paid in compensation for a slave gored to death by an ox. Peter had said, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you,” yet a few hours later he denied the Lord three times. How did Jesus respond? He did not scold, did not accuse and did not hold a grudge. After his resurrection he went looking for them himself. The doors were locked, and so were their hearts, and the Lord’s first words were not, “Why did you run away?” but “Peace be to you.”

Brothers and sisters, pay attention to that fire of coals by the sea. The word John’s Gospel uses appears only twice in the whole New Testament: once where Peter stood beside a fire of coals and denied the Lord three times, and once here. The Lord deliberately lit the same kind of charcoal fire, bringing Peter back to the scene of his fall in order to heal him. Three questions, answering to three denials. The Lord was not trying to shame him; he wanted to restore his calling: “Tend my sheep.” Did you notice? The Lord first asked, “Do you love me?” and only then said, “Tend my sheep.” This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, on the cross Jesus did not cry out in pain at the scourging, nor weep at the humiliation. His one loud cry was: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” That was not physical pain; it was the loneliness of being cut off from the Father. God made him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, and the Father turned his face away from him. And the word “forsaken” — Hebrews 13 uses the very same word to say to us: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.” Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? He was forsaken so that we would never again be forsaken. So when you feel lonely and forgotten, Jesus understands better than anyone.

Brothers and sisters, it was not that Jesus lacked the power to strike back. He said himself that he could ask the Father to send more than twelve legions of angels. Twelve legions — more than seventy thousand angels. Yet he did not ask. What he said was, “Father, forgive them.” The tense in the original tells us he said it again and again — as the nails came down, he kept on asking forgiveness for those who were nailing him. The 321 vision puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. So humility is not losing to others; it is winning over ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, this lesson gives us four practices. First, quietly entrust: when you are misunderstood, don’t defend yourself first; pray first. You can set yourself a twenty-four-hour rule. Second, choose to forgive: think of someone who has hurt you and bless them specifically. Change your prayer from “Lord, change him” to “Lord, heal me.” Third, respond with love: reach out in care to someone who has ignored you; the one who reaches out first is not the loser but the one who is like the Lord. Fourth, examine your conscience: each night ask yourself, Was I right today before God and before others?

Brothers and sisters, Jesus’ humility was not merely outward gentleness but inner strength. He was rejected by people, yet he did not reject people; he was humiliated, yet he still honoured others. A life like this is the glory of the cross. The Bible says that therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name. Brothers and sisters, the way down is the way up. Let us follow Jesus, learning to love amid rejection and learning humility amid the loss of respect, and let Jesus reign as King in our hearts.

Brothers and sisters, let us pray together. Lord, when I am rejected and misunderstood, help me to remember your example on the cross. I am willing to lay down the right to be respected, not arguing for myself, asking only that your love be made manifest in me. Lord, heal my wounded heart and remove the bitterness within me. I want to be like you — choosing to forgive, choosing to accept, choosing humble obedience. Reign as King in my family, my workplace and my church, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we come together to the fourth talk in the series “Jesus Our Role Model”: laying down the right to be respected. Our theme passage is 1 Peter 2:20–23, and its central sentence is: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Can you do that? Honestly, I can’t; when I am misunderstood, my first reaction is always to explain myself. But the Lord Jesus did it — and not once, but for a whole lifetime.

Brothers and sisters, before we begin, I’d like you to be quiet for thirty seconds and recall one thing: the last time something left you feeling really uncomfortable inside — did it have to do with “not being respected”? Perhaps in a meeting you were cut off before you had finished speaking; perhaps at home you worked all day and all you got back was, “What’s the big deal?”; perhaps you served for years, yet no one remembered your name. That feeling is not necessarily anger. More often it is a dull, unspoken ache. That heaviness — do you know it?

Why does “being respected” tug at us so strongly? Because being understood, accepted and appreciated makes us feel that we have worth and that we are secure. In 1995 the psychologists Baumeister and Leary published “The Need to Belong” in Psychological Bulletin, showing that belonging is one of the most basic human motivations. Leary also offers a picture: self-esteem is like a thermometer, and what it measures is not how good we are, but how far we are accepted by others. That is the truth: our emotions are held hostage by other people’s attitudes, and our worth is priced by other people’s opinions. But Jesus pointed to another way: laying down the right to be respected, and still choosing love. True humility is not being looked down on by others; it is no longer fighting for respect for ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, let’s first look at the scene of this letter. The author is the apostle Peter, writing around AD 62 to 64 to believers living as foreigners scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. “Living as foreigners” in the original means temporary residents without citizenship — they were already second-class people, and once they believed, their neighbours slandered them too. And the first century was an honour and shame culture: face mattered more than property, and not hitting back when insulted was seen as weakness. It was in exactly that atmosphere that Peter said, “But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God.” Notice the words “with God.” In man’s eyes it is being taken advantage of; with God it is commendable. And the word for “example” in the original is the copybook line schoolchildren traced over — the Lord has written his life on the first line, and we trace it.

Brothers and sisters, the first key point: rejected by the crowds, Jesus chose silent obedience. For three and a half years on earth he healed the sick, set the captives free and preached the gospel of the kingdom of heaven. Yet on the night he was arrested, not one person stood up to speak for him. Pilate asked, “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” They said, “Barabbas!” Who was Barabbas? Mark’s Gospel tells us he had committed murder in the insurrection. The crowd would rather have a murderous thug than the Lord who had healed them. Pilate asked again, and they all said, “Let him be crucified!”

Brothers and sisters, this was no accident. More than seven hundred years earlier Isaiah had seen it: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.” The most piercing part is the last line — not “they,” but “we.” John sums it up too: “He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.” And how did Jesus respond? Isaiah had written that down as well: “As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth.” He did not defend himself; he bore the humiliation in silence and let God vindicate him.

Brothers and sisters, someone may say: it’s only rejection — grit your teeth and it’ll pass. Is that really so? In 2003 Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams published a brain-imaging study in the journal Science: when participants were shut out of an online ball-tossing game, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex in their brains became markedly active — the very region that becomes active when the body is in pain. So the pain of being excluded uses the same circuitry as physical pain. If you feel heavy inside, it is not that you are too fragile; and what Jesus bore was real, genuine pain too. He was not numb; he held it in. But his quietness was not cowardice: cowardice is not daring to speak; trust is knowing there is a higher Judge. So Scripture says, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.” When we are misunderstood, we need only ask one question: Is my conscience clear before God, before others and before myself?

Brothers and sisters, the second key point: rejected by his disciples, Jesus still chose to receive and restore them. The deepest wounds often come from those closest to us. Judas went to the chief priests and said, “What are you willing to give me, that I should deliver him to you?” And they weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver. The Old Testament law provided that if an ox gored a servant, thirty shekels of silver were to be paid to the master — the price of a slave’s life. And Peter boasted, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” A few hours later, before the rooster crowed, he denied the Lord three times, and went out and wept bitterly.

Brothers and sisters, if you were Jesus, what would you have done? Most of us would scold them, accuse them, or keep our distance from then on. But Jesus did not scold, did not accuse and did not hold a grudge. After his resurrection he went looking for them himself: on that evening, when the doors were locked where the disciples were, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle and said, “Peace be to you.” The doors were locked, and so were their hearts, and the Lord’s first words were not, “Why did you run away?” Later, by the sea, when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there. Notice that fire of coals — the word John uses appears only twice in the whole New Testament, and the other time is where Peter stood beside a fire of coals and denied the Lord three times. The Lord deliberately lit the same kind of fire, bringing Peter back to the scene of his fall to heal him.

Then the Lord asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Three questions, answering to three denials. Not to shame him, but to restore his calling: “Tend my sheep.” In fact the Lord had said long before, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” The Lord did not start looking for a solution after the fall; before the fall he had already said, “when once you have turned again.” Unforgiveness has a physical cost too. In 2001 Witvliet, Worthington and colleagues published a study in Psychological Science: while imagining unforgiveness, people’s blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension all rose significantly. Holding a grudge is punishing your own body for someone else’s wrong. And the order in which the Lord restored Peter was this: first “Do you love me?”, and only then “Tend my sheep.” This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, the third key point: forsaken for a time by the Father, Jesus still obeyed to the end. The Roman cross was the cruellest punishment of the ancient world; Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty, and Josephus called it the most wretched of deaths. Yet Jesus did not cry out in pain at the scourging, nor weep at the humiliation. His one loud cry on the cross was: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” That was at the ninth hour, three o’clock in the afternoon; before that, from the sixth hour until the ninth, darkness lay over all the land. He did not cry out because of the nails, but because of his separation from the Father. Because the sin of humanity was laid upon him, the fellowship that had been perfectly one from all eternity was veiled. Paul says: God made him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.

Brothers and sisters, there are two key words here. The first is “forsaken,” in the original egkataleipō, meaning to leave behind, to abandon and leave uncared for. Remarkably, the same word appears in Hebrews 13: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.” Do you see it? Jesus experienced being left behind so that we would never again be left behind. The second word is “It is finished,” in the original tetelestai, a perfect tense, meaning it has been completed and its effect continues for ever. The scholar Deissmann found that this word was often written on ancient receipts, meaning: the debt is paid in full. So the Lord’s final declaration was not “I am finished,” but “The debt is paid.” And one more detail: that cry comes from the first verse of Psalm 22, a psalm that ends in victory. His faith never wavered — he still called him “my God.”

Brothers and sisters, there is a very simple comparison: if you want to show someone that you understand the road they have walked, the best way is not to explain how hard that road is, but to let them see the mud on your shoes. A mother who has lost a child does not most need a perfect answer; she needs another mother who has also lost a child, sitting beside her. Hebrews describes our Lord like this: “For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” So when you feel lonely and abandoned, Jesus understands better than anyone. In Man’s Search for Meaning, Frankl recorded what he saw in the concentration camps: everything can be taken from a man but one thing — the freedom to choose his attitude. Brothers and sisters, others can take away your face, but they cannot take away your freedom to choose humility. 321 reminds us: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, the fourth key point: holding to humility amid rejection, laying down the right to be respected. We must see one thing clearly: it was not that Jesus lacked the power to strike back; he had the power and did not use it. When Peter drew his sword, he said, “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” A legion numbered about six thousand men, so twelve legions would be more than seventy thousand angels. He had the power to take revenge, but he did not do it. Hebrews says that for the joy set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame. Despising the shame does not mean it didn’t hurt; it means he saw a greater joy. Paul learned the same lesson: “Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.” What Paul laid down was not his responsibility but his right.

Brothers and sisters, the prayer on the cross was this: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” In the original it is the imperfect tense, showing that he kept on saying it — as the nails were driven in, blow after blow, he asked again and again for forgiveness for those who were nailing him. When we are rejected, our most natural reactions are three: we want to prove ourselves, we want to retaliate, we want to be understood. But at the very moment the Lord had most right to retaliate, he chose to forgive. Paul says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” Our forgiveness is not goodwill squeezed out by force; it flows from the place of having already been forgiven.

Brothers and sisters, 321 puts this very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. This is exactly the picture of the cross. Satan’s way is, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God!”; Christ’s way is that he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” One grasps upward; the other goes downward. And the outcome? “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” In Mere Christianity C. S. Lewis points out that pride is essentially comparative — a person is proud not of having something, but of having more of it than others. So 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, the truth has to walk into daily living. This lesson has four practices, and we deepen them through 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Practice 1, quietly entrust: when you are misunderstood, don’t defend yourself first; pray first. Copy out 1 Peter 2:20–23 once — that is Information; ask the Holy Spirit to show you before whom you most often rush to defend yourself — that is Revelation; acknowledge that “my innocence does not need my own mouth to protect it” — that is Conviction; set a twenty-four-hour rule, praying for a day before you respond — that is Implementation. Practice 2, choose to forgive: think of someone who has hurt you and pray specifically for three good things for them; if your chest still tightens, correct your prayer from “Lord, change him” to “Lord, heal me.”

Practice 3, respond with love: reach out in care to someone who has ignored you. Remember that scene — it was Jesus who took the first step towards that group behind locked doors. So the one who reaches out first is not the loser but the one who is like the Lord. This week, send a greeting or arrange a meal. If they are cold, don’t withdraw your love; just adjust your expectations. Practice 4, examine your conscience: each night set aside five minutes of stillness and ask yourself, Is my conscience clear today before God and before others? Paul says, “In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.” Harvard’s Study of Adult Development has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, and its conclusion is clear: what keeps people healthy and happy is neither wealth nor fame, but good relationships. And good relationships are never sustained by respect we fight for.

Brothers and sisters, let’s place today’s message within the framework of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back; that is our copybook line. The Bible is my standard — when I am rejected, I go not by my feelings but by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — by our own strength we can’t hold out for three days. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — in the moment I am misunderstood, who sits on the throne of my heart? — and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The self-centred life is the root of the fall, and “the right to be respected” is the self-centred life’s most attractive disguise. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” “No longer I” — that is selflessness; “Christ lives in me” — that is the fullness. Here is where the 920 practice comes in: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; live out selflessness before them, and let the Holy Spirit bear his ninefold fruit. The person who rejects you is not your obstacle — he is your orchard.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus’ humility was not merely outward gentleness but inner strength — laying down the right to be respected, and still choosing love and forgiveness. He was rejected by people, yet he did not reject people; he was humiliated, yet he still honoured others. A life like this is the glory of the cross. And the Bible tells us where this road ends: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” The way down turns out in the end to be the way up; the hand that lets go turns out in the end to be the hand that is lifted high. And please remember that gentle reminder: being rejected does not mean you have failed; on the contrary, it is an opportunity to become more like Jesus. Let us follow Jesus, learning to love amid rejection and learning humility amid the loss of respect. Let Jesus be King, and let the glory go to the Lord who was crucified.

Brothers and sisters, let us pray together. Lord, when I am rejected and misunderstood, help me to remember your example on the cross. I am willing to lay down the right to be respected, not arguing for myself, asking only that your love be made manifest in me. Lord, I confess that there is a self in me that longs to be noticed. Deal with my self-centred life through your cross, and live out selflessness in me by your Holy Spirit; heal my wounded heart, and remove the bitterness that has grown in me from not being respected. I want to be like you — choosing to forgive, choosing to accept, choosing humble obedience. Reign as King in my family, my workplace and my church, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Message No One Answered
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we begin with a picture that is very small, and very real.

At half past five in the morning a sister wakes up, reaches for her phone, and sees the message she posted in the group chat last night — a message she wrote three times and deleted twice before she finally sent it. Beside it, the little word “Read.” Beneath it, nothing at all. No one replied. Not a single emoji. The conversation had long since moved on to something else. She lays the phone face down on her chest, and an ache she cannot put into words wells up inside her. “It’s fine,” she tells herself. “Everyone’s busy.” But the ache does not go away just because she said so.

Brothers and sisters, have you had mornings like that? Perhaps it wasn’t a group message. Perhaps it was a dinner you weren’t invited to; a piece of service you prepared for weeks that was passed over with a word; a proposal you thought of first that ended up with someone else’s name on it. These are small things — so small you’re embarrassed to mention them to anyone. Yet pile them up, and they are enough to press a deep, dark dent into a person’s heart.

Why is that? Because inside every one of us lies a very deep longing: to be accepted. To be accepted means I am seen, I matter, I am loved; it means I have a place in this world. In 1995 the psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary put forward their well-known “need to belong” theory. Having reviewed a large body of research, they concluded that forming and keeping stable relationships with others is one of the most fundamental of all human motives. We need more than bread. We need to be accepted.

More startling still: rejection really does hurt. In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman and Kipling Williams of the University of California, Los Angeles, published a study in the journal Science. They had volunteers lie in a functional MRI scanner and play a computer ball-tossing game called “Cyberball.” Partway through, the two other “players” suddenly stopped throwing the ball to them. At the very moment of being left out, a region of the volunteers’ brains called the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex lit up — one of the very regions that responds when the body is in physical pain. So it turns out that, as far as the brain is concerned, being shut out and given the cold shoulder is the same kind of pain as being cut or burned.

So, brothers and sisters, you need not be ashamed of the ache in your heart. It isn’t that you are too fragile. That longing was put there by God when he made us. The problem is not “I long to be accepted.” The problem is this: on whom have I placed that longing? If we lay the weight of that hope on people, then our emotions, our sense of worth and our sense of security become like a boat floating on the clouds, rising and falling with whatever people think of us. Today he praises me, and I soar; tomorrow he ignores me, and I sink. A life spent under the remote control of other people’s expressions is not freedom. It is slavery.

But this morning Jesus wants to remind us of something: true acceptance is not found in people; it is found in him. His love is unconditional. Whether we are good or not, whether we succeed or fail, he accepts us. And he wants us to learn that same acceptance — to accept ourselves, to accept others, and not to be governed by rejection.

That is the lesson before us today. We are learning from Jesus as our role model, learning how he “laid down the right to be respected.” Today we go one step further: when I lay down my right to be respected, what do I fill that space with? The answer is: with Jesus’ unconditional acceptance of me. A person who has already been fully accepted by the Father no longer needs to go begging the world for scraps.

In the 321 vision we say that the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. A self-centred person is bound to live under other people’s gaze, because the “self” needs to be fed, needs to be affirmed, needs to be respected. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Today’s four key points begin with “Jesus accepts me” and travel all the way to “I no longer live on people’s acceptance.” It is a road that sets out from being loved and leads to freedom.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Letter to a Church Whose Members Couldn’t Stand One Another
sections.html:
To grasp the true weight of the word “accept,” we have to go back to the scene behind our key passage.

The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. He is generally thought to have written it between AD 56 and 57, in Corinth in Greece, as his third missionary journey was drawing to a close and he was preparing to take the gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia up to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28). So Romans is a letter of introduction, and also a letter that prepares the way: Paul wants to set out the gospel he preaches, in full, before a group of brothers and sisters he has never met.

The church in Rome, which received the letter, was not founded by Paul. Quite possibly it grew, little by little, out of the “visitors from Rome” (Acts 2:10) who heard the gospel in Jerusalem at Pentecost and went home, together with the merchants, soldiers and servants who came and went through the imperial capital. A church like that has one distinctive feature: it is extremely mixed. There were Jews and there were Gentiles; there were free people and there were slaves; there were those from a synagogue background who took food laws and feast days very seriously, and there were those who had turned to the Lord from idol worship and had no idea such rules even existed.

More important still is a piece of history. The Roman historian Suetonius records that the emperor Claudius ordered the Jews expelled from Rome, and Acts 18:2 mentions the same event — it was because of that decree that Aquila and Priscilla left Italy. Scholars generally date the edict to around AD 49. This means that for several years the church in Rome was left with only Gentile believers; when Claudius died and the Jewish believers gradually returned, the church they came back to was “not quite the same” church.

And so tension arose. Romans 14 speaks of those who are “weak in faith” and those who are “strong,” and this is exactly what it is about: some eat anything, while others eat only vegetables; some esteem one day above another, while others esteem every day alike. How does Paul handle it? He does not begin by ruling who is right and who is wrong. He begins by saying, “God has accepted him” (Romans 14:3). Then in 15:7 he gives that famous command: “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.”

Brothers and sisters, notice how that sentence is built. “Accept one another” is not a moral exhortation to be nice. It has a basis, and it has a goal. The basis is “even as Christ also accepted you.” The goal is “to the glory of God.” This is precisely what 321 calls the Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. I accept you not because you are lovable, but because Christ accepted me first; and I accept you not so that we can look harmonious, but so that the glory goes to God.

The Greek word for “accept” is proslambanō, which literally means “actively to take someone to one’s own side.” It is not passive tolerance; it is reaching out a hand and drawing that person into the circle of one’s own life. Paul uses the same word in Philemon 17: “If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.” Concerning the runaway slave Onesimus, Paul asks Philemon to receive him — not as a slave, but exactly as he would receive Paul himself. That is the force of proslambanō.

As for our key verse, Romans 5:8, it sits at the hinge of the whole letter. In chapters 1 to 3 Paul has shown that “all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23); in chapter 4 he has used Abraham to explain justification by faith; and in chapter 5 he sets out to show what solid ground the justified person now stands on. Romans 5:6 says, “For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.” Verse 8 says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Verse 10 goes further still: “For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see how it deepens, layer upon layer? While we were weak; while we were yet sinners; while we were enemies. God did not wait for us to become good before he loved us. God proved his love at the moment we were least lovable. The word “commends” is sunistēmi in the original, carrying the sense of “to recommend, to establish, to demonstrate to others.” The cross is not a passing mood of God. The cross is a piece of evidence God has set before the whole universe.

So the four key points of this lesson are four streams flowing from the cross: because Jesus accepts me unconditionally, I can accept myself; because I have accepted myself, I can accept others; and because my worth has already been settled in Christ, whether others accept me is no longer the purpose of my life.

sections.heading: 3. Jesus Accepts Me Unconditionally
sections.html:
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)

1. He Doesn’t Love Me Because I’m Good Enough

Brothers and sisters, most of the love in this world comes with conditions. It all follows the same sentence pattern: “If … then I’ll …” If you do as you’re told, I’ll be fond of you; if you get good marks, I’ll be proud of you; if you stop embarrassing me, I’ll accept you one more time.

Jesus’ love doesn’t follow that pattern at all. He never said, “Change first, and then I’ll accept you.” His acceptance flows from grace, not from a trade. The Greek word for grace is charis, and at its heart it means “given freely, with nothing to repay.” If it had to be repaid, it wouldn’t be called grace; it would be called wages. Paul puts it plainly in Romans 4:4: “Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.”

Listen once more to the timing: “while we were yet sinners.” Not after we repented. Not after we had tidied our lives up. God’s love did not wait for our performance; God’s love went first. 1 John 4:19 says, “We love him, because he first loved us.” That little word “first” is the foundation stone of the whole gospel.

2. Scripture Interprets Scripture: A Father Who Ran

The Lord Jesus himself told the most moving of all his parables. In Luke 15 the younger son takes his share of the estate, goes off to a far country, lives recklessly, and squanders everything. When he is at the end of his rope and has rehearsed a confession to take home, Scripture says: “He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20)

Brothers and sisters, notice three details.

First: “while he was still far off, his father saw him.” For the father to see his son while he was still far off means he had been watching every day, waiting every hour. Acceptance is not a sudden softening of the heart; it is a long vigil.

Second: he “ran.” In the culture of the ancient Near East, a man of standing did not run; to run he had to hitch up his robe and bare his legs, which was beneath his dignity. Yet this father ran. Why? Because he wanted to reach his son before the villagers could heap shame on him, and wrap him first in his own embrace. Brothers and sisters, that run is the most beautiful picture of “laying down the right to be respected” — a father laying down his own dignity to restore the dignity of a son.

Third: the father orders the best robe, a ring and sandals to be brought, and the fattened calf to be killed (Luke 15:22–24). The robe is identity; the ring is authority; the sandals are the mark of a free man — servants went barefoot. The father did not put him “on probation as a servant for a while.” In one stroke he restored his full standing as a son. This is the very heart of Jesus: he does not tally up our wrongs; he welcomes our return.

3. What Psychology Confirms — and Where It Stops

The “Cyberball” experiment we mentioned shows that being excluded switches on the brain’s pain circuitry. In 2010 Nathan DeWall of the University of Kentucky and his colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science that went further: volunteers who took acetaminophen, an ordinary painkiller, every day for three weeks reported significantly less daily “social pain” than a control group taking a placebo. Social pain and physical pain really do overlap considerably in their neural mechanisms.

Brothers and sisters, this study shows us the limits of human remedies: a painkiller can dull the feeling of pain, but it cannot deal with the root of the pain. The wound of rejection does not need an anaesthetic; it needs acceptance. In the 1950s and 60s the psychologist Carl Rogers put forward the idea of “unconditional positive regard.” He found that when a person is fully accepted and listened to without being judged, change truly begins to happen. But the unconditional regard people can give is limited; it wears thin; it can be withdrawn. Only the One on the cross offers an acceptance that is infinite and never taken back. Psychology’s observations confirm the need of the human heart; Scripture points to the one supply that meets it.

What does God himself say? “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness.” (Jeremiah 31:3) What does the Lord Jesus say? “He who comes to me I will in no way throw out.” (John 6:37) Brothers and sisters, keep these words in your heart: no matter how others see you, even if the whole world rejects you, Jesus still says, “My child, I accept you.” His love never changes.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: From Man’s Perspective to God’s

321 tells us that change begins with a change of mindset: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The first mindset we most need changed is this: who decides what I am worth?

From man’s perspective, my worth is a share price that floats up and down: affirmed today, it rises; ignored tomorrow, it falls. From God’s perspective, my worth was settled long ago on the cross — Jesus set that price with his own life, and he has paid it in full. From a temporal perspective, one cold remark can ruin my whole day; from an eternal perspective, that remark won’t even last until next year, but God’s love for me will endure for ever.

Brothers and sisters, this is the first of 321’s Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model; and the second — the Bible is my standard. When people’s verdict and the declaration of Scripture collide, I choose to believe Scripture. That isn’t consoling myself. That is putting the standard back in its rightful place.

sections.heading: 4. I Accept Myself Unconditionally
sections.html:
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. (1 John 1:9)

There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. (Romans 8:1)

1. The Hardest Person to Forgive Is Often Yourself

Brothers and sisters, the lesson text says something that cuts close to the bone: very often our greatest enemy is not someone else, but ourselves. We regret our failures, we blame ourselves for our weaknesses, we feel inferior because we compare — and we even find it hard to believe God’s forgiveness.

There was a brother who, many years ago, said harsh words in a quarrel and wounded his family. Afterwards he confessed it, he apologised, and they forgave him. Yet twenty years on, whenever he woke in the middle of the night, those words still played over and over in his head like an echo. He could believe that God had forgiven him; he could not stop condemning himself. Brothers and sisters, do you recognise that struggle?

Henri Nouwen says something very deep in Life of the Beloved. In essence: self-rejection is the greatest enemy of the spiritual life, because it directly contradicts the voice that calls us “the Beloved.” Satan’s favourite move is not to get you to commit a new sin; it is to get you to keep looking back at an old sin that the precious blood has already covered. Accusing is Satan’s trade. Forgiving is Jesus’ work.

2. Scripture Interprets Scripture: What the Blood Has Cleansed, the Conscience Must Not Condemn Again

The lesson text says that “his precious blood has washed away our sins.” Here we should be clear about where each verse comes from. Cleansing by the blood is 1 John 1:7: “the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin.” Being forgiven when we confess is 1 John 1:9: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” The two verses belong together: one gives the foundation, the other the way in.

Notice the words of verse 9: God forgives us not because he is “soft-hearted,” but because he is “faithful” and “righteous.” Faithful, because he will keep what he has said. Righteous, because the price of sin has already been paid in full on the cross; if he demanded payment a second time, that would be unrighteous. Your forgiveness is not built on God’s moods; it is built on God’s character and on the merit of Christ.

Then what about our conscience? 1 John 3:20 says: “if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.” Your heart tells you, “You don’t deserve it.” God says, “I am greater than your heart.” Your heart digs out an old account; God says, “I knew all of it long ago, and I still accept you.”

Next comes the declaration of Romans 8:1: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” The Reformer Martin Luther has an often-quoted Latin phrase, simul justus et peccator, meaning “at the same time righteous and a sinner.” Looked at in myself, I am still weak; looked at in Christ, I have already been declared righteous. Romans 5:1 says, “Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Peace has already been made. So stop living like a wanted fugitive.

3. A Parable and a Study

I often use a picture. A mother puts a height chart on the wall of her child’s room, and every time the child grows a centimetre she draws a line. One day the child falls and hurts himself, gets angry at his own clumsiness, and tears the whole chart off the wall. The mother comes in. She doesn’t scold him. She simply sticks the chart back up and says, “Getting hurt doesn’t mean you haven’t grown.” Brothers and sisters, accepting yourself means not writing off all of God’s work in your life because of one fall. Philippians 1:6 says, “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.”

There is a related piece of psychological research worth mentioning. In 2003 Professor Kristin Neff of the University of Texas at Austin proposed the concept of self-compassion and developed the Self-Compassion Scale, dividing self-compassion into three components: treating yourself with kindness rather than harsh self-criticism; recognising the imperfection common to all humanity; and meeting pain with mindfulness. A large body of research since then has consistently found that people higher in self-compassion experience lower levels of anxiety and depression — and that they do not become self-indulgent or irresponsible as a result.

That answers a common misunderstanding: “Won’t accepting myself turn into indulging myself?” No. Truly accepting yourself does not mean saying “I didn’t do anything wrong.” It means saying, “I was wrong, but I am still under grace.” Condemnation makes people hide; grace makes people return. After Adam sinned he hid among the trees; but Peter, after denying the Lord three times, came back to him on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias. The one who hides is the one who has been condemned; the one who returns is the one who has been accepted.

So when you get it wrong, don’t condemn yourself. Learn to say to yourself: “I am willing to repent, and I am willing to accept myself again.” Because Jesus hasn’t given up on you, and you shouldn’t give up on yourself either.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Selflessness Is Not Self-Contempt

Brothers and sisters, there is a very important distinction to be made here. 321 teaches that “the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.” Does that mean we are to loathe ourselves and run ourselves down? Absolutely not.

The self-centred life puts the self in God’s place: it seizes rights and wants to take God’s place. Selflessness puts the self back in its place as a creature: let God be God and let man be man. So the opposite of selflessness is not low self-esteem; it is pride.

Low self-esteem and pride are really two symptoms of the same disease: both have their focus on the self. Pride says, “I’m better than others.” Low self-esteem says, “I’m worse than others.” Both sentences are comparing, and in both the subject is “I.” 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus truly moves onto Jesus, I no longer need to keep measuring my own height.

Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” The first half says, “no longer I”; the second half says, “Christ lives in me.” Selflessness does not leave behind an empty hole; selflessness lets Christ fill us. It is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

Only those who can accept themselves have the strength to love others. Someone who is fighting a lawsuit against himself in his heart every day has nothing left over to love with. 321 says that the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Only when we are at peace with God can we be at peace with ourselves; only when we are at peace with ourselves can we be at peace with others. That order cannot be skipped.

sections.heading: 5. I Accept Others Unconditionally
sections.html:
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34)

Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God. (Romans 15:7)

1. “As Long as He Changes” — the Invisible Small Print

Brothers and sisters, we often say, “I can accept him — as long as he changes.” Sounds reasonable, doesn’t it? But hidden in that sentence is a piece of small print that turns “acceptance” into a conditional contract. “As long as he changes” means: until he changes, I reserve the right to reject him.

Jesus’ acceptance, though, says, “even though he hasn’t changed yet.” That is the most astonishing thing about the gospel.

Look at the cross. The soldiers have just driven the nails through his wrists; the crowd below is still jeering at him. And at that very moment Scripture records: “Jesus said, ‘Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.’” (Luke 23:34)

Notice the timing: then and there. Not after the wounds had scabbed over. Not after those people had apologised. Then and there, at the moment the wound was freshest and most painful. Jesus’ forgiveness arrived before people’s repentance did.

The original word for “forgive” is aphiēmi, whose basic meaning is “to release, to let go, to let it leave.” The core action of forgiveness is letting go — loosening my grip on the debt I’ve been holding on to. We tend to think forgiveness means “I let him off.” In fact, forgiveness means even more that “I lay down the chain in my hand,” because the other end of that chain has been fastened to my own wrist all along.

Stephen, as he died, followed the same example: “He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, ‘Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!’” (Acts 7:60) Someone who can still pray for people while the stones are crashing down is certainly not running on willpower. He is running on a life that has already been accepted.

2. Scripture Interprets Scripture: The Basis and the Command for Acceptance

Why should I accept others? Scripture gives an answer on three levels.

First, because I was accepted first. “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.” (Romans 15:7) Not because others deserve it, but because we have received grace.

Second, because this is the Lord’s command and promise. “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matthew 6:14) The next verse is even more sobering: “But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” (Matthew 6:15) This does not mean we “buy” God’s forgiveness with our forgiveness. It means that someone who has truly tasted forgiveness cannot turn round and seize his brother by the throat. The Lord Jesus makes this vividly clear in the parable of the unforgiving servant in Matthew 18: a man who has been let off ten thousand talents refuses to let someone else off a hundred denarii — the most absurd contradiction there is. Accepting others is the mark of walking with our heavenly Father.

Third, because this is how a new creation looks at people. Ephesians 4:32 says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.”

Here a boundary also needs to be drawn. Accepting a person unconditionally does not mean unconditionally approving of what he does, nor does it mean letting evil run unchecked. God accepts us, yet he means to change us; the father accepted the prodigal, yet he did not send him back to the pigsty. Acceptance is directed at the person; discipline is directed at the behaviour. We accept a person’s worth while still holding to the standard of truth. This is exactly what 321 teaches: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; life first, then relationships, then ministry.

3. The Weight of Forgiveness: a Physiological Study and a Picture

What price does an unforgiving person pay? In 2001 Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet and her colleagues published a study in Psychological Science. They asked volunteers to recall someone who had genuinely hurt them, and to imagine that person under two different mindsets: “holding a grudge” and “forgiving.” In the grudge-holding state, the volunteers’ heart rate, blood pressure and the electrical activity of the frowning muscles all rose significantly, and their negative feelings were stronger; in the forgiving state, those physiological measures were clearly lower.

Professor Robert Enright of the University of Wisconsin–Madison has been called a pioneer of the psychology of forgiveness. From the late 1980s onward he developed forgiveness therapy, and a number of controlled studies have shown that groups receiving forgiveness therapy improved significantly in anxiety, depression and anger.

Brothers and sisters, refusing to forgive is like gripping a red-hot coal in your hand, ready to hurl it at the person who hurt you. You’re waiting for the right moment to throw it — and all the while you wait, the palm being burned is your own.

Unconditional acceptance is not only an act of love; it is even more an expression of humility. When we lay down the pride of “I’m right and you’re wrong,” we can embrace people’s hearts with gentle love, just as Jesus did. 321 puts it well: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: the 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

Brothers and sisters, accepting others cannot stop at being moved; it has to come down to practice.

This is how 321 describes the 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of each “2” we practise living out the “0” life of selflessness, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice this: the person you find hardest to accept is exactly the “2” God has given you. The co-worker who always interrupts you, the family member who always has an opinion, the friend who once hurt you — they are not your obstacle; they are your training ground. Without them, how would patience ever bear fruit? And to whom would gentleness ever be shown?

And the “0” is the key. If I am still self-centred, I will have only one reaction in front of that person: defence. The self-centred person only calculates, “Have I been respected?” Only the selfless person can simply ask, “Lord, what do you want me to do in this person’s life?”

Next come 235 relationships. From among selfless people God will prepare a “2” for you — a spiritual companion; then build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally form a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Healthy spiritual relationships grow out of selflessness; put a group of self-centred people together and you don’t get a team, you get a battlefield. Dietrich Bonhoeffer warns us in Life Together that whoever loves his dream of community more than the actual community in front of him will end up destroying that community.

When we choose to accept others and stop demanding that they change first, we become a channel through which grace flows. A channel’s value lies not in how much water it holds, but in not being blocked.

sections.heading: 6. Others Accepting Me: God’s Fruit, Not Our Aim
sections.html:
For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ. (Galatians 1:10)

1. Fruit and Aim: One Step Apart, a Whole Road Apart

Brothers and sisters, this is the point in today’s lesson that most needs careful discernment, so please pay special attention.

When we are willing to live out unconditional acceptance, others will be touched by our lives too. Love can melt coldness; grace can mend relationships. That is true. But — it does not mean that everyone will accept us straight away.

So the lesson text gives this point a very precise title: others accepting me is God’s fruit, not our aim.

Fruit is what grows naturally when you walk the right road; an aim is the target my heart is fixed on. The two are only one step apart, and yet a whole road apart.

If “being accepted by people” becomes my aim, my love goes sour: I’m kind to people so that they’ll be kind to me; I serve so that I’ll be noticed; I forgive so that I’ll earn a good name. And as soon as the other person doesn’t respond, I’m hurt, disappointed, I pull back — I may even doubt God. Brothers and sisters, love like that is still self-centred love; it is just wrapped in more spiritual packaging.

But if “being accepted by people” is only a fruit, then I am free. If he accepts me, I give thanks; if he doesn’t, I go on loving all the same. Because from the very start I was never trying to buy his acceptance.

2. Scripture Interprets Scripture: How the Apostles Lived

The apostles of the early church give us the best demonstration. As they preached they were often persecuted, misunderstood and reviled, yet they were not ashamed, because what they pursued was not people’s acceptance but the Lord’s pleasure. Paul says: “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” (Galatians 1:10) And in 1 Thessalonians 2:4 he says again: “But even as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Good News, so we speak: not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts.”

This was even more true of our Lord himself. More than seven hundred years beforehand, Isaiah prophesied: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.” (Isaiah 53:3) John 1:11 says, “He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.” 1 Peter 2:23 describes his response: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.”

Brothers and sisters, look at that last phrase — “committed himself to him who judges righteously.” Jesus could refrain from answering back, not because he didn’t care, but because he had handed the “right to judge” back to the Father. When a person hands over the right to judge, he no longer has to defend himself; when a person keeps the right to judge in his own hands, he spends his whole life in court.

The Lord Jesus also warned against the kind of religious life held captive by people’s eyes: “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.” (John 12:43) Proverbs 29:25 goes straight to the point: “The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in Yahweh is kept safe.”

3. The Snare of Conformity: a Classic Experiment

In the early 1950s the psychologist Solomon Asch carried out a famous series of conformity experiments. He asked volunteers to judge which of three comparison lines was the same length as a standard line — a judgement so simple that, answering alone, people got it wrong less than one per cent of the time. But when the other “volunteers” in the room (who were in fact all research assistants) unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer, about three-quarters of the real volunteers went along with the wrong answer at least once.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: over something as objective and as trivial as the length of a line, people will go against their own eyes so as not to be left out. Then where truth is at stake, where there are things that need to be said — how far will the pressure of people push us?

This is the snare Proverbs speaks of. There is only one way to break the net: move your eyes off people’s faces and set them before God. 1 Samuel 16:7 says, “for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” There is only one scorecard that truly counts, and it is in God’s hands.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Not Living for People’s Reactions

Brothers and sisters, 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

What does it mean to “rely on the brain and ourselves”? It means running through it in your mind all day long: What did he mean by what he just said? Why hasn’t he answered my message? What should I do to win back his good opinion? Spend a whole day doing that, and it would be a wonder if you weren’t troubled. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

What does it mean to “rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit”? It means taking that person, that matter, that remark, and handing it over to the Lord on the spot: “Lord, your view is the final view.” This is the third foundation — the Holy Spirit is my guide.

We accept others not to get their acceptance in exchange, but to respond to Jesus’ love. We do not live for people’s reactions; we live for God’s heart. When we are no longer held captive by people’s eyes, we can truly live in love and freedom.

And this is the real meaning of “laying down the right to be respected.” Laying it down is not degrading yourself, nor letting people trample on you. Laying it down means no longer making “I must be respected” the condition for living. I still have dignity — but my dignity is not given by people; it is given by God, and so no one can take it away.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision: From Being Accepted, to Selflessness, to Glory to God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s step back and look at this lesson once more within the whole picture of 321.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he was despised yet still embraced, rejected yet never stopped loving. The Bible is my standard — when my feelings say “I don’t deserve it,” Romans 8:1 says “no condemnation”; when people’s verdict says “you’re worthless,” Romans 5:8 says “Christ died for us.” The Holy Spirit is my guide — accepting myself, accepting others, living without depending on people’s acceptance: not one of these can be done by willpower. Only the Holy Spirit can pour God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

Second, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: when I am still haggling over “who ought to apologise first,” it is really I who am being king; when I am willing to let go first and accept first, I am letting Jesus reign as King. Let Jesus receive all the glory: the command of Romans 15:7 ends with exactly these words — “to the glory of God.” The end point of acceptance is not harmony between people; it is God being glorified.

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system runs on power — whoever is strongest does the talking. God’s system runs on grace — whoever loves stoops down. If the Jewish and Gentile believers in the church at Rome had not accepted one another, the gospel in that city would have been nothing but theory. It is the same today.

Fourth, the self-centred life and selflessness. A self-centred person must be respected, because the “self” lives on applause; a selfless person doesn’t need it, because he has already been filled in Christ. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When I say, “He has to change first before I’ll accept him,” I am sitting in the judge’s seat; when I let go, I return to my originally intended position. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Fifth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. A change of mindset: my worth is not decided by people’s acceptance but by the cross. A change of life: I no longer need to be on the defensive; rest begins to grow within me. A change of daily living: when I wake up in the morning I’m no longer in a hurry to see whether anyone has answered my message. A change of relationships: I can take the initiative to love that difficult person. A change of ministry: my service is no longer about being seen, but about Jesus being seen. And the order cannot be reversed — life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Sixth, the four shifts of perspective. From man’s to God’s: no longer asking “How do others see me?” but “How does God see me?” From the earthly to the heavenly: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) From the temporal to the eternal: a hurtful remark is temporary; God’s love is for ever. From the worldly to the godly: worldly acceptance has conditions; godly acceptance is grace.

Seventh, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit leads me to see my own self-centredness; Scripture enlightens me to understand what true acceptance is; and so my life is renewed, and in my service I can let Jesus reign as King and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Eighth, the 920 practice and 235 relationships. The training ground for this lesson is every person you will meet today. Everyone is your “2”; every time you are misunderstood is a chance to practise the “0”; every time you choose to accept, a fruit of the Spirit is growing. When a group of people who are also practising selflessness gathers around you, God’s system is being established in your home, your small group and your workplace.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Walking Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson text gives us four practices for daily living. 321 tells us that changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Let’s now walk each practice through those eight stages.

Practice 1: Quiet meditation — spend five minutes each day sensing Jesus’ unconditional love for you

Information: first let the truth in — memorise Romans 5:8.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this verse from your head down into your heart. When one day you are reading it and suddenly your eyes fill with tears, that is revelation arriving.

Conviction: declare to yourself — my worth is not my performance; it is the cross.

Implementation: five minutes every morning — asking for nothing, arguing for nothing, simply being still before the Lord and letting him love you.

Evaluation: after a week, ask yourself: have these five minutes changed the way I see myself?

Correction: if your phone keeps interrupting those five minutes, put it in another room.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row. A mindset isn’t changed by hearing something once; it is changed by repetition.

Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to do it with you, and report to each other.

Practice 2: Accept yourself — when you get it wrong, don’t condemn yourself; instead pray, “Lord, you still love me”

Information: remember 1 John 1:9 and Romans 8:1.

Revelation: ask the Lord to shine his light on the root behind your self-condemnation — is it pride demanding that you be perfect, or are you afraid to believe in grace?

Conviction: “confessing sin” and “blaming yourself” are two different things. Confession hands sin over to God; self-blame clutches it to your chest.

Implementation: the next time you get it wrong, let your first words not be “How can I be so awful?” but “Lord, I was wrong; please forgive me. You still love me.”

Evaluation: in the evening, look back: were the words I spoke to myself today words of accusation or words of grace?

Correction: write down the accusation that replays most often in your heart, and beside it write a verse of Scripture that answers it.

Repetition: stick that sheet of paper somewhere you can see it, and read it every day.

Multiplication: when someone near you is caught up in self-blame, share with them the grace you have experienced.

Practice 3: Accept others — take the initiative to show kindness or a blessing to someone you find hard to get along with

Information: read Romans 15:7 and Ephesians 4:32.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you see the hurt behind that person’s weakness, and also to see the pride of “I’m right and you’re wrong” in your own heart.

Conviction: I accept him not because he deserves it, but because I have received grace.

Implementation: pray for him today, and do one specific small thing: a message asking how he is, or a greeting you offer first.

Evaluation: as I did this, was my heart waiting for his response, or simply giving?

Correction: if you find you are waiting for something in return, come back before the Lord and readjust your motives.

Repetition: keep it up for four weeks, and don’t stop just because he doesn’t respond.

Multiplication: share the journey of this practice in your small group, so that others find the courage to love someone hard to love.

Practice 4: Release control — no longer let other people’s reactions decide your worth; seek the Lord’s pleasure alone

Information: memorise Galatians 1:10.

Revelation: ask the Lord to point out the one person whose opinion of you matters most to you, and ask yourself: have I put him in God’s place?

Conviction: I have only one Judge, and he has already pronounced me not guilty at the cross.

Implementation: once this week, when you badly want to defend yourself, choose to be quiet and entrust the matter to the Lord.

Evaluation: after being quiet, is my heart more at peace, or more churned up? If more churned up, it means I have only suppressed it and haven’t truly entrusted it yet.

Correction: whatever you are still clinging to, hand it over piece by piece in prayer.

Repetition: treat every misunderstanding as a practice session, not as an accident.

Multiplication: take along a brother or sister who is often held captive by people’s eyes, and walk this road to freedom together.

sections.heading: 9. A Gentle Reminder and Closing Word: True Honour
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson text contains a gentle reminder that I want to say once more: rejection is not the end of the world; it is the starting point for coming to know God’s love afresh. When you no longer live by people’s verdicts, you will discover that the deepest acceptance has been in Jesus all along.

When we are rejected, we usually ask only, “Where am I not good enough?” But perhaps, through that closed door, God is asking us a different question: “My child, if no one were applauding you, would you still be willing to live for me?”

C. S. Lewis says something unforgettable in The Four Loves: to love at all is to be vulnerable; a heart that wants never to be hurt has to lock itself away, and in the end it becomes hard and impenetrable. Brothers and sisters, Jesus chose to be vulnerable. He knew his own would not receive him, and still he came.

Our Lord was rejected by people, yet he never stopped loving; he was despised, yet he was still willing to embrace. His life tells us that true honour lies not in being respected, but in choosing to love all the same. The world thinks honour means “standing higher than others”; Jesus shows us that honour means “being willing to bend lower than others.” Though he existed in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped; instead he emptied himself, took the form of a servant and was made in human likeness; and being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death — even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). Then verse 9 says, “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” Brothers and sisters, see this heavenly order: whoever goes down, God lifts up; whoever denies himself, God causes to receive.

So when we learn to lay down the right to be respected, we gain the deepest freedom there is in Jesus — a life that sets out from being loved, is not shaken by rejection, and lives only to glorify God.

This morning, let’s make this decision in our hearts. Let Jesus be King: no longer letting people’s verdicts be king, no longer letting past failures be king, no longer letting the “self” that must be respected be king in my heart. Let Jesus receive all the glory: I accept myself, because his precious blood is worth it; I accept others, because his acceptance is worthy of praise; I no longer live for applause, because all glory belonged to him in the first place.

The Lord Jesus says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:28–29) Brothers and sisters, the heavy burden of trying to win people’s acceptance can be laid down today. Come to him, learn from him, and your soul will find rest.
