prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We bow before you. You died for us while we were yet sinners; your love was shown to us on the cross. Lord, we so often forget, and so day after day we go begging people for the acceptance you have long since given us freely. Please forgive us.
Lord, please heal the wounds of rejection inside us, and with your word replace “I don’t deserve it” with “no condemnation.” Help us to stop condemning ourselves, and to stop condemning others.
Lord, we place in your hands the debts we have been clutching in our hearts. Give us the grace to let go, so that like you, while the wound is still fresh, we can say: Father, forgive them.

Lord, please remove the self-centred life within us, so that before every person you place in our path we may live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit — not living for people’s reactions, but for your heart alone.
Lord, reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord’s acceptance be our strength for the day, and may the Lord’s love be the worth of our whole life.
discussion: Romans 5:8 says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Is there something in your life that you still find hard to forgive yourself for, even today? If God accepted you “while you were yet a sinner,” what would he say to you today? Write that sentence down and read it aloud in your small group.

Romans 15:7 says, “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.” Think of someone you have quietly attached small print to in your heart: “As long as he changes, I’ll accept him.” This week, what one small thing are you willing to do for him that sets that small print aside? Say it out loud, and ask your small group to check on your progress in four weeks’ time.

blog.title: The Message That Was Read but Never Answered

blocks.x: Only When You No Longer Need Other People’s Acceptance Are You Truly Free

At half past five in the morning she wakes up and reaches for her phone. Beside the message she posted in the group chat last night is the little word “Read.” Beneath it, nothing at all. No one replied; the conversation had long since moved on to something else.
“It’s fine,” she tells herself. “Everyone’s busy.” But the ache inside does not go away just because she said so.

Have you had mornings like that? Perhaps it wasn’t a message. Perhaps it was a dinner you weren’t invited to; a piece of service you prepared for weeks that was passed over with a word; a proposal you thought of first that ended up with someone else’s name on it.
Rejection Really Does Hurt

It isn’t that you are too fragile. In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman and Kipling Williams of the University of California, Los Angeles, published a study in the journal Science: at the very moment volunteers were left out of a computer ball-tossing game, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex in their brains lit up — one of the very regions that responds when the body is in physical pain.
So it turns out that, as far as the brain is concerned, being given the cold shoulder is the same kind of pain as being burned.

In 1995 the psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary also showed that forming and keeping stable relationships with others is one of the most fundamental of all human motives. We need more than bread. We need to be accepted.
So the problem has never been “I long to be accepted.” The problem is this: on whom have I placed that longing?

If we place it on people, our sense of worth becomes like a boat floating on the clouds: today he praises me, and I soar; tomorrow he ignores me, and I sink. A life spent under the remote control of other people’s expressions is not freedom. It is slavery.
There Is an Acceptance That Doesn’t Wait for You to Get Better First
The Bible says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
Look at the timing — not after we repented, not after we had tidied our lives up, but “while we were yet sinners.”

On the day the prodigal came home, his father did something that in that culture was quite undignified: he ran. In the ancient Near East a man of standing did not run. Yet he wanted to reach his son before the villagers could heap shame on him, and wrap him first in his own embrace.
That run is the gospel. A father laid down his own dignity to restore the dignity of a son.
Three Turnings

The first turning: accept yourself. Very often our greatest enemy is not someone else, but ourselves. Yet the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), and “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Confessing sin is not blaming yourself — confession hands sin over to God; self-blame clutches it to your chest.

The second turning: accept others. We often say, “I can accept him — as long as he changes.” But at the very moment the nails had just been driven through his wrists, Jesus said, “Father, forgive them.” Refusing to forgive is like gripping a red-hot coal, ready to hurl it at someone else — and all the while, the palm being burned is your own.

The third turning: stop making “being accepted by people” your aim. Others accepting me is God’s fruit, not the purpose of my life. If he accepts me, I give thanks; if he doesn’t, I go on loving all the same.
True Honour

In the 321 vision, a self-centred person must be respected, because the “self” lives on applause; a selfless person doesn’t need it, because he has already been filled in Christ. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Jesus was rejected by people, yet he never stopped loving; he was despised, yet he was still willing to embrace. He shows us that true honour lies not in being respected, but in choosing to love all the same.

Rejection is not the end of the world; it is the starting point for coming to know God’s love afresh. When you no longer live by people’s verdicts, you will discover that the deepest acceptance has been in Jesus all along.
A Question for Reflection

This week, who is the person you have quietly attached the small print to — “as long as he changes, I’ll accept him”? What is one small thing you are willing to do for him, setting the small print aside?

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to look at “Unconditional Acceptance.” This is the fourth lesson in the series “Jesus Our Role Model,” on laying down the right to be respected. Our theme verse is Romans 5:8: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Please hold this verse in your heart; today we are going to walk into it together.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you a question first. Have you had a morning like this? You wake up, reach for your phone, and see the message you sent last night. Beside it, the word “Read.” Beneath it, nothing at all. You tell yourself, “It’s fine, everyone’s busy.” But the ache inside does not go away.

Why is that? Because inside every one of us lies a very deep longing: to be accepted. Rejection really does hurt. In 2003 a research team at the University of California, Los Angeles, published a study in the journal Science: at the moment people were left out of a game, the pain region of their brains really did light up.

So you need not be ashamed of the ache in your heart. The problem is not “I long to be accepted.” The problem is this: on whom have I placed that longing? If we place it on people, we are like a boat floating on the clouds, rising and falling with their verdicts. Brothers and sisters, true acceptance is not found in people; it is found in him.

Let’s look first at the background. The apostle Paul wrote Romans around AD 57, in Corinth. The church in Rome that received it had Jewish believers and Gentile believers. Because the emperor Claudius had once expelled the Jews from Rome, by the time they came back the church was no longer the same. And so tension arose: some ate anything, while others ate only vegetables.

What did Paul say? In Romans 15:7 he gave a command: “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.” Brothers and sisters, acceptance has a basis — even as Christ accepted us; and acceptance has a goal — to the glory of God.
The first key point: Jesus accepts me unconditionally.

The love of this world so often follows the pattern “If … then I’ll …” If you do as you’re told, I’ll be fond of you; if you stop embarrassing me, I’ll accept you one more time. But Jesus never said, “Change first, and then I’ll accept you.” He died for us while we were yet sinners.

When the prodigal came home, “while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck.” In that era a man of standing did not run. Yet this father ran — he laid down his own dignity to restore the dignity of his son. Brothers and sisters, this is the very heart of Jesus.
The second key point: I accept myself unconditionally.
Very often our greatest enemy is not someone else, but ourselves. We regret our failures, we blame ourselves for our weaknesses, and we even find it hard to believe God’s forgiveness.

But listen carefully: the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, has cleansed us from all sin — that is 1 John 1:7; if we confess our sins, God will forgive us — that is verse 9. Romans 8:1 says, “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.”

Confessing sin is not blaming yourself. Confession hands sin over to God; self-blame clutches it to your chest. Brothers and sisters, Jesus hasn’t given up on you, and you shouldn’t give up on yourself either.
The third key point: I accept others unconditionally.
We often say, “I can accept him — as long as he changes.” But Jesus’ acceptance says, “even though he hasn’t changed yet.”

On the cross, the nails had only just been driven into his hands, and he said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” It happened then and there — not after the others had apologised, but at the moment the wound hurt most. Brothers and sisters, Jesus’ forgiveness arrived before people’s repentance did.
Accepting others is not only an act of love; it is even more an expression of humility.

The original word for “forgive” means to let go, to release. We think forgiveness means letting him off; in fact, forgiveness means laying down the chain in my hand, because the other end of that chain has been fastened to my own wrist all along.

Psychological research has found that when people hold a grudge, their heart rate and blood pressure rise markedly. Refusing to forgive is like gripping a red-hot coal, ready to hurl it at someone else — and all the while, the palm being burned is your own.
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
The fourth key point: others accepting me is God’s fruit, not man’s aim.
When we are willing to accept, love really can melt coldness. But that does not mean everyone will accept us straight away.

As the apostles preached, they were often persecuted and misunderstood, yet they were not ashamed. Paul says, “For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” Brothers and sisters, if being accepted by people becomes my aim, my love goes sour; if it is only a fruit, then I am free. If he accepts me, I give thanks; if he doesn’t, I go on loving all the same.
Brothers and sisters, let’s place this lesson within 321.

A self-centred person must be respected, because the “self” lives on applause; a selfless person doesn’t need it, because he has already been filled in Christ. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The 920 practice is this: everyone I relate to is my “2.” The person you find hardest to accept is exactly the training ground God has given you. Live out the “0” life before them, and you will bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.
Next come this week’s practices — four in all.
First, quiet meditation: five minutes each day, asking for nothing, simply letting the Lord love you.
Second, accept yourself: when you get it wrong, don’t condemn yourself; instead pray, “Lord, you still love me.”
Third, accept others: take the initiative to show kindness to someone you find hard to get along with.
Fourth, release control: no longer let other people’s reactions decide your worth.
Brothers and sisters, a mindset only changes through repetition. Please take these four practices home and keep them up for four full weeks.

Brothers and sisters, our Lord was rejected by people, yet he never stopped loving; he was despised, yet he was still willing to embrace. His life tells us that true honour lies not in being respected, but in choosing to love all the same.

The world thinks honour means standing higher than others; Jesus shows us that honour means being willing to bend lower than others. When we learn to lay down the right to be respected, we gain the deepest freedom there is in the Lord.
This morning, let Jesus be King, and let all the glory go to him.
Let us pray together.

Lord, thank you for your unconditional love and acceptance. I will no longer seek people’s approval; I will find my worth in your love. Please heal the wounds of rejection within me, and give me the grace to let go. I am willing to accept myself and to accept others, and willing to lay down the right to be respected, so that my life may glorify you alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord’s acceptance be our strength for the day, and may the Lord’s love be the worth of our whole life. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you.

Brothers and sisters, have you had mornings like that?

Rejection really does hurt. In 2003 Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams of the University of California, Los Angeles, published a study in the journal Science: at the very moment volunteers were left out of a ball-tossing game, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex in their brains became markedly active — one of the very regions that responds when the body is in physical pain.
Why is that? Because inside every one of us lies a very deep longing: to be accepted.

In 1995 the psychologists Baumeister and Leary put forward their “need to belong” theory: forming and keeping stable relationships with others is one of the most fundamental of all human motives. We need more than bread. We need to be accepted.

So you need not be ashamed of the ache in your heart. The problem is not “I long to be accepted.” The problem is this: on whom have I placed that longing? If we place it on people, we are like a boat floating on the clouds, rising and falling with their verdicts.
Brothers and sisters, Jesus reminds us: true acceptance is not found in people; it is found in him.
Let’s look first at the background.

The apostle Paul wrote Romans between AD 56 and 57, in Corinth. The church in Rome was not founded by him; it had Jews in it, and Gentiles too. The emperor Claudius had once ordered the Jews expelled from Rome, and by the time they came back, the church was very different.

And so tension arose: some ate anything, while others ate only vegetables. Paul did not begin by ruling who was right and who was wrong. He said, “God has accepted him.” Then in 15:7 he commanded them to accept one another.

Brothers and sisters, acceptance has a basis — even as Christ accepted us; and acceptance has a goal — to the glory of God. The Greek word for “accept” means actively to take someone to one’s own side.
The first key point: Jesus accepts me unconditionally.
Most of the love in this world follows one sentence pattern: “If … then I’ll …” If you do as you’re told, I’ll be fond of you; if you stop embarrassing me, I’ll accept you one more time.
But Jesus never said, “Change first, and then I’ll accept you.” His acceptance flows from grace, not from a trade. The Greek word for grace, charis, means given freely, with nothing to repay.

Listen once more to the timing: “while we were yet sinners.” Not after we repented. Not after we had tidied our lives up. God’s love went first. 1 John 4:19 says, “We love him, because he first loved us.”
The Lord Jesus told the most moving of all his parables.

When the prodigal, at the end of his rope, set out for home, Scripture says: “But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”

Notice three things. First, he saw him while he was still far off — which means he had been watching every day, waiting every hour. Acceptance is not a sudden softening of the heart; it is a long vigil.

Second, he “ran.” In the ancient Near East a man of standing did not run; to run he had to hitch up his robe, which was beneath his dignity. Yet this father ran. That run is the most beautiful picture of “laying down the right to be respected.”
Third, the robe is identity, the ring is authority, and the sandals are the mark of a free man; in one stroke the father restored his son’s full standing as a son.
Brothers and sisters, 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.
The first mindset we most need changed is this: who decides what I am worth?

From man’s perspective, my worth is a share price that floats up and down: affirmed today, it rises; ignored tomorrow, it falls. From God’s perspective, my worth was settled long ago on the cross — Jesus set that price with his own life, and he has paid it in full.
So the Bible is my standard, not my feelings. The Lord says, “He who comes to me I will in no way throw out.” Even if the whole world rejects you, Jesus still says, “My child, I accept you.”
The second key point: I accept myself unconditionally.
The lesson text says something that cuts close to the bone: very often our greatest enemy is not someone else, but ourselves.

There was a brother who, many years ago, said harsh words and wounded his family. He confessed it, and they forgave him. Yet twenty years on, those words still played over and over in his head like an echo. He could believe that God had forgiven him; he could not stop condemning himself. Brothers and sisters, do you recognise that struggle?

Henri Nouwen says something very deep, in essence: self-rejection is the greatest enemy of the spiritual life. Satan’s favourite move is not to get you to commit a new sin; it is to get you to look back at an old sin that the precious blood has already covered.
Accusing is Satan’s trade; forgiving is Jesus’ work.
So what does Scripture say?

Cleansing by the blood is 1 John 1:7: “the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin.” Being forgiven when we confess is verse 9: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins.”
Notice: God forgives us not because he is soft-hearted, but because he is faithful and righteous. Your forgiveness is not built on God’s moods; it is built on the merit of Christ.

Then what about our conscience? 1 John 3:20 says, “God is greater than our heart.” Your heart tells you, “You don’t deserve it.” God says, “I am greater than your heart.” Romans 8:1 declares: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Here we need to make an important distinction. When 321 teaches that “the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless,” does that mean we are to loathe ourselves? Absolutely not.

The self-centred life puts the self in God’s place; selflessness puts the self back in its place as a creature — let God be God and let man be man. So the opposite of selflessness is not low self-esteem; it is pride.

Low self-esteem and pride are two symptoms of the same disease: both have their focus on the self. Galatians 2:20 says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness does not leave behind an empty hole; selflessness lets Christ fill us.
Brothers and sisters, only those who can accept themselves have the strength to love others.
The third key point: I accept others unconditionally.
We often say, “I can accept him — as long as he changes.” But hidden in that sentence is a piece of small print: until he changes, I reserve the right to reject him.
Jesus’ acceptance, though, says, “even though he hasn’t changed yet.”

The soldiers had just driven the nails through his wrists; the crowd below was still jeering at him. And Scripture records: “Jesus said, ‘Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.’”
Notice the timing: then and there. Not after the others had apologised, but at the moment it hurt most. Jesus’ forgiveness arrived before people’s repentance did.
The original word for “forgive” means to release, to let go. The core action of forgiveness is letting go — loosening my grip on the debt I’ve been holding on to.
Why should I accept others? Scripture gives three answers.
First, because I was accepted first. “Accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you.” Not because others deserve it, but because we have received grace.

Second, because this is the Lord’s command. “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” A man who has been let off ten thousand talents refusing to let someone else off a hundred denarii — that is the most absurd contradiction there is.
Third, because this is how a new creation looks at people: being kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other.
A boundary needs to be drawn too: accepting a person does not mean approving what he does. The father accepted the prodigal, yet he did not send him back to the pigsty.
What price does an unforgiving person pay?

In 2001 Witvliet and her colleagues published a study in Psychological Science: as volunteers recalled someone who had hurt them, in the grudge-holding state their heart rate, blood pressure and the activity of the frowning muscles all rose significantly; in the forgiving state they were clearly lower.

Brothers and sisters, refusing to forgive is like gripping a red-hot coal, ready to hurl it at someone else. You’re waiting for the right moment to throw it — and all the while, the palm being burned is your own.

321’s 920 practice says: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” The person you find hardest to accept is exactly the training ground God has given you. Practise the “0” life before them, and you will bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.
The fourth key point: others accepting me is God’s fruit, not man’s aim.
When we are willing to accept, love really can melt coldness. But that does not mean everyone will accept us straight away.
A fruit is what grows naturally when you walk the right road; an aim is the target my heart is fixed on. The two are only one step apart, and yet a whole road apart.

If being accepted by people becomes my aim, my love goes sour: I’m kind to people so that they’ll be kind to me; I serve so that I’ll be noticed. That is still self-centred love; it is just wrapped in more spiritual packaging.
But if it is only a fruit, then I am free. If he accepts me, I give thanks; if he doesn’t, I go on loving all the same.

The apostles of the early church give us the best demonstration. They were often persecuted and reviled, yet they were not ashamed, because what they pursued was not people’s acceptance but the Lord’s pleasure.
Paul says, “Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.”

This was even more true of our Lord. Isaiah 53:3 says, “He was despised and rejected by men.” 1 Peter 2:23 says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.”
Brothers and sisters, Jesus could refrain from answering back, not because he didn’t care, but because he had handed the right to judge back to God the Father.
Proverbs 29:25 says, “The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in Yahweh is kept safe.”

How real is that snare? In the early 1950s the psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his conformity experiments. Judging which lines were the same length was so simple that, answering alone, people got it wrong less than one per cent of the time; yet when everyone else gave the same wrong answer, about three-quarters of the real volunteers went along with it at least once.
Over the length of a line, people will go against their own eyes so as not to be left out. Then what about where truth is at stake?

321 says: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Laying down the right to be respected is not letting people trample on you; it is no longer making “I must be respected” the condition for living.
Next come this week’s practices. 321 says that changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1, quiet meditation. Memorise Romans 5:8, and ask the Holy Spirit to carry it from your head down into your heart. Five minutes every morning — asking for nothing, simply letting the Lord love you. Keep it up for forty days in a row — a mindset isn’t changed by hearing something once; it is changed by repetition.

Practice 2, accept yourself. The next time you get it wrong, let your first words not be “How can I be so awful?” but “Lord, I was wrong; please forgive me. You still love me.” In the evening, look back: were the words I spoke to myself today words of accusation, or words of grace?

Practice 3, accept others. Take the initiative to show kindness to someone you find hard to get along with. Pray for them today, and do one specific small thing. Then evaluate: am I waiting for their response, or simply giving? Keep it up for four weeks, and don’t stop just because they don’t respond.

Practice 4, release control. Ask the Lord to point out the one person whose opinion of you matters most to you, and ask yourself: have I put him in God’s place? Once this week, when you badly want to defend yourself, choose to be quiet and entrust the matter to the Lord.
Brothers and sisters, the last stage is multiplication. Take along a brother or sister who is often held captive by people’s eyes, and walk this road to freedom together.
Let’s place this lesson within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he was despised yet still embraced; the Bible is my standard — when my feelings say “I don’t deserve it,” Scripture says “no condemnation”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — acceptance cannot be done by willpower.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — when I am haggling over who ought to apologise first, it is really I who am being king; let Jesus receive all the glory — that command ends with exactly these words, “to the glory of God.”
The Goal: establish God’s system. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
Brothers and sisters, the lesson text contains a gentle reminder: rejection is not the end of the world; it is the starting point for coming to know God’s love afresh.

When we are rejected, we usually ask only, “Where am I not good enough?” But perhaps, through that closed door, God is asking us: “My child, if no one were applauding you, would you still be willing to live for me?”
Our Lord was rejected by people, yet he never stopped loving; he was despised, yet he was still willing to embrace. True honour lies not in being respected, but in choosing to love all the same.

The world thinks honour means standing higher than others; Jesus shows us that honour means being willing to bend lower than others. He emptied himself, humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death; therefore God highly exalted him. This morning, let Jesus be King.
Let us pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, we bow before you. You died for us while we were yet sinners. Lord, we so often forget, and so day after day we go begging people for the acceptance you have long since given us freely. Please forgive us.

Please heal the wounds of rejection inside us, and replace “I don’t deserve it” with “no condemnation.” Give us the grace to let go, so that like you, while the wound is still fresh, we can say: Father, forgive them.

Please remove the self-centred life within us, so that we may live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit. Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord’s love be the worth of our whole life. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Who Sits at the Centre?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Let’s begin with a story from the history of science.

In 1543 a Polish astronomer, Nicolaus Copernicus, published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres as he lay dying. In that book he did something almost no one at the time dared to do — he moved the earth out of the centre of the universe and made it go dutifully round the sun. In the years that followed, the idea provoked endless argument and resistance. Why? Because what was truly hard to accept was not the astronomy; it was the unspoken line beneath it: so I am not the centre after all.

It took humanity several hundred years to accept, in astronomy, that “I am not the centre.” And in the spiritual world every one of us must go through a Copernican revolution of our own — God does not revolve around me; I must revolve around God. If that revolution never happens, we may read the Bible every day and gather for worship every week, and still be the sun of our own lives.

In our age “human rights” has become almost the most sacred phrase there is. People have the right to choose, the right to speak, the right to decide. Brothers and sisters, please note: none of this is wrong in itself. In fact, the very idea of human rights came from the Bible. The American Declaration of Independence of 4 July 1776 declares at its outset that all men are created equal and are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights. Look carefully at the foundation of that sentence — human rights are unalienable precisely because they are “endowed by their Creator.” The source of human rights was always the rule of God. Human beings have dignity because they bear the image of God; human beings have worth because they were made by God and bought with his precious blood.

So where does it go wrong? It goes wrong when we strike out the words “endowed by.” When people snatch their rights out of the hand of the One who gave them and declare that these rights are their own and have nothing to do with God, “human rights” turns from God’s gift into a human idol — and the rights of man become the rule of man.

History has given us one clear contrast. On 26 August 1789 the French Revolution adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Yet barely four years later, on 10 November 1793, the revolutionaries held a so-called “Festival of Reason” in Notre-Dame de Paris, dressed a young woman as the “Goddess of Reason” and carried her into that house built for the worship of God to be acclaimed. Man showed God out and showed himself onto the throne. And the result? By then the period history remembers as the Reign of Terror had already begun, and over the months that followed it grew ever more savage. A revolution that exalted the rights of man ended up devouring its own children.

Brothers and sisters, this is not a call to oppose human rights. It is a call to see a spiritual law: once human rule departs from God’s rule, it will always go bad. Like a river cut off from its source — at first there is still water, but further downstream it dries up and turns foul.

Our lesson text puts it very precisely: people have the right to choose, the right to speak and the right to decide, and none of these is wrong in itself; but when people place themselves above God and put “what I want” before “what God wants,” “human rule” replaces “God’s rule” — and that is exactly where humanity’s fall begins.

Allow me to put three questions to you, brothers and sisters. They will run through the whole of today’s message:

First, in your life, who has the final say?

Second, when “what I want” collides with “what God wants,” which one gives way?

Third, how long has it been since you said this from your heart — “Lord, may you reign”?

Psychology has made a fascinating discovery that can help us see ourselves. In 1975 the Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology on what she called “the illusion of control.” She had a group of people buy lottery tickets: half could pick their own numbers, and half were handed numbers chosen by someone else. Before the draw she asked how much they would want to sell their ticket for. Those who had picked their own numbers asked roughly four times as much as those whose numbers had been assigned. Notice: the odds of winning were exactly the same, not changed in the slightest. Only one thing had changed — “I” picked it.

“I picked it” — we often have no idea how much those three little words weigh in our hearts. It isn’t that we truly believe we choose better; we simply can’t bear to open the hand that is holding on. That is the self-centred life.

So the next sentence in our lesson is the key to today: the heart of humility is being willing to lay down our own rights and come back under the government of “God’s rule,” letting God be King once again. When we lay down our self-assertion and submit to God’s will, life enters true freedom — no longer “I must be in control,” but “Lord, may you reign.”

Today we will walk four stretches of road together: from the beginning of creation, seeing that God’s rule was God’s original intention; from the history of Israel, seeing the tragedy of human rule replacing God’s rule; from the situation of the church, seeing the danger of God’s rule sliding into human rule; and finally back to ourselves, learning to let Jesus be King again.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: 1 Samuel 8
sections.html:
Today’s theme verse is 1 Samuel 8:7. To hear it properly, we first have to step into that moment in history.

In the Hebrew Bible, Samuel was originally a single book, belonging to the “Former Prophets.” Jewish tradition holds that part of it came from Samuel’s own hand and the rest was continued by Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer (see 1 Chronicles 29:29). The whole book records the critical turn in Israel’s history from the age of the judges to the age of the kings, around the eleventh century BC.

What kind of age was it? The last verse of Judges sums it up: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.” (Judges 21:25) Brothers and sisters, doesn’t that sound remarkably modern? It is the standard outcome of “human rule” once it has thrown off the restraint of God’s rule — everyone their own standard, everyone their own judge.

Notice something important: the problem in the age of the judges was not that Israel “had no king,” but that Israel would not acknowledge the true King. God had always been their King. In Exodus 15:18, the victory song that Moses and the Israelites sang beside the Red Sea ends with this line: “Yahweh will reign forever and ever.” After Gideon’s victory, the people wanted to make him king, and he flatly refused: “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you. Yahweh shall rule over you.” (Judges 8:23) That is God’s rule — what theology calls a theocracy.

Then, when Samuel grew old, it happened. 1 Samuel 8:1–3 records that Samuel made his two sons judges over Israel, but “His sons didn’t walk in his ways, but turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice.” So the elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah and said: “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5)

Brothers and sisters, look at how that request is built: the first half is fact, the second half is the root of the trouble. “Your sons don’t walk in your ways” was true; but “like all the nations” is the heart of the problem. They wrapped a fleshly solution inside a real problem.

Samuel was deeply displeased, and he went to pray. God’s answer is our theme verse for today: “Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.’” (1 Samuel 8:7)

Two words here are worth stopping for.

The first is “rejected,” in Hebrew mā‘as: to refuse, to cast off, to look down on, to throw away as worthless. The same word appears in 1 Samuel 16:7: “But Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him.’” The “rejected” there comes from the same root. Israel was not simply swapping one leader for another; in their hearts they were “throwing God away.”

The second is “king over them” — behind it stands the Hebrew verb mālak, “to be king, to reign, to rule.” God did not say, “They don’t want my help,” but, “They don’t want me to reign.” Brothers and sisters, that distinction matters enormously. So often it isn’t that we don’t want God; we just don’t want God to be King. We welcome God as a consultant, as an insurance policy, as an emergency-relief resource — but not as King. What we want is a God who comes when called and otherwise leaves us alone.

Next God instructed Samuel: “Now therefore listen to their voice. However you shall protest solemnly to them, and shall show them the way of the king who will reign over them.” (1 Samuel 8:9) So Samuel laid out “the way of the king” to the people point by point (1 Samuel 8:11–18): the king will take your sons for his chariots and his horsemen; he will take your daughters to be cooks and bakers; he will take your best fields, vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants; and the last line is the heaviest of all — “you will be his servants.” (1 Samuel 8:17)

In this passage one Hebrew word comes back again and again: “take” (lāqaḥ). God says, “I give to you”; the king says, “I will take from you.” Brothers and sisters, here is the starkest contrast between God’s rule and human rule: the essence of God’s rule is to give; the essence of human rule is to take. Whichever one is King, that is the direction your life will flow.

Did the people listen to all this? They did. And their answer was: “No; but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations.” (1 Samuel 8:19–20) You have been told the whole cost, and you still want it — that is the stubbornness of the human heart.

In the flow of the book, 1 Samuel 8 is the watershed of the whole. The first seven chapters tell how God rescued his people through prayer, through Samuel and through the repentance at Mizpah; the chapters that follow begin the long story of Saul, David and the kings of Israel. And God did not abandon his purpose because of man’s choice — within the monarchy that people had demanded, he prepared David step by step, and from David’s line he brought forth the true King, Jesus Christ. That is our God: the paragraphs people write in rebellion, he can rewrite into chapters of salvation.

sections.heading: 3. From the Beginning of Creation: God’s Rule Was God’s Original Intention
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, to understand what “God’s rule” means, we have to go back to the very first page.

“God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. God blessed them. God said to them, ‘Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.’” (Genesis 1:27–28)

Notice that from the very start God handed the right of stewardship to man. Man is not a slave; man is a steward. Not a machine, but a creature bearing God’s image. What an honour that is! “Subdue” here is the Hebrew kābaš, and “have dominion” is rādâ — both are strong words of rule. God truly gave authority to man.

But then God added a sentence: “Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, ‘You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.’” (Genesis 2:16–17)

Brothers and sisters, count how much freedom is in that sentence: “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden” — every tree, freely. The limit was a single tree. God gave man ninety-nine point nine per cent freedom and kept back only that tiny portion, as a sign that “I am God and you are man.”

What did that tree mean? It wasn’t poisonous fruit; it was a boundary line. It was the one place in the whole of Eden where man had to say to himself: on this matter, I don’t get the final say. That is the essence of God’s rule — God hands the stewardship to man, yet his word remains the highest standard. Man has immense authority, but he is not the final authority.

I often use an illustration: a managing director may run the whole company’s operations, but he is not the chairman of the board. He can deploy every resource, yet the one thing he cannot do is rewrite the company’s charter. In Eden, man was that managing director. And the devil’s temptation of Adam and Eve, stripped down, was a single sentence: you could be chairman too.

“The serpent said to the woman, ‘You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.’” (Genesis 3:4–5)

“Like God” — in Hebrew, kê‘lōhîm. The heart of the whole temptation was not whether the fruit tasted good, but “who defines good and evil.” In Hebrew usage, “knowing good and evil” carries the sense of deciding and judging; to eat that fruit was to declare: from now on I will define good and evil myself — I will be my own standard.

Brothers and sisters, this is the original scene of “human rule” replacing “God’s rule.” Had Adam and Eve held fast in obedience, they would have lived under God’s rule; but when they chose to listen to the serpent and act on their own wishes, “God’s rule” was rejected and “human rule” took its place. From then on man became the master of his own life — this is the root of pride, and it is what the 321 vision calls the self-centred life.

In fact, this rebellion had already happened once before, in heaven. In Isaiah 14:13–14, through the downfall of the king of Babylon, the prophet portrays the fall that lay behind it: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” Brothers and sisters, listen to those five “I will”s in a row. Satan did not fall because he committed some monstrous crime; he fell because of five “I will”s. The fall of man is the same — it didn’t begin with doing something wicked; it began with wanting that seat.

The 321 vision puts it with great clarity: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The tragedy of Eden can be told in a single sentence: man refused to be man and wanted to be God. And more than thirty centuries later, in another garden, the true God willingly became man.

One passage sets out this contrast more clearly than anything else: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

“Emptied himself” — the Greek is kenoō, to pour out, to make empty. Look at these two pictures side by side: Adam is “man trying to seize the place of God”; Christ is “God willingly emptying himself of his place.” One is “a thing to be grasped” (Greek harpagmos: something snatched, seized for oneself); the other is “emptied himself.” Adam grabbed upward; Jesus went downward. In the end Adam was driven out of paradise, and Jesus was exalted by God.

This is the core of the 321 vision: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, living out that fullness. When Jesus emptied himself he did not lose his deity; he poured himself out, and received “the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Brothers and sisters, laying down your rights never makes you smaller; it only brings you into God’s fullness.

At the opening of the first book of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a prayer that has been repeated for over a thousand years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” As a young man he chased after everything he could grab — learning, reputation, lust — and finally discovered that the human heart has a throne, and that throne is a size only God fits; put anything else on it and it wobbles.

So we must ask ourselves: is that “tree of the knowledge of good and evil” in my life still standing today? Is that boundary — “on this matter, I don’t get the final say” — still there? Brothers and sisters, the first step in obeying God is always on something you are perfectly able to do, and choose not to.

sections.heading: 4. The Lesson of Israel: The Tragedy of Turning from God’s Rule to Human Rule
sections.html:
Israel was originally a nation governed by God himself. In Moses’ day, God himself gave the law; in Joshua’s day, God himself led them in battle; in the days of the judges, God raised up judges to rescue and govern the people — “Yahweh raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.” (Judges 2:16)

From the Red Sea to Canaan, not one of this nation’s victories came from human strength. Jericho was not stormed; it was circled. When Gideon went against the Midianites, God said he still had too many men and cut them from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, and the reason was spelled out plainly: “The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2) What God cared about was never whether the battle could be won, but who would get the glory once it was.

Yet by Samuel’s time the people were saying: “Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5) And God said to Samuel: “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.” (1 Samuel 8:7)

This is precisely where “human rule” began to replace “God’s rule.”

Brothers and sisters, notice that Israel’s motive for wanting a king looked, on the surface, like administration; underneath it came down to a few words: “like all the nations.” They envied the nations their visible kings, visible armies and visible chariots, and forgot that they themselves were the people “governed by God himself.” They would rather have a king they could see than a God they could not. How deep a sorrow that is — they traded a real King for a visible one.

From that moment the story began to go downhill. After Saul became king, Samuel spoke these severe words to him: “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim.” (1 Samuel 15:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, here “rebellion” is set equal to “witchcraft,” and “stubbornness” equal to “idolatry.” Why? Because witchcraft is the use of supernatural means to make things turn out the way I want — and that is exactly what rebellion is at heart: I want things my way. Idolatry is making a god who goes along with my wishes — and that is exactly what stubbornness is at heart. So self-will is the oldest witchcraft of all, and my own way is the idol I keep closest.

And how did it end? After Israel had its king, three kings came and went — Saul, David and Solomon — and in the hands of Solomon’s son Rehoboam the kingdom split apart (1 Kings 12). Rehoboam ignored the counsel of the old men and listened to the young men instead, telling the people: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke.” (1 Kings 12:14) — those who grab for power always end up with their own hands bleeding. After that the northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6), and the southern kingdom of Judah fell to Babylon in 586 BC (2 Kings 25). The verdict of 2 Kings 17 on the fall of the north is plain: “They abandoned all the commandments of Yahweh their God, and made molten images for themselves, even two calves” (2 Kings 17:16).

This reminds us that any person or any community that will not let God reign will in the end go to ruin.

Scripture gives us another, even more dramatic witness. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon stood on the roof of his palace and said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) The words were still in his mouth when a voice came down from heaven. After those seven periods of time had passed, this king who had once looked down on the whole world lifted his eyes to heaven, and his final conclusion was: “those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)

Brothers and sisters, history keeps repeating the same script. In 1887 the English historian Lord Acton, in a letter to Bishop Mandell Creighton, left us a famous line: “Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.” People often quote it about politics, but it is even more a spiritual diagnosis. Once a person puts himself in God’s seat, he cannot bear the weight of that seat.

Seen through the 321 vision, Israel’s failure was a failure of perspective. They retreated from God’s perspective to man’s; from heaven’s perspective to earth’s; from the eternal perspective to the temporary; from the godly perspective to the worldly. Those few words, “like all the nations,” are the most honest confession the worldly perspective ever made.

And once the perspective changes, everything after it changes. The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. And the reverse is just as true — let the mindset drift and life drifts; let life drift, and daily living, relationships and ministry all drift with it. Israel did not perish suddenly one day. They began to perish on the day they said, “like all the nations.”

Brothers and sisters, today we too must honestly ask ourselves: is there a “like all the nations” in my heart? What others have, I must have too; the road others take, I must take too; the way others arrange their children’s lives is the way I must arrange my children’s lives. When we measure our lives by the world’s standard, we have already quietly changed kings.

sections.heading: 5. A Warning Bell for the Church: The Danger of Sliding from God’s Rule to Human Rule
sections.html:
Jesus said: “on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the possessive in this verse: “my” church. The foundation of the church is Jesus himself, and the ownership belongs to Jesus himself — it belongs to no one else. Paul put it even more plainly to the elders of Ephesus: “Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.” (Acts 20:28) The church was bought with precious blood, and the buyer is Jesus. Colossians 1:18 says: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” — preeminence “in all things,” not in some things.

The early church let the Holy Spirit reign: in everything they prayed, sought and obeyed. There is a deeply moving detail in Acts. The Jerusalem Council had to deal with the problem of the Gentile believers — the thorniest issue of the day and the one most likely to split the church. The decision they finally wrote down began like this: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you” (Acts 15:28). Look at the order — “the Holy Spirit, and to us”: the Holy Spirit first, ourselves second. That one sentence is the loveliest mark of a church under God’s rule.

But as time went on, people gradually came to govern the church by human methods. Structures, rules, power and titles slowly took the place of the Holy Spirit’s leading. “God’s rule” became “human rule,” and believers leaned on organisation, tradition and influence, losing their sensitivity to God’s voice and their reverence for it.

In fact, this danger had already appeared in New Testament times. The apostle John wrote these grieved words: “I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say.” (3 John 9) “Loves to be first” is the Greek philoprōteuō, literally “to love being first.” Brothers and sisters, this word appears only once in the whole New Testament, and it is used to describe a leader in the church. The most dangerous disease in a church is not a lack of gifts; it is the love of being first.

Let me use an illustration from the body. In our hearts there is a very small cluster of tissue called the sinoatrial node. It is the heart’s natural pacemaker, normally firing about sixty to a hundred electrical signals a minute, and the whole heart muscle contracts together in time with that one signal. It is tiny, yet it is the only one giving the orders. What happens if many stray pacemaker points spring up in the atria, each demanding its own contraction? That is atrial fibrillation. From the outside, the heart looks busier than usual and beats faster, but the amount of blood it actually pumps drops sharply.

Brothers and sisters, that is a church that has lost God’s rule. It isn’t that there’s no activity — there’s too much; it isn’t that no one is working — too many people are giving their own orders. On the surface the calendar is full; inside, the blood supply is failing. A church’s health doesn’t lie in how many programmes it runs, but in whether it has only one pacemaker.

Here the 321 vision gives us a very practical measuring rod: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When a church runs into trouble, it is almost always because that order has been turned upside down. Once ministry is put first, people become tools for getting ministry done, and relationships start to strain; once relationships strain, life is drained; once life is drained, ministry is left with nothing but technique and emotion. Turn it the right way round and put life first, and ministry doesn’t shrink — it gains roots, strength and joy.

The 321 vision also says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. How many church conflicts have been over a budget, a venue or a position? In the end the job got done, but the people scattered. Brothers and sisters, pride stirs up pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. One person insists on his rights, another insists on hers, and in the end both are right — and the church is the loser.

Yet in these last days God is calling his people back to the starting point — back to the government of “God’s rule,” letting the Holy Spirit reign once more. Church history has borne witness to this again and again: every true revival has had at its heart not a new strategy but the same old thing — God’s people letting God be King again. On 13 August 1727, at a gathering in Herrnhut, the Spirit of God was poured out on the Moravian Brethren, and this band of refugees, who until then had been endlessly quarrelling with one another, began a round-the-clock relay of watchful prayer that went on for a hundred years. Revival did not begin with a meeting but with repentance; not with a strategy, but on our knees.

When the church is no longer built for people and glorified for people, but exists for Jesus and is glorified for Jesus, God’s glory will once again be revealed among his people.

This is exactly the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. It is also the Goal of 321: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, the difference between God’s system and man’s system is not whether there is organisation, but who sits in the middle. Man’s system is centred on man and uses structures to protect people’s positions; God’s system is centred on Jesus and uses order to serve God’s will.

John the Baptist left us a short but weighty sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) His disciples had come to complain that everyone was going off to follow Jesus. John didn’t say a word in his own defence; he said he was only the friend of the bridegroom, and that hearing the bridegroom’s voice filled him with joy. Brothers and sisters, being able to rejoice when someone else increases is the surest evidence that God’s rule is reigning.

sections.heading: 6. Our Personal Response: Letting Jesus Be King Again
sections.html:
Having spoken of creation, of history and of the church, the message now comes back to you and me.

The lesson text says: “laying down our rights” does not mean abandoning our responsibilities; it means acknowledging that God is wiser than we are. That needs to be made clear. Laying down our sovereignty doesn’t mean being passive, it doesn’t mean lying flat and giving up, and it doesn’t mean refusing to make decisions. Quite the opposite — those who hand their sovereignty to God act with greater courage, because they know the outcome is not in their own hands.

“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) Notice: the verse does not say “don’t use your own understanding,” but “don’t lean on your own understanding.” God still wants you to use your mind; he simply won’t let you treat your mind as God.

In daily life we often slip into living under “human rule” without even noticing — wanting to control outcomes, wanting to manipulate others, wanting the final say. Brothers and sisters, let’s do a small check-up.

Have you ever chosen a path for your child that was really a dream you never finished yourself? That is wanting to control outcomes.

Have you ever hidden a hook in something you said, so the other person would answer the way you wanted? That is wanting to manipulate others.

Have you ever said out loud, “Let’s pray and seek God together,” when in your heart you’d already decided and were only waiting for everyone else to agree? That is wanting the final say.

In 1966 the psychologist Julian Rotter put forward the theory of “locus of control,” distinguishing an “internal” from an “external” locus: people with an internal locus believe outcomes are in their own hands; people with an external locus believe outcomes depend on luck or on others. Research shows that those leaning towards an internal locus are generally more proactive and more successful. But brothers and sisters, the Christian life has a third kind, one this scale cannot measure — not handing sovereignty to myself, nor to fate, but to a Lord with a name, who loved me and gave himself up for me. That isn’t an external locus of control; that is trust. Trust doesn’t mean you stop putting in effort; it means you know whose hands you are working in.

The heart of “human rule” is “for myself”; the heart of “God’s rule” is “for God.” When we lay down our self-centredness, Jesus’ sovereignty can be restored in our lives.

To know whether this road can really be walked, we have the most reliable role model there is. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus fell to the ground, his sweat like great drops of blood falling on the ground, and his prayer was: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

Brothers and sisters, notice the shape of this prayer. Jesus didn’t pretend he didn’t want the cup taken away — he really did say, “remove this cup.” True obedience isn’t having no opinion; it is having an opinion and still placing it under the will of God. So you don’t have to pretend you aren’t struggling; you only have to say that “nevertheless” after the struggle. Between “my will” and “your will” stands only one word: “nevertheless.” That one “nevertheless” is the place where human rule is handed back to God’s rule.

Once that turning point comes, the formula of life changes: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

This is what the 321 vision calls “selflessness.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness doesn’t mean there is no me; it means “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” You have not disappeared; you have been filled by a greater Person. Think of a glove: an empty glove can do nothing at all, but once a hand fills it, it can do everything the hand can do. The glove hasn’t lost itself; the glove has found itself.

And what does Jesus promise on this road? “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice that rest does not come from taking the yoke off; it comes from changing yokes. The yoke of human rule you carry alone; the yoke of God’s rule you carry together with the Lord.

The gentle reminder in our lesson puts it beautifully: “human rule” pursues control and ends in anxiety; “God’s rule” pursues entrusting and ends in peace. Humility is not losing strength; it is letting strength return to its proper source — God.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Brothers and sisters, look at which way the verbs run in these two verses: humbling yourself is what you do; exalting is what God does. Our greatest mistake is trying to snatch God’s work and do it ourselves — and when we exalt ourselves, God resists us.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set today’s message within the framework of 321 and see it all clearly at once.

The Three Foundations. First, Jesus is my role model — in Gethsemane he said, “not my will, but yours, be done,” the perfect demonstration of returning from human rule to God’s rule. Second, the Bible is my standard — the content of God’s rule is not some vague feeling but what God has said; that tree in Eden was a boundary precisely because God had spoken. Third, the Holy Spirit is my guide — “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28): God’s rule is not a distant government but the Holy Spirit’s present leading in your heart and mine.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — this is the very theme of this lesson: from “I am king” back to “he is King.” Let Jesus receive all the glory — the word “all” cuts deepest, because we so often keep a little bit back for ourselves.

The Goal. Establish God’s system. The most fundamental difference between God’s system and the Worldly system is who sits on the throne. When Israel said “like all the nations,” that was the Worldly system.

From the self-centred life to selflessness. The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life; the root of the problem is pride. The five “I will”s of Isaiah 14, that one bite of fruit in Genesis 3, that one sentence “like all the nations” in 1 Samuel 8 — at heart they are exactly the same. And there is only one remedy: selflessness. Selflessness is not the passivity of self-negation; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan cannot get a grip on a person who has nothing for him to grab. If you have no seat to defend, he has no leverage to threaten you with; if you don’t care who gets the glory, he has no bait to lure you with.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Be transformed” is the Greek metamorphoō, “to change form” — the thorough change of a caterpillar into a butterfly, not a change of clothes. When the mindset changes, life changes; when life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry at last bears real fruit.

The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s subject, God’s rule, begins with our relationship with God. If you have not let him be King in your relationship with God, the other three layers will all be out of place: your relationship with yourself turns into self-condemnation or self-inflation, your relationship with others turns into competition and control, and your relationship with things turns into anxiety and performance.

A change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. “Human rule” is the human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective; “God’s rule” is the divine, heavenly, eternal, godly perspective. Look at the same matter from different perspectives and you reach completely different conclusions.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — so that the Holy Spirit bears his fruit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice that these nine graces have one thing in common — every one of them requires you to lay down a right of some kind. Patience lays down the right to have it now; gentleness lays down the right to hit back; self-control lays down the right to indulge. So the fruit of the Spirit turns out to be the fruit God’s rule bears in a person.

The 235 relationships. Become a “2” with selfless people — spiritual companions who remind each other who is King; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing on the life that lets Jesus be King; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together. Brothers and sisters, it is hard to hold on to God’s rule alone, because we cannot see our own pride; but a “2” can help you see it.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — that is Spirit; the Bible is my standard — that is Understanding; Jesus is my role model — that is Life; let Jesus be King — that is Service; let Jesus receive all the glory — that is God. Today’s lesson is really the whole road, from “Spirit” all the way to “God.”

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Brothers and sisters, human rule is the product of the brain — calculating, comparing, scheming; God’s rule is the surrender of the heart — trusting, entrusting, resting.

sections.heading: 8. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing the word is where the real work lies. Our lesson gives us four practices; let’s take them one at a time.

Practice 1: A Prayer Entrusting My Rights

Each morning in your prayer time, declare: “Lord, today I hand the sovereignty of my life over to you.”

Notice the words “each morning.” Handing over sovereignty has an expiry date, just as manna couldn’t be kept until the next day. What we handed over yesterday, we quietly take back again this morning. So this isn’t a one-off ritual; it is a daily practice. I suggest, brothers and sisters, that you say this sentence as soon as you open your eyes, before you reach for your phone. Whoever’s voice you hear first in a day is most likely whoever will govern that day.

In the Twelve Steps of Alcoholics Anonymous, the third step reads: “Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.” Even people in the world know that some bondages are only broken when sovereignty is handed over — how much more we who have the true and living God.

Practice 2: Obedience in Decision-Making

Before every decision, first ask: “Is this what I want, or what God wants?”

Ask this question before you decide, not after. We are very good at finding spiritual reasons for decisions we’ve already made, so the order matters enormously. You can add two follow-up questions: will this decision still count five years from now, in the light of eternity? And if the spiritual companion I respect most found out about this decision, would I feel the need to explain myself?

Note too that “what God wants” is not something we guess by feeling. The Bible is my standard. Where the Bible speaks plainly, there is no need to ask again; where the Bible does not speak plainly, seek the Holy Spirit’s guidance within its principles, and have it confirmed in community.

Practice 3: God’s Rule in the Family

In family prayer, let God’s word be the final standard, rather than emotions or habit.

Brothers and sisters, the family is the first place God’s rule is lost and the place it most needs to be won back. At home we are most prone to let two things be king: one is emotion — whoever shouts loudest wins; the other is habit — this is just how our family has always done it. Neither of these is the word of God.

Here is one concrete suggestion: in family prayer, read a short passage of Scripture first, and only then discuss things. When opinions differ, the question isn’t “who’s right?” but “what does God’s word say?” The most powerful lesson a parent can teach is not “do as I say,” but saying in front of the children: “I was going to do it that way, but God’s word says this, so Dad has changed his mind.”

Practice 4: Obedience in the Church

In serving, seek not position and control, but room for the Holy Spirit to move freely.

The temptations of serving are subtle: we may not covet a title, but we very often covet “being needed.” When something can’t get done without me, there’s a secret satisfaction in my heart. Brothers and sisters, that too is grabbing for power.

The practice is simple: hand over to someone else the area of service you do most easily, and resist the urge to correct the way they do it; and when your own proposal isn’t adopted, go home and pray a blessing over the brother who suggested something different. These little things are the church’s Gethsemane.

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

The 321 vision teaches that changing our mindset goes through eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Let’s place today’s practices within these eight stages.

Stage one, Information. You have received the information today: human rule began in Eden, Israel’s tragedy is in 1 Samuel 8, and the way out for each of us is in Gethsemane. Please write these things down.

Stage two, Revelation. For information to become revelation, the Holy Spirit must open your eyes. Ask the Lord in prayer: “Lord, please show me the one thing in my life I have not yet handed over.” Usually your heart already knows what that one thing is.

Stage three, Conviction. For revelation to become conviction, you must say yes. Conviction isn’t saying, “That’s a good teaching”; it is saying, “That teaching governs me.” Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that we don’t know; it’s that we won’t submit.

Stage four, Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, take up at least one of the four practices. Don’t try all four at once — that usually doesn’t last three days. Begin with “a prayer entrusting my rights,” because it is the source of the other three.

Stage five, Evaluation. Set a regular time each week to look back: in what matter did I take sovereignty back? What triggered it? Usually it is one of three situations — things getting out of control, losing face, or falling behind schedule.

Stage six, Correction. When you see it, change it — and make the change specific. Not “I’ll be more humble,” but “at the next meeting, I’ll wait until three other people have spoken before I say anything.” God’s rule is restored in specific, small things.

Stage seven, Repetition. Doing it once isn’t practice; doing it again and again is. Brokenness isn’t a one-time operation; it is a lifelong lesson. Going straight back to stage one after a failure is itself a victory.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Once you have tasted the sweetness of God’s rule, take someone along with you. Find your “2,” share these four practices with them, and ask each other once a week: “This week, who has been King in your life?” This is how 235 relationships begin, and how God’s system is established.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, from Eden until today, humanity has kept wrestling between “human rule” and “God’s rule.”

Adam reached out his hand in the garden, wanting to be his own god; Israel opened its mouth at Ramah, wanting a king like the nations; Diotrephes loved to be first in the church, wanting to be number one; and you and I, on every ordinary morning, are quietly deciding as well: who will be King today?

But Jesus’ example has already shown us clearly — true freedom is letting God be King.

In The Great Divorce, C. S. Lewis wrote what is widely seen as one of his sharpest and tenderest insights: in the end there are only two kinds of people — those who say to God, “Thy will be done,” and those to whom God says, “Thy will be done.” Brothers and sisters, this morning, which kind of person will you be?

When we lay down our sovereignty and hand over control, we are not losing; on the contrary, we gain a more abundant life. This is not a spiritual slogan; it is a spiritual fact. When your hand is clenched, all it can hold is what fits inside your fist; when your hand is open, it can receive as much as the sky is wide.

Let us turn from “human rule” back to “God’s rule,” from “relying on ourselves” back to “letting God reign,” so that Jesus truly reigns as King within us and receives the glory.

One day this proclamation will ring out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15) Brothers and sisters, since that day is certain to come, why not begin this very morning? Hand the kingdom over to him, give the throne back to him, give the glory to him.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
