A prayer of reverence: say every day, “Lord, let me walk in your order, turning neither to the left nor to the right.”
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
You are the God of order, not a God of confusion. From the farthest star to the smallest cell in our bodies, everything moves along the course you have set.

Lord, forgive us. So often we are not content with the place you have given us; our eyes are fixed on other people’s offices, and our hands reach for authority that does not belong to us. So often, too, we neglect our own originally intended position and push onto others the responsibilities that are ours to carry. Have mercy on us, we pray.

We ask that the Holy Spirit would guide us and bring us back each day to the place you have appointed. Let us return to the order of love in our families, to our originally intended position of faithfulness in our workplaces, and in the church let each joint do its own part, as we bow quietly before you.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you willingly emptied yourself and became obedient to the point of death. Give us that same mind, we pray. Let us never overstep, never exalt ourselves, and turn neither to the left nor to the right.
May you reign in our lives, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6). In your family, workplace or church right now, is there a place God has given you where you are unwilling to stand? What makes you unwilling?

“For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3). Please share a time when you “overstepped” or “left your place empty.” How did God later bring you back to your originally intended position? What did that experience teach you?

blocks.x: — Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 91: Order
True humility is not bowing our heads, but going back to our place

On the afternoon of 14 August 2003, North America suffered the largest blackout in its history. Some fifty million people lost their power in the sweltering heat of high summer; New York’s subway trains stopped dead in pitch-black tunnels, and every traffic light in the city went out at once.

The investigation afterwards found that the starting point was almost unbelievably small: a high-voltage transmission line in Ohio heated up and sagged until it touched a tree that had not been trimmed in time — and the alarm system happened to fail at that very moment.
One line left the place where it was meant to be, and within a few hours the whole grid went down like a row of dominoes.
Disorder seldom begins with something big. Disorder almost always begins with “one little thing that is not where it is meant to be.”
1. The essence of sin is often standing in the wrong place
There is a verse in the Bible that puts this in the weightiest terms:
“Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6)
The Greek word behind “first domain” means “the office and sphere of authority entrusted by God.” Notice this: what those angels lost was not power, not intelligence, but their place.

Isaiah 14 records the fall of the “shining one, son of the dawn,” and in it are five “I will”s in a row: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High.
These five “I will”s are the anatomy of pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to take God’s place. He wanted to go up, and went down.
2. God establishes order to protect us, not to restrict us

In Genesis 1, day after day, everything proceeds in perfect order: first light, then the separation of day and night; first the sky and the waters, then the birds and the fish; first the land and the plants were prepared, and only then was man created to live among them. God always prepares the home first, and then brings in those who will live there.

It is the same in relationships. Paul first lays down the overarching principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). Only then does he speak of husbands denying themselves, wives submitting, children honouring their parents, and fathers not provoking their children. This is not a matter of higher and lower status; it is the order of love.

The World Health Organization describes cancer as abnormal cells growing uncontrollably, going beyond their usual boundaries and invading other parts of the body. Cancer cells are not an enemy invading from outside; they were originally our own cells. What makes them deadly is that they have left their originally intended position.
It is the same in families, workplaces and churches. What hurts most is often not persecution from outside, but someone inside who has left their originally intended position.
Railway tracks are not there to restrict the train but to let it run at full speed. A train without tracks is not called free; it is called derailed.
3. Humility is recognising our own place
Many people think humility means constantly saying, “I can’t, I’m not worthy.” But that isn’t humility; it is just another way of talking about yourself all the time.

Paul says: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3). Don’t overestimate, and don’t underestimate either — that is humility.

If the hand wants to see in place of the eye, if the foot fights to become the head, the whole body stops functioning normally. If a hand really grew an eye, that would not be called a gift; it would be called a deformity.

The one who said, “I will make myself like the Most High,” was brought down to Sheol; this One “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,” but emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death, and God highly exalted him. This is the law of the kingdom of heaven: those who grab for position fall; those who return to their originally intended position are lifted up.
How to practise this week
1. Reflecting on my place: write down all your roles and check each one — have I overstepped? Have I left it empty?
2. Practising submission: when you hear an opinion you disagree with, be quiet for three seconds and pray before you respond.
3. Restoring order: in conflict, don’t ask “Who is right and who is wrong?” — ask only “Am I standing in my own place?”
4. A prayer of reverence: say every day, “Lord, let me walk in your order, turning neither to the left nor to the right.”

When people return to their originally intended position, God’s order is restored, relationships are healed and lives are built up. True humility is not bowing our heads; it is returning to God’s order.
Reflection
Right now, is there a place God gave you that you have left? Is there a place God did not give you that you are clinging to?

• Genesis 2:15: “Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden” — human dignity is bound up with place.
• Application: God never places a person somewhere that has not been made ready.
Everything in the universe has its place
Earth to sun: about 150 million km
Earth’s axis tilted about 23.4 degrees
The moon’s gravity pulls the tides
“In him all things are held together” (Colossians 1:17)
Key points:
• Data: the average distance from the earth to the sun is about 149.6 million km (one astronomical unit).
• The axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, giving us the seasons; the moon averages about 384,000 km away.
• Kepler (1571–1630) discovered the three laws of planetary motion; Newton, Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, 1687.
• Scripture: Colossians 1:17, “in him all things are held together.”
Order displays God’s glory
The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1)
2017 Nobel Prize: the biological clock
Augustine: peace is the tranquillity of order
321: the Bible is my standard
Key points:
• Scripture: Psalm 19:1.
• Science: the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Hall, Rosbash and Young for discovering the molecular mechanisms of circadian rhythm.
• Church father: Augustine, The City of God, Book 19 — the peace of all things is the tranquillity of order.
• 321: the Bible is my standard; a standard is the line on the track, not a railing.
2. The principle of mutual submission
Submit to one another in the fear of Christ
(Ephesians 5:21)
The head of Christ is God (1 Corinthians 11:3)
Submission is not inferiority
Key points:
• The overarching verse: Ephesians 5:21.
• 1 Corinthians 11:3: “the head of Christ is God” — submission does not mean inferiority.
• In the triune God there is the most perfect order and the most perfect love.
• 321: the priority of relationships — first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, last with things.
The order of love in the family
Husbands love wives as Christ loved the church
Wives submit to husbands as to the Lord
Children obey and honour their parents
Fathers don’t provoke their children
Key points:
• Scripture: Ephesians 5:25, 5:22, 6:1–3, 6:4.
• Emphasis: God’s command to husbands is weightier — wives are to submit; husbands are to deny themselves.
• Not a matter of higher and lower status, but the order of love.
• 321: the 920 practice — spouse, children and co-workers are all my “2.”
Jesus our role model
He went to Nazareth and was subject to his parents
(Luke 2:51)
“The will of my Father who sent me”
(John 5:30)
Key points:
• Scripture: Luke 2:51; John 5:30; Philippians 2:5–8.
• Thirty hidden years: the Lord lived as a carpenter’s son, quietly in his originally intended position.
• Example: the centurion of Capernaum (Matthew 8:8–10) — those who understand being under authority have the greatest faith.
• Application: he did not rise above the order, but fulfilled God’s will through submission.
The cost of leaving our place: psychology agrees
Minuchin: family boundaries and subsystems
A child pulled into a parent’s place
Bowen: tension forms triangles
Role ambiguity brings stress and exhaustion
Key points:
• Salvador Minuchin (1921–2017), Families and Family Therapy (1974): subsystems and boundaries.
• Parentification: when a child is pushed into the role of a spouse or parent, the family system stops functioning.
• Murray Bowen (1913–1990): triangles ease tension in the short term but lock the problem in place in the long term.
• Rizzo, House and Lirtzman (1970), role conflict and role ambiguity scales: unclear roles bring stress and exhaustion.
• Reminder: psychology is only corroborating evidence; the Bible is the standard.
3. The five “I will”s
I will ascend into heaven
I will exalt my throne
I will make myself like the Most High
Key points:
• Scripture: the whole of Isaiah 14:12–15 — count the five “I will”s.
• Getting the names right: “Lucifer” comes from the Latin translation; the Hebrew means “shining one, son of the dawn.”
• The Bible never calls him an archangel; the title is used only of Michael and an unnamed archangel (Jude 9; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).
• The definition of pride: leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to take God’s place.
• The result: he wanted to rise, and fell to Sheol.
Three warnings about leaving our place
Korah grabbed for the priesthood — the earth opened
“Is it a small thing?” (Numbers 16:9–10)
Uzziah burned incense — leprosy broke out
Saul offered sacrifice — to obey is better
Key points:
• Korah: Numbers 16:3, 9–10, 32, 35.
• Emphasis: Korah already had the honourable office of a Levite, yet looked down on the place God had given him.
• Uzziah: 2 Chronicles 26:16–19 — when he was strong his heart was lifted up, and leprosy broke out on his forehead.
• Saul: 1 Samuel 13:8–9; 15:22–23, “to obey is better than sacrifice.”
• The trajectory: dissatisfaction → grabbing → confusion → destruction.
Order is protection, not restriction
Cancer cells: our own cells crossing boundaries
Everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25)
Tracks don’t restrict the train; they let it run
Pride provokes pride; both sides lose
Key points:
• Scientific illustration: the WHO description of cancer — abnormal cells crossing their boundaries and invading other parts.
• The key: cancer cells are not an outside enemy but our own cells that have left their place.
• Scripture: Judges 21:25, “everyone did that which was right in his own eyes”; Genesis 3:5, “like God.”
• 321: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
• Illustration: tracks let the train run at full speed; no tracks is not freedom, it is derailment.
4. Think reasonably
Don’t think of yourself more highly than you ought
(Romans 12:3)
Neither inflating nor belittling yourself
Humility is recognising our own place
Key points:
• Scripture: Romans 12:1–3, from the renewing of the mind to thinking reasonably.
• Original language: sōphroneō means to be clear-headed, of sound mind.
• Clarify: constantly saying “I can’t” is not humility; it is just another way of talking about yourself.
• C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, Book 3, “The Great Sin”: pride is the complete anti-God state of mind.
Every joint doing its part
God set the members in the body as he desired
The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you”
Hand doesn’t replace eye; foot doesn’t fight to be head
Grab for position, fall; return to your place, be lifted
Key points:
• Scripture: Romans 12:4–5; 1 Corinthians 12:18, 21; Ephesians 4:15–16.
• Illustration: if a hand grew an eye, that would not be a gift but a deformity.
• Example: the conductor Bernstein is widely said to have called second violin the hardest place in the orchestra.
• Philippians 2:9–11: the One who emptied himself was highly exalted.
• 1 Peter 5:5–6: clothe yourselves with humility, and God will exalt you.
Practices (1)
Reflecting on my place
Have I overstepped? Have I left it empty?
Practising submission
Be quiet first, then seek God’s heart
Key points:
• Practice 1: write down each of your roles and check each one for overstepping and leaving it empty.
• Reminder: overstepping hurts people, and so does leaving a place empty.
• Practice 2: when you hear an opinion you disagree with, be quiet for three seconds and pray before you respond.
• Scripture: Romans 13:1; but if authority goes against God’s word, we must obey God (Acts 5:29).
Practices (2)
Restoring order
Not who’s right or wrong, but where am I?
A prayer of reverence
Walking in your order, not left nor right
Key points:
• Practice 3: swap “who is right and who is wrong?” for “where should I be standing?”
• Explain: when both people sit on the judgment seat, no one in the home is left in the place of love.
• Practice 4: pray daily to turn neither left nor right; scriptural basis Deuteronomy 5:32 and Isaiah 30:21.
• The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Summing up the 3-2-1 vision
Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard
The Holy Spirit my guide; let Jesus be King
The old self is self-centred, the new self selfless
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Key points:
• The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
• The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
• The old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; selflessness is not having nothing, but entering into fullness and living it out.
• The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; life first, then relationships, then ministry.
• A change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal.
Back to our place, glory to the Lord
True humility is not bowing our heads
but returning to God’s order
When people return, order is restored
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Key points:
• Call: ask the Holy Spirit to show a place I have left, or a place I am clinging to.
• Illustration: a kite flies high not because it has broken free of its string, but because it has a string.
• The lesson’s conclusion: when people return to their place, order is restored, relationships are healed and lives are built up.
• Point to: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Prayer of response and blessing
Lord, let me walk in your order
Never overstepping, never exalting myself
Turning neither to the left nor to the right
Reign in my life and be glorified
Key points:
• Lead the congregation in saying the six lines of the declaration of faith together.
• Prayer: confess leaving our place; ask the Holy Spirit to bring us back to it each day.
• The two small-group discussion questions can be handed out here.
• Blessing: may God’s order be the track you run on all through today.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we’re reading Lesson 91 together. The title is “Return to Our Originally Intended Position,” and the theme is “Order.”
Our theme verse is just one sentence: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).
Over the last few lessons we learned that true humility is laying down our rights. Today we go one layer deeper: true humility is, even more, returning to our originally intended position.
Let me start with a true story. On the afternoon of 14 August 2003, North America suffered the largest blackout in its history, and some fifty million people lost their power in the sweltering heat.
The cause was almost unbelievably small: a power line in Ohio overheated and sagged until it touched a tree that hadn’t been trimmed — and the alarm system happened to fail at that very moment.
Brothers and sisters, disorder seldom begins with something big. Disorder almost always begins with “one little thing that is not where it is meant to be.”
The Bible gives a very weighty definition of leaving our place.
“Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).
The Greek word behind “first domain” means the office and sphere entrusted by God.
Hear this clearly: what those angels lost was not power; it was their place. The essence of sin is often not doing something bad, but standing in the wrong place.
First, God is a God of order.

In Genesis 1, day after day, everything proceeds in perfect order. First light, then the separation of day and night; first the sky and the waters, then the birds and the fish; first the land and the plants were prepared, and only then was man created to live among them.
God always prepares the container first and then puts in the contents; he prepares the home first and then brings in those who will live there.

Look up at the sky and it’s the same. The average distance between the earth and the sun is about 149.6 million kilometres, and the earth’s axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and so we have the seasons.
The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to three scientists who discovered the molecular mechanisms of the biological clock. Even our tiniest cells run to the rhythm God has set.
Brothers and sisters, order is the display of God’s glory.
Second, there is a God-appointed order in our relationships too.
Before Paul speaks of any particular role, he first gives an overarching principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21).
So the order the Bible speaks of is never the strong crushing the weak; it is every person, in the fear of Christ, returning to their own place.

Someone may ask: if we are to submit to one another, why do we still need an order? Paul says: “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3). The Son shares equal honour and glory with the Father, yet willingly stands in the place of submission.
This is not a matter of higher and lower status; it is the order of love.
Worked out in the family, this means three sets of relationships.
Husbands are to love their wives, even as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for it; wives are to be subject to their own husbands, as to the Lord.
Brothers and sisters, did you notice? God’s command to husbands is weightier. Wives are to submit; husbands are to deny themselves.
Children are to obey their parents in the Lord and honour their parents; fathers are not to provoke their children to wrath, but to nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Jesus himself is our role model. He is the Lord who created all things, yet he went back to Nazareth and was subject to his earthly parents (Luke 2:51).
Third, there are consequences to leaving our originally intended position.

Isaiah 14 records the fall of the “shining one, son of the dawn.” Count them with me: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High.
Five “I will”s in all.
Brothers and sisters, this is the anatomy of pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to take God’s place.
He wanted to go up, and went down; he wanted to rise, and fell.
The Bible gives us three more warnings.

Korah was a Levite who already held an extremely honourable office, yet he grabbed for the priesthood — and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up. Moses asked him one question: “Is it a small thing to you?”
When King Uzziah became strong, his heart was lifted up; he went into the temple on his own to burn incense, and leprosy suddenly broke out on his forehead.
Saul couldn’t wait for Samuel and offered the sacrifice himself, and God said: “to obey is better than sacrifice.”
Brothers and sisters, God establishes order not to restrict us but to protect us. Railway tracks are not there to restrict the train but to let it run at full speed.
Fourth, humility is returning to order.
“Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

Humility isn’t constantly saying “I can’t, I’m not worthy” — that’s just another way of talking about yourself. Humility is taking our eyes off ourselves and letting them rest on the place God has appointed.
If the hand wants to see in place of the eye, if the foot fights to be the head, the body stops functioning normally.
Only when every joint does its own part does the body grow and build itself up in love.

The one who said, “I will make myself like the Most High,” was brought down to Sheol; this One “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,” but emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death, and God highly exalted him.
Brothers and sisters, this is the law of the kingdom of heaven: those who grab for position fall; those who return to their originally intended position are lifted up.
There are four practices today.
One, reflecting on my place: in my roles in the family, the workplace and the church, have I overstepped, or have I left my place empty?
Two, practising submission: when you hear an opinion you disagree with, be quiet for three seconds and say, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?”
Three, restoring order: in conflict, don’t ask who is right and who is wrong; ask only, “Am I standing in my own place?”
Four, a prayer of reverence: say every day, “Lord, let me walk in your order, turning neither to the left nor to the right.”
Brothers and sisters, a kite flies high not because it has broken free of its string, but because it has a string. Once the string snaps, the kite doesn’t fly higher; it crashes faster.
When people return to their originally intended position, God’s order is restored, relationships are healed and lives are built up.
True humility is not bowing our heads; it is returning to God’s order.
Let us learn from Jesus, our role model, submitting to God’s will in the right place — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let us pray together.
Dear Heavenly Father, you are the God of order, not a God of confusion. Forgive us that so often we are not content with the place you have given us, and our eyes are fixed on other people’s offices.
We ask that the Holy Spirit would bring us back each day to the place you have appointed. Let us never overstep, never exalt ourselves, and turn neither to the left nor to the right.
May you reign in our lives, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May God’s order be the track you run on all through today. Brothers and sisters, peace be with you.
Brothers and sisters, good morning.
This morning we’re reading Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 91, together. The title is “Return to Our Originally Intended Position,” and the theme is “Order.”
Our theme verse is just one sentence, but it carries real weight: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

Over the last few lessons we have been learning about humility together. We learned that true humility is laying down our rights. Today the Bible takes us one layer deeper: true humility is not only laying down our rights; it is returning to our originally intended position.
On the afternoon of 14 August 2003, North America suffered the largest blackout in its history. Some fifty million people lost their power in the sweltering heat of high summer.

The investigation found that the starting point was almost unbelievably small: a power line in Ohio overheated and sagged until it touched a tree that hadn’t been trimmed — and the alarm system happened to fail at that very moment.
One line left the place where it was meant to be, and within a few hours the whole grid went down like a row of dominoes.
Brothers and sisters, this is what disorder looks like. Disorder seldom begins with something big; disorder almost always begins with one little thing that is not where it is meant to be.
So humility has two levels.
Laying down our rights is being willing to stop insisting on “what I deserve”; returning to our originally intended position is being willing to go back to “the place God has appointed for me.”

Let me ask two questions. Why is it that in some families everyone works so hard and everyone loves one another so much, and yet they keep quarrelling until they are utterly worn out? Why is it that in some churches everyone is so gifted and so zealous, and yet in the end they go from co-workers to combatants?

Very often the problem is not too little love or too few gifts; the problem is being in the wrong place. The hand is working very hard — but it is doing the eye’s job. The foot is doing its best — but it wants the head’s seat.
“Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).

The author of this letter is generally held to be Jude, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. He did not call himself the Lord’s brother; he called himself only “a servant of Jesus Christ” (Jude 1) — and that in itself is a declaration of returning to his originally intended position.
The Greek word behind “first domain” is archē, meaning the office and sphere entrusted by God.
Brothers and sisters, this is one of the Bible’s most profound definitions of sin: the essence of sin is often not doing something bad, but standing in the wrong place.
Our first main point: God is a God of order.

The very first sentence of the Bible proclaims this God: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The second verse says the earth was formless and empty. God’s work of creation is precisely turning chaos into order.

Then, day after day, everything proceeds in perfect order. First light, then the separation of day and night; first the sky and the waters, then the birds and the fish; first the land and the plants were prepared, and only then was man created to live among them.
Do you see it? God always prepares the container first and then puts in the contents; he prepares the home first and then brings in those who will live there.
Order isn’t only in the first six days of creation; it is in the universe today.

The average distance between the earth and the sun is about 149.6 million kilometres; the earth’s axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and so we have spring, summer, autumn and winter; the moon is on average about 384,000 kilometres away, and its gravity pulls on the tides of the oceans day and night.
Brothers and sisters, what scientists actually do is just one thing: describe the order God has established.
Paul says: “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together” (Colossians 1:17). The universe does not hold itself up; it is upheld by him.
Order is the display of God’s glory.
The psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1).

Order is inside our bodies too. The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to three scientists who discovered the molecular mechanisms of the biological clock. It turns out that even the tiniest cells in our bodies run to a twenty-four-hour rhythm.
The church father Augustine said in The City of God: the peace of all things is the tranquillity of order.

From the perspective of 321, this is the second of the Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard. A standard is the line God has painted on the running track — the white lines don’t restrict the athletes; they make the race a race.
Our second main point: there is a God-appointed order in our relationships too.
Before Paul speaks of any particular role, he first gives an overarching principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21).

Someone may ask: if we are to submit to one another, why do we still need an order? Paul says elsewhere: “the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

Brothers and sisters, notice that last phrase — the head of Christ is God. The Son shares equal honour and glory with the Father, yet the Son willingly stands in the place of submission. So submission never means inferiority.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25). “Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22).
Brothers and sisters, did you notice? God’s command to husbands is weightier. Wives are to submit; husbands are to deny themselves.
“Children, obey your parents in the Lord” (Ephesians 6:1). “You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).

This is not a matter of higher and lower status; it is the order of love. When every person stands in their originally intended position, the family is full of peace; but when someone leaves their place, the family falls into confusion.
Of all role models, the most beautiful is Jesus himself.
He is the Lord who created all things, yet he submitted to his earthly parents: “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them” (Luke 2:51).
All his life he also submitted to the Father: “I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 5:30).

The centurion of Capernaum said to Jesus: “For I am also a man under authority, having under myself soldiers” (Matthew 8:9). Jesus marvelled, and said he hadn’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel.
Brothers and sisters, only a person who knows he is under authority can truly recognise who is in authority; those who understand submission have the greatest faith.

Salvador Minuchin, the founder of structural family therapy, pointed out in his 1974 book Families and Family Therapy that healthy families have clear boundaries. When the boundaries blur, and a child is drawn in to fill a spouse’s place and carry emotional responsibilities that don’t belong to them, the whole family stops functioning.

Murray Bowen, a pioneer of family systems theory, also observed that when a relationship becomes tense, people easily pull in a third person to form a triangle — which eases things in the short term but locks the problem in place in the long term.

Brothers and sisters, what wears people out most is often not having too much to do, but not knowing where they stand. This research is not meant to replace the Bible; it only confirms what the Bible said long ago.
Our third main point: leaving our originally intended position has terrible consequences.

Isaiah 14 records these words: “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! … You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly … I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:12–14).
Count them — five “I will”s in all.
A note in passing: “Lucifer” comes from the Latin translation, while the Hebrew simply means “shining one, son of the dawn”; and the Bible never calls him an archangel.
Brothers and sisters, these five “I will”s are the anatomy of pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to take God’s place.
“Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:15). He wanted to go up, and went down.
The Bible gives us three more warnings.

The first is Korah. He was a Levite who already held an extremely honourable office. Moses asked him: “Is it a small thing to you … Do you seek the priesthood also?” (Numbers 16:9–10). And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up.
Brothers and sisters, Korah’s problem was not that he had no place; it was that he looked down on the place God had given him.

The second is King Uzziah. He was a good king, but “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up”; he went into the temple on his own to burn incense, and leprosy suddenly broke out on his forehead (2 Chronicles 26:16–19). His failure was this: he did something that looked spiritual from the wrong place.
The third is Saul. He couldn’t wait for Samuel and offered the sacrifice himself, and Samuel said to him: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22).
These examples follow the same trajectory: dissatisfied with the place God has given, reaching out to grab a place that is not ours, then confusion, then destruction.

Let me use an illustration. The World Health Organization describes cancer as abnormal cells growing uncontrollably, going beyond their usual boundaries and invading other parts of the body. Brothers and sisters, cancer cells are not an enemy invading from outside; they were originally our own cells. What makes them deadly is that they have left their originally intended position.
That is why 321 puts it so precisely: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Please remember this: God establishes order not to restrict us but to protect us. Railway tracks are not there to restrict the train but to let it run at full speed. A train without tracks is not called free; it is called derailed.
Our fourth main point: humility is returning to order.
“Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).
The original word behind “think reasonably” means to be clear-headed, of sound mind: don’t overestimate, and don’t underestimate either.
Brothers and sisters, some people think humility means constantly saying, “I can’t, I’m not worthy.” But that isn’t humility; it is just another way of talking about yourself.
True humility is taking our eyes off ourselves, letting them rest on the place God has appointed, and saying: Lord, this is what you have given me; here I will be faithful.

Paul uses the body as an illustration. “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired” (1 Corinthians 12:18). “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

If the hand wants to see in place of the eye, if the foot fights to become the head, the whole body stops functioning normally. If a hand really grew an eye, that would not be called a gift; it would be called a deformity.

Put these two passages side by side. The one who said, “I will make myself like the Most High,” was brought down to Sheol; this One “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,” but emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death, and so God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6–9).
Brothers and sisters, this is the law of the kingdom of heaven: those who grab for position fall; those who return to their originally intended position are lifted up.
There are four practices today; let’s take them one at a time.

First, reflecting on my place. Write down every role you currently have, and then ask two questions: have I reached out to do things that are not mine to do? Have I dumped onto others the things I ought to do? Overstepping hurts people, and so does leaving a place empty.
Second, practising submission. This week, when you hear an opinion you disagree with, please be quiet for three seconds first and say in your heart, “Lord, what do you want me to learn from this?”

The Bible says: “Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities” (Romans 13:1). Of course, if an authority asks us to go against God’s word, we must obey God (Acts 5:29); but apart from that, submission is our safest place.
Third, restoring order. In a relationship conflict, don’t ask who is right and who is wrong; ask: am I standing in my own place?

Brothers and sisters, “Who is right and who is wrong?” pushes both people into the judge’s seat — and there is only one Judge. When both people sit on the judgment seat, no one in the home is left standing in the place of love.

Fourth, a prayer of reverence. Say every day: “Lord, let me walk in your order, turning neither to the left nor to the right.” This prayer has a scriptural foundation: “You shall not turn away to the right hand or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32).

And to keep going for the long haul, use the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. When you’ve done it, evaluate; when you get it wrong, correct; once corrected, repeat; and finally, multiply it to one person near you.
Let’s place what we have seen today within 321.

The Three Foundations are three declarations about place. Jesus is my role model — with his whole life he demonstrated what it means to return to our originally intended position. The Bible is my standard — I don’t find my place by feelings; I find it by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — every day it is the Holy Spirit who brings me back to where I ought to stand.

The Two Core Values are the core of order. To let Jesus be King is to acknowledge that there is only one on the throne. To let Jesus receive all the glory is to send every bit of credit back to where it was always meant to go.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Self-centred people spend their whole lives asking, “Why him and not me?” Selfless people ask only one thing: “Lord, where do you want me to stand?”

The fivefold change is here too: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. How many ministries have broken apart not because someone did the wrong thing, but because someone stood in the wrong place!
A kite flies high not because it has broken free of its string, but because it has a string. Once the string snaps, the kite doesn’t fly higher; it crashes faster.
When people return to their originally intended position, God’s order is restored, relationships are healed and lives are built up.
True humility is not bowing our heads; it is returning to God’s order.
Now please grow quiet and let the Holy Spirit ask you a question: Lord, is there a place you gave me that I have left? Is there a place you did not give me that I am clinging to?
Come back. There you will find God’s protection, God’s provision and the peace God has prepared for you.
Let us pray together.
Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. You are the God of order, not a God of confusion. From the farthest star to the smallest cell in our bodies, everything moves along the course you have set.
Lord, forgive us. So often we are not content with the place you have given us; our eyes are fixed on other people’s offices, and so often we neglect our own originally intended position.
We ask that the Holy Spirit would guide us and bring us back each day to the place you have appointed: in our families, back to the order of love; in the church, each joint doing its own part.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you willingly emptied yourself and became obedient to the point of death. Give us that same mind, we pray. Let us never overstep, never exalt ourselves, and turn neither to the left nor to the right.
May you reign in our lives, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May God’s order be the track you run on all through today. Brothers and sisters, peace be with you.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Universe Doesn’t Need You on Night Shift
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Let me begin with a very ordinary, homely question: when you opened your eyes this morning, what was the first thought that surfaced in your heart?

My guess is that, for many of us, that first thought was not thanksgiving but a list. The children’s grades, a parent’s test results, the case that’s stuck at work, the bills, the knots in our relationships — one after another they queue up beside the bed, waiting for you. The sun isn’t even up, and your shoulders are already aching. Deep in our hearts lies an assumption we rarely say out loud: if I don’t hold all this up, it will all collapse.

But listen to a fact. In the hours you slept last night, your heart did not take the night off. At seventy beats a minute it beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day, and you have never once given it an order. Right now the earth beneath our feet is racing around the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second, without a hair’s breadth of error, and nobody is working the night shift to push it. In 2013 a study published in the journal Science by Lulu Xie and colleagues at the University of Rochester in the United States found something more: while we sleep, the brain’s glymphatic system speeds up the clearing away of the metabolic waste that has built up during the day. God even cleans out your brain for you while you sleep.

The psalmist put this into poetry long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain. It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.” (Psalm 127:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, the universe doesn’t need you on night shift. God is never late, and he never drops anything. So why are we still so tired?

The introduction to this lesson gives us a very simple yet very profound sentence: “Let God be God, and let man be man.” Our greatest pride is wanting to “replace God”. We think we can help God do things faster and better; we think he is too slow, too quiet, too inactive. With one breath we cry, “Lord, I trust you,” and with the next we slot his work into our own diary.

This kind of replacing usually wears two faces.

The first face is “replacing God in the doing” — I’m going to produce the result for God. If the sick person isn’t healed, I blame myself; if my child doesn’t turn back, I double the pressure; if the promise hasn’t yet come true, I come up with a clever plan to help God get it done early.

The second face is “replacing God in the glory” — I’m going to take the applause on God’s behalf. The thing succeeds, people praise me, and my lips say, “Thank the Lord,” while my heart quietly makes a note: that was my gift, my hard work.

These two faces actually grow from one root: pride.

The Bible has a very short and very sharp verse that cuts straight to the heart of this: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6) Where our English Bible has “first domain”, the Chinese Union Version reads “proper position” — the very word this lesson keeps returning to. The Greek word is ἀρχή (archē), which means “beginning”, and also “office” or “position of authority”. The angels did not fall because they lacked ability, but because they refused to stay in the place God had assigned them. Sin has never been only doing the wrong thing; it is standing in the wrong place.

The core message of Kingdom 321 Online Fellowship puts it precisely: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

In this lesson we will follow the text along four steps: recognising our position — I am human, not God; learning to let go — let God be God; seeing the danger of replacing God — the example of Abraham; and giving the glory to God — not grabbing what belongs to God.

May the Holy Spirit, this morning, bring us back to the place where we ought to stand.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Source, the Means and the End of All Things
sections.html:
The theme passage of this lesson comes from the close of Romans 11. To understand these four verses, we first need to stand where they were written.

The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. From the clues in the letter — he commends Phoebe, “a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae” (Romans 16:1), and mentions “Gaius, my host and host of the whole assembly” (Romans 16:23), and Cenchreae was the port of Corinth — scholars generally conclude that the letter was written around AD 56–57, in Corinth, towards the end of Paul’s third missionary journey. At the time he was preparing to take the churches’ gift to Jerusalem, and then to travel by way of Rome to Spain (Romans 15:24–26).

The church in Rome that received the letter had not been founded by Paul, and it was a mixture of Jewish and Gentile believers. In AD 49 Claudius had ordered the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2); a few years later they began to return, only to find that the church was now mostly Gentile. And so a question arose: could the Gentile believers now think themselves superior?

Romans 9 to 11 is Paul’s answer to that question. He works his way through God’s election, Israel’s stumbling and the grace given to the Gentiles, and finally gives the Gentile believers a stern warning: “Don’t be conceited, but fear.” (Romans 11:20) For the branches cannot boast over the root; the wild olive shoot that was grafted in draws its richness from that root.

At this point Paul’s pen suddenly stops. He no longer argues; he worships. Romans 11:33–36 is one of the most magnificent doxologies in the New Testament. The three questions he fires off in a row are all drawn from the Old Testament: the first two come from Isaiah 40:13, and the third echoes Job 41:11. These three questions press right on the deepest root of the sickness in the human heart: we always assume we can serve as God’s adviser, that we can give God ideas, and even that God owes us something.

Then Paul writes the verse that sums everything up: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things.”

Here the Greek uses three prepositions, like three pillars holding up an entire temple: ἐξ (of him) — God is the source of all things; διά (through him) — God is the sustainer of all things; εἰς (to him) — God is the destination of all things. He is the beginning, he is the way, and he is the end.

If all things are “of him”, then my gifts, my health, my family and my service are all received. If all things are “through him”, then there is not a single moment when I am holding myself up — not even the breath I am drawing now. If all things are “to him”, then none of the fruit or the glory should stop with me.

Genesis 1:26 says that God made humankind to have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky and all the earth. What we were given is “stewardship”, not “ownership”. A steward may use all of his master’s resources, but he may not sit in his master’s chair. “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2) A steward’s duty is to be faithful, not to be almighty.

The last line of this doxology is the conclusion of the whole Bible, and the destination of this lesson: “To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”

This is exactly the Two Core Values of the 321 vision: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. To let Jesus be King is to live out “of him and through him”; to let Jesus receive all the glory is to give back what is “to him”.

Now let us follow the text and walk back to our own originally intended position.

sections.heading: 3. Recognising Our Position: I Am Human, Not God
sections.html:
1. The position we most easily confuse

Right at the start the text points out a mistake we often make without noticing: “taking over” God’s place.

The example it gives is very true to life: we pray for someone who is sick. If they are not healed, we blame ourselves and suspect our faith is not strong enough; if they recover, we easily become smug and think, “My prayers are powerful.”

Listen carefully to what these two reactions have in common: whether it is self-blame or self-congratulation, the focus is on “me”. The first is the pride of discouragement, the second the pride of success; they are two sides of the same coin.

But the authority to heal belongs to God, not to us. Our responsibility is to pray and to trust; the outcome rests in God’s will. We are responsible for obeying; God is responsible for accomplishing. If the sick person gets well, God receives the glory; if they do not, we still hold on to our faith.

The text draws this boundary in a single, crystal-clear sentence: “I am human; I pray. You are God; you heal.”

This is the humility of standing in our originally intended position.

2. Scripture interpreting Scripture: even the Son of God stayed in his place

There is a sentence worth remembering for the rest of our lives. The one who said it was not a weak disciple but the Lord Jesus himself:

“Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19)

Think about it: even the Son of God made flesh deliberately lived on earth in a place of obedience to the Father. Before he died he said, “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). If even Jesus did not grab the Father’s place, what right do we have?

The Lord also said, “Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’” (Luke 17:10) “Unworthy servants” doesn’t mean we have no value; it means we claim no credit and seek no reward.

Paul says as well: “Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3) “To think more highly” is the Greek ὑπερφρονεῖν (hyperphronein), literally “to over-think” — to let your thoughts spill over into a space that doesn’t belong to you.

3. The boundary of responsibility: the backpack and the boulder

In Galatians, Paul uses two verses that seem to contradict each other to mark out the boundaries of our position.

“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:2)

“For each man will bear his own burden.” (Galatians 6:5)

The second verse says each person carries his own; the first says we are to carry one another’s. Is that a contradiction? No. In English both verses say “burden”, but the original uses two different words. The “burden” of verse 5 is φορτίον (phortion), the pack a soldier carries on his back — each person’s own share of responsibility, a load he can manage. The “burdens” of verse 2 are βάρος (baros), a crushing boulder — a disaster no one can carry alone.

Our pain often comes from getting these two the wrong way round: we toss onto God the backpack we ought to carry ourselves, and then snatch up the boulder that only God can lift, and carry it until our spine is bent out of shape.

Psychology offers corroborating evidence here. In 1966, in Psychological Monographs, the American psychologist Julian B. Rotter introduced the idea of the “locus of control”. Research since then has broadly found that a healthy state of mind is neither to take everything on ourselves nor to blame everything on our circumstances, but to discern accurately what lies within our control and what does not. In their 1992 book “Boundaries”, the clinical psychologists Henry Cloud and John Townsend also observe that many Christians are worn out not because they love too much, but because they have drawn their boundaries in the wrong place.

The sixteenth-century French surgeon Ambroise Paré is called the father of modern surgery. He is generally credited with a saying that is still repeated today: “I dressed him, and God healed him.” The beauty of that sentence lies in its division of labour: dressing the wound is my job, and I give it everything I have; healing is God’s job, and I entrust it to him completely. Brothers and sisters, do today’s dressing well, and then leave the healing to God.

4. The hardest test of all: at home

The text then carries this principle into the closest place of all: the family.

We often want to “change other people” — to change our husband, our wife, our children. We draw up a list of their problems, remind them again and again, raise our voice, even put pressure on them with spiritual language. The result is that the relationship grows tighter and tighter, and the person does not change.

But the only one who can truly change a human heart is the Spirit of God. Our responsibility is to change ourselves and to love to the end.

The text says something I really love: “Give the hard part to Jesus, and do the easy part ourselves — that is the dividing line between humility and wisdom.”

Changing other people is hard; changing ourselves is hard too, but that is the part God has handed to us. In his 1961 book “On Becoming a Person”, the American psychologist Carl Rogers wrote: “The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.” The idea of “differentiation of self” put forward by the family-therapy pioneer Murray Bowen points to the same thing: the less a person is pulled along by the other’s emotions in a close relationship, the healthier the relationship becomes.

You don’t have to control someone in order to love them; it is when you let go of control that love truly begins.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision: The Priority of Relationships
sections.html:
The 321 vision speaks of “the priority of relationships”: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

The chaos in our homes often comes from getting the order upside down. We deal with “things” first — whose turn it is to wash up, who came home late again; then we deal with “people” — how could you do that? — and we never first become quiet before God. Returning to our originally intended position means setting the order straight: first with God — this home today is yours; then with ourselves — please change this controlling heart of mine first; then with others — I am going to love him, not manage him; and only last of all, things.

The 321 vision also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. Manage your child as an item on your to-do list, and you will lose the person he is.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, ask yourself honestly: in my daily living, which matter have I been sitting on God’s seat over all this time?

sections.heading: 4. Learning to Let Go: Let God Be God
sections.html:
1. The root of anxiety is gripping too tightly

The text says that the reason we grow anxious, troubled and disappointed is often that we “grip too tightly”. When money runs short, we worry about what tomorrow will bring; when the future is unclear, we try to find our own way. Yet provision is God’s responsibility; obedience is ours.

Brothers and sisters, notice this word: “grip”. The essence of anxiety is not caring, but gripping. Caring is love; gripping is control. A father caring about his son’s future is love; wanting to decide every step for his son and hold every outcome in his hand — that is gripping.

The Lord Jesus put it very bluntly: “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?” (Matthew 6:27) What have we gained in exchange for our worrying? Sleepless nights, stomach aches, quarrels with our family — everything except one extra moment of life.

“To be anxious” in New Testament Greek is μεριμνάω (merimnaō), from the same root as “to divide” (μερίζω). The true face of anxiety is a heart torn in two: half of it here eating breakfast, half of it inside tomorrow’s disaster; half of it worshipping, half of it calculating.

2. The theme promise: seek his Kingdom first

The text quotes that familiar verse: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33)

Notice the word “first”. The Lord did not say “seek only” his Kingdom, nor did he say those other things don’t matter; he is speaking about order. Food and clothing do matter, but they may not take first place.

The context of this verse is Matthew 6:25–34. The Lord first speaks of the birds of the sky: “See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns” — and the heavenly Father feeds them. Then he speaks of the lilies of the field. Finally he draws his conclusion: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.” (Matthew 6:34) God wants us to focus on trusting, not to be anxious about outcomes.

Notice, though: the birds neither sow nor reap, but they aren’t lying about either. Every morning they go out as usual to find food. God’s provision never cancels our duty; it only cancels our anxiety. You are to work, but you don’t have to be afraid; you are to do your best, but you don’t have to guarantee the outcome on God’s behalf.

3. Two actions: casting off and being still

Peter uses a very vivid word: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:6–7)

“Casting” is the Greek ἐπιρίπτω (epiriptō), meaning “to throw forcefully upon”. The same word appears in Luke 19:35, where the disciples “threw” their cloaks on the colt. It is a decisive action, done once and done fully — lifting the load off your own shoulders and flinging it onto someone else’s back.

Notice Peter’s order: first “humble yourselves”, then “cast”. For the person who will not come down low cannot cast off his worries. Beneath worry there is often an unspoken sentence: “Only I can deal with this.” That is pride, not a sense of responsibility.

David models another action: “Yahweh, my heart isn’t arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.” (Psalm 131:1–2)

What a beautiful picture. A baby not yet weaned lies in its mother’s arms wanting something; a weaned child lies in her arms wanting simply its mother. Brothers and sisters, as you lie in God’s arms today, are you wanting something, or wanting God?

4. Psychology as a witness: white bears and stress

In a classic experiment published in 1987 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Daniel M. Wegner and his colleagues asked participants “not to think about a white bear”. The result was that the participants not only kept thinking of white bears while they were suppressing the thought, but once the restriction was lifted, they thought of them even more often than people who had never been asked to suppress the thought at all.

Here is a reminder: gritting your teeth and telling yourself “Don’t worry” usually doesn’t work; the harder you try, the more you worry. The Bible doesn’t tell us to press our worries down by willpower, but to “cast” them away onto a God who cares for us. “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6–7) Not suppressing, but handing over.

Brothers and sisters, this is the first of the changes the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life. How you see a matter affects you more than the matter itself.

5. An illustration from life: struggling in the water

Any swimming coach will tell you that when people sink in the water, it is usually not because they can’t swim but because they are too tense. The human body is very close to water in density; with the lungs full of air and the body relaxed and lying flat, most people will float. But the moment you panic, thrash your arms and legs and let all your breath out, you go under.

The water hasn’t changed; you have. Faith is the same. The hands that hold you up have been there all along; it is our struggling that drags us down. Letting go doesn’t mean not moving; it means not flailing. It doesn’t mean not trying; it means not overstepping.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: rely on the heart and not the brain

The 321 vision has a very down-to-earth reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. The wellspring of life flows from the heart (Proverbs 4:23).

“Relying on the brain and ourselves” means moving God’s seat into our own heads, rehearsing every worst-case scenario over and over and preparing a plan for each one. It is exhausting, and most of the disasters we rehearse never happen. “Relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit” doesn’t mean not thinking; it means surrendering before we think: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

The 321 vision also speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. If you weighed the thing you are anxious about today on the scales of eternity, how heavy would it still be?

If we let God be God, life becomes light and free, no longer weighed down.

sections.heading: 5. The Danger of Replacing God: The Example of Abraham
sections.html:
1. Ten years of waiting, and one clever plan

The text says that Abraham’s story is the deepest warning of all.

Let’s lay out the timeline. Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4); after he had lived in Canaan for ten years, Sarai gave Hagar to him, and he was eighty-five (Genesis 16:3); and when Isaac was born, he was a hundred (Genesis 21:5).

In other words, they very nearly made it. Only fifteen years to go.

This is how the Bible records it: “Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. Sarai said to Abram, ‘See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.’ Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” (Genesis 16:1–2)

Notice Sarai’s wording. “I will obtain children by her” is the Hebrew אִבָּנֶה (’ibbaneh), literally “I may be built”; the root “to build” (בנה, banah) is related to “son” (בֵּן, ben) and “house” (בַּיִת, bayit). What Sarai wanted was not just a child, but a life that had been built up. Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of us: we rush ahead, not because we don’t believe there is a God, but because we are afraid our own lives won’t get built, and so we start building God’s house for him.

And please pay close attention to another sentence: “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” It carries an ominous echo — in Genesis 3:17 God says to Adam, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice …” When a human voice replaces God’s voice, the ending goes wrong. Sarai acted with good intentions, Abram acted out of compliance, and neither of them was a bad person. Replacing God is very often done by good people.

2. The result: human methods produce human problems

The text asks the right question: what was the result?

Ishmael, born through “human methods”, brought conflict and division. God said of this child: “He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him.” (Genesis 16:12) As soon as Hagar conceived, she looked down on her mistress; Sarai mistreated her; Hagar ran away; and from then on the household had no peace (Genesis 16:4–6). By Genesis 21:10 Sarah is saying, “Cast out this servant and her son!” Abraham’s good intentions brewed long-lasting bitter fruit.

Later Paul, interpreting Scripture by Scripture, spelled out the spiritual principle in this event: “For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the servant, and one by the free woman. However, the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise.” (Galatians 4:22–23)

“According to the flesh” and “through promise” — these are the two roads. What is born of the flesh has to be kept going by more and more of the flesh; what is born of promise, God himself takes responsibility for to the end. Any result forced through by human methods will have to be propped up afterwards by still more human methods: obedience gained through pressure needs ever greater pressure to keep it in place. It is a road that grows more exhausting the further you go.

3. Human good intentions are not necessarily God’s intention

The text puts it with great insight: human good intentions are not necessarily God’s intention; wanting to help God is really replacing God. Pride doesn’t always shout out loud; sometimes it comes wrapped in the kindness of “I just want to help you”.

“‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.’” (Isaiah 55:8–9) He does not need our help; what he wants is our trust and obedience.

So it was with Saul as well. At Gilgal he waited seven days for Samuel; unable to wait any longer, he offered the burnt offering himself, and the moment Samuel arrived he said, “You have done foolishly.” (1 Samuel 13:13) He was only a little early. The greatest failures in the spiritual life are often not doing bad things, but grabbing God’s timing in doing the right thing.

4. Psychology as a witness: the action bias

This urge — “I can’t wait any longer; I have to do something” — is what psychology calls the “action bias”.

A study by Michael Bar-Eli and colleagues, published in 2007 in the Journal of Economic Psychology, analysed 286 penalty kicks in top-level football matches. Goalkeepers dived left or right more than 94 per cent of the time and stayed in the centre only about 6 per cent of the time; yet nearly 30 per cent of the kicks actually went down the middle, and goalkeepers who stayed put had the highest save rate. So why do goalkeepers still dive? Because conceding a goal while standing still feels more embarrassing than diving the wrong way. People would rather do the wrong thing than look as if they did nothing.

Brothers and sisters, that was Abram’s psychology exactly. Waiting ten years looked like doing nothing; taking Hagar at least looked like “moving God’s plan forward”.

Our hearts are by nature wired to grab hold of something; and faith is precisely the work the Holy Spirit does within us that runs against that nature.

5. The turning point: letting go on Mount Moriah

Thank the Lord, the story didn’t stop with Hagar. The text says that later, when God commanded Abraham to offer up Isaac, he learned to let go completely. This time he no longer used his own methods, but simply listened to God’s voice.

Notice what happened in between. Between Genesis 16:16 and 17:1, the Bible is silent for thirteen years. For those thirteen years he held the son he had produced by his own methods, yet he could not hear God’s voice — what a costly lesson.

Then, on Mount Moriah, the man who had once come up with plans on God’s behalf had the son he had received by faith asked of him by God. This time he offered no ideas; he simply rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey and walked for three days. As a result he not only experienced the provision of “Yahweh Will Provide”, but also received God’s blessing and trust.

“Abraham called the name of that place ‘Yahweh Will Provide’. As it is said to this day, ‘On Yahweh’s mountain, it will be provided.’” (Genesis 22:14)

“Yahweh Will Provide” is the Hebrew יְהוָה יִרְאֶה (YHWH yir’eh), which translated literally means “Yahweh will see”. God’s provision begins with God’s seeing. When Abraham reached the mountain, God had long since placed the ram in the thicket (Genesis 22:13) — that ram was not created at the moment he raised the knife; it was just that Abraham had not seen it before. Brothers and sisters, the provision you need today may already be on the mountain; you simply haven’t got there yet.

This is how Paul assesses Abraham’s final faith: “Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.” (Romans 4:20–21) Look at the order in this sentence: grew strong through faith, gave glory to God, and was fully assured. The final outlet of faith is giving glory to God — which is exactly our fourth key point.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan

The 321 vision says that pride is the root of the problem, and the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The Hagar episode was a product of the self-centred life: my calculations, my methods, my timetable. Mount Moriah was the practice of selflessness: “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (see Galatians 2:20). Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When Abraham laid Isaac down on the mountain, what he received back was not only Isaac but the promise, “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring” (Genesis 22:18). Those who let go do not lose; those who let go gain God.

Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission, is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” Brothers and sisters, if God’s work is done in man’s way, it will certainly lack God’s supply — and we will try to make up the shortfall with more and more human methods, until we are utterly spent.

sections.heading: 6. Giving the Glory to God: Don’t Grab What Belongs to God
sections.html:
1. Another kind of replacing: keeping the applause for ourselves

The text reminds us that we may replace God not only in the “doing” but also in the “glory”. The first grabs God’s work; the second grabs God’s name. And the second is often more hidden, because it doesn’t need a hand to move — only a thought in the heart.

The text gives an example that makes us smile, yet stings: ask Sunday-school children, “Who parted the Red Sea?” and most will answer, “Moses.” But in fact it was God who parted the sea; Moses was only the vessel who stretched out the staff. The Bible says: “Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.” (Exodus 14:21)

Look at the structure of that verse: Moses stretched out his hand; Yahweh sent the wind. Moses was responsible for a one-second gesture; Yahweh was responsible for a whole night’s mighty work. And before that, Moses had already made it plain: “Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.” (Exodus 14:14)

The children get it wrong because they only see the person standing at the front. Brothers and sisters, so do we — and sometimes that person is us.

2. Scripture interpreting Scripture: the planter and the waterer are nothing

Paul also says: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6)

The background of this verse is the factional quarrelling in the Corinthian church. Some said, “I follow Paul”; others said, “I follow Apollos” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Paul’s answer was to move everyone’s position down a notch: “So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:7)

“Is not anything” isn’t self-deprecation; it is accuracy. From the moment a seed sprouts to the moment it bears fruit, no farmer can produce the mystery of “growth” in between; all we can do is put the seed in the ground and pour on the water. All we can do is our duty; the result always lies in what God does.

Paul shuts every human mouth with a question: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) Brothers and sisters, think about it honestly: your mind, your health, the mentor you happened to meet, the door that happened to open — which of these did you earn yourself?

3. A sobering example: Moses strikes the rock

Grabbing God’s glory can carry a heavy price.

Numbers 20 records that at Kadesh the Israelites quarrelled because there was no water. God told Moses to take his staff and to speak to the rock so that it would give out water. But what Moses said was: “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Numbers 20:10)

The Chinese Union Version reads “Must I bring water …”, but in the Hebrew the verb is first person plural — “Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” With a single sentence Moses turned God’s act into “our” act. Then, instead of speaking to the rock, he struck it twice with his staff. The water still came out, but God said to Moses: “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.” (Numbers 20:12)

Forty years of patience, brought down by one sentence.

Brothers and sisters, the fact that God made the water flow does not mean he approved of that “we … for you”. Fruitfulness in ministry does not mean God agrees with our taking the credit for it.

4. Three pictures from the New Testament

The New Testament gives us three vivid pictures of “giving the glory”.

The first is a negative one. In Caesarea, Herod put on his royal robes and addressed the people, and they shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” The result: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

The second is a positive one. In Lystra, Paul and Barnabas healed a man who had been lame from birth, and the crowds wanted to offer sacrifices to them as gods. At once they tore their clothes and shouted: “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you.” (Acts 14:15)

The third concerns an angel. In a vision John fell down to worship the angel who was speaking to him, and the angel said, “Look! Don’t do it! … Worship God.” (Revelation 19:10)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The apostles, even the angels, refuse to give an inch on this one thing: I too am human, I too am a servant, and the glory must not stop with me.

So however fruitful your service may be, however much people praise you — remember: we are human, not God. That God uses us is grace, but the glory must go to him.

The text also reminds us of the other side: don’t turn a prophet into a god, because prophets can be wrong too; don’t make an idol of God’s servants, because the power comes from God. Lifting a person up onto God’s seat harms him; being lifted up by others and not coming down harms yourself. “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

5. Witnesses from psychology and nature

When it comes to assigning credit, the human heart has a built-in bias. In a 1975 review published in Psychological Bulletin, the American psychologists Dale T. Miller and Michael Ross pointed out that people commonly display a “self-serving bias”: they attribute success to their own ability and effort, and failure to circumstances, luck or other people.

This is exactly the pair of reactions the text described at the start. Our hearts automatically pull credit inwards and push blame outwards; that is why we need, every day, to send the glory back on purpose.

Nature gives us a beautiful picture. The moon lights up the earth, but the moon itself gives off no light; it only reflects the light of the sun, and very inefficiently at that — the moon’s albedo is only about 12 per cent, and nearly nine-tenths of the sunlight that falls on it is absorbed. Yet that tenth or so reflected back is enough to light up an entire wilderness.

Brothers and sisters, we are the moon. We have no light of our own. What we can do is not shine, but not block the light; not manufacture glory, but reflect it. “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7)

The English writer C. S. Lewis wrote in “Mere Christianity” that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind. Humility is not putting yourself down; humility is knowing exactly where you stand.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: let Jesus receive all the glory

The text closes with Romans 11:36, which is also the theme verse of this lesson: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” This is the second of the Two Core Values of the 321 vision: let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, God’s glory never belonged to us in the first place. If we take it, we can’t keep it; it will only crush us. How many gifted servants in history fell not in suffering but in applause.

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) These words of John the Baptist are the freest declaration of everyone who has returned to their originally intended position.
