script12.title: Cover
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 92 together: “Return to Our Originally Intended Position: Do Not Take God’s Place.” Our theme verse is Romans 11:36: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” God is the beginning, and God is the end.

script12.title: The universe doesn’t need you on night shift
script: Brothers and sisters, when you opened your eyes this morning, what was your first thought? My guess is that it wasn’t thanksgiving but a list. The children’s grades, a parent’s tests, the case that’s stuck at work — one after another they queue up waiting for you. The sun isn’t even up, and your shoulders are already aching.

But listen to a fact. While you slept last night, your heart did not take the night off; it beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day, and you have never once given it an order. Right now the earth is racing around the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second, without a hair’s breadth of error, and nobody is working the night shift to push it.

The Bible says: “for he gives sleep to his loved ones” (Psalm 127:2). Brothers and sisters, the universe doesn’t need you on night shift; God is never late, and he never drops anything. So why are we still so tired? Because our greatest pride is wanting to replace God.

script12.title: The source, the means and the end of all things
script: Our theme verse was written by Paul around AD 57, in Corinth. When he speaks of God’s wonderful plan, he stops arguing and starts worshipping. The original uses three prepositions: “of him” — the source; “through him” — the sustainer; “to him” — the destination.
Brothers and sisters, what God gave us is stewardship, not ownership. A steward may use all his master’s resources, but he may not sit in his master’s chair.

script12.title: Recognising our position: I am human, not God
script: The lesson says that we often take over God’s place without noticing. We pray for someone who is sick; if they aren’t healed, we blame ourselves; if they recover, we become smug and think our prayers are powerful. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? Self-blame and self-congratulation both have their focus on “me”: one is the pride of discouragement, the other the pride of success.

But the authority to heal belongs to God, not to us. We are responsible for obeying; God is responsible for accomplishing. So the lesson teaches us to say: “I am human; I pray. You are God; you heal.” The Lord Jesus himself said: “the Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19). If even the Son of God stayed in his place, what right do we have not to?

script12.title: Give the hard part to Jesus
script: At home, this test is the hardest of all. We want to change our husband, our wife, our children; we remind them again and again, we raise our voice — and the relationship grows tighter and tighter, and the person doesn’t change. But the only one who can truly change a human heart is the Spirit of God; our responsibility is to change ourselves and to love to the end.

The lesson says something really beautiful: give the hard part to Jesus, and do the easy part ourselves. Changing his heart is hard — give it to Jesus; giving him a smile at dinner tonight is easy — we do that.
The 321 vision says relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. You don’t have to control someone in order to love them.

script12.title: Learning to let go: let God be God
script: The lesson says that we grow anxious often because we grip too tightly. Caring is love; gripping is control. The Lord says: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33). Notice that the Lord didn’t say “seek only”; he is speaking about order.

Peter says: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). “Casting” in the original means to throw forcefully upon — lifting the load off your shoulders and flinging it onto someone else’s back. It is an action, not a feeling.
The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

script12.title: A warning from Abraham
script: Abraham’s story is the deepest warning of all. He left Haran at seventy-five, took Hagar at eighty-five, and Isaac was born only when he was a hundred. Brothers and sisters, they very nearly made it — only fifteen years to go.

Sarai said: “It may be that I will obtain children by her.” The original says, “I may be built.” We so often rush ahead, not because we don’t believe there is a God, but because we are afraid our lives won’t get built, and so we start building God’s house for him.

And the result? Ishmael brought conflict and division. What is born of the flesh has to be kept going by the flesh; what is born of promise, God himself takes responsibility for to the end. Wanting to help God is really replacing God.

script12.title: Letting go on Mount Moriah
script: Thank the Lord, the story didn’t stop there. Later, when God commanded Abraham to offer up Isaac, this time he offered no ideas; he simply rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey and walked for three days.

As a result he experienced “Yahweh Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14). Translated literally, the name means “Yahweh will see”; God’s provision begins with God’s seeing. The ram had long been in the thicket on the mountain; he simply hadn’t seen it before.
Brothers and sisters, the provision you need today may already be on the mountain; you simply haven’t got there yet.

script12.title: Giving the glory to God
script: We don’t only replace God in the doing; we also take his place in the glory. Ask Sunday-school children, “Who parted the Red Sea?” and most will answer, “Moses.” But the Bible says it was Yahweh who divided the waters by a strong east wind (Exodus 14:21). Moses was responsible for a one-second gesture; Yahweh was responsible for a whole night’s mighty work.

Paul says: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Brothers and sisters, we are like the moon: it gives off no light of its own, only reflecting the light of the sun — and it reflects barely a tenth of it, yet that is enough to light up an entire wilderness. What we are to do is not shine, but not block the light.

script12.title: Practices
script: The lesson gives us four practices. First, entrusting in prayer: after you pray, declare, “Lord, I hand this over to you.” Second, changing myself: when you want to change someone else, first ask the Lord to change you. Third, waiting in faith: while you have not yet seen the promise fulfilled, choose trust, not agitation. Fourth, giving the glory to the Lord: when someone praises you, say in your heart, “Lord, this is your doing.”
Brothers and sisters, please choose one and do it for seven days first; one at a time, and it only counts if you actually do it.

script12.title: Letting God be Lord is the greatest humility
script: The lesson reminds us: wanting to help God is really taking his place; wanting to control the outcome is really usurping his sovereignty. Letting go is not failure but trust; letting God be Lord is the greatest humility.

The greatest weariness of our lives comes not from having too much to do, but from sitting in the wrong seat. This morning the Lord issues you and me a gentle call: come down, return to your originally intended position. Returning to our position is not being demoted; it is being set free.

script12.title: Prayer of response and blessing
script: Let us pray together.

Dear Lord, I am willing to return to my originally intended position — to let you be God, and to be your servant. I lay down my anxiety and my control; I will no longer use my own methods to help you finish things. I place in your hands the person and the matter that weigh on me. You are God; you are responsible for accomplishing it. I am human; I need only obey. All glory, honour and power be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, the Lord bless you and keep you. May you walk lightly today, for of him, and through him, and to him are all things. Amen.

script21.title: Return to Our Originally Intended Position
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 92, together: “Return to Our Originally Intended Position: Do Not Take God’s Place.”
Our theme verse is Romans 11:36: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”
God is the beginning, and God is the end. May this verse be our anchor point this morning.

script21.title: The first thought of the morning
script: Brothers and sisters, when you opened your eyes this morning, what was the first thought that surfaced? My guess is that it wasn’t thanksgiving but a list. The children’s grades, a parent’s test results, the case that’s stuck at work, the bills, the knots in our relationships — one after another they queue up waiting for you. The sun isn’t even up, and your shoulders are already aching. Deep in our hearts lies an assumption we rarely say out loud: if I don’t hold all this up, it will all collapse.
Brothers and sisters, that assumption is the starting point of “replacing God.”

script21.title: The universe doesn’t need you on night shift
script: But listen to a fact. While you slept last night, your heart did not take the night off; at seventy beats a minute it beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day, and you have never once given it an order. Right now the earth is racing around the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second, without a hair’s breadth of error, and nobody is working the night shift to push it.

The psalmist said it long ago: “for he gives sleep to his loved ones” (Psalm 127:2). Brothers and sisters, the universe doesn’t need you on night shift. God is never late, and he never drops anything.

The Bible has a very short verse that cuts straight to the heart of this: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place …” (Jude 6). Sin has never been only doing the wrong thing; it is standing in the wrong place.

script21.title: The source, the means and the end of all things
script: Our theme verse was written by Paul around AD 57, from Corinth, to the church in Rome. He gave the Gentile believers a stern warning: “Don’t be conceited, but fear” (Romans 11:20). At this point Paul’s pen suddenly stops; he no longer argues, he worships. The original uses three prepositions, like three pillars holding up an entire temple: “of him” — the source; “through him” — the sustainer; “to him” — the destination.
Brothers and sisters, what God gave us is “stewardship,” not “ownership.” A steward may use all his master’s resources, but he may not sit in his master’s chair.

script21.title: Recognising our position: I am human, not God
script: The lesson says that we often take over God’s place without noticing. We pray for someone who is sick: if they aren’t healed, we blame ourselves and suspect our faith isn’t strong enough; if they recover, we become smug and think, “My prayers are powerful.” Brothers and sisters, self-blame and self-congratulation both have their focus on “me.” But the authority to heal belongs to God, not to us: we are responsible for obeying; God is responsible for accomplishing. If the sick person gets well, God receives the glory; if they do not, we still hold on to our faith.

So the lesson teaches us to say: “I am human; I pray. You are God; you heal.” The Lord Jesus himself said: “the Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19). If even the Son of God stayed in his place, what right do we have not to?

script21.title: The backpack and the boulder
script: Paul uses two verses that seem to contradict each other to mark out the boundaries of our position: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2), and “For each man will bear his own burden” (Galatians 6:5). The original uses two different words: the “burden” of verse 5 is a soldier’s backpack; the “burdens” of verse 2 are a crushing boulder.

Brothers and sisters, our pain often comes from getting these two the wrong way round: we toss onto God the backpack we ought to carry ourselves, and then snatch up the boulder that only God can lift. The psychologists Cloud and Townsend say in Boundaries that many Christians are worn out because they have drawn their boundaries in the wrong place.
The French surgeon Ambroise Paré left us a saying: “I dressed him, and God healed him.” Do your dressing well, and leave the healing to God.

script21.title: Give the hard part to Jesus
script: At home, this test is the hardest of all. We want to change our husband, our wife, our children; we remind them again and again, we raise our voice — and the relationship grows tighter and tighter, and the person doesn’t change. But the only one who can truly change a human heart is the Spirit of God; our responsibility is to change ourselves and to love to the end.
The lesson says something really beautiful: give the hard part to Jesus, and do the easy part ourselves — that is the dividing line between humility and wisdom.

The psychologist Carl Rogers wrote: “The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.” The 321 vision says relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. You don’t have to control someone in order to love them.

script21.title: The root of anxiety is gripping too tightly
script: The lesson says that the reason we grow anxious, troubled and disappointed is often that we grip too tightly. Brothers and sisters, notice this word: “grip.” Caring is love; gripping is control. The Lord Jesus put it very bluntly: “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?” (Matthew 6:27). What have we gained in exchange for our worrying? Sleepless nights, stomach aches, quarrels with our family — everything except one extra moment of life.
In Greek, “to be anxious” shares a root with “to divide.” The true face of anxiety is a heart torn in two.

script21.title: Seek first his Kingdom and his righteousness
script: The lesson quotes that familiar verse: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).

Notice the word “first”: the Lord didn’t say “seek only” his Kingdom; he is speaking about order. And he draws his conclusion: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow … Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matthew 6:34).

Brothers and sisters, the birds neither sow nor reap, but they aren’t lying about either; every morning they go out as usual to find food. God’s provision doesn’t cancel our duty; it only cancels our anxiety: you are to do your best, but you don’t have to guarantee the outcome on God’s behalf.

script21.title: Cast it on God, for he cares for you
script: Peter says: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). “Casting” in the original means “to throw forcefully upon.” Notice the order: first humble yourself, then cast. The person who will not come down low cannot cast off his worries; beneath worry there is often an unspoken sentence: “Only I can deal with this.”

In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner asked participants “not to think about a white bear,” and they ended up thinking of white bears more often than people who had never been asked to suppress the thought. The Bible doesn’t tell us to press our worries down, but to cast them away.
David says: “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother” (Psalm 131:2). As you lie in God’s arms today, are you wanting something, or wanting God?

script21.title: A clever plan after ten years of waiting
script: The lesson says that Abraham’s story is the deepest warning of all. He left Haran at seventy-five, took Hagar at eighty-five, and Isaac was born only when he was a hundred. Brothers and sisters, they very nearly made it — only fifteen years to go.

Sarai said: “It may be that I will obtain children by her.” The Hebrew literally says, “I may be built.” What she wanted was not just a child, but a life that had been built up. That is a picture of us: we rush ahead, not because we don’t believe there is a God, but because we are afraid our own lives won’t get built.
The Bible goes on: “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” Sarai acted with good intentions, Abram acted out of compliance — replacing God is very often done by good people.

script21.title: Human methods produce human problems
script: And what was the result? Ishmael, born through “human methods,” brought conflict and division. God said of this child: “He will be like a wild donkey among men” (Genesis 16:12). Abraham’s good intentions brewed long-lasting bitter fruit. Later Paul, interpreting Scripture by Scripture, said that the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise (see Galatians 4:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, what is born of the flesh has to be kept going by more and more of the flesh; what is born of promise, God himself takes responsibility for to the end. God says: “my ways are higher than your ways” (Isaiah 55:9). He does not need our help; what he wants is our trust and obedience.

script21.title: Why goalkeepers always dive
script: This urge — “I can’t wait any longer; I have to do something” — is what psychology calls the “action bias.” In 2007 Bar-Eli and colleagues analysed 286 penalty kicks in top-level football: goalkeepers dived left or right more than 94 per cent of the time and stayed in the centre only about 6 per cent of the time; yet nearly 30 per cent of the kicks actually went down the middle, and goalkeepers who stayed put had the highest save rate. So why do they still dive? Because conceding a goal while standing still feels more embarrassing than diving the wrong way.
Brothers and sisters, that was Abram’s psychology exactly. Waiting ten years looked like doing nothing; taking Hagar at least looked like moving God’s plan forward.

script21.title: Letting go on Mount Moriah
script: Thank the Lord, the story didn’t stop with Hagar. Between Genesis 16 and 17, the Bible is silent for thirteen years. For those thirteen years Abram held the son he had produced by his own methods, yet he could not hear God’s voice.

Then, on Mount Moriah, the man who had once come up with plans on God’s behalf offered no ideas this time; he simply rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey and walked for three days. As a result he experienced “Yahweh Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14). Translated literally, the name means “Yahweh will see”; God’s provision begins with God’s seeing. The ram had long been in the thicket on the mountain; he simply hadn’t seen it before.

Brothers and sisters, the provision you need today may already be on the mountain; you simply haven’t got there yet. Hudson Taylor is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.”

script21.title: Who parted the Red Sea?
script: We don’t only replace God in the doing; we also take his place in the glory. The lesson gives an example that stings: ask Sunday-school children, “Who parted the Red Sea?” and most will answer, “Moses.” But the Bible says: “Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night” (Exodus 14:21). Moses was responsible for a one-second gesture; Yahweh was responsible for a whole night’s mighty work.

Numbers 20 gives another sobering example. God told Moses to speak to the rock so that it would give out water, but Moses said: “Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” With a single sentence he turned God’s act into his own; the water still came out, but he would not bring the assembly into the promised land. Brothers and sisters, forty years of patience, brought down by one sentence.

script21.title: We are the moon
script: Paul says: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). He goes on to say that neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters. That isn’t self-deprecation; it is accuracy — no farmer can produce the mystery of “growth.”

In 1975 the psychologists Miller and Ross pointed out that people commonly display a “self-serving bias”: they attribute success to themselves and failure to circumstances; that is why we need, every day, to send the glory back on purpose.

The moon lights up the earth, but the moon itself gives off no light; it only reflects the light of the sun, with an albedo of only about 12 per cent — yet that tenth or so reflected back is enough to light up an entire wilderness. Brothers and sisters, we are the moon; what we can do is not shine, but not block the light.

script21.title: Practices (1 and 2)
script: The lesson gives us four practices; today let’s look at the first two. First, entrusting in prayer: after every prayer, declare, “Lord, I hand this over to you; its fulfilment is up to you.” To go deeper: hand the matter over out loud, and then stop going over it again and again. You could keep an “entrusting notebook”: write down the matter and the date, then turn the page. Look back three months later and you’ll be amazed how much God has already dealt with.

Second, changing myself: when you want to change someone else, first ask the Lord to change your own heart. Set yourself a house rule — “one reminder costs one prayer”; after you have prayed, what you want to say will come out softer.

script21.title: Practices (3 and 4)
script: Third, waiting in faith: while you have not yet seen the promise fulfilled, choose trust rather than agitation. Find a verse for the thing you are waiting for and read it every morning. While you wait there are three “don’ts”: make no major decisions, take no shortcuts and don’t force things through by manipulation.
Fourth, giving the glory to the Lord: when someone praises you, say in your heart, “Lord, this is your doing.” You don’t need to deny the praise; just add, “Thank you — this really is God’s grace.”

321 says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Choose one practice and do it for seven days first, then arrange the four over four weeks; and finally, don’t forget Multiplication — teach this lesson to your “2.”

script21.title: Summing up the 3-2-1 vision
script: Brothers and sisters, let’s place today’s lesson within the whole picture of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he existed in the form of God, yet emptied himself and took the form of a servant; the Bible is my standard — I won’t let “what seems reasonable” replace “what agrees with God’s word”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — those who are led walk behind.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King answers the question of who makes the decisions; let Jesus receive all the glory answers the question of who gets the credit. The Goal: establish God’s system — God on the throne, people in their originally intended position.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The road of the new self is this: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20). Remember: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

script21.title: Letting God be Lord is the greatest humility
script: Brothers and sisters, the lesson leaves us a few beautifully concise reminders: wanting to help God is really taking his place; wanting to control the outcome is really usurping his sovereignty. Letting go is not failure but trust; letting God be Lord is the greatest humility.
Replacing God is pride at its most extreme; letting God be God is humility at its most complete. True faith is not doing things for God, but letting God work within me.

The greatest weariness of our lives comes not from having too much to do, but from sitting in the wrong seat. This morning the Lord issues us a call, gentle yet firm: come down, return to your originally intended position. Returning to our position is not being demoted; it is being set free. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

script21.title: Prayer of response and blessing
script: Let us bow our heads and pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, I am willing to return to my originally intended position — to let you be God, and to be your servant. I confess that when I so often want to help you, I really want to replace you; I so often speak of trust while my hands grip tightly. Forgive me all my pride wrapped up in good intentions.

I lay down my anxiety and my control; I will no longer use my own methods to help you finish things. Right now I place in your hands the person and the matter that weigh on me. You are God; you are responsible for accomplishing it. I am human; I need only obey.
All glory, honour and power be yours, for ever and ever. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, the Lord bless you and keep you. May you walk lightly today, for of him, and through him, and to him are all things. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: Pride Is Being Out of Position; Humility Is Returning to Position
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. First, let me ask you to picture a scene with me.

A symphony orchestra walks onto the stage, and more than a hundred musicians take their places. The bows of the first violins are already raised, the double basses lean against shoulders, the French horns rest quietly in their players’ hands, and the timpanist stands guard over two drums that, by the look of it, will be struck only a few times all evening. Suddenly someone asks: since the violin sounds so beautiful, why not have all hundred of them play the violin? The answer is simple — then what is on stage would no longer be an orchestra, but a hundred violins. The volume would go up, but the music would vanish.

The church is the same. God never intended to make a hundred identical copies of you.

In church we often say, “Christ is the head, and we are the body.” Say it long enough and it can turn into a pleasant but empty slogan. In fact it is not an abstract metaphor but a truth about our “originally intended position”. Paul says: “He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” (Ephesians 1:22–23) And again: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18) There is only one head, but there are thousands upon thousands of members.

So true humility is not only knowing “I am not God”; it also means knowing “I am not the head”.

That sentence is worth growing quiet over this morning and chewing on slowly. Many Christians acknowledged long ago that they are not God — that is the starting point of faith, and it isn’t hard. What is hard is acknowledging “I am not the head” in the church, in the small group, in the family, in the serving team. I am not the one who sets the direction; I am not the one who must always be heard; I am not the one they cannot do without.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever met a scene like this in church? Over some small matter two people each think their own way is better; back and forth it goes, the tone grows harder and harder, and in the end the job gets done but the relationship is ruined. Or at home, a husband and wife argue over some trivial thing, and before long they are no longer really arguing about that thing at all, but about “who has the final say”.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In the words of today’s lesson, it comes down to this: pride is being out of position; humility is returning to position.

“Offside” is a term from the football pitch. However fast a player runs, however skilful he is, if he is standing in the wrong place, the goal doesn’t count. The spiritual world has its offside too. However many gifts a person has, however great their zeal, if they stand in the wrong place, that service will hardly endure before God.

In this lesson we will learn together to “return to our originally intended position”. The text takes us down this road through three key points: first, we are different, and that is why we belong together; second, no one is the best, everyone else is better than me, and together we are at our best; third, let Jesus be the head, and let me be just a member.

May the Holy Spirit, this morning, personally put each one of us back in the place God has arranged for us.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter to a Divided Church
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of 1 Corinthians 12, we first need to know the author, the date, the recipients and the situation of this letter.

The author is the apostle Paul. He states who he is at the very start of the letter: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes, to the assembly of God which is at Corinth” (1 Corinthians 1:1–2). It was written around the spring of AD 55, while Paul was on his third missionary journey and living in Ephesus. He leaves a clue at the end of the letter: “But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost” (1 Corinthians 16:8). In other words, this letter was written with tears by a pastor far from home, for a church he had planted with his own hands, which was now splitting apart.

The recipients were the church in Corinth. The city of Corinth sat on the isthmus in southern Greece, with the port of Cenchreae to the east and the port of Lechaeum to the west — the throat linking central Greece and the Peloponnese. In 146 BC the Roman general Mummius destroyed the city; in 44 BC Julius Caesar ordered it rebuilt as a Roman colony, and it later became the capital of the province of Achaia. The rebuilt Corinth flourished rapidly. Merchants and travellers crowded in, and the population was a mixture — Roman veterans, Greeks, Jews, slaves and freedmen from the East all lived in one city. There was much wealth, and there were many idols; in the city stood the temple of Apollo, whose remains survive, and on the acropolis a temple to the goddess of love. Corinth’s licentiousness was famous throughout the world, so much so that Greek gained a verb, “to Corinthianise”, meaning to live a debauched life.

A city like this produced a church like this: gifts, but no character; excitement, but no order; spiritual displays, but no spiritual life.

In the letter Paul deals with their problems one by one: factions and divisions (chapter 1), pride and boasting (chapter 4), sexual immorality (chapter 5), suing one another (chapter 6), confusion about marriage (chapter 7), food offered to idols (chapters 8–10), disorder in their gatherings and at the Lord’s Supper (chapter 11), and disorder over spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14).

And all these problems had one single root. Paul points to it at the very beginning: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” (1 Corinthians 1:12) And again: “For you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?” (1 Corinthians 3:3)

Jealousy and strife. Put plainly, it is the self-centred life. Everyone wanted to stand at the front; everyone thought their own way was the right one.

So when he reaches chapter 12, Paul writes out his prescription. He doesn’t begin with rules; he begins with “the body”. He says: “For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12) And then: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit.” (1 Corinthians 12:13)

In its day this verse was earth-shattering. In the Roman world a high racial wall stood between Jews and Greeks, and a deep class divide lay between slave and free. Yet Paul says: in the body of Christ, you all drink of the same Spirit.

There is a piece of history here worth mentioning. Using “the body” as a picture of a community was nothing new in the Greco-Roman world. The Roman historian Livy records that in 494 BC, when the common people of Rome withdrew to the Sacred Mount, the senator Menenius Agrippa told them a fable about “the belly and the limbs”, urging the commoners not to complain about the nobility but each to keep to his station. That used the image of the body to maintain the class system. Paul turns the image completely on its head: far from telling the lesser members to keep quiet, he says, “those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary” (1 Corinthians 12:22), and that God gives “more abundant honor to the inferior part” (1 Corinthians 12:24).

Brothers and sisters, this is the gospel. The Worldly system uses “the body” to keep the little people down; God’s system uses “the body” to lift the little people up.

Notice too the overall flow of chapters 12 to 14: chapter 12 speaks of the diversity of gifts and the unity of the body; chapter 13 speaks of love as the most excellent way; chapter 14 speaks of how to use gifts in an orderly way in the gathering. The love chapter in the middle is not a wedding poem but a healing medicine placed right in the middle of their rivalry over gifts. Paul’s logic is this: however many gifts you have, without love they count for nothing; and the first concrete form love takes is each person returning to their own originally intended position.

The verses we read today, 1 Corinthians 12:17 and 21, fall right in the middle of this flow.

sections.heading: 1. We Are Different, and That Is Why We Belong Together
sections.html:
Paul says: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?” (1 Corinthians 12:17)

It is a question asked with a smile, yet it reveals a serious spiritual fact: God’s design is unity in diversity.

Look at the context. Paul first says: “For the body is not one member, but many.” (1 Corinthians 12:14) Then he describes two opposite emotions. The first is inferiority: “If the foot would say, ‘Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body,’ it is not therefore not part of the body.” (1 Corinthians 12:15) The second is superiority, which is what verses 17 and 21 deal with. The person who feels inferior says, “I’m no use”; the person who feels superior says, “You’re no use.” Both sentences deny the very same thing — God’s arrangement.

So in between, Paul sets down a sentence that steadies everything like an anchor: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18)

Key word: set

The word “set” is the Greek etheto, the aorist middle of the verb tithēmi, meaning “to place, to establish, to appoint”. It is a completed action, and its subject is God himself. In other words, your place in the body was not drawn by lot, was not assigned by the pastor, and was not won by your own striving — God personally “put” you there.

Add to that the phrase “just as he desired”. The Greek is kathōs ēthelēsen, “as he willed”. Your position comes from God’s heart, not from human ratings.

Brothers and sisters, if this sentence sinks into your heart, you no longer need to envy anyone else’s position, starting today.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: dividing is the first act of creation

From the very beginning God is a God who “divides”. Genesis 1 records that when God said, “Let there be light,” he “divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4); he made the expanse and “divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse” (Genesis 1:7); and he made the dry land appear and gathered the waters into one place. Dividing is not the beginning of chaos; dividing is the beginning of order. Chaos is chaos precisely because everything is churned together.

The New Testament follows the same logic. Paul says: “For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us.” (Romans 12:4–6) Peter says: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” (1 Peter 4:10) The word for “various” is the Greek poikilos, which originally means “multicoloured, richly patterned”. God’s grace is not one colour; it is a full spectrum.

That is why Paul says: “Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. There are various kinds of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all.” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6) Three times “various kinds”, three times “the same”. Diversity and unity have never been enemies; they are the fingerprints the triune God has left on the church.

Illustration: thirty-seven trillion cells, one blueprint

Let’s look at our own bodies. In 2013 Eva Bianconi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy published a study in the Annals of Human Biology estimating that an adult human body contains about thirty-seven trillion cells. Thirty-seven trillion is an unimaginable number.

But what is truly astonishing is not the quantity; it is this: almost every one of those thirty-seven trillion cells carries exactly the same set of DNA. One blueprint, growing into completely different functions — the light-sensing cells of the retina capture light, red blood cells carry oxygen, neurons transmit signals at over a hundred metres a second, and bone cells silently bear the weight of the whole body.

One blueprint, different callings. That is a picture of the church: we read the same Bible, we receive the same Holy Spirit, yet we are placed in completely different positions.

Back to the orchestra. In a performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony, the timpanist may strike only a few dozen times all evening, and the triangle player may sound just a handful of notes. But take those few notes away and the music is missing a piece. The conductor won’t say to the triangle player, “You’ve got too little to do — switch to the violin.” Because he knows those few notes are exactly what he wants.

Research: the cleverest team is often not the strongest team

In 1981 the British researcher Meredith Belbin published his research on team roles from Henley Management College. He did something very interesting: he put together a team of the people with the highest intelligence-test scores, called it the “Apollo team”, and had it compete in a management simulation against other ordinary teams. The result was unexpected — the Apollo team often came last. The reason was that everyone was too good at analysing and too eager to lead, so the whole team spent its time debating; no one was willing to carry things out, and no one took responsibility for pulling things together.

From this Belbin coined a well-known saying: nobody is perfect, but a team can be.

Brothers and sisters, this is a modern footnote to what Paul said more than nineteen hundred years ago. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?

Applying the 321 Vision: difference is a blessing, not a threat

The text puts it well: if we want to change others so they become like us, we are in fact denying God’s creation.

That one stings. We rarely admit that we are “remodelling other people”, but think about it: when I say in my heart, “Why is he so slow?”, “Why does she go on so much?”, “Why does this person never do things the normal way?”, what I am really saying is: why aren’t you me?

That is the self-centred life. Self-centred people measure the whole world with themselves as the ruler; selfless people look at everyone through God’s heart. The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having no self; it is no longer making yourself the centre, the standard and the end point. Jesus is the focal point — not myself, not others, not my circumstances.

Paul has a sentence worth reading once a day: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

If you preach better than others, you received it; if you cook better than others, you received it; if you are more patient than others, you received that too. Since it is all received, none of it can be used for comparison.

The first of the 321 vision’s fivefold changes is “mindset”. Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. The mindset to change today is this: difference is not conflict; difference is richness.

Returning to our originally intended position means respecting God’s arrangement, appreciating other people’s differences, and accepting our own uniqueness.

sections.heading: 2. No One Is the Best, Everyone Else Is Better Than Me, and Together We Are at Our Best
sections.html:
Paul reminds us: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

This is an attitude of spiritual humility — no member is dispensable. Everyone matters, but no one matters most.

Notice how precise Paul’s examples are. He doesn’t say “the foot can’t tell the eye”; he says “the eye can’t tell the hand” and “the head can’t tell the feet”. He deliberately has the higher speak to the lower. Because the damage done by pride always flows downhill. In church it is rarely the new believer who looks down on the senior co-worker; it is usually the senior one who looks down on the newcomer. It is rarely the one who cooks who looks down on the one who preaches; it is usually the one on the platform who looks down on the one in the kitchen.

Key word: necessary

Next Paul says something that almost goes against common sense: “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” (1 Corinthians 12:22)

“Necessary” is the Greek anankaia, meaning “essential, indispensable, impossible to do without”. Paul doesn’t say the weaker members are “of some use too”; he says they are “much rather necessary”.

And he presses further: “Those parts of the body which we think to be less honorable, on those we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable parts have more abundant propriety; whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part, that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another.” (1 Corinthians 12:23–25)

The word “composed” is the Greek sunekerasen, carrying the sense of “blending, mixing”, as one blends colours or seasonings. God didn’t just pile the members together any old how; like a master chef, he blended them. And the way God blends them is to give, on purpose, double honour to the one who is lacking.

So the result is: “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:26)

If you have ever been woken in the middle of the night by a toothache, you understand this verse. One tooth, less than a ten-thousandth of your body’s volume, can keep the whole person awake all night. The body never says, “It’s only one tooth — just put up with it.”

Illustration: glands the size of a grain of rice that govern the whole body

The human body has a pair of often-overlooked organs — the parathyroid glands, usually four of them, attached to the back of the thyroid. Each is only the size of a grain of rice; all four together weigh less than 0.2 grams. In the whole body they are so small you would hardly know they were there.

But the parathyroid hormone they secrete governs the level of calcium in the blood of the whole body. Medicine has long known that if these four little things are accidentally removed during thyroid surgery, the patient develops low blood calcium and spasms in the hands and feet, and in severe cases it can be life-threatening.

“Those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” Brothers and sisters, God has placed a design like this in your body so that you can understand his heart for the church. The older saint who comes half an hour early every week to open up, set out chairs and boil water; the sister who prays for the meeting in a corner and never goes up front — they are the church’s parathyroid glands. Normally you don’t notice them; once they are gone, the whole body starts to go into spasm.

Research: the more people there are, the less effort each gives

But “together” does not mean “lots of people”. A warning is needed here.

In 1913 the French agricultural engineer Maximilien Ringelmann ran a rope-pulling experiment, something like a tug-of-war. He found that a person pulling alone gives 100 per cent of their strength; when two pull together, each gives on average only about 93 per cent; when eight pull together, each gives on average only about half. Later, in 1974, Alan Ingham and other researchers repeated the experiment and confirmed that this was not just poor coordination but a drop in motivation — with more people around, I put in a little less effort. Psychology calls this “social loafing”.

This is the exact opposite of “together”. People gathered in one place do not automatically become a body; people gathered together who each hide themselves only become a heap.

So what kind of team truly multiplies its strength? From 2012 to 2015 Google carried out an internal study called “Project Aristotle”, analysing more than 180 teams to discover the secret of high-performing teams. The conclusion surprised them: the key was not who was on the team or how many clever people it had, but a quality called “psychological safety” — a concept introduced in 1999 by Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, meaning that members dare to speak up, dare to admit mistakes and dare to reveal what they don’t know, without fear of being humiliated or punished.

Brothers and sisters, does that sound familiar? A church that dares to admit weakness is a strong church. And what makes people dare to admit weakness is exactly this: no one is the best, everyone else is better than me, and together we are at our best.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: each counting others better than himself

The text’s motto is really a plain-speech version of Philippians: “Doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.” (Philippians 2:3)

“Counting others better than himself” is neither self-deception nor talking yourself down as worthless. The Greek hēgeomai means “to weigh, to judge, to regard”: in your thinking you deliberately put the other person first. It is a choice of the will, not an emotion.

The Bible gives a sad example. Samuel said to Saul: “Though you were little in your own sight, weren’t you made the head of the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17) Saul was once so small he hid among the baggage, but later he grew so big he would not listen to God’s word. Once people see themselves as big, they can no longer hold the position God gave them.

The Lord Jesus takes this principle all the way: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:26–28)

Mother Teresa is generally credited with saying something like this: I can do things you cannot, you can do things I cannot; together we can do great things. That is another way of saying the text’s motto.

Applying the 321 Vision: pride provokes pride, humility inspires humility

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Have you noticed that almost every conflict in church starts like this? One barbed remark gets an even more barbed reply; one disrespectful look gets an even colder look back. That is pride provoking pride. In the end there is no right or wrong, only winning and losing — and both sides lose.

The other way round, a simple “I didn’t think this through properly” will often be met with “No, I was too hasty as well.” That is humility inspiring humility.

That is why the 321 vision has the 920 practice: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Paul says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice that not one of these nine graces can be borne by a person on their own. Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards. God places different people around you precisely so that you can bear fruit.

In our service we must remember: each person’s gifts and calling are given by God. They are not capital for comparison but tools for serving. When each of us does our own part, the glory goes to Jesus, not to people.

sections.heading: 3. Let Jesus Be the Head, and Let Me Be Just a Member
sections.html:
Having come this far, we arrive at the heart of the lesson. The first two key points were horizontal — my relationships with my brothers and sisters; the third is vertical — my relationship with Christ. If the horizontal is to be level, the vertical must first be upright.

The text goes straight to the point: the core of pride is wanting to “take the place of the head”. Wanting to control, direct and dominate others is in fact usurping the sovereignty of Christ.

The Bible defines this very clearly: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

Key words: head and preeminence

“Head” is the Greek kephalē. In Paul’s usage the word carries two layers of meaning at once: first, “source” — life comes from him; second, “ruler” — authority goes out from him. So “Christ is the head of the church” doesn’t only mean that he governs us; it means our life comes from him. Cut off from him, we don’t just become weaker — we cannot live at all. The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

“Have the preeminence” is the Greek prōteuōn, a word that appears only once in the whole New Testament, right here in Colossians 1:18. Paul seems to have chosen a rare word on purpose, to say something utterly unique: only one has the preeminence in all things.

Notice the words “in all things”. It isn’t that he has first place in church but not at the office; it isn’t that he has first place on Sunday and someone else takes over on Monday. It is in all things.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: who was it that did not keep their position?

The first pride to appear in the Bible was not in a human being but in an angel. The prophet Isaiah records that chilling monologue: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Five “I will”s. Five times out of position.

Jude sums it up with one precise word: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6)

“First domain” — in the Chinese Union Version, “proper position” — is the Greek archē, whose basic meaning is “beginning, the original office and rank”. The angel did not fall for committing some monstrous crime, but for “not keeping its position”. Its original place was that of a worshipper, yet it wanted to sit on the throne of the one who is worshipped.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the 321 vision means: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God. The essence of Satan is not some evil innovation, but a confusion of position.

And Christ took the completely opposite road: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

Satan said, “I will make myself like the Most High”; Christ “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped”. Satan wanted to go up; Christ was willing to come down. “Emptied himself” is the Greek ekenōsen, literally “poured himself out until empty”.

So humility is not putting yourself down; humility is returning to your originally intended position. Satan left his position and fell; Christ came down to the position of a man and was exalted: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” (Philippians 2:9)

Illustration: what snapped was not the gift but the connection

The human body has an awe-inspiring design: the spinal cord. It is the information superhighway between the brain and the limbs.

A person with a severe neck injury may have perfectly healthy arms — the muscles are there, the bones are there, the joints are there, the blood is flowing. But he cannot lift them. It isn’t that the arms are broken; it’s that the connection between the arms and the head has been cut.

The paralysis of a church is often like this. It isn’t for lack of gifts, nor for lack of talented people, still less for lack of resources; it is because somewhere the connection to the head has been cut. Paul puts it beautifully: “But speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” (Ephesians 4:15–16)

First “him who is the head, Christ”; only then “every joint” and “each individual part”. The order cannot be reversed.

Illustration: the price of being out of position

On 27 March 1977, on the island of Tenerife in Spain’s Canary Islands, the deadliest accident in aviation history took place. Two Boeing 747s collided on a fog-shrouded runway, and 583 people were killed.

The investigation afterwards revealed a heartbreaking detail. The captain of the plane that was taking off was the most senior pilot in his whole airline, the chief pilot who trained others. He pushed the throttles forward before he had received take-off clearance from the tower. The co-pilot hesitantly voiced a warning, and the flight engineer asked, “Is he not clear, that Pan American?” But before a captain of such great authority, neither of them pressed the point any further.

A few seconds later, it was too late for everything.

That tragedy changed the whole aviation industry. Since then airlines around the world have adopted “crew resource management” training, whose core principle is this: the captain is not an unquestionable head, and every member of the crew has a duty to speak up loudly when they see danger.

Brothers and sisters, the church is not an aeroplane, but the principle is the same. When someone sits in the seat that only Christ deserves, the other members gradually stop daring to speak; and once the members don’t dare to speak, the body loses the safety mechanism God built into it.

In 1951 the psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his famous line-length conformity experiment: faced with an obviously correct answer, as long as everyone around them gave the same wrong answer, about three-quarters of the participants gave in at least once. Our tendency to conform is real, and startling. That is all the more reason the church needs a head who never makes mistakes.

Applying the 321 Vision: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory

The text says: the “head” determines the direction; the “members” carry out the mission. Our responsibility is not to take control but to obey.

This is exactly the Two Core Values of the 321 vision: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Letting Jesus be King means that whenever we disagree, the first question I ask is not “Who’s right?” but “Lord, what do you want?” It means that in every place of service I don’t compete for position or grab for power, but gladly stand in the position God has given me and faithfully complete the work he has entrusted to me.

The 321 vision also maps out the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, and so we let Jesus be King, and in the end let Jesus receive all the glory. Every step on this path is a step back for me and a step forward for Christ.

And stepping back like this is no loss. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. What you give up is one small place; what you gain is an infinite Christ.

If a church lets a human being be the head, it will lose its balance; if a family lets “self” be lord, it will fall into chaos. Only when Jesus is the head can every member work together as one under his leading.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The Body Is God’s System
sections.html:
Place this lesson within the whole picture of the 321 vision and you will see something beautiful: the “body” Paul speaks of is exactly what the 321 vision calls “God’s system”.

The Three Foundations are crystal clear in this lesson. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, showing us what it means to return to our originally intended position. The Bible is my standard — not where I feel I ought to be, but where God’s word says I am. The Holy Spirit is my guide — “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit.” (1 Corinthians 12:13) Unity isn’t produced by holding meetings; it comes from drinking of the one Spirit together.

The Two Core Values are in this lesson too. Let Jesus be King — he is the head of the whole church and has the preeminence in all things. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when each of us does our part, the glory goes to Jesus, not to people.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. What is a system? A system is a living organism with a head, members, order and connection, able to grow. Paul says: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

Look again at the fivefold change of the 321 vision: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. The first key point of this lesson changes the mindset — difference is a blessing; the second changes life and relationships — everyone else is better than me; the third changes the foundation of ministry — let Jesus be the head. And the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. How many churches have ministries that blaze with activity while their relationships lie shattered in pieces — simply because they have turned the order upside down.

The same goes for the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Today’s lesson begins precisely “with God” — confirming that he is the head; then “with ourselves” — accepting the unique me God has made; then “with others” — appreciating the members who are different from me; and only last of all “with things” — being faithful at our post.

There is also the shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. From man’s perspective, position means status: the front is better than the back, the platform matters more than the floor. From God’s perspective, position means trust: faithfulness matters more than visibility. From a temporary perspective, not being noticed this time feels unfair; from an eternal perspective, on that day the Lord himself will say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” (Matthew 25:21)

The 920 practice of the 321 vision has its most direct use in this lesson: every person I am in relationship with is my “2”. The co-worker I disagree with is my “2”; the family member who makes me impatient is my “2”. Before them, live out the “0” — the selfless life — and let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine of its expressions.

The 235 relationships of the 321 vision are also the body in concrete form: become a “2” with a selfless person, supporting one another; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of comrades — the very team spoken of in Ephesians 4:11.

Church history has a beautiful testimony. In the eighteenth century the Moravian Brethren — a group of refugees from different countries and backgrounds who quarrelled endlessly among themselves — gathered at Herrnhut in Germany. On 13 August 1727, during a communion service, the Holy Spirit was poured out on them together; they confessed their sins to one another, forgave one another, and from then on were one. After that they began a relay of prayer that went on day and night without a break for a hundred years, and they sent out a great host of missionaries. They did not become identical people; each of them simply returned to their originally intended position and let Christ be the head.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Truth into Daily Living
sections.html:
The text gives us four practices. The 321 vision says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s place the four practices within these eight stages, so that they become not just things we know, but truly our life.

Practice 1: Accepting difference

In team ministry, deliberately appreciate people who are different from you, and give thanks for them.

Information: first remember today’s truth — “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18) Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you that the brother who tries your patience most was placed beside you by God’s own hand. Conviction: tell God in your heart that you believe his arrangement is not a mistake. Implementation: this week, pick the co-worker whose style is most different from yours, write down three of their strengths specifically, and tell them one of them face to face. Evaluation: a week later, ask yourself whether your inner verdict on them has softened. Correction: if critical thoughts still come, bring them into prayer and turn them into intercession. Repetition: choose a different person each week and keep practising. Multiplication: do it together with your small group, so that acceptance becomes the culture of the team.

Practice 2: Humble submission

When you disagree, first ask the Lord: “Lord, what do you want me to learn?”

Information: remember, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). Revelation: let the Holy Spirit show you that what you really want in the argument is not to be right but to be valued. Conviction: admit that pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Implementation: the next time you clash, stay quiet for thirty seconds, ask this question in your heart, and only then speak. Evaluation: that evening, look back — was my tone fighting to win, or seeking the Lord’s heart? Correction: if you said something wrong, go and apologise within twenty-four hours. Repetition: until “ask the Lord first” becomes your instinctive reaction. Multiplication: teach this practice to your family.

Practice 3: Respecting our originally intended position

At your post of service, faithfully play the role God has given you, and don’t overstep into other people’s callings.

Information: remember the sobering reminder of “angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place” (Jude 6). Revelation: ask the Lord to let you see clearly where you have in fact reached across the boundary. Conviction: believe that faithfulness pleases God more than visibility. Implementation: this week, write down what your “God-given calling” is in the church or the family, and write down one thing you should let go of and hand back to someone else. Evaluation: check whether you often play backseat driver in other people’s affairs. Correction: sincerely hand the authority back into the hands of the person it belongs to. Repetition: review your post once every quarter. Multiplication: help the people you lead to find and keep their own originally intended position too.

Practice 4: Praying for unity

Pray every day for the unity of the church, asking the Lord to help every member do their part and glorify him with one heart.

Information: remember the prayer of the Lord Jesus: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Revelation: understand that unity is not something we manufacture but something the Holy Spirit gives; our responsibility is to “keep” it eagerly — “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). Conviction: believe that unity carries heavenly power. Implementation: every morning, spend three minutes praying by name for three members of the church. Evaluation: after a month, see whether your feelings about the church have changed. Correction: if your prayer turns into a list of complaints, change it into a list of thanks. Repetition: make it a fixed part of your morning prayer every day. Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to keep watch in prayer with you, becoming what the 321 vision calls your “2”.

A Gentle Reminder

Difference is not a threat but a richness.

Don’t envy other people’s positions, and don’t look down on your own role.

God’s body has no spare organs; every person is indispensable.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, true unity is not “sameness” but “working together in difference”.

The beauty of an orchestra is not that every instrument plays the same note, but that different notes sound together and become harmony. The health of a body is not that every organ grows into the same shape, but that each stays in its place and all are connected to one another. The beauty of the church is the same.

When every member humbly returns to their own originally intended position, the whole body can grow healthy and display the beauty of Christ.

Pride puts us out of position; humility returns us to our position.

This morning, let me extend three invitations to you.

First, accept your own position. Perhaps your position isn’t prominent; perhaps you have served in that corner for many years without applause. Remember: God arranged it just as he desired, and God never wastes a single member.

Second, respect other people’s positions. Stop remodelling others and start appreciating them. When you say to someone, “I have no need for you,” you are really speaking to the God who placed them there.

Third, hand over the position of head. A church can have only one head; a family can have only one Lord. Today, please hand back to Jesus the steering wheel you have been gripping all this time.

“Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)

Let us learn together to return to our own positions and let Jesus be the head, so that his church is knit together in love and made one in the truth.

May Jesus have the preeminence in all things, and may all the glory go to him.

keyVerses: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?” (1 Corinthians 12:17)
“The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)
“Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)
declarations: Lord, you are the head of the church. I am willing to return to the position you have given me — not striving, not grabbing, not comparing. Thank you for making me unique and making others different, so that in unity we may build one another up, that your body may grow healthier and your name be glorified.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You are the head of the whole church, and you have the preeminence in all things. This morning, through your word, you have reminded us: pride is being out of position; humility is returning to position.

Lord, forgive us. Forgive us for so often wanting to remake others in our own image; forgive us for the unspoken “I have no need for you” in our hearts; and forgive us for having, without even noticing, sat down in the seat that only you deserve.

Let us see your wonderful arrangement, and see that the members around us who are different from us are blessings placed there by your own hand. Give us a humble heart that can count others better than ourselves; give us a faithful heart that, at the post you have given us, does not strive, does not grab and does not compare.
Lord, be our head. May our families, our small groups and our church all hold fast to you, the head, with every joint doing its part and helping one another, building itself up in love.
May your body be healthy, and may your name be glorified.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18) Think about your present position in the church, the family or the workplace. Have you ever envied someone else’s position, or looked down on your own role? If this position really was arranged by God himself, how will you see it afresh today?

“The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21) Think honestly: is there a brother or sister whom, in your heart, you have felt you “have no need for”? This week, what concrete step could you take to express your appreciation or thanks to them?

blog.title: A Hundred Violins Don’t Make an Orchestra

blocks.x: Why didn’t God make us all the same?
Picture a symphony orchestra walking onto the stage. Someone asks: since the violin sounds so beautiful, why not have all hundred of them play the violin?

The answer is simple — then what is on stage would no longer be an orchestra, but a hundred violins. The volume would go up, but the music would vanish. The church is the same. God never intended to make a hundred identical copies of you.

In 1 Corinthians Paul asks a question with a smile that is nonetheless deeply serious: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?” (1 Corinthians 12:17)

Some people are like eyes that see far ahead, some like ears that listen well, some like feet that quietly bear the load. God’s wisdom is to make us different from one another, yet needing one another. If we keep trying to remake others in our own image, we are in fact denying God’s creation. Difference is not conflict; difference is richness.
Your Place Was Set There by God Himself
Paul goes on to say something that can heal a great deal of hurt: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18)

“Set” in the original means “to place, to appoint”, and its subject is God himself. Your place was not drawn by lot, was not assigned by someone else, and was not won by your own striving — God put you there with his own hand.

In 2013 Eva Bianconi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy estimated that an adult human body contains about thirty-seven trillion cells. What is astonishing is not the quantity, but that almost every one of these cells carries the same set of DNA, yet grows into completely different functions: light-sensing cells capture light, red blood cells carry oxygen, bone cells hold up the whole body. One blueprint, different callings.

The human body also has a pair of often-overlooked organs — the parathyroid glands. All four together weigh less than 0.2 grams, yet they govern the level of calcium in the blood of the whole body; if they are removed by mistake, the patient goes into spasms in the hands and feet. The church has its “parathyroid glands” too: the older saint who comes half an hour early to open up and set out the chairs, the sister who prays in a corner but never goes up front. Once they are gone, the whole body starts to go into spasm.

That is why Paul says: “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” (1 Corinthians 12:22) No one is the best, everyone else is better than me, and together we are at our best.
Pride Is Being Out of Position; Humility Is Returning to Position

True humility is not only knowing “I am not God”; it also means knowing “I am not the head”. Acknowledging that we are not God isn’t hard; what is hard is acknowledging, in the small group, at home and in the team, that I am not the one who sets the direction.

The first pride in the Bible was not in a human being but in an angel. The prophet Isaiah records that monologue: five “I will”s, five times out of position. Jude sums it up with great precision: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place.” (Jude 6)

Christ took the completely opposite road. He “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). Satan wanted to go up; Christ was willing to come down.

So humility has never been putting yourself down; humility is returning to your originally intended position. Pride puts us out of position; humility returns us to our position. The 321 vision puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When every member returns to their originally intended position, the body can display the beauty of Christ.
Three Things You Can Begin Today
First, accept your own position. Perhaps you have served in that corner for many years without applause; God never wastes a single member.
Second, respect other people’s positions. When you say to someone, “I have no need for you,” you are really speaking to the God who placed them there.
Third, hand over the position of head. A church can have only one head; a family can have only one Lord. Hand back to Jesus the steering wheel you have been gripping.

Reflection: In your church, family or workplace, is there a position you have never been willing to accept, or one you have refused to let go of? If it is God’s own arrangement, how will you respond to him today?
