notes: Return to Our Originally Intended Position
Position (Part 1): Let Jesus Be the Head; I Am Only a Member
“Now you are the body of Christ,
and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)
1. Open with the symphony orchestra: a hundred musicians take their places; if they all played the violin, the volume would rise and the music vanish.
2. State the lesson’s one-line summary: pride is being out of position; humility is returning to position.
3. First read the key verse, 1 Corinthians 12:27, then preview the three key points.
4. Keep a warm tone, inviting brothers and sisters to grow quiet and receive in the early morning.
Pride is out of position; humility returns to position
A hundred violins are not an orchestra
God didn’t make a hundred copies of you
True humility knows not only “I am not God”
but also “I am not the head”
1. Quote Ephesians 1:22–23: the church is his body; Christ is head over all things for the assembly.
2. Ask: acknowledging you are not God isn’t hard; what is hard is acknowledging you are not the head.
3. Give an everyday scene: a husband and wife argue over a trifle, and in the end they are arguing over who has the final say.
4. Explain “offside” in football: however fast you run, if you stand in the wrong place, the goal doesn’t count.
5. The 321 vision: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position.
Key Verse and Background
“If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?”
(1 Corinthians 12:17) Paul writes from Ephesus
around AD 55, to a divided church
Many gifts, little character; self is the root
1. The author is Paul, writing from Ephesus around AD 55 (1 Corinthians 16:8, “until Pentecost”).
2. Corinth was the capital of Achaia, destroyed in 146 BC and rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BC; crowded with merchants and travellers, and famous for its licentiousness.
3. The church’s root problem was jealousy and strife (1 Corinthians 3:3) — put plainly, the self-centred life.
4. Paul’s prescription doesn’t begin with rules but with the body (1 Corinthians 12:12–13).

5. You may mention the fable of “the belly and the limbs” recorded by the Roman historian Livy: the world uses the body to keep the little people down; Christ uses the body to lift the little people up.
We are different, so we belong together
If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?
(1 Corinthians 12:17)
God’s design: unity in diversity
Inferiority says “I’m no use”; superiority says “You’re no use”
1. Read 1 Corinthians 12:17 word by word, pointing out that it is a question asked with a smile.
2. Context: verse 14, “the body is not one member, but many”; verse 15 deals with inferiority; verses 17 and 21 deal with superiority.
3. Inferiority says “I’m no use”, superiority says “You’re no use” — both deny God’s arrangement.
4. Scripture interpreting Scripture: the “dividing” of Genesis 1 — dividing is the beginning of order, not of chaos.
God set them just as he desired
God has set the members, each one of them,
in the body (1 Corinthians 12:18)
Thirty-seven trillion cells, one blueprint
No need to envy anyone’s position
1. Key word: “set” is the Greek etheto (aorist middle of tithēmi) — a completed action of God personally placing.
2. “Just as he desired” is the Greek kathōs ēthelēsen, “as he willed”.

3. Scientific illustration: in 2013 Eva Bianconi and colleagues, in the Annals of Human Biology, estimated that an adult has about thirty-seven trillion cells, almost all carrying the same DNA yet growing into different functions.
4. Team research: Meredith Belbin’s 1981 “Apollo team” experiment — the cleverest team often came last; nobody is perfect, but a team can be.
5. 321 application: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; quote 1 Corinthians 4:7, “For who makes you different?”
No one is the best
The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you”
nor the head the feet, “I have no need for you”
(1 Corinthians 12:21)
Everyone matters, but no one matters most
1. Note that Paul deliberately has the higher speak to the lower — the damage done by pride always flows downhill.
2. The reality in church: usually the senior looks down on the newcomer, the one on the platform on the one in the kitchen.
3. Scripture interpreting Scripture: Philippians 2:3, “each counting others better than himself”; the Greek hēgeomai is a choice of the will, not an emotion.
4. A cautionary example: Saul, “though you were little in your own sight” (1 Samuel 15:17).
5. The Lord Jesus’ standard: Matthew 20:26–28 — whoever desires to become great shall be your servant.
The weaker are necessary
Members which seem to be weaker are necessary
(1 Corinthians 12:22)
Glands the size of rice govern the whole body
Everyone is better than me; together we’re best
1. Key word: “necessary” is the Greek anankaia — “indispensable”, not “of some use too”.
2. “Composed” is the Greek sunekerasen, with the sense of blending; God deliberately gives more abundant honour to the part that lacks (1 Corinthians 12:23–25).
3. Everyday illustration: one decayed tooth wakes the whole body, and the body never says, “It’s only one tooth.”

4. Scientific illustration: there are usually four parathyroid glands, each the size of a grain of rice, together under 0.2 grams, yet they govern the whole body’s blood calcium; remove them by mistake and the hands and feet go into spasm.

5. Psychology: Maximilien Ringelmann’s 1913 rope-pulling experiment and Alan Ingham’s 1974 replication show “social loafing”; Google’s “Project Aristotle” (2012–2015) found the key was “psychological safety”, a concept introduced by Amy Edmondson in 1999.
Let Jesus be the head; I am only a member
He is the head of the body, the assembly
the preeminence in all things (Colossians 1:18)
The head sets direction; members carry out the mission
Our duty is not to control but to obey
1. The first two key points are horizontal, the third is vertical; if the horizontal is to be level, the vertical must first be upright.
2. Key word: “head”, kephalē, means both “source” and “ruler”; apart from him we can do nothing (John 15:5).
3. “Have the preeminence”, prōteuōn, appears only once in the New Testament, right here in Colossians 1:18 — stress “in all things”.

4. Illustration: a person with a broken spinal cord has healthy arms but cannot lift them; a church is paralysed not for lack of gifts but because its connection to the head has been cut (Ephesians 4:15–16).
Pride is out of position; humility returns to position
Angels who didn’t keep their first domain (Jude 6)
Five “I will”s, five times offside (Isaiah 14:13)
Christ emptied himself (Philippians 2:7)
Satan wanted up; Christ came down
1. Isaiah 14:13–14: five “I will”s, five times out of position.
2. Jude 6, “first domain”: the Greek archē, the original office and rank; the essence of Satan is a confusion of position.
3. Philippians 2:5–8: he didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself; “emptied himself”, ekenōsen, means poured himself out until empty.

4. Historical illustration: the Tenerife air disaster of 27 March 1977, in which 583 people died; a senior captain took off without clearance and no one dared to press their objection; afterwards the whole industry adopted crew resource management.
5. Psychology: Solomon Asch’s 1951 conformity experiment — about three-quarters of participants gave in at least once; all the more reason the church needs a head who never makes mistakes.
Practices for Daily Living
Accepting difference: appreciate others
Humble submission: ask the Lord first
Respecting position: don’t overstep
Praying for unity: pray daily for the church
1. Keep the four practices in the lesson’s order, adding and removing nothing.
2. Deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
3. Accepting difference: this week, write down three strengths of the co-worker most different from you, and tell them one face to face.
4. Humble submission: in a clash, first stay quiet for thirty seconds and ask, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?” If you said something wrong, apologise within twenty-four hours.
5. Praying for unity: quote John 17:21 and Ephesians 4:3, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace”.
Closing and Call
Unity is not sameness, but working together in difference
Accept your own position
Respect other people’s positions
Hand over the head’s position; let Jesus be King
1. Return to the orchestra: the beauty is not in one note, but in different notes becoming harmony.
2. Three invitations: accept your own position, respect other people’s positions, hand over the position of head.
3. Reminder: when you say to someone, “I have no need for you,” you are speaking to the God who placed them there.
4. Close with 1 Corinthians 12:27, pointing to letting Jesus be King and giving the glory to Jesus.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, you are the head of the church
I will return to the position you gave me
Not striving, not grabbing, not comparing
May your name be glorified. Amen
1. Lead the congregation in proclaiming the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
2. Prayer content: confession — wanting to remake others, saying in our hearts “I have no need for you”, sitting in the seat only the Lord deserves.
3. Petition: a humble heart to count others better than ourselves, and a faithful heart that does not strive, grab or compare at our post.
4. Blessing: may your body be healthy and your name be glorified; pray in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

1. Key word: “necessary”, anankaia — “indispensable”.
2. “Composed”, sunekerasen, has the sense of blending; like a master chef, God blends the members together (1 Corinthians 12:23–25).
3. The result is 1 Corinthians 12:26: when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.
4. Everyday illustration: woken in the night by a decayed tooth — less than a ten-thousandth of the body, yet it keeps the whole person awake all night.
Glands the size of rice govern the whole body
Four parathyroid glands, under 0.2 grams
yet they govern the body’s blood calcium
Remove them, and the whole body spasms
The unseen ones are the most necessary
1. There are usually four parathyroid glands, attached to the back of the thyroid, each only the size of a grain of rice.
2. The parathyroid hormone they secrete governs blood calcium; if they are removed by mistake in thyroid surgery, the patient develops low blood calcium and spasms in the hands and feet.
3. The church’s parathyroid glands: the older saint who comes half an hour early to open up and set out chairs, the sister who prays in a corner and never goes up front.
4. A warning: Maximilien Ringelmann’s 1913 rope-pulling experiment and Alan Ingham’s 1974 study show “social loafing” — with more people, each puts in less effort.
5. Google’s “Project Aristotle” (2012–2015): the key was psychological safety, a concept introduced by Amy Edmondson in 1999.
Humility inspires humility — both sides win
Pride provokes pride — both sides lose
Count others better than yourself (Philippians 2:3)
920 practice: everyone is my “2”
Before them, live out the selfless “0”
1. The cycle of conflict: one barbed remark gets an even more barbed reply; in the end there is no right or wrong, only winning and losing — and both sides lose.
2. The other way round: “I didn’t think this through properly” is often met with “No, I was too hasty as well.”
3. Philippians 2:3, “counting others better than himself”: the Greek hēgeomai is a choice of the will.
4. The nine fruits of Galatians 5:22–23: patience needs someone to be patient with, kindness someone to be kind to, gentleness someone to be gentle towards.
5. Gifts and callings are not capital for comparison but tools for serving; each doing our part, the glory goes to Jesus.
Let Jesus be the head; I am only a member
He is the head of the body, the assembly
that in all things he might have the preeminence
(Colossians 1:18)
The head sets direction; members carry out the mission
1. The first two points are horizontal, the third vertical; if the horizontal is to be level, the vertical must first be upright.
2. Key word: “head”, kephalē, means both source and ruler; apart from him we can do nothing (John 15:5).
3. “Have the preeminence”, prōteuōn, appears only once in the whole New Testament; stress “in all things”.
4. It isn’t first place on Sunday and someone else taking over on Monday.
Who didn’t keep their position?
Five “I will”s: I will ascend into heaven
I will make myself like the Most High (Isaiah 14:14)
Angels didn’t keep their first domain
(Jude 6) Pride is a confusion of position
1. Isaiah 14:13–14: five “I will”s, five times out of position.
2. Jude 6, “first domain”: the Greek archē, the original office and rank.
3. The essence of Satan is not some evil innovation but a confusion of position: he was a worshipper, yet wanted to sit on the throne of the one who is worshipped.
4. The 321 vision: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to replace God.
Christ emptied himself
Didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant
(Philippians 2:6–7)
Satan wanted up; Christ came down
1. The whole of Philippians 2:5–8: obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
2. “Emptied himself”, ekenōsen, literally means poured himself out until empty.
3. Humility is not putting yourself down; humility is returning to your originally intended position; Satan left his position and fell, Christ came down and was exalted (Philippians 2:9).
4. Illustration: a person with a neck injury has healthy arms but cannot lift them — what snapped was not the gift but the connection to the head (Ephesians 4:15–16).

5. Historical illustration: the 1977 Tenerife disaster killed 583 people; a senior captain took off without clearance and no one dared to press the point; in Solomon Asch’s 1951 conformity experiment about three-quarters of people gave in at least once.
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
I don’t compete for position or grab for power
I gladly stand at the post God gave me
It is no longer I who live
but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20)
1. The Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.
2. In disagreement, the first question is not “Who’s right?” but “Lord, what do you want?”
3. The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — every step is a step back for me and a step forward for Christ.
4. Selflessness is not having nothing, but entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out; you give up one small place and gain an infinite Christ.
5. If a church lets a human being be the head, it loses its balance; if a family lets self be lord, it falls into chaos.
Practices for Daily Living (1)
Accepting difference: deliberately appreciate others
and give thanks for them
Humble submission: in disagreement, ask the Lord first
“Lord, what do you want me to learn?”
1. Follow the lesson’s order, adding and removing nothing.
2. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
3. Implementing acceptance of difference: this week, write down three strengths of the co-worker most different from you, and tell them one face to face.
4. Implementing humble submission: before a clash, stay quiet for thirty seconds; if you said something wrong, apologise within twenty-four hours.
5. For Information, remember 1 Corinthians 12:18 and Philippians 2:3.
Practices for Daily Living (2)
Respecting position: faithfully play your God-given role
Don’t overstep into others’ callings
Praying for unity: pray daily for the church’s unity
Ask the Lord to help each member do their part
1. Information for respecting position: the sobering reminder of Jude 6, angels who “didn’t keep their first domain”.
2. Implementation: write down the calling God has given you, and one thing you should let go of and hand back to someone else.
3. Information for praying for unity: the Lord Jesus’ prayer in John 17:21.
4. Unity is given by the Holy Spirit; our responsibility is to be “eager to keep” it (Ephesians 4:3).
5. Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to keep watch in prayer with you, becoming what 321 calls your “2”.
The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
Three Foundations: Jesus, the Bible, the Holy Spirit
Two Core Values: Jesus as King, all the glory to him
The Goal: establish God’s system
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
1. The “body” Paul speaks of is exactly what 321 calls “God’s system”.
2. The Three Foundations: Jesus our role model emptied himself; the Bible tells me where I am; the Holy Spirit makes us all drink of one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13).
3. The Goal: a living organism with a head, members, order and connection, able to grow (Ephesians 4:11–12).
4. The order of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.
5. Testimony: on 13 August 1727 the Moravian Brethren at Herrnhut in Germany received the outpouring of the Holy Spirit together and began a relay of prayer that ran unbroken for a hundred years.
Closing and Call
Unity is not sameness, but working together in difference
Accept your own position
Respect other people’s positions
Hand over the head’s position; let Jesus be King
1. Return to the orchestra: the beauty is not in one note, but in different notes becoming harmony.
2. Three invitations: accept your own position, respect other people’s positions, hand over the position of head.
3. Reminder: God never wastes a single member.
4. Close with 1 Corinthians 12:27; may Jesus have the preeminence in all things, and may all the glory go to him.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, you are the head of the church
I will return to the position you gave me
Not striving, not grabbing, not comparing
May your name be glorified. Amen
1. First lead the congregation in proclaiming the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
2. Confession: wanting to remake others in our own image, the unspoken “I have no need for you” in our hearts, sitting in the seat only the Lord deserves.
3. Petition: a humble heart to count others better than ourselves, a faithful heart that does not strive, grab or compare at our post.
4. Ask the Lord to let our families, small groups and church all hold fast to him, the head, every joint doing its part, building itself up in love.
5. Bless, and close in the Lord’s name: Amen.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we look together at Lesson 93, entitled “Return to Our Originally Intended Position”. First, let me ask you to picture a scene with me: a symphony orchestra walks onto the stage, and more than a hundred musicians take their places. Suddenly someone asks: since the violin sounds so beautiful, why not have all hundred of them play the violin? The answer is simple — then what is on stage would no longer be an orchestra, but a hundred violins. The volume would go up, but the music would vanish.

Brothers and sisters, the church is the same. God never intended to make a hundred identical copies of you. We often say, “Christ is the head, and we are the body.” That is not an abstract metaphor but a truth about our originally intended position. True humility is not only knowing “I am not God”; it also means knowing “I am not the head”. Acknowledging that we are not God really isn’t hard; what is hard is acknowledging, in the small group, at home and in the serving team, that I am not the one who sets the direction. Pride is being out of position; humility is returning to position.

Paul wrote 1 Corinthians around AD 55, while he was living in Ephesus. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, crowded with merchants and travellers, with much wealth and many idols. The church in Corinth that received the letter had gifts, but no character; excitement, but no order; spiritual displays, but no spiritual life. Their problems had one single root — jealousy and strife; put plainly, the self-centred life. So the prescription Paul writes out doesn’t begin with rules; it begins with “the body”.

Paul says: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?” This sentence reveals a spiritual fact: God’s design is unity in diversity. Brothers and sisters, there are often two voices in church. The person who feels inferior says, “I’m no use”; the person who feels superior says, “You’re no use.” Both sentences actually deny the very same thing — God’s arrangement.

That is why Paul says: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” Your place was not drawn by lot, and it was not won by your own striving; God personally put you there. Our bodies have about thirty-seven trillion cells, and almost every one carries the same set of DNA, yet they grow into completely different functions. One blueprint, different callings. Brothers and sisters, from today you no longer need to envy anyone else’s position.

Paul goes on: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” Notice that he has the higher speak to the lower. Because the damage done by pride always flows downhill. In church it is rarely the newcomer who looks down on the senior; it is usually the senior who looks down on the newcomer. It is rarely the one who cooks who looks down on the one who preaches; it is usually the one on the platform who looks down on the one in the kitchen. Brothers and sisters, everyone matters, but no one matters most.

Paul also says: “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” We have parathyroid glands, usually four of them, each only the size of a grain of rice, together weighing less than 0.2 grams, yet they govern the level of calcium in the blood of the whole body; if they are removed, the whole body goes into spasm. The older saint who comes half an hour early every week to open up and set out the chairs is the church’s parathyroid gland. No one is the best, everyone else is better than me, and together we are at our best.

The third key point is the heart of this lesson. The core of pride is wanting to take the place of the head. The Bible says: “He is the head of the body, the assembly … that in all things he might have the preeminence.” The word “preeminence” appears only this once in the whole New Testament. Notice the words “in all things”. The head sets the direction; the members carry out the mission. Our responsibility is not to take control but to obey.

Brothers and sisters, the first pride in the Bible was not in a human being. Isaiah records that monologue: five “I will”s, five times out of position. Jude puts it even more precisely: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place.” But Christ took the completely opposite road — he “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”. Satan wanted to go up; Christ was willing to come down. So humility is not putting yourself down; humility is returning to your originally intended position.

The lesson gives us four practices. First, accepting difference: this week, deliberately appreciate the co-worker most different from you, and give thanks for them. Second, humble submission: when you disagree, first stay quiet for thirty seconds and ask in your heart, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?” Third, respecting our originally intended position: faithfully play the role God has given you, and don’t overstep into other people’s callings. Fourth, praying for unity: spend three minutes every day praying by name for members of the church.

Brothers and sisters, true unity is not “sameness” but “working together in difference”. This morning, let me extend three invitations to you. First, accept your own position, because God never wastes a single member. Second, respect other people’s positions: stop remodelling others and start appreciating them. Third, hand over the position of head: hand back to Jesus the steering wheel you have been gripping all this time. Pride puts us out of position; humility returns us to our position.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, you are the head of the whole church, and you have the preeminence in all things. Forgive us for the unspoken “I have no need for you” in our hearts, and forgive us for having, without even noticing, sat down in the seat that only you deserve. Give us a humble heart that can count others better than ourselves; give us a faithful heart that, at the post you have given us, does not strive, does not grab and does not compare. May your body be healthy, and may your name be glorified. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we look together at Lesson 93 of Morning Devotion 321, entitled “Return to Our Originally Intended Position”, with the subtitle: Let Jesus Be the Head; I Am Only a Member. Let us first read today’s key verse: “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” This verse comes from 1 Corinthians 12:27. In one short sentence it says two things: we belong to the same body, yet each of us is a different member. May the Holy Spirit, this morning, put each one of us back in the place God has arranged for us.

First, picture a scene with me. A symphony orchestra walks onto the stage, and more than a hundred musicians take their places. The bows of the first violins are already raised, and the timpanist stands guard over drums that will be struck only a few times all evening. Suddenly someone asks: since the violin sounds so beautiful, why not have all hundred of them play the violin? The answer is simple — then what is on stage would no longer be an orchestra, but a hundred violins. The volume would go up, but the music would vanish. Brothers and sisters, the church is the same. God never intended to make a hundred identical copies of you.

In church we often say, “Christ is the head, and we are the body.” Say it long enough and it can turn into a pleasant but empty slogan. In fact it is a truth about our originally intended position. Paul says God “gave him to be head over all things for the assembly”. There is only one head, but there are thousands upon thousands of members. So true humility is not only knowing “I am not God”; it also means knowing “I am not the head”. The 321 vision puts it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In a few words: pride is being out of position; humility is returning to position.

Today’s text comes from 1 Corinthians. The author is the apostle Paul, who wrote it in Ephesus around AD 55. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, crowded with merchants and travellers, with much wealth and many idols. A city like this produced a church like this: gifts, but no character; excitement, but no order. Paul says: “For you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly?” Jealousy and strife — put plainly, it is the self-centred life. So when he reaches chapter 12, Paul writes out his prescription. He doesn’t begin with rules; he begins with “the body”.

Paul says: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?” Brothers and sisters, this is a question asked with a smile, yet it reveals a serious spiritual fact: God’s design is unity in diversity. Some people are like eyes, seeing far ahead; some are like ears, good at listening; some are like hands, able to serve; some are like feet, quietly bearing the load. In the same chapter Paul says: there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. Diversity and unity have never been enemies.

Notice the context. Paul first writes about the person who feels inferior: “If the foot would say, ‘Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body’”; then about the person who feels superior. Brothers and sisters, the one who feels inferior says, “I’m no use”; the one who feels superior says, “You’re no use” — both deny the very same thing: God’s arrangement. So Paul sets down a sentence that steadies everything like an anchor: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” The word “set” in the original means God personally placing and appointing, and it is a completed action. Your place was not drawn by lot, and it was not won by your own striving.

Let’s look at our own bodies. In 2013 Eva Bianconi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy estimated that an adult human body contains about thirty-seven trillion cells. What is astonishing is not the quantity: almost every one of these cells carries exactly the same set of DNA, yet grows into completely different functions — light-sensing cells capture light, red blood cells carry oxygen, bone cells silently hold up the whole body. One blueprint, different callings. In 1981 the British researcher Meredith Belbin put the people with the highest intelligence-test scores into one team, and it often came last. He said: nobody is perfect, but a team can be.

The lesson has one sentence that really stings: if we want to change others so they become like us, we are in fact denying God’s creation. Brothers and sisters, we rarely admit that we are remodelling other people. But when I say in my heart, “Why is he so slow?”, what I am really saying is: why aren’t you me? That is the self-centred life. 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Paul asks it well: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” Since it is all received, none of it can be used for comparison. Returning to our originally intended position means respecting God’s arrangement, appreciating other people’s differences, and accepting our own uniqueness.

The second key point. Paul reminds us: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” Notice how precise Paul’s examples are. He doesn’t say “the foot can’t tell the eye”; he says “the eye can’t tell the hand” and “the head can’t tell the feet”. He deliberately has the higher speak to the lower. Why? Because the damage done by pride always flows downhill. In church it is usually the senior who looks down on the newcomer, the one on the platform who looks down on the one in the kitchen. Everyone matters, but no one matters most.

Next Paul says something that almost goes against common sense: “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” He doesn’t say the weaker members are “of some use too”; he says they are “much rather necessary”. And he presses further: God gives “more abundant honor to the inferior part”. So the result is: when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. If you have ever been woken in the middle of the night by a decayed tooth, you understand this verse. The body never says, “It’s only one tooth — just put up with it.”

The human body has a pair of often-overlooked organs — the parathyroid glands, usually four of them, each only the size of a grain of rice, together weighing less than 0.2 grams. Yet the parathyroid hormone they secrete governs the level of calcium in the blood of the whole body. If they are accidentally removed during surgery, the patient develops low blood calcium and spasms in the hands and feet. Brothers and sisters, the older saint who comes half an hour early every week to open up and set out the chairs, the sister who prays in a corner but never goes up front — they are the church’s parathyroid glands. Normally you don’t notice them; once they are gone, the whole body starts to go into spasm.

But “together” does not mean “lots of people”. In 1913 the French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann ran a rope-pulling experiment: a person pulling alone gives 100 per cent of their strength; when eight pull together, each gives on average only about half. Psychology calls this “social loafing”. People gathered together who each hide themselves only become a heap, not a body. 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. That is why 321 has the 920 practice — every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0”, the selfless life, and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards.

The third key point is the heart of this lesson. The first two points were horizontal — my relationships with my brothers and sisters; the third is vertical — my relationship with Christ. If the horizontal is to be level, the vertical must first be upright. The lesson goes straight to the point: the core of pride is wanting to take the place of the head. The Bible says it very clearly: “He is the head of the body, the assembly … that in all things he might have the preeminence.” The word “preeminence” appears only this once in the whole New Testament. Notice the words “in all things”: it isn’t first place on Sunday and someone else taking over on Monday. The head sets the direction; the members carry out the mission.

Brothers and sisters, the first pride to appear in the Bible was not in a human being but in an angel. The prophet Isaiah records that chilling monologue: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will make myself like the Most High. Five “I will”s, five times out of position. Jude sums it up with one precise word: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place.” Its original place was that of a worshipper, yet it wanted to sit on the throne of the one who is worshipped. The essence of Satan is not some evil innovation, but a confusion of position.

And Christ took the completely opposite road. Paul says: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” Satan wanted to go up; Christ was willing to come down. “Emptied himself” in the original literally means poured himself out until empty. So humility is not putting yourself down; humility is returning to your originally intended position. A person with a severe neck injury may have perfectly healthy arms, yet cannot lift them — it isn’t that the arms are broken; it’s that the connection between the arms and the head has been cut. The paralysis of a church is often like this.

Brothers and sisters, our responsibility is not to take control but to obey. This is exactly the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Letting Jesus be King means that whenever we disagree, the first question I ask is not “Who’s right?” but “Lord, what do you want?”; it means not competing for position or grabbing for power at my post. And stepping back like this is no loss. Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out. What you give up is one small place; what you gain is an infinite Christ.

The lesson gives us four practices, and we deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset. The first practice is accepting difference. Information: remember, “God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” Implementation: this week, pick the co-worker most different from you, write down three of their strengths, and tell them one of them face to face. The second practice is humble submission. Information: remember, “each counting others better than himself.” Implementation: the next time you clash, stay quiet for thirty seconds and ask in your heart, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?” If you said something wrong, go and apologise within twenty-four hours.

The third practice is respecting our originally intended position. Information: remember Jude’s reminder — the angels who didn’t keep their first domain. Implementation: write down the calling God has given you, and also one thing you should let go of and hand back to someone else. The fourth practice is praying for unity. Unity is not something we manufacture but something the Holy Spirit gives; our responsibility is to be eager to keep it. Implementation: every morning, spend three minutes praying by name for three members of the church. The last stage is Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to keep watch in prayer with you, becoming what 321 calls your “2”.

Brothers and sisters, the “body” Paul speaks of is exactly what 321 calls “God’s system”. The Three Foundations are crystal clear in this lesson: Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself and showed us what it means to return to our originally intended position; the Bible is my standard — not where I feel I ought to be, but where God’s word says I am; the Holy Spirit is my guide — in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. And the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, true unity is not “sameness” but “working together in difference”. The beauty of an orchestra is not that every instrument plays the same note, but that different notes sound together and become harmony. This morning, let me extend three invitations to you. First, accept your own position. Perhaps you have served in that corner for many years without applause; remember, God arranged it just as he desired, and God never wastes a single member. Second, respect other people’s positions. Stop remodelling others and start appreciating them. Third, hand over the position of head: hand back to Jesus the steering wheel you have been gripping. Pride puts us out of position; humility returns us to our position.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, you are the head of the whole church, and you have the preeminence in all things. Lord, forgive us for so often wanting to remake others in our own image; forgive us for the unspoken “I have no need for you” in our hearts; and forgive us for having, without even noticing, sat down in the seat that only you deserve. Give us a humble heart that can count others better than ourselves; give us a faithful heart that, at the post you have given us, does not strive, does not grab and does not compare. Be our head, and let our families, our small groups and our church all hold fast to you, the head, building itself up in love. May your body be healthy, and may your name be glorified. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Mutiny of a Single Cell
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion I’d like to begin by asking you to think about something that happens in your body every single day, yet you never notice it.

Scientists estimate that the human body is made up of roughly thirty-seven trillion cells. Every one of those thirty-seven trillion cells is alive; every one has its own work to do; and every one has its own lifespan. More astonishing still: every day, somewhere between fifty and seventy billion cells in your body quietly “die by themselves.” Medicine calls this “programmed cell death” (apoptosis). It is not an accident and it is not a disease. It is a programme the Creator wrote into the cell: when a cell grows old, becomes damaged, or has finished its task, it takes itself apart, hands its usable materials back to the body, and lets a new cell take its place.

In other words, your body is healthy not because every cell is fighting desperately to stay alive, but because the overwhelming majority of cells are willing, at the right time, to stand in the right place and do the right thing — and even, when it is time to leave the stage, to leave it quietly.

So what happens if one cell refuses?

What if one cell says, “I won’t die. I want to live for ever. I won’t stay where I was put — I want to expand. I won’t listen to the body’s instructions — I’ll be my own master”? Brothers and sisters, that cell has a name we all fear. It is called a cancer cell.

What is cancer at its core? Medically, cancer cells have three classic hallmarks. First, they refuse apoptosis — they will not die. Second, they multiply without limit, endlessly expanding themselves. Third, they “metastasise” (metastasis): they leave the place where they belong and travel to other parts of the body. Refusing to die, insisting on expanding, leaving their proper place — taken one at a time, each of these might look like nothing more than “being full of vitality.” Put all three together, and they are enough to take a person’s life.

C. S. Lewis, the most influential Christian apologist of the twentieth century, wrote a chilling sentence in Mere Christianity: “Pride is spiritual cancer: it eats up the very possibility of love, or contentment, or even common sense.” He wasn’t exaggerating for effect. He was describing a spiritual fact: what pride does in the human heart is exactly what a cancer cell does in the body — it refuses to die, it insists on expanding, and it leaves its proper place.

In our last lesson we reflected together on “position.” Today we take one step further. The lesson’s introduction puts it beautifully: every member of the body matters, but when a member leaves its proper place and harms the whole, it is no longer a blessing — it is destruction. God established order to protect the life of the whole, so that every part can function in the right place. Humility is staying in the place God has given us; pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place.

Today we will reflect together on two crucial truths: first, “the body matters more than the member,” and second, “the end of pride.” We’ll begin with one of the sternest sayings Jesus spoke in the Sermon on the Mount, and then we’ll climb onto the roof of the palace in Babylon to watch a king of the world brought low by God for seven times — and restored by God in the instant he lifted his eyes to heaven.

Brothers and sisters, this lesson isn’t for someone else. A cell never thinks of itself as cancerous, and a proud person never thinks of himself as proud. So let us ask the Lord to shine his light on each one of us today, so that we can see in our own hearts that little bit of “self” that refuses to die and refuses to return to its place.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Truth
1. Matthew 5: Spiritual Surgery in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector. It is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians. Matthew quotes the Old Testament again and again, because he wants to prove to his own people that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah King the Old Testament promised. So the “Sermon on the Mount” in Matthew 5–7 is not a set of moral maxims; it is the charter of the kingdom, proclaimed by the King of heaven’s kingdom.

In Matthew 5:20 Jesus says, “For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.” Then, using six sayings of the form “You have heard that it was said … but I tell you,” he pushes the law from the level of behaviour down to the level of the heart. The passage around Matthew 5:29–30 is about adultery: the Lord says that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. And then at once he says it — if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away.

This is hyperbole, a common device in Jewish rabbinic teaching. Its aim is not to make people maim themselves but to shock them. After all, if plucking out an eye or cutting off a hand could really deal with sin, then blind people would never sin — yet Jesus says plainly that the problem lies “in the heart.” He uses the most violent surgical image to teach the most serious principle: deal with sin the way you would deal with a deadly disease; to preserve the life of the whole, you must have the courage to cut away the part that is bringing corruption.

Notice the Lord’s wording: “it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.” The Greek for “whole body” here is holon to sōma — the entire body. The Lord’s logic is crystal clear: which weighs more, the one member or the whole body? The whole body. This is the biblical foundation for the first key point of this lesson — the body matters more than the member.

sections.heading: 2. Daniel 4: A Royal Proclamation
sections.html:
Daniel 4 is unique in the whole Bible. It is not a prophet’s account; it is a public decree issued in the hand of a pagan king. Daniel 4:1 opens like this: “Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all the peoples, nations, and languages, who dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you.” The whole chapter is written in the first person — “I, Nebuchadnezzar” — a testimony signed by the king himself.

Nebuchadnezzar was the greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. He reigned from 605 to 562 BC — forty-three years. He defeated Egypt at Carchemish, captured Jerusalem, brought the kingdom of Judah to an end, and carried the temple vessels off to Babylon. He made the city of Babylon one of the wonders of the ancient world: its massive walls, the magnificent Ishtar Gate (now housed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin), and the legendary Hanging Gardens.

Archaeology gives the Bible a remarkably powerful piece of corroboration. The British Museum holds a cuneiform inscription unearthed at Babylon, which scholars call the East India House Inscription. On it is Nebuchadnezzar’s own account of himself, boasting again and again of how “I” built, how “I” fortified, how “I” made Babylon a city of glory. Brothers and sisters, the boast recorded in Daniel 4:30 was not invented by the biblical writer to blacken his name — it was the very tone in which this king spoke all his life, the “self” he carved into brick and left to posterity.

The book of Daniel was written by Daniel, who was carried off to Babylon in 605 BC, lived through two empires, Babylon and Persia, and served four kings. The book’s central message, which recurs in chapters 4 and 5, comes down to a single sentence: “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will” (Daniel 4:25). The whole book of Daniel was written for God’s people in exile, people who seemed to have been abandoned by history: don’t think the king of Babylon is the greatest. There is a King in heaven who is greater than every king on earth.

So when we put today’s two passages side by side, they form the skeleton of this lesson: Matthew teaches us how to see “the whole and the part,” and Daniel shows us “where leaving our proper place ends.”

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Body Matters More Than the Member — Choosing for the Sake of the Whole
sections.html:
“If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna. If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off, and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.” (Matthew 5:29–30)

This is an extremely forceful image. The Lord isn’t asking us literally to harm ourselves; he wants us to understand that preserving the life of the whole matters far more than protecting any individual part.

Let’s first look closely at the words. “Causes you to stumble” is the Greek skandalizō, from the root skandalon, which originally meant the trigger stick in an animal trap — the part that springs the whole thing at the slightest touch. By extension it came to mean a “stumbling block,” the “trigger of a trap.” What the Lord is saying is not “this member is bad,” but “this member is becoming the trigger that springs the whole trap.” In Jewish culture the right eye and the right hand stood for the most precious, most useful, most indispensable parts. The Lord deliberately chose the most valuable — he didn’t say cut off your little finger; he said cut off your right hand.

Why? Because the Lord knows that the part we are always most reluctant to deal with is the part that is most useful, contributes the most, and is most gifted.

Every member of the body is cherished and valued. When God made us, he didn’t make a single unnecessary organ. Paul says, “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired” (1 Corinthians 12:18). Every member was placed there by God himself; not one is an accident, not one is optional.

But if one of the members stubbornly refuses to repent — not only failing to work with the whole but actually spreading corruption — it may put the entire body in danger. At that point, to protect the health of the whole, a choice has to be made.

Let’s go back to medicine. When a diabetic patient develops gangrene in a toe, the doctor’s first step is never amputation. It is debridement, blood-sugar control, antibiotics, hyperbaric oxygen, fresh dressings every day. The doctor will try everything to save that toe. But if the necrosis keeps spreading and bacteria enter the bloodstream, sepsis could take the patient’s life at any moment — and then the doctor does something that looks terribly cruel: he amputates.

Let me ask you: does the surgeon who amputates hate that toe? No. The surgeon who amputates loves that person. He removes a toe in order to save a life.

It is the same in the church. If a member is weak or has fallen, we should support and help them, as we would wash and dress the wound on an injured foot. Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). The word “restore” is the Greek katartizō. In the New Testament it is also used of fishermen “mending” their nets, and in medicine it was used for “setting” a broken bone. The first thing God gives the church to do is always to mend the net, set the bone, bring healing.

But if that member refuses to repent and even goes on causing damage, then, out of love and a desire to protect, spiritual surgery may sometimes be necessary — cutting away the influence of sin so that the church is not defiled.

In Matthew 18 the Lord Jesus gave the church a very clear sequence: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15); if he won’t listen, take one or two others along; if he still won’t listen, tell the church; “If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector” (Matthew 18:17). Notice that the Lord gives three lines of defence, three chances, and the aim of every step is “gaining back your brother.” Spiritual surgery is the last step, not the first.

Protecting the body is not cruelty; it is the courage of love. When the Lord Jesus cleansed the temple and overturned the money-changers’ tables, he wasn’t losing his temper; he was restoring the holiness of the temple. John records: “He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money and overthrew their tables” (John 2:15). And what his disciples remembered then was a line from the Psalms: “Zeal for your house will eat me up” (John 2:17). The Lord’s fierceness did not come from temper; it came from love for his Father’s house.

In the same way, if the church is to be healthy, it must bravely face sin and deal with pride. For a little yeast of pride can leaven the whole lump. When Paul dealt with sin in the Corinthian church he said, “Your boasting is not good. Don’t you know that a little yeast leavens the whole lump?” (1 Corinthians 5:6). And in Galatians he says, “A little yeast grows through the whole lump” (Galatians 5:9). What is yeast like? It is quiet, tiny, invisible — and yet it transforms the whole batch of dough. Sin and pride are just the same: they never stay where they are.

From the 321 perspective, this point touches the most fundamental distinction of all: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. For the self-centred, the measure of everything is always “What will happen to me, this one member?” For the selfless, the measure of everything is “What will happen to the body of Christ?” What the Lord Jesus wants us to learn here is precisely to move from the outlook of “one member” to the outlook of “the whole body” — the shift in perspective that 321 speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from the temporary to the eternal.

Brothers and sisters, I invite you to ask yourself one honest question today: in your small group, your team, your family, is there something you know full well is hurting the whole, but because it involves your face, your gifting, your position, you have kept refusing to deal with it? That may be your “right hand.”

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Humility Is Returning to Our Originally Intended Position; Pride Is Leaving It
sections.html:
Humility is the willingness to lay down our rights and return to the place God has appointed. Pride is clinging to our rights and wanting to stand in God’s place.

There is a verse in the Bible that is enormously important yet often overlooked, and it makes the idea of “our originally intended position” clearer than any other: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).

“First domain” is the Greek archē, which originally means “beginning” or “origin,” and also “office” or “sphere of rule.” The reason the angels fell was not that they committed some earth-shattering atrocity, but simply this — they did not keep their position. They left the sphere God had appointed for them.

This is the very prototype of Satan. Isaiah describes the fallen shining star: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Five times, “I will.” Brothers and sisters, the first sin in the universe was not murder and it was not adultery; it was five “I will”s — a created being refusing to stay in a created being’s place.

And the way of salvation runs in exactly the opposite direction. Philippians 2: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8). “Emptied himself” is the Greek kenoō — to pour oneself out. Satan is a creature trying to climb up to God’s place; Jesus is God himself coming down to a servant’s place.

So 321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Does that sound abstract? The lesson gives us two very concrete tests.

The first test: when someone wrongs us. If we insist, “I have the right to hold a grudge,” that is pride. If we can choose to forgive, laying down the right to “avenge ourselves,” that is the response of humility.

Why is insisting on a grudge pride? Because the Bible says, “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). Whose authority is vengeance? God’s. When I hold on and refuse to forgive, what I am really saying is, “God, I don’t trust you with this; I’ll do the judging myself.” — and in that moment I have climbed onto the judgment seat. And the judgment seat is God’s place.

That is why the Lord teaches us: “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” (Matthew 6:14–15). And Paul says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

Someone once said that refusing to forgive is like drinking poison yourself and expecting the other person to die. Medically, this is more than a metaphor. Long-term hostility and resentment are an established psychosocial risk factor for cardiovascular disease; the American Heart Association and a large body of epidemiological research point out that chronic anger and hostility are associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and coronary artery disease. Brothers and sisters, the one a grudge really hurts is very often the body of the person who holds it.

The second test: when we want others to see what we’ve given and acknowledge what we’ve achieved, we have in fact already left our originally intended position and, in our hearts, seized God’s glory.

The Lord Jesus said, “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1). Notice the Lord’s wording: not “don’t do good works,” but “not … to be seen by them.” The very same good deed can be an offering or it can be a theft — the only difference is the heart: whether the glory is sent upward or gathered onto ourselves.

The fruit of pride is being brought low by God; it is the humble life that God lifts up. Scripture repeats the same sentence more than once: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Peter goes on: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). Notice — lifting up is God’s work, not mine. My only work is to humble myself, to return to my place.

Psychology holds up a rather merciless mirror. In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University published a famous study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that the least competent people tend to overestimate their own performance the most — because the very skills that make someone good at a task are the same skills needed to judge whether they are doing it well. It came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect.” Earlier still, in a 1981 study, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that about ninety-three per cent of the American drivers he surveyed believed their driving skill was above the median — which, by definition, is mathematically impossible.

Brothers and sisters, these two studies tell us the same thing: by nature we cannot see our own pride. The most terrifying thing about pride is not that it is strong, but that it is invisible.

That is why 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is on myself, I am forever measuring my own height; only when the focus is on Jesus do I discover my true proportions. And that is why the 920 practice of 321 is so practical: every person we are in relationship with is our “2,” and in every relationship we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). You cannot prove you are humble when you are alone; humility is only tested in relationships.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The End of Pride — Nebuchadnezzar’s Testimony
sections.html:
The Bible tells us of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, whose kingdom was mighty and whose fame was great. One day he stood on the roof of his palace and boasted, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30)

Listen to the three key phrases in that one sentence: “the might of my power,” “I have built,” “the glory of my majesty.” One sentence, three times “my.” This is the classic grammar of leaving our originally intended position.

And none of this happened suddenly. A full twelve months earlier, God had already warned him through a dream. After interpreting the dream, Daniel pleaded with him earnestly: “Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps there may be a lengthening of your tranquility” (Daniel 4:27). God gave him twelve months to repent. Brothers and sisters, God’s judgment is never an ambush. God always warns first and waits first.

Before he had even finished speaking, God’s word came upon him and took away his reason. “While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, ‘O king Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you’” (Daniel 4:31).

“This was fulfilled the same hour on Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from men, and ate grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky, until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.” (Daniel 4:33)

Notice what the text describes: living with the beasts of the field, eating grass like an ox. This king, who had once fancied himself the first man under heaven, was put by God among the cattle. Some scholars of medical history have suggested that this may have been an extremely rare delusional disorder in which the sufferer believes he is an ox, known as “boanthropy.” Whatever we call it, the point Scripture is making is perfectly clear: if a man insists on being God, God lets him see that, apart from God, he cannot even manage to be a man.

There is a sobering contrast here. God made man in his own image — “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Man climbed upward trying to be God, and fell instead to the level of a beast. Brothers and sisters, we cannot rise above our originally intended position; the moment we try to go up, we are bound to fall down. That is the law of gravity in the spiritual world.

After seven times — generally understood as seven years — he lifted his eyes to heaven and acknowledged that God is the Most High. Then his reason returned, and his kingdom was given back to him. The text says, “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever; for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation” (Daniel 4:34).

Brothers and sisters, notice the order here: first he lifted his eyes to heaven, and only then did his understanding return. It wasn’t that his reason came back first and then he worshipped; the moment he worshipped, his reason returned. The moment he looked up was the moment he returned to his place. A man who had spent seven years with his head down eating grass among the cattle needed only to be willing to look up once, and God gave everything back to him.

In the end he testified: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37).

This episode gives us much to ponder: pride costs us our reason, our position and our glory; humility brings us back under God’s blessing and authority.

However great our achievements, however fruitful our ministry, we have nothing to boast about. For everything we have, we have received. Paul makes the case unanswerably: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

As Job said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name” (Job 1:21).

When Job said this, he had lost in a single day seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred female donkeys — and ten children. And still he said, Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. How could he stand? Because he had known from the beginning that none of it had ever been “his.” A person who never thought things belonged to him will not collapse when he loses them.

In Good to Great, published in 2001, the management thinker Jim Collins studied eleven companies that leapt from mediocrity to excellence and sustained it over the long term, and he found that their leaders shared a common combination, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: extreme personal humility joined to intense professional will. When these leaders spoke of success, they always pointed to others, to the team, to good luck; when they spoke of failure, they always pointed to themselves. Collins said he had not expected to find this — the data forced him to admit it.

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research has found that the people who go the distance are the ones who send the glory outward. How much more should we, who believe in the Lord who emptied himself and took the form of a servant?

This is the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Nebuchadnezzar’s failure was not that he built Babylon — there’s nothing wrong with building. His failure was that, once he had built it, he credited both the place of “king” and the ownership of the “glory” to himself. Brothers and sisters, our ministry is the same: the question has never been how much we’ve done, but where the applause goes once we’ve done it.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Humility Keeps the Church Healthy; Pride Corrupts It
sections.html:
Pride makes people overstep, sets members in conflict and throws the body off balance. Humility brings people back to their place, so that the church can be knit together in love and united in the truth.

Paul’s picture of the church as a body is the fullest and warmest teaching on the church in the New Testament. “For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12). “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).

In a healthy body, no organ fights for credit for its own performance. The heart never says to the lungs, “I’m the one who delivered today’s oxygen.” The liver never complains, “Why does the brain get all the applause?” The body is beautiful because every organ stays in its own place, quietly working for the others.

But brothers and sisters, have you ever wondered what happens when an organ starts “fighting for more” for itself? When the heart decides to beat faster than the body needs, that’s an arrhythmia. When cells decide to grow more than the body allows, that’s a tumour. When the immune system decides to attack its own body, that’s an autoimmune disease. Almost every conflict in a church can be put into one of these three categories: someone rushing to beat faster, someone rushing to grow bigger, someone starting to attack their own people.

All these problems have one and the same root: forgetting who the head is.

Paul says, “He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:22–23). And again: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18).

Physiologically, this image is astonishingly precise. All the coordination in the human body depends on the central nervous system. When the spinal cord is injured and the signal is cut off, the limb itself hasn’t broken — the muscle is still there, the bone is still there, the blood is still there — but it can no longer move, because it has lost its connection to the head. The church is the same: the gifts are still there, the numbers are still there, the activities are still there, but once the connection to Christ the Head is broken, all that remains is religious motion with no spiritual life.

So Paul gives a definition of a healthy church: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:15–16).

Look at four keys in this passage: speaking truth in love; being joined to Christ the Head; every joint doing its own part; building itself up in love. “Speaking truth in love” — not love without truth, and not truth without love. “Every joint supplies … according to the working in measure of each individual part” — in the Greek, each joint supplies according to its own measure, and no joint does another’s work. That is returning to our originally intended position.

A church that exalts only human achievement and will not submit to Christ as its head will end up like Nebuchadnezzar — torn down by God and forced to learn humility.

This is a heavy word, but it has to be said. Almost every fall in church history began with the same thing: treating God’s work as man’s achievement. The medieval church had boundless wealth and power, and what it got in return was the thunderbolt of the Reformation. It is the same today: when a church begins to measure whether it is blessed by its numbers, its offerings, its buildings and its reputation, that church is already standing on the palace roof.

But if the church is willing to confess, “Christ is the head; we are only members,” then God’s glory will fill his house once again.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in human history. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has distilled decades of data into one conclusion: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout their lives is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. It took the world eighty years and several generations of scholars to confirm what the Bible had long since said — God made us to live in relationship, and for relationships to be healthy, each person must return to their own place.

The 235 relationships of 321 put this very principle into practice: with selfless people we become a “2,” spiritual companions who support one another; we build a “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and we go on to become a “5,” a team of spiritual comrades in which the fivefold ministry works together. Notice that 2, 3 and 5 are all numbers of relationship; none of them is a “1.” There are no lone rangers in the church — only members.

In a letter to Dioscorus, Augustine was asked what the way to truth is, and he answered: the first is humility, the second is humility, and the third is humility. Brothers and sisters, the health of the church has the same answer.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
When we set this lesson back within the framework of 321, the thread becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — when it comes to keeping our originally intended position, Jesus is the only perfect demonstration: he existed in the form of God, yet willingly emptied himself and took the form of a servant. The Bible is my standard — the surgeon’s knife in Matthew and the palace roof in Daniel are not our opinions; they are God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — because pride is invisible, we cannot see ourselves by our own light; we need the Holy Spirit to shine on us. The psalmist says, “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — the church’s problem has never been who should be the leader, but who is sitting on the throne. Let Jesus receive all the glory — Nebuchadnezzar’s failure lay in keeping the glory for himself; Job’s victory lay in giving everything back to Yahweh.

The Goal. Establish God’s system. The one condition for any system to work is that every part is in its own place. Parts scattered across the floor are not a machine; members each going their own way are not a body. God’s system is made up of people who have returned to their originally intended position.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Satan’s five “I will”s and Nebuchadnezzar’s three “my”s are all the self-centred life. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, living out that fullness; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Why? Because the only thing Satan can attack is the “self.” With a person who has no “self,” Satan has nowhere to get a grip. You cannot humiliate someone who isn’t seeking his own glory; you cannot provoke someone who isn’t avenging himself; you cannot buy someone who isn’t grasping at his own rights.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Almost every conflict in a church begins like this: he oversteps, I won’t submit; and the moment I won’t submit, I overstep too; and so both of us have left our originally intended position, and both of us lose. But as soon as one person returns to their place first, the whole atmosphere changes. Humility is contagious.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The mindset this lesson sets out to change is exactly that sentence — the body matters more than the member. When that mindset really gets inside you, your life will loosen its grip; once your life loosens, your daily living no longer needs to prove itself at every turn; once your daily living changes, your relationships with others are healed; and once relationships flow, ministry bears fruit naturally.

A shift in perspective. From man’s perspective, cutting something away is a loss; from God’s perspective, it is preservation. From an earthly perspective, being brought low is humiliation; from heaven’s perspective, being brought low is rescue. From a temporary perspective, Nebuchadnezzar lost seven years; from an eternal perspective, he traded seven years for the knowledge of the everlasting God. Brothers and sisters, sometimes God brings us down from the roof to the grass not to destroy us, but to save us.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The place where pride flares up first is always the heart; and the place where returning to our position happens first is the heart as well.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. The Holy Spirit leads us to see that we have left our originally intended position; the Bible makes us understand where we ought to stand; Jesus’ role model makes us willing to go back; and so our ministry becomes ministry that lets Jesus be King; and in the end all the glory goes to him.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: An Order Check

Consider: am I overstepping in the church or in my family? Have I taken God’s place?

Information: Today you have heard two passages — Jude 6, on the angels who did not keep their position, and Daniel 4:30, on the three “my”s on the palace roof. Start by copying these two passages into your notebook.

Revelation: Be still for ten minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you by name: at home, am I overriding my spouse, overriding my parents’ authority? In the church, am I overriding the pastor, overriding my co-workers’ roles? In my heart, have I already sat down on the judgment seat where only God may sit?

Conviction: Settle this — returning to our originally intended position isn’t a demotion; it’s coming home.

Implementation: This week, choose one concrete situation and practise “not taking over.” When something lies outside your role, hand it back to the person responsible for it, and pray for them.

Evaluation: Every evening ask one question: was there anywhere today where I made a decision on God’s behalf?

Correction: Confess at once; give it back at once.

Repetition: Keep practising for forty days in a row, until returning to your place becomes instinct.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion, teach them the “order check,” and remind each other.

Practice 2: Protecting the Body

Learn to admonish in love and build up in truth, never sacrificing truth to please people.

Information: Get to know well the three steps of Matthew 18:15–17, and Ephesians 4:15, “speaking truth in love.”

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you — which kind of person am I usually? Someone with love who dares not speak the truth, or someone with truth but no gentleness?

Conviction: Believe that real love is willing to risk being misunderstood for the other person’s good.

Implementation: If there’s a true word you ought to say and have been swallowing for a long time, find a chance this week to say it — privately, gently, clearly. Pray first, then speak; affirm first, then remind; and when you’ve said it, go on loving them.

Evaluation: When I spoke, was my motive to win them back, or to prove I was right?

Correction: If the motive wasn’t pure, deal with your own heart first, then deal with the matter.
