Repetition: Build the habit of not bottling things up and not judging behind people’s backs.

Multiplication: Build a culture in your small group of “say it face to face, bless them on the spot.”

Practice 3: Practising Forgiveness

Lay down the pride of “I have the right to hold a grudge”; choose to forgive and heal the relationship.

Information: Memorise Romans 12:19 and Ephesians 4:32.

Revelation: Write down a name — the name that makes your chest tighten the moment you think of it.

Conviction: Admit this: my refusing to forgive won’t make them hurt; it will only make me sick. Vengeance belongs to God, not to me.

Implementation: Say it out loud to God: “Lord, I now lay down my right to hold a grudge against them, and I hand the right of vengeance back to you.” Then bless that name, for seven days in a row.

Evaluation: Over these seven days, has my heart loosened a little?

Correction: If the feelings come back, don’t condemn yourself; pray the same prayer again. Forgiveness is often not a single decision but a whole series of decisions.

Repetition: Keep going until, when you think of that name, what rises first in your heart is a blessing, not a bill.

Multiplication: Turn your experience of healing into a testimony, and use it to lift up someone else who is bound by bitterness.

Practice 4: A Prayer of Humility

Declare every day: “Lord, keep me in the place you have given me; let me not steal your glory.”

Information: Write this declaration on your phone’s home screen, above your desk, on the kitchen wall.

Revelation: Every morning, before you speak the declaration, be still for a minute and let the Holy Spirit remind you of the moment today when you’re most likely to overstep.

Conviction: Be fully persuaded that lifting up is God’s work — “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6).

Implementation: Declare it once every morning and once again every evening.

Evaluation: Was there a word or an action today that I did so that people would see me?

Correction: Right then, in your heart, pass that glory on to the Lord and say, “Lord, this is yours.”

Repetition: Let the declaration become your breathing.

Multiplication: Declare it together with your whole family and your small group, so that returning to our originally intended position becomes a habit of the whole community.

A Gentle Reminder

Pride makes the members rot; humility can bring the body back to life.

Protecting the health of the church sometimes means forgiving and supporting, and sometimes means cutting away and dealing with things. But the final goal is always that the body of Christ might receive glory.

Brothers and sisters, please remember this balance. A church that only cuts away and never supports is cold; a church that only supports and never dares to cut away is indulgent. True spiritual wisdom is knowing when to apply the dressing and when to pick up the scalpel — and both come from the same motive, which is love.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
The body matters more than the member; unity matters more than performance; obedience matters more than achievement.

When everyone returns to their own place, Christ can reign as King in the church. Humility is the church’s root; unity is the church’s fruit.

Brothers and sisters, let’s close this morning’s devotion with a picture.

A symphony orchestra has nearly a hundred players, and each one has a part in front of them. On that part there are many bars of whole rests — which means that for long stretches they must sit there quietly and do nothing at all. A good player never feels those blank bars are wasted, because he knows those blanks are someone else’s melody. And there is only one person in the whole hall who makes no sound at all and yet decides everything — the conductor.

The church is an orchestra like that. Your notes may be few, but they are your notes; someone else’s solo may be long, but that is their calling. When everyone follows the score and watches the conductor, a hundred people make one sound. When someone decides on their own to play two extra beats, the music is ruined.

God’s call to us today is not to become bigger, but to return to the right place.

Perhaps what you need to lay down today is a right you’ve clung to for a long time. Perhaps it’s something you’ve given that nobody has noticed, which leaves you feeling hard done by. Perhaps it’s a name you’ve never been willing to forgive. Perhaps it’s a “right hand” that you know full well is hurting the whole, but that you can’t bear to deal with.

Nebuchadnezzar tells us one thing: it’s all right to look up. A man who had spent seven years in the fields needed only to be willing to lift his eyes to heaven, and God gave everything back to him. Wherever you have fallen today, looking up is the first step home.

May we spend our whole lives learning to lay down pride, return to our originally intended position, and let Jesus receive the glory that is his due.

keyVerses: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna. If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off, and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.” (Matthew 5:29–30)
“Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)
declarations: Lord, you are the head of the church;
I am willing to return in humility to the place you have given me,
not grasping at your glory, not overstepping your authority.
Guard my heart,
and let me serve in love and in truth.
May the church be built up and the body be healed,
and may the glory be yours for ever.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you that you are the head of the church, the Head over all things. We confess that we often leave the place you have given us — we want to be seen, we want to be affirmed, we cling to our right to hold a grudge and won’t let go, and we quietly keep your glory for ourselves.
Lord, make your word our mirror and your Holy Spirit our light. Shine on the “self” within us that refuses to die and refuses to return to its place.

Give us the courage of love: when it is time to support, let us gently lift up the members who have fallen; when it is time to deal with things, let us face sin and pride with clean hands, and not for our own satisfaction.

Lord, we are willing to return to the place you have given us. We are willing to let man be man and let God be God. Heal our families, build up our small groups, and let your church be knit together in love and united in the truth.
Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours, for ever and ever.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Discussion 1: The Lord Jesus said, “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna” (Matthew 5:29). In your life, family or ministry right now, is there something you treasure that is nevertheless hurting the whole? How are you willing to place it in the Lord’s hands?

Discussion 2: Nebuchadnezzar said, “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37). Share a time when God brought you low. Looking back, what was God doing in you during that time? How did you “lift your eyes to heaven”?
l094.title: Humility Returns Us to Our Place
l094.subtitle: The Body Matters More Than the Member
l094.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

blog.title: The Cell in You That Refuses to Die

blocks.x: — Why the Body Matters More Than the Member

Your body is made up of roughly thirty-seven trillion cells. Every day, tens of billions of them quietly die by themselves — what medicine calls “apoptosis”, programmed cell death. It is not an accident; it is a programme the Creator wrote into the cell: when a cell grows old or becomes damaged, it hands its materials back to the body of its own accord and lets a new cell take its place. Your body is healthy not because every cell is fighting desperately to stay alive, but because they are all willing to stay in the right place — and even, when it is time to leave the stage, to leave it quietly.
So what happens if one cell refuses?
Refusing to Die, Insisting on Expanding, Leaving Its Place

What if one cell says, “I won’t die; I want to expand; I’ll be my own master”? That cell has a name we all fear: a cancer cell. Its three hallmarks are refusing apoptosis, multiplying without limit, and leaving its proper place to spread elsewhere. Taken one at a time, each might look like nothing more than “being full of vitality”; put all three together, and they are enough to take a life.
The apologist C. S. Lewis wrote in Mere Christianity that pride is spiritual cancer. He wasn’t exaggerating — what pride does in the human heart is exactly what a cancer cell does in the body.

The Bible is remarkably precise. In describing the fallen angels, it needs only a few words: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness.” (Jude 6)
The first sin in the universe was not murder and it was not adultery; it was a created being refusing to stay in a created being’s place.
The Most Forceful Words Jesus Spoke

In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said something extremely stern: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.” (Matthew 5:29)

This is hyperbole, a device common among Jewish rabbis — not to make us maim ourselves, but to shock us. He deliberately chose the most precious part: not the little finger, but the right hand. Because the part we are always most reluctant to deal with is the most useful one. Which weighs more, the one member or the whole body? The whole body.

It is the same in the church. When a member is weak or falls, the first move is always to support and restore. It is like a doctor facing a gangrenous toe: he will always clean the wound and give medicine first, trying everything to save it; only when sepsis threatens life at any moment will he amputate. The surgeon who amputates doesn’t hate that toe; he loves that person. Protecting the body is not cruelty; it is the courage of love.
From the Palace Roof to the Grass

The most dramatic lesson in humility in the Bible took place on the roof of the palace in Babylon. Looking down over the city he had built, Nebuchadnezzar said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) One sentence, three times “my”. Before he had even finished speaking, a voice came from the sky, and the kingdom departed from him. He was driven from the palace and ate grass like an ox for seven times.

But the story doesn’t end on the grass. The text says, “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me.” (Daniel 4:34) Notice the order: first he lifted his eyes to heaven, and only then did his understanding return. It wasn’t that his reason came back first and then he worshipped; the moment he worshipped, his reason returned. The moment he looked up was the moment he returned to his place. His final testimony was: “Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)
Returning to Our Place Is Not a Demotion — It’s Coming Home

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

There are two very concrete tests. First, when someone wrongs you, if you insist, “I have the right to hold a grudge,” that is pride; because the authority to avenge belongs to God, when I hold on and refuse to forgive, I have climbed onto the judgment seat myself. Second, when you want others to see what you’ve given, you have already, in your heart, quietly gathered the glory onto yourself.

A symphony orchestra has nearly a hundred players, and every part has long rests on it. A good player never feels those are wasted, because those blanks are someone else’s melody. And the one person in the hall who makes no sound decides everything — the conductor. When everyone follows the score and watches the conductor, a hundred people make one sound.
The body matters more than the member; unity matters more than performance; obedience matters more than achievement. God’s call to us today is not to become bigger, but to return to the right place.
Reflection: Right now, in your family, workplace or ministry, is there a place you have refused to go back to? And is there some glory you have been unwilling to hand back to God?

brief12.title: Humility Returns Us to Our Place
notes: The Body Matters More Than the Member
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 94
“Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.”
Daniel 4:37
Key points:
• This lesson is the second talk in the “Return to Our Originally Intended Position” series; the theme is position.
• The lesson’s introduction: when a member leaves its proper place, it is no longer a blessing but destruction.
• Two key truths: the body matters more than the member; the end of pride.
• The other key passage: Matthew 5:29–30.

brief12.title: Introduction: The Mutiny of a Cell
notes: About 37 trillion cells in the body
Tens of billions quietly die each day
Refusing to die, expanding, leaving its place
That’s called cancer — and also pride
Key points:
• Apoptosis is a programme the Creator wrote into the cell.
• Three hallmarks of cancer cells: refusing apoptosis, multiplying without limit, metastasising out of place.
• Quote C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity: pride is spiritual cancer.
• Reminder: a cell never thinks of itself as cancerous; a proud person never thinks of himself as proud.

brief12.title: Key Verses and Background
notes: Matthew 5: the scalpel of the kingdom’s charter
Daniel 4: the testimony of Babylon’s king
The Most High rules in the kingdom of men
Daniel 4:25
Key points:
• Matthew was written between about AD 50 and 70, for Jewish Christians.
• The Sermon on the Mount is the charter of the kingdom proclaimed by the King of heaven.
• Daniel 4 is a decree signed by Nebuchadnezzar himself, written in the first person.
• Nebuchadnezzar reigned from 605 to 562 BC — forty-three years.

brief12.title: 1. The Body Matters More Than the Member
notes: If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out
Better that one of your members perish
than your whole body be cast into Gehenna
Matthew 5:29
Key points:
• This is hyperbole common among the rabbis, not a call to self-harm.
• “Causes you to stumble”, Greek skandalizō, originally the trigger stick of an animal trap.
• The right eye and right hand stand for the most precious, most useful parts.
• Which weighs more, one member or the whole body? The whole body. That is the criterion for choosing.

brief12.title: Cutting Away: The Courage of Love
notes: First support: restore gently (Galatians 6:1)
Then surgery: three steps (Matthew 18:15)
A little yeast leavens the whole lump
1 Corinthians 5:6
Key points:
• Medical picture: gangrene is debrided first, amputated only as a last resort; amputation is to save a life.
• “Restore”, katartizō, is also used for mending nets and setting bones.
• When the Lord cleansed the temple he wasn’t out of control; it was for the holiness of his Father’s house.
• Spiritual surgery is the last step, not the first.

brief12.title: 2. Humility Is Returning to Our Place
notes: Pride: grasping rights, wanting to replace God
Humility: laying down rights, returning to our place
Angels who left their domain are kept in bonds
Jude 6
Key points:
• “First domain”, Greek archē: beginning, office, sphere of rule.
• Satan’s five “I will”s (Isaiah 14:13–14) are the first sin in the universe.
• Jesus instead emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–8); kenoō means pouring oneself out.
• 321: let man be man and let God be God.

brief12.title: Two Tests: Forgiveness and Glory
notes: Insisting on a grudge is pride
Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay
Wanting to be seen steals God’s glory
Romans 12:19
Key points:
• Refusing to forgive is climbing onto God’s judgment seat yourself.
• Chronic anger and hostility are a psychosocial risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
• Matthew 6:1: don’t do your giving before men, to be seen by them.
• The Dunning–Kruger effect (1999): by nature we cannot see our own pride.

brief12.title: 3. The End of Pride
notes: Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?
Before he finished, the kingdom departed
He lifted his eyes, and understanding returned
Daniel 4:30, 34
Key points:
• One sentence, three times “my”: the might of my power, my royal dwelling place, the glory of my majesty.
• God first gave him twelve months to repent (Daniel 4:27–29).
• The East India House Inscription in the British Museum has exactly the same boastful tone.
• First he looked up, then his understanding returned; looking up is returning to our place.

brief12.title: 4. Humility Keeps the Church Healthy
notes: Christ is the head; we are only members
Every joint supplies its part
Joined to the head, built up in love
Ephesians 4:15–16
Key points:
• The heart doesn’t compete with the lungs for credit; the body’s beauty is each part in its place.
• Three church diseases: rushing to beat faster, rushing to grow bigger, attacking our own people.
• With a spinal injury, the limbs are all there but cannot move; cut the connection to the head and only motion remains.
• 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry; the 235 relationships contain no “1”.

brief12.title: Practices
notes: Order check: am I overstepping?
Protecting the body: admonish in love
Forgiveness: lay down the right to a grudge
Prayer of humility: not stealing your glory
Key points:
• Deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
• Practising forgiveness: write down a name and bless that person for seven days.
• Declaration of humility: Lord, keep me in the place you have given me.
• 1 Peter 5:6: humble yourselves, and God will exalt you.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: The body matters more than the member
Unity matters more than performance
Obedience matters more than achievement
Return to your place; let Jesus be King
Key points:
• The orchestra picture: the rests are someone else’s melody; the conductor makes no sound yet decides everything.
• The call: lay down the right you cling to, the name you won’t forgive, the right hand you can’t bear to deal with.
• Nebuchadnezzar’s hope: looking up is the first step home.
• Humility is the church’s root; unity is the church’s fruit.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
