Not grasping your glory or overstepping your authority
May the church be knit together in love
Glory to you for ever
Key points:
• Lead the congregation in praying aloud together.
• Intercede for the healing and unity of families, small groups and the church.
• Blessing: may God help us each do our part and build ourselves up in love.
• Closing declaration: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief21.title: Humility Returns Us to Our Place
notes: The Body Matters More Than the Member
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 94
“Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.”
Daniel 4:37
Key points:
• This lesson is the second talk in the “Return to Our Originally Intended Position” series; the theme is position.
• The lesson’s introduction: God established order to protect the life of the whole.
• Two key truths: the body matters more than the member; the end of pride.
• The other key passage: Matthew 5:29–30.

brief21.title: Introduction 1: Thirty-Seven Trillion Cells
notes: About 37 trillion cells in the body
Tens of billions die each day
Giving up their place keeps the body healthy
A programme written by the Creator
Key points:
• Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not an accident.
• Health is not every cell fighting to live, but each staying in its place and leaving on time.
• Order is not restriction; it is protection.
• Pave the way for today’s theme: position determines blessing or destruction.

brief21.title: Introduction 2: The Cell That Refuses
notes: Refusing to die, expanding, leaving its place
That’s called a cancer cell
Pride is spiritual cancer
C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity
Key points:
• Three hallmarks of cancer cells: refusing apoptosis, multiplying without limit, metastasising out of place.
• Lewis’s own words: pride eats up the very possibility of love, or contentment, or even common sense.
• A cell never thinks of itself as cancerous; a proud person never thinks of himself as proud.
• Ask the Lord today to shine on the little bit of “self” in us that refuses to return to its place.

brief21.title: Key Verses and Background
notes: Matthew 5: the scalpel of the kingdom’s charter
Daniel 4: the testimony of Babylon’s king
The Most High rules in the kingdom of men
Daniel 4:25
Key points:
• Matthew was written between about AD 50 and 70, for Jewish Christians.
• The context of Matthew 5:29–30 is adultery; the Lord pushes the law down into the heart.
• Daniel 4 is written in the first person, a testimony signed by the king himself.
• Nebuchadnezzar reigned from 605 to 562 BC — forty-three years in all.

brief21.title: 1. The Body Matters More Than the Member
notes: If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out
Better that one of your members perish
than your whole body be cast into Gehenna
Matthew 5:29
Key points:
• Rabbinic hyperbole — not to make people maim themselves, but to shock them.
• “Causes you to stumble”, skandalizō, originally the trigger stick on an animal trap.
• The right eye and right hand stand for the most precious, most useful, hardest-to-give-up parts.
• Greek “whole body”, holon to sōma: which weighs more, the one member or the whole?

brief21.title: Every Member Is Placed by God
notes: God has set the members
in the body, just as he desired
1 Corinthians 12:18
Support first, then decide what to cut
Key points:
• God made no unnecessary organ; not one member is an accident.
• Galatians 6:1: restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.
• “Restore”, katartizō, is also used of fishermen mending nets and doctors setting bones.
• Matthew 18:15–17: three lines of defence, all aimed at gaining back your brother.

brief21.title: Cutting Away: The Courage of Love
notes: Gangrene: clean first, amputate last
Amputating isn’t hating the foot, but loving the person
A little yeast leavens the whole lump
1 Corinthians 5:6
Key points:
• The doctor tries everything to save the toe, and amputates only when sepsis comes.
• When the Lord cleansed the temple and overturned the tables, he wasn’t out of control; it was for the holiness of his Father’s house.
• Yeast is tiny, quiet, invisible, yet it transforms the whole lump.
• 321: move from the outlook of “my one member” to the outlook of “the body of Christ”.

brief21.title: 2. Humility Is Returning to Our Place
notes: Pride: grasping rights, replacing God
Humility: laying down rights, returning to our place
Angels who left their first domain and dwelling
Jude 6
Key points:
• “First domain”, Greek archē: beginning, office, sphere of rule.
• The reason the angels fell comes down to this: they did not keep their position.
• 321: pride is leaving our originally intended position; humility is returning to it.
• Let man be man and let God be God.

brief21.title: Five “I Will”s vs One Emptying
notes: I will ascend into heaven
I will make myself like the Most High
He emptied himself, taking a servant’s form
Isaiah 14:13–14; Philippians 2:6–8
Key points:
• The first sin in the universe was not murder but five “I will”s.
• “Emptied himself”, kenoō, means pouring oneself out.
• Satan is a creature climbing up; Jesus is God himself coming down.
• Jesus is my role model — the first of the Three Foundations of 321.

brief21.title: Two Tests: Forgiveness and Glory
notes: Insisting on a grudge is pride
Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay
Wanting to be seen steals God’s glory
Romans 12:19
Key points:
• Refusing to forgive is climbing onto God’s judgment seat yourself.
• Matthew 6:14–15; Ephesians 4:32.
• Matthew 6:1: not to be seen by them.
• The Dunning–Kruger effect (1999): by nature we cannot see our own pride.

brief21.title: 3. The End of Pride
notes: Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?
One sentence, three times “my”
Before he finished, the kingdom departed
Daniel 4:30–31
Key points:
• Three times “my”: the might of my power, my royal dwelling place, the glory of my majesty.
• God first gave him twelve months to repent (Daniel 4:27–29).
• The East India House Inscription in the British Museum has exactly the same boastful tone.
• God’s judgment is never an ambush; God always warns first and waits first.

brief21.title: From the Palace to the Grass
notes: He was driven from men
Ate grass as oxen, wet with the dew of the sky
Hair like eagles’ feathers, nails like birds’ claws
Daniel 4:33
Key points:
• Man was made in God’s image; trying to be God, he fell to the level of a beast.
• Some medical historians suggest the rare delusional disorder “boanthropy”.
• The spiritual law of gravity: try to climb up, and you are bound to fall down.
• If a man insists on being God, God lets him see that he cannot even manage to be a man.

brief21.title: Looking Up Is Returning to Our Place
notes: At the end of the days I lifted up my eyes to heaven
and my understanding returned to me
Those who walk in pride he is able to abase
Daniel 4:34, 37
Key points:
• The order: first he looked up, then his understanding returned — not sobered first and then worshipping.
• 1 Corinthians 4:7: what do you have that you didn’t receive?
• Job 1:21: Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away.
• Jim Collins, Good to Great, Level 5 Leadership: extreme personal humility plus intense professional will.

brief21.title: 4. Humility Keeps the Church Healthy
notes: Many members, yet one body
When one member suffers, all suffer
When one is honoured, all rejoice
1 Corinthians 12:12, 26
Key points:
• The heart doesn’t compete with the lungs for credit; the liver doesn’t complain that the brain gets the applause.
• The body’s beauty lies in every organ quietly working for the others.
• Three church diseases: rushing to beat faster, rushing to grow bigger, attacking our own people.
• All these problems have one root: forgetting who the head is.

brief21.title: Christ Is the Head; We Are Members
notes: Head over all things for the assembly
The church is his body
Joined to the head, every joint doing its part
Key points:
• With a spinal injury the muscles and bones are all there, yet the limb cannot move.
• Cut the connection to the head, and only religious motion remains, without spiritual life.
• Colossians 1:18: that in all things he might have the preeminence.
• “Speaking truth in love”: not love alone, and not truth alone.

brief21.title: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
notes: People matter more than tasks
Relationships matter more than things
235: “2” companions, “3” parents and children
“5” fivefold-ministry comrades
Key points:
• The Harvard Study of Adult Development, over eighty years: good relationships determine health and happiness.
• The conclusion of its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger.
• 2, 3 and 5 are all numbers of relationship; none of them is a “1”.
• Augustine: the first is humility, the second is humility, and the third is humility.

brief21.title: Practices (1)
notes: Order check: am I overstepping?
At home, in church, in my heart
Protecting the body: admonish in love
Never sacrifice truth to please people
Key points:
• Order check: have I made a decision on God’s behalf?
• Returning to our originally intended position isn’t a demotion; it’s coming home.
• Two ways admonishing goes wrong: love without truth, truth without gentleness.
• Pray first, then speak; affirm first, then remind; and when you’ve said it, go on loving them.

brief21.title: Practices (2)
notes: Forgiveness: lay down the right to a grudge
Bless that name for seven days
Prayer of humility: declare it daily
Lord, keep me in the place you gave me
Key points:
• My refusing to forgive won’t make them hurt; it will only make me sick.
• Forgiveness is often not a single decision but a whole series of decisions.
• 1 Peter 5:6: humble yourselves, and he will exalt you in due time.
• The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, all the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
Old self self-centred; new self selfless
Key points:
• The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.
• The shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from temporary to eternal.
• Humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan; Satan can only attack the “self”.
• Galatians 2:20: it is no longer I who live.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: The body matters more than the member
Unity matters more than performance
Obedience matters more than achievement
Return to your place; let Jesus be King
Key points:
• The orchestra: the rests are someone else’s melody; the conductor makes no sound yet decides everything.
• The call: lay down the right you cling to, the name you won’t forgive, the right hand you can’t bear to deal with.
• Nebuchadnezzar’s hope: looking up is the first step home.
• Humility is the church’s root; unity is the church’s fruit.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, I will return to the place you gave me
Not grasping your glory or overstepping your authority
May the church be knit together in love
Glory to you for ever
Key points:
• Lead the congregation in praying aloud together.
• Intercede for the healing and unity of families, small groups and the church.
• Blessing: may God help us each do our part and build ourselves up in love.
• Closing declaration: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 94 of Morning Devotion 321, entitled “Humility Returns Us to Our Place”, with the subtitle “The Body Matters More Than the Member”. Today we have two key passages: one is Matthew 5:29–30, and the other is Daniel 4:37: “Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” Let us grow quiet together and ask the Lord to shine his light on our hearts.

Brothers and sisters, did you know? Your body has roughly thirty-seven trillion cells. Every day, tens of billions of those cells quietly die by themselves — what medicine calls “apoptosis”. They give up their place so that new cells can take over. Your body is healthy not because every cell is fighting desperately to stay alive, but because they all stay in the right place.

So what happens if one cell refuses? If it won’t die, insists on expanding and leaves its proper place, that cell has a name: a cancer cell. C. S. Lewis said that pride is spiritual cancer. Brothers and sisters, refusing to die, insisting on expanding, leaving its proper place — that isn’t only a cancer cell; that is pride too.

Today we read two passages. Matthew 5 is the charter of the kingdom proclaimed by the King of heaven, and there the Lord takes out a spiritual scalpel. Daniel 4 is a testimony signed in his own hand by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and the whole chapter is written in the first person. Both chapters say the same thing: “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:25).

The Lord Jesus said: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.” (Matthew 5:29) Brothers and sisters, the Lord isn’t asking us to harm ourselves. This is hyperbole, common among Jewish rabbis, meant to shock us. He deliberately chose the most precious part — not the little finger, but the right hand; not the left eye, but the right eye. Why? Because the part we are always most reluctant to deal with is the most useful one. Which weighs more, the one member or the whole body? The whole body.

So what is the order in the church? Support first, then choose what must go. Paul says that those who are spiritual should restore the one who has fallen in a spirit of gentleness (Galatians 6:1). The Lord also gave three steps of admonition (Matthew 18:15). It is like a doctor facing gangrene: he will always clean the wound and give medicine first, trying everything to save that toe. Only if sepsis threatens life will he amputate. Brothers and sisters, the surgeon who amputates doesn’t hate that toe; he loves that person. Because “a little yeast leavens the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5:6).

The second key point: humility is returning to our originally intended position; pride is leaving it. Jude 6 speaks of “angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place”. Brothers and sisters, the angels fell for no other reason than this: they did not keep their position. Satan said “I will” five times, wanting to be like the Most High; but the Lord Jesus emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Pride is grasping our rights and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. Let man be man and let God be God.

Does that sound abstract? There are two very concrete tests. First, when someone wrongs you, if you insist, “I have the right to hold a grudge,” that is pride. Because the Bible says: “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay” (Romans 12:19). Refusing to forgive is climbing onto God’s judgment seat yourself. Second, when you want others to see what you’ve given, you have already, in your heart, gathered the glory onto yourself. The Lord said: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them.” (Matthew 6:1)

Brothers and sisters, psychology reminds us that in 1999 Dunning and Kruger found that the least competent people overestimate themselves the most. The most terrifying thing about pride is not that it is strong, but that it is invisible.

Third, let’s look at the end of pride. Nebuchadnezzar stood on the roof of his palace and said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) One sentence, three times “my”. Before he had even finished speaking, a voice came from the sky, and the kingdom departed from him. He was driven out and ate grass like an ox for seven times.

But brothers and sisters, look at what follows: “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me.” (Daniel 4:34) Notice the order — first he looked up, and only then did his understanding return. The moment he looked up was the moment he returned to his place.

Fourth, humility keeps the church healthy; pride corrupts it. The heart never competes with the lungs for credit, and the liver never complains that the brain gets all the applause. The body is beautiful because every organ stays in its own place, quietly working for the others. Paul says the whole body is joined to Christ the head, “being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part” (Ephesians 4:16). Brothers and sisters, once the spinal cord is injured, the muscle is still there and the bone is still there, but the limb can no longer move — because the connection to the head is cut. The church is the same.

Today there are four practices. First, an order check: at home, in church and in my heart, am I overstepping? Second, protecting the body: learn to admonish in love, never sacrificing truth to please people. Third, practising forgiveness: write down a name, lay down your right to hold a grudge, and bless that person for seven days. Fourth, a prayer of humility: declare every day, “Lord, keep me in the place you have given me; let me not steal your glory.” Because lifting up is God’s work; my only work is to humble myself (1 Peter 5:6).

Brothers and sisters, let me close with a picture. A symphony orchestra has nearly a hundred players, and every part has long rests on it. A good player never feels those are wasted, because he knows those blanks are someone else’s melody. There is only one person in the whole hall who makes no sound and yet decides everything: the conductor. The church is an orchestra like that. The body matters more than the member; unity matters more than performance; obedience matters more than achievement. God’s call to us today is not to become bigger, but to return to the right place.

Let us pray together. Lord, you are the head of the church. We confess that we often leave the place you have given us; we want to be seen, and we cling to our right to hold a grudge and won’t let go. Lord, shine on the little bit of “self” within us that refuses to return to its place. We are willing to return to the place you have given us, not grasping your glory, not overstepping your authority. May your church be knit together in love and united in the truth. May the glory be yours for ever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the Lord’s peace be with you this morning. Today we come to Lesson 94 of Morning Devotion 321, entitled “Humility Returns Us to Our Place”, with the subtitle “The Body Matters More Than the Member”. We have two key passages: Matthew 5:29–30, and Daniel 4:37: “Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.”

The lesson’s introduction puts it beautifully: when a member leaves its proper place and harms the whole, it is no longer a blessing — it is destruction. Today we will reflect on two crucial truths: first, the body matters more than the member, and second, the end of pride.

Brothers and sisters, let’s begin with something that happens in your body every single day, yet you never notice it. Scientists estimate that the human body is made up of roughly thirty-seven trillion cells. Every day, tens of billions of those cells quietly die by themselves — what medicine calls “apoptosis”.

It is not an accident; it is a programme the Creator wrote into the cell: when a cell grows old, it hands its materials back to the body of its own accord and lets a new cell take over. So your body is healthy not because every cell is fighting desperately to stay alive, but because they all stay in the right place — and are even willing, when it is time to leave the stage, to leave it quietly. Order is not restriction; order is protection.

So, brothers and sisters, what happens if one cell refuses? What if it says, “I won’t die; I want to expand; I won’t listen to the body’s instructions”? That cell has a name we all fear: a cancer cell. Cancer cells have three hallmarks: they refuse apoptosis, they multiply without limit, and they leave their proper place and spread elsewhere.

Refusing to die, insisting on expanding, leaving its proper place. The apologist C. S. Lewis wrote in Mere Christianity that pride is spiritual cancer. Brothers and sisters, this lesson isn’t for someone else. A cell never thinks of itself as cancerous, and a proud person never thinks of himself as proud.

Today we read two passages. The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, generally thought to be between AD 50 and 70, for Jewish Christians. The Sermon on the Mount in chapters 5 to 7 is not a set of moral maxims; it is the charter of the kingdom, proclaimed by the King of heaven’s kingdom.

Daniel 4 is even more unusual. It is not a prophet’s account but a public decree issued by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, written entirely in the first person. This king reigned from 605 to 562 BC — forty-three years. And the heart of the whole book of Daniel comes down to a single sentence: “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.” (Daniel 4:25)

The first key point: the body matters more than the member. The Lord Jesus said: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.” (Matthew 5:29)

Brothers and sisters, the Lord isn’t asking us to harm ourselves. This is hyperbole, common among Jewish rabbis, meant to shock. “Causes you to stumble” is the Greek skandalizō, originally the trigger stick on an animal trap that springs at the slightest touch. And the Lord deliberately chose the most precious part: not the little finger, but the right hand; not the left eye, but the right eye. Why? Because the part we are always most reluctant to deal with is the most useful one. Which weighs more, the one member or the whole body? The whole body.

But please don’t misunderstand. God’s first move towards a member is always to cherish it. Paul says: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18)

So in the church, if a member is weak or has fallen, we should support and help them. Paul says: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” (Galatians 6:1) The word “restore” is also used in the New Testament for fishermen mending their nets, and for doctors setting bones. In Matthew 18 the Lord gives three lines of defence, and every step aims at gaining back your brother. Brothers and sisters, spiritual surgery is the last step, not the first.

But if a member refuses to repent and even goes on causing damage, then, out of love and a desire to protect, sometimes the knife must be used. Think of the scene in a hospital: when a toe develops gangrene, the doctor’s first step is never amputation, but cleaning the wound and giving medicine, trying everything to save it. Only when sepsis threatens life at any moment will he operate. Brothers and sisters, the surgeon who amputates doesn’t hate that toe; he loves that person.

Protecting the body is not cruelty; it is the courage of love. When the Lord cleansed the temple and overturned the tables, he wasn’t losing his temper; it was for the holiness of his Father’s house. Because “a little yeast leavens the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5:6). Sin and pride never stay where they are.
The second key point: humility is returning to our originally intended position; pride is leaving it.

There is a verse in the Bible that is often overlooked yet enormously important: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness.” (Jude 6) “First domain” is the Greek archē, meaning beginning, office, sphere of rule. Brothers and sisters, the angels fell not for some earth-shattering atrocity, but simply this: they did not keep their position. 321 puts it precisely: pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Isaiah describes the fallen shining star saying: “I will ascend into heaven! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Five “I will”s. Brothers and sisters, the first sin in the universe was not murder; it was five “I will”s — a created being refusing to stay in a created being’s place.

The way of salvation runs in exactly the opposite direction. Christ, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). “Emptied himself” is the Greek kenoō — to pour oneself out. Satan is a creature trying to climb up to God’s place; Jesus is God himself coming down to a servant’s place. Jesus is my role model — the first of the Three Foundations of 321.

The lesson gives two concrete tests. First: when someone wrongs you, if you insist, “I have the right to hold a grudge,” that is pride. Because the Bible says: “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.” (Romans 12:19) When I hold on and refuse to forgive, I am really saying: God, I don’t trust you with this. In that moment I have climbed onto God’s judgment seat.

Second: when you want others to see what you’ve given. The Lord said: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them.” (Matthew 6:1) The very same good deed can be an offering or a theft; the only difference is whether the glory is sent upward or gathered onto ourselves. In 1999 Dunning and Kruger at Cornell University found that the least competent people overestimate themselves the most. The most terrifying thing about pride is not that it is strong, but that it is invisible.

The third key point: the end of pride. Nebuchadnezzar stood on the roof of his palace and boasted: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) Brothers and sisters, listen: the might of my power, my royal dwelling place, the glory of my majesty. One sentence, three times “my”.

And none of this happened suddenly. A full twelve months earlier, God had already warned him through a dream. God’s judgment is never an ambush; God always warns first and waits first. Yet “while the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, ‘O king Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you.’” (Daniel 4:31)

What follows is a startling picture: “He was driven from men, and ate grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky, until his hair had grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.” (Daniel 4:33) This king was put by God among the cattle.

Whatever illness this was medically, the point Scripture is making is perfectly clear: if a man insists on being God, God lets him see that, apart from God, he cannot even manage to be a man. Brothers and sisters, man was made in God’s image; man climbed upward trying to be God and fell instead to the level of a beast. That is the law of gravity in the spiritual world: the moment you try to go up, you are bound to fall down.

But the story doesn’t end on the grass. The text says: “At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me, and I blessed the Most High.” (Daniel 4:34) Brothers and sisters, notice the order: first he lifted his eyes to heaven, and only then did his understanding return. It wasn’t that his reason came back first and then he worshipped; the moment he worshipped, his reason returned. The moment he looked up was the moment he returned to his place.

His final testimony was: “Those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37) Paul also asks: “What do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) Job lost everything in a single day, and still he said: “Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away.” (Job 1:21)

The fourth key point: humility keeps the church healthy; pride corrupts it. Paul says the members, “being many, are one body”, and “when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12:12, 26).

Brothers and sisters, in a healthy body no organ fights for credit for itself. But what happens when an organ starts fighting for more for itself? When the heart beats faster than the body needs, that’s an arrhythmia; when cells grow more than the body allows, that’s a tumour; when the immune system attacks its own body, that’s an autoimmune disease. Almost every conflict in a church falls into one of these three categories, and they all have one root: forgetting who the head is.

Paul says God “gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body” (Ephesians 1:22–23), and that the whole body grows up “into him who is the head, Christ … through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part” (Ephesians 4:15–16).

Physiologically, this image is astonishingly precise. All the coordination in the human body depends on the central nervous system. Once the spinal cord is injured, the muscle is still there, the bone is still there, but the limb can no longer move, because it has lost its connection to the head. The church is the same: the gifts are still there, the numbers are still there, the activities are still there, but once the connection to Christ the Head is broken, all that remains is religious motion with no spiritual life.

That is why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years. Its current director, Professor Waldinger, concludes: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout their lives is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

The 235 relationships of 321 put this very principle into practice: with selfless people we become a “2”, spiritual companions; we build a “3”, spiritual parents and children; and we become a “5”, a team of spiritual comrades in the fivefold ministry. Notice that 2, 3 and 5 are all numbers of relationship; none of them is a “1”. There are no lone rangers in the church — only members. Augustine said: the first is humility, the second is humility, and the third is humility.

Next come the practices. The first is an order check: am I overstepping in the church or in my family? Be still for ten minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you — at home, am I overriding the authority of my spouse or my parents? In the church, am I overriding the pastor’s role? In my heart, have I sat down on the judgment seat where only God may sit? Brothers and sisters, returning to our originally intended position isn’t a demotion; it’s coming home.

The second is protecting the body: learn to admonish in love, never sacrificing truth to please people. Admonishing can go wrong in two ways: love that dares not speak the truth, or truth without gentleness. Remember: pray first, then speak; affirm first, then remind; and when you’ve said it, go on loving them.

The third is practising forgiveness: lay down the pride of “I have the right to hold a grudge”. Write down the name that makes your chest tighten the moment you think of it, then say it out loud to God: “Lord, I lay down my right to hold a grudge against them, and I hand the right of vengeance back to you.” Then bless that person for seven days. Forgiveness is often not a single decision but a whole series of decisions.

The fourth is a prayer of humility: declare every day, “Lord, keep me in the place you have given me; let me not steal your glory.” Because lifting up is God’s work — “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Please walk these four practices through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Let’s set this lesson back within the framework of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself and took the form of a servant; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide, because pride is invisible. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system — and the one condition for any system to work is that every part is in its own place.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Satan’s five “I will”s and Nebuchadnezzar’s three “my”s are all the self-centred life. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus. Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan, because the only thing Satan can attack is the “self”. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, let me close with a picture. A symphony orchestra has nearly a hundred players, and every part has long rests on it. A good player never feels those are wasted, because those blanks are someone else’s melody. And there is only one person in the whole hall who makes no sound and yet decides everything: the conductor.

The church is an orchestra like that. Your notes may be few, but they are your notes. The body matters more than the member; unity matters more than performance; obedience matters more than achievement. Perhaps what you need to lay down today is a right you’ve clung to for a long time, a name you won’t forgive, or a right hand you can’t bear to deal with. Nebuchadnezzar tells us: it’s all right to look up. Wherever you have fallen today, looking up is the first step home.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you that you are the head of the church, the Head over all things. We confess that we often leave the place you have given us — we want to be seen, we cling to our right to hold a grudge and won’t let go, and we quietly keep your glory for ourselves.

Lord, make your Holy Spirit our light, and shine on the “self” within us that refuses to return to its place. Give us the courage of love: when it is time to support, let us gently lift up the members who have fallen; when it is time to deal with things, let us face sin and pride with clean hands. We are willing to let man be man and let God be God. Heal our families, build up your church, and help each of us do our part, building ourselves up in love. May all the glory be yours, for ever and ever. In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: An Honest Complaint
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Once, after a small-group meeting, a brother stayed behind and said to me very honestly, “Pastor, I understand everything about humility, and I really want it, but I just can’t do it. When someone shoots me down in a meeting, I’m churning inside straight away; when my child talks back to me, my voice goes up instantly. Humility feels far too hard to me, and pride comes all too easily.”

I believe those words speak the truth that is in many of our hearts. We often picture humility as a high mountain: standing on the summit are a few saints — Moses, David, Paul, Andrew Murray — while we can only gaze up at them from the foot of the mountain. We picture pride as a downhill road: no effort needed, just follow your natural bent and you’re there. And so we conclude, “Humility is too hard; pride is too easy.”

But brothers and sisters, the Bible tells us exactly the opposite: humility is actually easy; it is pride that is hard.

This isn’t a motivational slogan; it’s the Bible’s declaration in black and white. Jesus said it himself: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). He didn’t say, “My yoke is heavy, but you must grit your teeth and hold on.” He said “easy”; he said “light.”

Why do our feelings run counter to the Bible? Because we are doing the sums wrong. We understand “humility” as “suppressing ourselves” — seething inside but pretending everything is fine; wanting to argue back but forcing the words back down. Brothers and sisters, of course that is hard, because that isn’t humility at all; it’s a disguise held in place until it explodes. True humility is not suppressing the self-centred life but laying it down. Suppressing takes every ounce of your strength; laying down only takes opening your hand.

Let me use a picture from sailing. With the wind behind it, a sailing boat can head straight for its destination; but to sail against the wind it can’t go straight — it has to keep changing course from side to side, tacking upwind in a zigzag. That is basic seamanship, and simple geometry too: tacking at forty-five degrees, the distance actually sailed is about 1.4 times the straight-line distance — in other words, going upwind you travel forty per cent further. And at every tack the crew have to haul the sails and reset the lines all over again, and the whole boat is in a flurry.

Brothers and sisters, pride is sailing into the wind. Humility is sailing with the wind behind you. It’s not that humble people have more strength; it’s that humble people take the course that runs with God’s wind.

In this lesson we’ll look at three things from the Bible: first, God does not ask people to do the impossible; second, Jesus himself says humility is easy; third, humility brings grace, and pride brings resistance. Let’s ask the Lord, through his word, to turn upside down the old mindset in our hearts that says “humility is too hard.” For in the 321 vision, all change begins with the mindset: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Setting in Which This Invitation Was Spoken
1. The Author, Date and Readers of Matthew’s Gospel
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, formerly a tax collector in the Capernaum area, who after the Lord called him became one of the twelve apostles (Matthew 9:9; 10:3). From Papias in the second century onward, church history has consistently attributed this book to Matthew. It is generally dated between AD 50 and 70, and it was written chiefly for believers of Jewish background.

So Matthew’s Gospel has a very distinctive feature: it constantly quotes the Old Testament to prove that Jesus is the Messiah the Old Testament promised — the offspring of Abraham, the Son of David, and the “new Moses,” greater than Moses. Moses gave the law on Mount Sinai; Jesus preached the charter of the kingdom of heaven on a mountain. Moses led the people out of Egypt; Jesus leads his people out of sin. Once we grasp this, we realise that when Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you,” he was speaking to people who talked every day about “the yoke of the law.”

sections.heading: 2. The Context of Our Key Passage
sections.html:
The atmosphere of Matthew 11 is actually rather heavy.

First, John the Baptist, in prison, sends his disciples to ask Jesus, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3). Even the forerunner who prepared the way for the Lord had begun to doubt in his cell.

Then Jesus rebukes Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum — the three towns that had seen the most miracles with their own eyes and yet still refused to repent (Matthew 11:20–24).

And then, amid all this rejection and disappointment, Jesus suddenly lifts his head and prays: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25).

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. “The wise and understanding” cannot see, but “infants” can. The difference isn’t IQ but posture; not ability but humility. Right after this prayer, Jesus issues that most tender invitation: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened.”

So Matthew 11:28–30 is not an isolated verse of comfort; it is the climax of the whole chapter, the conclusion to the contrast between “the proud wise and understanding” and “the humble infants.” Jesus is in effect saying: if you are willing to come humbly, like an infant, there is rest with me; if you insist on being one of the wise and understanding, these things will be hidden from you.

sections.heading: 3. The Historical Setting of “Labouring and Heavily Burdened”
sections.html:
The Jewish people of the first century really did carry a heavy yoke on their shoulders. On top of the law of Moses, the scribes and Pharisees had piled layer upon layer of oral regulations (later collected into the Mishnah). The Sabbath alone generated dozens of categories of prohibition: how many steps counted as a journey, how heavy a load counted as work, how many knots counted as a violation. Jesus later said bluntly, “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them” (Matthew 23:4).

More crucially, in the language of the Jewish rabbis, “yoke” was a technical term. They spoke of “taking the yoke of the law” and “taking the yoke of the kingdom of heaven,” meaning “becoming a certain teacher’s disciple and accepting his teaching on the law.” So when Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me,” he wasn’t talking about farm equipment. He was saying: come and be my disciple, accept my teaching, let me lead you.

Later, at the Jerusalem Council, the apostle Peter put it even more plainly: “Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). And Paul says, “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage” (Galatians 5:1).

Brothers and sisters, everyone has a yoke on their neck. The question has never been “Shall I wear a yoke?” but “Whose yoke shall I wear?” Wearing your own yoke is pride, and that yoke is unbearably heavy; wearing Jesus’ yoke is humility, and that yoke is easy and light.

sections.heading: 4. The Background of the Other Two Passages
sections.html:
This lesson will also draw on Deuteronomy 30:11 and James 4:6, so let’s first set out their background.

Deuteronomy 30 is Moses’ final exhortation to the second generation of Israelites on the plains of Moab. They were about to cross the Jordan into Canaan, and Moses set before them “life and death, the blessing and the curse,” urging them to choose life (Deuteronomy 30:19). Right at this point of decision between life and death, Moses spoke the comforting words of verse 11: God’s commandment is not too hard for you.

James, the author of the letter of James, was the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and later became a leader of the church in Jerusalem. He wrote to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — that is, Jewish Christians scattered abroad. At the start of chapter 4 he goes straight to the root of the strife and fighting in the church: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1). Pride sets people against one another, and the remedy lies in 4:6: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: God Does Not Ask People to Do the “Impossible”
sections.html:
The Scripture

“For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, ‘Who will go up for us to heaven, bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?’ Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, ‘Who will go over the sea for us, bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?’ But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.” (Deuteronomy 30:11–14)

A Light from the Original

The Hebrew word behind “too hard” is נִפְלֵאת (niphle’t), from the root פָּלָא (pala), whose basic meaning is “wonderful, beyond human reach, astonishing.” The same root appears in Psalm 139:6: “This knowledge is beyond me. It’s lofty. I can’t attain it.”

So Moses’ meaning is perfectly clear: God’s commandment is not some “unreachable wonder beyond human ability.” God never hands you a command and then stands back with folded arms to watch you fail.

“Too distant” is the Hebrew רְחֹקָה (rechoqah), distance in space. In one breath Moses closes off two routes of excuse: it is not in heaven (too high), and it is not beyond the sea (too far). And the positive declaration is: “But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart.” Paul quotes exactly this passage in Romans 10:6–8 to show that the word of justification by faith is “near you.”

Scripture Interpreting Scripture

God’s commands always go hand in hand with God’s grace.

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:12–13) We “work out” because God “works in” us.

“No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” (1 Corinthians 10:13) God will not give you a situation you cannot bear.

The most direct verse of all comes from the apostle John: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous” (1 John 5:3).

Brothers and sisters, listen to these three verses together: God’s commandment is not too hard; God’s testing will not go beyond what we can bear; God’s commandments are not grievous. So when God says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble,” could that command be impossible? Absolutely not.

The Hard Part, Jesus Has Already Done

Someone will ask, “But it really feels hard to me.”

Brothers and sisters, that is because we’ve got the division of labour wrong. The part that is truly hard, Jesus has already done for us.

“Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:4–5)

The price of salvation, the suffering of the cross, the power to overcome sin and death — not one of these could we carry. And on the cross Jesus said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). In the original it is a single word, τετέλεσται (tetelestai). In the commercial documents of the day, this word was stamped on receipts, meaning “paid in full.”

The hard part, Jesus did; the easy part, we learn. We have only one thing to do: believe and obey. So humility is actually easy, because it is not an achievement we squeeze out by sheer effort; it is the result of obedience, the natural outflow of faith.

An Example from Life

I remember learning to ride a bicycle as a child. My father held the back of the seat and ran alongside me, and I pedalled until I was dripping with sweat, thinking how clever I was. Only later did I realise that most of the balance on that stretch of road came from my father’s hand holding me up. He let go little by little without my knowing, but the moment I wobbled, that hand was there again.

Brothers and sisters, the practice of humility is just like that. You think you’re the one pedalling, but all along there’s a hand holding you steady. The hard part is that hand; the easy part is your two feet.

Confirmation from Psychology

In a 1977 paper in Psychological Review, the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his well-known theory of “self-efficacy.” He pointed out that whether a person attempts something, and whether they persevere after a setback, often depends not on their actual ability but on their belief about “whether I can do it.” People who believe they can’t usually won’t even try.

Brothers and sisters, that is the real reason so many of us fail at humility. It’s not that we can’t; it’s that we “believe we can’t.” And today the Bible sets out to renew that belief: God says, it is not too hard for you.

Applying the 321 Vision

The second of the Three Foundations of 321 is “the Bible is my standard.”

When our feelings say “humility is too hard,” our experience says “I’ve tried and failed every time,” and our circumstances say “that person doesn’t deserve my humility” — at that moment, what is the standard?

If feelings are the standard, we’ll never get out; if the Bible is the standard, we stand on one sentence: “It is not too hard for you.”

And this is exactly the first two of the eight stages of changing our mindset. First comes “Information” — I have heard the words of Deuteronomy 30:11. Then comes “Revelation” — the Holy Spirit makes those words come alive in me, and I suddenly see that God has never been making things hard for me. Once the mindset changes, the life begins to change.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Jesus Himself Says Humility Is Easy
sections.html:
The Scripture

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:29–30)

Brothers and sisters, notice: this isn’t a theologian’s deduction; it’s the Lord Jesus’ own definition. In all the Gospels, this is the only time Jesus directly describes his own heart, and the two words he uses are — gentle and humble.

A Light from the Original

“Gentle” is the Greek πραΰς (praus). In classical Greek this word was often used of a trained warhorse: its strength not diminished in the slightest, yet wholly responsive to the reins in its rider’s hand. So gentleness is never weakness; gentleness is “strength tamed by the hand of God.”

“Humble” is the Greek ταπεινός (tapeinos). In Graeco-Roman culture this word was originally pejorative, carrying a flavour of “base, low, servile”; no Greek philosopher would have counted it a virtue. It was the cross of Christ that turned this despised word into the noblest character of the kingdom of heaven.

“Easy” is the Greek χρηστός (chrestos), meaning “useful, well-fitting, kind.” The same root appears in Romans 2:4, “the goodness of God” (χρηστότης). So “my yoke is easy” can also be heard as “my yoke fits well” — as if made to measure, not chafing the neck or crushing the shoulders.

“Light” is the Greek ἐλαφρός (elaphros), simply “light in weight.” Paul uses the same word when he says, “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Two Yokes Compared

The Bible sets two yokes before us.

One is the yoke of religion, the yoke of self: “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them” (Matthew 23:4). This yoke has only demands and no help.

The other is Jesus’ yoke: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). This yoke has demands, but even more, it has companionship.

And the phrase “you will find rest for your souls” is in fact taken from Jeremiah. Yahweh says, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls” (Jeremiah 6:16). Jesus is in effect proclaiming: the “old path” the prophet pointed to is me; the rest promised so long ago is here with me.

The Picture of a Shared Yoke

Brothers and sisters, a “yoke” is a crossbeam set on the necks of two oxen so that they pull the plough together. A yoke always means two oxen.

In traditional farming, when a farmer trained an inexperienced young ox, he never had it pull the plough alone. He put it under the same yoke with an older, steady ox that knew the way. Almost all the weight of the plough fell on the old ox; the young ox had only one thing to do: keep pace with the old ox, not charge off and not stop. And as they walked on, the young ox learned.

Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you.” He didn’t say, “Go and pull your plough.” He said: come, be yoked beside me; I’ll do the pulling; you just keep pace.

That is why his yoke is easy. Not because the field is smaller or the plough lighter, but because the one beside you is Jesus.

Pride, on the other hand, takes the yoke off and carries it alone. Relying on self, carrying self, fighting for self — the result is that the longer we live, the wearier we get; the harder we try, the more we suffer. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that the most exhausted people are often not the busiest people, but the people least able to let go of themselves?

Confirmation from Science and Psychology

The cost of forcing ourselves to hold on can be measured.

In 1936 the Hungarian-born physiologist Hans Selye published research in the journal Nature proposing the “General Adaptation Syndrome,” which describes three stages of the body’s response to prolonged stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. A person can hold out in the “resistance” stage for a long time and still look as if they’re coping; but unless the stress is lifted, they will inevitably end in exhaustion.

Conversely, the benefit of companionship can also be measured. In 1997 the Carnegie Mellon psychologist Sheldon Cohen and his colleagues published a study in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA): they exposed volunteers to a cold virus and found that the richer people’s social connections, the lower the rate at which they actually developed a cold. Human beings are not designed to fight alone.

Brothers and sisters, pride puts you into the resistance stage and keeps you holding on all the way to exhaustion; humility puts you into companionship, with someone sharing the burden.

The Witness of Church History

One of the church fathers who valued humility most highly was Augustine of Hippo. In a letter to Dioscorus he left a famous saying: if anyone asks me what is of first importance in the Christian faith, I will answer: the first is humility, the second is humility, and the third is humility.

The nineteenth-century South African pastor Andrew Murray, in his book Humility, gave a beautiful definition: humility is nothing other than the creature taking its proper place before God, and letting God be all.

Brothers and sisters, listen to that definition — humility is “returning to our originally intended position.” This is exactly what 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God.

Why is returning to our originally intended position easy? Because it is the very place you were made for. It is easy for a fish to return to the water, easy for a bird to return to the sky, and easy for a human being to return to God’s presence. What is hard is a fish insisting on climbing onto the shore, a bird insisting on diving into the water, a human being insisting on being God.

Applying the 321 Vision

The first of the Two Core Values of 321 is “let Jesus be King.”

Sharing a yoke with Jesus means letting him decide the direction, decide the pace, decide when to turn. And this is often where our greatest struggle lies: we’re willing to have Jesus walk with us, but not so willing to let Jesus decide where we’re going. We want Jesus as our helper, not Jesus as our King.

321 also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. For the outcomes of a whole life flow from the heart. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

When we rely on the brain and ourselves, we are tacking into the wind, calculating and straining at every step; when we rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we are sailing with the wind behind us, going far and going light.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Humility Brings Grace; Pride Brings Resistance
sections.html:
The Scripture

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)

This verse is quoted from Proverbs: “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble” (Proverbs 3:34). The apostle Peter quotes the same sentence: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6).

The Old Testament says it once, James says it once, Peter says it once. Brothers and sisters, when the Bible says the same thing three times, it is no longer a suggestion; it is a spiritual law.

A Light from the Original

“Resists” is the Greek ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), made up of ἀντί (against, opposite) and τάσσω (to draw up in battle order, to deploy). It is a military term meaning “to draw up troops in battle array and stand opposite.”

Brothers and sisters, what a solemn picture this is. Towards the proud, God doesn’t merely frown, or shake his head, or ignore them — God draws up his battle lines and stands opposite them. However gifted, however talented, however well connected a person may be, if God stands against him, he cannot take a single step.

And to the humble, God “gives grace.” Grace (χάρις, charis) is given freely, not earned. Humility is not the price we pay to buy grace; humility is the vessel that receives grace — because a clenched fist cannot catch anything.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Two Contrasting Records in the Bible

The Bible demonstrates the end of pride again and again.

Lucifer, the morning star, with his five “I will”s: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). The essence of pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to replace God.

Uzziah, king of Judah: “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up, so that he did corruptly, and he trespassed against Yahweh his God; for he went into Yahweh’s temple to burn incense on the altar of incense” (2 Chronicles 26:16). Notice the turning point — “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up.” The most dangerous moment is often not our weakest moment but our strongest.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, after losing his reason for seven times, finally acknowledged: “those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37).

The Bible also demonstrates the end of humility again and again.

The supreme role model, of course, is the Lord Jesus: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:6–9).

Jesus also summed it up with a parable. The tax collector beating his breast in the temple said only one sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). And Jesus said, “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

With the Current and Against It

The lesson puts it precisely: humility is going with the current; pride is fighting upstream.

Obey God’s will, and life becomes light; resist God’s will, and life becomes toil.

We spoke earlier of the sailing boat. Against the wind, the boat has to tack in a zigzag; at forty-five degrees, the distance sailed is about 1.4 times the straight-line distance; and at every tack the whole crew must haul the sails and reset the lines all over again. With the wind behind it, the boat need only spread its sails, and the wind itself will drive it to its destination.

Brothers and sisters, the same wind is a driving force when you go with it and a resisting force when you go against it. It is the same God: obey him and it is grace; oppose him and it is resistance. The wind hasn’t changed, and God hasn’t changed; what has changed is our direction.

Tested in Relationships

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

This is easiest to test at home. When a husband and wife argue, if one raises their voice, the other is sure to raise theirs; if one drags up old grievances, the other is sure to drag up older ones. Pride is like an echo: whatever you shout out comes back to you. The result is that both sides lose — even if you win the argument, you lose the person.

But as soon as one of them softens first and says, “I’m sorry, I was too hasty just now,” the whole situation eases. Humility is like an echo too — only what comes back is peace.

Confirmation from Psychology and Management

In a 2013 study in the journal Organization Science, Bradley Owens of Brigham Young University and his colleagues examined “expressed humility” in organisations — including acknowledging one’s own limitations, appreciating others’ strengths and being teachable. They found that leaders’ humility was positively related to team members’ engagement, willingness to learn and job performance. Far from making people lose influence, humility amplifies it.

In Good to Great, published in 2001, the management scholar Jim Collins started from 1,435 companies that had appeared on the Fortune 500 lists between 1965 and 1995, and in the end only eleven had truly made the leap “from good to great.” He found that the leaders of these eleven companies shared one trait, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: a personality of personal humility combined with a will of professional resolve.

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research points in the same direction. How much more so, since this is a spiritual law that God himself has set.

Why Pride Is So Hard to Detect

The English writer and apologist C. S. Lewis devoted a whole chapter of Mere Christianity to pride. He called pride “the great sin” and said that pride is “the complete anti-God state of mind.” He also points out something that cuts deep: the great mark of pride is that you see it perfectly clearly in other people, yet almost not at all in yourself.

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely what makes pride “hard” — it keeps you from even knowing where the problem is. You think you’re just “a person of principle,” just “dealing with the facts,” just “someone who dislikes hypocrisy,” when in fact hidden inside is a self that refuses to come down from the throne.

That is why David’s prayer is so precious: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

The first step of humility is often not “I’m going to become humble” but “Lord, shine your light on me and let me see my pride.”

The Real Question

The lesson puts it well: the real question is not “Is humility hard?” but “Are we willing?”

If we are willing to lay ourselves down and let God be Lord, humility immediately becomes easy; if we insist on relying on ourselves and wanting to control everything, pride will make our road harder and harder.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. He said, “I am gentle and humble in heart … learn from me” (Matthew 11:29). Humility is not an abstract virtue on a list; humility has a face, and that face is the face of Jesus.

The Bible is my standard. When our feelings say “too hard,” the Bible says “not too hard for you” (Deuteronomy 30:11). We take the Bible as our standard, not our feelings.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. This point matters enormously. Notice: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). The word “gentleness” here is the Greek πραΰτης (prautes) — the very same root as “gentle” (πραΰς) in Matthew 11:29.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most important key in the whole lesson: gentleness and humility are not virtues we cultivate by our own efforts; they are fruit the Holy Spirit bears. A tree doesn’t squeeze out fruit by gritting its teeth; fruit grows naturally out of life. That is why humility can be “easy” — because it is the outflow of life, not the effort of the flesh.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. Sharing his yoke means handing him the steering wheel. Wherever he reigns as King, there is rest.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The deepest problem with pride is wanting to keep a little of the glory for ourselves; the deepest freedom of humility is being able to give all the glory to him. When I don’t need glory, I no longer have to prove myself; and a person who no longer has to prove himself is the lightest-burdened person in the world.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. The Worldly system is a pyramid: climb upward, grab a position, step on others to get there. God’s system is a body: each member doing its own part, caring for one another, with Christ as the head. The pyramid runs on pride; the body runs on humility.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, Satan fell in the first place precisely because of those five “I will”s. And when he tempted Eve he used the same script: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). That is why 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. When a person is truly selfless, Satan can find nothing in him to hook onto — because every bait he uses is cast to catch the “self.” The Lord Jesus put it most completely: “for the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, “no longer I” — that is why the yoke is light. Because the one pulling the plough is no longer me.

The Fivefold Change and the Path of Serving

Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. What this lesson sets out to change is the very first link — the old mindset that says “humility is too hard.”

321 also reminds us of the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Proud people often turn the order upside down, grabbing at ministry first and then at results, and in the end their life dries up and their relationships break down.

The Path of Serving is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Gentleness and humility are the very feet that carry us to the end of this path.

A Shift in Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: man says humility loses out; God says humility receives grace.

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective: on earth we fight for position; heaven looks at the heart.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective: will you even remember this battle over face ten years from now?

From a worldly perspective to God’s perspective: the world says, “Beat everyone else”; God says, “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

The 920 Practice

The 920 practice says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

And this lesson falls right at the centre of 920 — because the eighth of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit is “gentleness,” which shares a root with the “gentle” Jesus speaks of.

So this week, please choose one “2”: it might be your spouse, your child, your parents, a colleague — even the person who most often rubs you up the wrong way. In front of that person, practise selflessness; practise gentleness and humility. Not suppressing, but laying down; not pretending nothing’s wrong, but placing yourself in God’s hands.

The 235 Relationships

Humility is also the entry ticket to the 235 relationships. Become a “2” with someone who is also pursuing selflessness, reminding each other and praying for each other; go on to build a “3,” the relationship of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally become a “5,” a team of spiritual comrades in the fivefold ministry, serving together.

Brothers and sisters, proud people cannot build 235, because proud people won’t let their weakness be seen, nor will they let anyone else lead them. Only the humble can find their way in.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Taking the Lesson’s Four Practices Deeper
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four concrete practices. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

The Lesson’s Four Practices

First, the practice of obedience: every morning pray, “Lord, today I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility.”

Second, the practice of letting go: when pressure comes, stop first and ask, “Am I trying to rely on myself again in this?”

Third, reflecting on grace: list three things God has helped you through, and remind yourself, “The hard part, he has already done.”

Fourth, living lightly: learn to entrust things to God, stop being overly anxious about everything, and let Jesus walk with you under the same yoke.

sections.heading: 1. Information
sections.html: First, put the truth into your head. This week, copy three verses onto a card and put it where you’ll see it: Deuteronomy 30:11, Matthew 11:29–30 and James 4:6. Read them three times a day. Information is the starting point of all change — without a seed, there will be no fruit.

sections.heading: 2. Revelation
sections.html:
Ask the Holy Spirit to make these words “come alive” in you. Information is knowing; revelation is seeing. You might pray like this: “Holy Spirit, open the eyes of my heart, so that I truly see that you have never made things hard for me, and that your yoke really is easy.”

Revelation often happens in a concrete moment: just as you’re about to blow up, you suddenly remember, “My yoke is easy” — and in that moment, you see.

sections.heading: 3. Conviction
sections.html:
Having seen it, you still need to nod and say “yes.” Conviction is truly agreeing in your heart: humility is easy; it is pride that is hard.

Check honestly: do I still secretly feel that “humble people get pushed around”? If so, bring that mindset before God and let him replace it with his word.

sections.heading: 4. Implementation
sections.html:
Start with the lesson’s first practice — tomorrow morning, as soon as you open your eyes, before you scroll your phone or think about your schedule, say: “Lord, today I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility.”

Then add the second — today, the moment you feel the pressure rising or your emotions rising, stop for three seconds and ask in your heart, “Am I trying to rely on myself again in this?” Those three seconds are often the dividing line between winning and losing.

sections.heading: 5. Evaluation
sections.html:
Every evening, spend three minutes looking back honestly: how many times today did I take off the yoke and carry it myself? In what situation? With whom? What words stepped on my toes?

The lesson’s third practice fits best here: list three things God has helped you through, things you once thought you’d never get past. Write them down and read them aloud. This is to remind yourself of one sentence: the hard part, he has already done.

sections.heading: 6. Correction
sections.html:
Find the one point where you are most often self-centred — perhaps when you’re contradicted, perhaps when someone takes the credit, perhaps when your plans are thrown into disarray. For that one point, prepare a sentence to respond with.

For example: “Lord, I hand this over to you; I don’t need to prove myself.” A correction doesn’t need to be big, only accurate.

sections.heading: 7. Repetition
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, humility is a practice, not a switch. Once isn’t enough; a week isn’t enough; it has to be repeated.

The lesson’s fourth practice is precisely the work of repetition: learning to entrust things to God and no longer being overly anxious about everything. “Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Notice that this verse comes immediately after “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.” Humility and entrusting are two sides of the same thing.

sections.heading: 8. Multiplication
sections.html:
Finally, pass it on. Find a brother or sister and share one sentence from this lesson with them: “Jesus does the hard part; we learn the easy part.”

If a changed life isn’t multiplied, it stops with us. And as you pass it on, you’ll find you stand more firmly yourself — because you’re no longer just a student; you’ve become a fellow traveller too.

A Gentle Reminder

Humility is not “lowering your head” but “lifting your head to look at God.”

The more you look at God, the less you need to prove yourself.

Pride makes you want to “be God”; humility makes you willing to “let God do it.”

Brothers and sisters, these sentences are worth memorising. Because many people think humility means keeping your head down, keeping your voice small and talking yourself down as worthless — that isn’t humility; that’s low self-esteem, and low self-esteem is really just the other face of pride: its focus is still on the self.

In true humility the focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, but on Jesus. Once your eyes are lifted up, the self grows small; once the self grows small, the burden grows light.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have seen three things together.

First, God does not ask people to do the impossible — “not too hard for you” (Deuteronomy 30:11).

Second, Jesus himself says humility is easy — “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

Third, humility brings grace and pride brings resistance — “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

So humility is not the privilege of a few; it is a way of life that every one of God’s people can live out. God has not asked us to do the impossible; through Jesus he has already prepared for us that “easy road.”

Jesus does the hard part; we learn the easy part. When we choose humility, we are choosing grace.

So humility isn’t hard — as long as we are willing, God will surely help us walk in humility and enter into true freedom and rest.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you a call: take off that yoke you’ve been carrying on your own neck. You put that yoke on yourself, and only you can be willing to let it go.

Then come and stand beside Jesus and share his yoke. Let him be King — let him decide the direction, let him decide the pace, let him decide when to stop and when to go.

When you do, you’ll discover something wonderful: the field is still the same field, the plough still the same plough, but the weight is no longer the same. Because the one beside you is Jesus.

May all the glory be his. He is worthy, and we are not; and yet he invites us to walk with him.

keyVerses: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)
declarations: Lord, your yoke is easy, and your burden is light.
I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility, to lay down my pride and my control, and to let you lead my steps.
The hard part you have already accomplished; the easy part I am willing to do.
May I walk in humility all my life, and enjoy your rest and your grace.

The practice of letting go: when pressure comes, stop first and ask, “Am I trying to rely on myself again in this?”
Reflecting on grace: list three things God has helped you through, and remind yourself, “The hard part, he has already done.”
Living lightly: learn to entrust things to God, stop being overly anxious about everything, and let Jesus walk with you under the same yoke.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
On the cross you said, “It is finished”; the hardest stretch of the road, you have already walked to the end.

Lord, forgive us. So often we say with our lips that we want to be humble, while in our hearts we are still clinging to ourselves; so often we ask you for help, yet refuse to let you be King. We take off your yoke, put on our own, and then complain that life is too heavy.

Today we are willing to come before you afresh. Take away the lie in our hearts that “humility is too hard,” and rebuild our mindset with your word. Holy Spirit, bear the fruit of gentleness in us, so that gentleness and humility become the natural outflow of our lives.
Help us live a selfless life before every “2”; help us to see that choosing humility is choosing your grace.
May we walk with you under the same yoke all our lives, and enjoy the rest you have promised.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

If God says, “This is not too hard for you,” how would that change the way you face it?
