l095.title: Which Is Easier — Humility or Pride?
l095.subtitle: Jesus Has Done the Hard Part; We Are Willing to Learn the Easy Part
l095.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

blog.title: Humility Is Actually Easy

blocks.x: Jesus Has Done the Hard Part; We Are Willing to Learn the Easy Part

A brother once said to me, “I understand everything about humility, but I really can’t do it. When someone shoots me down in a meeting, I’m churning inside straight away; when my child talks back to me, my voice goes up instantly.”

I think that speaks for many of us. We picture humility as a high mountain with only a few saints standing on the summit; we picture pride as a downhill road — just follow your natural bent and you’re there. So the conclusion comes naturally: humility is too hard; pride is too easy.
But the Bible gives us exactly the opposite answer.
1. We Have Done the Sums Wrong

Most people find humility hard because they misunderstand it as “suppressing ourselves” — seething inside but pretending everything is fine; wanting to argue back but forcing the words back down. Of course that is hard, because that isn’t humility at all; it’s a disguise held in place until it explodes.
True humility is not suppressing ourselves but laying ourselves down. Suppressing takes every ounce of your strength; laying down only takes opening your hand.

That is why Moses said: “For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant.” (Deuteronomy 30:11) God never hands you a command and then stands back with folded arms to watch you fail. His commands always go hand in hand with his grace.

More importantly, the hardest part Jesus has already done for us. The price of salvation, the suffering of the cross, the power to overcome sin and death — not one of these could we carry. On the cross he said, “It is finished!” That was a commercial term, meaning “paid in full.”
The hard part, Jesus does; the easy part, we learn.
2. A Yoke Always Means Two Oxen
Jesus said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:29–30)
A “yoke” is a crossbeam set on the necks of two oxen so that they pull the plough together. So a yoke always means two oxen.

In traditional farming, when a farmer trained an inexperienced young ox, he never had it pull the plough alone. He put it under the same yoke with an older, steady ox that knew the way. Almost all the weight of the plough fell on the old ox; the young ox had only one thing to do: keep pace.
Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you.” He didn’t say, “Go and pull your plough.”
That is why his yoke is easy. Not because the field is smaller or the plough lighter, but because the one beside you is Jesus.

Pride, on the other hand, takes the yoke off and carries it alone. Relying on self, carrying self, fighting for self — the result is that the longer we live, the wearier we get. Have you noticed that the most exhausted people are often not the busiest people, but the people least able to let go of themselves?
3. With the Current, or Against It?

With the wind behind it, a sailing boat need only spread its sails to head straight for its destination; against the wind it can’t go straight, but has to keep tacking upwind in a zigzag. By simple geometry, tacking at forty-five degrees, the distance sailed is about 1.4 times the straight-line distance — and at every tack the whole crew must haul the sails and reset the lines all over again.
The same wind is a driving force when you go with it and a resisting force when you go against it.

The Bible says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) “Resists” here is a military term in the original, meaning “to draw up in battle array and stand opposite.” However gifted, however talented a person may be, if God stands against him, he cannot take a single step.
So the real question has never been “Is humility hard?” but “Are we willing?”

If we are willing to lay ourselves down and let God be Lord, humility immediately becomes easy; if we insist on relying on ourselves and wanting to control everything, pride will make our road harder and harder.
What You Can Do This Week
First, every morning begin with one prayer: “Lord, today I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility.”
Second, when pressure comes, stop for three seconds and ask yourself, “Am I trying to rely on myself again in this?”
Third, write down three things God has done for you that you once thought you’d never get past, and remind yourself: the hard part, he has already done.
Fourth, learn to entrust things to God, stop being overly anxious about everything, and let Jesus walk with you under the same yoke.

Humility is not “lowering your head” but “lifting your head to look at God.” The more you look at God, the less you need to prove yourself. Pride makes you want to “be God”; humility makes you willing to “let God do it.”
Brothers and sisters, choosing humility is choosing grace.
A Question for Reflection
This week, what is the one thing for which you took the yoke off your shoulders and carried it yourself? Are you willing to hand it back to the Lord today and walk with him under the same yoke?

notes: Which Is Easier — Humility or Pride?
Jesus does the hard part; we learn the easy part
“My yoke is easy,
and my burden is light.”
Matthew 11:28–30
1. Theme: this lesson overturns an old mindset — humility is too hard, pride is too easy.
2. Key verses: Matthew 11:28–30, where Jesus himself says, “My yoke is easy.”
3. Subtitle as a memory line: Jesus does the hard part; we learn the easy part.
4. Open in a warm tone, inviting brothers and sisters to grow quiet together.
Is humility really harder?
We think: humility too hard, pride too easy
The Bible says: humility is the easy one
Humility goes with the current
Pride fights upstream
1. Open with a real small-group conversation: “Pastor, I understand it all, but I can’t do it.”
2. Name the misunderstanding: treating humility as suppressing ourselves — of course that is hard.
3. True humility is laying ourselves down — suppressing takes effort; laying down just takes letting go.
4. Picture: against the wind a sailing boat must tack in a zigzag, sailing about 1.4 times the straight line.
5. Concluding line: pride is sailing into the wind; humility is sailing with the wind behind you.
Key Verse and Background
“Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened,
and I will give you rest.” Matthew 11:28
To people under the heavy yoke of the law
Jesus gives a gentle and humble invitation
1. Background: Matthew was written by Matthew the tax collector, for believers of Jewish background, between about AD 50 and 70.
2. Context: John the Baptist asks from prison; three towns refuse to repent; Jesus says the truth is revealed to infants (Matthew 11:25).
3. Historical setting: the scribes and Pharisees added oral regulations, and the people bore the heavy yoke of the law (Matthew 23:4).
4. “Yoke” was a rabbinic term meaning to become a certain teacher’s disciple.
5. Ask: the question isn’t whether to wear a yoke, but whose yoke to wear.
God doesn’t ask the impossible
“This commandment which I command you today
is not too hard for you or too distant.”
Deuteronomy 30:11
God’s commands always come with God’s grace
1. Scripture: Deuteronomy 30:11–14, Moses’ final exhortation on the plains of Moab.
2. Original: “too hard”, pala, meaning wonderful, beyond human reach.
3. Scripture interpreting Scripture: Philippians 2:13, 1 Corinthians 10:13, 1 John 5:3.
4. Psychology: Albert Bandura’s 1977 theory of self-efficacy — people who believe they can’t usually won’t even try.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to ask you a question: which is easier — humility or pride? I suspect most of us would answer in our hearts: pride is easy, humility is hard. But today’s lesson tells us the opposite: Jesus has done the hard part; we are willing to learn the easy part. Jesus said: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” These words are recorded in Matthew 11:30. Brothers and sisters, he didn’t say, “My yoke is heavy, so grit your teeth and hold on.” He said “easy”; he said “light”.

Brothers and sisters, a brother once said to me, “I understand it all, but I just can’t do it.” I understand completely. Because we often misunderstand humility as “suppressing ourselves” — churning inside while pretending on the outside that everything is fine. Of course that is hard! But true humility is not suppressing ourselves; it is laying ourselves down. Suppressing takes every ounce of your strength; laying down only takes opening your hand. That is why the Bible teaches that humility goes with the current, and pride fights upstream. Have you noticed that the most exhausted people are often not the busiest people, but the people least able to let go of themselves?

Let’s first look at the key verse. Jesus said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” These words are recorded in Matthew 11:28. The Jewish people of that time carried on their shoulders layer upon layer of regulations added by the scribes and Pharisees. Jesus said they “bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders”. Under that crushing weight, Jesus gave a gentle and humble invitation. Brothers and sisters, everyone has a yoke on their neck. The question has never been whether to wear a yoke, but whose yoke to wear.

First, God does not ask people to do the impossible. Deuteronomy 30:11 says: “For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant.” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully — not too hard for you. The original word for “too hard” carries the sense of “wonderful, beyond human reach”. God never hands you a command and then stands back with folded arms to watch you fail. God’s commands always go hand in hand with God’s grace. 1 John 5:3 also says: “His commandments are not grievous.” Since they are not grievous, how could the gentleness and humility he wants us to learn be impossible?

So why does it feel so hard? Because we’ve got the division of labour wrong. The hard part, Jesus has already finished. Isaiah 53:5 says: “The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.” On the cross he said: “It is finished!” In those days the original word was written on receipts, meaning “paid in full.” Brothers and sisters, Jesus does the hard part; we learn the easy part. We have only one thing to do: believe and obey.

Second, Jesus himself says humility is easy. Matthew 11:29: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” In all the Gospels, this is the only time Jesus directly describes his own heart, and the two words he uses are — gentle and humble. In the language of the Jewish rabbis, a “yoke” meant “being a disciple”. So taking his yoke means letting him lead me. The original word for “gentle” was used in ancient times of a trained warhorse — its strength not diminished in the slightest, yet wholly responsive to the reins in its rider’s hand. Gentleness has never been weakness.

The original word for “easy” means “well-fitting, kind” — made to measure, as it were, not chafing the neck or crushing the shoulders. Brothers and sisters, a yoke always means two oxen. When a farmer trains a young ox, he puts it under the same yoke with an old ox; the weight of the plough falls on the old ox, and the young ox only has to keep pace. Pride takes the yoke off and carries it alone, growing wearier as it goes; humility shares the yoke with the Lord, growing lighter as it goes.

Third, humility brings grace, and pride brings resistance. James 4:6 says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” The original word for “resists” is a military term, meaning “to draw up in battle array and stand opposite.” Brothers and sisters, this is serious. Towards the proud, God doesn’t just shake his head; he draws up his battle lines and stands opposite them. However gifted, however talented a person may be, if God stands against him, he cannot take a single step. But to the humble he “gives grace”. Humility is not the price we pay to buy grace; humility is the vessel that receives grace — because a clenched fist cannot catch anything.

So humility goes with the current, and pride goes against it. With the wind behind it, a sailing boat simply spreads its sails and goes; against the wind, it has to tack in a zigzag, sailing about 1.4 times the straight-line distance. The wind hasn’t changed; what has changed is the direction. 321 tells us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. When a couple argue, if one raises their voice, the other is sure to follow. Even if you win the argument, you lose the person.

Brothers and sisters, today there are four practices. First, obedience: every morning pray, “Lord, today I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility.” Second, letting go: when pressure comes, stop for three seconds and ask yourself, “Am I trying to rely on myself again in this?” Third, grace: count three hard things God has done for you. Fourth, lightness: learn to entrust things to God, and walk with the Lord under the same yoke. From Information to Revelation, from Conviction to Implementation, from Evaluation to Correction, do it again and again, and then pass it on to someone. And this week, please choose one “2” — your spouse, your child, or the person who most often rubs you up the wrong way — and before them, practise selflessness; practise gentleness and humility.

Finally, let me leave you with one reminder: humility is not lowering your head but lifting your head to look at God. The more you look at God, the less you need to prove yourself. Pride makes you want to “be God”; humility makes you willing to “let God do it”. Brothers and sisters, this morning, take off that yoke you’ve been carrying yourself, and come and stand beside Jesus and share his yoke. The field is still the same field, the plough still the same plough, but the weight is no longer the same at all, because the one beside you is Jesus. May all the glory be his.

Let us pray together. Lord, your yoke is easy, and your burden is light. I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility, to lay down my pride and my control, and to let you lead my steps. The hard part you have already accomplished; the easy part I am willing to do. Help us to choose humility, for choosing humility is choosing grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May you, brothers and sisters, walk in humility all your lives and enjoy his rest and his grace.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to ask you a very honest question: which is easier — humility or pride? I suspect most of us would answer in our hearts: pride is easy, humility is hard. But today’s lesson tells us something completely the opposite: Jesus has done the hard part; we are willing to learn the easy part. Jesus said it himself: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” These words are recorded in Matthew 11:30. Brothers and sisters, notice that he didn’t say, “My yoke is heavy, so grit your teeth and hold on.” He said “easy”; he said “light”. Today, together, we’ll let God’s word turn an old mindset upside down.

Once, after a small-group meeting, a brother stayed behind and said to me, “Pastor, I understand everything about humility, and I really want it, but I just can’t do it. When someone shoots me down in a meeting, I’m churning inside straight away; when my child talks back to me, my voice goes up instantly.” Brothers and sisters, doesn’t that speak for you too? We picture humility as a high mountain with only a few saints standing on the summit; we picture pride as a downhill road — just follow your natural bent and you’re there. And so we conclude: humility is too hard; pride is too easy. But is that really so?

The Bible gives us the opposite answer: humility is actually easy; it is pride that is hard. Why do our feelings run exactly the other way? Because we have done the sums wrong. We understand humility as “suppressing ourselves” — seething inside but pretending everything is fine; wanting to argue back but forcing the words back down. Brothers and sisters, that isn’t humility at all; it’s a disguise held in place until it explodes. True humility is not suppressing the self-centred life but laying it down. Suppressing takes every ounce of your strength; laying down only takes opening your hand. Against the wind, a sailing boat has to tack in a zigzag, sailing about 1.4 times the straight-line distance; with the wind behind it, it need only spread its sails, and the wind itself drives it to its destination.

Let’s look at the background of the key verse. The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, who once sat at the tax booth and, after the Lord called him, became one of the twelve apostles. He wrote it between about AD 50 and 70, chiefly for believers of Jewish background. The atmosphere of chapter 11, where our key verse sits, is actually rather heavy: John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask, “Are you he who comes?”; Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum had seen the most miracles yet refused to repent. Then Jesus lifts his head and prays that the Father has hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. And straight after that he gives his invitation: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” Brothers and sisters, the difference isn’t IQ but posture.

The first key point: God does not ask people to do the impossible. Deuteronomy 30:11 says: “For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant.” This was Moses’ final exhortation to the second generation of Israelites on the plains of Moab. They were about to cross the Jordan, and Moses set before them life and death, the blessing and the curse. Right at this point of decision between life and death, Moses said: God’s commandment is not too hard for you. Brothers and sisters, God’s commands have always gone hand in hand with God’s grace. Philippians 2:13 says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work.” We can do it because God is at work within us.

The Hebrew root behind “too hard” is pala, whose basic meaning is “wonderful, beyond human reach”. The same root appears in Psalm 139:6: “This knowledge is beyond me. It’s lofty. I can’t attain it.” So Moses’ meaning is perfectly clear: God’s commandment is not some unreachable wonder. In one breath Moses closes off two routes of excuse: it is not in heaven, and it is not beyond the sea. And the positive declaration is in 30:14: “But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.” The apostle John also says: “His commandments are not grievous.” That is recorded in 1 John 5:3.

So why do we still find it hard? Brothers and sisters, because we’ve got the division of labour wrong. The part that is truly hard, Jesus has already done for us. Isaiah 53:5 says: “The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.” The price of salvation, the suffering of the cross, the power to overcome sin and death — not one of these could we carry. On the cross Jesus said: “It is finished!” In the original it is a single word, stamped on receipts in those days, meaning “paid in full.” When I was a child learning to ride a bicycle, my father held the back of the seat and ran alongside me. I thought I was the one pedalling, but most of the balance on that stretch of road came from my father’s hand. The hard part was that hand; the easy part was my two feet.

This brings us to the first 321 application: the Bible is my standard. When our feelings say “humility is too hard,” our experience says “I’ve tried and failed every time,” and our circumstances say “that person doesn’t deserve my humility” — at that moment, what is the standard? In 1977 the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his theory of “self-efficacy”. He pointed out that whether a person attempts something, and whether they persevere after a setback, often depends not on their actual ability but on whether they believe they can do it. People who believe they can’t usually won’t even try. Brothers and sisters, many of us fail at humility not because we can’t, but because we “believe we can’t.” This is exactly the first two of the eight stages of changing our mindset: first Information, then Revelation.

The second key point: Jesus himself says humility is easy. Matthew 11:29: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” Brothers and sisters, notice one thing: in all the Gospels, this is the only time Jesus directly describes his own heart, and the two words he uses are — gentle and humble. Not “I am mighty in heart,” not “I am full of wisdom,” but gentle and humble. This echoes what came just before: the truth is hidden from the wise and understanding and revealed to infants.

Let’s look at four key words in the original. “Gentle” is praus; classical Greek used it of a trained warhorse: its strength not diminished in the slightest, yet wholly responsive to the reins in its rider’s hand. Gentleness is never weakness; gentleness is strength tamed by the hand of God. “Humble” is tapeinos; in Graeco-Roman culture it was originally pejorative, carrying a flavour of “base, servile”; it was the cross that turned it into the noblest character of the kingdom of heaven. “Easy” is chrestos, meaning useful, well-fitting, kind. So “my yoke is easy” can also be heard as “my yoke fits well” — not chafing the neck or crushing the shoulders. “Light” is elaphros; Paul uses the same word when he speaks of “our light affliction, which is for the moment”.

Brothers and sisters, a “yoke” is a crossbeam set on the necks of two oxen so that they pull the plough together. So a yoke always means two oxen. In traditional farming, when a farmer trained a young ox, he put it under the same yoke with an older, steady ox that knew the way. Almost all the weight of the plough fell on the old ox; the young ox only had to keep pace, and as they walked on, it learned. Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you.” He didn’t say, “Go and pull your plough.” And in the language of the Jewish rabbis, “taking someone’s yoke” meant “becoming their disciple”. By contrast, Jesus said the Pharisees “bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders” — that is recorded in Matthew 23:4. Peter too called it “a yoke … which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear”.

Here is the second 321 application: let Jesus be King. Sharing a yoke with Jesus means letting him decide the direction, decide the pace, decide when to turn. Brothers and sisters, this is often where our greatest struggle lies: we’re willing to have Jesus walk with us, but not so willing to let Jesus decide where we’re going. We want Jesus as our helper, not Jesus as our King. 321 also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, for out of the heart is the wellspring of life. In 1936 the physiologist Hans Selye proposed the “General Adaptation Syndrome”: facing prolonged stress, a person moves from the alarm stage into the resistance stage, and finally into exhaustion. You can hold out for a long time, but in the end you will collapse.

The third key point: humility brings grace, and pride brings resistance. James 4:6 says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” James was the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and later a leader of the church in Jerusalem. At the very start of chapter 4 he points out that the root of the wars and fightings in the church is the pleasures at war in people’s hearts. And this sentence is in fact quoted from Proverbs 3:34; the apostle Peter quotes the same sentence in 1 Peter 5:5. Brothers and sisters, the Old Testament says it once, James says it once, Peter says it once — when the Bible says the same thing three times, it is no longer a suggestion; it is a spiritual law.

“Resists” is the Greek antitassomai, made up of “against” and “to draw up in battle order”; it is a military term meaning to deploy troops and stand opposite. Brothers and sisters, what a solemn picture this is. Towards the proud, God doesn’t merely frown or shake his head; he draws up his battle lines and stands opposite them. Isaiah 14 records five “I will”s in a row: I will ascend into heaven; I will make myself like the Most High. That is the essence of pride — leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God. 2 Chronicles 26:16 says of King Uzziah, “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up.” The most dangerous moment is often not our weakest but our strongest. And Philippians 2 says Christ “emptied himself”, and therefore God highly exalted him.

The lesson puts it precisely: humility is going with the current; pride is fighting upstream. Let’s go back to the sailing boat. Against the wind, the boat can’t go straight; it has to keep changing course, tacking in a zigzag. By simple geometry, tacking at forty-five degrees, the distance sailed is about 1.4 times the straight-line distance. And at every tack the crew must haul the sails and reset the lines all over again, and the whole boat is in a flurry. And with the wind behind it? Just spread the sails. Brothers and sisters, the same wind is a driving force when you go with it and a resisting force when you go against it. It is the same God: obey him and it is grace; oppose him and it is resistance. The wind hasn’t changed, and God hasn’t changed; what has changed is our direction.

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This is easiest to test at home. When a husband and wife argue, if one raises their voice, the other is sure to raise theirs. Pride is like an echo: whatever you shout out comes back to you. The result is that both sides lose — even if you win the argument, you lose the person. In 2013 Bradley Owens of Brigham Young University found that the humility leaders express is positively related to their team’s engagement and job performance. And the management scholar Jim Collins, in Good to Great, found among more than fourteen hundred companies only eleven that truly made the leap, and their leaders shared one trait: a personality of personal humility combined with a will of professional resolve. Brothers and sisters, the real question is not whether humility is hard, but whether we are willing.

Now let’s practise. The lesson gives us four practices; let’s look at the first two. First, the practice of obedience: every morning pray, “Lord, today I am willing to learn your gentleness and humility.” Tomorrow, as soon as you open your eyes, before you scroll your phone or think about your schedule, say this first. Second, the practice of letting go: when pressure comes, stop and ask yourself, “Am I trying to rely on myself again in this?” Just stop for three seconds. Those three seconds are often the dividing line between winning and losing. A small change made every day is more powerful than one big decision.

Third, reflecting on grace: list three things God has helped you through, things you once thought you’d never get past. Write them down, read them aloud, and remind yourself of one sentence — the hard part, he has already done. Fourth, living lightly: learn to entrust things to God and stop being overly anxious about everything. 1 Peter 5:7 says: “Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” Notice that this comes immediately after “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.” Humility and entrusting are two sides of the same thing. And the eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. The last stage matters a great deal — pass this lesson on to someone.

Let’s draw the 321 threads together. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he says, “Learn from me”; the Bible is my standard — it says, “Not too hard for you”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — and here is the key: Galatians 5:22–23 says the fruit of the Spirit includes “gentleness”, and that word shares a root with “gentle” in Matthew 11:29. Brothers and sisters, this means gentleness and humility are not virtues we cultivate by our own efforts; they are fruit the Holy Spirit bears. A tree doesn’t squeeze out fruit by gritting its teeth; fruit grows naturally out of life. That is why humility can be “easy”. The Two Core Values are to let Jesus be King and let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal is to establish God’s system. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless — Galatians 2:20 says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” This week, please choose one “2” and practise selflessness before them.

Finally, let me remind you of the lesson’s gentle reminder: humility is not “lowering your head” but “lifting your head to look at God.” The more you look at God, the less you need to prove yourself. Pride makes you want to “be God”; humility makes you willing to “let God do it.” Notice that low self-esteem is not humility, because its focus is still on the self. The focus must be Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you a call: take off that yoke you’ve been carrying on your own neck. You put that yoke on yourself, and only you can be willing to let it go. Then come and stand beside Jesus and share his yoke. The field is still the same field, the plough still the same plough, but the weight is no longer the same at all, because the one beside you is Jesus.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. On the cross you said, “It is finished”; the hardest stretch of the road, you have already walked to the end. Lord, forgive us. With our lips we say we want to be humble, while in our hearts we are still clinging to ourselves; we ask you for help, yet refuse to let you be King. Today we are willing to come before you afresh. Take away the lie that “humility is too hard,” and let the Holy Spirit bear the fruit of gentleness in us. The hard part you have already accomplished; the easy part I am willing to do. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May you, brothers and sisters, walk in humility all your lives and enjoy his rest and his grace, and may all the glory go to Jesus.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Not “I Can’t” but “I’m Not Yet Willing”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning.

A brother had spent three months preparing a project at work. On the day of the presentation, a colleague on his own team took it and presented it to their manager as his own idea. When the meeting broke up, he sat alone at his desk, palms sweating, heart racing, and his mind began running a whole script: how he would post the timeline in the group chat, how he would drop a “casual” remark at the next meeting, how he would make sure the manager found out for himself. That night he couldn’t sleep. The next morning, as usual, he opened the link to the morning devotion and heard a familiar sentence — “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” At once a voice inside him talked back: “I understand all that. But this time, I can’t do it.”

Brothers and sisters, that little phrase “I can’t do it” — haven’t we all said it?

Let me take that sentence apart. Was it really that he “couldn’t”? Did he have the ability not to post the timeline? Yes. Did he have the ability to sit quietly in the meeting? Yes. Did he have the ability to say to that colleague, “You presented really well yesterday”? Actually, yes, he did. He “could” do every one of those things; he simply “didn’t want to” do any of them. So the sentence really in his heart was not “I can’t” but “I won’t.”

We often translate “I won’t” into “I can’t,” because “I can’t” sounds more innocent and lets us off the hook. Once we call it “I can’t,” the matter shifts from a question of will to a question of ability — from my responsibility to my limitation. But brothers and sisters, the Bible never files humility under ability. The Bible files humility under the will.

In the last lesson we saw a truth that overturns common sense: humility is actually easy; it is pride that is hard. Humility goes with the grain of God’s life; pride goes against the grain of how life was designed. Deuteronomy 30:11 says, “For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant.” God never issues a command without preparing the grace to fulfil it.

So if it isn’t hard, why do we still find it hard? In this lesson, the text gives two very honest answers: one is “unwillingness,” the other is “unfamiliarity.” Then it gives two answers full of hope: the power for humility comes from God’s grace, and the practice of humility begins with our circumstances.

Psychological research on humility points, remarkably, in the same direction as the Bible. Professor June Tangney of George Mason University, in a paper published in 2000 in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, argued that true humility is not self-abasement but a combination of several traits: an accurate assessment of one’s own abilities and limitations, a willingness to admit mistakes, openness to new ideas and advice, and — she noted in particular — “a relatively low self-focus,” that is, no longer keeping our attention fixed on ourselves. Brothers and sisters, that last item, in the language of 321, is “selflessness.”

So humility is not trampling yourself underfoot. Humility is moving yourself out of the centre of the picture and letting Jesus stand there. The hard part has never been moving aside; the hard part is that we can’t bear to move aside.

What did the Lord Jesus himself say? Matthew 11:28–30: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

The word “easy” in Greek is χρηστός (chrēstos), meaning “fit for use, well-suited, good.” In the Lord Jesus’ day, a good yoke was made by a carpenter who measured that particular ox’s shoulders and neck — snug, never chafing, spreading the load evenly. When the Lord Jesus says, “My yoke is easy,” he does not mean the yoke has no weight; he means it won’t rub you raw, because it was made to your measure. Brothers and sisters, humility is the yoke the Lord has tailor-made for us. It is not a rack of torture; it is a tool that fits the hand. What rubs us raw has never been the yoke itself, but the force with which we wear the yoke while straining hard in the opposite direction.

This morning, let us lay that straining force down.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Letter to a Quarrelling Church
sections.html:
To truly hear “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble,” we need to know the situation in which these words were first written.

Evangelical scholars generally hold that the author of the letter of James was James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh. In Galatians 1:19, Paul, recalling his visit to Jerusalem, says, “But of the other apostles I saw no one except James, the Lord’s brother.” Galatians 2:9 names him, together with Cephas and John, among those “reputed to be pillars.” Acts 15 records the Jerusalem Council, where it was this same James who gave the closing summary. It’s worth noticing that John 7:5 says, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” The Lord’s brothers did not believe in him at first; only when, as 1 Corinthians 15:7 records, the risen Lord “appeared to James” did this younger brother become a servant. So in James 1:1 he calls himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” — he does not say, “I am the Lord’s brother.” Brothers and sisters, this is humility: he had the most impressive title in the whole church to hang on his door, and the only title he hung there was “servant.”

As for the date, most evangelical scholars place it around AD 45–50, possibly making it one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written. And the recipients? James 1:1 says, “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion: Greetings.” These were Jewish believers scattered abroad by persecution. They lived as outsiders, life was hard, the gap between rich and poor in the church was wide, and friction between people ran especially high.

So James chapter 4 opens with a heavy blow. James 4:1: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” Verse 2 says, “You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” Verse 4 is sterner still: “You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?”

Brothers and sisters, notice this: when James traces the source of the church’s strife, he doesn’t stop at circumstances, and he doesn’t stop at the other person. He follows it all the way to “your pleasures that war in your members” — all the way to the “self.” In the language of 321, the root of every problem is the self-centred life, and the sharpest shape the self-centred life takes is pride.

Then, right in the middle of all this rebuke, verse 6 suddenly makes a great turn: “But he gives more grace.”

That word “but” is the turning point of the whole chapter. You quarrel, you fight, you befriend the world — but God gives more grace. Brothers and sisters, God’s grace is never just barely enough; it is “more.” Then James goes on: “Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”

An important correction needs to be made here. The lesson’s introduction says “God says,” but James 4:6 plainly says “it says” — that is, Scripture says. James is quoting the Old Testament, Proverbs 3:34, which reads, “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.” James follows the wording of the Greek Old Testament in common use at the time (the Septuagint). The same verse is also quoted in 1 Peter 5:5: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” Two apostles independently quote the same sentence — clear evidence that this was a spiritual law the early church held in common.

Two Greek words in this sentence deserve a closer look.

“Resists” is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” It is not a casual brush-off; it is lining up the ranks and meeting you head-on. Brothers and sisters, what this sentence means is this: when I am proud, I’m not up against my colleague — I am drawn up in battle array against God. No wonder pride is so exhausting: you are in a tug-of-war with the Lord of the universe.

“Gives grace” is δίδωσιν χάριν (didōsin charin), “keeps on giving grace.” And “the humble” is ταπεινοῖς (tapeinois), a word that in Greek culture originally carried a negative sense — “low, lowly, of no standing.” The Greeks looked down on this word; the Bible lifted it up and made it the passport of the kingdom of heaven.

After verse 6, James fires off ten commands in a row. James 4:7–10: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded. … Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.”

Look carefully at the order: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil. When 321 says, “Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan,” this is where it comes from. We do not overcome the devil by shouting louder than he does; we overcome him by first bowing our heads before God. Bowing the head is the posture of victory.

And “humble yourselves,” ταπεινώθητε (tapeinōthēte), is in Greek a command in the passive voice — “let yourselves be brought low.” This is wonderful: humility is both our choice and the work God does in us. Our part is to be willing; God’s part is to bring it to completion.

This is the backdrop to the lesson’s four main points. Now let’s look at them one by one.

sections.heading: 3. Humility Isn’t Hard — the Hard Part Is “Am I Willing?”
sections.html:
1. The Scripture: A Command That Seems Impossible

Matthew 5:44: “But I tell you, love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you.”

This is the most breathtaking sentence in the Sermon on the Mount. The lesson quotes it as “love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you,” which is correct, except that it leaves out the opening; in the Chinese Union Version the whole verse begins with “But I tell you.” Those four words matter, because the Lord Jesus is drawing a contrast: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you …” He is not adding a footnote to the old standard; he is issuing a new one.

Loving your enemies sounds far too hard, doesn’t it?

But, brothers and sisters, think it through clearly with me: what is the hard part — is it the “loving,” or is it something else?

2. The Hard Part Isn’t Love — It’s Letting Go of “My Right to Be Hurt”

The text puts its finger right on it: the hard part isn’t love; the hard part is “being unwilling to let go of my right to be hurt.”

Think about it. When we have been wronged, we hold several cards in our hand: I have a reason to be angry; I have a right to get justice; I’m entitled to demand an apology; I’ve every ground to let him have a taste of his own medicine. In a human court, every one of these cards holds up. And as long as we keep holding them, loving our enemies really does feel as hard as climbing to heaven — because love and revenge cannot happen at the same time, just as one hand cannot be clenched into a fist and held open at once.

A tug-of-war is a good picture. Two people pull on one rope, and as long as neither lets go, the struggle goes on until both are worn out and hurt. Ending it is actually very simple, so simple it’s almost absurd — one person just has to let go. Letting go takes no strength; letting go takes willingness. Brothers and sisters, our problem has never been that we can’t pull hard enough; our problem is that we won’t let go.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Laying Down Our Rights Is Not Abandoning Justice

Someone will ask: “So the wrongdoer just gets away with it? Doesn’t justice matter?”

The Bible’s answer is very clear: laying down our rights does not cancel justice; it hands justice back to its true owner.

1 Peter 2:23 describes the Lord Jesus this way: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” Notice the last phrase — he did not throw justice away; he “committed” it.

Romans 12:19 says too: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.’”

Brothers and sisters, laying down our rights does not mean saying, “This doesn’t matter.” It means saying, “This matters so much — so much that I don’t dare handle it with my own small hands. I will hand it to the God who sees most clearly and judges most fairly.” Pride scrambles to be the judge; humility is content to be the plaintiff, then steps back to the public gallery and lets God take the judgement seat.

This is exactly what 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When I insist on getting justice with my own hands, I have sat down in a seat that doesn’t belong to me. And the moment I sit there, God steps aside in my life, because that chair was his all along.

4. Once We’re Willing, Grace Begins to Flow

The text puts it well: once we choose humility and lay down our rights, God’s grace comes upon us, and he gives us the power to love those who are unlovable.

Here the text quotes a sentence: “It is not I who can do all things, but Christ who strengthens me.” The meaning is not wrong, but it is a reworded sentence, not the words of Scripture. Philippians 4:13 actually reads: “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.”

Paul wrote this in prison. The context is Philippians 4:11–12: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.” So the context of “I can do all things” is not that everything goes my way, but that I can be content whatever state I’m in. And the word “learned,” in Greek μανθάνω (manthanō), is the verb related to the word for disciple (μαθητής) — learning slowly, learning by following, learning until it becomes a skill.

Brothers and sisters, even Paul had to “learn.” If you and I are a little clumsy at learning today, there’s no need to lose heart.

5. Illustration and Research: Forgiveness Is a Road We Can Walk

Professor Everett Worthington of Virginia Commonwealth University has made forgiveness the subject of his research for decades and developed the well-known REACH model of forgiveness. A number of controlled studies by him and his colleagues consistently show that people who receive forgiveness interventions experience significantly lower levels of depression and anxiety, and a markedly greater sense of hope. Even more striking, his own mother was murdered, and he carried on this research in the midst of the deepest grief. His conclusion is simple: forgiveness is not letting the offender off; forgiveness is letting yourself out of prison.

Brothers and sisters, what science has measured, the Bible said long ago. When we cling to “my right to be hurt,” that chain seems to bind the other person, but in fact its other end is fastened to our own heart.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: Change the Mindset First

321 speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Everything begins with the mindset.

Under this point, the mindset that needs to change comes down to just one sentence: it’s not that “I can’t”; it’s that “I’m not yet willing.”

Brothers and sisters, saying this out loud stings a little, because it puts the responsibility back into my hands. But that is exactly the good news — anything that is a matter of “I won’t” can still turn around, because willingness can change, while the limits of ability cannot. What God wants has never been our ability; what God wants is our willingness. He asks, “Are you willing?” All we need to answer is, “Lord, I am willing.” The rest is his work.

sections.heading: 4. Humility Isn’t Hard — the Hard Part Is “I’m Not Used to It”
sections.html:
1. Humility Is a Habit, Not a Temperament

The text says: humility is not an inborn reaction but a spiritual habit that is formed only through choice and practice.

That sentence deserves to be copied carefully into our notebooks. Many people spend their whole lives stuck at one hurdle: they assume humility is an “inborn personality” — some people are naturally gentle, some are naturally hot-tempered, and I unfortunately belong to the second group, so there’s no hope for me in this life.

Not so. The Bible never speaks of humility as a temperament; the Bible speaks of humility as training.

1 Timothy 4:7: “But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness.” “Exercise” in Greek is γυμνάζω (gymnazō), the verb behind the word “gymnasium” (γυμνάσιον). What Paul means is that godliness has to be trained the way an athlete trains.

Hebrews 5:14: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” “Exercised” is a perfect participle from the same root, γεγυμνασμένα — the condition left behind after long training.

Brothers and sisters, spiritual maturity doesn’t accumulate with seniority; it is trained into us through repeated practice.

2. The Text’s Picture: A Left-Hander Learning to Use the Right Hand

The text uses a very apt picture: it’s like a left-handed person learning to write with the right hand.

At first the letters are crooked, the hand aches, the pace is slow, and after two lines you want to give up, while a sentence keeps rising in your mind: “This isn’t me.” But if you’re willing to keep practising — one month, two months, six months — the right hand grows smoother and smoother, and the writing looks more and more like your own.

When we choose humility, it feels exactly the same. The first time you’re the first to fall silent in an argument, it feels awkward. The first time you’re the first to say sorry, it feels like you’ve lost out. The first time you hear criticism and don’t defend yourself, you toss and turn all night. That “this isn’t me” feeling will be very strong.

But brothers and sisters, hear this clearly — that feeling is not the truth. That feeling is just an old habit protesting.

3. Confirmation from Science: The Brain Can Be Rewritten

When God made us, he put something marvellous into our brains, called “neuroplasticity.”

Beginning in the 1990s, Professor Edward Taub of the University of Alabama at Birmingham developed “constraint-induced movement therapy”: the stroke patient’s healthy hand is restrained, forcing the patient to use the affected hand again and again. The result — not only did movement improve, but brain imaging showed that the area of the cortex corresponding to that hand had actually grown larger. In other words, the adult brain rewires itself according to what we do repeatedly.

Physiology offers a lovely parallel as well. A nerve fibre wrapped in myelin can carry signals at around a hundred metres per second; a fibre without myelin manages only one to two metres per second. And myelin is precisely what thickens, layer by layer, through repeated use. The more a path is travelled, the faster, easier and more natural it becomes.

Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, in a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, followed participants as they formed new habits and found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Brothers and sisters, please note that number: an average of sixty-six days. It tells us two things — first, it won’t come naturally right away; second, the day will come when it does.

Professor Wendy Wood of the University of Southern California and her colleagues, in a diary study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that about forty-three per cent of people’s everyday behaviour consists of habitual responses repeated in the same settings, almost without thought. Brothers and sisters, this means that nearly half our lives run on “autopilot.” So where is the real spiritual battle? It lies in this: who writes the program that runs that autopilot.

4. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Put Off the Old Self, Put On the New

Ephesians 4:22–24: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”

Put away, be renewed, put on — Paul uses the picture of getting dressed. Brothers and sisters, getting dressed is something you do every morning, not something you do once for a lifetime. The old self isn’t taken off all at once, and the new self isn’t put on all at once. Taking off every day, putting on every day — that is training.

It is generally held that the American historian of philosophy Will Durant, in The Story of Philosophy, summed up Aristotle’s thought in this sentence: “We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” The sentence is often attributed directly to Aristotle, but strictly speaking it is Durant’s interpretation. Yet the point stands: character never springs up in the decisive moment; character is trained in countless unremarkable moments, and merely shows itself in the decisive one.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

Pride is the inertia of the old life; humility is the training of the new life. The most frightening thing about inertia is that it takes no effort — do nothing at all, and you’ll slide back onto the old track automatically. So spiritual growth never happens of its own accord; it is one deliberate choice after another.

Among the eight stages of changing our mindset, there is one called “Repetition.” It is the least romantic stage, yet the most vital. You’ve heard the Information, received the Revelation, nodded in Conviction, done the Implementation once, gone through Evaluation and Correction — and then what? Then comes Repetition, repetition and more repetition, until humility changes from “something I try hard to do” into “who I naturally am.”

The text says it so well: at first it’s not easy, but keep at it, and it will become easy.

sections.heading: 5. The Power for Humility Comes from God’s Grace
sections.html:
1. Humility Is the Fruit of Grace, Not the Score of Effort

The text says: humility is not gained by effort; it is the result of grace.

This has to be said up front, or the previous point will be misread as “grit your teeth and push through on willpower.” Brothers and sisters, if humility were something we produced by sheer effort, then the people who pushed through most successfully would end up proud of their humility — the most absurd, and the most common, trap in the spiritual life.

Ephesians 2:8–9: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.”

“Grace” in Greek is χάρις (charis), meaning “free favour” — a gift we are utterly unworthy of and could never earn. Paul deliberately adds “that no one would boast” — so even the way of salvation God designed in such a way that no one could be proud of it.

The nineteenth-century South African pastor Andrew Murray, in his well-known book Humility, says that humility is simply the proper place of the creature before God — acknowledging that God is the one who does everything. Brothers and sisters, humility is not an achievement; humility is a kind of “seeing”: seeing that I am created and he is the Creator; seeing that I am limited and he is limitless. Once we see it, we naturally bow low.

2. The Moment We Believed Was Our First Lesson in Humility

The text has a very precious insight: when we admitted we were sinners and received Jesus as Saviour, that moment was the beginning of humility.

Why? Because in that moment we laid down our right to “save ourselves.”

In Luke 18:13–14, the parable the Lord Jesus told still pierces today: “But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

Brothers and sisters, every word of the Pharisee’s prayer was true — he really did fast, he really did give a tenth. He wasn’t lying; he was simply standing in the wrong place. He stood before God, yet used other people as his measuring stick. The tax collector had nothing, only “be merciful to me.” And the one who went home justified was the man with empty hands.

So every brother and sister who has truly been born again has already done the most thorough act of humility there is — you have already confessed before God, “I can’t.” Since you have already passed the hardest test of all, is it really so hard to bow your head first today over one small matter?

3. The Holy Spirit Is at Work Within Us

The text says: the Holy Spirit is constantly at work in our hearts, using circumstances, relationships and even setbacks to show us our limits and teach us to depend on him.

Philippians 2:13: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.”

Brothers and sisters, look closely: even the “willing” is God at work within us. That thought that suddenly rose in your heart this morning — “Should I be the first to say sorry to him?” — you didn’t come up with that yourself. That is the Holy Spirit knocking at the door.

Philippians 1:6 says as well: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” He is the one who begins the work, and he is the one who completes it. We are the building site, not the foreman.

I think of a sailing boat. A sailing boat crosses the ocean not by its crew rowing for dear life, but by raising the sails. Those who raise the sails do not make the wind; they simply place themselves in the wind. Brothers and sisters, humility is raising the sails — we don’t make grace; we simply put ourselves where grace can blow on us. And which way does the wind blow? God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The wind blows toward the low places; grace flows downhill.

4. God Has Done the Hard Part; We Only Do the Easy Part

The text concludes: we need not feel pressured over “whether we can be humble”; we need only be “willing” to choose humility. God has done the hard part; we only need to do the easy part — choose to obey.

This is exactly the logic of Philippians 2:5–8: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

“Emptied himself” in Greek is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), literally “poured himself out.” Brothers and sisters, the hardest act of humility in the universe has already been accomplished by the Lord Jesus: from the throne of glory to the manger, from the manger to the cross. Not one step of that road could we walk. He has walked it all.

Having walked the hardest part, he turns back and says to us, “Learn from me.” All we have to do is the far easier thing — in today’s office, at today’s dinner table, in today’s group chat messages: not answer back, listen to the end first, say “I’m sorry.”

Professor Carol Dweck of Stanford University, through her research on the “growth mindset,” tells us that people who believe ability can change through effort are more willing to persevere when they meet setbacks, and keep improving. It’s a very useful finding in education. But brothers and sisters, the Christian’s hope is sturdier than a “growth mindset” — what we believe is not “I can become better,” but “God will complete his work in me.” A mindset relies on ourselves; grace relies on God. A mindset grows tired; grace does not.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll fret, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice.

Proverbs 4:23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

Brothers and sisters, the reason we find humility hard is often that we are calculating with the brain — calculating how much I’ll lose if I do this, whether he’ll take a mile if I give an inch, what other people will think of me. The more precisely we calculate, the less we can move. Relying on the heart is different: the heart asks only one question — “Lord, what do you want me to do?” — and then goes and does it.

Of 321’s Three Foundations, the third is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” Humility can become our life not because our resolve is firm enough, but because the Holy Spirit lives within us. Galatians 5:22–23 says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Notice that it is fruit that is “borne,” not a product that is “made.” Fruit is grown, not manufactured. Our part is to stay joined to the vine, as branches. John 15:5: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.”

sections.heading: 6. The Practice of Humility Begins with Our Circumstances
sections.html:
1. What God Gives Is Not Comfort but a Classroom

The text says: God often uses people and circumstances to give us one opportunity after another to practise humility.

Brothers and sisters, the first sentence of our prayers is often “Lord, please take this difficulty away” or “Lord, please change that person.” God hears such prayers, but what weighs on his heart is often a different question: can this situation teach you humility?

Romans 5:3–5: “Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope: and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.”

Paul does not say suffering is good; Paul says suffering “produces” something. It’s a production line: suffering, perseverance, proven character, hope. And this production line has only one entrance — you have to stay in the suffering and not jump off halfway.

Psalm 119:71 puts it even more directly: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.” Hebrews 5:8 even says this of the Lord Jesus: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” If even the Son of God “learned” obedience through suffering, how much more you and I.

2. Rather Than Asking God to Change Others, Ask God to Change You

The text’s second reminder is the key to this whole section: rather than asking God to change others, ask God to change you.

When you find someone hard to get along with, someone who makes you uncomfortable, that is precisely God’s “humility classroom” for you. And the most unusual thing about this classroom is that you don’t get to choose your classmates.

Moses is the best example. He spent forty years in Pharaoh’s palace and was taught all the learning of the Egyptians; then he spent forty years tending sheep in the wilderness of Midian — forty years with no learning, no stage, no applause, only sheep, sand and wind. God spent forty years grinding down a prince who thought “I’ll take charge on God’s behalf” into a servant who said, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?” Numbers 12:3 says, “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” That sentence was carved out in the wilderness.

Nature, too, offers a quiet testimony. When a grain of sand gets inside an oyster’s shell and the oyster cannot push it out, it begins to secrete layer upon layer of nacre around it. The grain of sand never leaves, yet a few years later it has become a pearl. Brothers and sisters, sometimes God doesn’t remove the grain of sand; he wants to make a pearl around it.

3. Don’t Complain — Give Thanks Instead

The text says: when things go wrong, don’t complain; give thanks instead.

1 Thessalonians 5:18: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” Notice it is “in everything give thanks,” not “feel happy about everything.” Giving thanks is a decision, not an emotion.

Robert Emmons of the University of California, Davis, and Michael McCullough of the University of Miami, in a study published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, divided participants into groups, one of which wrote down each week the things they were grateful for. After ten weeks, this group felt markedly better about their lives as a whole, reported fewer physical complaints, and exercised more often.

Brothers and sisters, gratitude will not change what happened yesterday, but it will change the eyes with which we see things today. And 321 says our perspective must turn from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Seen through human eyes, this is a nuisance; seen through God’s eyes, it is a classroom.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

321 has a very concrete practice called 920.

Every person we are in relationship with is our “2” — spouse, children, parents, colleagues, neighbours, and that one person who is hardest to get along with. And the “0” is selflessness: before each “2,” we practise living out a selfless life. As we keep practising, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit will be borne: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

Brothers and sisters, notice one thing: not one of these nine graces is borne in easy times. Patience needs something to be patient with; kindness needs someone unlovable; gentleness needs a moment of being offended. So the person who gives you headaches is not an obstacle to your spiritual life; he is the garden of your spiritual life.

One step further on are the 235 relationships: first become a “2” with someone who is selfless — spiritual companions who support each other; then build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together. And all of this has only one foundation: selflessness. The self-centred cannot build a team, because the self-centred have to stand in the middle of everything.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Brothers and sisters, if in our circumstances we are only in a hurry to get the “task” dealt with, while offending the “person,” then we have turned the whole order upside down.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set this lesson back into the big picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he is gentle and humble, emptying himself and obeying to the point of death; the Bible is my standard — humility is not decided by how I feel, but by what God’s word says; the Holy Spirit is my guide — humility is not something I force out by gritting my teeth, but fruit the Holy Spirit bears.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — I step down from the judgement seat that doesn’t belong to me and give the throne back to him; let Jesus receive all the glory — only when I stop rushing to prove myself can others see the Lord.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, God’s system is a system in which no one scrambles for a seat. The driving force behind scrambling for seats is pride; the lesson of not scrambling is humility. So humility is not merely a personal virtue; humility is the foundation on which the system either stands or falls.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. The mindset this lesson exchanges is this — “humility is too hard” becomes “humility isn’t hard; I’m just not yet willing, and not yet used to it.” Change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes.

And there is that vital saying: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Walking Four Practices Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The text gives four practices for daily living. Let’s take them deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice One: The Practice of Choosing

Every day, when you face conflict, deliberately stop first and ask yourself: “In this matter, can I choose humility?”

Information: know that humility is a choice, not a personality trait. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let me see, at the very moment I’m offended, that this is a fork in the road, not a straight road with no turnings. Conviction: truly settle it in my heart that “it’s not that I can’t; it’s that I’m not yet willing.” Implementation: today, pause for at least three seconds before speaking. Evaluation: in the evening, look back — how many times did I pause today, and how many times didn’t I? Correction: identify the situation where I most easily lose ground — is it group chat messages? The dinner table at home? Late-night tiredness? Repetition: for forty days in a row, make a note every day. Multiplication: tell your “2” about this practice, and pause for three seconds together.

Practice Two: The Prayer for Grace

When you find it hard to be humble, pray like this: “Lord, please give me grace, so that I am willing to lay myself down.”

Information: the power for humility comes from grace, not willpower. Revelation: see that God’s grace is “more grace.” Conviction: believe he will provide. Implementation: save this prayer on your phone, and in the moment of conflict open it and pray it silently once. Evaluation: notice whether, after praying, the temperature in your heart has come down. Correction: if it still won’t come down, pray the prayer out loud. Repetition: let it become a reflex. Multiplication: teach your children to pray this way.

Practice Three: Building the Habit

Set yourself a “humility challenge” — be the first to apologise in an argument, the first to listen in a meeting.

Information: on average a habit takes sixty-six days to become automatic. Revelation: understand that what God wants is not one heroic performance but a long, long road. Conviction: accept that at first it is bound to feel awkward. Implementation: this week, start with just one thing — only “listen first, don’t interrupt.” Evaluation: each night, mark a tick or a cross. Correction: if you’ve set the bar too high, shrink it until it’s something you can certainly do. Repetition: sixty-six days without a break. Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to walk it with you, and report your counts to each other.

Practice Four: Thanksgiving in Our Circumstances

When things go wrong, don’t complain; give thanks instead: “Lord, thank you for giving me an opportunity to practise humility.”

Information: giving thanks in everything is God’s will. Revelation: see that person, that situation, as a classroom God has arranged. Conviction: believe that suffering produces perseverance. Implementation: today, give specific thanks once for one thing that has gone wrong. Evaluation: a week later, look back — has the number of complaints gone down? Correction: change a vague “thank you, Lord” into a specific “thank you for using this to deal with my impatience.” Repetition: make it a daily three-line thanksgiving. Multiplication: share one “classroom testimony” in your small group.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
The text ends with a beautiful reminder: those used to pride find humility unnatural; those used to humility find pride uncomfortable.

Brothers and sisters, which kind of person do you want to be?

Humility is not asceticism; it is grace overflowing. It is not an unreachable ideal, but a way of life we can choose every single day. God will not send us down a road that goes nowhere; he has long since prepared the help of his grace.

So please remember the four sentences of this lesson:

Humility isn’t hard; the hard part is whether we’re willing — so today, say to the Lord, “I am willing.”

Humility isn’t hard; the hard part is that we’re not used to it — so start practising today, and keep at it until it comes naturally.

The power for humility comes from grace — so don’t grit your teeth; raise the sails.

The practice of humility begins with our circumstances — so don’t waste today’s lesson in the classroom.

The hard part, the Lord has already finished; the easy part, let us go and do. When we are willing, humility becomes easy, life begins to be transformed, and the glory goes to the Lord Jesus, who is gentle and humble.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Dear Lord Jesus,
Thank you, thank you that you have already placed a humble life within me.

Lord, I confess that in the past I often said “I can’t,” when deep down I knew it was that I wasn’t yet willing. Today I lay before you, one by one, the rights I have been clinging to — the right to justify myself, the right to hit back, the right to prove myself.
I also confess that I am still very unused to this. Please give me perseverance, so that through one choice after another your likeness may be trained into me.

Thank you that the hard part you have already finished; the easy part I am willing to do. Please give me grace to live out a selfless life before every person I meet today, and to see, in every difficulty I meet today, the classroom you have prepared for me.

discussion: Think back honestly over this week: was there something you told yourself “I can’t do,” when really it was “I won’t”? When you read Matthew 5:44, “But I tell you, love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,” who is the first person who comes to mind? Are you willing to pray for him or her once today?

Right now, which person or which situation is God’s “humility classroom” for you? Set it against Romans 5:3–4, “Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope,” and talk it over: what does God want to produce in you? Which one thing will you practise concretely this week?

blog.title: Humility Isn’t Hard — You’re Just Not Yet Willing

blocks.x: A brother had spent three months preparing a project. On the day of the presentation a colleague took it and presented it to their manager as his own idea. That night he couldn’t sleep. The next morning he read James 4:6: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” At once a voice inside him talked back: “I understand all that. But this time, I can’t do it.”

You and I have probably said “I can’t do it” too. But take that sentence apart: he could keep from answering back, he could sit quietly, he could even say, “You presented really well yesterday.” He could do every one of those things; he simply didn’t want to do any of them. The sentence really in his heart was not “I can’t” but “I won’t.”
The Hard Part Isn’t Love — It’s Letting Go of My Right to Be Hurt

The Lord Jesus said, “But I tell you, love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Loving our enemies sounds as hard as climbing to heaven. But the hard part isn’t the “loving”; the hard part is laying down that card in our hand — I have a reason to be angry, I have a right to get justice.

It’s like a tug-of-war. Two people pull on one rope, and as long as neither lets go, the struggle goes on until both are worn out and hurt. Ending it is actually very simple: one person just has to let go. Letting go takes no strength; letting go takes willingness. And laying down our rights does not cancel justice; it hands justice back to its true owner. The Lord Jesus, “when he was cursed, didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23).
It’s Also Hard Because We’re Not Used to It — So We Train

Humility is not an inborn personality; it is a spiritual habit that has to be trained. It’s like a left-handed person learning to write with the right hand: at first the letters are crooked and the hand aches, and a sentence keeps rising in your mind: “This isn’t me.” But that feeling is not the truth; it is just an old habit protesting. Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London found in a 2010 study that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic. That tells us two things: first, it won’t come naturally right away; second, the day will come when it does.

And we don’t do it by gritting our teeth. Paul says, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Even the thought “Should I be the first to say sorry?” isn’t something we came up with ourselves; it is the Holy Spirit knocking at the door. Humility is not rowing; humility is raising the sails — we don’t make the wind, we simply put ourselves where the wind can blow on us. The wind blows toward the low places, and grace flows downhill.

If humility were something we produced by sheer willpower, then the people who pushed through most successfully would end up proud of their humility. That is why Scripture says, “for by grace you have been saved through faith … not of works, that no one would boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Our Circumstances Are God’s Classroom of Humility

The first sentence of our prayers is often “Lord, please take this difficulty away.” But what weighs more on God’s heart is this: can this situation teach you humility? That person who is hard to get along with is not an obstacle to your spiritual life; he is the classroom God has given you. Rather than asking God to change others, ask God to change you.

This week, why not start with four small things: in a conflict, pause for three seconds and ask yourself, “Can I choose humility here?”; when it’s hard, pray, “Lord, please give me grace, so that I am willing to lay myself down”; practise just one thing — listen first, don’t interrupt; and when things go wrong, say instead, “Thank you for giving me an opportunity to practise humility.”

Those used to pride find humility unnatural; those used to humility find pride uncomfortable. The hard part, the Lord has already finished; the easy part, let us go and do. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Question for Reflection
This week, is there something you have told yourself “I can’t do”, while deep down you know the truth is “I won’t”?
