l098.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

blog.title: Three Sentences That Are Hardest to Say

blocks.x: Practising Humility Daily (Part 2)

An elderly preacher who had served for more than forty years was once asked, “What lesson have you been slowest to learn in your whole life?” He thought for a long time, and answered with a single word: “Humility.”
Preaching, he said, gets more polished the more you do it, and you memorise more and more Scripture — but that “I” in your heart swells more easily the longer you serve.

Have you ever had that experience? You thought you were very humble — until someone corrected you in public. You thought you had already denied yourself — until someone took the credit for your work. The thing that stood straight up in that moment shouting “I’m not wrong!” is the self-centred life.

Humility is not a theory; it is a daily practice. The opportunities God gives us are sometimes hidden in conflict and sometimes hidden in success. Today there are three sentences that are hardest to say, and each one is an act of laying down a right.
The First Sentence: I Will Change Myself to Fit In with You
The greatest tension between people often comes not from “badness” but from “difference.” Different personalities, different styles, different habits — and so conflict arises.
We often ask God, “Change him!” But God gently asks a question back: “Are you willing to change yourself first?”

Paul says, “To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). He did not demand that people accommodate him; he took the initiative to adjust himself, so that through him people could come to know Jesus more easily.

When you travel abroad and your plug won’t fit the socket, however right you are, the power simply won’t come — unless you’ve brought an adapter. Humility is that adapter: it doesn’t change the nature of the current; it only changes the shape of the contact.

We cannot change people — that is God’s work; but we can change our own attitude, tone, expression and reactions. Pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
The Second Sentence: I Am Really Nothing Special
Failure often makes people humble; it is success that most easily makes people proud. When people praise us, a sentence quietly rises in our hearts: “I worked hard to get where I am.”

But Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Planting is something people can do; watering is something people can do; but you cannot make a single seed sprout.

The moon is beautiful at night, yet it gives off no light of its own; moonlight is sunlight. When is the moon at its brightest? When it is directly facing the sun. When is it at its darkest? When the earth squeezes in between. We are just the same: the moment the self gets in the way, there is an eclipse.
So when people praise me, I say, “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.” Humility does not deny our worth; it recognises our source. I am only a channel of grace; the glory belongs to God.
The Third Sentence: I Don’t Understand Anything

Spiritual pride is more dangerous than worldly pride, because it wears the coat of godliness. Some people feel they understand the truth, understand the church, understand spiritual principles — and so they are no longer teachable and no longer depend on God.
Scripture says, “But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2). The truly wise are those who know what they don’t understand.

Three times in the Bible the waters were parted: Moses raised his rod and the Red Sea parted; Joshua led the priests into the water and the Jordan stopped flowing; Elijah struck the water with his cloak and it too was divided. The same parting of waters, yet three different ways — because God is never boxed in by our experience.
Yesterday’s method cannot guarantee today’s results. Only those who admit they don’t understand will depend more on the Holy Spirit and walk in God’s fresh works.
Four Practices You Can Start Today
1. Adjust yourself: in a conflict, ask first, “What can I change to fit in with him?”
2. Give the glory to God: when praised, respond, “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.”
3. Admit your limits: pray every day, “Lord, I don’t understand anything; please teach me.”
4. Look to the Holy Spirit: ask him first in everything; don’t go by experience, don’t rely on yourself.
The practice of humility is not about how much we do, but about each willing choice we make. A heart like that is where revival begins.
Let us practise humility every day, and have less and less of self and more and more of Christ.
Question for reflection: of these three sentences, which is the hardest for you to say today? With which person, or which situation, does God want to start training you?

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we read together the second talk on “Practising Humility Daily.” Peter says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). Today we will learn three practices: I will change myself to fit in with you; I am really nothing special; I don’t understand anything. These three sentences are three acts of laying down our rights.

A preacher who had served for more than forty years was once asked what lesson he had been slowest to learn in his whole life. He answered with a single word: humility. Brothers and sisters, have you ever had that experience? You thought you were very humble — until someone corrected you in public. You thought you had already denied yourself — until someone took the credit for your work. The voice that stood straight up inside you in that moment is the self-centred life. Humility is not a theory; it is a daily practice. The opportunities God gives us are sometimes hidden in conflict and sometimes hidden in success. When conflict comes, God is asking, “Are you willing to change yourself first?” When success comes, God is asking, “Where are you going to put this glory?”

Peter was writing to a group of resident aliens who were being bullied and misunderstood. The first thing he says to these suffering people is not to fight for their rights but this: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another” (1 Peter 5:5). The word for “clothe yourselves” refers in the original to the apron a slave tied at his waist while working. Why did Peter choose this word? Because he could never forget that night when the Lord tied on a towel and knelt down to wash his feet. Then Peter goes on: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). First humbled, then exalted — the order cannot be reversed.

The first practice: I will change myself to fit in with you. Brothers and sisters, the greatest tension between people often comes not from “badness” but from “difference.” So we pray, “Lord, change him!” But God gently asks a question back: “Are you willing to change yourself first?” Paul says, “I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). Paul was a free man, yet he willingly became everyone’s servant. What he changed was his method, not the standard; his posture, not the truth.

When we travel abroad and our plug won’t fit the socket, however right we are, the power simply won’t come — unless we’ve brought an adapter. Brothers and sisters, humility is that adapter. Not one bit of the gospel’s power is reduced; only the shape of the contact has to change. When Hudson Taylor went to China, he put on a Chinese long robe; his own countrymen mocked him, yet he carried the gospel into the interior. We cannot change people — that is God’s work; but we can change our own attitude, tone, expression and reactions. Changing first is not weakness; it is humility that springs from faith. Pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

The second practice: I am really nothing special. Failure often makes people humble; it is success that most easily makes people proud. When people praise us, a sentence quietly rises in our hearts: I worked hard to get where I am. But Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Planting is something people can do; watering is something people can do; but you cannot make a single seed sprout. The force that pushes the seed coat open belongs to God.

The moon is beautiful, yet it gives off no light of its own; moonlight is sunlight. When is the moon at its brightest? When it is directly facing the sun. When is it at its darkest? When the earth squeezes in between. Brothers and sisters, we are just the same: the moment the self gets in the way, there is an eclipse. Paul asks, “What do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). So when people praise me, I say, “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.” Humility does not deny our worth; it recognises our source. I am only a channel of grace; the glory belongs to God.

The third practice: I don’t understand anything. Spiritual pride is more dangerous than worldly pride, because it wears the coat of godliness. Scripture says, “But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2). And the Lord Jesus said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25). What abilities does an infant have? None — only simplicity, dependence and a willingness to learn.

Three times in the Bible the waters were parted. Moses raised his rod and the Red Sea parted; Joshua led the priests into the water and the Jordan stopped flowing; Elijah struck the water with his cloak and it too was divided (Exodus 14:16; Joshua 3:8; 2 Kings 2:8). The same parting of waters, yet three different ways — because God is never boxed in by our experience. Brothers and sisters, yesterday’s method cannot guarantee today’s results. So let us rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice, rely on the brain and you’ll fret.

There are four practices today; please take them home. First, adjust yourself: in a conflict, ask first, what can I change to fit in with him? Second, give the glory to God: when praised, respond, thank the Lord — it’s his grace. Third, admit your limits: pray every day, Lord, I don’t understand anything; please teach me. Fourth, look to the Holy Spirit: ask him first in everything; don’t go by experience, don’t rely on yourself. 321’s eight stages remind us: once we have Information and Revelation, we still need Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, the practice of humility is not about how much we do, but about each willing choice we make. God is not up in heaven holding a scoreboard, counting how many times you gave way today and how often you held your tongue; he is looking at your heart. Revival doesn’t begin with big meetings; it begins with a heart willing to go low. Today, let Jesus reign as King over your emotions, as King over your achievements, as King over your opinions. Let us practise humility every day, and have less and less of self and more and more of Christ.

Let us pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, we confess that we often ask you to change others but refuse to change ourselves first; we often treat your grace as our own achievement. Please forgive us. Lord, I am willing to change myself first; I am really nothing special; I don’t understand anything — please teach me. Holy Spirit, please be our guide all through this day; make us vessels fit for your use, and may all the glory go to Jesus. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This early morning, let us read together the second talk on “Practising Humility Daily.” Peter says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). Today we will learn three practices: I will change myself to fit in with you; I am really nothing special; I don’t understand anything. 321 tells us: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. May the Lord engrave these three sentences on the tablets of our hearts today.

An elderly preacher who had served for more than forty years was once asked, “What lesson have you been slowest to learn in your whole life?” He thought for a long time, and answered with a single word: “Humility.” Preaching, he said, gets more polished the more you do it, but that “I” in your heart swells more easily the longer you serve. Brothers and sisters, have you ever had that experience? You thought you were very humble — until someone corrected you in public. You thought you had already become gentle — until the person closest to you at home spoke to you in the very tone you can least stand. In that instant, the voice that stood straight up inside you is the self-centred life.

321 tells us: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Today’s three sentences are three acts of laying down a right: laying down the right to make others change, laying down the right to be seen, laying down the right to think I already understand. When conflict comes, God is asking, “Are you willing to change yourself first?” When success comes, God is asking, “Where are you going to put this glory?” And when we think we understand, God is asking, “Are you still willing to learn?”

Our key passage comes from 1 Peter chapter 5. Peter was writing to Christians scattered across Asia Minor, called people “living as foreigners”; the letter was written around AD 62 to 64, on the eve of persecution. To a group of people being bullied, the first thing Peter says is not to fight for their rights but this: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another” (1 Peter 5:5). The word “clothe yourselves” appears only once in the whole New Testament, and in the original it refers to the apron a slave tied at his waist while working. Why did Peter choose this word? Because he could never forget that night when the Lord laid aside his outer garments, wrapped a towel around his waist and knelt down to wash his feet. Then Peter says, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). First humbled, then exalted; the one who lifts us up is God, not ourselves.

The first practice: I will change myself to fit in with you. Brothers and sisters, the greatest tension between people often comes not from “badness” but from “difference.” One person works fast, another works carefully; one says exactly what he thinks, another always considers other people’s feelings first. They both love the Lord, yet after three months of serving together they’ve started sighing at each other. It’s the same at home: where to squeeze the toothpaste, what to set the air conditioning to. Not one of these involves sin, yet day after day they grind out a temper. So we pray, “Lord, change him!” We even put it very spiritually: “Lord, shine your light on him.” But God gently asks a question back: “Are you willing to change yourself first?”

Paul says, “To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). In this chapter Paul is talking about rights: he had the right to eat and drink, the right to make his living from the gospel, yet he says, “But I have used none of these things” (1 Corinthians 9:15). He also says, “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more” (1 Corinthians 9:19). Those words “brought myself” matter a great deal: no one could compel him; he chose it himself. What he changed was his method, not the standard; his posture, not the truth.

When we travel abroad, what do we dread most? Bringing our appliances and finding they won’t fit the sockets. However right you are, the power simply won’t come — unless you’ve brought an adapter. Brothers and sisters, humility is that adapter: it doesn’t change the nature of the current; it only changes the shape of the contact. Not one bit of the gospel’s power is reduced, but without a connector willing to change its shape, the current cannot get into the other person’s life. When Hudson Taylor went to China as a missionary, he put on a Chinese long robe and grew his hair into a queue, and his own countrymen mocked him for lowering himself. He would rather the Chinese see not a foreigner but simply a man bringing the gospel. The psychologist John Gottman, in a marriage study published in 1998, also found that husbands who were willing to accept influence from their wives had markedly more stable marriages. What decides how far a relationship can go is not who is more in the right, but who is more willing to adjust first.

We cannot change people, because that is God’s work; the human heart is God’s territory, and you and I cannot get in. But we can change our own attitude, tone, expression and reactions. The Lord Jesus said, “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5). The Lord did not say there is no speck in your brother’s eye; he said the order cannot be reversed. Changing first is not weakness — weakness keeps quiet because it is afraid of the other person; humility gives way because it trusts God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. 321’s 920 practice reminds us: every person connected to us is our “2,” and the person you find hardest to get along with is not your obstacle but your lesson.

The second practice: I am really nothing special. Brothers and sisters, the first practice is learned in conflict; the second is learned in success. Many people think pride comes in through failure, but in fact failure often makes people humble; it is success that most easily makes people proud. Pride doesn’t knock; it comes in by the back door, wearing a very respectable coat called “I earned this on my own merit.” One brother put it very honestly: “My most dangerous moment isn’t when people criticise me. It’s the drive home after people have praised me.” Brothers and sisters, do you have a drive home like that?

Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). The background to this passage is the factions in the Corinthian church. How did Paul handle it? He took everyone’s name down: “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants” (1 Corinthians 3:5). “Servants” in the original means the waiter who serves the food; no one thanks the hand that carried the plate for a good dish. People can plant and water; but you cannot make a single seed sprout. The Lord Jesus said the same: “We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty” (Luke 17:10).

“I am really nothing special” is not a polite formula, nor is it false modesty. False modesty says out loud, “Oh, not at all,” while inwardly waiting for the other person to say it again. True humility sees one fact clearly: “What do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Brothers and sisters, who gave you your mind? Who arranged the moment you heard the gospel? Without Jesus I can do nothing; with Jesus I can do all things. The Lord said, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Paul said, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

I love comparing Christians to the moon. The moon is beautiful at night, lighting the path in front of the lost traveller; but it gives off no light of its own — moonlight is sunlight. When is the moon at its brightest? When it is directly facing the sun. When is it at its darkest? When the earth squeezes in between, and there is a lunar eclipse. Brothers and sisters, we are just the same: the moment the self gets in between the Lord and people, there is an eclipse. John the Baptist put it most beautifully: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). In a 1981 study, the psychologist Ola Svenson found that nearly nine in ten of the drivers he tested believed their skill was better than average; yet by definition it is impossible for nine in ten people to be above average. So when people praise me, I say, “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.” I am only a channel of grace; nobody thanks a water pipe.

The third practice: I don’t understand anything. Spiritual pride is often more dangerous than worldly pride. Worldly pride boasts of wealth and status, and is easy to spot; spiritual pride wears the coat of godliness — boasting that I understand the truth, that I understand the church — and so that person is no longer teachable and no longer depends on God. Paul says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). “Puffs up” in the original means “to inflate by blowing air into” — the size grows, the weight doesn’t increase, and one pin will burst it. Then he says, “But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

The Lord Jesus also said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25). The Lord is not saying that cleverness is a sin. “The wise and understanding” are those who think they already have the answers and no longer need to be taught; earlier in the same chapter the Lord had just rebuked Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum — they knew everything, except how to turn back. “Infants” in the original is a child who cannot yet speak: no abilities, only simplicity, dependence and a willingness to learn. He never says, “I already knew that.” The Lord says, “unless you turn, and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

Psychology confirms this too. In their 1999 study, Kruger and Dunning showed that those least competent tend to be the most likely to overestimate themselves, because the very ability needed to judge their own performance is the ability they lack. In 2002, Rozenblit and Keil asked participants to rate how well they understood how a flush toilet works, and most gave themselves fairly high marks; but when asked to write out in detail how it works, their self-ratings dropped sharply at once. Brothers and sisters, if we can overestimate ourselves about a flush toilet, how much more about the God who sits enthroned above the heavens? Even Paul said, “Now I know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:12). If a cup is already full, however good the tea you pour into it, it only overflows.

There is an even deeper reason why we are willing to say, “I don’t understand anything”: God’s works are limitless. Three times in the Bible the waters were parted. The first time, God said to Moses, “Lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it” (Exodus 14:16). The second time, God commanded Joshua to tell the priests bearing the ark, “you shall stand still in the Jordan” (Joshua 3:8) — no rod, and they had to step into the water first. The third time, “Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters, and they were divided here and there” (2 Kings 2:8) — neither rod nor ark. The same parting of waters, yet three different ways, because God is never boxed in by our experience. He says, “Behold, I will do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:19). Brothers and sisters, yesterday’s method cannot guarantee today’s results. So let us rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice, rely on the brain and you’ll fret.

The lesson gives us four practices. First, adjust yourself: in a conflict today, ask first, “What can I change to fit in with him?” Second, give the glory to God: when others praise you, respond, “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.” Brothers and sisters, people’s praise is like a ball passed into your hands. You can hold on to it, or you can pass it on to the Lord. Those who hold on to it have their hands full and can’t catch anything else; those who pass it upward always have empty hands. The first four of the eight stages of changing our mindset are Information, Revelation, Conviction and Implementation: hearing isn’t enough — let the Holy Spirit put his finger on it in your heart, be won over heart and mouth, and then act on it concretely today.

Third, admit your limits: pray every day, “Lord, I don’t understand anything; please teach me.” Fourth, look to the Holy Spirit: in everything ask the Holy Spirit first; don’t go by experience, don’t rely on yourself. The Lord promised, “when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). The last four of the eight stages are Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Before bed tonight, take three minutes to think: was there any moment today when my “self” took the throne again? When you find something, change it; don’t let it pile up. Repeat it every day, and only then does it become character. Then go and walk alongside someone, and take him along the road you have travelled once more.

Let us put today’s message back into the picture of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Today’s three sentences take aim at exactly three strongholds of the “self”: my rights, my achievements, my opinions. Three times laying down is three times tying on the apron. 321 says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. So it is life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, the practice of humility is not about how much we do, but about each willing choice we make. God is not up in heaven holding a scoreboard, counting how many times you gave way today and how often you held your tongue; he is looking at your heart — at that crossroads where you could have argued your case, which road did you take? At that moment when you could have caught the applause, to whom did you pass the ball? A gentle reminder: humility is not putting yourself down; it is seeing yourself rightly — I am only a vessel, not the master; I am only a worker, not the owner. Today, let Jesus reign as King over your emotions, as King over your achievements, as King over your opinions. Let us practise humility every day, and have less and less of self and more and more of Christ.

Let us pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for shining your light on us through your word this early morning. We confess that we often ask you to change others but refuse to change ourselves first; we often think we understand and stop looking to you. Please forgive us. Lord, I am willing to change myself first, and no longer to demand that others accommodate me; I am really nothing special — everything is your grace; I don’t understand anything — may the Holy Spirit teach me. Lord, make us vessels fit for your use, living out the selfless life at home, at work and in the church, so that you receive all the glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
